I hate to be the bearer of bad news, but I have to say that Bioshock 2 is a very lackluster sequel to the marvelous, original Bioshock. It's not that Bioshock 2 sucks. Don't get me wrong, it's a great game. What it lacks most though, are improvements. Much of the game felt like an addon to the first Bioshock. There are new areas to explore and new weapons, but that's all that's new. You do get to dual wield plasmids and weapons, but as exciting as that sounds, it's not much of a departure from the first game. Fortunately, the strength of the original's story still resonates in its sequel. The plot is still captivating and there are still the twist and turns we've come to love as a fan of Bioshock. As for the multiplayer, all I have to say is that it sucks.
Grade: B

I was initially disappointed in this game. It felt too much like Civ 5 and didn't exactly meet the standard for storytelling set by its spiritual predecessor. Yet despite this, I've returned time and again for another round. I won't lie, this game will not appeal to anyone who doesn't enjoy Civ 5. But for those of us who enjoy Civ 5 style 4X gaming but feel that Civ 5 has gone stale this is a breath of fresh air. I especially enjoy the nonlinear tech web approach to technology and the customization allowed by building events and by affinities.
The recent patch has fixed most of the egregious balance issues that plagued the game since release. With trade units more properly balanced and the various slingshots nerfed the game now allows a multitude of different strategies. With 5 distinct victory conditions (Though the affinity based ones are rather similar tbh) and 3 affinities there is enough replayability but add in multiplayer and It'll do until Civ 6 eventually hits.

I've played through all the saints row games now save for the first one (Can't seem to find it for the pc) and this is by far the shortest.
It kind of feels like they were trying to trim away bits from the game. I don't know why they would do this but, they did.
Don't get me wrong though. I do like the game. Not love, but like.
I would love the game but there's some things that give it bad points. So... I'll make the list of positives and negatives.
Pro:
1. You get to play as Gat.
This is cool since we get to dive into the charicter more. It kind of felt like there was a disconnection from the other charicters in the series other then the boss. This made it so we got to know the charicter more. Which is kinda cool.
2. Get to play as Kenzi (did I spell that right?)
Same as above.
3. Creative weapons.
Self explanitory.
4. Flight. (which is the biggest positive)
The flight mechanics alone in this game (assuming you have your controls set up right) are fantastic in my opinion.
They make the game. I find myself flying around, swooping through wrecked buildings and over lava pits just for the fun of flying. Wishing that flying in saints row 4 was like this. (Maybe a mod could be done to transfer it? Or DLC for a winged flight power in 4?)
The Cons:
1. Short story.
It felt like they rushed it. The story -is- good, but it just seems like they needed more charicter interaction.
2. Shortage of mini-games
The games they do have are fun. But there's a lot of diversity which has gone missing.
3. Teaser of what they could have had in ending.
I'm not going to give it away here, but I'm going to say that after you get some things acomplished, there's a story book telling ending segment that tells a story that would have been better if played through. At first when I saw it I thought "Cool! I get to face them to then?" but no. It's only part of a story instead. A small segment. Almost trollish really. I'm -hoping- they add them in through a patch or something but... anyways....
For those of you who have played through it you'll know what I mean. For those who haven't it's a negative point for the moment unless they add it as a not too expensive or free DLC.
4. The settings were hellishly dull (pun intended).
I understand that it's hell and there's not too much you can do with it. They -were- creative with what they had. But... why did they have to spend -all- the time in hell? They couldn't have gone back to the ship? Maybe seen the alien ship some? Had some nightmare dream scenes in other settings to save people from?
The part of 4 that makes it such a negative point is that we have such beautiful flight controls, but enjoying them is hard to do because the scene is always so terrible and... well... hellish.
Over all I give the game 7/10 for the time being depending on what they do with it in the future. Given the right DLC (given it's not too pricey) I may revisit this review.

There's a lot of talk about CBE not doing enough different, being just 'Civ V with different textures'. After having played it somewhat, it is surprising how wrong it seems those statements are. Yes, of course it is similar to civilization. You start with one town, you explore and build more.
However: Instead of barbarians you have aliens. These are not a minor nuisance soon to be eradicated, but a driving force in the game between those who want to eliminate them, and those who want to ally with them.
You have several levels of choices - wether to go for purity, harmony, or supremacy. (Exterminate, symbiosis, or kinda neutral.), with their own progress trees.
Neutral settlements are handled differently - they don't control territory, for instance; trade with them is still rather useful. (Trade also improves depending on how long the trade route has been going).
Instead of a huge unit tree, you have a very basic selection of units, but with four or so upgrade levels (and options depending on which attitude you choose).
The tech tree is instead a tech bush. Plenty of wonders.
Every building you build has two upgrades you must choose between.
Spying is reworked completely.
Basically, it has almost everything civ V has without needing to buy expansion packs, and each element has been reworked to be new and interesting.
I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of the series. It is enough of a change of scenery to make it seem new and fresh, at least to me. If you expect it to be a completely different game, then you may be disappointed. It will still have hexes, population, gold equivalent (energy) etc. But then, it still has Civilization in the name.

After 190 hours of game time, I just finished my first playthrough of this game.
To be fair I nearly did 100% of its content. But yeah, it has a LOT of content, if you do everything.
So what is this game about? You assemble a team of people, put them together into units (called unions) and do battle in turns. Depending on who you put together into a union the actual commands they get in battle change and depending on which skills your guys/gals use they level different abilities and stats, which in turn affects which classes they will get into. There are also different formations for your unions to use, which affects the stats of the union.
Well, that sure sounds complicated, but rejoice most of this game is easily beatable by just doing whatever sounds good to you.  So you don't have to get into the depth of it if you don't want to, though for me that was part of the fun. It is a really good easy to use but hard to master/really understand type of system.
There are a few optional bosses that are very very hard and beating them may require some kind of special tactics. It feels incredible rewarding when you are finally able to beat them, though.
Does the game have any drawbacks? To be honest the story is kinda "eh whatever", but there are tons of optional stuff to distract you from it. The story battles however are pretty awesome. Another negative point is that a few enemies have really really cheap skills, which can be quite frustrating.
Overall I really liked this game a lot and might even start up a ng+ run of it. Yes, that is a recommendation.

I've been gaming for more than a decade yet I've never come across a game as unique and thought-provoking as The Stanley Parable. One might think that the concept of the game and the sole intention of the developer is to teach the player a thing or two about choices and decision-making in game design, development etc, but I'd argue that they can also be applied to real life as well. The game almost forced me to think about where life came from, where it is now, where it is going, where it will end up at and whether it really matters at all.
"When every path you can walk has been created for you long in advance, death becomes meaningless, making life the same. Do you see now? Do you see that Stanley was already dead from the moment he hit start?"

The game has an interesting take on turn-based combat (directing multiple parties of characters that share stats  and move as one unit rather than as individuals); however a lot of the nuances of the mechanics are not well-explained within the game itself. I'd recommend browsing a wiki on basic gameplay to get a better handle on the mechanics the game has.
If you like JRPGs and turn-based games it's worth checking out, imo, though for people who prefer 100% control over every combat decision the variable nature (based on party makeup, party leader, and positioning) of combat commands in battle might be annoying. Basically, most of the strategic thought goes into setting up your parties' characters and their skills beforehand, and then adapting to whatever options you get during the actual combat turns. It may feel a little too random for some people, though you can stack the deck in your favor if you know what you're going for with your group/skill makeup. There are around fifty unique characters that you can choose to recruit into your parties -- some are linked to the main story while others are hidden and can only be obtained after doing certain side quests, as well as 'generic' soldiers that you can hire to pad your army.
The art direction and music are top-notch -- the game looks beautiful on the PC. Areas themselves are linear, though there are many side quests and hidden regions available if you want a break from the main storyline. A lot of the side content can become unavailable permanently if you progress too far in the main story without exploring every area (though there is the benefit of being able to start a New Game + after your first playthrough).
Despite the game's setting being original and interesting, the lead character is a bit of a dope and the main story is not that great, unfortunately (the writing is pretty weak). I honestly enjoyed doing the side content (which includes defeating rare miniboss monsters) more than following the main scenario.
The Last Remnant is unique compared to any other turn-basd RPG I've played, so it's hard to make a blanket statement of recommendation; it really depends on your personal tastes. Basically, your mileage may vary; if you play JRPGs primarily as visual novels and prefer an epic cinematic storyline  with typical gameplay, then this may not be a game for you. But if you are a fan of turn-based combat and are open to investing the time to learn the nuances of this game's unique mechanics (and are a collector and completionist-type), then you might enjoy it.

While the battle system is interesting, and certainly different than the usual affair for an RPG, it misses the mark... as does the rest of this game. The turn based battle system puts you in control of multiple "troops" who operate with vague and often times unpredictable mechanics. You would expect that since you are incharge of a small army, you would also have a good understanding of the terran, troop movements, ect. Wrong. You have no sense of space whatsoever during any point of the battle. This eliminates gameplay as sound strategy and makes each encounter a crapshoot with the player often times hoping for the best.
As for the characters and story... there is none. The characters are souless and without clear motivations. Their relationships are never well established or developed. Essentially, everybody is just there and has a loose reason to be on this "quest". The story is choppy, full of glaring plot holes and is as ill defined as its characters. It gives no real sense of threat or urgency when it's time to go out and face the bad guys, nor does it explore why each character would be vested in the story's goals. You just have to do cuz there's nothing else to do... except side quests. Speaking of...
The side quests are a bunch of repetative nonsense that feel tacked on to the story and service no real purpose except to be finished by completionists. (This is not to say that other RPG's do it better, but it contributes to the souless nature of this game. There is just no drive, interest or reason to really do much of anything. You do it because it's there. The end.)
At least the art and music are good. But if that's all that interests you... Go to the symphony.

Free-running controls can be a bit all over the place when in close proximity to lots of objects but easy enough to get a handle on (I play with an XBox360 controller).
Good story with a few plot twists and enough side missions/activities to keep you busy when taking a break from the story. Side missions and prowling the ocean for plunder are pretty much the go-to method for upgrading Kenway's ship and gear.
The protagonist is also likeable enough this time round (better than Connor but not quite on Ezio's level imho)
New 'gimmicky' weapons are good enough but darts can make the game a bit easy i think and the combat system is a little more straightforward than the AC2 franchise but fun none-the-less.
Graphics are quite good for a PC port but to have all settings maxed (not really needed) your rig might need a bit of muscle for steady 60fps**.
All that said I was already a fan of the AC franchise and really enjoyed this addition to the series.

Cute idea but ultimately fails to deliver. The paywall is an enormous issue; it takes forever to make a reasonable amount of cards without spending money. The game is fine until one gets to a higher matchmaking rank where the problems stick out more. Since they exclude large portions of the paper releases on this platform, certain strategies suffer to the point of being unplayable (B/G delirium without Grim Flayer, Emrakul). One particularly surprising exclude is planeswalker removal entirely. As soon as a 'walker hits the board, they are only removable with combat damage and "Anguished Unmaking". Control strategies are forced to move to creature strategies, but with the 1 mythic, 2 rare, 3 uncommon etc rule, efficient creatures are few and far between. This also makes aggro strategies really fragile. The games in the higher ranks become a race to see who can draw their 'walkers first and clean up with a sweeper or just midrange Ob-Nixilis mirror grindfests ala Khans of Tarkir-OGW standard.
The exclusion of some rare land cycles (but strange inclusion of the old core set "check lands") from sets released on this platfrom makes for unbalanced opportunities for multi-color decks. The varriance associated with playing a two color deck and getting "color screwed" is compounded by the allowance of only two of each rare land. 3-color Shards get much better manabases than Wedges since they have more options for come-in-to-play-untapped lands and two color manabases are a mess of too many basic lands or too many "guildgate" lands that come into play tapped all the time.
The simplicity of the removal of the ability to stop the timer on an opponent's upkeep step makes cards like "Elder Deep-Fiend" a whole lot worse and suseptable to countermagic than in paper.
The list of complaints goes on and on. I used to be a fan of this casual way to play Magic at home but it seems the fun ends once WOTC has one in their pockets already. This game is pretty much just an advertisement for MODO or paper Magic and is not nearly as fun or emersive as previous DOtP installments. It certainly isn't on par with Hearthstone, the game this is supposed to be copying.

This game is a very generic-feeling beat 'em up. I played through the game with a friend quite some time ago and we found ourselves trudging through the game for completion's sake more than anything. We stopped after one play through, unable to muster the gumption needed to play through the campaign a second time on new game +.
The few characters you have to choose from are all rather boring archetypes. You gain new class abilities over time that let you perform special moves, but nothing here seems particularly inspired.
There was also pretty severe bug on a couple of the levels that was causing the to become exceptionally bright, almost to the point of the screen being a blinding white color. And sometimes it would rapidly blink in and out of this mode. I'm not sure if it was some intense bloom effect bug, or what it was, but it nearly made those levels unplayable.
The game was bland and over all boring. It was certainly not for me, so I cannot recommend it to others, however if beat 'em ups are your thing then perhaps you will still find something here worthwhile.

Recommended for newcomers to Magic for sure--if you've had your eye on the Duels of the Planeswalkers series before, this version is the friendliest yet to newbies. It eases you into the basic rules and then takes you by the hand when new rules pop up for the first time (as they so often do).
Magic veterans rejoice--there is full deck building available from the start. In terms of player vs. AI--the main way to get coins, and thus packs, at first--there's nothing here that is especially challenging for you, although some of the story battles pit you with an inferior deck. You'll need to rely on a fair dose of luck to get through those. There's a second deck builder (called a deck wizard) geared toward less experienced players, but it's not very good at allowing you to put in newly obtained cards or even the best/most synergistic available.
That's a problem since there's a bug involving quests with deck archetypes--you have to use decks built by that deck wizard to get credit toward those quests. At least, that better be a bug. If veteran players are forced to use the wizard for daily coins, they are going to pull their hair out. Considering this, and that the servers aren't fully stable yet, I would suggest veteran Magic players wait a bit until those kinks are straightened out.

Hollow knight is a game that showcases some of the things I love best about videogames. Fast-paced action combat with great graphics all while not sacrificing that good clasic game feeling. Despite the prior statement, this game does however have its flaws.
Starting with the graphics: Simple but effective. The character itself can't be comprised of more than a handful of lines, but it works. The lategame becomes so fast-paced that the simple art style of the character will be the last thing you would pay attention to, while also being less distracting. Meanwhile, the background is actually incredibly complex if you bother to dig deep enough into it. Almost every level has at least 3 layers, while some have more than 5, all at incredible resolutions. Unfortunately, the graphics may also be one of the lower points of this review. My computer runs a gtx 970 graphics card and an amd fx 8320 8-core cpu, (which is far beyond what should be necessary for the game). Yet still, on certain stages, I would get some random framerate between 20-50, and trust me, for this game you'll need every frame you can get.
Gameplay: Early game you will probably feel open, vulnerable and weak. However, the early game bosses are weak enough that it probably won't matter. Room enemies are barely a mild nuisance early on. Mid game is where you start to feel strong. Having obtained items that make you faster, stronger and offering more degrees of movement will make you start to feel powerful, and then you fight the mid game bosses and realize it still may not be enough. Suffice to say that even some of the most skilled players will probably die at least once. Once again, random enemies are barely a mild nuisance, but they can bring your health down over time if you aren't careful. Late game you will probably feel like a monster. Reaction time and dexterity become an absolute necessity at this point. The scaling in this game is absolutly insane. You will go from what might feel like super mario to something that might feel like geometry dash, or touhou, or darksouls, or "Insert stereotypically hard game here" on 2X speed. Unfortunately, the hitboxes seem slightly off in certain cases. Generally speaking, most of the hitboxes are pretty accurate, but in my case there were some very iffy hits.
Soundtrack: Absolutely astonishing. Music makes the mood for a game, and they picked the perfect mood. To give an image of how the soundtrack might feel to someone playing the game without having heard it while also void of spoilers: imagine a feeling of visiting a place that feels like it had been much more in the past and is now a shell of it's former self, almost as if looking back on it like a dream. The soundtrack manages to keep the mood for pretty much the entire game with one of the sole exceptions being the intense music for some of the boss fights (which are beastly by the way).
Difficulty: Early game is easy. My nine-year-old brother could beat it if I let him play. Mid game can be frustrating, but far from impossible for any decently experienced gamer. Late game... I would say there are 2 answers. 1: If you really want a challenge, go in to boss fights unprepared. There are plenty of items to help you snowball out of control, but these bosses deserve to be showcased without being outscaled by the power of grinding items. 2: Like previously stated, you can get items that will make these boss fights 10X easier, not to say that they will be easy even with the items though. The choice is yours.
Summary: If you bothered to read this review to the end, you clearly have at least some interest in this game. In which case I say you would be foolish not to give it a shot. I personally assure you that the only problem you would have with the game is the difficulty (and/or graphics, depending on your computer). In fact that's basically a summary of every negative review for this game out as of right now. Do yourself a favor and buy this game.

This is a bite-sized version of a full game. GOOH has the possibility of being a real gem as a forerunner to SR5. The events in SR4 would inevitably lead to the take over the underworld and depose the Prince of Darkness, right?! Can a Saint reach Sainthood? (Vaguely reference from tatoos in SR3 and 4, so Volition had an idea to start with.)  Can Gat catch the eye of the Big G on borrowed wings? Will the Saint bring fire and brimstone upon the universe?! Who knows.
The content is sufficient enough to urguably price at $20. Wait till it's on sale on Steam. Had it been priced 12.99 I'd say pick it up right now and enjoy. GOOH hovers in a weird area between where it feels more like DLC and less standalone and missed out on being a full release. It takes up what SR does well (weapons, combat style, skyscraper set pieces etc) and cuts out a lot the shortcomings (annoying repetition on NPC 'pickle' phrases) but doesn't supply much more than that.  Mostly filler challenges and some loyalty and side quests and the chance to enjoy flight. BUT in the tradition of Buffy the Vampire Slayer, GOOH also has a musical to enjoy. WOOT!
Be aware of no additional clothing customizations, so you can't dress up as a Grim Reaper or Mistress of the Dark, no licensed soundtrack (just have Michael's 'Thriller' nearby and other pop-horror tunes handy or maybe Meatloaf, Audioslave, Godsmack, Gorillaz, Queens of the Stoneage, Benni Benasi, Pitbull on standby.) No witty references to Elvira, or other pop, zombie, horror, vampire, werewolf culture appear at all.
Had this title recieved a proper numbered sequel budget it could have easily transitioned into a stand alone, spin-off franchise while still maintaining Saints Row status without officially being Saints Row 5 (if they had done what they originally did with SR4, which originally was slated as a SR3 expansion then released as a full game I wouldn't hesitate so much over the lack of what's missing.)

While it had a few interesting twists (paradigms, and these weird "aeresol" spays you could use before and after battle), that was pretty much where innovation ended.  You had no control over party members, and you can almost literally "auto battle" through the entire game.  The combat is boring, repetitive, and does almost nothing to make the player feel like they have something invested in any of the fights.
My only hope is that future FF games take some lessons from some of the better games of the last few years; Mass Effect, Witcher series, Dragon Age series...JRPG's are in desperate need of abandoning tired old combat systems and reinventing themselves....

I've played this game a great deal, and I have to say, it just doesn't live up to snuff. It's not as good as Civilization 5: Brave New World on the strategy front, nor is it challenging or exciting.
Why is it bad?
- Affinity system makes beakers the *only* important resource; rush tech 100% of the time, and you will win 100% of the time
- The A.I. doesn't seem to have any programming. They often just idle the entire game, while occasionally deploying a poorly organized army at you once, and then begging for your forgiveness while rewarding you with tons of favors and resources.
-  The aliens don't scale; they're a challenge for 40 turns, and then they are just fodder for the rest of the game. For something to be an integral part of the game, it needs to serve some sort of purpose beyond "Wefuxurexplorers" for a few turns
- The jumps between tech levels are too drastic; a tech 1 unit, fully leveled and with virtue support, has almost no chance of contending with a tech 2 unit; the auto-upgrade immediately happening further rewards players for fast teching, instead of making them strategically utilize their resources on a per-unit basis.
- Diplomacy is a complete and utter joke. Literally the worst iteration in the franchise history, I would say.
- Randomly appearing trade outposts always take up the best land spots; you have to decide whether you want their bonus, or their location for tiles... and they always spawn in between the best locations, strategically.
The game has a long way to go. The only positive I can say about it is that, it's a Civ game, and they do always get better with time/expansion packs/DLC. Wait until a few patches drop and and the game is fine-tuned. In it's current state, it feels like a fleshed out, early-access game that is still months away from being a complete game

I was looking forward to this game. A graphically enhanced version of the original classic? Let's ♥♥♥♥ing go!!!!
The first scene was a little dubious as the graphics really didn't seem too "remastered", but I let it slide. The first combat scenes seemed a little off, but we'll get to that later. I had already done a playthrough of the original on Hard, so I figured I'd give Survivor a shot for some real difficulty. Right off the get-go, it seemed entertaining, and a well-polished remake of the classic.
Then the Medical Pavilion came in, and likewise my first Big Daddy encounter. I took him on in that general area with all my turrets hacked, as well as a Security Bot flying around my head for extra damage. It took me nine lives to finally kill him, in which during the last couple of lives I was suicide rushing in with the wrench, as my EVE had depleted and so too had my patience.
The problem was not in my lack of skill, nor the Survivor difficulty (although partly a reason why it took so long). The hitboxes for this PC game were vastly changed from the original PC version. Plasmids used to be generally friendly with aiming. As long as the target was in your crosshairs, 9 times out of 10 you'd hit em with an Electro Bolt, or an Incinerate, whichever. Here, it's an absolute mess. Your splicer will be in your crosshair, at about 5 steps' range, and your Electro Bolt will be just to the left. Or just to the right. Or actually, no, it landed right behind him. Or actually, I've run out of EVE and he's gunned me down. I acknowledge that this could be the way the developers intended to make aiming for Bioshock on PC, but it's a very inconsistent process and the hitboxes in general need to be looked at.
Without Plasmid usage, the game is a very tilted affair on Survivor. The generic Leadhead Splicer will only need 3 random shots to any part of your body to kill you, while you need to unload the equivalent of Hiroshima and Nagasaki's atomic payload to kill them. Throw in peeker's advantage, where any enemy will instantly hit you as soon as you move a pixel out of cover, and your 9 first aid kits? Gone.
TL;DR I'd prefer it if they kept the gameplay like the 2007 version, while graphically improving the game a LOT more. I was expecting a game that graphically kept up with 2016 standards, but instead it's like a little improvement here, and there, but nothing when you add it all up. Hitboxes are a serious issue, I don't remember it being that inconsistent on the original version. There are many enjoyable moments, but they are ruined by the firefights where aiming is such an issue.
EDIT: one year later and still no fixes - $$$$$ grab by slapping on the title and stepping all over the consumers who just wanted a huge graphical overhaul!!

It's a shame that the review page for this game is plagued by complaints about connectivity issues from the first few days after release. As it stands now most of those problems seem to have been overcome.
In-game UI is functional but gameplay is a little sluggish. No idea why the devs insisted that every animation should move at a snail's pace. Ultimately it feels a little clunky but so long as you're not after lighting fast gameplay it should not prove too much of an issue.

The card pool in this game is rather shallow at the moment though I understand it will be expanded upon in future. Even with this in mind there are a lot of aspects to the paper version of the game which are absent here at least for now.
The game is pretty generous with gold to begin with and it isn't too hard to grind for a pack or two each day. Also the current system makes it far easier to amass a full collection than a lot of comparable games. A lot of people are mad about the 'always online' feature but I can't see how it could have worked in any other way so those complaints are a little unwarranted.
All in all it's the cheapest way to enjoy what is often times a prohibitively expensive pastime. It wasn't the ultimate electronic version of MtG we've all been waiting for but maybe it could be one day. Yes, it feels unpolished and clunky, yes, it had an awful PC launch, yes, you can't grind endlessly for gold but it's still well worth a look and will only become more worthwhile as time goes on.

One of the best games I have ever played, and most definitely the most impressive space based RTS/4X game I've ever had the joy of playing. Stunning visuals and solid gameplay make this game a must have.
This game is made great for any playstyle, with versatile early game units to quickly rush your opponents, and beefy end game starships for trully epic encounters and turtling. For those with quick fingers and reflexes, every single unit has some kind of ability that is great when auto-cast, but even better when manually timed making micro a viable option. On the other hand, by late game you can bunch up a ton of poweful units and capital ships with abilities on auto-cast to make short work of any traget or fleet of any size.
The three factions are balanced to a key. The Vasari are built around hit-and-running lightly defended planets, and completely strip mining less useful planets. The Advent are good for more tactical and micro-managerial attacks, relying on shields and debuffs to overpower opposing fleets. The TEC are built around smashing bulky and heavily armed and armored ships against even the strongest defenses and fleets while remaining safe behind powerfull starbases. On top of that, each faction is split into a Loyalist and Rebel faction creating even more diversity with six different abilities and ultra-ships, the titans.
With solid action-filled gameplay and thought out lore (found mainly in the research you do) this game will provide a satisfying experience for anyone; casual or skill-based, turtling or rushing, fast or slow, strategy and action, visually and technically it is one of the best investements in a game you can make.

2/5
I have a shorthand of my review below, but I go into more detail about each point below that, so if you're looking for detailed info for a purchasing decision, I recommend reading this review in it's entirety.
TL;DR: Really most of the crappy stuff (like the platforming) is forgivable if the combat with basic enemies (non bosses) was really fun, but it isn't. To me it really just feels bland and straightforward, and doesn't have the satisfying controls and combat that say, Bloodborne, employs. Also, I really wasn't getting what was so great about the NPCs, they're nice I suppose but nothing to write home about. The experience is lacking because the combat is nothing to fall in love with, and frankly neither are the bosses, but if you're an artist or animator and love cute/dark art that oozes personality, there is love to be had with the art-style (once again, a great achievement and what makes me so dissapointed that everything else was so meh).
Now for detail...
Pros.
The world has a fun style and looks great. The drawing's are gorgeous and the music is fantastic. This is a greatly realized world and the idea's behind it's inception and what it truly is make it interesting. By far the biggest driving force for actually wanting to decend into the forgotten kingdom.
Decent Stuff.
The combat is only ok as far as fun factor; honestly it serves as a nice marker of your progression as a player (skill wise) but not much else. This is the honestly the biggest problem. While the world is beautiful and there's definitely a fun element to finding more on the map and finding Geo/charms, the enemy to enemy combat just isn't especially fun. Part of this has to do with the fact that the controls aren't as tight/perfect as some lead to believe; there's definitely been plenty of times when my jump had an unexpected delay (PLAY WITH THE CONTROLLER!).
- The NPCs are nice to talk to I guess, but are we really going to act like they have some incredible stories to them? I get it, you meet one, and it progresses and plays itself out and there's some big character portrait/story being drawn (Zote being one that comes greatly to mind), but I just don't find these stories interesting! Alot of them beg to be ignored (once again, Zote being a fantastic example :/ ) but even the one's that don't just really don't add a huge amount. I put them here because I think they are technically a positive addition to the story, but really nothing to write home about and not a massive bonus to overall experience.
Bad Stuff
- The Platforming! Most of it is bearable (not good, bearable) but frankly, I just think incoroporating the "Souls" system of losing everything until you get back to your ghost and kill it is made more obnoxious by the fact that there is F*ing platforming. I'm personally not a huge platformer, but I definitely play some and I get enjoyment out of them. But being precise with your jumps just to move throughout the world is just frankly annoying. Additionally, the areas in which you have to avoid a bunch of dangers while using the Mantis Claw (wall drag) or the dash or whatever ability it is, were really F*kd for me. Example (one of many) I'm using the Claw and try to go into my  next jump, but it just doesn't do it at all, and I die. Oh boy! now I get to go ALLL the way back, because my jump didn't time right. Lovely...

Remastered isn't quite the appropriate term. The graphics have been updated, but only in the sense that it now resembles how you remember it in your mind, and nothing more. It was provided for free due to owning the original Bioshock, so I did not intend to complain a great deal about it.
For the most part it appears to be a ported version of the console Bioshock, due to the removed graphics options. I only suspect this is because they are releasing this upon the new consoles, and PC was somewhat of an afterthought. Physics and gameplay have not changed at all.
My only true complaint is that upon crashing, which only occurred twice during my playthrough, the game seemingly wipes the player's settings. This is especially problematic as it will change your difficulty setting. If one intends to acquire any of the difficulty related achievements, be mindful of this. Launch the game, load your save and change the difficulty back to what it was, before closing it again so that the settings save.
I unfortunately only noticed after I had saved once, forcing me to reload a fair distance back just in case. I doubt I would buy this, especially if the original Bioshock is still available. For free however, I can hardly complain.

Epic dark fantasy turn-based strategy with role-play elements. Used to be a big Dark Prophecy fan back when it came out and now I snapped Rise of the Elves, which adds another playlable side. The game should be right up the alley to any HoM&M fan, sans some differences in gameplay like the inability to move your characters during combat (was changed in DIII, but we Disciples fans prefer such) and the more strategic rivalry with other sides for land and resource. The art and sound in the game was one of the best I've seen in it's time for fantasy 2D games and it still holds up just nicely and the game is just massive with all the quests, sagas and the mission editing tools that come with it. But beware, this game will eat your time like it's nothing - this is no fast paced arcade game that you can play for a few minutes and feel content, minutes here will turn into literal hours, so keep this in mind before you grab it (although it's very cheap on a discount so you might as well just support the developer in doing so). Basically, this is a game that made me a fan of fantasy turn-based strategies, as I also enjoy the HoM&M games, but Disciples will always be my first choice when it comes to such games. Also, for those wondering how it runs on modern hardware - it runs just fine on W10 and Intel HD graphics (which I currently use), just make sure you set it to "compatability mode" and tick some other settings.

A classic I feel, it has its moments and charms.
Pros:
- Beautiful art style and world setting with background story, mission dialogue and set-pieces.
- A fun hybrid of RPG and Strategy, take your main party and destroy everything in the map in any order you choose.
- Lots and lots of units types to try out, and the races feel different. There's also a nice variety of enemies types to fight, and of course always a bigger and nastier critter out there to defeat.
- The missions unfold a linear narrative but is quite fun to follow all the races story modes in order.
- Carry over your main hero to the next mission, this makes the game feel a little RPG like – although the Strategy aspect of the game feels very weak in my view.
Cons:
- Tech issues to start up – though I've figured out the issues and written a guide to help with this here:


- Some units feel a little useless compared to alternatives, though for a first run though it can be fun trying things out.
- The mechanics are simple, you can't have multiple attack types for a unit and you can't upgrade a unit down both sides of the tech tree – you choose the path and all units of that type follow it. You can however choose a different path on the next mission (everything resets).
- The normal difficulty seems a little out of touch, and will be very challenging. In contrast the easy difficult might feel more like a breeze.
Overall it is an interesting and somewhat unique game.

Multiply my "hours on record" by 2 or so to get closer to the real amount of time I've so far spent with this game.
Greatly underrated game. While certainly not perfect, it does its job really well of delivering a battle-heavy stroll through really beautiful and atmospheric locations of War of the Ring Middle-Earth, following a plot that is simple and yet of some very respectable quality.
Gameplay is straightforward click/key-to-hit combat with a number of abilities based on button combos. While the characters do not always respond optimally, a few hours of play and you'll be more than at ease as you go toe to toe with big nasties. A regular stat & talent-tree based progression with unlockables as well as upgradeable equipment give it the little RPG flavor that deepens gameplay a bit, without complicating things too much or making the game try to be something other than it is: a very decent hack and slash experience.
The rendition of all the places we visit is beautiful due to how much personality and distinctiveness each environment has and the characters certainly work well, surprisingly being generally closer to book than film in terms of how they speak and behave, which is really pleasant. The focus on oft-neglected Book 1 environments (Barrow Downs, Fornost, Ettenmoors, Misty Mountains... with a very nice escape through Mirkwood) is also a very pleasant change from the usually inevitable tropes of Rohan and Mordor.
While somewhat repetitive as all games of this type are, the game throws enough action and enough variety in enemies (from goblins to trolls all the way through uruks, savages, spiders...) to keep things interesting from the first level to the last. A good bunch of abilities and three quite different playable characters help in that regard.
It was never game of the year material but it scores points for being a mostly well done product into which a lot of care has gone, despite its shortcomings and limitations. Very decent gameplay, beautiful environments, high quality music, interesting story moments. I recommend it. It deserves the follow-up that it will unfortunately never get.

Before I begin, please understand that Magic: Duels has its own set of quirks just like the Magic games before it (both good and bad).
Anyways... I will start with the good:
M:D is completely free, and it is possible to acquire the gold you need to buy boosters without spending a dime of real money - spending real money just accelerates the process (which for some, may constitute P2W).
What makes Magic Duels better than previous iterations is how they've toned down certain types of cards that have proven to be very annoying (remember those one or two mana black magic death cards that insta-killed your monsters? Well, they're still there, but they require the opponent to sacrifice one of his monsters as well [which would only be a problem if the opponent steals one of your monsters, or has disposable summons]).
The more powerful insta-kills, insta-counters, and raw damage spells require more mana to cast, thereby eliminating decks that, for one or two mana a peice, could render your brilliant strategy into a puddle of curd. More strategy is required, and if you want the decks of old, you're gonna have to mix colors, which can reduce your odds of getting something decent.
Most recently, Wizards gave everyone playing the game 400 gold for free as a compensation for some of the troubles the game has been having. Nice touch.
The one thing you have to consider, before buying this game, is that the story mode can be difficult (but I like to think that the Story mode games really just tutorial matches teaching you how to address different strategies/playstyles that you will encounter when facing other players, or at least, some of them).
Always-Online-required feature can be a bit of a let-down, but as of late, the game servers have become more stable (though the devs, as of this writing, have warned to expect the possibility of some instability in the near future - part of the reason they gave out the free 400 gold, which is worth 2 boosters).
There is a learning curve when it comes to building decks, but there's a deck wizard that "helps" you build an archtype. The reason I say "helps" in quotation marks is because while the game does help you establish a basic deck, it does not let you pick all of the cards you want (you get about 4-5 cards to choose from that, once chosen, fade out and either a duplicate of that same card that you might have will show up, or another will take it's place. Even when you get ot hte filling out your deck portion, the limitations in selection can be a bit problematic, but the game probably figures that you can simply make your own custom deck if you want more choice. The ability to customize your archtype decks, and name them, help you keep track of which decks do what.
New daily quests provide objectives that award gold as well.
All in all, a fun game.

A minor spoiler alert for anyone reading the below. If you're looking to play the game as someone who has to make some really tough decisions without really knowing the outcome of your choices; maybe skip this review and know that it's a great game and I'd recommend it. Otherwise, read on!
---------
If you enjoyed the Oregon Trail for letting you take a plucky group of people, and navigate a precarious balance in supplies and risky gambles to hopefully win the day; I think TWOM would really appeal to you. The desperate need to balance long term goals with short term survival is a wonderful puzzle to play. The investments you make into your local infrastructure, whether its defense, economy, or supplies for scavenging all pay out dividends against a difficulty curve that is relentless. Sometimes you make good logistic decisions, and sometimes you make bad ones; and to the victor goes the prepared and adaptable.
If you enjoyed Spec Ops: The Line; and the narrative it tried to deliver about the ugliness that war represents, I would definitely recommend this. It's a very fresh breath into a genre that isn't really talked about (the ugly side of war; that lacks in glory or patriotism, and is really just about the people who get caught in the cross fire to pay the price).
Mechanically, I think TWOM's a triumph. The dull washed out colors, the punishing lack of a manual save system to give your decisions gravity, and the mathematical impact of poor choices all reinforce the game's theme and storyline of survival in an horrible land.
For better or worse though, the story is one of hope. That may seem like an odd comment, but the eventual end to your playthrough (assuming you survive) is that good people doing good things are rewarded; and bad people doing bad things are punished (the impact of stealing from the good, or harming the innocent, or turning your back on those who need help is overwhelmingly steep compared to the price of going without a few supplies or sending someone out for a night).
Games trying to force difficult moral choices are great and its a mechanic I enjoy, but I think this is one area that TWOM fell a little short. You are almost never punished for making selfless decisions (the countless random encounters where I was asked to send someone out to help either went with a great reward, or no reward rather than catastrophe), and you almost always face swift retribution for unjust choices. All the food and medical supplies in the world will be worthless if someone in your group has a mental breakdown over having to steal, and it can start a very slippery slope as depression kicks in. To it's credit, the epilogue goes through these decisions you made during your adventure to stay alive in an almost Fallout-esque way which I was very pleased to see.
TL;DR: Buy this game. It's fun, easy to get into, savagely difficult, with a beautiful story and moral, and like all excellent games: forces you to make interesting and impactful decisions.

Hollow Knight is an excellent MetroidVania title with quite a bit to offer a prospective buyer, though the game does have a few flaws that can make sections of the game irritating.
Pros:
- Art style: the hand drawn enemies and environments look absolutely great, and the amount of character the designers manage to portray in the NPCs of the game with very minimalistic designs is rather impressive in its own right.
- Score: Normally when I game, I listen to podcasts or music or audiobooks. Hollow Knight is the first game I've played in months to have a score good enough to have me turning off all my other devices. The game's areas each have extremely atmospheric pieces, with eerie chimes echoing down the tunnels of old Hallownest, light bassoon-flute duets setting a peaceful mood in the forests of the outer areas, and understated woodwinds setting the bleak atmosphere of the surface regions. The boss fight scores are intense, though they don't edge into the bombastic. This game easily has the best score of any 2d sidescroller I've ever played.
- Value: for $15, this game packs an incredible amount of content. Each playthrough of the game runs the better part of twenty hours. If you're on a tight budget, Hollow Knight offers literally days of entertainment for the price of a map pack for a bland multiplayer shooter.
- Story: The game offers a surprisingly large amount of lore and NPC interactions, allowing for storytelling both in the environment designs of the kingdom of Hallownest itself and in interactions with a multitude of in game characters.
- Challenge: I love games that can offer up a good challenge. Hollow Knight is one of the most difficult platformers I've played in years. While this difficulty can occasionally come from random undodgeable enemy attacks, the game's challenge typically comes down to timing and good reflexes.
Cons:
- Boss Fights: while most of the fights in Hollow Knight are excellent and challenging, a fair number of the boss fights produce challenge not through skill testing, but through RNG dependent attack patterns that can leave you dead without any chance to heal or defend yourself.
- Backtracking: I know, complaining about backtracking in a MetroidVania game seems like complaining that ice cream is cold. However, if someone handed you chilled cream at ten degrees kelvin, you'd be justifiably irritated at them. Hollow Knight often leaves one or two collectable items or bonus areas in every area of the game that can only be reached with new powers, so that unlike most MetroidVanias, where new powers simply open up the story, Hollow Knight can often have the player walking back through literal miles of tunnels every time they get a new dash attack or wall climb in the hopes of remembering where one rescuable NPC was eight hours ago.
Conclusion:
I would highly advise buying Hollow Knight. Though the game does have issues worth noting, its low price tag, respectable difficulty and excellent art design make it well worth a playthrough.
*Oh, and it's hard and has boss fights in it so it's basically 2D Dark Souls.

Hollow Knight, the difficult platforming metroidvania. Maybe a bit like a LOZ:II that never came (but with bugs). Here's my review of this beautiful game:
Pros:
Gameplay -> Wow. The controls are precise and 'pack a lot of punch'. You start off with 4 directional movement, a 4-directional attack and means to regenerate health (masks). In these 3-simple mechanics there is a lot of complexity and brilliance. The jump button can be held or tapped for short or high jumps, something the user will need to learn when dealing with enemies like the first boss. A 4-directional attack allows flying enemies to be less irritating and allow for 'nail pogoing' where you can swing your sword (nail) down on enemies from above whilst always staying above them. And then there's the soul meter (allowing for regeneration). This slowly fills up as you defeat your foes and can then repair damage, however the knight (you) are very vulnerable during this animation (no instant movement on cancelling), this means that boss fights are much more of a challenge.
Abilities -> As you proceed through the game you will encounter new items (like double jump, dash and wall climb). Some people don't like how you don't start out with these items. But I'm fine with this as the enemies’ scale with this progression and the game wouldn't flow as well without it. Thanks to these items, bosses can get harder without going with the 'give it more health' or 'more is harder'. This leads to kore enjoyable boss fights.
Boss Fights -> I have never played a game where the majority of the boss fights have so much tension that my heart starts racing and I shiver for a while after defeating the boss. This feeling has made every boss that much more memorable, unlike other games. The boss fights are (normally) balanced (looking at you flukemarm and crystal guardian II) leading to a healthy 'I can do this next time' attitude towards them. None of this 'Well that's utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t', and 'how the ♥♥♥♥ am I supposed to do that' or even 'I quit'.
Art style -> Mmmmmm. I like this game's art. Fits the theme well, every area looks different (maybe greenpath and queen's gardens are kinda similar), and every area has its own personality. which brings me right onto:
Music -> Yay, everyone loves a bit of music don't they? The music here is memorable, each piece suits the area it's assigned to. But the real point here, is that it makes the boss fights. As mentioned earlier my heart raced during the majority of bosses, the music generated this tension, just thinking of it gives me those great memories of overcoming each boss. truly fantastic
Characters -> All the characters have nice little quirks. I love the little noises each bug makes. This didn’t really help drive the game in anyway. But it sure did drive the plot (if you research anyway) and is actually pretty interesting.
Free DLC and low price -> It's an indie game that's not driven by stupid AAA titles. What isn't there to like. Stop ♥♥♥♥♥ing and buy the freaking game it’s so cheap for the amount of content (and there’s still more coming)
Cons:
Progression -> If you are impatient. The progression feels a little slow. 1st spell after the about 40 minutes. Dash after about 1h 30. A health upgrade after a few hours, it feels quite slow. I think this is fine, it provides more of a challenge and is all well and good. I can see why it may cause problems for some however.
Charms -> Whilst I do like the charm SYSTEM. I do struggle to see the point in a lot of charms. Some charms become straight up useless after some time and some I never even used (I only got them for them sweet sweet achievements). I do however like the charms that combine in new ways (like defender’s crest + glowing womb which effectively grants you homing bombs every few seconds).
Spell builds -> Spells are good fun in this game. There are 3 one for each direction and they can be very powerful after upgrading them. The problem is that they can easily ruin some boss fights. Using flukenest + spell twister + shaman stone is fairly OP and can allow you to breeze through bosses that would usually pose a much greater threat. Oh well I guess you don't have to use them.
Cheese (smelly, smelly cheese) -> Nosk and dung defender (and white defender). These bosses are made very easy through some easy positioning, taking a lot of the oomph out of the fight. knowing that you'll rarely be hit and can easily regen after being hit destroys the tension in the fight.
Zote ->  Zote is a haxing pile of willies. He is too hard and must be taken out of the game. How can anyone defeat his 56 precepts and his supreme nail 'Life Ender'. See? The clues in the name, you'll want to end your life just after seeing this fight.

Since my review for the vanilla game is still available feel free to check it out. Here, I'll be focusing on the aspects of the remastered edition only. As for BioShock: I consider it one of the best games I have every played. --- crashes, crashes and crashes everywhere; the game can crash if you open a door or if you pick up a new plasmid.

Don't be fooled by the similar look, because this game is most certainly not Civ V: Just A Reskin.
Civilization Beyond Earth is exactly what I was hoping for. The tech web is much more enjoyable than the Tech Tree, and every civ is unique as a result of the affinity system. There's no more of two archers fighting with no visible differences, now you have hovertanks fighting giant turtle-like genetic constructs and 40k-esque battlesuits. The affilities give your nation a personality, one that other nations consider worthy of going to war over. The game is very much playable if you're inexperienced, but players who know every little nook and cranny of the game and  like to minmax in an attempt to defeat an unbeatable enemy will not be dissapointed, as the difficulty levels mean exactly what they say (Or, you know, what they would say if they weren't named after milestones in space exploration history). As someone who likes to roleplay, I had great fun with the affinities and tech web. The aliens are definitly not barbarians, and will act different to you depending on your actions. However, they become less and less important as time goes on, and eventually even Harmony players just start killing them off to make room for a new mine. This feels intentional, like the devs wanted to show that over time, humanity just asserted it's dominance over the planet.
Now, the game isn't a unicorn farting rainbows while eating cake. There are some very real problems. Just like Civ V, it can get boring over time. The different sponsors feel very, very similar. The affinities are where the different units come into play, and the bonuses from the sponsors really don't matter unless you're minmaxing. It is also very much a base game, after being spoiled by Civ V's numerous expansion packs, it feels tiny.
Overall, I would definitely reccomend this game. While there are drawbacks, it's a fun game and the expansions will inevitably fill in the gaps. I would go so far as to reccomend it at full price. If you liked Alpha Centauri, this is a must-have. Not the same game, but worthy of being called a spiritual successor.

I played Bioshock extensively back on the Xbox 360 and thoroughly enjoyed it. Yet, I haven’t played it in years, so when the opportunity came up to play a ‘remastered’ version, I couldn’t resist. Pros:
. It’s Bioshock.
. PC controls are great, not sure about controller support
. Steam cards
. Steam achievements
Cons:
. It’s not a remaster
. The visuals and animations have dated quite a bit now, and aren’t as impressive as they were
. It’s very expensive for what is, or rather what it isn’t
. Riddled with bugs that were in the original PC release and haven’t even been fixed yet!

Bioshock is a fantastic game, but this is disappointing remaster.

If you loved X, X2, or X3, then you probably won't love this failed console port waste of time. What could you do in the other games that you can not do here? Almost everything. They dumbed down about every part of the X franchise for 8 year olds that throw games on the floor with any depth.
Now, all that being said, Egosoft has always had a hell of a community. They were always modding the game, improving it for the better. Egosoft realized this and has in the past released player created content as 'Signed' content, meaning its possible to obtain it without modding the vanilla game.  So could modders do something crazy with this game in the future, I'm sure they could.
Like I hinted at above, they have dumbed down about every aspect of the game here to appease a younger generation with a higher need for instant gratification. You pilot one ship, not a super awesome highly customizable ship that you can really make your own either. There's like 5 different types of components that you can buy for your ship, and maybe a variety of 3 for each component. One engine gives more speed, and less maneuverable thrust, one gives more maneuverable thrust less speed, and one is a 'balanced' option. Could having one ship if dont correctly be ok? I'm sure it could be, but this wasn't it. It's not exciting to buy upgrades for your ship when there really is only a couple ways to go.
Another problem, not only could you not really customize your ship, but you are not worthy of a cargo bay. Modders have attacked this already, but the base game left out your personal ability to trade. To trade you had to take one of your ships that is meant for the ware you are trying to buy and order it to make the purchase while you are there in sector. What a most horrible system. In the other X games you could order your ship half way across the galaxy to do something, true freedom
The weapons made for your player ship are dumbed down versions of the older X games as well. Maneuvering your ship is easy, and fighting is as advertised, but like I said, no customizability. 5 Different weapons, MK1 and MK2 of each, what trash.

This is a great way for PC gamers to play a turn-based, strategic RPG, which unfortunately, has been a dying genre for the platform since the 90s. There are also many sidequests, and you'll probably need to do a lot.

I just finished Final Fantasy XIII and I'm still planning on going back and completing all the remaining sidequests.  I wouldn't say this game ended up as my absolute favorite in the series, but it's still very much worth playing through.
First off, I'm going to discuss the main point of criticism everyone keeps bringing up about this game: the linearity.  I would definitely say that I prefer games that are more open and adventurous instead of games that constantly force you in one direction.  However, while the first part of the game is extremely linear, it actually didn't bother me as much as I was afraid it would.  Many of the game's 13 chapters consist of your team running down long, narrow pathways (with the occasional offshoot containing treasure) while fighting enemies and watching cutscenes.  All shopping and upgrading is done at save points; there are no minigames or towns (well, there are "towns" but you'll be running through them fighting enemies just like in the other parts of the game).  On the bright side, the story, combat, and character progression system were all engaging enough to keep me entertained throughout all the linearity.  Still though, when first starting the game one might wonder why Square-Enix would ever decide to make it so ridiculously linear.  My guess is that it's their way of making the player focus on the story during the first part of the game without getting sidetracked - most sidequests in the earlier parts of these types of games tend to yield insignificant rewards, anyway, so the developers opted to save all of the sidequests for the later part of the game.  Indeed, if you are able to make it through the first 10 chapters without getting sick of all the corridors and pathways, chapter 11 finally presents you with the expansive, wide-open, sidequest-filled world you've been craving.  At first, it may seem like too long of a wait to reach chapter 11 out of 13, but believe me, this open part of the game is HUGE and is very well worth the wait.  Don't be thrown off by the fact that it's just one chapter.  To put it into perspective: if you plan on completing everything there is to do in the open section, it will likely take you more time than the main story by itself.  Also, even if you decide to move on and finish the last two chapters of the game, you are still allowed to return to the open world.
People tend to have different opinions on this game's battle system, but personally it's one of my favorites in the whole series.  It introduces enough new aspects to make it unique and refreshing, but at the same time it doesn't stray too far from Final Fantasy tradition like I feel FF12's combat system did.  Combat is fast-paced and engaging, but you still have enough time to strategize.  There are six different roles that a character can assume during battle, and you can instantly change those roles by shifting the party's "paradigm" (set of roles for all three active characters) depending on what you need to do at any particular moment, whether it be healing, attacking, buffing/debuffing, etc.  Speaking of roles, the character progression system strikes a perfect balance between customization versus character uniqueness.  You are free to choose which role you want a character to improve in by spending CP (the game's term for EXP) wherever you please.  At the same time, even though every character will eventually be able to access all roles, each character will still have three roles that they are better at than the others, and these roles vary depending on the character.  Even characters who are both good at a certain role will each have access to their own unique abilities for that role, so they're definitely not blank slates that you have to build from the ground up.
To top it all off, the game's soundtrack is pleasant for the most part and the environments are beautiful and full of color.  I'm aware the voice acting has occasionally been criticized with regards to certain characters, but I've heard much worse - in fact, I didn't find it bad at all.  My final word: if you never had the chance to play this game on a console, now's the time to get it.

The latest Magic game is both a step in the right direction but also plagued by lackluster design decisions and bugs.
I would recommend it for people unfamilliar to Magic, just be sure you aren't expecting Hearthstone-level of polish and smoothness. I wouldn't recommend spending any money on this at least for now.
The Good:
- UI continues to be smooth and keeping in mind the baggage of implementing from physical card game the flow of the gameplay is ok.
- F2P, with grinding you can get everything free
- Campaign is actually rewarding since you get in-game currency from it.
- Community quests are an awesome idea
- Has potential
The Bad:
- Netcode seems to not have improved and continues to be as bad as previous installations. Joining online game is still a hassle since game keeps popping up "Session full" almost half the time and forcing you to keep hitting retry yourself. This is weird since you no longer select a specific game from a list, so you are not trying to join a specific session.
- There is no proper concede option, if your opponent leaves you are still forced to play the match to the end against AI.
- Numerous bugs. Gamepad has some issues. Some daily quests won't progress even if you meet the requirements*.The developer is notorious for leaving many bugs unfixed in previous installations of Magic franchise.
- If connection to server is lost (and this happens a lot) mid-game, there goes your reward.
- Current card selection is smallish. First decks you can make feel very poor and lack consistent theme.
*EDIT: So now I get it how the quest thing works. You have to build the deck with deck wizard in order to progress in the "archetypal" daily quests. It does not count towards the quest if you build the deck without deck wizard even if the colors are correct. But after you have the deck built you can even battle against AI to complete the daily quests! That's nice, since the decks are still quite awkward since the card selection is so limited, would not go online with them.
80 / 100 for totally new players
70 / 100 to people familliar with previous MtG DotP games
60 / 100 for people with Hearthstone only background

I, personally, enjoy this game, and if you are into space combat games at all, you will enjoy Sins of a Solar Empire. The original game was fantastic, and with Rebellion, comes even more fun! Take command of one of three factions, and choose whether you are a Loyalist or a Rebel. Each faction has their own backstory and reasons for why they are fighting, and the sins they are paying for.
The technology trees have been expanded ever so slightly, and the tech from before has been reworked. Perhaps you want to upgrade how effecient your mining is or maybe you want to start broadcasting how amazing your civilization is across space. Choose whether you want to upgrade your ships' weaponry or armor, to field more variations or ships, or build your defenses.
Speaking of ships, they have added in two new classifications: the Corvette and the Titan. The Corvette is a fast little attack ship, sporting a few weapons, and a debilitating effect. They take only a research upgrade to start producing. And then comes the Titan. These behemoths take several research upgrades, not-to-mention an arm and a leg worth of resources to start producing. You can only field one at a time, but these monsters are devastating.
Each faction has one new capital ship as well, which can be of varying use in certain aspects of the game. The original five capital ships have been revamped, with their abilities being reworked and revamped. Not everything has been changed, but a few tweaks have been made, to make sure they are still viable and fun to use.
This is the only part that I still have a problem with: the planetary upgrades. Planets can be upgraded in a handful of different areas, and different types of planets can receive a different number of upgrades, up to a maximum of four. These upgrades can allow a larger planetary population or increasing the number of tactical (defensive structures and the like) or logistical (research platforms, broadcasting stations, shipyards). It could increase the health of the planet (and thus how much damage it can take from enemy bombardment), or explore the planet. This could lead to planetary anomalies that could be beneficial or penalize the planet, or even discover a long-lost artifact, which would have beneficial affects for your empire as a whole. The reason I have a problem with this is because it is too streamlined. Once a planet is upgraded, there is no reason to keep coming back to it, unless it is being attack.
That being said, do I recommend the game? Yes. Absolutely. Gameplay is almost never stale, as the game changes every time you start it again. Anyone that enjoys the aspect of large naval space engagements would positively love Sins of a Solar Empire. And with this 75% off deal going on for this weekend, I would jump at the opportunity.

Quote from the game's store page (still current at time of writing):
We strongly believe in words: 'Pay once, Play forever' and will provide all future content updates for free.
There are at least two planned expansions with new ships, abilities, campaigns and a multiplayer support.
Those two lines were there when I bought the game, and are still part of the game's marketing right now. That said, neither promise has eventuated. On top of the lack of this promised content, the devs have been actively promoting a planned sequel, which is to include multiplayer. When asked about this game's multiplayer, which does not yet exist, they have so far failed to respond to those queries.
I would love to recommend the game. It takes a little figuring out at first, but once you get it, it flows quite well. Anticipating enemy movements to line your torpedoes up can be a lot of fun. Timing a shield for a turn where you would have otherwise gotten shredded by enemy fire or torn open by a volley of missiles is tense and challenging. Using abilities at the wrong time, or using the wrong ability for a situation, can lead very quickly to an early grave. I don't want this to be a negative review, but with the developers putting up SERIOUS reasons to doubt their promises, I can't in good faith recommend supporting them. The game doesn't feel polished or entirely finished in some ways, which could be forgiven with the pricetag and the promise of extra content to come. Unfortunately, given the suspicious silence from the devs, part of the reason to hope for improvement and polish is being buried.

, a metroidvania that focuses on exploration and combat
This is where I think the game truly shines, the game gave freedom and does not hold your hand, which is a pro
, the freedom provides satisfaction whenever I find a new place because I felt like "I found it" and not because the game led me to it.
But it also brought me to moments where I don't have an idea on where I should go anymore, I still love it though, since the moments where I hated it are too few
The map system is something you would either love or hate, as a map is one of the most important things on a metroidvania. It will affect the exploration the wrong way sometimes, it felt like you have to find the cartographer before even trying to explore.
Personally, I was not a fan of the part where you need to buy the maps, but I loved the part where you have to go there to map it (Again the feeling of "I found it").
The checkpoint system is similar to a bonfire on dark souls game, you would rest and if you die or quit the game you would go back to the certain place where you rested.
It was not the checkpoints I hated, but the lack of them on certain important places, I had to walk up to 4 levels I got to 5 times. I even did the "quit the menu then load the game" so you would go back to the rest point faster once (Yes, I am sorry) because I was tired of going back to a rest point just to map it out.
The combat is fluid, the ability to attack on four directions and control the height of your jump worked well, not only on combat but also on platforming levels.
Every enemy is not that unique on how they try to kill you, some goes and walks a random pattern, most will try to kill with ranged attacks or by charging at you.
But I learned how to love them on my trials on the Colosseum of Fools, where they would pair enemies with each other, I felt how different they really are from each other.
All bosses were unique with interesting attack patterns, all with a right amount of difficulty that will make you want to try fighting them again and provide satisfaction once you defeat them.
Though I hate that there are certain bosses that can be easily killed just by going ham and taking advantage of the invulnerability frames, and so far there were four bosses. And also that there are certain bosses that have mechanics that will try to cripple you (like falling rocks on a random pattern), even though bosses are a test of reaction time and reading of patterns.
You will start with no idea, get certain clues on certain areas, then learn about the secrets of the place.
One thing I learned when I played Undertale, is that interactions with NPCs can be so smart that they will leave a smile on your face, same goes to Hollow Knight.
The game takes account on how you approach certain characters, either you pass by them without even trying to talk to them, or just straight up approaching without turning you back on them.
And with an adorable voice acting with unique and lovable characters, they make the world feel alive somehow.
Because clues are tied to certain areas, the story will pretty much go on your own pace. I don't know if it will be a bad thing for others, but it was a good thing for me.
The "not so real" ending was unsatisfying, so in most cases you will try and get the true ending of the game as there are more secrets to uncover.

If you're looking for the ultimate game to end all other games, this is probably not your game.
If you're looking for you're gonna marry and have kids with, this is probably not your game.
If you're looking for an AAA title with the best graphics of the century, this is definitely not your game.
But if you're looking for a simple but challenging game to have a few hours of fun with, this is it.
Star Tactics takes the mantra "less is more" as its basis and creates great game around it.
It is based on very simple mechanics, but these open up to a quite large amout of tactical decision making, sometimes even feeling similar to chess.
Sure, the graphics are nothing to write home about, but I feel the minimalistic wireframe-like style actually adds to the immersion, making you really feel like a commander directing the battle through his tactical display.
The UI is similarly minimalistic as the grapics and I think it might even be the best part of the game. It's intuitive, clear, and doesn't feel cluttered or complicated at all. While part of this might be due to the simple underlying mechanics, I feel like many bigger game companys could learn one thing or the other from this game.
The levels are quite well designed. Most of the time you're facing a larger opponent fleet, so you actually need to gain an advantage through better positioning and using your ships' abilities well.
While this game is great, I have found four notable flaws.
One, Torpedoes/Rockets are really overpowered. Many battles, you can win through "french-american" tactics: Run away as fast as you can while bombing the hell out of your enemy. If your battleship or dreadnought isn't already in range of the enemy ships, it's a sitting duck.
Two,  sometimes, the enemy AI is dumber than bread. Lay a line of mines, hide behind it and wait for the enemy to run into its doom. Most of the time this is mitigated by being outgunned or outnumbered, though, so it's actually a balanced fight.
Three, the game has no gamemode where you can build your own fleet.
And last: NO MULTIPLAYER. I'd love to play this game against a friend!
