I got into this game via a demo. The demo left me wanting more, and Steam had it on sale, so off I went to get it.
I'm on my second play through. The first play through was messed up beyond believe. I didn't know what was what and got stuck in a boss battle that I could not win. That bit frustrated me to no end and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off greatly. I went off in search for a guide to overcome the boss battle. To my dismay, none of the guide helps as I've done something I should not have done: killing everything in sight and trying to spread the EXP love with all my party members. The end result was a severly gimped party lacking in both stats and skills.
I stopped playing for a couple of days and dived deep into the wiki. I learn the proper way to play the game, picked up a majority of the content that I just zipped past without realizing it, and focused on growing my party members the proper way. Second time around, the game was infinitely less infuriating and way more fun. The boss that I was stuck at in my first play through became a breeze, though the game did something rather nasty after that particular fight. Thank god I was somewhat prepared for it, equipped with both knowledge and power to overcome that nasty bit. The resulting satisfaction was very, very high.
From then on, the game became something I want to explore in depth. I trawled through the wiki and its discussion pages to learn more about the mechanics of the game. Although I've been vigilant in keeping track of the missable content, there are still a number of things that I inadvertently got locked out of without realizing it. I am currently one boss fight away from the end of the game and already I am laying down the foundation for my new game plus.
Despite the amazing depth of the game, or rather, due to it, the game will eat you alive if you don't know what you’re doing. The game does not make obvious certain crucial information from the get go. Playing the game with a lack of information can lead to a really bad experience, especially if you play this game the way you would a normal RPG.
With that said, the game is excellent for those wanting a good challenge. There is a vast amount of content within the game, and it should keep someone busy for the next 100-200 hours.
Update (22 Feb 2014): I've just finished my third playthrough and I'm taking a break to plan for my fourth playthrough. It seems that once you've finished the game once, you just keep going back for more. This game is one of my best investments in Steam.

This is NOT a full out written review; I HAVE NOT COMPLETED THE GAME AS OF THIS WRITING,  just sharing how much I LOVE this game
===============================================================================
I honestly REALLY love this game so far, I don't understand the internet hate against it. I personally LOVE how creative the developers were with the story. I love gameplay so far but I already know I have not gotten far into it. Basically I just want to express that I have never played a game like this. Its so unique and fun to play, the visuals were spot on.
OPINIONS
Storyline: I like how creative the developers were with explaining the plot. You dive right into the world without any introduction, but you learn what is happening and where you are in the datalogs and as you progress through the game. I love that fact alone, that you dive into the story without any introductions. It makes easier for not making some cheasy introduction like, "Welcome to the city of cocoon" etc.    Some people hate how you dive straight in, but for me, they executed it very well.
Gameplay: The battle system is no easy task later in the game. At first you go through the battle system nice and slow. This is VERY good for newcomers to the game like myself, it lets you progress and process what you do in battles. (You will fight ALOT in this game) What is the battle system like, you ask? Here it is.
Battle: To put it simply, you have a party with you consisting of people that have roles such as Medic or Damage. You the player, may be any of those roles. In order to use your moves, you have to choose them like Pokemon (Clicking on potions, attacks and abilities.) But the thing is, you don't take turns like in Pokemon; It is realtime and the enemies can attack you whenever. You must be REALLY fast paced and have knowledge of the enemy, along with your own moves and party, to defeat them.
All in all, I really like this game, AND I FULLY RECOMMEND IT TO EVERYONE. This game is for you if you love story in a game, because this game's story is explored ALOT.

Tl;DR Good game. Some flaws but worth buying if you like a good story and fast paced battles.
Looking at the reviews for this game, many seem to criticise it for two main problems: first is the lack of port and second is the corrider/linear styled gameplay that could potentially restrict the freedom you have when playing. However, I personally didn't have a problem with either.
The games's port for my laptop was absolutely fine. I experienced very minimal to absolutely no framedrops throughout my game time, even during battle scenes, and my laptop kept the game to a steady 60fps.
The linear styled gameplay, however, may put off some people from buying this game and I personally can understand that opinion. The game starts off very slowly at the beginning and most of the early hours spent on this game will consist of you of either watching cut scenes or simply swatting away easy enemies that adds very little experience in terms of content in the game.
Even so, if you're a major FF fan or if you're a patient type, like me, the late game experience is certainly a reward for toiling through countless yet pointless hours. In my experience, the story line starts to bring life and excitement at around chapter 7 (some may disagree) and once you're about 20 hours in, the game finally provides an alternative to the monotonic, corridor styles gameplay and introduces the player to a vast, open world in which you can finally participate in some side missions or just explore and generally have fun. In addition, the battles start to feel more challenging, and with the entry of the paradigm shifts and techniques such as libra or summon, they begin to feel enjoyable and rich in content with great, fast paced action that'll keep you on your toes throughout the whole fight.
In conclusion, Final Fantast XIII is a good game. There are definitely some flaws that some gamers may not like and if they're the reason why it's preventing them from buying or liking this game, then I can only wave away what little argument i have and simply agree with them: everyone has their opinion. However, I think there are some who are too critical and too unfair which could then upset the true reflection of a solid, good game. Personally, I think this game is worth buying.

I have played a lot of paper magic, about 60 hours of Duels of the Planeswalkers (Wizards of the Coast's previous online magic game), and have dabbled in Hearthstone, I thought I would give some comparisons between the different games.
Compared with Paper Magic:
+ Costs much less, even if you spend fourty dollars to get a bunch of cards at the start
+ Doesn't require friends or other people to play
+/- Less cards and mechanics means there are fewer complications
+/- There is a story mode, which unfortunately only serves as a more efficient way to earn gold
- No way to interact with opponents
- Matches are generally slower
- Sometimes there are connectivity issues
- There are less gamemodes (no free-for-all, Commander, or anything wacky)
Compared with Duels of the Planeswalkers:
+ Free to play
+ No restrictions on deck building
+ Cards retain some value since there won't be a new game every year
- Takes longer to unlock cards
- No challenges or puzzles
I never really tried to play online Duels of the Planeswalkers, so unfortunately I can't remark on the differences in community, connectivity, etc.
Compared with Hearthstone:
+ Much faster progression
+/- More complicated gameplay (instants and planeswalkers in particular cause these complications)
- Unlockable cards are much more powerful than initial cards, unlike Hearthstone
- More connection problems
- Less polished
- When opponents concede they are replaced with an computer, rather than losing
- Smaller card selection (Will become less noticable with time)

So why do I recommend this game even though there seem to be so many issues with it? Simple: I like Magic, and I am familiar with the cards, the rules, and the little worlds that are supposed to make up the game. I like the complexity it allows both in deck building and in use of cards. I like that I can have good cards without spending any money. Most of all though, it would feel really hypocritical of me if I didn't recommend a game I was planning on playing.
TL:DR I enjoyed playing paper magic back in the day so this is fun, even if there are problems.

Here is my unbiased review of this game.
This game at its core is very simple once you figure out what you're doing. The learning curve is fairly steep so I recommend going through ALL of the skill quests as well as through as many of the story missions as possible.
As a beginner this will get tedious and if you're experienced it'll just be downright annoying to see the same things repeated to you over and over.
The only reason you'll want to do this is for the TONS of free gold the skill quests and story missions give you. However if you can get past that you'll have a GREAT sense of accomplishment and lots of gold to buy new booster packs with. After that its all about Multiplayer and earning gold to buy more cards. If you like Deckbuilding this game is a nice little timewaster if you need one.

Verdict: People might actually think that I don't like FFXIII, but it's the other way around. Out of the three from the Lightning Saga, XIII is my favorite because of its atmosphere, lore and world. All the nonsense added in XIII-2 didn't appeal to me (not to mention that the story was far more confusing than XIII's in many aspects) and Nova Chrysalia, while gorgeous and with a stabe lore, didn't feel as great as the original party's fight against fate. XIII has problems though, starting with its extremely linear nature and flawed battle system (which was greatly improved in XIII-2). Don't get me wrong, I don't mind a good linear game and I understand that many previous FFs had a linear nature even though they were open world, but the early level designs of XIII are really just terrible (as many would put it, "it's like being on rails"). The story and lore can also be a problem for some people as they're not easy to get into. The story requires a lot of interpretation, while much of the lore is hidden behind datalog entries. General FF fans are not used to either as previous entries in the franchise were pretty straightforward with their stories and didn't have a very deep lore, or at least not deep enough to require a detailed explanation through walls of text. The last problem is that the game is just too big for Western Steam users. A 50GB download is absurd for a game this old, which shouldn't be necessary because many of the pre-rendered cutscenes could run on the engine if Square Enix made the effort. Alternatively, they should've provided the Japanese VOs as a free DLC.
All in all, is not that easy of a game to get into and newcomers may need the help of other players and/or wikia to understand what's going on. If you play this without being spoiled by haters and can get over its performance issues (which are not as bad as XIII-2's, but are still there), it's a hell of a game with high production values. Fans of sci-fi fantasy might find the lore appealing and the environments, breathtaking.

+ When on sale, it is usually $9.99. Not bad at first glance.
- Pre-discount price is still the same as the launch price in 2012: $39.99 (for a small expansion added onto a game going back to 2008). A 75% discount only looks impressive because the price has never been adjusted.
- Graphics and gameplay haven't been much improved from Trinity. It's an example of something old given a touch here and touch there, and repackaged and priced as something "new".
- It has 'super-capital-class' (aka titan-class) ships that are overpowered and limit the gameplay. All roads lead to building a titan, whether you wanted to use one or not.
- It doesn't truly have six factions; more like what should have been additional tech options for each original faction, got marketed to "hey, now you have double the number of factions".
'Old Games, Same Debut Prices'
Stardock is one of thousands of publishers on Steam that list their old games at ridiculous regular prices. When these overpriced games go on sale, the discount by themselves are high - 50%, 75% -  many of us get distracted by that percentage figure and buy old games at what should really be regular prices, but are advertised as "discounted prices".
They have all the advantages (reduced costs, easier marketing, global distribution, greater profits) through Steam, selling copies upon copies of old hits that would receive little attention and garner little sales without this platform. But they do not change their prices from launch and profit even more greatly, all without offering any added value for  customers. I hope Steam's userbase becomes more tight with their wallets - it's the only way publishers that offer good value for their games (both old and new products) will benefit, while publishers who 'double dip' on cost savings and price gouging, will adapt.

As much as I want to give Magic Duels a positive review, as the game stands currently I cannot in good conscience do so.  There are just too many issues with the game, both technically and from a design standpoint as of this writing.  First would be the connectivity issues that have plagued the game since launch.  Many times I would be unable to connect to the servers for an entire day, although Wizards has made strides in makes the servers more stable as of late.  Why is this a problem when you can play offline (although obviously not against other people)?  Magic Origins awards you coins for purchase of booster packs to expand your collection upon successfully completing duels, either against a computer opponent or another player.  Therefore in offline mode you cannot make any progress towards improving your collection in any way, which is a tough thing to swallow.
Another large issue is the very grindy nature of the game.  Veterans of the Duels of the Planeswalkers series will know it takes a significant time commitment to gain access to every card in the game, but Magic Duels takes this to an entirely new level.  Matches against either the computer at the hardest difficulty setting or another person give you 15 and 20 coins upon a win respectively, while you need 150 coins to "purchase" a single booster pack in game.  Furthermore, a booster pack in Magic Duels only gives you 6 cards, a far cry from the 15 in an actual Magic pack or the DotP 2015 packs.  To make matters even worse, there is a cap on the amount of coins you can earn in a single day from online/offline matches, somewhere in the range of 500 total coins.  This is obviously to facilitate the microtransactions of buying the in game coins and make Wizards and Stainless money, but this can make it feel like a significant chore to improve any deck you make without sinking a large amount of money into the game.  This situation will only get worse as Wizards is planning on releasing each new Magic set in Magic Duels to coincide with the real life release.
There are other issues with the game (troubles with the online matchmaking system, the "deck construction wizard" offered to novices when creating new decks is laughably bad, etc.) but the online issues and the amount of effort needed to improve your collection without sinking a ton of money into the game outweigh those by a significant margin.  Although the gameplay itself is fine and the addition of planeswalkers a definate positive, as the game stands as of this writing it is not worth the time and money needed to spend on it to make a deck that doesn't feel underwhelming.  Only if Wizards addresses these issues either with more coins per win/lower booster pack "cost"/more cards per booster pack would I check out Magic Duels .

REVIEW:
Saints Row: Gat out of Hell is the latest installment in the often hilarious, over-the-top, ridiculous, & insane Saints Row series. This game feels and plays actually like a stand-alone expansion pack or DLC (depends on how you look at it) to Saints Row 4, for better and/or for worse. If you liked how SR4 was controlled mechanically, you'll feel right at home with that, for the most part: action + gunplay feel a lot similar to the previous game (SR4). Throw in a blender some old elements, some new elements, and some removed elements - it's hard to actually quantify this experience. This expeirence has more ups + downs than a roller coaster, for better and/or for worse.
I wish GooH had more than mostly just Activities (side-quests) + MMO type of stuff, more or less. And more or less, most of your time here in GooH, you will be doing side-quests. If you liked doing Activities in Saints Row 4, you'll probably feel right at home here. Since this feels mostly like a stand-alone SR4 expansions/DLC, some of the activities feel similar or have been reskinned + re-tweaked to suit the new location of Hell. Others like Hellblazing (in which you fly around at reach checkpoints, in a certain amount of time) - feel completely new here.
The only real problem is - well, most of this game consists of just Activities. One of the joys of previous SR games like SR2, 3, and 4 was that a lot of the main missions were absolutely unique and excellent - especially when compared to the Activities. Not here, as you mostly have just Activities. You build-up your Satan's Wrath meter by doing whatever you do in the game-world - from Activities, completing Challenges, doing Loyalty Quests, and whatever else you can think of. Once this meter has been built-up, then you can confront Satan for an epic conclusion.
So, why are you in Hell? The Boss (i.e. the player character from the previous SR games) gets kidnapped on Kinzie's birthday by Satan, after all goes wrong when messing around with a Ouija board. Satan decides to take the Boss and have his daughter marry him. The player can play as either Kinzie or Johnny Gat, in which these two are going to get The Boss back and stop Satan. Every now and then, once you've done certain quests and/or you've raised your meter to a certain point, you will be greeted with something hilarious & funny - in typical Saints Row fashion, of course. While many of these are well-written & very funny. the game certainly could've used more of these cut-scenes + hilarious moments.
While it's pretty cool to play as either Johnny Gat or Kinzie (you can switch b/t the two at a certain location in the game), there's another issue here with GooH. Unfortunately, by being stuck w/ Gat and Kinzie - the player now does not have much customization on their looks, outfits, or anything of that sort...which is unlike most Saints Row experiences. SR experiences are usually overloaded with kind of customization - but, not here in SR: GooH.
Another drawback of the game not being a typical DLC and standing-alone on its own is that this game is not loaded with the music found in SR4. It's not like much music was created just for this game, either. You can't access music in a car or even at any time, which is what SR4 had going on - since there really isn't much for music here. Since this game seems to be lacking any of the licensed music from SR4, something feels completely lacking here in this department. This game certainly could've benefitted from having a MP3 Player Station like many of the GTA games on the PC feature.
One of the best new features here is, once you earn it: how to fly. If running up walls, jumping around insanely, and knocking over cars at fast speeds wasn't enough fun already (especially once you gain them and do improve + upgrade these abilities a bit), which all returns here in SR: GooH, BTW - the player can now also fly. Once the player learns how to fly + has leveled-up their character enough, the flying gets better and easier to handle. Oh, and it's a hell of a lot more fun, too! Flying is one of the best, coolest, and most fun new features in this game. Just exploring the sandbox of Hell itself and flying around it is pretty sweet, to say the very least.
While it took me 10 hours or so to finish my 1st playthrough (even though I did not do everything here), it certainly could take players a lot less time if they do not decide to keep on exploring the game-world and just do whatever activities they need to do to get fill up Satan's Wrath meter to get to the final encounter. It should be noted that there are actually multiple endings here, if you actually do feel up to experiencing the game more than one time through.
Saints Row: GooH is a very tough game to place somewhere b/c there are some cool + awesome things here, yet it feels like quite a bit is actually missing here. While that is to be expected with a stand-alone expansion or DLC, it still doesn't shake the feeling of how this could've turned out. With its crazy premise and many of the things this game has going for it, it could've been great. But, it's not - only having greatness in flashes of brillance, when it does. Maybe if Volition and High Voltage do feel up to it, they could offer up later some DLC (free and/or paid), to enhance + expand upon this experience.
For the time being, though: this game is certainly not worth the usual MSRP of $20 since there is hardly any main quests here; no real customization of your character's looks + outfits; and no real music here (licensed or not). On the other hand, it's certainly worth it if you can actually get this game really cheap, so you can check out the hilarious humor (which I wish there was more of); the new flying mechanics and gameplay is awesome (especially when you actually level-up your character); and there is the nice + cool new sandbox of Hell to explore.
Final Grade = C-.

Gat out of Hell is a small slice of the Saints Row insanity, following Johnny Gat and Kinzie Kenzington tearing up hell after Satan kidnaps the President of the USA.
The game revolves around filling up a &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥of-Satan-o-meter" by completeing activites and being a general pain in the♥♥♥♥♥for Satan. At certain points the story segments are unlocked but the main plot rather bare, so don't expect more than 3-4 hours of gameplay if that's all you care about.
New additions include the hell cityscape, a wide variety of very interesting weapons (the armchair with the miniguns is my favourite), a few new hell themed enemies and some slightly re-imagined powers. Instead of gliding, Gat/Kinzie has the ability for proper flight, which is by far the most entertaining form of travel in the Saints Row Series. You also have the option of switching between Johnny and Kinzie, but unfortunately this means all character customization has been removed.
There are plenty of new and old characters making an appearence, but they're heavily under used. There is little interaction with any of them aside from basic quest giving and scenes that are described by a narrator rather than acted out. Fortunately, there are audio logs scattered throughout the world that can give you a little more insight into their backstories.
If you're itching for some more Saints Row and you aren't tired of doing the same activities in the previous, then it's might be worth it, but personally, $20 is a bit much of an ask. Definately grab it on sale sometime.

This game is great. It's nothing like the traditional mobas that so many people compare it to, so you should give it a go regardless of whether you like them. (especially during the free weekends). The only problem with this game is that no matchmaking system can commonly create balanced matches with such a small playerbase. If there are only two teams queueing and one of them is high ranked, and the other low ranked, the game is going to put them together eventually because it doesn't want you to sit in a queue forever. (although there is an option to just... sit in the queue until it can find you a balanced game, if that's your thing) - more people need to play this game to fix that!
To clarify a few things people have incorrectly stated in whingy negative reviews;
- If you buy the game for $20 before it becomes free to play, you will have access to all the heroes forever. You do not have to unlock them individually with ingame currency.
- If you play the game free to play (during this free weekend or once it becomes free to play) you will NOT have access to all heroes and will have to unlock them individually (I believe you can do this with real money too).
There are microtransactions for cosmetic items even if you buy the game for $20, but this isn't really unusual these days. (Overwatch, Siege, CS:GO, etc) - and you can unlock all the cosmetic items without spending any money if you play enough.

A watered down, featureless and uninspired add-on to Civ 5.  Seems to have been rushed and lacks in depth compared to Civ 5, which is essentially the same game.  Roads, farms, boats, Civ 5 with a different art set.  And saying that it has unique art is stretching, there is limited, terribly rushed and re-used art for the Wonders, both the static images and what you see on the map.  Hey I built a "Xenoswarm" and there's a wireframe outline of it.. whatever the heck it is.  It;s as thought they randomly assigned future-sounding words together to form the technologies and buildings, which have simplistic base stat bonuses and little else.  Oh, a Biodrome, and a monochrome wireframe image.. and nothing appears on the map, and I get +5 energy, no text or backstory tells me what it is, no sage man with a deep voice reads a quote from the annals of history, it's just "Hey you got this thing, good for you".  The lack of narrative and background information in this game really kills it, and detracts heavily from the experience.  Every faction has the same units, for example.  They only start to differ once you advance along a course of one of three different viable technology routes (and if you don't focus in one, you don't get more powerful units, so you lose).
How can you trade in geothermal energy?  You can trade energy, but geothermal energy is a unique resource for some reason.  Am I scooping up lava and putting it on a truck to send out on the roads? This game is just mind bogglingly light on thoughtfulness.  It can be fun to play through once, but once you realize how little there is to do, you'll tire of it.  I recommend you get the excellent Civ 5 and expansions instead of this botched, rushed, missed opportunity for a great game.

Verdict: People might actually think that I don't like FFXIII, but it's the other way around. Out of the three from the Lightning Saga, XIII is my favorite because of its atmosphere, lore and world. All the nonsense added in XIII-2 didn't appeal to me (not to mention that the story was far more confusing than XIII's in many aspects) and Nova Chrysalia, while gorgeous and with a stabe lore, didn't feel as great as the original party's fight against fate. XIII has problems though, starting with its extremely linear nature and flawed battle system (which was greatly improved in XIII-2). Don't get me wrong, I don't mind a good linear game and I understand that many previous FFs had a linear nature even though they were open world, but the early level designs of XIII are really just terrible (as many would put it, "it's like being on rails"). The story and lore can also be a problem for some people as they're not easy to get into. The story requires a lot of interpretation, while much of the lore is hidden behind datalog entries. General FF fans are not used to either as previous entries in the franchise were pretty straightforward with their stories and didn't have a very deep lore, or at least not deep enough to require a detailed explanation through walls of text. The last problem is that the game is just too big for Western Steam users. A 50GB download is absurd for a game this old, which shouldn't be necessary because many of the pre-rendered cutscenes could run on the engine if Square Enix made the effort. Alternatively, they should've provided the Japanese VOs as a free DLC.
All in all, is not that easy of a game to get into and newcomers may need the help of other players and/or wikia to understand what's going on. If you play this without being spoiled by haters and can get over its performance issues (which are not as bad as XIII-2's, but are still there), it's a hell of a game with high production values. Fans of sci-fi fantasy might find the lore appealing and the environments, breathtaking.

TLR is a fantastic game. Sadly the game has an extremely poor reputation from the xbox world where I understand that it is sub par. On the PC however, the game is absolutely beautiful and suprisingly deep. The story won't win any awards for originality I suppose, but personally I really enjoyed it.
The main draw of the game however is the turn based combat with a twist. Instead of giving individual party members a command, you assemble small armies and assign them a general strategy to execute over the course of a turn. While this system can seem shallow and perhaps frustrating to those without the patience to learn its intricacies, it is one of the most enjoyable battle sysyems I have ever used in an RPG. Building and customizing each union and your overall team is a lot of fun. If you seek out the sidequests in the game (which easily adds more than 50% more content) you will often find yourself with access to many more allies with which to customize your team.
In all honestly if you have no interest in making a decent investment into learning the sysyem then this may not be the game for you. If, on the other hand, you enjoy learning and mastering an intricate combat system, turn based combat, hours and hours of sidequests and a beautiful world to explore, extremely challenging optional bosses, and beautiful looking combat, you will probably love TLR as much as I do.

I'm mostly a console gamer these days(even though I've been playing PC and Console games both since I was 4 in 1987), so I live for Square Enix games and know their history very well. I worshipped at their feet in the glory days before the merger. They haven't been great since, but for me, The Last Remnant is one of the few standout IPs they've had since they left their old Squaresoft monicre behind them.
This game is equal parts JRPG, strategy, and story-driven RPG. The combat is the main draw and probably the most unique form of turn-based I've seen in many years. Battles take place in a pseudo-strategic form where the player holds many groups of 3+ toons forming smaller parties broken off from the main group of up to 25 party members. You can fight groups of enemies as large as 75+ forming wave after wave and it really lends itself to the whole "continental war" vibe that the story tries to evoke. It's something you don't see often, if ever and it's very engrossing.
There is well over 100 hours of content to explore from sidequests to mob hunting to the main story itself and it very rarely gets old. On the pc, t graphics shine and the art style and creativity of the world is awe-inspiring at times. It is, again, something largely unique in the world of JRPGs. It doesn't feel too much like Final Fantasy, but you can see the influence.
One of the best aspects of this game, believe it or not, is the music. Take the best soundtracks of the FF franchise and combine it with hard rock compositions by some of Japans best and you have a soundtrack unlike any other out there. I bought the 3+ disc soundtrack I love it so much. It really heightens the impact during combat and brings you in that much more.
All in all I'd say any lover of JRPGs will love this game. It didn't get it's fair chance because SquEnix botched their chance with the ill-adviced 360 version. Rest assured that this game is 100% playable and will be well worth the cost.

Sins of a Solar Empire (SoaSE) could be such a great game, if it weren't for the god-awful multiplayer.
The game is an RTS in space which unlike Starcraft puts a much greater emphasis on "macro" (long-term economic management) than "micro" (fast command in battle). By itself the game is great and very well designed. So why do I still not recommend it?
Easy. It's because the multiplayer is ♥♥♥♥ed, you really can't say it in a better way and Stardock hasn't made any effort to fix some fundamental flaws.
1. The demands the player faces in multiplayer are light-years away from those he has to face in singleplayer against AI. The learning curve in Multiplayer is extremely steep and so getting better requires a huge amount of time, nerves and will to be invested. By itself this wouldn't be a problem for a casual RTS-player like me, but...
2. The multiplayer does not have leagues or divisions. There is no real way to divide players into categories depending on their skill like there is in Starcraft. All that's known to others is the number of games one has played and won/lost. However since SoaSE is usually played by more than two players at once, these figures don't really say anything. Also I can play 100 games for all I care, if I only play them in a casual way, I still won't become a "veteran". By itself this wouldn't be a problem, either, but...
3. There are simply not enough people playing this game. As a casual player who does not want to have a second job he's not getting paid for, I want to use games like these for relaxing and enjoying battles in space. Min-maxing to the largest extent possible is NOT what I want to do. I am fine with knowing which ship counters which other ship and which technologies are more useful early on than later. I neither have the time nor the nerve to turn a game into a university degree. I simply don't want it to matter that a Marza Dreadnought as a starter capital ship might be very useful 40 minutes later when it reaches level 6 because then it can bombard planets more effectively or whatever. You get the idea. This game is deep, but it does not allow casual players to join the party, simply because the more experienced players behave like♥♥♥♥♥♥♥towards noobs and so most people don't even try to enter multiplayer in the first place.
These three factors combined make the multiplayer experience about as pleasant as hitting your foot with a rusty nail. Not enough players and not enough differentiation between player levels just takes away all the fun.
Singleplayer is not worth it in long-term simply because the AI is about as smart as a brick and on higher difficulties it simply gets more resources than the player (i.e. cheats) instead of actually playing better.
I have played this game for over 150 hours (about 50-50 between Singleplayer and Multiplayer) and I still don't know♥♥♥♥♥♥about the huge variety of strategies and decisive differences between races. Also there is no encyclopedia or anything where you could look up some basic strategies. Elder players however seem to know all of them, so you are better off not even trying to get in in the first place unless you have a thing for masochism. Basically this game is both bland and incredibly deep at the same time and the developers have done their best to raise a massive entry barrier for newer players.
Edit: Also there are quite a large amount of negative reviews on Steam pointing this out that were downvoted extensively. So it seems that this game also calls a number of fanboys spitting on other peoples' opinions their property.

This game gives a very love hate relationship. I'll try my best to split the good and bad because i find it easier to point out the bad rather than what i actually like/love about this game. (SPOILERS AHEAD)
Good:
-Square Enix hardley ever dissapoint when it comes to delievering a lore and setting for a Final Fantasy title. The whole L'cie concept and how it can result is to me, original. The design of Cocoon and Gran Pulse feel very natural with the story arch alongside the whole Fal'cie and L'cie idea.
-Music. Now this i can say whole heartedly that Square Enix NEVER dissapoint when it comes to scoring a Final Fantasy game. If i were to give you a taste of why i think it's amazing then listen to this song.
The music in every big Final Fantasy title always make the lore feel very alive and rich, this part of the series that we all know and love is fortunately carried through in this title and i'm sure you'll all enjoy it.
-Game length. While i have 102 hours on my record i truly completed the game in 83 hours and the rest is where i left the game on and fell asleep but Final Fantasy only tracks time i've been actually playing. Final Fantasy is never usually a short game, especially because these titles are in development for many, many years. Don't worry about not thinking you might not get your money's worth out of this game because trust me, you will and there's still another 2 titles ahead of this that you have to play still.
-For the overall goodside i'm still not sure on what makes me love this game even with all of it's flaws (which i state below). I think the character i love the most is Sazh, he's the one who seems like he's the only one who's slightly true to the objective of the game. Getting Dajh back as a father figure is his biggest drive, even though he doesn't seem very driven throughout most of the game because he proclaims himself as "old" and "tired/fed up". Like i said, this game gives a very love/hate relationship between itself and the player.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Bad:
-Snow Villiers.
-A lot of the characters just moan throughout the game and a lot of the lines are pretty tacky/cheesy/cliche. Snow Villiers is the biggest example. Not only is he a cocky character but the majority of his lines are super far fetched about being a "hero" and if it's not that then he's always screaming and crying about Serah and holding that damn crystal tear. I also find Hope to be very annoying throughout the first half of the game, yes he lost his mother but he bottles his emotions towards Snow and starts to give of the vibe of an annoying little emo kid that only has character development because of a dead mother.
-The last boss, Orphan. Not only do you fight barthandelus for the third time in the game but you then go on to fight Orphan straight after without any preperation and by then you might have used all of your TP to even have any left against Orphan. My biggest complaint about Orphan is the attack it uses and it's name ends in "Wrath". I can't express how ******* ANGRY that move makes me. That move has a chance, yes, A CHANCE, of instant killing either you, your party members or nobody at all. I want to put my keyboard through my ******* monitor when i'm close to killing Orphan and i get instantly killed by ******* CHANCE! To put the very final boss fight to rest in review, After you defeat the annoying Orphan you go on to fight Orphan's "final form" which is literally the easiest boss fight ever. Spam buffs and debuffs and Orphan II goes down in like 1-3 staggers.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Overall:
I do recommend this game a lot as it is one of my favorite Final Fantasy titles and because in the ending i felt nothing but relief and i cried tears of joy, but i do warn you of the bad things about this game, seriously.

Hitman Absolution could have been one of the greatest stealth action games ever made if it did not have so many problems. The first of many issues with the game is the stealth system. If you are not disguised as what ever an NPC is dressing at that moment then you get detected really quickly. Which is fine and makes sense. If the NPC is hostile then he will shoot you and such, but if he is a friendly then you are good to go. This is all well and good untill you have a disguise on. Wearing a disguise does not give you a free pass to not-getting-shot-land, it just makes it take a bit longer for an enemy to realise taht you are not one of them. This is a problem, because of how quickly and enemy realises that you are a fake. So apparently evey mobster, cop, gangster and chef knows how every other mobster, cop, gangster and chef looks. This causes the player having to awkwardly crouch while enemies are looking at you just to reset the detection meter. As you do this not only do you look stupid because you are crouching in plain sight and staying behind a table for 3 seconds and then going back as if you are a stealth ninja. Even the NPC's mock you as you do this. They say things such as "Hey buddy what are you doing" as if this broken core mechanic of the game is the incorrect way to play. Also often disguises are more of a burden than a help. If you are wearing the same disguise as a non hostile NPC then they will realise you are wearing a disguise within secodns and then try and kill you for no reason. The entire disguise system is broken and makes the entire game frustrating to play. If that was the only problem then the game would still have been bad, but the level design is also a huge flaw. You don't feel liek you are searchign for a target and waiting for the perfect moment to strike. You are just looking for the target and when yo usee him you probably have no other choice but to kill him jus there because he probably won't move anywhere opportunistic. The only level where you feel like an assassin that is stalking his target is when you are with a huge crowd of people and looking for blind spots. Even this is filled with terrible level design because of hwo small it is. The mission could be finished with a brillaitn score by in 2 minutes by just picking up a brick, going to a corner and hitting the target with it. This is not fun or immersive, it is annoying. This game is a huge missed opportunity that is not just a game that I do not like, but I strongly believe that it is a terrible game that should not be played by anybody. If you want a good Hitman game then play Hitman Blood money, because that game is a true masterpiece.

The quickest and easiest way to describe Star Tactics is this: imagine taking Steambirds (an old Flash-turned-mobile game involving an air war during a Steampunk timeline) and changing the setting to outer space with starships.
Instead of airships, you have capital ships; instead of propeller-driven or jet-powered aircraft, you have space fighters, etc.
That's pretty much it. Even the control scheme (where you guide your units using arrows) and special abilities (such as a defensive shield or a 180 degree turn) are nearly identical to Steambirds.
After requesting an options menu be implemented, the developer readily responded and added one. The options menu now lets you set music and sound effects, as well as resolution, advanced effects, and gives you the choice to play in windowed mode.
Despite my harsh comparison to Steambirds, the fact remains that Star Tactics is an entertaining, albeit somewhat simple, game. It's not meant for people to spend all day playing, but for those who have limited time and want to play a game in short spurts.
Overall, I'd recommend Star Tactics, so long as you realize you're getting a relatively simple strategy game. There's nothing wrong with that at all, but just be aware of that before purchasing.

This game is so heart-wrenchingly surreal that it gets my physical heart to beat at key moments. Here's a little taste:
Day 17. I'm desperately low on food and the survivors are starving. I decide to raid a nearby house in the hopes of stockpiling food. Uponarriving, I find the jouse inhabited by two brothers and their elder parents. I sneak in through the back unnoticed. One of the brothers is about to walk through the door so I ascend to the second. Through the keyhole, I see an old woman come down from the attic and approach the door. I ready my knife and pray that she doesn't come any closer to the door. I don't want to kill her. She stops, idles for a moment in self pity, and then turns back around and enters a different room. I enter and scavenge for supplies when the same brother enters, causing me to hide. He finds the place suspicious and approaches my hiding place. I panic and lunge at him from hiding. He dies noisily, and his brother hears. He runs to apprehend me, but he is unarmed. I dispatch him quickly. The old mother hears and comes down. She sees one of her dead sons and weeps above him. I pause before her as I realize what I've done to them. She cries as she says their names. In one final act of pity, I kill her where she kneels. I loot the rest of the house and escape to my shelter, food in tow. The father, out of earshot to it all and asleep, I've left to awaken to the massacre.
This game touches me so deeply that these actions of mine caused me to ask myself, "what if this was a choice that I couldn't just hit the resatrt button to?" Then I realized: that question is the game.

If your expectation of this game is not to do much overall, you will surely be a happy customer like most people that like this game. Build a couple of items in a day, maybe eat, sleep rotation and wait to see if someone knocks at your door - this is an in depth summary of your day. During the night you will scavenge for items. You will do your best to avoid other people, but this isn't a stealth game. Sometimes you will fight, but there is no fighting mechanic at all to make that interesting either. You will bring stuff back to your house - this was an in depth summary of every night you will play.
People you meet have one liner dialogues in a loop and add nothing to the story. Information you find is equally inconsequencial. The people you meet at your door are totally random and you won't be seeing them again. There is no sense that something bigger than your group is operating outside despite having a radio which has nothing of use to say other than flavourless text. The locations you scavenge do little to add to the story, your experience or your interest. There is no world economy or society functioning in the background (which technically, in all wars, these two elements keep functioning unless everyone is dead).
If this is supposed to be a game to make us aware that war is horrible it does so in a very "light" way. Yes people are bored, sad, hungry and tired but rarely will you be doing anything that feels important, stressful, linked to morals or truly atrocious. I met a Bosnia war survivor who saw a pregnant lady lose a leg to a mortor shell and witnessed people resorting to eating wood to survive - in comparison, this game shows that war is really an inconvienence more than anything else. Another thing: war torn cities have curfews with "shoot on sight" rules during the night since its harder to tell who's who, hence scavenging occurs mostly during daytime for civilians.
I don't normally slam games that cost 20$ but all the awards and the hype just created expectations that were painfully absent. I wanted to love this game but I really cannot understand how so many people seem to like playing such a boring game where most of its components exist in other games which are better made. I'm almost thinking that there must be fake accounts to write so many loving reviews that are so obviously exaggerated.

It's a fairly good game, entertaining enough so far. It seems to have fairly decent depth, the world seems moderately vibrant, the combat is complex (perhaps a tad much) and the animations and graphics are solid.
There's two big gripes I have with this game, one being a lack of aesthetically impactful design in terms of music. The music is bland and barely memorable. Not much more to be said for it.
The other gripe is that the game is a tremendously lazy port, to the point where all instructions show an Xbox controller button rather than a keyboard key. Rewriting the tutorials would've done wonders, but instead, players are forced to look up and perhaps even jot down all the important keys. This is particularly painful with the battle mechanism of critical calls, something akin to the action commands from Mario & Luigi and Paper Mario. The screen will show the A, B, Y and X buttons or the Right Trigger, and you're supposed to figure out what to press without any appropriate visual cue. (In case you're interested, it's the arrow keys for the A, B, Y and X buttons, and space bar for the Right Trigger)
Other than that, the game seems rather promising and I hope it will continue to deliver.

This game is not necessarily a waste of your time.  Since it's free you should definitely play it just for the story mode.  Wizard/Stainless had one job.  Make a collectible card game(a 'CCG', if you want a TCG play cardboard Magic or MTGO).  They have failed, by definition of CCG.
You can't collect all the cards from the Origins set, and they've said that future expansions won't include all the cards either.  I did not expect to have every Magic card ever made, that would be far more work than I would consider viable.
I expected, wanted desperately, to play Magic: The Gathering.  This is not Magic, you can tell because it doesn't have the cards you need.  They even have the gall to put cards into the single player campaign (which is pretty fun and close to real MTG) but not into circulation.  So it is not laziness on their part, it was a choice.  It is not a choice I can respect.  It is a choice meant to, I don't know.  Presumably usher you toward 'real' Magic.
Dear WotC, if I had the time and patience and money to play MTG, I would already be playing MTG.
So ultimately I suppose I am not the target demographic and it does not satisfy my needs nor was it intended to do so.  However, assuming they are going for newbies, well, play the tutorials and campaign and find out if Magic is for you.  If you stay with this program longer, you will come up against limitations within a week.

This game is so heart-wrenchingly surreal that it gets my physical heart to beat at key moments. Here's a little taste:
Day 17. I'm desperately low on food and the survivors are starving. I decide to raid a nearby house in the hopes of stockpiling food. Uponarriving, I find the jouse inhabited by two brothers and their elder parents. I sneak in through the back unnoticed. One of the brothers is about to walk through the door so I ascend to the second. Through the keyhole, I see an old woman come down from the attic and approach the door. I ready my knife and pray that she doesn't come any closer to the door. I don't want to kill her. She stops, idles for a moment in self pity, and then turns back around and enters a different room. I enter and scavenge for supplies when the same brother enters, causing me to hide. He finds the place suspicious and approaches my hiding place. I panic and lunge at him from hiding. He dies noisily, and his brother hears. He runs to apprehend me, but he is unarmed. I dispatch him quickly. The old mother hears and comes down. She sees one of her dead sons and weeps above him. I pause before her as I realize what I've done to them. She cries as she says their names. In one final act of pity, I kill her where she kneels. I loot the rest of the house and escape to my shelter, food in tow. The father, out of earshot to it all and asleep, I've left to awaken to the massacre.
This game touches me so deeply that these actions of mine caused me to ask myself, "what if this was a choice that I couldn't just hit the resatrt button to?" Then I realized: that question is the game.

With the 60+ hours, I have put into this was an incredible experience. I have 101% in my first playthrough and I'm thinking of replaying this game more times than I should have.
To start, you'd think that for a $15 game, you'd get around 15-20 hours if you're a completionist, but Hollow Knight feels more like a $60 game with the amount of content it provides. It feels like a 40-60 hour game if you want to go for 100%. Like videogamedunkey said, "That's what we call a masterpiece for your wallet".
The atmosphere is dark and gloomy. When you start the game, you get this sad tune featuring a viola and a piano in the main menu, which is just a beautiful score. You first stumble upon this deserted city which has only one bug living in this city, Elderbug. The story behind the city that is Dirtmouth is a tragic one as almost everyone but the Elderbug have gone down the well where there are creatures that can kill them. The start may sound a bit too dark for a game, but the game, in general, doesn't hammer in that darkness. There is just a finite amount of light-hearted moments and characters like Zote, the Dung Defender, and Cornifer while there is also a finite amount of serious characters like Hornet, Quirrel, and Tiso.
The presentation is outstanding for a game with a $40,000 budget that had been in development for 2 years. Each enemy and character has a different design. Some you may find cute like Booflys and Funglings. Others you may find disturbing like Corpse Creepers and Grub Mimics.
The mechanics are extremely tight. The combat is amazing. Consisting of a cast of 150+ enemies, about 30 of them are bosses, I love almost every one except for those at Deepnest. They're just 2spooky4me

This game is really kind of like a pizza without the crust to me. Lot's of delicious toppings, melted cheese, and yummy sauce but with nothing really holding them all together for you to fully enjoy them.
If you don't really want to read a long review, then this is a short and simple sentence that sums up Gat Out of Hell.
Buy it on sale.
Now if you are looking for a little more detail, welcome to the detail giving part of the review.
First off, what does Gat Out of Hell do right?
It is really fun. The characters are entertaining, it has some pretty comical dialouge at times, and seeing Shakespeare as a DJ was amusing. You get your powers fairly early on in the game, which is good since you most likely don't want to play through an entire game to get the powers you already unlocked in Saints Row 4.
The Blast and Stomp powers return from Saints Row 4, with different elements to use this time. You also get a new power that lets you summon minions to aid you in battle. They are all fun to use in combat and go well with the new guns you get to use.
Speaking of Guns, you get some pretty neat Hell based guns. The first real gun you get is the Lava Assault Rifle, which is great for getting headshots. You get some real world weapons from the Ultor corporation like a shotgun and machine gun. You also get some really unique weapons like the sloth weapon. A laz-e-boy chair you sit in and run around shooting gattling guns and firing missles.
Flying is a new feature in this game, and is pretty fun to play around with. It is done in a way that gives you a good bit of freedom while giving you some limits so you can't just fly away from your problems. (You are Johnny Gat, you don't fly around from problems, you stab them in the eye and kick them in the♥♥♥♥♥♥
What Gat Out of Hell does wrong.
Do you like doing side missions? Because you are going to do some side missions. You don't have to do them of course, you can just not beat the game. But if you do want to beat the game eventually, you are going to do some side missions.  They pretty much got rid of the traditional story mission format for a meter that shows how angry Satan is at you. You open with some storyish missions, but nothing like in previous games. I can't knock them for trying something new, but it really just doesn't work out that great in all honesty. Loyalty missions return but unlike Saints Row 4 they are just a group of side missions and you don't get super powered homies.
Your homies are gone as well, which really kind of disappointed me. I kind of loved listening to the different characters interact with each other, in Gat Out of Hell though they are in the opening cut scene and in one or two endings. You get some help from Shakespeare, Vlad, Blackbeard, and the Twins from Saints Row 3, but they don't really interact that much with well.. anyone really. They have some dialouge with you but nothing that is really completely interesting.
Customization is completely gone too, and that really kind of sucks. I can understand not being able to change their physical features, but I would have enjoyed changing their clothes or at least the looks of the guns. The thought of Kenzie killing demons dressed up all bdsm mistress like seems kind of fun and like something that would have included.
The last thing I will go into is that Johnny and Kenzie really are not that interesting on their own. Gat and the boss were a massacre when together. Kenzie and the boss were humerious with their exchanges, but on their own I really can't get that into them. It's not bad writing or anything, it is just the characters themself.
Remember the time I said "The last thing"? Yeah I changed my mind, you get another! The endings were all kind of empty. They are like midgame cutscenes without the game to follow. Only one really feels like a definitive ending, but really felt like it could have had a little bit more.
Oh, and also Carlos from Saints Row 2 wasn't a big part of anything in this game, and I was kinda hoping he would be like, an angelic ally or something. Not really good or bad, just a hope not realized.
Anyways, this is a fun game, but really not a 20 dollar fun game. If it is on sale for like, 10 or 5 dollars, definitly pick it up, but for 20 dollars I feel that there could have been more. I gave up a bottle of Baileys Irish Creme for this game and I'm not sure it was a worth while sacrifice.
So there you have it, a full review of Gat Out of Hell.

If your expectation of this game is not to do much overall, you will surely be a happy customer like most people that like this game. Build a couple of items in a day, maybe eat, sleep rotation and wait to see if someone knocks at your door - this is an in depth summary of your day. During the night you will scavenge for items. You will do your best to avoid other people, but this isn't a stealth game. Sometimes you will fight, but there is no fighting mechanic at all to make that interesting either. You will bring stuff back to your house - this was an in depth summary of every night you will play.
People you meet have one liner dialogues in a loop and add nothing to the story. Information you find is equally inconsequencial. The people you meet at your door are totally random and you won't be seeing them again. There is no sense that something bigger than your group is operating outside despite having a radio which has nothing of use to say other than flavourless text. The locations you scavenge do little to add to the story, your experience or your interest. There is no world economy or society functioning in the background (which technically, in all wars, these two elements keep functioning unless everyone is dead).
If this is supposed to be a game to make us aware that war is horrible it does so in a very "light" way. Yes people are bored, sad, hungry and tired but rarely will you be doing anything that feels important, stressful, linked to morals or truly atrocious. I met a Bosnia war survivor who saw a pregnant lady lose a leg to a mortor shell and witnessed people resorting to eating wood to survive - in comparison, this game shows that war is really an inconvienence more than anything else. Another thing: war torn cities have curfews with "shoot on sight" rules during the night since its harder to tell who's who, hence scavenging occurs mostly during daytime for civilians.
I don't normally slam games that cost 20$ but all the awards and the hype just created expectations that were painfully absent. I wanted to love this game but I really cannot understand how so many people seem to like playing such a boring game where most of its components exist in other games which are better made. I'm almost thinking that there must be fake accounts to write so many loving reviews that are so obviously exaggerated.

As of late October 2015, I am
unable to 100% complete the game thanks to a glitch preventing me from completing one of the Torment Fraud exercises.
Let's get one thing out of the way right now: for every positive thing this game boasts, there's also something negative that detracts from the experience. Though you may like something as a hardcore Saints Row fan, you will be unable to deny that there's something that turns you off to it. If you don't want to read everything, I've been so kind as to add a little 'TL;DR' at the bottom so that people can scroll to the end or Ctrl+F their way to it. So... let's start with:
• First off, being able to explore an entirely new overworld in the form of New Hades is amazing and much more refreshing than Steelport from Saints Row 3 and 4. It gives the game an entirely new feeling, making it stand out much more on its own, and gives you so much more to explore and discover.
• Another great thing is the powers; yes, you have some rehashed abilities from SR4 and that's to be expected, but they all have their own unique flair. I loved being able to summon a Titan against one of Satan's archdukes, or surrounding myself in a heavenly glow that made all the demons of Hell bow in reverence... and gave me a massive damage boost.
• Free-form flight is something I would've absolutely loved in SR4, and just the ability to soar through the sky dodging missiles and going through narrow passages in this game is euphoric for lack of a better word. Being able to jump multiple times in the air helps you keep better control, and just being able to descend for extra momentum during flights to preserve your 'flap' meter gives an even better sense of speed than super-sprinting or driving in cars.
• Moving right along, the weapon selection is both creative and phenomenal. Being able to get seven different weapons that correspond to the seven deadly sins is definitely a nice spin on the more traditional SR formula where you just pick a weapon or two that you really like (
) and upgrade it to its maximum potential. Each weapon brings something funny and new to the table without seeming like a blatant rehash.
• Finally, the story is fun and inventive, and it throws a few curveballs your way that you really don't expect part of the way through. I was flabbergasted when Satan, Jezebel, and even Kinzie and Johnny busted out in a full-blown Disney-esque musical.
Unfortunately, all that glitters is not gold, as they say. And as I said above, every silver lining in the sky is only overshadowed by the little thundercloud waiting to rain on your parade. Here come...
• The overworld, for all its new luster and polish, is pretty scant once you get rid of all the collectibles. It is as you would expect Hell to be: it's barren and full of fire in most places, and being able to fly over the map at top speeds really shows you how small it is by comparison. Granted, I was as annoyed as anyone in Saints Row 3 and 4 by Steelport being three kilometers across or so end-to-end, but with your many power-ups and weapons, there was always a creative way to travel (
); with this game, you're flying everywhere at top speeds almost immediately.
• Speaking of powers, if you're quick about it, you can get all the powers and a fair number of the upgrades and elements for them in less than the first hour. In SR4, I don't recall getting the Buff power until the start of the game's third act. It added longevity to the game, making you
to keep playing to fully upgrade yourself. Having access to the most powerful abilities in the game practically by default, I might as well be playing SR4 still.
• Flight in this game, for as fun as it is, can be
hard to grasp and sometimes very finicky. I can be flying along without a care in the world, hit something I didn't see immediately and either perform a wall-run for some reason (
) or careen into it and shoot upward, losing all momentum and control for a few seconds. Without the "Flight - Nimble" power-up, you're going to find maneuvering very hard for the first hour or two of your adventure.
• Some of the weapons in the game quickly lose their fun factor after a little while, and there's going to be a lot of shooting in this game... after all, it's a Saints Row game and you're playing as Johnny Gat, who can only be described properly as 'trigger-happy' and 'murderous'. While it may be gratifying to kill enemies with the Diamond Sting weapon and collect all the money drops with your Vacuum Stomp power, it starts to become
. Most times, I find myself going to a Sinterpol store and switching out for my less powerful weapons like the Energy Caster and the Damned Impaler just to challenge myself further. You're already in Hell; dying literally has no consequence in this game aside from a few thousand currency units from your pocket... oh, and if you're looking for customization beyond choosing between Johnny and Kinzie and deciding what seven weapons you want to carry around, go back to the previous installments—Gat Out Of Hell boasts a total of ten stores, and they're all weapon shops... or rather, weapon vending machines. If you're looking for character customization in any form, please go back to Saints Row 3 or 4.
• Finally, and it pains me to say this... the story is just so damn short. I thought I had so much more left to do, but by the time I actually got to Satan, I was less than four hours into the game! For a $20 USD title, I was kind of expecting at least double that, especially when the last game incorporated all sorts of side activities in their loyalty missions. In this game, however, all you do is: get buddy-buddy with people like William Shakespeare and Vlad the Impaler, go on one loyalty mission for each of your five new friends, save them from ritual sacrifice by a few Dark Inciters (
), and then go shoot Satan in the face with RPG rounds... I beat the game in less than four hours, and I was taking a leisurely stroll through the entire game.
Personally, because I liked the last two games so much, I paid full price and pre-ordered the game in hopes for getting something more than I did. Does that mean I didn't enjoy it? ♥♥♥♥ no, it's phenomenal... but the problem is that I don't feel right calling this a "game" when it feels like glorified DLC at best. The pre-order rewards were absolutely not worth it, either, as I rarely found myself using Yorick (
) to fight enemies when it was constantly overheating, and the Saints wing skin is a pretty lackluster change even by cosmetic standards. Enemies and their overall typings in the game suffer the same problems as they did in SR4, and beating the game is the worst part because there's little else to do after you're done and have collected all seven deadly weapons... the worst of which is tied between the 'Boom Chicka' and the 'Armchair-A-Geddon'.
Is this game as good as previous installments in terms of gameplay? Yes, as there are a few new spins on familiar side missions that will occupy your time for a few hours, and the story is captivating if leaning heavily on the 'short' side.
Is this game as good as previous installments in terms of content? Gat Out Of Hell is to Saints Row 4 what SR:TT was to SR2—all you're really getting is a graphical overhaul with no real changes to the core mechanics.
Should you buy this game? If you're a die-hard Saints Row fan, yes... but even then, I would recommend waiting until a substantial (≥25%) price drop.

NASCAR Heat 2..
How much closer to a blessing could we get?
Not sure, but In comparison to recent years of NASCAR licensed games, this is a major step forward.
My opinion is this: I love the game, and I play it all the time. Sure, it has it's little issues, and wonky cautions but it's a playable NASCAR game that makes you feel like you're really doing it. I have a blast playing by myself in the new (and super mega awesome) career mode and online with my friends. I'd recommend this game to anyone interested in getting a recent NASCAR game that is worth buying.
Here are my cons:
-The AI online WILL NOT HESITATE to race as the same driver as you and it can be a bit aggravating
-There is no countdown given as to when a "challenge" starts so you can be blindly thrown into a corner and randomly lose AI control and have no chance
-You are forced to use your gamertag in career mode and on single player leaderboards and as someone who enjoys feeling like I'm racing with the pros, I'd like the option to use my name in single player.
-No burnouts after victory, all I want to do after I win is celebrate, and jumping around my room doesn't cut it. I'd like the option to do a burnout in singleplayer at least
-NO FULL PAINT BOOTH! PLEASE GIVE US FULL CUSTOMIZABILITY!
-Not much setting/option customizability as in cosmetics like sounds and music, no biggie though
-No onboard online chat, this could be good or bad, I'd like to see it implemented
-The spotter isn't helpful, he clears one lane lower than you are, maybe this isn't a problem for most but it's small for me.
-If I get offered a Hot Seat, and "race later" then come back..later.. the car/team changes, which is sorta strange.
MY PROS:
-This is definitely playable
-The cautions were acknowledged, and somewhat fixed.
-The addition of the Truck Series and the Xfinity Series make the game
-AI can give challenge, which makes career mode very fun
-the career mode overhaul was absolutely wonderful, the best career mode I've played. Ask about my PS2 game collection.
-There is so much room for improvement that it makes me excited for the next game.
-If I get mad while playing, it's not at the game but at myself and that's a sign of a good game.
Most of the cons are small, little things that only stand out because the rest of the game is very well done. This is a major improvement for 704 Games and it is well-earned. if you want a NASCAR game that is casual, and will allow you to have a bunch of fun, NASCAR Heat 2 is your best option right now, that is if you can't buy Dirt To Daytona. haha.

Very easy game and I am putting down a recipe for scones once you've finished this game.
INGREDIENTS:
225g/8oz Self Raising Flour
150ml/¼ pint Milk (approx)
Pinch Salt
25g/1oz Caster Sugar
25g/1oz Margarine
METHOD:
Sieve flour and salt into a bowl, stir in sugar, if used.
Rub in margarine.
Add sufficient milk to make a soft dough.
Turn onto a floured board and gently knead to remove any cracks.
Roll out lightly to 1” in thickness. Cut into scones with a cutter dipped in flour.
Place on a floured pre-heated baking sheet/tray, glaze if liked with beaten egg or milk.
Bake in a pre-heated oven 425°F/220°C/Gas 8 on upper shelf position for 10 mins. approx .
Cool on a wire tray.

To clarify a few things people have incorrectly stated in whingy negative reviews;
- If you buy the game for $20 before it becomes free to play, you will have access to all the heroes forever. You do not have to unlock them individually with ingame currency.
- If you play the game free to play (during this free weekend or once it becomes free to play) you will NOT have access to all heroes and will have to unlock them individually (I believe you can do this with real money too).
There are microtransactions for cosmetic items even if you buy the game for $20, but this isn't really unusual these days. (Overwatch, Siege, CS:GO, etc) - and you can unlock all the cosmetic items without spending any money if you play enough.

Comming From the Xbox 360 Version, this game has undone some extreame polish for PC since it's release. i've endured the major issues with the console version of this game from start to finish, and have recently moved to the PC version because of it's much needed updates.
This is an outstanding game. Using the best of SAGA character development, an innovative combat engine modeled off of squad tactics, but with each character being individualy accounted for (if they are the one attacked, thier chance to dodge is what matters, but formations and current tactics effect who is at risk) an intruiging and well told plot (note, "side" quest are essential to experience the majority of it), outstanding graphics (as played on a PC), and most of all, constantly fun.
There is something of a steep curve to get good at combat, and if you do not wrap your mind around it, it may seem random, but it isn't very random at all, and a keen understanding of pre fighting tactical choices (setup) and in combat tactical choices is essential to beat any of the major monsters from about the first 1/5 of the game on. fortunately there are numerious (really unlimited) fights with lesser monsters, and so equally limited (or not) chances to experament.
Worth playing by all rpg fans, this manages to be unique and present some experamental ideas with polish and mechanical balance that makes it seem like a much more mature project. on a side note, many reviewers were turned off by the combat engine. I suspect this came from not indulging enough in the gameplay, it is not a standard console rpg, mechanically, and one should not expect to succeed without some new ways of thinking. That said, it is something that the rpg (jrpg especially) market really needs. LR's combat engine is also important as a story telling device, because it is not the story of a few super heroes, but rather of a world war, and the player controls an army. The combat engine allows the player to quickly, elligantly, with simple menu choices and just a few buttons, control a small army of 36 unit (6-10 squads if mem serves), and fight even larger ones, as well as fascilitates massive bosses attacked by your army. For instance, your army fighting a dragon and its horde of followers, in one large battle.
So far, no J-styled rpg has greatly surpased the techniques used in the earliest FF games, a big fight as described above would just be your 1 squad fighting a series of battles without a break, followed finally by the big bad, and *maybe* letting you fight the big bad with more than one squad. Games which have used engines to deliver more, have been too convoluted for simple menu based play. LR manages to be simple to control, fun to think about (as a tactical puzzle, which is the big draw of JRPG combat) and delivers a constantly rewarding and enthralling experience.
In spite of a few small flaws, LR remains a well designed and built game, consnstantly fun and hcallenging, and truly innovative and worth the time of any player looking for a brilliant new idea

This is how my experience with Bioshock Remastered went whilst I was doing an achievement run (trying to get them all in one playthrough like I did on the original Bioshock 2): I started a game on Hard, and it crashed when I looted the first Splicer, resetting all of my settings and forcing me to restart the game and watch all of the cutscenes again. I then started a new game on Hard and got all of the audio diaries and tonics on Medical Pavilion, and it crashed just before I fought Steinman, erasing my quicksaves, settings, and forcing me to reload my autosave at the beginning of Medical Pavillion. I then proceeded to get all of the audio diaries and tonics on Medical Pavilion again and reached Neptune's Bounty, only to realize that the game had for some reason changed the difficulty of my playthrough to Medium after loading the autosave, rather than Hard (thereby forfeiting my ability to get the 'Beat the game on Hard' achievement for the playthrough). I then restarted the game completely on Hard, raced through Medical Pavilion again while getting all of the audio diaries and tonics, and was 1 room away from reaching the bathysphere to the next level before it crashed on me again. Once again my quicksaves were erased, my settings were reset, and the only thing available was an autosave that put me back to the beginning of Medical Pavillion (on Normal rather than Hard once again). Fortunately this time I had backed up a copy of the quicksave file that had the vast majority of Medical Pavilion on Hard complete, and I proceeded to replace the current file with it. However, this didn't work, and the game still only recognized my autosave.
And like many others have reported, the game consistently had major freezes/stutters, audio glitches (skipping and repeating), props occasionally disappearing and reappearing, and terrible mouse acceleration.
Thus I can safely conclude that Bioshock Remastered is currently unplayable. DO NOT buy this game (or even try to install it if you were given it for free) until 2K releases some solid crash and stability fixes for the game.

Ahh, Bioshock....hello old friend.  You're looking well.  Seriously, you haven't aged a day and if I'm not mistaken your resolution is looking particularly fit.  You always were the best aquatic-based steampunk game. Hell, you're the only one of those games that I can think of. What's more, your action rpg elements ensure that players will have plenty to do as this dark  journey takes them ever closer to Andrew Ryan and a rather morbid revelation of sorts.  Furthermore, the recorders collected throughout the game really add depth to the story as they often reveal the twisted, intricate plot details as both the story and the very foundation of Rapture itself unravels.
Alas, the remastered version, though better than the original, is not without issues.  My personal experience with this game was for the most part exceptional in that I only suffered several crashes and a bizarre glitch that apparently caused the game to be set to normal difficulty when I had clearly selected the hardest setting from the outset - throughout the game the damage inflicted on enemies and caused by the same appeared to be the higher difficulty setting but it was only after beating the game and not unlocking the difficulty level associated achievements I was expecting to unlock that I realized there was an issue. Solution: reload the final battle, confirm that the game was for some reason stuck on normal, reset it to survival, and proceed to unlock the achievements I should have already unlocked.
Those things aside, Bioshock still remains one of the greatest/most important game series to date and shouldn't be passed up by any gamer that's a fan of shooters with a hearty dose of action rpg elements and even a touch of sci-fi horror as garnish. There are apparently some fixes in the works for those suffering major issues, so hang tight and have fun when you finally do get around to playing this modern classic.
