Saints Row Gat out of Hell is a standalone DLC for saints row 4 featuring Gat and Kinzie as playable characters. Game’s main length is around 3-5 hours long and full completion is 10+
+Audio logs are nice way to flesh out allies
-Princess of Satan feels underused (more missions would have helped)
Satan has taken the president’s soul and it’s up to Gat and Kinzie to bring him back home. Hell is full of disgruntled citizens, a promising avenue to recruit new allies for the confrontation against Satan, and his armies. Your allies all have hidden motivations to fight against Satan that is revealed as you discover tapes scattered throughout hell
+Doing what you want advances the story
+Repeatable last mission (Ability to watch all endings without loading)
-Only 2 main missions that feel unique (Operation Rescue + Defeat Satan)
The gauge has two events that trigger before the final confrontation. The first one being anti-air spires planted around the city to shoot you out of the sky. The second involves freeing the allies you gained throughout the story. There are multiple endings to pick from once defeating Satan in the final confrontation, since the boss is repeatable, seeing all endings is possible, without loading a previous save or restarting the game.
+Abilities to increase time needed in activity is handy
+Flying is fun without being too difficult
The side missions are fun just like the previous saint row games. They range from murder with powers, collecting souls by flying into them before they disappear into the air, throwing yourself into cars, and more murder with weapons until you survive all the waves.
There were minor cosmetic done to the side missions that separate it from the previous games for example instead of fraud being paid in money its been substituted by years.
The missions that put your powers to the test, gained throughout Saints Row 4, have returned as alter missions that you can find throughout the city, to unlock further elements.
+CO-OP still fun to play with friends!
The achievements in this game don’t require you to do the online profile thing which means getting 100% is a lot easier now, especially with CO-OP since the only achievement I saw requiring it was the 3 hour one.
Note: You play as the opposite character of whoever your friend picks.
+7 Deadly Sin Weapons are a treat to use
+Ability to upgrade weapons
-Customization is gone
The customization is gone the only cosmetic change you can really make is for people who have the alternate wings from the pre-order dlc.
The 7 deadly sin weapons are great fun to use and I do enjoy how diverse they are in both manner and execution similar to how creative previous saints row games have been with their weapons. Having jackpot weapons that explode enemies into gold is great fun and while I would rant more about the other weapons I’ll leave it up to you to discover them :)
The ability to upgrade weapons in various ways is still here. I tend to upgrade clip size even though I got the infinity ammo perks which made… that completely pointless (I never claimed I was smart!)
+Abilities are complimentary and worth to switch back and forth from.
+Summons have replaced calling up allies
-Losing the ability to fight alongside your new allies
-There are two less abilities than previous game (SR 4)
The abilities this time around in my experience feels like they compliment each other alot better. For example I can summon a titan that likes to charge enemies while i switch to stone spell and cast it on enemies for him to break into rubble. Another example is using stampade to vacuum up enemies while you have vamp drain active which drains enemies that are close to you. Due to the vacuum element of stampede this allows me to get enemies within range and clustered up for maximum effect supposing they don’t die.
Removing the ability to call up homies is the biggest con in the game. Being able to call on homies you unlocked throughout your journey was always fun in other saint row games. Considering you have new allies like shakespeare and Vlad the impaler it would have been interesting to fight alongside them. Summoning unlike calling homies doesn't require menu navigation and flows better.
There is two less abilities in this game than the previous one. If they are in the game I must have missed them (98% of game done) and I am only missing Kill X with Y powers/guns and some souls to collect. They could patch in either new powers or sell them as DLC we will see what happens in the future.
+Fresh Setting: Hell (allows for some interesting cosmetic choices)
-Where the physical barriers are can be misleading at times
The game looks very fresh and different from the other saints rows considering the setting and all it allowed for some interesting cosmetic changes. I believe its map design is structured after steelport (and mentioned in the game as looking similar in that sense) though I could be wrong. It looks different enough as a result of the setting to not feel like a clone.
The physical barriers can be quite misleading at times, what i mean by this is when i shoot at a enemy and I thought i aimed far away enough from a spire for example it still gets blocked magically. Other times I would be above a hole and go a bit closer and fall through the metal floor.
Note: Cars look horrible and explode randomly after curving off into buildings - awesome
+Flying is a vast improvement over gliding
Navigation in Saints Row 4 focused super speed and gliding while Gat out of Hell switched up gliding for a pair of wings. One would think that it would only be a small improvement but since it was designed with momentum in mind and upgrade abilities its actually pretty big improvement over gliding. It feels more rapid and exciting especially to fly down from great heights or flapping your wings to gain speed and maneuver around buildings at a rapid pace. It’s also quite fun to shoot down those pesky Spire missiles that home-in on you.
+Collecting souls for skills
+Stacked data is replaced by a mini-game of grabbing a series of souls quickly (4-5)
+Commentary collectibles for both characters (Adds amusement/personality)
+Finding Glyphs unlocks treasure chests
There are 5 audio logs per ally that you can obtain in order to understand their motivations for helping you. There is also audio logs that Satan himself personally records that you can collect. The commentary for the two playable characters is spread out throughout the map in key points to comment about their surroundings.
Collecting 3 glyphs per distract allows you to open a chest for nice soul rewards and a weapon once you finish getting them all. The souls you collect throughout the city are useful for upgrading your powers.
Instead of grabbing stacked data like in saints row 4, you have to grab a series of souls after initiating the mini-game by touching the big glowy soul in the sky that is pointing at the direction it will launch the souls to. So it’s best to be facing that way whenever you plan to win them since they are TIMED.
Saints Row: Gat Out of Hell is alot of over the top fun with a variety of creative weapons and some laughs here and there at the absurdity of it all. I recommend getting this game if you're a fan of Saints Row the 4th.

The Hitman series has continually challenged players with tracking and assassinating various targets across the world, while providing multiple routes in which to accomplish the particular tasks at hand. Absolution marks the first true entry in the current generation of games built upon its powerful, in-house built Glacier 2 graphics engine. In addition, the gameplay has been altered with the introduction of new features associated with the Instinct and Contracts modes.
Set directly after the events of the previous game, Hitman: Blood Money, Absolution tasks Agent 47 with tracking down his series handler Diana Burnwood after she goes rogue and reveals the agency's identity to the public. The new Agency director Benjamin Travis orders Agent 47 to kill Diana and capture a teenage girl by the name of Victoria that has been under her care. Upon reading a letter left from Diana, the narrative spirals into a chaotic set of events interwoven with Agent 47 being hunted by both the police and a cast of villains that aim to capture the mysterious Victoria from him. The majority of levels are set in various exterior and interior locales in Chicago and a small town in South Dakota.
A major contrast from past games in the series is the addition of entire level sequences that focus on evading the police while reaching a designated exit. In these particular sequences, players aren't even provided with particular targets to assassinate that results in the gameplay resembling a generic shooter versus a Hitman game. Some sections feel eerily similar to the gameplay of IO Interactive's past Kane and Lynch series of games. The levels that do offer particular targets to assassinate and multiple routes in which to accomplish that task are the most memorable of the narrative and beg for multiple playthroughs.
Each playthrough of a level is continually scored based on each action taken by the player from killing civilians to being detected by patrolling enemies. The game has a way in which it wants the player to complete each level and any deviations result in the loss of points. Compared with recent games in the Hitman series, Absolution includes far too many linear paths and evade the police scenarios that result in an overall more restrictive experience.
The major change in the Hitman gameplay formula in Absolution revolves around the addition of the Instinct mode. Instinct in the game is displayed through a meter that regenerates overtime through various actions taken. There are a variety of uses that involve Instinct mode from scanning the environment for enemies and their movement, which is similar to the detective mode in Batman Arkham Asylum, to a quick shot kill system, which is similar to the mark and execute feature in Splinter Cell: Conviction. While both are not original concepts, they work exceptionally well in surveying the environment and when in difficult situations that require a quick takedown of multiple enemies.
The major aspect of Instinct mode that will cause some frustration with players is how it handles disguises. NPCs in the game can detect that the player is lying about their identity if wearing the same disguise, with the example that other police officers would be able to spot someone new in their ranks. To counter this, Agent 47 can either wear disguises that aren't of the same group of NPCs or use Instinct mode to hide their true identity. Unfortunately, Instinct mode when used for disguises drains at an alarmingly quick rate that makes it useful for only brief scenarios. In later levels, disguises feel completely useless when nearly all of the NPCs are of the same group and can quickly discover Agent 47.
Aside from the new Instinct mode and cover system, nearly all of the Hitman series basics return with the infamous fiber wire and dual Silverballer pistols. Along with a host of other weaponry from pistols and shotguns to rifles and explosives, Agent 47 has the ability to utilize various weapons and staged accidents located throughout levels. Makeshift weapons appear in the form of small objects like knives, hammers, and even bongs. While some of them aren't the most practical to use in combat situations, they serve as great alternatives to when a more specialized approach is required for a certain situation.
Following with the tradition of past games in the series, Agent 47 has the ability to utilize conveniently-placed staged accidents around the level that range from a hoisted car on a lift to food items that are ripe for poisoning. While some staged accidents are simple to put in motion, others require carefully-planned timing and execution to perform the perfect assassination. Absolution stays true to the Hitman series by continually providing players with a near endless amount of options in assassinating targets from going completely Rambo style to a more subtle approach with a knife stab in the back.
Levels completed in the campaign mode can later be played through in the Contracts mode that has players setting their own targets and selecting loadouts of unlocked disguises/weapons. The points earned in the both modes can be used to unlock additional disguises, weapons, and gun modifications ranging from silencers to extended clips. Contracts mode introduces the Hitman series first online feature in that the scenarios that players devise can be uploaded online for others to download and play. When creating a custom contract, players walk through a level and assassinate whom they wish and with what disguise and weapon they feel is right for the particular task. When the target eliminated, players then rush to an exit point to complete the level. With the level complete and statistics tracked for the time taken for both assassinating the target and reaching the exit, players can then proceed with uploading the contract for other players to compete in beating their score. Players that use the particular disguise and weapon that the creator did in their original playthrough will earn additional points when completing the contract.
Contracts mode seems to be the developer's answer to the restrictive campaign levels and escape from the police sections. The Contracts mode is clearly not the perfect solution for fans that were looking for similar gameplay from the previous Hitman game, but it's a step in the right direction considering that players can select their own disguise and weapon loadout. Contracts mode will be interesting to watch as more players upload their specialized combination of levels, targets, disguises, and weapon loadouts.
IO Interactive's Glacier 2 engine can be summarized with 1 word: stunning. From the massively-rendered crowds to the detailed interior/exterior environments, Absolution never ceases to amaze with visuals that beg to be set to max. Absolution debuts as the first real entry of the Hitman series in the high-definition era of gaming and succeeds at trumping nearly all of the current game releases. The sound effects and most notably the music succeed at impressing with loud and bold gunfire and mesmerizing classical scores. The soundtrack composed by Thomas Bärtschi fits the atmosphere of Absolution perfectly whether it may be a hectic gun battle or silent takedown.
Absolution marks a bold new direction for the Hitman series that focuses less on player freedom and more on telling a defined narrative. While the levels and poorly-implemented Instinct mode are sure to anger and frustrate fans of the series, Absolution still succeeds at providing an entertaining and most importantly, engaging gameplay experience that is difficult to put down until the credits roll. Both the expansive Contracts mode and stunning graphical overhaul help in overcoming the issues associated with the restrictive campaign levels.

I always felt like there I was making progress and combing over the map for locations I had missed or places I could use new abilities in was highly rewarding. Every boss fight was easy to learn but difficult to master and usually took me multiple attempts without feeling like I was being killed unfairly.

If you enjoy Super Smash Bros. you'll like Rivals of Aether.
Created by the same person who made Super Smash Land, a free PC fan-made Smash game, Rivals of Aether is a fast-paced fighter that adopts the Smash Bros. formula. Play as 8 different characters, each with their own very unique set of play styles. Fight it out with up to 4 players, smacking each other around until one gains victory.
If the normal fighting isn't enough for you, well this game also has a Story Mode! Dwell into the lore o fthe Rivals of Aether story and learn more about the characters.
There's also an Abyss Mode, where you get put into many different trials that require you to complete in order to set on into the next wave. Level up your characters and give them over powered skills that'll make Abyss Mode more fun and exciting.
New to the game? Well the Tutorial will help you get started,  not only does it teach to the common core basics of the Smash Bros. formula, but also teaches you advanced skills that the pros use such as teching and wavedashing.
Simply put: A game for casual players to have some fun. Exciting and intense for the competitive players.
The achievements in this game aren't especially hard to get. There's some that require you to KO opponents using specific moves, but most of them you'll get by playing the Story Mode, there are some Tutorial achievements and some Abyss achievements. Don't think this will be an easy trip though, there's an achievement that requires you to basically git gud in Story Mode by getting Gold Medals on all the different Story Modes.

First off, I think this game is excellent and the visuals are amazing, especially for a game that isn't exactly new.
Problem is this release is buggy as hell. I was having the same problems with constant crashing that everyone else with a 64 bit OS was having until I ran the game in 'Windows Vista Service Pack 1' compatability mode, which solved the problem.
But the big thing that stopped me from being able to finish the game was the framerate. I did alot of research around the forums and it seems that Crysis doesn't like newer hardware. I have a R9 390x and no matter how much tweaking of the graphics settings and config files I did I couldn't get the game to fully utilize my gpu, instead it would only use between one half and two thirds of its potential. This was with the CPU (Intel 3570K) at 50% utilization and the graphics card running at about 50 degrees Celcius (water cooled), so no CPU bottleneck and no need for clock speed throttling.
This caused the framerate to be all over the place now matter what graphics settings I had, from 10-60 fps, with VERY inconsistant frame times. I don't know whether AMD, the developer or steam are responsible but from my experience and many other cases I have read this game needs patching before it can be considered functional.
If you have similar hardware to me then I would be wary of this release, if you can get a refund I would recommend it as it will send a message to Valve that this game needs to be fixed. I would whole heartedly recommend this game if it was fixed.

This is a game about how far you are willing to go to survive in a war-zoned city.
You start out with 1-4 playable characters, each with their own set of skills. Your goal is to survive, how you do this is up to you. The game begins with you arriving at an abandoned building, and you have to clear out piles of rocks and locked doors to open up the house, this in turn gives you resources you can use to build different things like beds, chairs, ovens, workshops and so forth.
When the night arrives you have to venture out into the war filled city to scavenge for supplies where you will meet homeless people, or perhaps an elderly couple that is just trying to get by, do you steal their food? their medicine? and in turn leave them to their fate just so you can survive another day? There are also bandits, traders and people just trying to keep to themselves that will defend what is theirs.
You will also be visited by people that needs help, some children perhaps that needs medicine for their dying mom, do you give it to them and risk the chance of you not having enough for your own people, or do you turn them down? Your shelter will also get raided so you might want to put some people on guard duty during the nights unless you want to come back from your scavenging runs and all the food is gone.
How you survive is up to you, but be assured that your choices will have consequences for your group. My first playtrough took about 13 hours to finish and I thoroughly enjoyed every minute of it.

I normally don't enjoy games which tend to avoid combat, however "This War of Mine" has pulled it off in such an amazing way. The world really does pull you in, I love the encounters with the rebels or soldiers.
Some key points:
- Each play through is different, maps do change!
- A decent amount of events.
- Real sense of a post-apoc world.
- Loads of crafting! (Weapons, ammo, armour, household objects, medical supplies, food)
- Can't let your people die via starvation, health... they can even commit suicide if they become depressed (gain by killing innocent people, your people have decent morals).
Real fun game, still playing it now. Thought id take the time to write a decent review for it as I haven't been pulled into a game this much for a long time.

I have been playing Magic: The Gathering for the better part of 20 years.  I play casual Magic in real life very often, I am familiar with all the rules to a high degree and have played approximately 1000 online matches of the Duels of The Planeswalker games in years past.
Although it had some weird drawbacks--namely not being able to remove any unlocked cards from your deck--the first iteration of this game was awesome.  It got me back into the game: here was something that was easy to play, had a good mix of different card and deck types, and was just a really streamlined, accessible way to play casual M:tG games without having to get a group together and worry about deck balance.
The next two (or three, I forget how many now) were similarly excellent.  Rudimentary deck editing allowed seasoned players much greater control over how they played, and was a much more managable way for new players to learn the ins and outs of what makes or breaks a deck.
Magic 2015 and this new Duels have just taken huge strides backwards.  Forcing players to build their own decks without actually providing any information on why and how the old archetypes were constructed makes the gap between pros and newbs that much wider, and makes for a much more narrow metagame than previous years.  Add in the lack of extra modes, the inability to skip a patronizingly hand-holding tutorial for advanced players, and a cap on how much you can progress in the game ON YOUR OWN TIME to further encourage spending extra money on the game, and in my opinion you have the worst game Stainless has put out yet.
Obviously I haven't played it very much, and I may go back and slog through the intros to sink my teeth in a little deeper, but this game is exactly what no one was asking for.
"The ones who just don't get it are the ones who scream the loudest."  I've heard WotC say players have been clamoring for open-ended deck editing for years, so that's why these last two have looked like the did, but look what happened:  the worst sales and reviews of the series for two years straight.
WotC, Chris, whoever reads this, take note:  GIVE US BACK DUELS OF THE PLANESWALKERS.  Your company already offers platforms that meet the needs of people who want open-ended deck editing and microtransactions, what about those of us who, for three years in a row, happily paid $20US for a main game and also several expansions that allowed casual players a fair and streamlined platform for playing M:tG?
TL;DR - It's free so you might as well get it, and there's certainly fun to be had, but by comparison DotP:2014 is the cream of the crop, offering 21 different 100 card decks, 2HG and several other modes, and, if you buy it on Steam, unlimited modification options.

Shelter is a surprising delight of a game.
With aesthetics that bring you back to the days of your childhood storybooks, Shelter throws you into an unexpected frenzy of emotions.
In Shelter, you play as a mother badger trying to safely lead her pups through a vast and intense forest. You come to love these children programmed to you, and might even name them or manufacture little personalities for each of them. Either way, you become attached, only for the game to start throwing curve balls left and right.
You hear the screech of a bird of prey, the crackle of a forest fire, the roar of a raging river, and your heart starts racing. You know that the death of one of your beloveds is a possibility, and you will do all in your power to crush that possibility into the dust... Unfortunately, you are but one badger and not every badger-plan plays out as intended.
There's also one big KERBLAM in this game that you won't want to miss, so pick it up! Whether it's on sale or not, for $10 or less, this game is definitely worth the time and money. For about an hour or two, it'll suck you in for one heck of a ride.

I really wanted to like this game, and I do, but I can't play it anymore because of the little game-breaking bugs and "features" this game offers. I've put a good amount of time into it and have done multiple seasons in the career mode. The last race I did actually gave me one of the worst experiences I have ever had from a video game. Before I go into that I just want to say where this game is most successful...
Pros
- AI is fun to race against and gives a decent challenge (when up to speed). They could be a bit harder. 105 is fairly easy on some tracks to be honest. But the AI is also the weakest point which I will highlight in the Cons section.
- Lots of good tracks. I can feel every little bump and they are very nicely captured. I've been to many of the circuits and can say most of them are not far off.
- Graphics are fine. I don't really care about people who argue over graphics. It's a waste of breath. The overall style is simple and clean. Would definitely like to see some anti-aliasing and anisotropic filtering options though.
- Plenty o paint schemes and most drivers are in the game. Having the 3 series structure is nice, with each series feeling like has its own driving style.
- Physics and controls are manageable. They have some options to customize all of that. Overall, it fells like I'm driving a racecar. Enough said. Though I would like to see a bit more wheel support. A buddy of mine can't get his wheels to work. Force feedback is actually surprisingly good, so I am happy with that.
Cons
- The engine sounds like an 8-bit soundbyte from the 80's. Seriously? It's 2017.
- The driving physics were fine, but when i slam into another car with my 3,300 pound car, i expect some sort of reaction from them. The AI is unwreckable. They must be made of solid adamantium or something because they will not budge when they wreck you or when you try to wreck them. You'll always end up wrecking yourself so there's no point.
- AI is oblivious to you if you go about 5 mph slower than them. If they see a wreck, they will go plowing into it, head first, without even thinking about letting go of the gas. This makes it impossible to just have a simple spinout. I guess yellow means 'go faster' for the AI. Or maybe they wanted to make it more action packed. They might as well add explosions at this point.
- Freight Training is back from everyone's favorite nascar game: Nascar '15 (sarcasm). The AI gets some magic banana rocket boost when they take the low line behind you. If you even give them an inch, they will hit the nitrous button and plow through you. It is toned back from the other games, but I can feel it kick in, especially when I see that I'm catching the AI in front of me, yet I'm getting freight trained by AI that is going at least 10-20 mph faster than me. It's fairly difficult to run the low line because of this "feature".
- The Rival system is trash and has always been trash. I remember when they first announced it and I genuinely considered not buying this game. My experiences with rival systems in past nascar games were not pleasant. Even after the update that was supposed to fix it, I couldn't even race the AI because all they wanted to do was wreck me. I only wrecked one or two people in about half a season on accident and I managed to make the entire nascar roster hate me. They are just programmed to leave you no room on the track and even sacrifice a win just to be annoying to you. It's the laziest programming I've ever seen. Also, don't bump draft them because that really pisses them off. Hell, just being in their vicinity pisses them off. If I had known how bad this rival system was gonna be, I would have saved my $50. It ruins career mode for me. I mean c'mon, rubbin is racin.
- The cautions are my least favorite part about this game. They don't seem to come out when you need them to, even the strict yellows. The last race I did, I ended up going from 2nd to 40th on the last lap because the flag twirler was picking his nose for 20 seconds before he heard explosions in the distance as I was getting gang banged by 3 different rivals at the same time. Normally, it takes anywhere from 3-5 seconds for the caution to come out, but it actually took around 17 seconds from the time I was sideways (I timed the game footage after I watched the replay). So the game waited for me to be in last to call the race. It almost brought tears to my eyes because of how beautifly choreographed it was. It was almost as good as real nascar. The best part was that i plowed into everyone in the field and I was thinking "Oh this is the Big One". But whoops, I was the only one wrecking while the AI kept it straight at full speed.
I really don't want to hate on the devs but there's so many little problems that add up to be game breaking. Some of them are simple fixes, like the draft cutting out randomly at Daytona/Talladega. There's plenty of other things that i reframed from saying in the cons section which I did because I really don't want to talk about this game anymore. Unless there's a massive overhaul of the AI and Career mode in this game, I won't be playing it anytime soon. So, for now, it's a thumbs down.

8 stars out of 10. This is a huge improvement over the previous iteration from this company.  It still feels game-y and there is some further improvement to be had, but it is much more enjoyable.  704 seems to be listening to us fans and trying to make a better game for us.
If 704 sees this, my only gripes right now are that Hot Seat races aren't skippable.  I prefer running the truck series, I don't wish to be forced into running an Xfinity race, I wish to see this as an option for those of us who wish to make a career in either of the two lower series.
The AI are vastly improved over Heat Evolution.  They don't rubberband like the did when you made an impressive pass in Heat Evolution, but they do seem to not give as much as they take.  For example, if you get a little loose on the inside and dive down onto the apron a little, they will move down into the lower groove and you will have no way to get back in line if you save it.
Plate racing is also improved and it is very difficult for a car to break away from the pack, player or AI.  The experience I've had on normal difficulty so far is very enjoyable.  I'm qualifying in the middle-front of the field with 5 star equipment and having to work to get to the front.  It's not cake, but its not starting dead last like Heat Evolution.  Even 4 star and 3 star equipment is competitive if you drive it right, though expect to qualify closer to the back, realistically.
I would like to see more customizability in the Customs Cars, maybe shapes placement like some of the late 2000s games. More sponsors and numbers would be nice, but licensing is an understandable difficulty.  Also, crew firesuits do not change color with vehicle color options, I think that would make a nice addition.
Over all, I will give this game an 8 out of 10 where Heat Evolution only got 4 out of 10. Keep Trucking 704!

I'm going to open this review with an analogy. Gat out of Hell is like the Weezer album "Make Believe". It's sell-out pop garbage and you're sitting there wondering what is happening to your favorite band, but all I'm thinking is: 'Well...The Green Album wasn't great either. I can't say that I'm surprised."
...Ehh..Okay that doesn't really work. I don't listen to Weezer.
Here's a much better analogy: Gat out of Hell is the equivalent of sneezing so hard that you crap your pants.
Look, I'm not critical of Saints Row because I get paid off by Rockstar, I do it because I'm passionate about the series. I've been here since the beginning, the demo for Saints Row 1 being the first game I played on my brand new Xbox 360. Even though I don't like Saints Row 4, I still applaud Volition for its success, they deserve it. However, it seems like no matter how low I set my expectations, Volition/Deep Silver have to find ways to disappoint me. Saints Row $: Gat out of Hell 44 1/4: All Saints go to Hell: The Final Insult is a blatant low-budget cash-grab. Here's a transcript from an actual* conversation at Volition.
Deep Silver: "Sup? What are you working on?"
Volition: "Currently I'm developing content for a new Saints Row game."
Deep Silver: "Excellent. What is it about?"
Volition: "Well, we decided to expand on what made SR4 so popular. This game is going to take place in Hell, and the Boss is going to have a lot of really unique demonic powers. There's also going to be this really good story, with lots of twists and turns. This is definitely going to be our biggest game yet."
Deep Silver: "Hmm..About how far along are you?"
Volition: "Ehhh only 10% at best. Right now it's mostly just place-holder content."
Deep Silver: "I see..*gasps* What in the world could that be!?"
Volition: "Huh?"
Deep Silver: "YOINK!"
Volition: "Hey! My workstation PC!"
High Voltage: "Why are you giving me a PC?"
Deep Silver: "Just...do something with all this."
Gat of Hell is a strictly Gat (and/or Kinzie) affair. The Boss has been kidnapped by Satan, and it's up to a couple of Mary Sues to save her. It seems odd that Kinzie would get involved, and not...Shaundi. Shaundi's been there for the boss since Saints Row 2. If I had to guess, it's because she doesn't have a personality. Anyway they arrive in Hell, get superpowers, and do a bunch of activities until the final boss battle unlocks. Note the word activities, there are no actual missions in this expansion. There are a few interactions with various "wacky" characters like Vlad the Impaler and Shakespeare, but they don't amount to anything beyond cut-scenes and a lot of talking while you're exploring. While the city feels new and different enough, its inhabitants are soul-less husks. Yeah I know, eternal torment and all, but Hell still looks very much like an actual city. There are bars, clubs, and all sorts of other places to go, but they're all closed-off to you.
The chief superpower you receive in this game is the ability to fly. I...I actually can't hate on this at all. The flying in Gat Out of Hell is great. I loved soaring around, through narrow passages, diving, and even collected all 940 of those freakin' orbs. It's a damn shame that nothing is actually done with this ability. There aren't any missions, no enemies that specifically target flying Saints (aside from the lame spires), and all you really can do is stupid pet tricks like flying through hoops. While a few of Satan's minions can fly, Big Red never got the bright idea to finance some demonic flying vehicles to complement his tanks. The rest of the superpowers are reskins, and just like SR4 they are ridiculously over-powered. Satan himself isn't immune to the coldfire aura, he spent most of the final battle frozen. Several new weapons round out the Saint's arsenal. My personal favorite is Sloth. Nothing says effort like sitting back in a chair while twin-miniguns and rockets do all the work.
While is is appealing having 666 methods for wrecking adversaries, it all seems wasted due to the pitiful level of difficulty. Like most other gamers, I like big explosions and huge body-counts, but I also want to feel like they were earned. I want close-calls, near-deaths, or even just to be slightly threatened. I'll admit, I'd be happier if Saints Row went back to the early games, where explosive options were kinda limited. But if we're planning on sticking to this route, at least go all the way. If I'm going to be an ultimate badass, I want ultimate odds to match.
Actually, I take that back. I suddenly envisioned the end-game. Imagine a Saints Row MMO. It'd probably play like Marvel Heroes 2015 or DC Universe Online. It would take place in a bland feature-less city (like Steelport), and you'd create a Saint to go kill gang-bangers, aliens, and demons with dozens of dull super-powers. It'll be challenging only in the sense of "you can't go here yet because you'll get one-shotted". There would be all these quests with punny titles, and I'd probably be the only idiot wondering why I can't drive a car. I'd ask someone and they'd say "Why would you drive a car?! You have super-sprint and flight already."
It sounds ridiculous but what other conclusion can I draw? Saints Row has fallen into the trap of constant escalation. When your last game ended with the world getting blown up and the Saints getting a sweet space-ship and time-travel, you have to wonder what could possibly happen next. Well apparently it involved going to Hell, but that was basically wasted. What's next then? Do we just go back to thug-life and stealing cars? Or do we time-travel to the distant future to save neo-earth from the cyborg-dinosaurs? Nobody wants to get stuck with a pistol, when they can shoot lasers out of their finger-tips that cause massive explosions.
And yet with all that said, I've barely talked about Gat out of Hell. You know why? Because there's nothing to talk about. This expansion is for SR4 fans that want a change of scenery. If you've already played through SR4, play through it again and save some cash instead. All you're actually missing out on with this game is a half-baked city and the (really sweet) ability to fly. The activites are retreads or stupid stuff like hitting frat-demons through giant hoops. There aren't any missions, and all you ever really do is kill things. Sadly, that isn't even the worst part. There are those times when I actually want to mindlessly kill stuff, but then some Archduke(mini-boss) appears, all of the other demons leave, and I think to myself "Maybe I should wait for the F2P Saints MMO".
Oh! Before I forget. The cutscene before the final boss bugged out on me. I'm not sure how this got past testing.

DO NOT BUY. This game is a train wreck, even if you looked at it with fresh eyes ignoring all the glaring things it's missing from past games, it's still just a terrible clunky unoptimized game that's bad at the core level and no amount of bugfixing or patches is going to redeem it.
A once great space sim series has been gutted and everything that made it unique and fun and interesting has been dumbed down or just removed. All the menus are clunky and simplified, the game is the definition of unintuitive. Where once you could command fleets and build empires and easily issue orders to specific ships or set them up to autonomously run actions, now you do none of that in X rebirth. Fleet commands? What fleet commands?
Any cool ship you see is instantly made uninteresting when you realize the fact you will never ever get to fly it, enjoy being confined to your boring one ship that can't even be customized or upgraded that much, heck it can't even hull cargo. The devs teased that you would be able to walk around capital ships and command them from the deck indirectly. But this was debunked by them weeks before launch, but I mean they were happy to let rumors run their course. You can dock at capital ships sure, but they can't move around while you're on them, and the interior in them is very small and lackluster, no bridge view whatsoever, in fact no view at all because rendering the outside "living" world while on a space station or Capital ship would have just been to much I guess. We can just chalk all that up to unfinished game syndrome.
On the note of space stations, they all look the same, enjoy going to the same looking bar over and over again while you search for an npc to trade with that has the one item you need. Trading is awful, in past X Games it was simple, certain stations produced certain products and it was easy to go between them trading. In X rebirth you have to randomly land at a station and blindly talk to NPC's in hopes they have the products you need. It's very time consuming and pointless, the worst possible way they could have handled trading.
This isn't a series reborn, it's a series aborted. This game feels like a tech demo for their new engine or worse yet, and I honestly feel this way, this game seems like some kind of weird spin off egosoft was making for nextgen consoles but due to whatever reason they had to abort and release on PC only. The clunky turbo-bad menu systems feel like they were designed to be controlled solely with a gamepad without the aid of a keyboard or mouse, and they can be.
By now this rant has gotten kind of long and I could keep going because I haven't even gotten through half of why this game is such a massive disappointment but I don't think anyone's going to even read this far. This has to be the worst game of 2013. If you want a space game go play X3:Terran Conflict/Albion prelude. Egosoft has one of the most loyal community and fanbase that mod and help fix their games over the years, and they are rewarded with this steaming pile of consolized homgeneous crap.

I'll just start by saying that I already owned Bioshock on steam and therefore, in a way recieved this for free, thanks to the free upgrade program, thus my opinion on the remaster will be somewhat biased because of this. I also played through the original back in the day when it came out, so nostalgia may somewhat cloud my judgement too.
I intend to review this game in 2 ways, firstly as a game, secondly as a remaster, scoring each part separately, whilst listing the pro's and con's in each instance and then I'll close with an overall statement and score.
Firstly, as a GAME (10/10):
PROS
- Story: From the characters, the setting, the way events unfold, I can't really fault it.
- Gameplay: The variety of powers and weapons makes for some really interesting combat, and the light RPG elements of upgrades and character customisation are great too.
- Graphics: Whilst the visuals are a bit dated now the art direction of the game is still top notch, Rapture is a beautifully realised city heavily influenced by Art Deco and due to it's fall from grace has a destroyed beauty appeal to it as well.
CONS
- Length: If anything I just wished the game was longer as I enjoyed every minute of it.
Secondly then, as a REMASTER (4/10):
PROS
- Extras: It's good to have all DLC bundled together, as well as Developer Videos to find throughout your journey.
CONS
- Graphics: Not much care seems to have been taken to vastly improve the graphics, as I said before the art direction is strong, still it would have been nice to see, for example, better textures.
- Customisation: There are very few graphics options with this remaster, whilst not a deal breaker for me, I know this is something sort after by a lot of people.
- Stability: Game crashed on me a handful of times during my initial playthrough, whilst not the end of the world, each time this happended it reset my graphics and gameplay options, as well as which developer vidoes I'd collected (I kept saves near each one in the story to combat this). Specifically, each time this happened the difficulty and vita chamber options reset (I was playing on survivor with vita chambers off) so when the game loaded back up I changed the difficulty back up and the vita chambers back off, I still got the achievements associated with the higher difficulties and vita chambers thankfully.
- Controls: Whilst I play with a controller and didn't run into any issues, I've read that there are issues when using a mouse and keyboard so I'll simply state that here as a con for controls. I have read that they are working on patching this soon, at the time of writing this review.
OVERALL (7/10)
In the end I would still recommend this to any fan of Bioshock, or anyone who has never played the game before, perhaps with the caveat that you use a controller (due to the known mouse issues). Bioshock for me is one of my all time favourite games and it really is good to be back in Rapture.

Amazing game.  Hours of fun in this survival game with a somber war setting that places you as the civilians that get caught in the midst of a war struggling to survival.
The challenges/encounters you face in game feel very real and the dialogue really immerse you into the cold and war struck city.  Challenges include spending your day time reinforcing your shelter and making sure you provide food and warmth to your survivors.  Once night hits you set jobs for your survivors and the options to scavenge other parts of the city for supplies. The combat requires some planning and strategy when you decide to dispact of foes in your way or even murder the innocent and elderly with a crowbar then you reap their meds and food.
The game has a lot of replayability as the experience will be different from the areas you explore to the survivors you start with from the begining.  This game is very worth the money for those who enjoy the survival, strategic, or morally questioning decision making experience in this game.

I can't ever do this game and why it's unbelievably good, justice. The concept of realistic wars in games never struck me as the kind to hold my attention, yet this game, mixed with its survival elements and its whole new take on what war means and what it does to an individual, has managed to do just that, and has done so extremely well.
The game is based on true life events from the Siege of Sarajevo in 1992 (and countless more perspectives I imagine). A video in particular, shows Emir Cerimovic's accounts of what daily life was like, struggles for basic needs (no water, food, electric), what it was like to be involved in war as a child, the unimaginable terrors that come with war, seeing those you believe to be good, turn into monsters when filled with desperation and despair. That video, along with several other videos is what made me buy this in the first place. This War of Mine, on all accounts, did close to what I believe to be justice in trying to convey what it means to survive, what you'll do to survive, and what it truly means to be in something so horrific.
If you have some spare time, please go and check out 11bitstudios's YouTube channel and have a look at the game.

Sins of a Solar Empire has been a top-shelf 4X game for a long time, and probably the only successful Real-Time galaxy-based strategy game I know of.  Think Empire at War, Endless Space, Galactic Civilizations, or Master of Orion with an updated, streamlined interface, in full 3D (you can zoom to almost any level of magnification), and in Real-Time, and you'll have a good idea of what to expect.  The game eschews a traditional single-player campaign in exchange for more emphasis on instanced gameplay, and provides a wide variety of pre-designed maps along with random maps in various sizes and a scenario builder for the more hands-on type.  In Rebellion (over and above SINS: Trinity), the three races are here split into two factions apiece, each with unique technologies and units, without sacrificing the careful balance among the factions.  Additionally, Rebellion includes the immense Titans, a large, expensive combat ship which moves and levels like a capital ship but has the strength and stamina of a starbase.  The Forbidden Worlds DLC adds three additional planet types (all of which require research to colonize and have particular strategic value), while the Stellar Phenomena DLC adds a number of non-colonizable objects, as well as some hazards and environmental events to create a less predictable experience.  Both are a little expensive for what you get, though they're interesting additions nonetheless.
In short: Sins is pretty much the best game of its kind out there - if you're a fan of the strategy/4X game, you should absolutely give it a look.

Real review:
Once in a while, a game comes along that you notice by sheer chance and buy on a whim only to find yourself realizing that it blew a lot of purchases that you had much higher hopes for out of the water. This War of Mine is such a game. I personally only bought it after noticing a small 2BFP playthrough of it as a YT recommendation, and don't regret it at all.
Your €/$19 will buy you a ticket to a game that essentially Oregon Trail on steroids. Plot-wise, the game is said to be inspired by the experiences of the civilians during the Siege of Sarajevo, which was the longest siege of a capital city in the history of modern warfare. As a result, you'll be given control of up to 5 (out of a pool of 12 at the time of review) surivors trying to live another day in Pogoren, the fiercely contested capital of Graznavia. Both are of course ficticious.
However, to try and keep the gaming experience 'fun', the siege of Pogoren doesn't last more than a few months. That being said, a lot of the things that exacerbate the attrition your group faces do happen during the siege. Thus the choices you have to make will get harder as Pogoren slowly runs out of all resources that it once had.
TWoM is remarkable in how it manages to set a scene by clever usage of pencil drawing effects, bleak colors and a mere radio. If you permit yourself to vest interest in the game, you won't feel like you're being slammed with a moral lesson and guilt like so many aid organizations like to do. Instead, you'll be trying to do the best you can for the group and only at the end of the game, when it presents you an epilogue will you think back about the journey you have made.
Gameplay follows what is arguably the core doctrine of the industry in that it is 'easy to pick up, hard to master'. Your gameplay moments are split in a daytime mode, spent by allowing the injured & sick to recover, by preparing food or material or building new installations for your shelter. After that, night begins and one member of your group has to go out into other areas and scavenge for components. Those components are needed to allow you to prepare food, materials or even build installations. As war rages on, you'll find yourself going from scavenging abandoned places left in a hurry for tons of parts without any danger to trying to find just 4 pieces of wood you can steal from an army base.
After you've scavenged/stolen all you can carry, you return home and the grueling daytime starts anew, now compounded by the events that happened in your shelter while you were gone + the reaction of your group to the stuff you did in the night. The reason I say the core doctrine is followed is because anyone can scavenge the safe areas, yet it does take some time, mastery and luck to be able to take out a psychopath wearing body armour and his 5 goons before scavenging his base, for example.
Information about how your game is progressing can be heard over the radio, and once the war ends, you'll be given a small timeline + epilogue on how your characters fared. At that point, as I mentioned earlier, you'll stop and reflect in amazement at how you had to kill 5 hobos for a pair of bandages, or how you had to steal from the hospital twice.
You will never be able to be a gun toting hero that enforces his will in this. And that alone, for once, makes war hell.

TLDR:  This is a cool tractor driving simulator, it is not an in-depth 'run a farming business' simulator.  Don't buy if you are looking for the economic depth of something like Tropico...
I bought this game based on the reviews here, knowing that the majority of what people were talking about was the cool tractor driving, and assuming that surely there was an underlying economic business model behind the running of the farm.  Unfortunately, I was wrong in that assumption, and hence I only played the game for a few hours and won't be returning to it.  If all you are looking for is a cool tractor driving simulator, then cool, enjoy.  But, if you are looking for something where you can dig down in a ledger and see what fields have been producing well, what's the impact of fertilizing to the bottom line, how does the return on investment in the fields compare to the return on investment of buying bee houses or lettuce houses, etc, then this isnt the game for you.  The accounting ledger is extremely simple, doesn't allow you to see where all the in/outflows go, and doesn't allow you to see any history.  This may be a fun game for some, but it lacks the depth that I was hoping for, and I just wanted to warn others like myself.  Peace.

Heat 2 is a huge imrpovement over the last title, and the work the devs have put into the game really shows.
First the cons:
-Physics could use some work. The car seems to get loose too easily, but maybe that's because I'm used to more of the sims rather than using a controller and arcade like physics.
-AI pit strategy could use some work.
-AI could be a little more difficult to race against
-Limited camera angles
Pros:
+ The latest update made cautions more sensitive, a feature many requested in the community, and it feels good.
+ Career mode is excellent. It takes time to progress, and it feels well though out. However, earning money is totally useless and should either be removed, or should be put to use somehow.
+ Plate racing has improved dramatically. Now I can qualify decently, and race in a pack around Daytona.
+ Limited paintbooth allows for some car customization, which is great considering last year there was nothing.
+Rivalries make racing harder, and teaches you not to be a turn 1 hero. The update also allowed rivalries to go away if you race clean, adding incentive to not drive like Kevin Lepage.
Overall the experience is a lot better than last years title, and for any casual NASCAR or racing fan, the game is a buy. If you enjoy sim racing, you may find this less enjoyable in that aspect, but it is nice to have a solid arcade racing title to just have fun in every once in a while. I look forward to seeing what the devs can do with this title going forward.

A great game for those seeking an intro to semi-competitive level of Magic. Easy to follow tutorial that teaches new and experienced players about some common mechanics in 2 minutes at most. You even get rewarded for these tutorials with about 2 booster packs worth of gold, as well as a booster for each of the 5 campaign chapters (battles using a preset deck that tells the story of popular planeswalkers in Magic lore).
After getting these cards you are given a starter pack containing enough cards for several decks. If you're new, you can use the "deck wizard" which helps you build a deck around a certain theme (graveyard, aggro, elves, auras, etc) in an easy step-by-step manner (things like "pick 10 early creatures" or "pick 7 aura/buff cards"). More experienced players can, of course, have complete freedom in the builder. The UI and filters in the deckbuilder are a bit messy, not being able to sort for a keyword or name, but are only a minor annoyance. You can save 30 decks as of now.
Now you can play vs easy, medium, or hard ai for 5,10,or 15 gold for winning, or play against other players and win 20 gold for a victory. A daily as well as community quest will also grant you 40-60 gold when completed. This allows purchase of a booster pack (150 gold) every 1-3 days depending on your time available. Another mode which was added due to its popularity in the Magic community is Two-Headed Giant. In this mode you team up with another player in a 2v2 match (Seperate decks but a shared turn and lifepool). A few minor gripes with this is that you can't earn gold, can't play solo vs AI (which for many doesn't matter but it would be nice), and the server issues at times.
When actually in a game, the UI is clean and allows you to easily see abilities and judge the current situation (though there are a few times where I will need to zoom in order to see the P/T of a creature because the dispaly has bugged). If you've played any Duels game before this will be familiar.
Overall, this game is great for anybody who has even considered trying Magic or is trying to fall back in love with the game. It's free and has no Pay-to-Win or locked content for new players (Duels:2015 I'm looking at you), so why not give it a try, it's only a few hours out of your life.

Magic the Gathering has been a game I've enjoyed for over 15 years and the DoTP series has been (except for last year) one I've quite enjoyed despite its shortcomings. I've looked forward to what the developer could do with the next iteration.
Well, this developer has done a poor job. As others have mentioned the series has regressed, losing features. The series is obviously mimicking Hearthstone but doing a bad job of it.
My main gripes:
15g per win (20g vs online opponent) and 150g to buy a booster pack of only 6 cards. No discount for buying packs in bulk. Plus a weak card pool (not just the rares, but even more importantly the commons and uncommons) for every archetype (aggro, midrange, control, ramp, combo). This means a long and rather uninteresting grind.
A frustrating beginner experience because of the above. Its not much fun to use a very limited, weak, and uninteresting pool of cards against more interesting decks played by the AI.
The AI has not improved in this series for over four years. It doesn't seem to have been worked on.
Removed different gameplay modes and challenges from the campaign.
Can't get gold from 2 headed giant games? So you put in a feature and penalize players who enjoy that feature. Again, these players already have to slowly grind for gold. How does that make sense?
Can't save account/game data across platforms. Their excuse for this was lame. Hearthstone can do it and its been out for a while. Who cares if its out on iPhone, iPad, Steam, and console if you have to create an account for each one? Discourages players from long term play and investing $$ in the game for gold and packs. This is a major, major flaw.
Can play a 30-40 minute game against an online opponent, right before winning the opp quits/disconnects and you lose connection to the game and will not gain any gold for the win. This just happened to me. The payout is bad enough without this disconnects.
Solutions:
Increase the amount of gold per win to 25g.
Quests should give at least 75g each. These massive worldwide coop quests should be even more. A worldwide quest today has a 40g reward. Not even 1/3 of a pack.
Increase booster packs to AT LEAST 8 cards  per pack, but preferably 9-10.
Do whatever coding you have to do to make it cross platform compatible.
Hire a new developer.
Give free packs to all customers for all the grief with the servers and all these letdowns. This costs you no money but makes the customer base feel listened to and happy. Happy and loyal customers is a good thing.
Broken, and just not full of promise.

My favorite part of this game is the variety. They took the basic formula from Civilization V and blended it with a sci-fi motif, in the fullest sense of the word. The new affinity system determines your corporation's philosophy towards dealing with the new world, including special passive upgrades and units. Speaking of units, while they probably over-simplified the promotion system for units, as you increase your affinity levels, you get to make your units stronger, and in some cases give them new abilities. THis makes for a much smaller, but tighter, roster of units. I found it quite refreshing, and definitely preferable to the plethora of units in older civilization games.
Being an RPG aficionado, I also really enjoyed the quests that were added to this iteration. Not only do they give you smaller goals to work towards over time, lending you motivation to get through some of the boring parts, and even telling a decent story. The game really does a good job of getting you into the mindset of this setting. Furthermore, there are new and interesting victory conditions that go way beyond just "get a lot of culture" or the like from Civ V. They also tell a story, and each affinity has one specific win condition for them.
The game has some technical difficulties, and I still want more to it (after a few games in a short time I was a little burnt-out). However, the game has already built an avid modding community, and they recently released a patch to work out some of the kinks in the software. All in all, this game gets a 9/10 for strategy games.

It been almost two years since I played FF XIII for the last time. However I decided to write a review anyway. I have to admit, that I'm not a huge fan of the franchise, but it doesn't means I don't know nothing about it.
As in every game, there is no strict story line between each game. Final Fantasy is rather brand which keep well known product and tries to maintain some basics of game mechanics and each of them has own story.
In final fantasy XIII's storyline is placed in world called Cocoon, that want to be destroyed by lords of Santctum under command of Galeth Dysley. In the game we are steering as 6 main characters. These are Lighting, Snow, Vanille, Katzroy, Hope, and Fang. They are trying to prevent of human destruction of the cocoon. Each of them has on own expressive personality, history and different behavior during the fight.
Gameplay is very controversial. Some of fans complain on dead linearity which does not give us opportunity to discover the world. We are traveling from point A to B. But, to be honest I actually enjoyed it. FF XIII isn't hack n' slash game, which means we cannot keep press repeadle mouse button as fast as possible to kill  as much as we can. In this game we have old school Nintendo's RPG style. Where for fights shows a different screen and to attack our enemy we have to choice enemy, and the attack of which we have to destroy him. For some beasts some attacks are more effective and for other less.
Music and Visual part is really charming. I have couldn't imagine the game without high contrasts and so good music themes. From very beginning we have feelings like we are watching good quality Asian TV series. It is done by great story and lots of high quality of cinematic - one after another.
For the bad aspect, I have to admit, even if music is good, it's also very repetitive. It's getting a bit annoying when we hear the same theme during 999999'th fight. And I cannot say lot of good about the PC port. Even with high end PC, horrible FPS drops (60/30) are on main curse on this adventure. Anybody who did this, didn't try to make anything about shaders or increasing/decreasing graphics, to keep game stabilised or looking better than consoles. What's worth to say. My GTX 970 is using 30% of its performance during playing this game. Other words we could say it is 100% PlayStation 3 emulator.
But even with this defects I would to recommend this amazing masterpiece.

After years of waiting to give this title a try, the opportunity finally presented itself and I carved out some time to really get into it.  Unfortunately, although it is a decent and mildly enjoyable game, I can't personally recommend Crysis.
What I had thought would be a unique experience turned out to be a run-of-the-mill, fairly generic First-Person Shooter that failed to draw me in.  The suit mechanics are the game's strong point, as they are entertaining to use, but the rest of the game is quite lackluster in comparison.  As I played, it seemed to me that what got this game its hype was, by and large, the advanced graphical features of its day.  On this end, I will say that the game still holds up even eight years later.  The game looked good and the animations were smooth.
As I stated previously, this is not a bad game, just one that no longer stands out for anything in particular.  If you're a huge fan of First-Person Shooters and need another to hold you over to the next release, I'd say go ahead and get it.  If you're looking for a new experience that's going to keep you enthralled for the length of the game, I would look elsewhere.

One of the most compelling games I've played this year. This War of Mine puts you in control of a small band of intrepid survivors trying to survive in a battered city in the midst of a civil war. Every night you must scavenge the city for supplies, and every day you must trade some goods for others in order to keep your survivors fed, warm, healthy and happy. With realistic mechanics that deal not only with your survivors physical health, but their mental state as well, This War of Mine is a bleak look at the side of war video games don't show often enough. You are not a mighty warrior, cutting a swath through enemies with your machine gun. You are trying not to die while far greater powers struggle for dominance around you—something you almost never even get to see.
There are as many ways to play this game as there are people who play it. You can attack other survivors and steal their things—though this, of course, will have a huge impact on your survivors' morale. You can try to hoard some supplies and trade them out for food and materials, but if your supply runs dry, you'll swiftly starve. Events and your survivors are randomized, so the game has great replay value.
Is This War of Mine FUN? No, not in the last. At least not for me. But it's tremendously compelling, in the same way as a sad book or a Shakespearean tragedy. You don't need to be laughing or cheering to be deeply emotionally invested in a game, and This War of Mine proves that in spades.

Holy crap, being a badger mom is tense. You've got five badger cubs to keep alive, and while they're occasionally clever - they run towards food and away from predator sounds in the dark - for the most part they just follow you around. It's up to you to lead them past fires and rushing waves and foxes and all kinds of nasty eagles in the air, and yikes, it's hard. I tried as hard as I could but I just couldn't save them all - no matter what I did, one cub got eaten while we were running across open ground towards a shelter. I've seen videos of other people get through that unscathed but I can't tell what I'm doing differently. It's a sad day in badgerland.
The UI minimalism really helps, in a way - I felt like I was learning how things worked, and it felt very animalistic in terms of there being no words and varying levels of dread and apprehension. The art style looks a bit weird in screenshots but ends up working really nicely in motion, and the music and sounds do a great job of matching the mood and giving you gameplay callouts.
Also, it's suprt short - I probably spent an extra 30 minutes restarting levels to try and save cubs, and even so it didn't take that long. It really puts you in the role successfully. Give it a shot!

I bought this game because of the co-op and because there aren't many RPG-Action Co-Ops out there. It seemed like a great opportunity to play my favourite game genre with my friend. And it might be a decent experience, if you get around the bugs, some of which might force you into restart.
My rating without the bugs is 7/10. My rating with bugs is 4/10. I would not recommend this game for its full price, but with discount and some friends to play with, you might give it a try.
PROS:
Apart from being a co-op game there really isn't any other positive outstanding feature in this game, because as an Action-RPG game it provides only a mediocre gameplay experience and boring dialogues.
CONS:
-Pour graphics even for 2011. Compared to Witcher 2, which was released in the same year, LoR: War in the North is something from Stone Age.
-Simple battle system: just fast attack and strong attack, blocking and few skills. There are no combos and, if you are patient enough, you can just hold block and attack simultaneously, without taking any damage (apart from ranged attacks)
-Confusing crafting system, unless you learn the names of all the plants and components, it's hard to understand what will be the result of your crafting.
- There is no push-to-talk, you are forced to listen to all the background noise from your gaming buddy's microphone.
-If you finish a quest, you can return to complete it again. I can't understand whether it's meant to be like that or it's a bug. Either way it doesn't help you to understand what to do next.
- No mini-map. It's a big problem in Burrow-downs cave system and Forest for apparent reasons.
- Bad camera work – does not always follow the character.
- BUGS!!!
1. Some quests get stuck. No solution. Restart the game or change the host (if co-op).
2. Completed quests revert back "in progress", if you return to the same area.
3. Some enemies (bosses), which should spawn, do no appear.
4. Sometimes it's not possible to revive your allies. Normally it's possible.
5. I started to play this game with my friend. But on our second co-op session this game told me that he has progressed further than me and that I will not be able to get achievements and to save my progress. However none of us had played the game in single-player mode after the previous session, so we were on the same line.
6. Graphical glitches.
Enjoyed it from start to finish. Took less than 8 minutes. ;)

Being loosely familiar with the franchise, I thought the newest installment in the series would be a good place to start. While it is an overall solid game, a few things along the line really kept me from truly thinking of this game as great.
What it does right: The gunplay is smooth and enjoyable. Being able to snap between headshots quickly is satisfying enough to make me want to replay the more action-heavy missions again. The arcade-style, open world sections where you had multiple ways to kill a target were a blast to play through and try to get every challange or complete it with a silent assassin ranking, even if it was frustrating to constantly retry after every ♥♥♥♥ed section.  The score system was a good way to bring replayability to the game. The variation in the missions was great, too. I was never bored or wishing things would just hurry along, even when I was trying a mission again for the fifth or so time. The stealth system was alright mostly. I never got terribly frustrated with it, but more of that in the bad.
What it does wrong: I think calling the story lackluster would be giving it too much credit. While it was easy to follow, it never really made much sense at times. Like how a team of skilled, covert assassins' first move against their target was to blow the front door down with a rocket, or how 47 just instantly cared for this girl without ever knowing her, and swears to protect her with his life. This might've been touchd on in a previous game, but it was just not engaging at all on a narrative level. I feel like this detracted from the gameplay as well. It felt like it was trying to have that arcade feel of one level at a time, but it tried to tie in story to it. Like some missions I had to question why it was even necessary to kill certain targets. My overall story objective had nothing to do with these people and they've had zero prior introduction. And they missed a massive opportunity for 47. A hardened assassin having to learn to get along and care for a teenage girl would've made for some great character development, but in the end, the sushi guy was a more in-depth character than our protagonist.
After my story complaints, the disguise system felt more aggravating than anything, especially on the higher difficulty levels. Having a guard instantly see through my disguise at a side glance when I ran out of instinct was beyond frustrating, and suddenly running out of instinct to blend in seemed weird to have a master of disguise suddenly not know how to blend in anymore. A prolonged detection system might've worked better, like have the same detection mechanic, but if you're blending in, it takes a lot longer, but you move slower. I don't know.
While the score system added replayability, it really took a lot of fun out of certain segments. Some missions did call for being silent, and a covert assassin, but giving you a loaded rifle, dozens of targets, only four actual assassinations, and a big empty space? That's just cruel to visible downgrade your score every time you want to open fire. It took the fun out of being good enough to clear out an entire room with just the silverballers. I understand that's probably just to encourage a silent approach, but it made the whole "choose your playstyle" thing into "do this specific playstyle or you'll get a bad grade".
Last but not least: Contracts. The initial concept of contracts had me excited. The prospect of player-made contracts where you could choose your own loadout and playstyle sounded good on paper, but the end product wasn't nearly as satisfying. I tried playing through a couple different ones, and it was only a slight twist on the story missions. Instead of player-created maps and targets, you just pick out a target from within one of the story maps. This isn't really a big enough difference to make me care about having to go through and do all these different contracts and gain a bunch of money for upgrades. Maybe if it was like hitman vs. hitman in an area, and you had to figure out who was the other hitman and kill him before he could find you, or if there was actual, player-created maps that were completely new content. As it stands it's really just not worth the time.
All in all, I'd say about 8/10 for the campaign, and probably a 4/10 for contracts.

I think this actually was the first PC game that I have ever played (well apart from those pre-installed games on Windows XP like Solitaire). I enjoyed it back in the days. I still do.
Disciples II is a turn-based strategy game with beautiful graphics (even for today) and rich storyline. Unlike other turn-based strategy titles like Heroes, the battle system offers a control over individual units instead of stacked units, which I find very convenient. Also the different strategies you can use to complete a map and the rich storyline guarantees that the gameplay does not get repetitive as it is with Heroes of Might and Magic.
In Disciples II, you get to choose from five different races (Elves, Humans, Dwarfes, Demons and Undeads) with their own unique agendas and characteristics. Also you can choose one of three classes for yourself as a strategist: Mage (cast spells twice a day), Warlord (restore Health more quickly) or Guildmaster (more resources and actions for the Thief). So when you've completed game with one race/leader class you can try another.
This game offers three elements of gaming experience that I value the most: great style, rich storyline and character development/customization. Also, this game rewards exploring and there are plenty of quest maps to try after the campaign mode is complete.
What I didn't like about this game however was that you can export only one leader and only five items to the next campaign, so lot of valuable equipment is lost in the process. Also I didn't like that only a particular development branch could be chosen for a unit class instead of them all. Also, the Multiplayer via Directplay does not work anymore. I guess, you need to try external services like GameRanger for that.
Nevertheless, Disciples II is a great classic turn-based strategy game. My overall rating is 10/10.
p.s. Don't believe other reviews. This game works on Windows 8.1 like a charm. I had some issues with fullscreen on my laptop (I had to choose a lower resolution, otherwise the game won't fit the screen), but with external monitor there are no problems at all.

I've decided to change the name of this game. It shall now be called: Doorman Repetition. That's all you really do. This game has a lot going wrong, yet it has some great aspects. Let's start with the bad. The story is horrible. Hitman has never been known for good storytelling, but that didn't matter because the gameplay came first. The levels in Bloodmoney and Contracts weren't made in any real order. They were random, and the story came afterwards. That was fine, we all liked that. Absolution though...with it's brain cell killing plot decided to shape the levels based on what the story is, and that ruined the gameplay to some degree. Because the levels are determined by the story we didn't really get the massive, open, levels from previous games. We got "escape through this door." The levels are puny, and cramped, and along with the story not making any sense (and being a cliche as hell action game and not an assassin game) the gameplay is repetitive.
So, let's talk about the good stuff. The game is beautiful. Graphically it's amazing, especially with all the little things within the cramped levels. Mechanically the game is good as well. The controls are smooth, and the detail with bullet impacts and stuff are great. Though the levels are small, there are lots of little, small, blunt, sharp objects to slay people with, and that's awesome. Contracts mode is pretty cool as well, but the same level flaws apply.
Overall, Doorman Repetition is disappointing, but it's still enjoyable to a certain extent. The mechanics are crisp, and very solid along with the amazing graphics and attention to detail. The only issue is that the levels (while some are really cool) are designed around a story that is, quite frankly, very bad, and as a result almost every other aspect of the game suffers. Bloodmoney is still the greatest Hitman game, but if you want a fun action game with a cliche/stereotypical/ridiculous/brain cramp inducing story, while having great graphics and fun gun play you should buy this when it's on sale.

X Rebirth is both a step forward and a step backward for the X Series.  An all-new game engine provides for gorgeous vistas and a truely open world, where you can, with enough patience, fly from one place to almost any other place you can see (and some which you can't).  The underlying simulation promises the same degree of complexity seen in previous games, while the simplified user interface makes the most basic aspect of the game, flight and space dogfighting, easier and more accessible.  However, that same new interface lacks the fine grained control over player owned ships and stations that X players have come to expect.  Add to that a very rocky launch, with arguably every aspect of the game being broken in some way, and it's clear that X Rebirth is not quite ready for mass consumption.  Fortunately, the dev team is working tirelessly on bringing the game up to speed, and the modding community is plugging away intently adding features that are either broken or perceived as missing.  Overall, X Rebirth is a flawed gem, not yet ready for the average gamer, but stands as an excellent platform for the next generation of X games, and, with the dedicated developers whom Egosoft has proven themselves to be, will hopefully soon be the X game we've always wanted, and worthy of a spot in every spaceie's Steam Library.
