Disclaimber: This review was written 11/09/2010
The Last Remnant is about a kid who's sister become kidnapped and he ventures on a journey to save her. The game is mainly marketed of it's "strategic" combat system where you can flank, intercept and such while still being a "faithful" JRPG.
When you start up the game you are greeted with awesome music and some really sweet battles and I love large battles. It gives me chills in all the Total War games, but this game is nothing like Total War. The graphics use the unreal engine are alright (when it gets going), although this game is especially slow on loading textures in relatively small areas, which will mean that you're going to watch a lot of low-res textures (this might be fixed by defraging the hard drive though). The art style is a joke. If you didn't like Final Fantasy IX for it's art style you're going to hate this game because it's inhabited by giant fish people, small rabbit-frogs and orcs... no wait, those are just guards. All especially bred to be as cartoony as possible. The main characters are ridiculously emo-looking, and I mean all the main characters, which is why this style needs to die, right now.
The biggest problem with this game however is the combat system. It sucks♥♥♥♥♥because it has nothing to do with strategy. Since it uses turns you cannot in reality intercept someone because you never know who they're trying to go after. You "flank" your opponents by sending more than one unit towards them, if you're opponent is then fighting more than one squad in the same time you'll flank them and this is regardless of squad size so 1 squad vs 2 squads equals flank but the nice thing is that the squad can be surrounded and that happens when they're fighting over 3-4 enemies I believe. When the fighting starts it only looks like a giant brawl without any kind of structure, and since the game deals with relatively low numbers of units it wont look as epic as the brawls in the Total War series where they're mostly chaotic because here the characters take turns to hit each other. You get 3 squads in which you can have max 5 people in them it's kinda strange that they would even be able to flank someone and quite fitting it all turns into a brawl. Your performance of the battles are entirely luck based because you never really directly command your units in battle. If you want them to heal themselves you gotta wait until they're bleeding to death before the option is even available. I thought this didn't sound so bad before I bought the game but in practice it ruins the "tactics element" of it all, if you could call it that.
So basically you can't flank your opponents if you don't outnumber them and you cannot directly control your squadmates. This is a game where the player doesn't have much control over and you would probably have better control when trying to win at ♥♥♥♥ing slot machines! The control you do have is where to send your squads, vague pointers on how they should fight and who goes in what squad. Oh and by the way, you don't get to choose their equipment either. Poof, now a RPG element are gone too.
Do I even have to say more? The story mayhap? When you meet (what the ♥♥♥♥ his name was) you befriend him and the story turns over to him for a moment while he tries to make his vassal state independent from another vassal state. Yes, this game deals in Feudalism (kind of) and you get to follow his struggle for his state's independence for a little while. He promises you that he will find your sister in the process but it have to be done methodically. The story isn't half bad I think and it would be really interesting to follow up on if only the game actually let you control the battles. It becomes increasingly difficult to control the outcome of the battles and you would probably lose quite a few battles because you simply cannot control anything that's happening during the course of it.
Decent story and graphics, poor characters and art style and a bad gameplay. If you could control the game it would be alright but a game that cannot interact with the player isn't worth spending many hours of frustration on. And don't even get me started on the giant learning curve, why is it so big? Because no one tells you squat and the game is so unorthodox in almost every way. There's a stat that is different for each character that seems more like a characteristic. It changes with levels but what does it do? No, this game is hopelessly bad, don't even try it.

Don't get me wrong this game has more than a few flaws but personally I managed to look past them. It's kind of hard to persuade people in this situation because the problems this game has I don't really pay attention to. Also for the price it's at I doubt anyone would be interested.
Plot-Personally I liked it, it was something different as to what I have played before, really I don't have a problem with it. However that is one to be disagreed with because according to some people it's hard to understand, which I can relate to at times.
Gameplay-One of the major problems in the game for me. Yes, the game does have a very nice switching paradigm system but it's all dumbed down by the fact that you can just auto-battle and win.
Graphics-I love this game's graphics, the enemies, the surroundings. When you get to Chapter 11 you will see how great it is however it will take a LONG time to get there and when I got there my fps dropped substantially.
Characters-I believe most people have problems with the same ones namely Hope, Vanille and Snow. I can agree with Hope to some degree but he gets less "hopeless" *wink* as time goes on. Vanille is extremely kooky and at first I didn't like her but I started to like her as time went on. Snow is my favourite character but he's a complete idiot.
Finally the part almost everyone has a problem with...corridors. It's all good saying "oh well if you get to chapter 11 it opens up" ok bright idea I will play over 30 hours of your game to get to the fun part, nope, it isn't going to happen. Needless to say I persevered and I tried to ignore it and to be honest I didn't have to try hard. To me as long as a game has interesting parts that keep me preoccupied I couldn't care less about corridors. However that is down to opinion, also one last thing I want to state before jumping to my conclusion, the New-Game+ is good but a few things are getting on my nerves. If you do get to the end and you actually do like it there are a few things you can do afterwards like the remaining quests (stone missions), maxing out COMPLETELY (trust me it's going to take years to do so) and getting all achievements. Where most of my beef comes from is maxing out, it will take ages, there is however a way to speed it up. One of the missions will give a Growth Egg doubling xp so when you need it is when your low levelled (logic). However that's where the problem comes in, to beat the boss that drops it you can either be almost maxed out (if so what's the point of the reward) or test your luck at getting a 1% chance instant kill move. Good Luck...
So I can only really say buy the game if you can look past its problems which I did but I am not saying it will work for you. I liked it because I tried to look past all of it and in the end I succeeded, I came out pleased. I was stuck on what to give this because in many ways it can be considered a really bad game. Its lacklustre start will put of most people but as long as you can endure it until the half way point hopefully it will start to change your mind. I reccommend it just purely because I found it fun. Even though I have covered more than a few things to me the game has so much more good things about it than bad.

The Last Remnant is a really good attempt for Square Enix to establish itself on PC gaming ( though I still play it with PS3 controller since it's easier to control, I used a 3rd party controller program to disguise it as 360 controller ).
Graphics : The game's graphic is a little bit on the middle ground for PC ( and especially for SquareEnix ) though the game show much of its details and the true power of SE-animated on the battleground rather than the cutscene ( Maybe my PC sucks but the grame drop during some of the gigantic animation are quite bad ).
Control : The game is console controller friendly and I would suggest you to use one since It's much nicer to get around using controller.
Game's Mechanics : The game use its old and all popular turn base mechanics from the final fantasy series, with a really nice touch here and there. A big improvement though is apart from the main character, anybody else will be treated equally on the battlefield which make the game extremely interesting and fun to play.  Speaking of the amount of characters, the game offer you up to 25 chatacters to be on the battlefield at one time ( 5 team of 5 ), you will be controlling a team called "union", to give order to your troops, the action each troops can take are very situational base, since you are controlling up to 5 characters at one time, the game use a function to give each troops their own chance to use their skills. This might cone at a negative to some person since you can't directly control one particular character and command him to use certain skill at that specific time, but he/she will be using it automatically if the situation is met. The tutorial is there, though it doesn't go in depth of how and when is the appropriate time to use some of the function. The QTE they include in the fight are extremely nice, it make the game goes from spam Attack to win to you have to pay attention on the game in case some of those QTE come in so you can power up your attack or counter the enemy attack with your own for HUGE damage. Which of course have its down side on that it's more centered toward luck-base than strategy for the QTE. Speaking of QTE, another HUGE downside of the game came from the fact that it have the "turbo mode" option available for you to speed up the fighting progress of the game, it speed up the animation of the fighting scene and here is a problem that they might not noticed before, the QTE's speed in turbo mode is also much, MUCH quicker, so quick that it's impossible for any human to react to the right QTE sequence on time which in turns, making the QTE in turbo mode, impossible and thus, might lose you in the match that require some QTE action.
Sound : Oh my god, SE did it again with its awesome soundtrack that will capture anyone's heart.
In total, for the price tag of 10$, I would recommend this game to anyone that is a fan of RPG ( first timer are not the target audience of this game ). If you're a fan of ANY of the FF series, Dragon Quest series or  just any game from SE in general, you will probably love this game. I have no idea why metacritics critics have been giving this game a low score of 66 ( users at 82 ), I think it deserve better though the story line is, as you guess it, very final fantasy-like.

You can only control a single character at a time (the rest are controlled by AI), and fights are basically made obsolete by an auto-attack button that chooses the best attack option for you. There is no leveling up through fights (so one may ask why even bother to engage enemies), and most engagements can be avoided by walking around an enemy. Combining all this with save points every 30 seconds (literally), just makes me wonder why even bother playing?
The story line is completely lackluster and mind numbingly dull, yet you are forced to sit through an eternity of cut-scenes after every linear corridor you walk through. It makes little to no sense if you don't intend on reading the never ending amount of side notes in the menu, and is possibly the worst in the entire Final Fantasy series.
Don't waste your money on this.

One of the most compelling games I've played this year. This War of Mine puts you in control of a small band of intrepid survivors trying to survive in a battered city in the midst of a civil war. Every night you must scavenge the city for supplies, and every day you must trade some goods for others in order to keep your survivors fed, warm, healthy and happy. With realistic mechanics that deal not only with your survivors physical health, but their mental state as well, This War of Mine is a bleak look at the side of war video games don't show often enough. You are not a mighty warrior, cutting a swath through enemies with your machine gun. You are trying not to die while far greater powers struggle for dominance around you—something you almost never even get to see.
There are as many ways to play this game as there are people who play it. You can attack other survivors and steal their things—though this, of course, will have a huge impact on your survivors' morale. You can try to hoard some supplies and trade them out for food and materials, but if your supply runs dry, you'll swiftly starve. Events and your survivors are randomized, so the game has great replay value.
Is This War of Mine FUN? No, not in the last. At least not for me. But it's tremendously compelling, in the same way as a sad book or a Shakespearean tragedy. You don't need to be laughing or cheering to be deeply emotionally invested in a game, and This War of Mine proves that in spades.

I had high hopes for this game but was disappointed by the mixed reviews on release day. I heard lot of discussion about wheel bugs, graphics bugs, and bad gameplay. I hesitantly placed my order, fully expecting to ask for a refund. I had doubts that my wheel would work at all. Well I was pleasantly surprised.
I have a Thrustmaster T300RS wheel along with T3PA pedals and TH8A shifter. Everything works great! I had no problems with the game detecting them. I thought the sensitivity was way too low by default, so I increased it some along with the force feedback strength, and also lowered the deadzone, and it feels perfectly fine to me! There is some tendency for the wheel to oscillate some if you don't hold it well (I turned FFB back down a tad). Overall, I am very pleased with the wheel performance and overall control of the game.
I play iRacing, so I've grown accustomed to the simulation feel. NH2 is not a simulator of the same caliber by any means, but that is actually what I was hoping for in NH2. iRacing can feel a little too hardcore sometimes, and I wanted something a little more casual and fun to play that I could just jump into, but I also wanted something that functions properly (not buggy or ridiculous). I'll will say this: NH2 is very forgiving of dumb driving. You can bump other cars and get away with it where iRacing would send you in a spin in an instant. NH2's handling overall feels a little more "muddy" than iRacing, but that actually makes it a little more casual and fun to play. I also don't mind really that cautions are automated. It's not as realistic, but it keeps things moving. NH2 is not a simulator, but it still feels real enough to me. It's still quite a few steps above Mario Kart. Even though NH2 forgives a lot of dumbness on the player's part, I'm pretty satisfied with how the AI acts. It's a tad silly sometimes, but don't feel like I'm being screwed over by them as long as I'm not too dumb. It does seem like positions 20-40 are really slow AI, and 1-20 are quite a bit tougher.
I will admit that what causes yellow flags or doesn't is odd. Sometimes you get them and sometimes you don't, but I think it acts that way just to keep the game moving along. People have also mentioned the spotter being a little odd, and while I agree it's not a 100% accurate simulation, the spotter is quite sufficient in my opinion. He seems to almost always tell me what I want to know for the most part. Sometimes iRacing will keep saying "Outside. Outside. Car on your outside" over and over (which is good), NH2 sometimes just settles for saying "Easy, easy" if there is someone close by. It's not as specific, but it still clues me into what is going on well enough for NH2's arcade level of racing.
I'm also quite pleased with the graphics. People have mentioned it needs anti-aliasing, but mine was off by default. You can turn it on in options, and it didn't hurt my performance much. It looks much better with it turned on. I have everything on high except for shadows (medium), and it is running great. I love the bloom effect. It's a pleasant change coming from iRacing. Everything looks bright and lively.
I've done a couple hundred laps at Charlotte, about 100 at Atlanta, along with a few online races, and an Eldora race. So far everything has been enjoyable. I think the UI and menus are great. The menu music is also cool (it may grow old after a lot of hours of play time, but I'm pretty sure it can be turned off).
I'm running a 21:9 monitor, and the game runs fine with it. I also love the feature that lets me set the game to always run on my secondary monitor (which is my ultrawide that has my steering wheel setup in front of it). NH2 is the first racing sim I've played that lets me do it that way, and I am very grateful!
So yeah: Graphics, sound, wheel support, controls, menus, AI, and gameplay are all to my personal liking. NH2 is most definitely a sim-cade (not a fullblown simulator). If you want a fun NASCAR game, I think this fits the bill. Thank you, developers!

Bottom line: The Stanley Parable is an awesome piece of video gaming,
A little tip - play the demo BEFORE playing the full game. The demo is not acctually a part of the game, but more like a standalone introductory chapter to the game, and it will give you the taste of what this game is all about.
Which is necessary, because The Stanley Parable is probably unlike any other game you've played before.
Not much puzzles in here, not much action, not much of a big, complex story. Not much characters, not much music, and not much of anything you'd expect from a standard video game.
Without spoiling the experience too much (although, if you haven't played the game yet and reading through those reviews you're probably already spoiled!), I'd tell that the Stanley Parable explores the concepts of choices and consequences and narration in video games. And it does so very wittingly and and elegantly.
The game has many secrets and things for you to reveal and find out, and therefore the experience is based mainly on your will to explore and try out new things. And while you can "complete" the game within 10 minutes or even less, each gameplay can and probably will look completely different.
I've played the game for about 5 hours in total which I spread across many short "sessions" of playing the game, and I feel I haven't revealed the entire content of the game (even when using a walkthrough).
Technically, there's not much to say, the game is built with the Source engine used in the famous HL games, which is highly stable and still looks good even after aging quite a bit. You'll find out that the game has plenty of "atmospheres" throughout the different paths you can take, and it seems there was much thought put into every detail of the game, It plays fantastically, but as I said before, this is not a usual game.
I highly recommend it for anyone which can appreciate something a bit different, where the center is about how the story is told rather than the story itself, or rather than who's the next target to shoot

X: Rebirth is not an X series game. If you are trying to buy it while expecting such, dont. It is simply unsatisfying to play if you are looking for anything more complex than a space shooter.
The developers spent 7 years working on the game to release for console, so the interface, options, and controls suffer from that design decision. As of this review, there is no way to target enemies besides clicking on them, all the menus are radial and difficult to navigate, and overall the performace of the game, even on high-end rigs, is poor.
Being stuck in the same ship the entire game (The Albion Skunk, endearing..) is unsatisfying, especially when you see all the other cool looking ships flying around. Your co-pilot is annoying as humanly possible, your ship is invulnerable if you activate a drone, and you cannot carry any cargo inside of it. You have to hire other people to fly your other ships and carry cargo for you, and they have to be the most ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ pilots ever.
The combat is weak and unchallenging. Enemies have spawned inside other ships and inside stations on several occasions, or they will just spawn in empty space and sit there, doing nothing as you blow them up. Though, why you would blow them up is a mystery, as they never shoot at you.
The only good thing about the game is that stations look and feel truly alive and massive, with tons of npc ships flying around them and giving them satisfying feel. Unfortunately even this is ruined as the developers turned it into a minigame, making you fly and look at every inch of these massive stations to get missions and discounts. I won't even go into detail about docking and walking around inside of them, as that has to be the absolute worst part of the game, and you should live in fear of it.

Got this on sale for $5 and it's mostly excellent.
======
the bad
======
You are basically the d-list team fighting evil while all the cool stuff from Lord of the Rings is happening elsewhere.
Story is totally forgettable and non-canon as far as I know.
At the last location of the game, it's like QA completely ran out of time to validate anything. The framerate throughout the beginning of this section is choppy as hell, 2 specific rooms have absolutely bonkers graphics glitches, and I crashed multiple times during this section of the game. At one point, I had finally defeated the first phase of the last boss after 3 attempts - and the game crashed; that was a "ARE YOU F***ING KIDDING ME!?" moment. The first 90% of the game was pretty much bug-free during my multiple playthroughs minus a few rare game lockups during load screens. It's like the QA / development team just didn't have enough time to fix all the bugs in this game. It's freakin' great and smooth and nice like 90% of the time, but the remaining 10% are like no QA tester ever looked at it.
UPDATE: I can't really tell you why, but a recent playthrough in 1080p resolution didn't have nearly the amount of issues on the last map - no idea why though!
Solo with AI companions - there's not a way to easily see their equipment. You can quit, select a different character, manage their equipment, and repeat to set everyone's equipment the way you want - but that's pretty tedious. I never found it necessary to micro AI companion equipment - they upgrade themselves with random pickups just fine - but it seems bizarre that there's no such feature.
======
the good
======
combat, progression, loot, finding secrets - all of these systems are great and totally satisfying.
It really feels good to build up to an eviscerating strike on an enemy and then knock their head clean off, chop off an arm, or knock them down and skewer them for the finisher.
Getting a good hit streak and just going berserk on stuff is awesome, too.
The skill trees and stat point systems really provide a variety of playstyles and builds for each character, and all of them feel useful.
Active dodging and blocking, well done enemy tells, hit reactions, and misc animations - man combat is satisfying in this game.

Do I recommend playing this game? Yes.
What's the catch? Of course there's a catch:
STORY: The story in this is interesting, but don't expect some major twist. If you played the Third Age, it's kind of that same setup. Your mission is to support the fellowship by distacting Sauron's forces away from Frodo and gang. You'll meet the likes Aragon and Gandalf, but there's one problem: the voice acting. I'll give Gandalf's voice actor credit, he really tries to sound like Sir Ian, but he just falls short. Aragon's is just awful. It's not to the point where I can't listen to it, but don't be suprised when he sound's nothing like his film counterpart.
GAMEPLAY: The gameplay is what I imagine would happen if you took Dragon Age and Skyrim and paid them to make a baby. You've got the run around and find loot off of enemies and hidden chests like Skyrim (Yes, I know Dragon Age has it but I don't have to go find a Rogue whenever I find a chest in this game). The combat itself feels like a mix of Dragon Age, Skyrim, Arkham, and only the slightest hint of Gears of War. You have your two team mates that do somewhat support you unless you're playing in Coop (That's an entirely different discussion) and in a way it reminds me of Dragon Age, except that I have no control over them. It's like Skyrim in that there is no pause feature; you are constantly in the midst of the battle. It's like Arkham in the sense that you have really neat slow motion finishing moves occasionally (Yes, I know Skyrim has those, too, but I think that Arkham's has more in common with the style this game has). When I saw Gears of War, though, I don't refer to the cover shooting mechanic, I mean more of the coop system. Even in a singleplayer game, when you lose all of your health, you will go into a downed position and can slowly crawl to your teammates like in Gears. The constant, "Get on that turret!" command also seems reminicient of Gears to me, also. Aside from combat, you will be navigating a fairly linear world populated with breakable barrels, secret caches, and tons of Orcs. It's fairly simple in that regard. You progress through the level, break barrels for ammo, loot, and coins, occasionally stop at random places to purchase new gear or sell loot, and then carry on.
GRAPHICS: I would say these Graphics remind me of Dragon Age 2, particularly in the environment. The way it's textured and modeled just reminds me of it. The ground doesn't look like, say, Halo or Crysis where you look at the ground and think how pretty it looks (I know that sounds weird, but seriously look down sometimes.) The ground looks like it kind of all blends together and there is no distinct place where a rock sticks up or grass ends and sand or dirt starts aside from a bland change in texture on a flat face. The characters, on the other hand, are an entirely different story. The characters look really sharp and well rendered. The clothes flow when you run, there aren't random sharp edges on the character, etc.
OVERALL: Overall I'd say this is a neat game. If you like Lord of the Rings or want an RPG that you won't spend 50+ hours running around in like Dragon Age or Skyrim, absolutely invest in this game, but I'd stick to buying it on a sale. This game is by no means remarkable. It isn't going to astound you with its story, blow you away with its soundtrack or voice acting, etc. It's a game that manages to ride right in the middle where you'll enjoy playing through it, maybe play it again with some friends, and then occasionally look at it as you scroll through your Steam library and think how much fun it would be to play Shadow of Mordor which sits right above it.

Now I realize my review will be just another grain of sand on the beach of Normandy that was the disaster called X Rebirth and that my voice will most likely be drowned out by the shouts and cries of those others who purchased the title alongside me. Close to countless reviews found on just about any gaming website can elucidate the extent of the problems this game presented. I just wanted to highlight some that mattered most to me.
Given that it's near impossible to get a game released these days without a slew of bugs and glitches, I don't want to spend too much time focusing on those errors. That said, it is worth asking how on earth a company as established as Egosoft could have possibly thought XR was worthy of release. A few glitches here, maybe a bug or two in that feature there, sure but what they gave us was just an utter shock. And you have to imagine that at some point, they sat down during some meeting just before launch and said "well this is ready to hit the mainstream. We have a good product, a functioning product or at the very least a passable product but as we all know now, not one of those held true. NOT a one.

To be frank, as consumers we have a right to expect a game to not have at least half the bugs XR had, especially in a AAA title. I'm not implying that every game released be absolutely bug free, but I equate this to gas prices. At a certain point in time, our country raises gas prices from oh, let’s say $2.00 a gallon to $4.50. Of course we're outraged but this persists for such a long time that when they finally reduce the price to $3.95, we jump for joy and hug our pets in excitement. Again, I don't expect the gas to be free, but I expect it to be reasonable. The games that have been released over the last few years are akin to charging a good $6.00/g for gas and nowhere has this been more true for me than with XR.
I was so utterly frustrated doing the infamous 100 energy cell mission within the first hour of the game that my gf had to pull me away and take me to dinner to calm me down a bit but I let the game continue in hopes that my ship would find it’s way. Two and a half hours later and my freighter is still taking a sightseeing tour of whatever galaxy we're in (something I doubt I'll ever learn given the incomprehensible map system). Unfortunately, when I submitted for a refund 4-5 times, Steam laid this  as evidence against me stating I had played 20 some odd hours and therefore must have in some way approved of the product. Like most people I've spoken to or read about, the vast majority of that time was spent alt tabbed checking forums, practicing calming breaths, thinking about taking up religion again or going out to more dinners aimed at diffusing my ticking time bomb of frustration. Many others have stated this very thing in their own way and yet it shows us logging on more hours than we ever actually played.
SO that all said, let’s say the Egosoft fairy waived her magic wand, which I'm sure is rife with glitches and probably using the wrong batteries and fixed every bug and glitch in the game. Know what we're left with? An glitch free POS. Look, I'm not trying to be some kind of hater. I, like everyone else tried time and again to justify the money I threw away in this game. And like some others also stated, there is the skeleton of a game buried in there somewhere, but I really did try. I have everything to gain in liking this game given the brick wall I've ran into with steam customer service. All the bugs aside, the design decisions they made in this day and age are just beyond understanding. I understand these guys are based in Germany but could they really not afford getting just one guy, ONE GUY who speaks native English on their staff to share some phrases with them that would pass off better than "Go Boil your Head" or, "Nice talking to you...NOT". Forget how utterly annoying it is that nearly every NPC is angry at you for no reason....well wait, they all appear to be over 70 years old, so maybe they're just old grouches.....that are supposedly piloting space and building empires......sigh.., forget the annoyance, if you can anyhow, but the dialogue left me embarrassed for them in some odd way.  How full of yourself and out of touch must you be? And How many times did Bernd say the word "Immersion"? Yisha, the co-pilot is by far and away on my top three list of hair pullers. Forget her really creepy incomprehensible animation, not sure if she's pooping in her ventilated space suit, is she's part arachnid, fighting the urge to eat me, or doing calisthenics. What I don't understand is why they put her there. I know others have voiced this in their own way, but here's the bottom line. She doesn't do anything. At all. She doesn't pilot, trade, she is nothing more than a permanent plot prop piece. I've tried finding the woman who did the voice acting for her without success. Perhaps that's for the best. She doesn't need career changing advice from some yankee. But oh my sweet jesus is it awful. It again, ruins the whole immersion. Poorly written dialogue, made worse by the worst voice acting. Missions requiring me to go here to pick this up, then there to drop it off, then here to pick up something else, then there to deliver it. I'm a fed ex truck in space stuck on rookie training duty.
What i did find funny was how very early in the game, the crew to which Yisha belonged to paid me good money (I'm assuming its good since I haven't really had a chance to see an economy function) to keep her with me. It totally sounds like a made up excuse to get rid of her now that she's no longer on their ship. Out of the  literally 12 times I had to restart the game, that was the only thing that made me smile until I realized it was me they pawned her off on. If I could have ejected her from my latrine shoot, I would have right onto their windshield.
I mean the list goes on and on and on. The one thing everyone was really excited about, or at least most people, myself included, was walking around space stations. God what an exercise in frustration that was. Cookie cutter, with every NPC doing the same task  in the same corner. Every box and locker making the same sound and getting you stuck in the process 25% of the time. It was all just one big horrible horrible horrible experience. And they charged us $50 for it. They made a lot of money while many of us gave a significant chunk of our meagerly paychecks for something we were hoping would take our minds off our meagerly paychecks. Instead, I’m forced to face the harsh realities of just how much spending $50 on the wrong present for myself can impact my life in a negative way. I’ve since moved on but then I saw that Steam is finally allowing us to write reviews so here is me waving my hands telling anyone thinking of XR to change course, go somewhere else. Dive into an empty swimming pool and incur more enjoyment.
One a last note, I emailed egosoft early on and the Bernd man himself replied. I wont bother with the details cuz he didn’t give me any. It was short, condescending, blowing off my thoughts and recommendations and still full of himself with regards to that incredibly inappropriate “We’re a Success!” message he tied onto his failing apology. In short all that said was, we failed, you bought it, and we MADE MONEY OFF YOU!!! Yay!
Sigh. Hey Egosoft, if any of you ever read this, go and apologize. Not to us cuz that would take the remainder of your lives to do. Rather, apologize to every other gaming company for the bad faith you instilled in all the gamers out there that will inevitably think twice about purchasing something at launch. You screwed up the curve in the worst possible way. So to all of you that made these decisions to the ones that knew better but lacked the courage to tell those in power  what time of day it was and that they’re releasing a big failure, I say SHAME on you.

This is a top tier game, hitting every element that makes the classic Metroidvanias great without just reskinning the classics and makes the formula its own.
There's just so many great things about this game that it's hard to nail down a few to highlight for a succinct review, so I'll just offer up a random selection of features that make me love this game.
- The story is amazing, if a bit mysterious, without forcefeeding it to you, yet still creating enough attachment to the characters and the setting that you actually care what happens to them.
- Plenty of opportunities to properly sequence break, without built in secret shortcuts, but instead natural sequence breaks by a combination of a variety of movement abilities that can be applied in unexpected ways, and simply not patching out ways to bypass soft locks that should prevent progress from lack of appropriate movement ability.
- Beautiful art. Not much to say about this that you can't see in screenshots.
- Continued updates. There have been, so far, 2 free content updates, with more expected in the future. While fairly small, they add interesting additional options and story elements.
- Many ways to build. While you main abilities are set and doled out in classic metroidvania style, with charms you can focus your build towards how you like to play, and what may be needed to beat a given boss. While many players may have their preferred builds, there's enough variety that to bypass any one challenge two different players' "perfect build" may be wildly different.

Gameplay wise this is honestly my all time favorite JRPG. The game gives you control of up 18 characters at a time from a pool of hundreds, most of which have their own unique story line and a quest associated to them. Every character develops in their own way and loosely follow a unique leveling tree. However probably the best thing is that every character has their own individual weapon tree, class tree, skill pools, and leveling patterns, but you see NONE of them and they are constantly changing, the more you use a character the more they grow. The game adapts to how you play, depending on how you use a character that character develops to follow how you use them. If you go out and grind endlessly to make your party stronger, enemies will in return grow stronger to match your party, as a result the game constantly challenges you. It also has a pretty good story line, I am currently holding off on finishing the final sequence to finish the last of the side quests but I can say I was/am definitely emotionally invested in the story line. It doesn't have the GREATEST story, but it's definitely not just a mediocre story. It also has a stupid amount of side quests, I have 126 hours sunk into this game and am basically at the end of the game yet I still missed 2 side quests.
All in all 10/10 and I plan on playing the game through again on hard mode with a new game+ when I beat it. Best $10.00 I've ever spent.
If you do decide to get this game let me give you a few quick tips (things I wish I had known/was glad I knew) that I'll try to make as unspoilery as possible. (they probably won't make any sense until you reach said point in the story, but try to keep them in mind)
Every available side quest becomes unavailable as soon as you enter the area called the Aqueducts.
You can't defeat the fallen if you set foot in Underwalt, making an entire area of the game unavailable.
Talk to the Duke of Ghor after every time you clear one of the bases.

While there is a certain guilt I might feel for my actions towards other survivors, I ultimately justify my actions by believing that there was no other way. I'd rather it be us than them. I really felt attached to all of my characters and after I stopped restarting when one died, I began to realize the beauty this game offers. It's a unique, and somewhat chilling perspective on the side-effects of war.
I failed to protect some of these people. I believed they were invincible and many of my people died because of my delusions. On several separate occasions, I sent a scavanger to seek revenge for a comrade which ended up with more deaths on my hands... And it was weird at how troubled I would get: these were video game characters and I was guilty, even angered, by their deaths.
Winter was one of the most grueling gaming experiences I've ever had. There was this constant struggle to bring home enough food to eat and enough wood to burn. After a month, components started to become scarce and I was trading valuable supplies for it, so I could build equipment like water filters or to enhance my defenses.
The game kind of throws you in media res to figure everything out on your own. I didn't understand it at first but I eventually realized how symbolic that was: nobody really knows what to do when war breaks out.
9/10, I feel combat could be improved, there were a few times where I was trying to shoot a bunch of thugs and my scavenger would run right out of cover headfirst into them, which obviously wouldn't turn out so well. I'd like to see them add more content to the game: extra areas, more characters, more events, more weapons, more equipment, etc.
This game has a limitless potential and it's already quite the masterpiece.

Final Fantasy XIII reminds me of the South Park episode where we meet the Marklar aliens.  Replace every noun in FFXIII with Marklar and you would not be any more lost as to what is going on or why.  There is an entire encyclopedia that opens up as you play the game, but it only opens up when it feels like it.  I would figure having all the information ahead of time and studying said encyclopedia would allow the player a better understanding about the story from the start.  Then again, if I wanted to read a story about another world and people saving the day, I'd read a book, not play a game.
I made it 16 hours in and I'm still on rails, following character stories that I am barely starting to understand about characters that I really don't care about.  You jump from one group to the next with no real reason and lacking context of their world or situation.  I found it very difficult to connect to them in any way.  At least beyond the ideas of, Snow is an idiot, Hope is a cry-baby, Lightning is a robot, Vanille makes the most annoying sounds, and Sazh is what you would expect of people trying to be PC about a character.  My favorite character so far, is the chocobo chick that lives in Sazh's hair.  That little guy is more expressive than any of the other characters, and that's just out of his 20 minutes of screen time.
While times change, so do games and everything else.  Final Fatnasy XIII is less fantasy and more sci-fi.  Albeit 1970's, B-rated, acid trip sci-fi.  Horrible storytelling, un-relatable characters, constant tutorials, game mechanics that play the game for you, an unnecessarily convoluted leveling system(one that puts the sphere grid of FF-X to shame), and a world so lost in itself it requires a dictionary and encyclopedia to understand.  If you're new to the FF series, you might like it, especially if you are into sci-fi.  If you are one of the "old school" FF players, that loved anything 7 or under, you should skip it, the series is dead.
Oh, and motorcycle twins Shiva summons.  Yes, Shiva are twin sisters with wheels for hair that wrap their legs around each other and become a motorcycle for a character to ride around on.
Final Score:

One of the most compelling games I've played this year. This War of Mine puts you in control of a small band of intrepid survivors trying to survive in a battered city in the midst of a civil war. Every night you must scavenge the city for supplies, and every day you must trade some goods for others in order to keep your survivors fed, warm, healthy and happy. With realistic mechanics that deal not only with your survivors physical health, but their mental state as well, This War of Mine is a bleak look at the side of war video games don't show often enough. You are not a mighty warrior, cutting a swath through enemies with your machine gun. You are trying not to die while far greater powers struggle for dominance around you—something you almost never even get to see.
There are as many ways to play this game as there are people who play it. You can attack other survivors and steal their things—though this, of course, will have a huge impact on your survivors' morale. You can try to hoard some supplies and trade them out for food and materials, but if your supply runs dry, you'll swiftly starve. Events and your survivors are randomized, so the game has great replay value.
Is This War of Mine FUN? No, not in the last. At least not for me. But it's tremendously compelling, in the same way as a sad book or a Shakespearean tragedy. You don't need to be laughing or cheering to be deeply emotionally invested in a game, and This War of Mine proves that in spades.

This year’s iteration includes all three major NASCAR series (Monster Energy, Xfinity, and Camping World Trucks); the lower two series are essentially slower versions of the Monster Energy cars with different vehicle models and drivers. 2017 race rules are in effect, with stage racing and the new points system. Beyond simple quick races, there are single championships for each series (including just playing the 10-race playoffs) and a career mode where you start out in the Truck series and work your way up. Challenges give scenarios on specific tracks with specific drivers and objectives, but there is no countdown timer for when control becomes manual, leading to a lot of crashes until the timing is memorized. A split-screen mode and online multiplayer are also available, but there are no tutorials or racing line to learn each track. NASCAR Heat 2 is clearly designed with consoles in mind, with simplified handling and abbreviated controls; in-game information is hard to come by, as gaps to the car in front or how many laps of fuel are remaining are impossible to find. In addition, race starts and pit stops are automated and cannot be manually controlled. The spotter is very inconsistent, sometimes ignoring surrounding cars or giving useless information. Car handling is very tight off the corner (possibly because I am accelerating too early), but can be slightly adjusted using the setup options. Damage (minor contact sometimes causes damage, but flipping over may not) and cautions (Single car wreck? Yellow. Multi-car wreck involving the player? No flag) are inconsistent. The AI isn’t quite up to par: while it doesn’t do anything outrageously terrible, computer drivers routinely ignore the player’s position when deciding to go three-wide into a corner (which happens frequently), and they recklessly dive into corners when given a little room at speeds far too fast than normal. NASCAR Heat 2 is an arcade racing game through and through, exchanging accessibility for realism and showing cracks in several areas.

Bottom line: The Stanley Parable is an awesome piece of video gaming,
A little tip - play the demo BEFORE playing the full game. The demo is not acctually a part of the game, but more like a standalone introductory chapter to the game, and it will give you the taste of what this game is all about.
Which is necessary, because The Stanley Parable is probably unlike any other game you've played before.
Not much puzzles in here, not much action, not much of a big, complex story. Not much characters, not much music, and not much of anything you'd expect from a standard video game.
Without spoiling the experience too much (although, if you haven't played the game yet and reading through those reviews you're probably already spoiled!), I'd tell that the Stanley Parable explores the concepts of choices and consequences and narration in video games. And it does so very wittingly and and elegantly.
The game has many secrets and things for you to reveal and find out, and therefore the experience is based mainly on your will to explore and try out new things. And while you can "complete" the game within 10 minutes or even less, each gameplay can and probably will look completely different.
I've played the game for about 5 hours in total which I spread across many short "sessions" of playing the game, and I feel I haven't revealed the entire content of the game (even when using a walkthrough).
Technically, there's not much to say, the game is built with the Source engine used in the famous HL games, which is highly stable and still looks good even after aging quite a bit. You'll find out that the game has plenty of "atmospheres" throughout the different paths you can take, and it seems there was much thought put into every detail of the game, It plays fantastically, but as I said before, this is not a usual game.
I highly recommend it for anyone which can appreciate something a bit different, where the center is about how the story is told rather than the story itself, or rather than who's the next target to shoot

I'm running a championship with 25% distance races and tried increasing to 2x tire wear and fuel consumption. The AI had no clue that they needed to pit following the stages and instead started pitting a few laps into the second stage. After stage 2 they would also stay on track resulting in a green flag stop in stage 3 unless a caution came out.  I ended up changing the fuel and tire wear back to 1x because of this. I just ran the 1st Michigan Cup series race of the season and after stage 1 I pitted and for whatever reason the free pass car was Martin Truex Jr. No idea why or how he was lapped. I decided to follow him through traffic for a few laps. He quickly worked us back into the top 20 before I turned under him on the backstretch to try for a top 10 on the stage. At the end of the stage we were 8th and 10th. which having pitted and not needing fuel put us 1 and 2 on the restart.  I took off and the pack quickly started working us over after a few laps and we fell back into the top 10. I decided to hook back up begind him and started bump drafting down the back stretch to get us back out front. We had a 2 second gap over 3rd when he dropped to pitroad. they can and will race you hard if you have them set right. The game is really good. Few things to note: I tried this with an old XBox 360 wired controller and the handling was awful. Very sensitive and uncomfortable. A brand new wired Xbox One controller (bought for another game I had recently purchased the same day) and the handling is much much better. I don't know the specifics to why this is since I dont use gamepads often but keep this in mind I guess.
The AI at 105% with the default setups are too fast in qualifying but only fast in the top 10 during the race so most of your races without car setup adjustments will consist of you starting last and having to cut through the field. Using custom setups however, I get either pole or top 5 consistantly and completely destroy the field in race with the same setup, often by half a lap after about 10 laps. For the best experience in quickplay I'd suggest making a Q setup (old NHE ones from last year still work fine) but sticking to default race setup.
Another note is that most of my practice races were at Atlanta which currently has very worn racing surface. Despite this, the track behaves like its from 1997-2002 being freshly paved in other words very little tire fall off. Granted, I was running sprint races with 1x wear but even after 15 laps on 1x you should lost at least half a second. This isn't gamebreaking but just keep in mind the cars/tracks are simplified thus the tracks lack some personality.
IN SHORT: the game exceeds where it needs to. Hardcore players will always prefer iRacing and NR2003, but for console gamers or sim racers who just want a laid back offline experience with a solid career mode, much improved AI, the game does just fine. Don't bother with DLC skins of course, just buy the base game, you can just edit and create your own skins with UABE anyway like any other sim. I don't mind DLC and would consider buying some but they need to provide more things than just skins.

Honestly, I want to like X Rebirth, I really do, but it's impossible. I've bought several early access (alpha) games on Steam in the past, and they were all in a better shape than X Rebirth is. The current state of things means you have to be a masochist to play the game, it's just frustrating and full of bugs.
With another year of development, it might have been a decent enough game to stand on its own, but even if all the bugs were to be fixed, it will never really be able to live up to the expectations people who have played the previous X games have. It will never be able to compete with them as a sandbox game due to design decisions (really, one flyable ship?), it will never be able to compete as a trade/economy game since that entire part of the game is underdeveloped and completely devoid of any automation. Due to the horrid UI (to be honest, the X games have always had a horrid UI, requiring mods to use fully, but I thought that was going to be improved and streamlined for X Rebirth?), you can't really quickly see what's going on with your ships and the trades and so forth. Also due to the horrid UI, it will never compete with the old X games as a fleet simulator game either, since it's virtually impossible to organize and order your ships to do anything.
All in all, don't buy X Rebirth yet. Wait until the bugs are fixed (if ever) and buy it when it's cheaper and try to play it at its own merits, and not an X game. Hopefully Egosoft will realize their folly and release a proper X game in the future.

The Last Remnant is a role playing that has you taking charge of large groups of soldiers as you fight to protect your kingdom from the threat of the Conqueror.
The game is split between a world area, a battle area, and a world map, you control Rush Sykes the protagonist and move him about the world and then use the made too outside of different areas.

I do find combat can get a little hard but once you figure out which combination of group’s works and what tactics to give them then you’ll have to problems mowing down your enemies

Awesome game! Although it's a very linear game, it's still very enjoyable. At first you might think this game is just pressing x (auto-battle) constantly, win the battle, rinse, repeat, but just wait until you reach the part where the crystarium is unveiled. Basically after each battle you earn Crystogen Points and you use them to unlock abilities and stats on the Crystarium, which is a sort of FFX sphere grid. There are also 6 different roles, each of them having their own abilities, stats, and different magics. So for example you can assign one character the role of physical attacker, the other one might be a healer, and the last one might be a support character. Or maybe you want two attackers and one magic user! You choose their roles, and the beauty of it is that one character might have several roles in just one battle (especially the end-game content.)
If you're a hardcore rpger, just wait till you get to the endgame content, hunting marks and achievements, I assure you, you will have a great time, especially those bosses where you just can't find the way or tactic to beat them, and then you finally realize which combination of roles to use. In my opinion this is a very rewarding game.
Story-wise, I have to say that I really enjoyed the narrative and characters. Although there are a few lines that make you say "WTF was that?", I have to say that most of the script was pretty enjoyable.
I remember playing it back in the day when it came out, so this was my second play-through, and I have to say that I enjoyed it as much as the first time. Got the ps3 platinum trophy back in the day, and 100% now!
Finally, do I recommend this game?! YES YES! BUY IT NOW!
- Battle System (Very dynamic and action-paced, constantly changing roles)
- Graphics
- Voice acting (Both English and Japanese are great)
- Music (Hamauzu did a great job)
- Mark hunting is awesome! Especially the last ones
- Unstable fps :( (I recommend using Gedosato)
- Moms are tough
- Leona Lewis ending theme
- Corny dialogue here and there

Such a good game. I got this from watching Dunkey's "The Good Year" video, somewhat skeptical but intrigued based off the little I saw. What I got was a game deep enough to make me fall in love with it despite all the bugs. The gameplay as well is solid, with platforming abilities hidden around the world that make getting around fun without warping all the time, and combat tense enough to challenge you but simple enough to leave you responsible for the outcome. Be warned: minor SPOILERS ahead!
With that out of the way, let's cut to the chase. Gat Out of Hell plays very similarly to SR4, so if you weren't a fan of beating everything to a pulp in some of the most comical/creative ways possible, this game isn't for you. Sorry. Also, because of that fact, there will be more than a few comparisons between the two games.
CONS:
Starting with drawbacks, the game is, as probably expected, very short. Runs from beginning to end can take as little as 5-7 hours, tops (unless you're an achievement hunter). The same amount of time would translate to roughly 40% in its predecessor, just to put things into perspective.
The final boss fight against Big Red was, in a way, less intense than the Zinyak fight due to the fact he can be stunlocked. Yes, the Devil himself can be kept from doing ANYTHING. The Archdukes of Hell put up more of a fight than this guy, and to be perfectly honest, that's a little sad.
Lack of customizable weapons. In hindsight, this is more of a nitpick than a legitimate critique given the location, but a little creativity beyond the "fire and brimstone" themed weapons would have been nice.
PROS:
While the game is short, it is VERY fast-paced. Depending on whether or not you like a little breathing room between missions, the side activities have you tearing up Hell in a way no one could do in the Simulation. I often found myself content with dodging missiles in mid-flight (improvement from the UFO laser blasts while gliding).
Powers make an encore with a vengeance. Instead of doing homie missions to unlock the next element, you're encouraged to go out with what you have to activate the next one, get a crash course in using your new ability against waves of enemies that CAN kill you (no safe zones in Hell, genius), rinse and repeat. Oh so satisfying.
The Seven Deadly Sins - weaponized. Haven't found them all yet myself, but this was a large part of what sold for me during the trailer. Name at LEAST two other games that let you kick back in a virtual recliner and blow the s*** out of stuff.
Clever writing is not lost here! Thank God! Seriously, find as many of Satan's "Orientation Books for the D***ed" as you can. Just do it. Oh, and something about a musical...?
Finally, next to being able to play as Kinzie and Gat at anytime, is flight. Admittedly, it takes some getting used to, and feels a little clunky early on, but with practice and the Manuevering upgrade, you'll not want to go back to gliding anytime soon. Not to mention it makes collecting the Soul Clusters that much more fun.
FINAL VERDICT: 8.3/10 Would fly again. (Please turn to page 528).

Bottom line: if you enjoyed Saints Row IV enough to finish it, buy this, and continue the craziness.
Highs:
If you love freedom of movement in video games, you'll love the flight mechanic.  The Tomb Raider reboot disappointed me mostly because Lara controlled like a comatose linebacker, and this is the polar opposite of that.  It'll take you 7-10 minutes of play time to get super sprint, and your wings.  You're on a fixed momentum budget when you take wing, so it's still (mostly) unpowered gliding, but being able to dive low, and then swoop upwards, is liberating and fun.  As soon as I got those wings, I forgot about everything else and just flew all over hell, picking up over 250 clusters before finally carrying on with the missions.
The writing and humour remain strong in this game, and wacky non-sequiturs (such as Satan breaking into song, Andrew Lloyd Webber-style) abound, and the voice acting is solid.
Middles:
Although I've always been a little stumped as to why Johnny Gat is always spoken of as though he's the star of the series, I'm not bothered by playing as him.  I much prefer Kinzie's personality, though, so I've mostly been playing as her.  I love her sardonic wit, her undisguised contempt for convention, and her character model.  Using her to make my enemies say "teacup" is just plain delightful.**
In spite of the opportunity to create even more outlandish weapons than the Black Hole, Dubstep, and Disintegrator guns available in SR4, this game's weaponry is fairly lacklustre.  The armchair with gatling guns is the best of them, and it's a little cumbersome to wield.  They're not bad or unusable or anything, but I was expecting to be wowed, and I merely found them thematically appropriate.
Lows:
It's pretty short, but it's also nowhere near typical AAA launch prices, so it's worth what it costs, I just wish there were more of it.
Engine looks pretty dated.  The graphics aren't bad, but they're sub-par.  I don't really care, personally, but it's something you'll notice.
The one thing I can't forgive, however (and the reason I'm keeping SR4 installed) is this game's total lack of actor Keith David.  I'm not sure what they were thinking.  If this game were "Keith David Out of Hell" they could charge twice the price and I'd still gladly pay it.  I'd like to think that Keith made some sort of principled, awesomeness-based objection to participating -- something like, "I'm not doing a Hell scene unless I can be Spawn again" --
but I think Volition just really likes Gat for some reason, and once they thought up a titular pun, there was no going back.
** In SR4, we learned that "teacup" is Kinzie's "safe word" but the enemies don't actually say "teacup" or anything.  I was just making an inside reference.

Sins of a Solar Empire is one of the few game series that I was introduced to by a friend, instead of the other way around, and I am very glad I was. Despite being several years old already, Rebellion is still an extremely fun game to play. If you played the original Sins of a Solar Empire game, there are several new additions that make Rebellion a whole lot more fun. The enormous titan class ships are an excellent addition and loads of fun, and each faction also gained a 6th class of capital ship. With some DLC, you can also add new planet types and random galatic events to your game. Rebellion also splits each of the 3 races into 2 seperate factions, namely Loyalists and Rebels. This affects a few different technologies and changes what your titan is, but mainly it just decides whether you're friendly to other races or xenophobic.
If you've never played a Sins of a Solar Empire game before, but you like space-based RTS games, then I highly recommend getting Rebellion. The game caters to a myriad of play styles with the various races, each having their own aesthetics, mindsets and strengths and weaknesses. If you're a turtler and enjoy sitting back and slowly building up immense power and wealth (like me), the defensive and economic powerhouse of the Trader Emergency Coalition is for you. The Advent are based around culture and abilities, and while their ships may appear to be built mainly for supporting roles, when you bring them all together they form one of the strongest fleets in the game. If you are an agressive player then the high mobility and sheer offensive power of the Vasari is probably your best bet.
A word of warning is that games of Sins of a Solar Empire tend to take a long, long time to complete. While this can make single player a bit tedious after a while, Rebellion is an excellent game for playing with friends, either online or over LAN. Have a game over several nights, or a weekend, and I can guarantee you'll have hours and hours of fun!

This is a game that is hard to judge. On one hand, it is a short game that does little interesting mechanically; you run around, press left click to collect various kinds of food, and hide in bushes when an enemy is around, avoiding pretty standard patrol patterns. It's basically one long escort mission (thankfully the little critters that you escort have decent AI) through various levels, which in theory isn't at all that interesting. On top of that, I simply don't know if I enjoyed playing it; it ended up being a slightly stressful experience, which I didn't quite expect.
On the other hand, the game is exactly what it should be with the premise it has. The game is stressful because you feel like an unforeseen predator could attack, or the critters might get tired and need food, or something else might happen. Which is, naturally, exactly what a badger taking care of her young would feel. The mechanics are simple because, well, that's what the life of a badger is; simple. Not easy, but just not complicated. Gameplay-wise it's sound, it does a decent job explaining everything you're supposed to do and in the end I can't say that I wasn't emotionally affected by it. You do end up caring for your little wards, which is pretty much the point, isn't it?
In the end, if the game seems interesting to you, give it a try. It's not an inherently revolutionary experience, but it's not bad either. An above average experience which does get carried by an interesting premise. I just wouldn't expect a mindblowing experience.

This game stands out from the crowd, to say the least.
While seemingly just a knock off of everyone's favorite Smash Bros. franchise, this game throws you into a conceptual fighting game that requires a good amount of time and dedication to get the hang of. It's true, some of the abilities certain characters have are obvious imitations from SSB; most of them are used in conjunction with the rest of that character's kit. This introduces a larger field of outplay potential than most other games. A battle can demand constant focus as to where your opponent(s) are setting up to potentially annihilate you and in turn, makes you play accordingly.
Despite the roster only featuring 8 playable characters at the moment, you may find yourself playing one for hours and all of a sudden discovering a new combo you can perform. What also sets this game apart from the SSB franchise is that there are 3 attack buttons and a larger amount of air attacks, which amount to somewhere between 15-20 attacks per character.
Rivals of Aether is an incredibly complex game for how simple it comes off as and while you may find yourself encountering a lag spike occasionally, I wouldn't consider it to make the game unplayable by any means.
Through the combination of art style, music, SFX and mechanics, this game is definitely worth your money if you're at all into fighting games and even more so if you're a fan of the SSB franchise.

WARNING: This game feels like a beta at time of writing (01-Dec-2013) thus my review is based on this premise.
NOTE: Do not buy this game if you are expecting a perfect/completed game but do buy it if you want to participate in it's evolution. The initial release is a starting point and may feel unplayable by some but Egosoft are now formally adopting a public Beta update strategy.
There is no neutral recommendation status so this will have to stand as a recommendation, this game is not perfect by any stretch of the imagination but it does show promise which is why I will let my recommendation stand as a yes rather than a no.
First off, I know there are a large number of long-time fans of the X Series of games from Egosoft that consider this game a failure and alot of new comers who also feel the same. Some feel like Egosoft have perhaps been not as open about the nature of the game pre-release as perhaps they should have and others complain about the price of the game but putting things simply IMO the game is not too far off what Egosoft were pitching it as and it "will be" worth the asking price in the long run.
If you are expecting a perfect game from X-Rebirth then you are going to be sorely disappointed, there are plenty of flaws with the quality of the software even a fortnight after release but Egosoft are working hard to make things better so lets not dwell on what it is not and more on what it is...
X-Rebirth is an attempt by Egosoft to relaunch their X game series with an engine that is more upto date and an interface that is easier for new comers. The latter part is one which many people will dispute it has failed at with the user interface simplified too far and I do agree with this assessment to a large degree but I do believe there is hope of it improving sufficiently based on the current efforts of the X-Rebirth modding community.
One of the primary things that is new to the X-series in X-Rebirth is better native support for modding, more specifically the ability to have more than one mod loaded at once. Older versions of the engine did include native modding support but in general it barely got used since most people would want to use more than a single mod package. This change is a welcomed improvement and long overdue. Especially since several mods may currently be necessary to help the game meet the expectations of some long term fans. X-games in general have typically had a strong modding community and this would appear to be continuing with X-Rebirth.
Unfortunately at this time, there is not much positive that I can actually write details about but this game does feel to me like it has promise and from my experience with past X games written by Egosoft they tend to improve after release both with the efforts of the modding community and the on-going development by Egosoft themselves.
Update: 31-Aug-2013
The game is currently at v2.20 and there is a pretty significant patch due in the near future and when this is released I will probably rewrite this review from scratch. In the mean time I felt a small update to this review was required.
If you are considering the X games as one series of games then I would stop there. From X-BTF to X3:AP the X-games are considered the X-Trilogy which is based on iterative revisions to the original X-BTF game. As of X-Rebirth, pretty much everything is new (except for lore and perhaps a few ship models). X-Rebirth also brings the game engine design pretty much up to date in technical terms and still requires work in many areas but IMO is still worth getting and playing. No doubt if/when you start playing it you will find it lacking in some areas but Egosoft have been listening to and responding to community observations (mostly in terms of results - patch changes - as they are not really big on getting embroiled in the discussions) but they do have some changes that they appear to consider red lines (possibly due to the Level of Effort required to implement them). We do know they plan to release another X-Game in the future (believed to be a follow on from X-Rebirth) thus the best hope for the red-line changes being addressed is probably in that future title.

Before I begin: I have a couple of years of experience with Melee and Project M, and this review is mostly my first impressions.  Rivals is much like the Smash games, but it introduces some new mechanics for better or for worse.
The classic rock-paper-scissors of Smash is attack/shield/grab.  In RoA, the latter two do not exist.  In their place is a lone "parry" feature that cancels out the opponent's attack and stuns them for 40 frames (and reflects projectiles).  In theory, this was intended to make the game more aggressive, but in my experience with netplay, it seriously hurts the neutral game.  Parrying a move is much more advantageous than blocking it would be if you had the option, and it is equal to or better than hitting the opponent with a combo starter... so obviously it's kind of busted.  Rivals' answer to this is to make the first hit of jab not recieve stun from a parry, and also to make it cancelable into any tilt.  I haven't made up my mind on whether or not this is worse.  The tutorial also teaches parry baiting, which is basically the same as spotdodge baiting, except it also removes things like OoS options and shield pressure (as a Falco player, the absence of the latter is disappointing).
There's also no ledges.  Melee ledges are really dumb (even as someone who religiously grabs ledge when the opponent is offstage) so I can see why this change would be explored, but in practice it seems to really hurt Zetterburn (PM Wolf, basically) most and Wrastor (Marth + Puff +  Falco, also the best character in the game) least.
As for the mechanics it borrows from Smash games:
Directional airdodges, and thus, wavedashes, are possible.  They accept digital inputs, do not put you into special fall, and can be buffered.
SDI does not actually take smash inputs at all.  The tutorial introduces it in the context of escaping multihits, but in my experience, there are practically none of those that are actually exploitable, so... I guess it's just an addition to combo DI?
Speaking of controls that aren't the way they should be, the right stick charges smashes when held, which is quite disappointing from a game that borrows so much from Melee since only Smash 4 does this.  And also like Smash 4, netplay is more often than not a lagfest.  I've had better experiences here than with For Glory, however.
...And now that I have torn as much out of this game as I can, it's still the best Smash-like experience you'll find on Steam.  I got it for less than $10 and it's easily worth it at that price, especially if you intend to play locally with other people.  There doesn't seem to be a huge scene for it, but it's fun enough to deserve one.

Was this worth my $20? Long story short, no. Do I regret buying it though? Also no. The game has its flaws, and I feel it doesn't really measure up to Saints Row IV or its Christmas DLC (which is apparently no longer canon as of this game. Sad, I really liked that DLC) as a result of those flaws, but I still had fun with it.
Let me get my biggest complaint out of the way right off the top: You bothered to put in the time to collect 100% of the clusters so you could max out all your powers? Well too bad! You can't. There are 940 clusters in this game, and purchasing and upgrading all of your powers would take at least 1120, if my calculations are correct. Unlike SRIV, which left you with a ton of clusters you'd never use, in this game, it's impossible to max out all your powers, so you have to pick and choose which ones you want to max (it would have been nice to know that BEFORE I spent clusters willy nilly grabbing every upgrade for the never-used 'Summons' power). Now if this were some sort of class/build-based RPG, that'd be fine, but this is a Saints Row game, and I expect to be rewarded for taking the time to collect everything.
Beyond that, the game lacks a lot of what gives Saints Row games their personality, such as 80s pop music and a large cast of colourful characters. Saints Row IV was a bit bland in the post-game, but this game feels very empty and lifeless. Makes sense for the setting, I suppose, but it could have been handled better. I miss being able to dress up my characters however I see fit, and buying things from actual shops. I miss being able to store/recall and/or modify vehicles (even though vehicles have been worthless since Saints IV). I even miss being able to taunt or compliment random passersby (I tried binding those actions to keys in the key setup menu, but it refused to bind those actions, probably because they didn't want to make taunts or compliments for each character). I really miss the "Death From Above" attack from Saints Row IV, since it's still possible to hover in midair, and it even still uses the same animation. With the new flight mode, it seems like it'd have been a perfect fit, but it was taken out for some reason.
Now on to the positive: The flight is fun. It's something that was SORELY missing in Saints Row IV, and I really enjoy screwing around with it. It takes a good while to get the hang of, and even longer to master, but when you do, it feels pretty natural (at least for mouse and keyboard, but I can't imagine why you'd be playing this game with a controller). At least one of the new powers and a couple of the new weapons are interesting. Not really anything too special, and I'd rather just take the Saints Row IV weapons and powers any day, but interesting. Switching off between Johnny and Kinzie is kind of a neat little gimmick, even though it seems to be mostly if not entirely a cosmetic difference (it feels like Kinzie takes damage faster, though I may just be imagining that. Other than that, the only difference I see is in the final boss fight, depending on who you are when you go into it). The humour is okay, though that's to be expected of Saints Row.
tl;dr: It's not as good as Saints Row IV or the Christmas DLC, I'm sad that the Christmas DLC is no longer canon, I'm not happy about not being able to max out my character, and I feel the price was much higher than it should have been, but I still enjoyed it, so I can't say I don't recommend it. I give Gat Out of Hell a C+.
