There aren't many JRPGs on PC, and on the surface it seems like The Last Remnant fills that gap to a T. The problems, and there are many of them, appear when you look deeper at the game; for most people, this will likely happen upon reaching a boss battle that seems (and may potentially be) impossible to win. If you can get past that, though, it can be a fun experience.
The first major problem with The Last Remnant is the battle system. Some of the decisions made by Square Enix are impossible to understand, as if battle mechanics were decided by throwing darts at a dart board.
To participate in battles, you need to create unions. These groups of up to 5 characters fight as a single entity (for the most part) in combat. When you take these unions into combat, you are given up to 5 generic commands (like an all-out attack, or healing, or inflicting ailments) which feature appropriate ability usage from each unit in the union. The issue is that you have no control over the specific abilities as well as no control over the general commands you give to your unions, leading to situations where you cannot use the command or specific ability you want for no reason at all.
Secondly: QTEs. Like some other modern turn-based RPGs such as Paper Mario, The Last Remnant uses quick-time events (QTEs) to keep the player engaged. In The Last Remnant, each QTE is a single press of one of 5 buttons, with the other change-up being how fast you must press it. Compare this to a game like Paper Mario, where abilities and attacks will generally each have their own unique interaction, and it's easy to see how tedious The Last Remnants QTEs can be.
Compounding upon the lack of variety and utilization of skill is the fact that QTEs in The Last Remnant can have an inordinate impact on the outcome of battles. Hitting QTEs successfully has several impacts on battle: 1) The next unit in the union has its turn come immediately after a successful QTE. 2) Hitting several QTEs in a row leads to automatic critical hits for the rest of the units in the union, provided you hit their QTEs as well. 3) Units can "reconsider" their attacks, changing what attack they are doing to what they feel is more appropriate, which is almost always a better option than their original one.
Worst of all, QTEs are random. They don't always show up, and you have no impact on when they do. Then, due to how impactful QTEs are, a battle can swing simply on whether or not QTEs show up.
Then there's the issue of leveling. The game gives you no information on how its non-traditional leveling works. Your units gain stats, new or upgraded abilities and your "Battle Rank" (BR) goes up every once in a while after battle. However, the game doesn't tell you that your BR is the measure of *the opponents strength*, where a higher BR makes enemies stronger in an attempt to have the game have a smooth difficulty curve. It also doesn't tell you that your BR isn't directly tied to your characters' strength, and you can use meta knowledge to have your BR stay low relative to your characters' power by fighting only the efficient battles. Unfortunately for average players (myself included), this leads to situations where you may fight most battles you come across and *hurt* yourself in the long run. And, again, due to lack of information, a player that falls into this pit won't know about this problem until they reach an impossible fight and search the internet for help, only to find out that everything they've done in the game was wrong and they may very well have to restart the entire game to fix it.
As you can see, there are many problems (and more I couldn't fit in this review) with The Last Remnant. It is a strategy game with a distinct lack of strategy in places where strategy should shine, and an RPG where how one levels is completely unclear to those who don't metagame. A dedicated player who researches can get past these problems, but the average person will become stuck and frustrated, thus I cannot recommend The Last Remnant.

Many negative reviews of this game are due to a misconception by that player. They are looking at this from an objective, shoot-to-thrill stance that games such as Call of Duty has instilled in them. They argue about the game forcing a moral code on them, they scream at some characters having skills/traits with no discernable impact, they scream that this game is not really a game.
Cause this is not a 'game', in the traditional sense.
This is an artistic expression, a view of the toll of war on civilians lies that only comes from one who has lived it. And the creators have indeed lived it, according to several interviews. You cannot go into This War of Mine, bringing in expectations and attitudes from other games. This isn't one of those typical games. Yet, for a game, it is surprisingly well done.
Looking at the game angle on this, This War of Mine has a very unique art direction with blinding lights, visibly dark rooms, and a vague pencilly fog of war for many areas. This was done from the perspective of someone who has lived in these dark houses, who's own eyes got adjusted to the low light and everything in the room was just so much visible. And when that sunlight comes in, it almost sears your eyes. The characters are unique, they have a life about them, and many of them you care about them beyond just what skills they bring to the table. And they all have useful traits, you just got to know when to best apply them. Want to have minimal morale loss when it comes to necessary killing? Send Emilia. Want to boost someone from depression? Send Zlata. (Well, Anton I can't yet figure out. I don't know WHAT his skill does. No one seems to really...). The music fits, the characters fit, the 'quests/events' fit. The game is designed around it's main statement about surviving war. It does not sacrafice stuff, to be more gamey, like some other games have. It isn't trying to cater to consoles or with cutting edge graphics. It's Master is first, and foremost, the story of war.
I could say more about how I think the inability to save is brilliant (You have to actually live with your consequences, but this is frustrating to a perfectionist like me. I must of restarted 10 times cause I didn't do a run perfect. Finally I decided just to..go with the story), or about how impressed I was with how the creator appealed to people on Pirate's Bay (He had a good product, he wanted people to enjoy it. He wanted this story to be heard).
My only one 'gripe' with the game, is that I want more. Not sure how more is possible, but I want more. Content, DLC, Patches that add things. Expansions. Whatever. More. Gimme. I know this game was finanically viable by November 16th, two days into it's sales. We are now nearing the one month mark, and I hope the game is still making them a profit.
But again, do not mistake this for just a game. It is artistic expression, interactive storytelling, walking beside you as you see a story on the horrors of war. The point of the game isn't to win, to kill all the enemy or really survive. The point is to look at what the creators saw, look at what they are trying to tell you..and to understand.
Simply sublime.

How much you enjoy this game probably depends a lot on if you can get it working acceptably. First up, my Thrustmaster wheel wasn't recognised, so over to Xbox controller. Game starts in a fullscreen window and has no in game way of setting an exclusive fullscreen, so unless you use an Aero desktop on W7 you will have broken vsync. Had more than a few crashes to desktop after launch with an "oops.." dialog box.
There are no problems with a tiny interface like Assetto Corsa here, the UI is so big it can be seen from space. Unfortunately, I experienced a horrible frameskipping that occurs momentarily every few seconds. No amount of fiddling with nvidia inspector could fix it even though CPU, GPU and memory were far below being maxed out (the GPU working at a pedestrian 30%). UI graphics are OKish, but rather low res, in game graphics are simple, clean and quite nice except for some very intrusive shadow draw-in which occurs right in front of your car at a static distance.  The views are terrible for sim racers. The bonnet camera is set very high and it's really a roof camera, the behind car view is OK for arcade racing but the in car view is so far back you may as well be sitting in the back seat. The view outside the car is a paltry third of the screen. There is no seat adjustment or FOV control to speak of.  There is also, other than the mirror, no look back view, which is a rather mystifying omission.
Pit crew animations are really good. Music is not. When you fire up Project Cars you're greeted with a tune that conjures up feelings of driving back from the opera in your BMW. Well, the music here will remind you of waking up covered in your own vomit in the toilet of a seedy bar. "Chemical Weapon" song? Seriously.
Overall, there maybe a fun racer in there if I could get past all the broken bits. Not everyone seems to suffer the framerate/vsync issues but many do if you read the discussion threads.  Unfortunately the game ends up more Buddy Bretherton than Cole Trickle. On the positive side, I don't live next to the guy that selected the soundtrack.

I really wanted to enjoy this game...
Ever since it was first announced I was really excited because it seemed that the Duels game I've always wanted was finally going to arrive: a free-to-play platform that wasn't pay-to-win, would continously update with new sets in the real-world card game, would bring back Two-Headed Giant and possibly add new modes in the future, and would have a diverse card set to freely build any deck with. Of course, cross-platform play was excluded, but at the time I didn't care too much as I knew I would mostly play here on Steam. I was a bit bothered when Wizards failed to communicate with the community about release dates and such, but in the end I waited patiently for it to finally release on Steam.
Now while the game did deliver what it promised, it ended up vastly failing to reach my expectations. First of all, while Two-Headed Giant did return, chat was removed. In which rational universe is this considered a good idea? It was there in previous iterations of the Duels. Why did they think this would be a good idea? It was just like Nintendo removing chat from Splatoon, a multiplayer shooter in which communication with a team really makes a big part of the fun. Did Stainless remove this feature because they feared online harassment? That is easily solvable with an option to mute players or turn off chat altogether. There is no reason chat should have been removed. Also, you don't even earn gold from Two-Headed Giant... what the hell?!?! What is the incentive then to play that mode?
Also, after several years of the Duels franchise and dealing with bugs, you would think that now in 2015 they would finally have been able to pull off a relatively painless and stable release. But no, this release is riddled with issues, glitches, and constant server downtime. It seems that the servers go down for at least a few hours every single day since it was released. People are encountering glitches where they don't get the gold they earned from duels or from what they have paid real money for. When the gold grind is a central aspect of the game, it's a waste of everyone's time when you put a lot of work into a duel and the servers crash so all that work was for naught. There was even one day where the game was inexplicably down for at least 6 hours straight in the middle of the day, and there was absolutely no word from Wizards or Stainless in regards to the situation.
Also, while I haven't unlocked the entire set of cards, from what I've seen and heard it's a very poor representation of the Duels set and Magic altogether. You can get 4 of every common, 3 of every uncommon, 2 of every rare, and 1 of every mythic. This isn't how it works in Magic, and I don't know why this was implemented. In real Magic, a play set consists of 4 of everything, excluding lands of course. I've heard from various people that the entire Duels set is not even included in this game, and what they have included are mainly the most basic of cards. I understand that it's a free-to-play game and is meant to teach new players the rules in hopes that they would buy the paper card game. But changing the way things work in Magic is unfair to those new players as well, and they will go into the paper game with wrong information when it comes to deck-building and what not. It's just another scumbag tactic employed by Wizards and Stainless. Also, the story mode shows that the AI has a lot of cards that are restricted to only the AI, and a lot of them are really unfair making the story mode quite difficult at times. This could easily scare off a lot of new players. Why could those cards not be added to the available pool?
They added a daily gold cap of 200 to the game after they had said in an interview before that no cap would be added. Eventually they raised it to 400, but still... And also, the daily and community quests continue to suffer issues where players aren't receiving their rewards, or quests are not resetting.
Sadly, I can't really tell you to not play this game so that we can teach Wizards a lesson and get them to give us a better game. The truth is, they could care less. They already ignore the fanbase in regards to all the issues with this game that people are encountering. In the end, make your own choice with this game that will make you happy, but be aware of the big issues present in it. I'd be willing to play again if they would just fix their servers so there isn't a daily downtime that may cause me to lose progress or any rewards I should have earned for my work. Chat and incentives for Two-Headed Giant are also a must. But until then, I can't recommend this game.

The core gameplay is fine, what with it being MTG and all, but this little PC port could be called an unworthy successor, what with multiple technical issues and design flaws throughout it.
Deckbuilding? Good luck navigating the maze that is your card collection, and don't use the "Deck Wizard". You see, the Deck Dictator actually forbids you from making any deviations from its suggested cards, even when you've finished the deck and want to make some changes to it. It's good only for learning how many lands you should put in a deck.
Story Mode? As confusing and disconnected as the whole affair was, what irked me the most was the true source of the bosses' difficulty; your own deck. Not only are there many bosses whose decks are built perfectly for countering yours (Not the final bosses of the campaigns, mind you; you'll have more trouble with some random hermit witch than with a council of ancient demons), you cannot make the slightest adjustment to the premade deck given to you to respond, even though half the strategy of these games is supposed to be building and adjusting a good deck.
The UI? It apparently hates people who like to bluff or change their minds, considering the moment you pick up a creature or untargeted spell, you can't put it back in your hand; it'll be played once you let go no matter where the cursor is and you can't go back on it.
The servers? Well, want to play sometime during the afternoon? Maybe late morning? Impossible!
You might like this game if you play Magic and want to do it on the PC. Do remember that I said "might", though.

In its current state I cannot recommend Beyond Earth, and I have been playing Civ since 1992 with Civ 1.
The game has its bright spots, and can be fun at times, but frankly the whole system is just broken. There are too many unbalanced aspects to the game (trade routes, battlesuits, planet carvers) that make it too easy to exploit the system to win no matter what.
The AI is so bad, and I mean BAD that it makes me want to cry. The AI in this game makes Civ 5's AI seem hyper-intelligent and cunning by comparison. It's just illogical, stupid, easily exploited, and irrational. And when it comes to diplomacy the AI gets even worse.
The wonders are boring and weak, which is a big deal considering wonders inject tension and the occasional rush into civ games, even when at peace. In Beyond Earth, most wonders aren't even worth bothering with. Aside from the Gene Vault, I can't actually remember or name any of them, they're so not memorable.
The soundtrack to the game is actually quite awesome. I'm happy that Firaxis allowed us to download it separately so we can listen to it outside the game. The music really stands out as top-notch.
Multiplayer is pretty much unplayable. Period. Don't even bother.
And I'm writing this review AFTER Firaxis has released the first major patch to the game. It fixes maybe 10% of the game's issues, and that's being generous.
It'll probably take 2 or 3 years for Firaxis to flesh out the game and really finish it. After a couple of expansions and maybe 6 or 7 major patches it may be worth playing. Until then I advise holding off.

As someone who never really played a stealth game before, I had a lot of fun with Hitman Absolution. Its not a perfect product, but its polished and just plain fun to play, which is what really matters in a video game.
Hitman: Absolution  is designed so that you can play it however you'd like: you can slink around in the shadows and never be seen, you can take someone out and don their outfit, or you can shoot your way through the enemies; as long as you reach your target, its Mission Passed. There is a score system that pushes the player towards a stealthy approach, but unless you are concerned with leaderboards and beating your friends' scores, they don't really matter.
I found the funnest way to play HItman: Absolution is to buy into the games' gimmick and put on a disguise, carefully plan my movements, and use the games' Instinct mechanic (which makes it harder for enemies to detect you) to navigate to the target. The shooting in the game is serviceable, but not good enough to play through the game as a third person shooter. I found a more traditional Hitman approach to be much more rewarding.
The story is nothing special, but well handled and intriguing at the least. The real aspect of note in Absolution's production is the voice cast; Powers Boothe, Keith Carradine and Vivica Fox (among others) join David Batesman (Agent 47) with some cheesiest lines in a video game in recent years. The writing is quite good, and the whole game has a great balance of self-serious and over-to-top themes (especially some of the more extravagent costumes)  that keep the game interesting.
A few cons:
The cutscenes have an odd smokey effect that is just plain unnecessary and detracts from the storytelling.
The scenario of the AI deciding that you are not a threat after losing sight of you for 30 seconds, despite you having murdered any number of their comrades, is still very much a part of the game. I understand this may be because IO Interactive wants to accomodate all playstyles, but again, I think this detracts from the game.
There are a few areas in the game with ridiculous lighting that cause the game to drop to around 40 fps down from the rest of the game running at a smooth 60. The difference is noticeable (at least to me) and takes me out of the moment a bit.
All in all, a very fun game that keeps the gameplay interesting and entertaining for the whole playthrough.
The game took me about 14 hours to beat with my playstyle, which is quite good and long for a non-open world AAA title.
Highly recommended.

I'm sorry. I really wanted to like this game. I have looked forward for a decade to someone making a worthy successor to Alpha Centauri, and I figured Sid's team would do it. Instead, we got a fairly boring version of Civilization.
The factions do not have any well-defined philosophy or attitudes. Instead, they sort of morph into one of them matching you and the others opposing using the affinities. The philosophical questions that AC raised in its story telling are gone. In its place, we have a bunch of small laugh quotes, not all of which make sense.
There's no sense of wonder or grandure. When you finish a wonder project, you see a static blue print screen. There's no sense of having completed something awesome like the movies of other Civ games. And when AIs complete projects first, it's just a small notification, with no sense of having missed out on a great opportunity. The tech tree of Beyond Earth has items so generically named that it is impossible to really grasp what any tech does from just its name, making it hard to aspire to any given technology.
The mini quests are just bizarre. Why do I have to choose between the ultrasonic fields protecting my traders or having an extra bit of range? Why wouldn't a civilization just build two different types of ultrasonic fields? Why not make these separate entries in the tech tree? Beyond the game play problem here, the dialog to justify some of these choices is just painful. False choices, misleading phrasing, and just plain stretching the point abound in those dialogs.
The game mechanics are all well and good, and I'm sure the patch will provide some game balance. But what this is TOTALLY missing is STORY. It is just a very long game of tactical positioning with no style points. Stick with Civ 5 or go back to Alpha Centauri. Or, as several others have suggested, try Endless Legend. But this... this just isn't worth the money.

2 mins in, I had purchased a 4 pack for me and some buddies. I was actually sat on the edge of my sofa waiting for the game to install.. It looked complex from what I could see.. but hey, that makes the game better!
Now as much as I want to recommend the tutorials..  it did take me 3 hours to run through all the tutorials, just because they're are as boring as hell to do. They did however prepare me for some basic gameplay so in I jumped ready for some action!
Now skipping past my first few games, or the learning phase, as I call it. I put myself against 3 Ai and no word of a lie, it lasted over 9 hours. For fans of older games like 'Birth of the Federation' 'Star wars Supremacy' 'Homeworld' or Civilisation, then be prepared to lose yourself inan absolutely incredible stratagy game!

Fantastic HoMM-style turn-based strategy RPG built around Norse mythology marred by some poor game design choices. Your favorite hero and his units will transfer between missions so this means if one of your super-units dies you can potentially throw the campaign. The terrain control mechanic is a great visual representation of your area control but I find it downplayed in many missions because of a turn limit or boss rush. Hero customization is diverse and has more options than HoMM but they are slower to level up. Although it has aged poorly, this is a great HoMM alternative that is worth checking out if you're a fan of strategy games.

It is sad, but true, that evidence indicates that Egosoft does not seriously beta test their games before release. It is now the first of December and there are, other than technical issues, still problems with the campaign mode, which should have been picked up by beta testers. It is a very pretty game though I suspect that modders will make it far prettier. What has frustrated many old supporters is the lack of all the old functions which made the previous X games complex but also relatively automated. The drones for instance are limited to Launch and Smart Defense. The ships captains don't appear have the functionality to trade independently. You are limited to flying one ship which you don't get to choose, though it's equivalent to an armed yacht. The AI is more prone to "breakage" where they stop functioning because there's no "Failure" Loop. Wait to buy until the second quarter of 2014, when Egosoft may have fixed some of these issues - or the modders have.

If you attempt to play through this game normally, even reading all hints, tips, and tutorials the game gives you, you will never fully learn or understand the battle system. It's a really cool battle system, in fact my favorite turn-based combat system, incorporating a little (dumb) use of RNG. This should be a fatal flaw of the game design by not telling you all the basics of a JRPG game, but it's fun if you figure it out. I had to reinstall and try this game three times before it clicked.
Things you should know before considering playing this game:
1: This is the Dwarf Fortress of JRPG's in complexity so you will probably need to read the whole game wiki to FULLY understand and prepare your unions/parties/units
2: If you are too low of a battle rank, the game is hard. If you are too high of a battle rank, the game is hard. If you grind, you will get punished. Basically, if you reach a point where a battle is super hard, you've either ♥♥♥♥ed up or you're just not high enough level. The game doesn't give you a clear idea of which it is.  By "grinding", I mean heading to an open field with monsters and clearing it all out just for the sake of grinding. If you're on your way to an objective or on a quest, do fight.
3: If you HAVE to battle, DO NOT BATTLE A SINGLE MOB AT A TIME. Battle Rank raises depending on the amount of battles you have, not experience from battles. Try to get every single possible mob in one chained link, then initate the battle. If it's too hard with all those monsters, do one by one anyway.
If you didn't read everything I typed above this line of text then do not play this game.
TL;DR it's an extremely complex game that offers zero explanation of it's systems because there's no tutorial or visual presentation of information, but the high points are addictive and very fun.

kay...Im going to re-recommend this now that I have completely finished the game.
Overall my thoughts..Its fairly decent and in ways i can see why people considered it an underrated RPG. It has a lot of highlights and from in somewhats I say it has the beginning elements of a battle style that is currently in final fantasy 13, only its heavily modified. Now to be fair, there are good things about this game and then there are some WTF moments because this kind of game..you don’t normally expect stuff like it.
I shall try my best to not spoil any game play, but no promises..
First off. This game is well worth the money and honestly, it is a game that, if you can get into it you can waste a good 80+ hours on. If I had spent my time maxing out my characters then I could of done this but I decided to go the casual route because it would take far too long for me to invest time into the characters.
This game is also is about 13GB on your drive so expect a huge chunk gone when you install it. Not that size is a problem, it makes up greatly for its long story line as well as its ability to visually please those people who think graphics are a major concern. So yes, this isn’t FF7 style graphics or anything, its more on the lines of FF13 despite this game coming out before it.
As for game play the over world is rather enjoyable. There are many animations that go on within the scenery depending on location and in someways it can make you sit there to watch the view. I do wish they added the option to take pictures because some areas of the game is very nice and worth looking into for projects or hell even a background on a PC.(yes i have done this.)
Moving into the main aspects of the game, The lead character is..well..like most other RPG characters I see nowadays, being that hes slow, an idiot at times and makes you want to slap him through your monitor because hes so...eh..but more onto the game play, unlike most other console style RPGs you actually get a ton of characters to play with. You can have up to 50 max, 18 in battle, but there are restrictions.
Battle mode is something you shall be in often as everything is centered around it. This game unlike other RPGs does not really have an minigames, but instead they give you a ton of side quests to do, however more on this later. Main point on the battle mode is that its entirely based on 1). your health 2). your morale and 3). luck.. So basically anyone with luckhax, you may enjoy this game greatly. Also just because the game was made in 2008 does not make it a bad game at all.
One thing I loved (and will be downloading later) is the Soundtrack.. I found it rather addicting, especially when you are over-leveled in battle at times. The music keeps you active, pumped and ready for more fun as it keeps being dumped upon you time after time. If anything the most memorable thing would be the soundtrack in my opinion, but again it is just my opinion.
Controller support for this game is fantastic. Not only that it naively supports the PC keyboard and mouse(not that I recommend) but it also supports third party controllers especially for big picture mode which is win. XINPUT is also supported so xbox controllers are available here as well.
On a minor note. the game actually runs fine on Linux for you WINE users out there. Didn’t bother testing controller support, My controller was undetected with big picture mode but worked with every game, even games that are designed only for the xbox controller.
Now, for the bad side of things.
1. Grinding. You start off the game rather slow, and it seems easy at first but then your hit with enemies that are completely BS at times especially the bosses because they often get more than one turn and near the end of the game you actually have to watch out because they gain the ability to attack up to 10 times in a row killing you entirely. But yeah, grinding in this game

I was not pleased with the changes made to Bioshock Remastered, there has been very little in the way of improvement particularly with the graphical sheen of the game. In fairness, Bioshock was an outstandingly beautiful game which brilliantly sold it's style and immersed players in it's dystopian underwater city named Rapture. This "remaster" is not only stagnant, in various ways it's a regression. In 8 hours of play, I experienced half a dozen situations where the game executable simply gave up and culmitavely wiped hours of progress. Not only does this make losing large chunks of game progression a risky threat it also annoyingly resets the games graphics, audio and gameplay settings each time it happens. In addition the map/quest sub-screen suffers from a two second delay in opening, a bug which was not present in the original Bioshock
Bioshock is an incredible game, even 9 years on from it's original release, it's world, it's characters, it's story-line and the delivery are all fantastic elements but this edition of it is simply not the optimal way to experience the game. It is a free update to those who owned the original Bioshock so that has to be taken into consideration but it's no excuse for a lazy and backwards stab at delivering this iconic game.
The developers have stated that a patch is in the works to aid with the crashing problems and menu freezes but until then would you kindly just play the original Bioshock?

The Last Remnant is one of the best fantasy role playing games from the 2009 era that I have played on PC. The visuals are what you would expect from a modern day game and the cinematics remind you of playing a Final Fantasy game.  The Last Remnant received below average reviews on the Xbox 360, but don't let that dissuade you from giving this one a try on the PC. Most of the bugs/problems were fixed outside of some noticeable texture pop-in. You can pause anytime in the game including the CG scenes! You can even skip the CG scenes if you doing a 2nd play through. The auto save feature will save your progress after each battle ensuring that you will never have to replay an hour of gaming session due to your gamble on a strategy to defeat an enemy. These are the features that I have been waiting for ever since I started playing RPGs.
A few things to note, this game requires a lot of forum reading. Not as much for the story progression as it is fairly linear, but more to understand the mechanics of the battle/formation system. Square Enix took a new direction in the battle system allowing for a very diverse and strategic game play but the in game tutorials will leave you scratching your head as to what is happening during the battles. This has to be the biggest issue that I have with the game. After reading the FAQs and forums I found that many others had the same questions that I ran into and most where answered in depth by users in the Steam community.
In summary, if you don't mind doing a little reading to nail down the game mechanics and you enjoy turn based battle systems I would highly recommend the Last Remnant. The price even when not on sale is well worth the content and enjoyment that you will get out of it. This is a AAA title from Square Enix with an Indie price tag. Go buy it right now if you are a fan of Fantasy RPGs!

Full disclosure, for the longest time I was one of those folks who would scoff at new FF games and simply say "It hasn't been good since FFIX." I still don't like FFX, have my doubts about FFXII, and will never play XI and XIV, but 14 hours into the game I can say one thing for certain: FFXIII has made me a fan.
Prior to playing the game, I heard all the usual criticism. They said the game was too linear. They said the game practically plays itself. I even heard that the plot was dumb and the characters were annoying. Some of that criticism has a little bit of truth to it, but here's the bottom line: Over the course of my time playing this game, I have discovered that this game is a wild adventure across a beautiful and chaotic world, and a desperate struggle for survival against all odds. As someone who plays RPGs for the story, I couldn't be happier with my decision to play this game. As someone who frankly doesn't care about graphics, I have to admit that this game is stunningly beautiful, and a treat for the eyes just as much as for the brain. And the best part? I know that there's still a lot more for me to see here, because I still have a lot further to go before the game is finished.
Anyway, those are my personal thoughts. Here's a brief rundown of some pros and cons.
Pros:
- The game takes place in a fascinating and beautiful world.
- You will find that the story is engaging and unique once you give it an honest shot.
- Although you don't always notice it, the game appears to have an excellent soundtrack. Several times in particular I have felt impressed with how well the music seems to fit the situation.
- Most of the characters will grow on you quite nicely as you progress through the story (at least, they did for me).
- Combat can be both simple and difficult depending on the enemy, and the paradigm system is an interesting departure from the standard ATB combat system most other FF games utilize.
Cons:
- The game throws you into the fray right off the bat and only gives you bits and pieces of the plot/backstory as you progress through the game.
- You will probably hate most of the characters the first time you meet them.
- The maps are extremely linear, as is the game itself. Don't go into it expecting an open world because there is none.
- Exploration is practically non-existent, and I haven't seen any minigames or anything like that yet.
The Bottom Line:
- You play this game for the story. FFXIII is the most story-driven game I've probably ever heard of, to be honest. There is really nothing you do in this game that is not done for the purpose of advancing the main storyline.
- Expect to be bombarded with strange terminology and seemingly unexplained conflicts early on. Much of it will be explained through dialogue shortly, but there is also an in-game database that you can use to learn more about the world and the plot in the main menu.
- If you are a fan of story-driven RPGs like myself, then you owe it to yourself to give this one a shot. Despite the criticism and the fact that it is a radical departure from the games that came before it, FFXIII is a great game that I highly recommend.

Google or look it up on youtube if your unaware who any of these are, and you'll understand. XD
The story concept to me is "out o the blue" so to speak. Not an idea I would have thought of or did I see coming with *without adding any spoilers* all that happens in Saints Row 4, so this is very cool *no pun intended XD *
Despite the smaller map size, its still fun and interesting to me to just freeroam and see things. I always loved that part in any game, and find it interesting in comparison to previous versions.
There's still a lot to do, again, despite the smaller map. I guess I'm a very "slow" player because I tend to take my time doing everything, and I try to take in the full aspects as well as the content offered, be it just the overall astetics of the games design. I know the game itself only offers a few hours of actual game driven play, then one or two more with the side quest/missions, but if your like me and take your time playing, its still very rewarding, none the less.
Cons:
Not a big surprise to me given Johnny's signature outfit and looks, but no character customization, not even cloths? Rather sad I think considering the wide variety of outfits in most of the games thus far, and I looked forward to seeing what kind of outfits were going to be available in "Hell", not to mention seeing Kinzie in some of the various outfits, if even the "hell" versions of.
No hommies, gang members, crew to back you up or help *aka meat shields XD * which is also rather surprising to me in that I would have thought at least some of them would have went ....down Not up? XD  None the less, its still rather disappointing.
No vehicle customization, which again is very sad and disappointing to me as I have always loved customizing and tweaking my vehicles, and which also has previously been available.
No vehicle saves/storage, also very sad and disappointing to me, considering previous versions, but being that there are no hommies thus no vehicle delivery or garages, and no customizations for them as well as the fact there are only like for or five types of vehicles in "hell", and considering this is not another full Saints Row game, still I find this sad and disappointing.
No weapon customizations again leaving me feeling a bit dissapointed as i usually prefered the reskins version as to the standard skins.
No radios/radio stations, just the in game music itself. This really shocked me in a couple different ways. I have always loved the radios in the Saints Row games for the music and often for the commentaries *Zynak in Saints Row 4 comes to mind* not to mention I loved the added feel the music provided to the game experience so I was very shocked as well as disappointed about this one. Saints Row has always had some of the best in game music in my opinion.
No cheat codes. OK, this isn't a big issue to me, however I add it because when I get tired of doing the missions, quest, or roaming about I love turning them on and just creating overall havoc and destroying stuff just for fun, without having to worry about burning through my ammo, and getting killed, and just seeing the game mechanics as I run amock creating overall mayhem....its Just a thing to me. XD
No Genki... Now, I didn't expect a Murder Brawl, or M.O.M. or anything like that, but was rather disappointed not to see Professor Genki  just roaming about as in Saints Row 4, which I thought would be both awesome and sensible because after all, he's Genki! XD
Only one safe house....again This isn't a big issue to me, considering Saints Row 4 *again trying not to add any spoilers*, but would be nice, none the less, to have more than just the one, even if the fact that you have no wardrobe or vehicle storage ability rather makes them pointless anyway, but still I find it a bit disappointing, even if the map itself isn't that big overall.
To wrap this up finally, I know this isn't meant to be Saints Row 5, nor was it designed to be, but again it feels very lacking and limited, and more like a demo of the actual game. Still despite all its fun and interesting.
Recommend.....at this time, no....simply due to what it lacks overall. As I said a few times, it feels more like a demo version of the game that you have to buy, rather than get free to try, and not a part of the game itself. Understanding though it was designed to be a DLC that they opted to make a stand alone, and not an actual game. Hopefully they may add more content to it and then I would recommend it, but unless you just want a lesser feel of Saints Row without having to buy the actual game, or just want it as part of the series, then not at this time.

So you will read mixed reviews on this title, and complaints about thin story and it running poorly. Disregard those reviews. FFXIII has quickly become one of my favorites of the series. I first started playing Final Fantasy with the original on the NES. I got it two days after launch, brand new, from the rack at our local walmart. Me and my mom (who also enjoyed RPGs) got it on a whim because the coverart looked really rad. We were pleasantly surprised by an amazing game, and have played the franchise ever since. This game's story is involving, evolving, and deep. You will get attached to the characters before you know it, and will start having emotional responses to the trials they encounter. The gameplay IS a bit linear, but if you have been playing Final Fantasy long, you will be accustomed to that and it will not feel odd. This is not World of Warcraft, this is not Final Fantasy XIV ARR. This is a single-player Final Fantasy title that lives up to it's namesake. The music is moving, and me and my wife have since downloaded the soundtracks for this, and the next two titles. We have gotten real-world merchandise from the game, and have become involved in the canon about the characters. So to make a summation: The game is lovely if you enjoyed previous Final Fantasy titles such as FF7/9/X, etc; you will love this one just the same. The game runs perfectly great if you are playing on a gaming computer, and not some Lenovo laptop you borrowed from work. The art, music, and combat system are all the quality you would expect from a Final Fantasy title. If you liked Final Fantasy 10, get this game. It's really just a newer version of that game with a different story; it's very comparable.

Day 16: Finally had to make a supply run to the quiet cottage; the other caches are either picked clean, or too dangerous. Before the war, I never thought about what I was capable of when things got desperate. The old couple were just surviving, like the rest of us. Good people, could have been my gran and pa in another world. But we need food, needed it more. Before the war, there were monsters and there were people. Now, only the people remain, and that scares me.
This War of Mine is ugly and cold. It strives to make you the same way, always offering small glimpses of hope through a veil of tragedy. It's not a survival story that closes by telling you everything will be alright, because the cost of making that far will have you questioning whether it was worth the price.
For every moment of humanity, there is a dark realization that your survive only because others have not. You want to trade, scavenge, and grow enough to feed your own, but the war doesn't make it easy. Robbers break in during the night, stealing away with hard earned medicine and food. Your comrades get sick, and can no longer help out with scavenging. Your trade options have dried up. But the family in the house two blocks away is doing well. They've been untouched by roaming gangs somehow, and they have plentiful food and supplies. If survival is the ultimate goal, would you shatter another person's safety and livelihood to reach it?
The War of Mine achieves it's opus in the hundred little stories it tells to punctuate the backdrop of gunfire and bombings. If it's a fitting summary of the actual toll that war takes, then it's to remind us that no wars are truly won, considering all the we lose in the process.

I highly recommend this game.
In my opinion Crysis is superior to the second and third installment of the series. The game grants the player with more freedom to view and explore the more open world-oriented environments, and all of the components of the environment can be interacted with for MAXIMUM enjoyment while traversing the missions. There isn't a bad amount of weapons for the variety of things you can do with each. There is just the right amount for each scenario, and there's nothing about the weapon systems in any given firefight that's broken or needs improvement. The gunplay is satisfying, and you absolutely realize when you kill an enemy.
The missions are very fun. The only complaint I have about Crysis is the fact that the game focused most of it's missions on the human antagonists rather than the aliens. I feel like the Crysis sequels nailed the antagonist's human-alien ratio. It gave variety to the gameplay. The majority of the missions in this game just focused on killing human enemies with guns, and advancing through the mission by doing so. With that said the gorgeous environment and free-roam aspect to each mission made this game a blast to play through.
The nanosuit's options were the highlight about Crysis in relation to the two sequels in the franchise (Along with Warhead). In this game, you have the option to maximize your strength, your speed, your damage resistance, and the option to cloak yourself for MAXIMUM stealth ability. The stealth system in all of the Crysis games works like a charm, and are a blast to utilize for tactical situations. So these heightened abilities give the player an edge in each firefight scenario, and they each work just as effective in the battle to give you the advantage over the opponents. Speed lets you move fast to avoid being hit, and gives you the speed edge to get away fast enough if you're on the verge of death. Strength actually does less in the way of combat unless you're going to run around punching your enemies. Punching while in strength mode kills an enemy in one hit. The ups of strength are basically in hand-to-hand combat and in jumping. The player jumps higher to clear high obstacles while in strength mode. The only downside to strength is that the character walks and runs slower due to the strength ability. Shield and cloak are self-explanatory, but quite obviously the most useful options in the game, which is why they were implemented in the sequels as the only two options for the nanosuit. Cloak gives the player the stealth edge, while shield gives the player increased damage resistance in the nanosuit.
Weapons also can be customized in this menu. On the AK(FY71) and SCAR variants, you have the option to add a suppressor, flash light, laser light, ACOG type scope, long range scope, red dot sight, and I might be missing a couple of options there. The options are limited with the pistol, and there are no options with the rocket launcher, minigun, alien minigun, and the gauss rifle can be outfitted with just sights for the top accessory rail. The submachine is able to be outfitted for a suppressor, and a few other options, while the shotgun is also limited in it's customization options, but can be outfitted for a suppressor.
In conclusion, Crysis is a blast for anyone with a desire to play an addictive FPS with an experience like no other.
Again, I highly recommend this game.

The whole way that the story of a few people's struggle for survival unfolds is very immersive. There are however plenty of things they could add to this game. Such as (and forgive for making this a suggestions list instead of a review):
Character Creation (where you can add your own photos, in essence adding yourself and even your
family and friends to the game {hehe, then it would really suck when someone dies}).
If not Character Creation then perhaps just heaps more possible characters for each playthrough.
More character interaction, perhaps even romance.
Longer daytime perhaps.
Child and teenage characters (though this might be hard because kids aren't allowed to die under gaming law I think).
A Bigger City (simply a lot more locations perhaps).
The ability to have your characters 'make a run' out of the city through a very hard level needing much preperation, ending (winning) the game early.

Derided by many as more of a techdemo than an actual game on release, Crysis actually revolutionised tactical first person shooters by virtue of two very smart (and intertwined) design choices: One, by setting the game on a large, semi open-world island, thus allowing the player to tackle seemingly simple "go to position X" missions in a variety of ways; and two -- and it is here that the game sets itself apart from Crytek's previous outing Far Cry --, by giving the player access to a variety of superpowers (speed, strength, invisibility, armor), as well as the ability to quickly change between these powers on the fly. In other words, the player is free to advance from checkpoint to checkpoint in his own way, both literally (as in choosing his path) and metaphorically (as in choosing his playstyle). And crucially, while a one-to-one combat situation is bound to be boring in a game that outfits the player with numerous superpowers, the enemies still hit hard and find strength in superior numbers, so as to not make the game a cakewalk.
Yet the plot of Crysis, unimaginative from the start but seemingly an afterthought anyway, eventually comes to influence the mechanics of the game and does so for the worse: Aliens briefly appear early in the game, then vanish again for several hours before becoming the principal antagonists of the second half of the game. Thus, the intricate setpieces  of the first half -- the infiltration of a shipyard a definite high point --, usually culminating in intense firefights against Korean soldiers, give way to monotonous battles against lazily designed aliens. Instead of infiltrating a base, the player suddenly finds himself following a very straight and narrow path for 20 minutes, steadily interrupted by groups of three identical enemies and packs of conveniently placed ammo, since the aliens do not drop any.

Anyone who's ever played Crisis will likely tell you to buy this game. And while I would as well, there's a few... let's call them 'interesting' problems that any prospective buyer should be aware of. With no further ado, let's go over the facts!
TL;DR... The Summary:
+ Stunning visuals and graphics, even today.
+ Entertaining, action packed gameplay.
+ Encounters change based on your play style.
+ Semi-open world maps for each mission.
+ Weapons and Tactical diversity.
- Multiplayer no longer exists.
- No real replayability.
- Physics glitching (Many 'LOLwut?' moments).
- SEVERE late game glitching and bugginess (almost unplayable).
- Cliche, generic plot and storyline.
- Cardboard NPCs.
- Still need to sell your soul (or your first born) for a system that can play this on high settings.
The Pros:
Without a doubt one of the very best things about Crysis is the stunning, mind-blowing visuals. Other, newer games have done better for themselves, but even today the game's environment is simply stunning. The controls take a little getting used to, but once you learn how to operate that nano-suit it's a very smooth and responsive ride. Normal Mode will seem like a cakewalk if you're a standard FPS gamer. The combat and gameplay in general is also quite diverse in that it lets you decide how you want to engage most scenarios, be it going all in with guns blazing or pretending you're Garrett from the Thief series (another good series, except for the most recent one Thief 4). Finally, without spoiling too much, you can modify most of the weapons you find or use in game to fit your personal needs. Good hunting!
The Cons:
Now we get to the not-so-fun part! Despite being a fairly well crafted game with plenty of bonuses and making for one hell of a high-tech commando simulator, this game is literally chock full of bugs and glitches that will likely never be addressed. Death by random physics (seriously, I was once killed by a gun I *dropped* because of physics in here) abound, and the last level is fiendishly notorious its illusionary floors, in which you can and will fall through either to your death or into the earlier parts of the level with no ability to continue. A lot. A whole freak'n ton of a lot. Be prepared to save often, reload twice as often, and restart your game a couple times to get through this beast. If you're one of the lucky few who don't suffer this horrendous fate? I salute you!
Alas, this isn't all that violates your precious cake and leaves it bitter-tasting. The storyline is... okay at best. It's nothing to write home about and you'll likely feel complete apathy when people start dying; the plot of Crysis is about as cliche as it gets, its characters pretty much one-dimensional. The game is also very short; you can beat this in eight hours or less, and despite the open world environment the story is so linear there's barely any replay value. Throw in the fact that Multiplayer for this game no longer exists, and you're actually only getting half the game it was meant to be.
In Conclusion:
While Crysis can be fun and engaging for a few romps, I can't recommend this game at its full price (even if it's only $10!) with the sheer amount of bugs and other problems piling onto what would otherwise be a masterpiece. My advice? Watch it on Youtube. Or if you *really* want to play it, get it on sale or in a sale bundle set with Crysis Warhead, Wars, and Crysis 2 for dirt cheap.
Trust me on this. You'll be happier if you save your hard-earned money for better things.

I give this game a solid 7.5/10.  As far as RTS games go, this one has a lot of customization options that allow you to tweak it to your liking.  I bought it on sale and am glad I did, because for the full price I would have been let down a bit but simultaneously it fulfills that RTS need in my gaming collection better than any other I've ever played.  Pro/Con as follows:
Pro:
Great look, its amazing to zoom into the battle and see ship fleets just tearing each other up.
Micro is there, and you'll be rewarded for your skill, but its not as in your face as SC and other RTS games I've played before.  Macro in this game is a big part and most of what you'll use as the empire you build can be enormous.
There are tons of maps to play, making the game very replayable and exciting.
6 somewhat unique races that carry specific abilities to fit your style of play (might i suggest picking one and sticking with it until you understand the game)
AI can be set to your liking and believe me, it delivers if you so choose it to.  Downright nasty even.
Con:
Battles can be so long. Honestly, even a 1v1 match can take more than an hour.  You'll definetely be saving and continuing at a later date with this game more often than not.  Not many people I would think have the time for large 50+ planet battles in one sitting.
Huge learning curve if you've never played the Sins of a Solar Empire games, took me several days to even understand what I was doing.  Do the tutorials as many times as need be, it'll save you time in the long run.
Maps are diff sizes, you can pick how big the map is and therefore roughly decide how long the battle will be, but know that most of the maps are bigger maps, and I feel the games just take too long.
The complexity of the game favors those that keep at it.  Just a little here and a little there won't cut it.  Those that practice their strategies and stick with their fav race will end up becoming extremely talented while those that play here and there will be left in the dust in online play due to the sheer amount of content you as an empire builder must be keeping track of at all times.  You've been warned.
Music is annoying.  Turned it off within the first few hours.
In closing, this game has so much to offer.  Those that want a very complex, high maintenance empire will love it.  Again, overall its a very good RTS game that I enjoy and it fulfills that role in my gaming collection extremely well, however, its not worth as much as they're charging at full price, sale price is where its at.  And I can't stress enough: make sure when you start a battle online that you've got some serious time on your hands.

The difficulty levels are steep as you progress through them and you will have to think quickly and tactically at a moments notice to stay competive on the higher levels, but it is ultimately a very satisfying feeling once you master it.
The only real drawback to this game is that there is no campaign mode, which would have been nice, and a couple of extra races just to add a little more diversity would have been welcome too. Overall, I highly recommend this game to fans of strategy and 4x games, you will not be disappointed....

Shelter is a charming game and really one of a kind. It could be described as a "mother simulator", where you take the role of a mother badger, in charge of 5 little badger cubs. You have to travel through beautiful but, at the same time, dangerous locations, in order to reach safe lands for you and your family to live and prosper.
The game is divided in 5-6 chapters/levels, each with its own style, mood and lighting. (My personal favourite was the nighttime one). There is no manual saving system, but that's actually a good thing, because it immerses you completely and makes the danger feel absolutely real. There is, thankfully, a checkpoint before every chapter.
The only problem is its -very- short length. Coupled with the fact that I found it quite easy, I finished it in just over two hours; I only restarted the river chapter a couple of times. Other than that, my badger babies were full of health and we reached the last chapter undivided! But, at the same time, because of this, Ι didn't feel any super strong emotional connection, neither do I have to replay the game to find a "better" ending (and as such, spend a little more time in the game).

Etc. etc., eventually, once I knew how to end my turn, I taught myself, making rookie mistakes, but adapting quickly after the first two games were a disaster.
Secondly, as far a I'm aware, this game doesn't even provide a single player campaign, I love myself a good story-line.
However, this game is quite boring to be fair. I do like the city building as I do with most strategy games, but it just seems a bit bland, the structures don't really seem to do anything apart from provide resources. To build different units I don't build buildings but I research tech, there are no defensive structures other than the cities itself (no walls, canons, soldiers on a watchtower or whatever I much prefer Total War, AoE, C&C (especially the Red Alert series), etc. Though only Total War seems to be somewhat comparable to Civ due to the world map perspective.
Also I don't like how an enemy can win a game without even encountering you in battle simply by building a gate of some sorts, though to be fair, I never liked when wonders helped you win a game, every since I started RTS games.
I had fun, but it felt more like an free to play online kind of fun. Not the traditional RTS base building and attack kind of fun.
But I guess that's just what Civ is. Either way, far too expensive for what it provides in my opinion, and simply not that fun.

Archetypal three-out-of-five star game. Probably at least 100 hours to finish everything, but the constant re-use of dugneons and areas fosters a "why bother?" kind of attitude.
The writing and story fall dead center into the average of what you'd expect from a smaller-budget JRPG -- it poaches and steals from every trope you can imagine, leaving no stone unmolested. Even the moldiest old concept is trotted out a few dozen times throughout the storyline. So if you've seen and liked it in a JRPG before, you'll probably see it again in The Last Remnant, just this time in a worn-out-STD-infected-completely-trashy kind of way,
In some ways this game makes me want to hire a skywriter to tour Japan and paint the heavens with a simple message: "<Blank> did <insert bad thing> to my <blank> is NOT AN ACCEPTABLE STORY." Because somehow, even in 2008, Square Enix appeared to believe that their customers could be hoodwinked into giving hafl a damn about some characaracter whom we were just introduced to 2 seconds ago, and the bad thing that happened to her. If you find this kind of lazy writing to be offputting, I implore you: stop reading right now, back out of this game's store page, and never let its pixels illuminate your screen again.
The art direction is okay, and the graphcis are decent for a game first released fairly early in the Xbox 360's lifespan. It runs well on a modern PC. If you hate the way Unreal Engine 3 games look, you'll probably hate the way this game looks.
The combat system is fairly atrocious. It wants to look complex, but anyone with half a brain can figure the ins-and-outs within a short period of time and turn the game into a mindless slog from start to finish.
Also, 52353253242345 unwanted fights while backtracking. And believe me, there's some backtracking in this game.
I freely admit that I didn't beat this game. I actually enjoyed it a lot of the time, and might finish it one day. But that's just because I'm into this terrible-but-enjoyable kind of game.

so far so good.
gameplay-wise i know a lot of people don't like the game as every action you take (or more like influence) in battle shapes the kind of battle style and stats your units will develop. it makes absolutely no indication as to what will change your class (but you can kind of figure melee will get you on the fighter route, magic on the mage route, etc) or how much experience is needed to advance to the next level. lots of people recommend you research which routes you want to take in advanced so you know what actions to choose in game... but i think that's kind of boring/cheaty honestly. i've had no trouble so far and intend to complete the game this way. maybe on new game+.
there's also the issue of battle ranks. battle ranks are this game's way of determining how well you are doing in battle, and are not to be confused with the traditional JRPG's levels. in order to gain stats quicker, you want to keep your battle rank fairly low. basically, in battle you should punish your units and suck as much as you can. this mechanic is definitely interesting but it's pretty damn masochistic.
what i've learnt is to get into battle with multiple semi-tough enemies that will give your units a good wolloping, and just chisel away at their HP in between healing/reviving and if things aren't as going as planned you can do the good old square enix soft reset by pressing all shoulder buttons as well as start/select or in my case back/start. it'll take you back to the title screen so you can load your last save and try again. you should be saving before every battle.
you should also be checking the pubs after every single advancement in the story. there'll be two NPCs standing behind the bar, the one the left is the bartender and the one on the right is the guy/girl you want to be talking to. they'll let you know if there's an available side quest. you should be doing these as soon as you can, and i suggest doing so before continuing with the story as they are constrained to certain plot points. save before you accept any, however, because some of them transport you to new areas that you can't exit unless you finish the quest objective or suspend the quest until later on.
this game was originally released on 360 and ported to pc much later, and because of that, in my medical opinion, this game suffers from mild consolitis.
controls... just use a controller. very bad port in this respect, having to navigate menus with arrow keys and enter is just incredibly lazy and wrong.
it also has major loading times if you have a dual core cpu, which i still do. to fix it, you either need to get the mass affinity.exe to launch the game (mass effect 2 had the same issue) OR do what mass affinity does manually by
going into task manager
right clicking TLR.exe process
set affinity...
then uncheck one of your cores, doesn't matter which.
click apply, then set affinity again
recheck the core you chose, and just leave it like that until you've exited the game.
FOV is also ridiculously small and it's really annoying in wide open areas as you can't see what you're pulling the attention of which is NOT good in this game. if you're willing to, you can change the settings in one of the ini files, and also bind keys that assign different FOV values.
overall there's nothing too much to complain about.

Many negative reviews of this game are due to a misconception by that player. They are looking at this from an objective, shoot-to-thrill stance that games such as Call of Duty has instilled in them. They argue about the game forcing a moral code on them, they scream at some characters having skills/traits with no discernable impact, they scream that this game is not really a game.
Cause this is not a 'game', in the traditional sense.
This is an artistic expression, a view of the toll of war on civilians lies that only comes from one who has lived it. And the creators have indeed lived it, according to several interviews. You cannot go into This War of Mine, bringing in expectations and attitudes from other games. This isn't one of those typical games. Yet, for a game, it is surprisingly well done.
Looking at the game angle on this, This War of Mine has a very unique art direction with blinding lights, visibly dark rooms, and a vague pencilly fog of war for many areas. This was done from the perspective of someone who has lived in these dark houses, who's own eyes got adjusted to the low light and everything in the room was just so much visible. And when that sunlight comes in, it almost sears your eyes. The characters are unique, they have a life about them, and many of them you care about them beyond just what skills they bring to the table. And they all have useful traits, you just got to know when to best apply them. Want to have minimal morale loss when it comes to necessary killing? Send Emilia. Want to boost someone from depression? Send Zlata. (Well, Anton I can't yet figure out. I don't know WHAT his skill does. No one seems to really...). The music fits, the characters fit, the 'quests/events' fit. The game is designed around it's main statement about surviving war. It does not sacrafice stuff, to be more gamey, like some other games have. It isn't trying to cater to consoles or with cutting edge graphics. It's Master is first, and foremost, the story of war.
I could say more about how I think the inability to save is brilliant (You have to actually live with your consequences, but this is frustrating to a perfectionist like me. I must of restarted 10 times cause I didn't do a run perfect. Finally I decided just to..go with the story), or about how impressed I was with how the creator appealed to people on Pirate's Bay (He had a good product, he wanted people to enjoy it. He wanted this story to be heard).
My only one 'gripe' with the game, is that I want more. Not sure how more is possible, but I want more. Content, DLC, Patches that add things. Expansions. Whatever. More. Gimme. I know this game was finanically viable by November 16th, two days into it's sales. We are now nearing the one month mark, and I hope the game is still making them a profit.
But again, do not mistake this for just a game. It is artistic expression, interactive storytelling, walking beside you as you see a story on the horrors of war. The point of the game isn't to win, to kill all the enemy or really survive. The point is to look at what the creators saw, look at what they are trying to tell you..and to understand.

It hurts to write this becuase I love MTG so much, but I just can't recommend this game.  You will see in other reviews that the servers have a lot of down time, and some of the mechanics of the game (like two headed giant) just don't work.  The parts that really bother me are:
1) After playing through story mode you'll have been able to open roughly 10 booster packs of cards that have 6 cards each.  The packs have one rare each.  I have four of the same rare after these 10 packs, and it may be the most useless rare in the game.
2) The cards I do have are no where near what you need to make a competitve deck to play in solo.  The only way to earn more coins for more booster packs is now to play through solo mode aginast AI opponents who have vastly better cards and always seem to get just the card they need.  Even if you win, you get 5 coins and a booster cost 150.  So you have to win 30 times to get one booster which seemingly is going to have the same cards you already have.
3) The game (certainly the cuts scenes) looks like it was made in 1995.  Even the background board you stare at for hours is a low res image you would find as a screen saver in Windows 95'.
I'm not sure if this game was rushed out, if there was no develoment money behind it, or no one at Wizards of the Coast cares anymore but the implementation of this game is just bad.  If you want to play a few hands for nostalgia sake, it may do the job, but I cannot in good faith suggest anyone spend money on this.

This is the second Assassin's Creed game I've played. I tried the second one, and half enjoyed it - I liked the locations, I liked the idea, but I stopped playing when I ran into some glitch which kept losing me half an hour of progress. That was years ago..
I picked Black Flag up in the sales, and I much like the second game I'm half enjoying it... But it's an Assassin's Creed game, which means simple controls that irritate due to their inaccuracies, and repetitive gameplay. Really repetitive. The things I hated about the second game have come flooding back to me playing this. And it's such a shame.
This is basically a pirate game. A triple A pirate game. Which is amazing really. I didn't realise how much I wanted a proper pirate game until now. And the graphics are lovely, the clothing and islands convincing, and the sailing is almost so good. But it's all too simple, of course. The combat is "mash mouse button, there's a red icon so press "e", mash mouse button"... It's boring. The stealth mechanics are still non existent, and for a game I always assume to be a stealth(y) game that's surprising.. The sailing is fun but already I feel I've seen it all after an hour or so of it. Ach it all could have been so, so good. All the basics are there, they just needed to go make a pirate game with a sharp, refined control method and proper stealth dynamics... An open world Hitman/Splinter Cell! Hell, even taking their Far Cry mechanics and applying them more would've been better..
But they made an Assassin's creed game. What's all the animus rubbish about?! It's utterly pointless. Just give me a bloody pirate/assassin game for goodness sake! What I'm not actually a pirate? Well that's immersion breaking, cheers. It's like the plot of a bad 90s B movie. I'll doubtless give this another 10 hours or so before getting really bored, maybe a total of 20 hours, which is pretty good for me. So I guess it's worth picking up if you just want an adventure game (sadly lumbered with outdated gameplay mechanics). It just pains me playing something so limited, which could have been so good..

I have a ton of PC sim racing experience, I began running online competitively on NR2002 and have spanned to NR2003 and iRacing and found some success in both. As someone who's very familiar with those games, I'm genuinely impressed with this one. Obviously it is not the super-realistic sim that either one of those are, but man is it nice to finally have an up-to-date NASCAR game with what seems to be a great career mode and just overall fun gameplay.

I have a Driving Force GT and the configuration took a few minutes, with an error, but it eventually was sorted out. I'm surprised that you have to turn the steering sensitivity down, but other than that seems to be no issues there.
The career mode seems like a climb like some of the older games, scratching and clawing for top20's and 15's initially with lower-tier rides. I really like that, brings back NASCAR Thunder 2003/D2D type of feeling. I wish career mode had more stats in it, but seems to be a step up with the addition of all the series from last year.
Perhaps an upgrade for next year could be more of an emphasis of adding in grooves at different tracks, since early on at Auto Club, Atlanta, Charlotte seem like perennial bottom feeders.
I know this isn't important to many people, but the soundtrack is actually pretty cool for this game. Been 2005 Chase for the Cup since I really loved a NASCAR soundtrack, and this game seems to have a good variety of some relatively unheard of songs that are quite good.

I originally wrote a bad review for Nascar Heat 2. I've since deleted it and spent a couple hours with the game.
I have been sim racing, simcade racing, and arcade racing since the late 90's. I've played just about every racing title released on PC. Over the years there have been some really good games. When talking Nascar games Papyrus was always the top dog in sim racing. We had Nascar Racing 2 and 3 that were awesome for their time, and then came the original Nascar Heat released around 2000. That was a fun game! It wasn't Papy, but it was just plain fun!
That's what I've had to tell myself and give Nascar Heat 2 another shot.
It's not NR2003, iRacing, or even Nascar Heat of yesteryear, but it's the best attempt at a Nascar game that we've had for a long time. It's not perfect, there are some handling issues, and poor AA. If you go into it just looking to have fun you won't be disappointed. If you're looking for a true sim, this isn't it, and it never really tries to be.
Nascar Heat 2 isn't really what I was hoping it would be, but its fun, and I will happily support any developer that's willing to produce a Nascar game. Doing that is what will get us another blockbuster Nascar game in the future.

This game blows.  I'm a big fan of the trading card game but rarely play because of cost, and have played other computer based TCGs like Hearthstone and Scrolls to try a fill that void.  If you are in the same boat and hoping that this will feel like playing Magic for real, you will be sorely disappointed.

In order to capture this in a game, you have pauses between every card played, every phase, and so on. I have a decent laptop that can run popular games like League of Legends, CS:GO, and Skyrim on low to medium settings with around 60 fps.  I rarely exceed 14 in this game. In Shelter, you play as a mother badger nurturing her five cubs while travelling through the wilderness.
The main game is about 1.5 hours long with little replay value. There is also an additional ‘Nurture’ mode, which is meant to be played in short intervals in the span of several days. The gameplay itself is pretty stale and repetitive, mainly consisting of gathering food for your cubs and protecting them from harm.
Throughout the experience you can lose your cubs in various ways, and it is naturally your main objective to keep them safe. Seeing one taken away does evoke a sense of loss, but, perhaps due to the short duration of the game, is not nearly as emotional as it could be. Especially when you lose one without even realizing it, only to find it missing later, making you wonder if your carelessness or the game’s bugs are to blame.
As to bugs, the cubs also occasionally get stuck against ‘walls’ or start spinning in circles standing on the food that you’re trying to give them. On top of that, in my 1.5hr playthrough, I regularly had issues with the camera clipping against trees and/or other bigger objects in the game. Another, although a minor, issue was the menu text colors blending with the background visuals, making it often difficult to read.
Nevertheless, I did enjoy Shelter’s unique visuals, although some levels definitely stood out more than the overs. The same can be said about the soundtrack, with a couple of pretty impressive pieces, and then some less notable ones.
All in all, I would consider Shelter to be more of an interactive story about loss and harshness of nature than 'a game’.
