While mainly taking plenty of steps forward and a few back, this is my favorite Hitman game.
Quick Vocabulary:
Blood Money=Referencing to Hitman: Blood Money, the game that came before Hitman: Absolution.
Pros:
-Great Price. $20.00 is definitely worth the buy. Even $60.00 is.
-The creative ways of dispatching your foes. This game takes focus and planning to take out your targets, and in the long run, easily worth it.
-The graphics are amazing for 2012. (Like Far Cry 3)
-More Story Driven. This Hitman is about learning what the Agency really is as Agent 47 feels guilt for killing his handler for the first time.
-Instinct. It's like Bullet Time but you mark your targets and let the bullets fly.
-Easily replayable. While having smaller levels, it gives Hitman sooo much more replayability. In the older games (Blood Money), if you screwed up once, you were dead. In this, it allows you to fix your mistakes a lot easier. The smaller level sacrifice is also a con, because this game is more linear than the others, which really wasn't.
-The guns and having to search for them is also very cool. Unfortunately, it leads to a con in which there is no loadout screen like in Hitman: Blood Money.
-Contracts. While you can only pick single-player levels, you can create a challenge, set an example, and see if your friends can beat your score. It's cool.
-12-18 hours is the length of the campaign. You might not want to play on Easy, even for the first time. Setting it on Normal or harder has you thinking strategies and that's what Hitman is about.
-The levels. While being linear, there are a few levels that aren't, like the Town (forgot the full name), Hotel Terminus and a few others. Set the difficulty on Easy once you beat the Gun Shop (My favorite) level so you can have Instinct on the range, unless you are practicing for the real game.
-A welcome cover system. In the older Hitman games (Blood Money), you would be trying to get behind walls. Finally, they added a cover system to assist you. It is sincerely welcome.
-Sooo many things to find in each level. Even if the level is linear, you won't find everything. As I am typing this review, I just found a few things. An Easter Egg I just found include Lynch from Kane and Lynch being on the gun range on the Gun Shop level (Far Right on the gun range). People also talk about him at the front counter about how he cuses like a sailor and uses all of the shotgun ammo. Speaking of talking, there are so many conversations you can listen to. That's a few of the things you can find in this game.
Cons:
-Smaller levels. While offering large replayability, it does suffer the game being more linear than the other Hitman games.
-No loadouts. In Hitman: Blood Money, you could have upgrades and choose which weapons and items you could carry into the mission. You have to scavenge around the mission for weapons and items, which since it's more linear, it isn't as hard as you might think.
-No extra DLC missions. The game does end when it ends (which is our next con) and unfortunately doesn't have any extra DLC missions. I wish it did. It only has extra DLC guns which are more like Camos for them, and aren't required. (It does have Hitman: Sniper Challenge and for some reason is $25.00. That was like a Demo for the Absolution and you should only get if you need more Hitman: Absolution)
-Awkward QTE Fist/Melee Fights (when you are detected). I never got into a Melee fight as I always relied on my guns, but it's there. It's not a big problem.
-When the game ends. Unfortunately, there is no Co-op with friends. That would have been awesome.
Overall Rating: (Non-Bias)
8.5/10-Worth Buying
Hardcore Hitman Fans:
9/10-Worth Buying

Just bought this game in the Summer Sale, as well as Shelter 2. I have finished this game in around 1.5hrs (went AFK for a while, so that's why my counter shows 3), and I would say that it was an Euro well spent. While I probably wouldn't buy it for 10 Euros, picking it up on a sale is very recommended.
Shelter is a very cute and emotional short story about a badger and its five babies, accompanied by a beautiful art style. Here is my rating of various aspects of the game:
Gameplay:
The gameplay of Shelter is very simple, most levels have a certain mechanic that they focus on. The way you play this game is walk through the levels, while encountering food, prey, predators and natural forces. The prey and food you feed to your babies, making sure to distribute it evenly, and the predators and nature's forces you will have to use a certain mechanic to avoid.
Controls are very simple: W, A, S, D, Sprint, Crouch, and Interact. The camera flows pretty well, even conquering common third-person issues like confined spaces.
Art:
The art style is beautifully abstract. In the beggining what I really noticed was the low contrast/high brightness of the game, but you will get used to it.
Music:
Music is mainly simple chords and short melodies that are very well mixed together to create beautiful sound effects. For example, when one of your pups eats something, a short guitar tune will play. When a bird of prey soars above you, a grim sounding bass guitar will play.
Story:
The story isn't really complicated, you are a badger with five pups that endures forces of nature in an adventure for food, and that is where I like it. There is no text in-game, no aggressive philosophical phrases that sound really cheesy, yet the game manages to express something that you can't really put into words about mothers.
Price:
While 10 Euros is a little pricey for a story this short, if you get it on sale it is well worth it. Would say a good price is 7 Eur, but getting it for 1 was a steal. If you live in countries that don't use the Euro or Dollar, then you should probably buy it for full price.
Overall:
The simplicity of the gameplay, story and art makes this game absolutely beautiful. Would strongly reccomend. Can't wait to get into Shelter 2, and then maybe I'll snag some of the other Shelter games.

I think it succeeds, personally. The world has enough going on, and feels open enough that you don't feel like you're being hand-held through a linear experience. The combination of feeding & protecting, I never felt bored, and I was sad when any cub died. And then the end (I won't say anything) came about  before you felt like it was dragging on.
This game took me less than 1.5hrs for a full playthrough, so it's not a long game, but for what it was, I think it was perfect. At this short length, it encourages you to try again and secure all your cubs to the end. There are also some extras I haven't really looked at too hard with some more gameplay, one about nurture, with the cubs starting from newborn, and another I haven't checked out yet.
I thoroughly enjoyed this experience, and I'll be playing Shelter 2 soon, so it will be interesting to see what that's like.
I highly recommend this game, and it's on sale now, so give it a try :)

This game is SquareJP's finest work this generation. The story, whilst being somewhat generic is a shining example of how you take a generic concept and make it more than that. In this game, you do not control a few singular characters, instead you have 'unions' which you form with a key character acting as a general so to speak, with bodyguards and special units in the union. You can have several unions depending on your battle level which allows for some jaw dropping gigantic battles against hostile unions. The traditional japanese roleplaying elements are heavily modified, with RTS style tactics of engaging and 'deadlocking' enemies in a close combat fight whilst your other unions move around to flank them or intercept enemies who are trying to flank your unions whilst they are in a deadlock. All of this is controlled with a sleek, stylish interface and battle controls identical to a traditional JRPG and is very easy to use whilst having respectable depth. If you think that the game is an actual RTS in the way it handles, and are put off by it, don't be because it isn't. This is a fantastic example of how you can merge two genres together whilst catering to everybodies tastes.
At £7.99, this game is more than worth it, and is a no brainer in a sale. I'm not even a huge JRPG fan at all, and other than Final Fantasy 4, 7, 13 and Lost Odyssey, I have never played any other ones and I have to say this one is easily the best. If like me you were left with a sour taste in your mouth after the latest, awful Final Fantasy games, The Last Remnant is a breath of fresh air, a fantastic new IP and proof that Square have not lost their touch.

Good, solid isometric ARPG which, at the time of publishing, helped to fill the gap between Diablo 2 and 3, as there weren't many decent ARPG's around (Titan Quest being a noteable exception). Outdated now as there are better alternatives in the same genre, but still a good game that you can safely pick up when it's on sale.
I'm assuming that everybody who reads this at least knows what an action RPG is, so I won't go into the mechanics of the game too deeply, since it doesn't stray far from the general mechanics of games in this genre. Basic attacks, special skills, potions, gems, randomly generated loot, it's all there.
In the game, you play as either a Destroyer (melee combat warrior), Alchemist (mage-type) or Vanquisher (ranged warrior). You arrive in the town of Torchlight, built on top of a big Ember vein (Ember being a kind of ore with properties to imbue people and items with magical power). The town is in trouble, since monsters start pouring out of the nearby mine, and one of the sages, Master Alric, is missing.
So down you go into the mines, where you quickly discover that below the mines, there's a huge dungeon that's basically a "layer cake" of different civilizations. As you delve deeper into the dungeon, and defeat several sub-bosses, the story progresses until you find the root of all evil at the bottom of the dungeon. This feels very, very much like Diablo 1, and in that way, it was quite outdated already upon release, since games like Diablo 2 and Titan Quest (released before Torchlight 1) already offered a far bigger, vaster world.
Regardless, Torchlight 1 has everything a basic ARPG needs and it does everything quite well. Some things that make (/made) it stand out are the fact that your pet is of actual use instead of it being just a visual addition (you can send it to town to sell loot, so you don't have to go yourself and you can continue going through the dungeon), it has great graphics and music (at least at the time of publishing), there's a great variety in monsters (one thing that I found lacking in Titan Quest), and that it was one of the first ARPGs to have an actual endgame (the endless dungeon) once you finished the main storyline. On the downside, it doesn't have a multiplayer mode, which a lot of players regard as a serious omission.
+ fresh visual style and good music & sound effects (by Matt Uelmen, who also did the music for Diablo 1 and 2)
+ nice mix of fantasy and steampunk
+ good amount of replayability with different classes, skills, items, difficulty settings and the "endless dungeon"
+ a lot of variety in items and monsters
+ big, unique boss monsters
+ a pet with multiple uses (attack / defend / sell goods at town)
+ moddable game with quite a lot of good mods available
+ fishing (which doesn't do much for me, but I guess it's a "thing" for some people :) )
- not much of a storyline
- small inventory size
- the worlds are a bit too big, so gameplay gets a bit repetitive before you reach the final boss
- no multiplayer mode
- trillbot :)

The Last Remnant is a fantastic game. I have spent over 60 hours playing it (my profile may say 40 but I've spent some time playing offline). If you like strategic but fast combat, this could be the game for you. There are tons of sidequests that give meaningful and useful rewards and many different characters that you can use in combat. For a JRPG, the story is not very strong, however it does have some interesting concepts.
The game can be complicated at times, with complex character progression as well as difficult concepts such as battle formations, but once you gain an understanding of these concepts the game can be very engaging. The Last Remnant Wiki will also help a lot.
Overall I'd give this an 9-9.5 out of 10. The game is very addictive and has great graphics (for its time) and good voice acting for the most part, but I believe you can choose to listen to Japanese voices if you like. An Xbox controller is highly recommended for this game, but not required.
Anyway, I obviously really like this game if you couldn't already tell from how much I've written about it. I've enjoyed all 60 hours of my game time and I bet you would too!

This game blows.  I'm a big fan of the trading card game but rarely play because of cost, and have played other computer based TCGs like Hearthstone and Scrolls to try a fill that void.  If you are in the same boat and hoping that this will feel like playing Magic for real, you will be sorely disappointed.
The gameply is incredibly slow.  Magic is a complex game because it requires interactions on your opponents turn.  In order to capture this in a game, you have pauses between every card played, every phase, and so on.  I get that this is necessary for PvP duels, but do I really have to sit through it all when playing NPCs in Story mode and the like?
While we are on the topic of story mode, let me just say how frustrating of an experience it is.  In addition to being incredibly slow, you have to play with a prebuilt deck that you can't even examine outside of duel.  Not only are these decks complete rubbish (and significantly worse than your NPC oppenent's), you have no idea what cards are included in them.  Good luck forming strategies like that.
And the icing on this horrible, horrible cake is the game performance.  I have a decent laptop that can run popular games like League of Legends, CS:GO, and Skyrim on low to medium settings with around 60 fps.  I rarely exceed 14 in this game.  The interface is really bizarre.  The game table is massive, but the cards are tiny.  The default option for the englarged card view is to scroll up on the card.  And selecting and playing cards from your hand is awful.  I've played the wrong card many times.  This is the most basic feature of the game and even that doesn't work well.
Oh, also, apparently turning off the music also mutes the cut scenes.  10/10

Spend the night scavenging the chosen areas, bartering with other survivors, sneaking though hostile camps stealing their goods, or searching abondoned sites for valuable items.
This War of Mine is an all around great game with high replay value. I highly suggest it if you're into survival style games.

This is a free to play MTG game that continues Wizards' DotP series' tradition of "2 small steps forwards, 1 giant leap backwards". As it is now, DotP 2014 is a better game, and I would recommend you play that instead of this. I hope that the devs will put in the work needed to make this game live up to its potential.
EDIT: 1 month later, still cannot recommend.  The list of significant bugs is massive, and to date there's only been one patch that addressed a small list of things.  To give you an example of a major bug present from day 1 with no timeline for a fix: One "day" is 2-3 days - you'll get a "daily" quest every 2-3 days, and have your "daily" limit on earning gold (400g) reset every 2-3 days.  6 cards cost 150g, a win gives 20g, and there are 480 cards... this makes earning cards agonizingly slow.
*** The Good ***
- Free to play: In game currency is earned at a fair pace, and, unlike Hearthstone, you will unlock all cards in a set number of booster packs (once you have the maximum number of a given card in your collection, that card will no longer appear in your packs).
- Noob friendly: The tutorials are simple, modular, and reward large amounts of gold. They do a good job of teaching the basic rules of the game. The overall power level of cards is low by MTG standards, and there are strict limits on how many powerful cards can go in a deck, which puts people with small collections on a somewhat even footing vs people with large collections.
-Persistant client: This game will continue to grow in terms of features and card sets. While you'd think this is standard for a video game, it is certainly a new and welcome concept for the DotP series.
-It's MTG: The artwork is beautiful and the cards are well designed. MTG is the king of card games for a reason.
-Interface: Although I still question a lot of the design choices (why is the perspective not top-down so that we can easily read the cards? Why are the enemy's cards upside down from my perspective? Why is there no history bar like in Hearthstone so I can review a confusing play the opponent made? Why do the in game decision pop ups completely obscure the playing field, which you need to see in order to make an informed choice?) the interface is undeniably cleaner and snappier than DotP 2014s. The auto targetting system is also quite good, almost always recommending the correct play
*** The Bad ***
-No chat: In what little promotion that they did do for this game, Wizards focussed on the fact that they brought back the much loved 2v2 mode, 2HG. What they didn't tell you is that there is no chat in this game whatsoever, making playing with other people lose all of its social value. Worse, it's super frustrating to be playing with a teammate in what boils down to a strategy/puzzle game, but not be able to coordinate strategy or puzzle solutions with that person. Fire the person who made this design decision - it wrecks the game in the short term, and without a community, your game will not last in the long term.
-Atrocious launch: No communication from devs about release date, server instability repeatedly causing progress to be lost, frequent periods of extended, unexpected downtime. The number of bugs I've discovered is what I'd expect from a game's beta, not the full release. For example, the cutscenes are silent - no music, voice acting, or SFX - which is awkward and embarassing. If I paid money for this I'd be furious.
-Stupidity: Offline progress in campaign and tutorials cannot be saved - you can't farm these for gold, so why require server connection? No cross platform support - if I want to play on my iPad, I need to start a new collection from scratch for iOS. No game lobbies means that you can't play against your friends in 2v2 mode. 2v2 mode does not award gold. 2v2 mode, the best part of the previous games, is not fun without chat. The 1v1 ranked queue often fails, requiring you to press buttons to requeue - I should be automatically requeued if matchmaking fails. It often takes FOREVER to get a 1v1 match because your first 10 matches fail to load.
- AI: The AI makes really really really bad mistakes. I suspect that it is worse than the previous DotP games. For example. it often attacks with all of its creatures, even if it cannot win and will lose next turn by doing so. It feels as though I only lose to the AI because I had a bad draw or because its deck is made from stronger cards than I have access to.
-Campaign: Overall, I enjoyed the campaign. Unfortunately, you can't create or edit a deck for the missions, so whether you win or lose is very much luck of the draw - this is frustrating and unfun. I get that they wanted to give you a feeling of starting from a weakling and becoming all powerful, but the hilariously bad cards in the early decks just get in the way of the fun. I think that next time we should be able to craft our own decks from a restricted pool for each mission.
-Long wishlist: Once the devs fix their servers, fix the bugs, and fix the stupidity outlined above, they need to add chat and lobbies back. Then we need some kind of sealed format (every f2p card game has sealed) and tournament support. Then I would like to see fun modes like Commander, Archenemy, Emperor, and Planechase.

If you want to have a fun, competitve NASCAR or Racing game, here ya go. If you think this is just like Heat Evolution, instead of trying to persuade you into thinking it is or isn't, let me note the differences between the two...
1.Stages, and Overtime
2.Kinda Paint booth
3.Very different Career, you have to jump into random trucks, and try and get rides.
4.Physics, if you hit the apron you get loose, just like you would in iRacing or even in real life, but your car doesn't just immedetley whip around like in Evolution..
5.All 3 series
6. Completley new soundtrack, and background, which is actually pretty cool
7. There is Split screen, and not just for console but also PC
8. You can have Cautions again in multiplayer
9. You can have AI fill all the empty spots in online
10.NO RUBBERBANDING AI!!!!
11. Rivals, if you continue to hit and crash into people in Career, they will slowly get mad at you.
12. Momentum, if you continue to do well in Career, with a full-time ride, you can upgrade/fix parts faster, and stuff like that.
13.The AI are improved, they don't crash in the triovals, and they usually know that you are there instead of just wrecking you.
14. No fake drivers, all real drivers whom started Daytona
15. Built-in DLC, almost at least 1 or 2 extra paint schemes for most drivers, not just Toyotas either.
16. Drafting, at plate tracks, and even any other track, you can sidedraft, just draft, or bump draft, and it actually will make you and the car whom your bump drafting/drafting go faster.
17. You can drive custom cars on online and in single player
18. Damamge model is much more realistic, the car with have the hood caved way in, or bent all the way up. Hard to describe, but it is greatley increased.
19. Not as twitchy when turning, the car is pretty stable, heavier, and more in control.
20. Brakes are ten times better, your not drifting in every corner.
21. Driver models of most real drivers
22. Victory music, if you win a race, online or offline, a song/tune in which you can choose plays, for all too hear.
23. Victory lane celebration, just a little scene of you, your car, and your team, and your trophy.
That's all I can think of, but there is certainly more.
What I wish they could fix/add:
1. Cautions, they come out better for a crash, but still if you crash by yourself, the caution usually doesn't come out...
2. Weird REV bug, where there is a weird random loud rev in the background that gets quiet, and then loud. Just a minor bug in which they could fix.
3. Crash physics, you still usually go flying into the air, not as bad, but you still usually get airborne, at least a little, and if you hit the wall diagloney, you spin out.
4. AI always crashing in turns 1 and two at Texas.
5.Private online races, like NASCAR The Game series, where you have only people that you want or invite
6. Random bug I found, I was in a race, and all of a sudden, it said I was in posistion zero, zero miles an hour, rpms, etc. I could change stuff like the leaderboard, but.....Only happened once though..
7.Would like victory burnouts
8. Would like a track map, especially for all the new road courses...
9. Would like it so you don't have to switch from leaderboard, to laps, to fuel, to damage, to water temp. NASCAR '15 had the track map, fuel gage, temperature, and a small leaderboard, all neatley on the screen.
Off the top of my head, that is all I can think of. On a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the best, I would rate this game at probably a 7.3/10. NASCAR Heat Evolution would probably be a 3.1/10, and NASCAR '15 would be a 7/10, but if they fixed the broken AI and all the stupid glitches, it would probably be a 9/10. All in all, this is a very fun, exciting, competitive, enjoyable fun NASCAR Game. I don't think that it should cost $50, I would have to say probably about $35 or so, which it will fall to $25 in a few months, so that won't matter. Not everything is the way it should be, and not everything that was complained about in NHE was fixed, but about 85% of it was, and they even added several new features and things.

OK so I admit I didnt have high hopes for this title after being burned by the last few... NH2 is not perfect but its better than the last versions of NASCAR we have had here on Steam. If you are looking to replace NR2k3, this isnt it... but  this is actually a  fun casual game. The addition of the top 3 touring series is nice. The cars/trucks handle differently as well.  I know that I would have like to have seen  a more sim oriented approach, but for an arcade game its fun... Case in point, I hooked the apron in Richmond and had it half spun but nothing happened... the car snapped back straight.
Graphically its ok - not the best but not the worst.   Maxed out on my system it looks ok -  but not what we should have for 2017. The vsync issue isnt one if you know how to use nVidia Nspector... just lock it there and you wont need to worry about it.
The pros are that its a massive improvement, and its actually fun  - not nearly as frustrating to deal with as the last few titles... and for that alone its worth a look.  The 3 touring series, the career mode, are nice to have too. The challenges bring me back to the old school Nascar Heat from 2000/01 ish, and are enjoyable.
Another thing I do enjoy about this version  - the REAL cars... none of those fake schemes.. or lower tier drivers in cars they never drove. Plus if you verify your age you get the beer cars... not a major deal to some but its a nice touch.
The cons for me at this point are the sound (isnt close to being what the real thing sounds like), the lack of pace car/manual caution laps, and the handling... its just too arcade for me. That said, I mainly got it to split screen with friends who are casual players, and its already been a big hit.
Id also like to have received the #41 Daytona winner post race car that console users got.
Id like a more robust replay system but its not a deal breaker at this point.

First of all let me say that this is a good game, not great, good, i've had at this time 149 hours of mostly a good time, now on to the review.
This game is all about farming, and getting the equipment to be more productive and expand until you own all the fields, that's basically the end goal, own every field (of varying sizes) and the best equipment, it's not an easy task in itself, specially in singleplayer, it's allso relaxing since you can change the game speed to fit your preference.
I've been playing this with my dad (im 34 hes 65+) and it's very fun to try and coordinate things so that each field is ready for harvest after the next one, you haveto take into account growth time, weather patterns, day and night, the economy, time it takes to transport etc. the only bad part is that the sky is pretty much static and you loose one hireable worker per multiplayer person besides yourself, the graphics are great, besides the sky
Theres three maps so far, various DLC's for machinery, an economic system, and rudimentary AI, traffic and pedestrians, singleplayer and multi aaand things do get dirty, very dirty.
Now (sigh) no game is perfect, that includes this one, there are a few bugs (not many actually) that may be annoying at times, the game at some point might become grindy and boring but there are aspects in this game you can change to instead of just working the fields, in a way you can "remotely" work the fields while doing other things by hiring workers, though keep an eye on them.
In this game there's one aspect that's pertinent to me, and that's forrestry (since im a trainee lumberjack) you can use various machinery to chop down trees, and make uses for them, such as selling the logs and grinding the branches into chips, and you can replant trees.
At the moment there seems to be a few problems with the physics part of this described now.
Forrestry is fun, it's a changer from the fields for sure, this is their first iteration of it (i think, seems like it) so there a few problems that stand out, one is the physics and strength of the claws, jaws, grabbers or whatever you prefer to call them, from logging forks to the ones on the crane, they're weak and loose grips alot on everything from logs to branches, you'll have a hard time holding on to 2 branches or logs no matter the size, and branches do fall into the ground and get stuck there, or just plain dissapear if you're using the harvester a tree top hits something while harvesting.
Now that said it's still a pretty decent attempt and since i bought the game i'll continue to do logging.
If you're into farming or wonder how things on a farm or logging work this a pretty good iteration, my recommendation is this, if you want this for the farming part then it's highly recommended, however if you want this for the forrestry part i'd say look around for something more dedicated to it, if you can't find anything then go with this.
Hope you found this review helpful in deciding what to do,

Hitman: Absolution does nothing by halves. When the game is good, it's fantastic and borderline brilliant. But when the game is BAD, woah boy, is it BAD. Missions are generally broken down into two different types; being given targets to assassinate by any means necessary, and Metal Gear Solid-esque sneaking through larger levels to get to the exit. The former can be absolutely stellar; you have to plan takedowns of other targets to get disguises to get close enough to your target (preferably without getting caught, as the best laid plans will understandably get torn asunder if someone sees you moving a body), and are then given a variety of methods to take your mark out, ranging from doing it personally with a gun or garotte wire, or, my personal favourite, using various parts of the environment to set up "accidental kills", like framing your target so he gets shot by police, setting a live wire to where they urinate in an alley in order to electrocute them, or less subtle methods like causing a crane's hook to come undone and crushing them with its contents.
Unfortunately, where the game falls apart is in the long stealth sections that make up the rest of the game. There's very few checkpoints, it's almost impossible to shake suspicion once you've lingered in an NPCs line of sight for too long, even while disguised, and with few exceptions (like one case where you can throw the police off your trail by dropping the body from someone else's murder into their line of sight), they feel very uninspired. Worse of all the AI is very buggy at times; I've been spotted through solid walls, had would-be victims magically turn around at random despite never going so in the previous dozen or so attempts, and on at least three occasions had to completely restart a level because an NPC spawned right in front of a checkpoint, facing me. Worst of all, checkpoints DON'T save progress between game sessions, meaning if you crash or have to exit for whatever reason, you have to start the entire section from the beginning.
There's a recipe for a truly unmatched stealth game here; if Hitman: Absolution had focused more on the actual "hits" and less on the horrendous stealth sections, it could have been darn near perfect. Unfortunately, those are diamonds in the rough, and there's a heck of a lot of rough to sift through. Thankfully the game's multiplayer "Contracts" mode, where players can set challenges for other players to beat by doing those actions in the in-game setting, provides a steady stream of decent diversions and while the stealth sections heavily bog down the early stages of the game, much of the later game brings the game back to form.
All told Absolution slips by with a recommendation, but with a lot of caveats. Sadly beyond Contracts mode you HAVE to endure the lousy stealth levels at least once to get to the good stuff, meaning those without a lot of patience for that sort of thing had best look elsewhere. The meat of the game is in replayability; thankfully replays break chapters up into sections that allow you to bypass the worst parts of them if you see fit.
I really, really hope that the next Hitman game learns from Absolutions' flaws and continues to polish its gems. For now, Absolution is fun-- just very flawed fun.

The game that you will Love-To-Hate TM.
There's a lot to like about Hitman: Absolution, but so, so much that is poorly excecuted.
The save system, or lack there of(ugh where to begin)? Do you like repeating the same parts of a game over and over hoping for a new result? Well the developer must've thought everyone who plays their games are masochists because without allowing you to save, it becomes repetition for the sake of repetition. It's not skill based at all in these situations just luck. So what it boils down to is less realism and taking you out of the experience due to frustation. I love a challenge, but my time is precious.
The Challenges that are setup are serioulsy contrived as well. Not only has the developer created these tasks for you to complete, but once you do there's no reason to replay a level. The desgin isn't well thought out either, requiring you to pause the game and access a menu to scroll through a vague list. It's a guessing game. The "challenges" aren't really that either, unless you think again redoing something over again to complete and earn points is challenging. Many of them are nonsensical too, i.e. making Agent 47 kill a certain number of goons in a particular costume, why would a hitman do that? I started consulting video guides just so I wouldn't miss anything. It's amazing that a developer would purposefully create content for a game that may never be seen.
Finally the disguise rules are a joke. Use a costume that other characters are wearing and they'll spot you; put your hand over your face and you can "trick them". Just writing that made me laugh.
All of these features seem like a badly coordinated rush job. Which is a shame because the world is beautiful to explore in this game. The character models and animation are well done. Shooting and stealth(when it works) are fun also. Honestly if the older Hitman games, with their open-world gameplay, were made in this new Glacier engine it would be a fantastic experience.
It's such a mixed bag that I had to write this review to vent about it. It's been theraputic, thanks for reading.

The game Bioshock on its own is a fantastically fun game to play.  However, this "remastered" version is far from being remastered.  I don't think a single bug or glitch was fixed from the original released nine years ago.  And I'm talking glaring problems that have been well listed and well known.  The controls are still awful and require major tinkering to create an enjoyable experience.  Luckily, having owned and gone through this before with the original game, I was able to modify configuration files until the game wasn't annoying to control.  Now, I'm not sure how easy it is to fix those control issues, but it appears and feels as if no effort was even attempted.
A simple bug I just recently encountered, however, I find almost impossible for whoever worked on the remaster to have had trouble fixing or impossible to not have known about.  On going through a playthrough I was carefully making sure I was aquiring all the audio diaries for the 'Historian' achievement.  Before leaving the area I carefully checked my list of audio diary messages and compared it to a guide of all the audio diaries.  One audio diary I knew I had picked up wasn't appearing in the list: the audio diary, Andrew Ryan - First Encounter.  I remember listening to this audio diary, but nevertheless went back to the spot to double check.  No audio diary was there confirming that I indeed picked it up.  A quick google search using "radio diary not showing up in message first encounter bioshock" popped up with many similar experiences.  First link I found gave me my answer... an answer from a post made seven years ago.  After picking up the audio diary, the diary appears in a different tab.  It appears in the Neptune's Bounty - Smuggler's Hideout section instead of the section for Arcadia - Farmer's Market.  To put it simply, it sounds like I'm still on track to (hopefully) finish the achievement.  A simple miscatagorization bug still haunting Bioshock into its "Remastered" version since its launch nine years ago.
I've heard that some of the issues may be under review for a future patch, but its incredibly saddening that this version is bascially the same exact game.  Nothing about the game was attempted to create a "remastered" version.  Luckily, I received the game for free owning the original Bioshock already, but expecting a game that's been fleshed out and refreshed from nine years down the line is not what this product delivers.
Buy the game and you can waste just as much of your life as i have.

First off. Don't listen to what the bad reviews have to say about this game. Just get the game, play some matches and have a great time.
So if you play any other MOBA, whether that be League Of Legends, Dota 2, Smite/etc. Y'know those good♥♥♥♥♥team-fights in the late-game that can win or lose a game? Imagine that, but that's the only part of the game, and you don't die in 1 shot. No armour that you have to take into consideration, no worrying about late-game. You have your damage, and your health. Some characters have more health, some have less.
So that's the main idea of the game, but now instead of items that you get throughout the game. You get buffs to your abilities. (Or, better known as "Battlerites") You get to choose from 3 each round. On the final round (If it's 2-2) You get to upgrade your ultimate ability.
If you play League of Legends (I dunno if this applies to other MOBAs) Imagine your battlerites as buffs to your champion that only last for that game. These Battlerites can be as simple as increasing the damage of one of your abilities, to pulling in all your enemies once you use your ultimate ability. And depending on who you're vsing, and what the enemies play-style is, your choices of your battlerites may change. You're playing a long-range character, the enemy is not bothering to focus you, and they are contesting Mid-Orb well? Get more damage on your "Snipe", or it's the opposite. The enemy is focusing you down as much as they can. Well you might want to get invisibility on your escape then.
I'd also like to point out that EVERYTHING. In the game is a skill-shot. There is no point and click♥♥♥♥♥♥here. Even if you're playing a melee champion, you still have to aim your attacks.
I highly recommend this game. The game will be going out of Early-Access and into Free-To-Play this year. With that change, I hope that lots of people start playing this game. The main reason I don't play this game more is due to the small player-base, and vsing the same players over and over.
(And now with the paragraph above being reality. The game's been more fun then ever!)
If any new players would like some tips and help to improve in Battlerite, send me an add in-game! If you show enough interest in the game and won't just dump it in a few days or so I'll happily help!

Having played both Torchlight 1 and 2, I would rate the first game below average. Compared to Torchlight 2 this is a really boring and repetitive game, with recycled monsters used continuously, some broken and in need of fix mobs (Accolytes) that will 1 shot you unless you play melee with maxed out defenses.
The maps are mostly the same, featuring a dungeon or a castle like theme, there is scarce diversity in maps, the enemies after a point are mostly the same, few bosses were interesting or unique looking, the active effects which you have to keep track of and renew every 20 seconds are way too many and make the combat feel like a chore.
The campaign is also very short (8 hours), the story is tiny and uninteresting and the optional end game is a 100-floor dungeon using again the same recycled maps and enemies.
Unfortunately this is a really dull and monotonous game and I do NOT recommend buying it in full price. Only perhaps for die-hard ARPG fans or if received for free or on a 3$ sale like I did.
Do not be fooled by the "Very Positive" reviews this game has on Steam. This is mostly because Torchlight 2 is such a big hit, it affected its predecessor aswell.
Speaking of which, the second installment in the series, Torchlight 2, is a really great game which solves almost all of the problems mentioned above, along with adding unique and immersive maps and epic boss fights. I definitely suggest giving the second game a try.

A well executed and properly involving survival and managing game.
I haven't put that many hours into the game (yet) however I would like to share my enthusiasm about this game with you all. This War of Mine puts the player in control of a small group of civilians in a dire, yet realistic setting in which survival truly is an every day concern.
It clearly doesn't need any zombies or post-apocalyptic events to transpire to have you feel you are in an endangered situation. You're in control of a group of survivors with real needs and emotions. The decisions you make, whether for good or ill will decide how they will feel. You're faced with a shortage of supplies and there is only so much you can scavenge and find within your safehouse or that you can craft. The game is solid and you can expect a real challenge from this game, it'll test out your decision making and your management skills. Since, from what I have noticed so far, there are a few random generated matters in the game it offers a proper replayability as well.
All in all I really recommend this game for those liking a strategic challenge. However, this game might not be for everyone as it does present itself differently from a lot of other games out there. If you want the full experience out of it I would also recommend you explore it without using any guides or similar as it takes a lot of the fun straight out of the game.

Greetings,
this review is quite late, as this game came out in 2009 and i am writing this at the end of 2017.
If you like action RPGs and if you liked Diablo 1, then this is the right thing for you.
What you get:
The 3 archetypes of classes: Warrior, Archer/Rogue, Mage. Each class has 3 destinctive talent trees.
I only played the mage Class. Every talent tree felt very unique and well balanced on it's own and followed a specific theme (Caster tree with insane mana regeneration and a lot of more damaging spells and CC spells; a Summoner tree with lots of minios and talents to enhance them and a Melee tree, with armor enhancing, a magic shield and close-up abilities).
The base game does not support resetting of spent talent points, but there is a mod for that.
If the loot lord is not with you, then you can buy stuff at the "gambler". Basically you can pick an unidentified item for a reasonable price. The item will have a certain quality, although the rolls on it are random.
Would only suggest that for weapons, because you get a good dps on it and thats kinda the most important thing on weapons. On armor it is too much hit or miss for my taste.
If you feel like playing different classes, then you get a shared stash in town, that is accessable at level 1.
If you want to enhance your gear, then you can also put random enchants on items at the town enchanter, to improve items.
Storywise you get the "Diablo 1" package. There is a mine at the town "Torchlight" and there is bad stuff going on in that mine. You have to fight all the way down to the big villan, with some minor "plottwists".
The graphic is still ok up today and it has a more comic like approach.
If you like ARPGs and havent stumbled on Torchlight yet, then it is worth your money.

Ok, I've changed this review to "recommend" because I had an issue with the price but seeing the hours I'm getting out of it, I no longer have an issue with it. Though as I stated below my main issue now is that the pace is too fast for the way I prefer to play. A simple "easy" setting which would slow the clock down would fix this.
What I do like about it:
1) It's a survival game.
2) The tech is sort of interesting, though odd in places i.e moonshine maker.
3) The animations are good.
4) Deeper than your average game and makes you think about the choices you make.
5) Very original and well thought out.
What I don't like about it:
1) Forces you to play at the pace the game developers want with a very annoying clock/countdown timer. No relaxing game session, unfortunately. Also makes for unrealistic sprinting everywhere in the "house" for your characters. "I'm tired"..sprint to bed.
2) The characters whine and complain a lot. Would this be realistic given the circumstances? Maybe...maybe not.
3) No difficulty level. This could be implemented by slowing down the countdown-clock on easy, for example.
4) No saving. If you leave, the day starts over. Would be nice if they explained this somewhere.
5) Combat is...automatic. No need to even point-and-click.  Except for the gun-fights. It's also hard to just run away while engaged in combat.
7) Doesn't give you enough time to build all the tech.
8) Can't enjoy the fruits of your labour as you're rushing everything and everywhere because of the annoying countdown-timer on the top left.
If it was half the price I paid for it, I'd probably recommend it but at £14.99? No. You can get far better games for that. If you want to try it I would suggest waiting until it's discounted.

This is a rewrite to this review. So...... Farming Simulator 2015 (Gold Edition):
First off, my father was a smalltime farmer. I used to help him. He's been playing this game for a quite some time and has logged many hours and loves it. I only purchased it with the intent of playing online with him. However......
I can't really give this game a good review. While it is somewhat playable, it is also laughable to even consider it as a simulation. First, you start off in a field with some equipment and your first crop ready for harvest. No tutorials (normal mode) and not a clue on what to do. So you basically run around checking things out, till you figure it all out. There's a small actions menu which can be confusing at times. Once you figure out the controls and the menu, you learn to harvest. Harvesting has a Minecraft feel to it (Never even played Minecraft!). The biggest issue with the game is rendering, which ties into the Minecraft feel. Crop renders in square patches and when plowing, some parts of the field don't get plowed right. Plowing and harvesting evenly is an issue, as well. You can "hire a worker", but expect to pay them on $3-4,000+ per field, which is rediculous. And sometimes, they're worthless. So, you harvest and either fill your storage with crop, or travel to businesses to sell your harvest. If you're in the negative cash-wise, you'll pay back your worker before making profit. If you took a loan out, you can pay it back $5,000 at a time. So you plow, wait, harvest and store or sell your crop to try to break even or profit, so you can buy more equipment, which is reasonably priced. You will get odd missions like mowing or forklift, mowing is okay, but the controls for the forklift are a pain on keys and mouse. By the way, took forever to realise not only did I need the blue tractor and forks, but also needed to buy the arms as well. WHAT THE HELL?! Couldn't just make it 1 or 2 purchases! Oh, and if you didn't ralise the weights are supposed to help keep your tractor from tipping and you so happen to tip it, no GTA style unflipping. Hit i for inventory/info and search for tractors owned. Then hit "Reset", which takes your equipment back to your farm. I'm sure there's more for me to nitpick at, but my biggest issure is paid DLC for a halfassed kind of ugly looking game that isn't really worth the $17 I paid for on sale. This game may be worth $5-10 for slight enjoyment. Don't expect a bunch of acheivements, either. Short short list.
In conclusion, mediocre graphics, horrible rendering, nowhere near simulation worthy, lack of tutorials during playtime, overly complicated controls and ♥♥♥♥ing pointless DLC. For my time spent, I can give it 4/10. But even giving it a 4 is being generous. I'd skip it, unless you can get an easy refund.

Having played SoaSE since its original release in 2008, I can say that this game is the definitive iteration a space RTS. It is a bit sandbox, since no campaign exists, but the back-story sets up skirmishs well enough. Rebellion has gorgeous graphics, and scales well on older machines (I had a budget laptop from 2010 that could play this on low, no dedicated graphics card).
The Titans are glorious beasts without being too overpowered, and the new Stellar Phenomena DLC adds more ambience to Rebellion. The sense of scale is astounding: you can go from managing a single colony ship, to watching a massive fleet duke it out over a resource-rich terran world.
Each race has a different UI, which helps with immersion, as well as very well-made musical pieces that is played during gameplay.

So, I got Shelter whilst it was pretty cheap in a sale and I've got to say for a game that only last around an hour it is a rollercoaster of emotions. You start the game with your five little cubs, off you go out into the world to find food to help them grow strong and healthy and then... you see it. That giant bird figure that swoops down and takes away something double the size of your babies. You quickly run for cover only to realise... it got one of your cubs.
So yeah, the game starts off very nice with some LOVELY music and BEAUTIFUL visuals and whilst these are retained throughout most of the game, the serenity is not. This beautiful bright landscape suddenly turns into a nightmare. This game is tense, VERY tense at some points. It will have you constantly looking over your shoulder making sure that your cubs are still there and it really does make you panic about these small creatures even though... it's only a game. The music just adds to how tense it can be and the game really portrays the struggles of animals in the circle of life really well. One thing this game really teaches you is that no matter how big and hungry you are, there is always something bigger and hungrier than you. Inevitably in the end someone has to die, will it be you or your cubs?
Brilliant game. If you like games like assasins creed then you will love this.

A new instalment to the Civ franchise that, whilst bringing new ideas to the table, fails to capitalise on what made its successors so great. A tactically underdeveloped game with a monotonous look and dull writing. The game isn't bad - it just fails to develop in any interesting ways from Civ V, and comes nowhere close to the full majesty of that game with all of the expansions. Even the most rabid of Civ fans should wait for the expansions, or at least a few patches.
Positives:
+ New ideas introduced to the Civ formula, with the Virtue trees and Tech Web changing the way research and cultural development work.
+ An interesting idea with the introduction of Affinities, presenting more development and unit choice.
+ Stays true to the usual Civ game mechanics - the familiarity helps you get into the game straight away.
Negatives:
- Tactically underdeveloped - the choices you make never really have much of an impact on your Civilization, and the only really viable strategy is war.
- Underwritten - the 8 Civs seem devoid of personality or culture, and the quests are uninteresting at best.
- The art style is just boring - the tiles are often hard to distinguish from one another, and with the size of the galaxy, the fact that each planet has exactly the same resources is disappointing.
- A large array of glitches and bugs that, while not game-breaking, present an annoyance in their regularity.
Rating: 63%

A truly amazing pirate adventure the likes of which I have yet to see!
This game is set in the golden age of piracy. It borrows heavily from historical figures and accounts while spicing it up just enough to make it a great adventure game.
You play a non-historical pirate who slips into the role of an assassin during the game's introduction. This is very interesting for many reasons. Firstly, it means this pirate game is unlike any other pirate game, because you have much more to do than just plunder, pillage and drink copiuous amounts of rum. Throughout the story, your character fights beside an ancient group of anarchists, but also many historical pirates such as Blackbeard, Hornigold and of course the legendary Bartholomew Roberts.
You start off with a small galleon named "Jackdaw". At first, it barely has enough firepower to threaten a lonely trade ship, and it's hull falls appart if a rock formation looks at it wrong. By the end of the game however, you can upgrade it so much that it can take on fortresses, ships of the line and even legendary ghost ships. This is where I think the fact that this is an AC game truly shines.
All other pirate games that I have played have distinct "game modes" such as "sailing mode", "land exploration mode", "ship combat mode", etc. Not so here! There is no transition from walking around the harbor to sailing your ship. This is because ships like nearly everything else save for sheer cliffs is climbable. So, if you are done on the shore and want to set sail, you climb on board your ship, walk to the helm and grab the wheel and off you go!
This is even more amazing if you board another ship. You will be presented with a series of objectives, but how you complete them is up to you. You can stay on board your ship, fight on the enemy deck or climb around aloft and do air-assassinations on their important fighters from above.
Add to this the great graphics engine that runs smoothly even on my old GTX 780. My GPU is 10 years older than this game, and yet it still looks amazing. This is because they took great care to make the interaction of the environment with your character to seem realistic. Anything from how you swing with a rope during boarding actions to brushing away leaves while strolling through a jungle looks very detailed and believable. I should also mention the water, which is another thing that works much better than most other pirate games I have played. It feels like a real ocean, up to the point where you have to factor it into your line of shooting during ship battles. Waves vary in size and have a direct influence on cannon trajectory. Also, huge waves look really scarey. They are less of a gameplay danger and more of a "holy crap look at that thing!" moment that sent shivers down my spine.
So, graphically, this game blew me away, even compared to newer games with "better graphics". I'd say it was less the technical specs and more the atmosphere and how the world was built. It just feels real!
There are many more things to go into, but one more thing I want to point out are the diving scenes. They are the only thing that are really "seperate", because you have to dive using a diving bell and you have no weapons. Instead of hiding from guards, you have to dodge sharks and sea urchins while searching through forgotted wrecks for lost treasure. Here again we see how much love the designers gave the concept of making the game feel real. It is loads of fun to explore the many caves and wrecks that hide on the ocean floor. There is even one quest that require you to navigate an abandoned mine shaft, take out a guard and then use only the weapons you find to assassinate a target in a cave that has no other access.
There is only one problem I have with this game: Once you complete all the quests, the game is over. Usually, end game content isn't something I need, but this game is so amazingly awesome that I really wish there was some sort of item I could spend 1000 hours grinding for. The crafting system is really cool, especially because you have to hunt down plans for maxing out your ship by opening chests. Having said that, I wish it was more like Skyrim where I could spend weeks or months trying to find ways to make my gear even better.
So basically the only complaint I have is that it is so awesome that I'm sad I beat it.

In Summary: After playing over 700 hours of Civ 5 (bnw) I was really looking forward to more. However, this game is actually worse in almost every way, making it a massive disappointment. If you must buy, wait for an expansion sorting out the issues
with a 50-70% discount at least.
Units:
- In this game there is much less upgrading of units (i.e swordman to knight) or ability gains (i.e +XX% on flat/hill/etc, +XX% v wounded/bunkered/etc, Gain XXhp on kill and so on.
- No special units between players, only between 'affinities'....think Civ 5, but minus all the special units between civs and instead have just 2 or 3 units depending on if you chose Freedom/military/authority later in the game
- Units all look similar and on upgrade some units don't even change.
- A lack of sea or air units (no subs, no helicopters), plus the ones which exist are pretty useless
Wonders:
- Most have Abilities which do very little, many just give basic resourse such as 'food' or 'energy'...something which a simply improved tile could do
- Very few of them
- The almost artistic images of wonders are gone, and are now replaced with what appears to be blueprints...literally barely reconisable white outlined images on a blue background
Tech:
- Techs don't follow from one to another...or even make sense. We travelled across the universe, but we need to learn physics and computers again?
- Again like the wonders, the beautiful images in Civ 5 after researching a tech are gone
- Tech research doesn't feel like it's going anyway, as the game play is pretty much the same regardless of where on the tech 'web' you are
Trade:
- Few tradible resources in game (i.e gold still present but no silver, no cotton/silk/etc but 'fiber' however not tradible)
- Not good balance on maps for resources. Some maps have very little or too much.
- Almost no sea resources
A.I
- Alien (barbarians) A.I don't improve as the game progresses, same weak units throughout making them simply annoying later n the game and ad no challage or even benefit
- Appear regardless of vision
- Rarely pilage
Others nags:
- Dispite finding the planet, knowing the planet supported life before going, then flying to it, finding a landing spot, our vision is merely around our settlement?
- Games too short
- OP early-mid game units
- Constantly resetting trade convoys, if you have over 7 cities it becomes every turn...I just gave up having full convoys at every city at this point.
- The female voice throughout the game gets annoying fast. The one in Civ 5 was much better.
- Miasama damaging everything at the same rate, surely if the first solider unit takes xx damage from it, then the late game LEV destoryer should take less...or at the very least solider take more
- Civs and station (the replacement for city states) start to appear after you've settled and you will see where they land. However, this is too much of an advantage on single player. The ignorance of your staring area makes for a better more challaging experiance
The Positives:
- Normal building have more options for abilities, most useful to manipulate 'health', especially with many cities.
- Quite like the digs and research pods
- I have mixed feelings on the victory stories, I'm glad that the concept is being tried, but the current ones aren't benefiting the game...
- I do like the idea of the satalities

Before anything else allow me to clarify that RoA is built from the ground up to be a competitive game. It is by no means a casual party game, as many understand the smash bros. games to be. There are no built in items to date, and I doubt there will be, there is no online support for anything outside of 1v1. It is meant for competitive tournament play, a breathe of fresh air for those of us getting a little exasperated with Nintendo's complete absence and apparant disinterest in supporting the competitive scene for the smash brothers games, melee in particular.
The game hasn't even seen its full release yet and it already strikes me as being more balanced than any of the smash bros. games. There are 8 characters featured and although the challenge is certainly stronger for certain matchups every character has the potential to beat any of the other characters in the cast, not to unlike melee's top 8 albeit without matchups as grossly difficult to surmount. Looking at you Peach vs. Ice Climbers. As someone who prefers a game where skill is the primary deciding factor in a competitive match this game is in many ways ideal.
The system allows for advanced movement with simplistic mechanics. The occassionally frustrating ledge grab mechanics present in the smash bros. games has been forgone entirely introducing a far more dynamic and skill dependent edge guarding system. However, things that were certainly good strengths in the smash bros. games have been abandoned alongside it. Grabbing and shielding have been removed entirely along with spot dodging and the ability to get knock down, you simply bounce of the ground instead. While the shielding has been replaced with the parrying system the absence of any sure form of defense makes the meta game very unlike any of the smash bros. games.
In terms of it's combos and flow it certainly feels fast and engaging like melee. However, at the upper level of play the metagame certainly emphasizes spacing to a level comparable to that of Smash 64. While the punish game might not be quite as insanely powerful as Smash 64, RoA's cast can still put the hurt on viciously off a single instance of poor spacing, sometimes even taking stocks outright. While this certainly makes for a fascinating neutral I would argue that it ultimately costs the game a level of depth that Melee in particular has.
The only other issue at present that persistantly frustrates me is the online coding. While the ping indicator is a great addition it has proven on occassion to be deceptive. I'll join into a match with as good as 40 ping. Only a few moments into the match it spikes into the 100's. Worse yet are the instances where the lag will spike suddenly ending the match prematurely. The Game at present is still in early access so I hope that the online scripting will be improved in that time but as of right now it leaves some things to be desired.
All that to say, Rivals of Aether is an excellent game, by a wide margin the best indie game I have ever enjoyed on steam well deserving of a flourishing competitive scene and a wider appreciation from its cousin smash bros. scenes. It's stages are excellent, characters well balanced, and soundtrack a top tier bit-symphony. But what seperates RoA from it's fighting game peers, and really what will indicate its importance in the long term, is what it represents.
For years Nintendo has a had a chokehold on the percentage fighting game market. The Smash Bros. series alone has been the standard for the genre that you could call platform fighting games or percentage fighting games and while there have been other entries into the genre all of them are remarkably lacking and comparatively forgettable. Until Rivals of Aether that is. With this game the lid that nintendo has had on the genre has truly been popped off for the first time, ever in my opinion.
People now know that it's possible to make a game with mechanics that remain faithful to the system introduced by the smash bros. games while branching out into new innovative character rosters & mechanics allowing for truly innovative play and depth. If Smash Bros. is the Street Fighter of the percentage fighting game genre (PFG) then RoA is definitely the Mortal Kombat. But what excites me even more is knowing that down the road comes the King of Fighters, the Killer Instincts, and the Guilty Gears of the genre that will take it to even greater heights. Rivals of Aether is the first step in taking the PFG genre out of the shadow of Nintendo's petty politics and casual market and into the light of esports where it belongs.

Where Saints Row IV took place in matrix version of Steel Port and revolved around you fighting an alien empire, Gat out of Hell take place in hell and involve you fighting demons to free The Protagonist of the Saints Row game. You gain angelic wings early on and the sky become your playground. Soaring is similar to the glide ability but this time you can gain altitude and control your speed. The new weapons are interesting. You can definitely tell the creators had fun coming up with even wackier weapons this time. With weapons based on the 10 plagues of Egypt and the 7 deadly sins, destroying demons with your weapons become more entertaining.
The game isn't that long. You could easily go through it in a couple of hours, but the real value come from enjoy hell and torturing the residents with your weapons and powers. Overall it a good add on to Saints Row IV, if you enjoyed that game then you will love this.

This is an excellent game for fans of the Super Smash Bros. Series.
It features similiar gameplay options: wavedashing, short hops, fast falls, specials, teching, wall jumps, DI, and SDI. While all of these mechanics are featured in Super Smash Bros. Melee, here in Rivals of Aether, they are much simpler to execute. The frame window for inputs is much greater allowing you to pick up these advanced techniques quite easily.
Ledge mechanics are different. You can not grab ledge, however it is still very important to prevent the opponent from recovering.
The combo game is a big part of Rivals of Aether. Similiar to Smash Bros. you can "free style" your combos by reacting to DI and tech.
Defense-wise, there are no shields. However, you do have a block. When timed correctly, this block can also stun the enemy for a short time. You also still have your standard rolls and air-dodges.
The game is wonderfully designed. You have 8 characters, all with a wide variety of movesets. You have a decent amount of maps, each with a "competitive" variant. You can create custom skins for characters. There is a button check mode right from the character select screen, excellent for quick handwarmers. There are in depth tutorials that teach the basics and advanced techniques of the game. There is local and offline play, against a second player or AI. There is also 4 player teams. Story mode and Abyss mode (a wave based gamemode) are on the way too. There are also new maps and characters planned for the future.
It is also important to note that you are able to use a GameCube controller (as long as you have the proper adapter). So if you have played any of the Smash games on the Dolphin Emulator or are coming from Anther's Ladder, you will be all set.
While this game isn't an exact copy of Super Smash Bros., fans of the series will find and enjoy many similarities. All in all, a great game designed with the player in mind. It is easier to pick up, yet still difficult to master. I highly reccomend it.

The Last Remnant was part of an experiment by Square-Enix to make two new Japanese RPG IPs with the Unreal Engine 3 side-by-side with the development of Final Fantasy XIII. In my honest opinion, this experiment was much more successful than the experiments they made with Final Fantasy XIII itself.
Final Fantasy XIII gave almost no player freedom while The Last Remnant allows players to make choices. Final Fantasy XIII had no towns and thus lost its sense of a cohesive and defined world while The Last Remnant has multi-sectioned town hubs ala golden-era Final Fantasies and tends to reward going off the beaten path. Final Fantasy XIII has a combat system that relies mostly on auto-battle with occasional 'paradigm shifts' and healing while The Last Remnant has a legitimately challenging combat system, even for vetern JRPG players. Lastly, Final Fantasy XIII had a story needlessly convoluted by invented words with no proper explanations to define them that essentially boiled down to 'we're cursed, we don't know why, let's pad out 40 hours talking about it amongst ourselves and then kill God' while The Last Remnant's story is more focused and explains itself better, allowing for a much better experience than looking up words in an in-game encyclopaedia.
That said, the main character, Rush Sykes, annoys me in this game almost as much as Tidus from Final Fantasy X, but the mechanics in this game really save it from me placing it in the same category as FF X, which I hate immensely.

Ok, I've changed this review to "recommend" because I had an issue with the price but seeing the hours I'm getting out of it, I no longer have an issue with it. Though as I stated below my main issue now is that the pace is too fast for the way I prefer to play. A simple "easy" setting which would slow the clock down would fix this.
What I do like about it:
1) It's a survival game.
2) The tech is sort of interesting, though odd in places i.e moonshine maker.
3) The animations are good.
4) Deeper than your average game and makes you think about the choices you make.
5) Very original and well thought out.
What I don't like about it:
1) Forces you to play at the pace the game developers want with a very annoying clock/countdown timer. No relaxing game session, unfortunately. Also makes for unrealistic sprinting everywhere in the "house" for your characters. "I'm tired"..sprint to bed.
2) The characters whine and complain a lot. Would this be realistic given the circumstances? Maybe...maybe not.
3) No difficulty level. This could be implemented by slowing down the countdown-clock on easy, for example.
4) No saving. If you leave, the day starts over. Would be nice if they explained this somewhere.
5) Combat is...automatic. No need to even point-and-click.  Except for the gun-fights. It's also hard to just run away while engaged in combat.
7) Doesn't give you enough time to build all the tech.
8) Can't enjoy the fruits of your labour as you're rushing everything and everywhere because of the annoying countdown-timer on the top left.
If it was half the price I paid for it, I'd probably recommend it but at £14.99? No. You can get far better games for that. If you want to try it I would suggest waiting until it's discounted.

This game is very good.  It even has a better apocolypse suvival feel to it than most zombie games.  The first several playthroughs as you learn the game are fantastic and everything feels like a hopeless struggle as you try and balance your ability to feed yourself, develop your home, fend off looters, and fight off depression.  Even as you have a good idea of what to do, you have to be very careful because one small mistake can be very costly, even fatal.
I give it a 9/10, with my only complaints being that you have a good understanding of game mechanics, most of the game becomes tedium.  Starting out is still the wonderful struggle, but once you stabalize (which can happen as early as day 5 if you are lucky and know what to do), your survival is pretty much assured and the game loses a lot of what makes it so good.

This is a game first and foremost about exploration, and every facet of its design is keyed precisely to make that exploration feel as good as possible. The deeper you go into the world the deeper you find you CAN go into the world; uncovering secret areas, interesting finds, characters, and fights, and slowly unearthing the story they all collectively represent. Almost any initiative you take, any time you have a go at a wall that FEELS like its hiding something, any time you want to go back and retry an earlier area with your newest power up, you are rewarded with a shortcut linking one area to another, or a new power, or a secret character, or just a silly frivolence to let you know that YES, the devs did know you’d go there and YES they want you to know that.
I could talk about the other amazing aspects of this game, the artstyle is beautiful and executed goddamn well, the story is well put together, it has a good mix of challenge and gameplay options, and it has one of the highest value-to-buck ratios of any game in the genre, but almost everything that can be said about this game has been said about this game by people slightly more eloquent than I, so I can only give what made this game so singular for me, in that it felt like I was exploring a world created with the one purpose of giving me as much pleasure as possible to slowly peel it away, until every single room of it is etched into my mind forever.
Buy this game.

Pros:
-Ability to quickly grow your collection (it's absolutely feasible to get every card for free, but it's a grind)
-Can't get duplicate cards in packs
-Streamlined turn sequence means the game does move along at a reasonable pace (a problem for digital versions of MTG)
-It's Magic
Cons:
-Strange deck construction limitations that effectively neuter the game, limit deck construction possibilities, and warp rarities such that commons are harder to finish than mythics (you can have only 1 of each mythic in a 60 card deck, 2 of each rare, and 3 of each uncommon)
-Rapid set releases mean you have to play a lot to get all the cards
-No ability to select which cards you get (no crafting like Hearthstone), complete RNG as to what's in your collection
-Terrible choice of starting cards (most are unplayable garbage that wouldn't even be playable in limited)
-Bad UI and playing field design (most of the screen is empty space, and you have to have a mouse to be able to actually click the tiny images on the screen with any accuracy -- don't play on mobile/tablet)
-Dumbed down ruleset prevents advanced level play (e.g. can't make a game action during a draw step)
-No drafting/sealed/tournament mode
-Broken and glitchy questing system (only gives you a quest if you log in for that day, can't log in after 3 days and get/do 3 quests)
-Have to use the atrocious deck-building wizard to complete quests (can't use custom decks for completing quests)
-Can't complete quests in 2HG
-Massive server issues (getting better)
-Bad AI
-No ability to communicate whatsoever
-Bad story mode (though it was nice that it was actually a story this time around)
-Non-skippable tutorials
-If a player quits (which almost always happens once they start losing) they get replaced by an AI, and you only get credit for winning if you beat the AI, which makes zero sense, prolongs games and only leads to frustration.
-Poor community interaction and communication/failure to address complaints and issues
-CG cutscenes are voiceless and look like they're twenty years old
-Poor card pool (which should get better in time, but right now is mostly unfun and unplayable junk)
-Low quest rewards (40g max, packs cost 150g), which leads to an emphasis on grinding the AI for gold
-Very easy to skip your attack due to how they've placed the buttons, which can totally ruin a game
-Oh yeah, and let's not forget that there's a non-zero chance of your collection literally disappearing, and their support team will not reinstate it (at best, you'll get a handful of packs)
To sum up, Magic Duels is a very mediocre, if not bad digital CCG. If you want to play a digital CCG, play Hearthstone. It's designed and implemented far better, and it saddens me as a veteran Magic player to see Wizards yet again ship an underwhelming and sub-par video game. At this point, I'm convinced that they are intentionally shipping mediocre video games because they're afraid that if they make a good one, they'd hurt their lucrative paper Magic business. Maybe the latest earnings reports regarding Hearthstone will convince them that this is ridiculous, but likely not.
It feels very much like they saw Hearthstone, and then decided to make a clone of it to emulate its success, but also decided to make every element of it at least a little worse, either out of incompetence or our of fear of making the game too good of an alternative to paper magic. Blizzard literally gave them the blueprint for a successful digital CCG, and they just ignored everything that has been working for Blizzard and produced this piece of garbage. If you squint your eyes, it looks like a Magic version of Hearthstone. But if you actually play the game, you quickly realize that most of the things that make Hearthstone worth playing are not here, and that Magic Duels is just a highly inferior experience. Since digital CCGs are a lot like MMOs in that I can only really play one at a time, the fact that Magic Duels is so incredibly inferior to Hearthstone makes it virtually unplayable.
Stay away unless you just have to play the Magic version of a digital CCG and don't want to pay the crazy high amounts of money it costs to play MTGO. Almost everything about this game is vastly inferior to its competitors. It feels designed to give people a taste of what Magic is like so as to lure them into the paper market, not as an avenue to actually enjoy playing the game of Magic on a digital device.
WOTC: if you're reading this, please hire a competent game developer from this decade to fix this mess. It's a crying shame that the leader of CCGs has one of the worst digital CCGs on the market, and it can only serve to damage your brand.

The game runs really well on PC, even though sometimes the sync between the voice actors and sound gets knocked off but that's just my PC being dumb on occassion, very rarely does it occur otherwise. I enjoyed the story on PS3, and was happy to replay it, but if you are looking for something that is nonlinear, you are looking in the wrong place.
For about the first 10-11 chapters (there are 13), you are constricted to hallways that determine your path, with the occasional offshoot (which deadend and force you to go back). In that sense it lacks the feel of some final fantasy games like FFVII or VIII. However, the character development and world building are very interesting, which is honestly the reason I keep going in the first place at this point. The normal mode is certainly brutal to those who cannot adapt to the ATB Gauge type of battle, where some battles seem impossible, which is why strategizing is key once you can switch people in your party. Like most people have said, the game is heavily tutorial-based, where 5-7 chapters are strictly teaching you how to play with the system and how to strategize with the mechanics. If you cannot deal with the mechanics or just want the story, there is an easy mode, which makes the battles easier to endure and grinding quicker than in normal mode. Also, once you get to a certain point, the open areas are really beautiful and give missions for you to do so that you can get better gear or more CP to level up. Overall, I feel it is a good game, though it lacks in some aspects.
