This game reminded me a bit of my first racing game, Bill Elliots Nascar Challenge (1990 on PC).  It was a terrible game but it was the only Nascar game  that was available.
First off, the AI isn't very good.  Going into the corners at Darlington or Dover, if you slow down or tap the brake, it will most likely result in you being freight trained by most of the field.  The AI doesn't seem to slow down  or try to avoid you.
Or if you are at Daytona or Talladega the AI will turn  into you from the front strech to the corner.  I've also had it where I've been sandwiched between 2 cars unable to steer out of it.  Generally what would happen is  I'd have to get out of the gas only to be rammed from behind.
Multiplayer is joke.  The most people I've seen on multiplayer was about, 20 spread between 4 lobbies.   So many griefers were present on multiplayer.   The first race online I did, one guy sat in the middle of track seeing how many people he could wreak into.   Then he had the gaul to add me as steam friend...
Another annoyance was the scoring system.   It happened many times when a player would finish 2nd and be scored in the 14th postion.   One of my seasons, I had won 18 races, including the last 3 before Homestead.   I  should have been in 1st place but for what ever reason I was scored in 2nd.
I'll say i got my moneys worth (37 cents/hour)  but its hard to recommend this game.   If the game was more polished, I would recommend it.  It would be amazing to have games come out in a finished state, rather than them coming out with problems.

and

A truly amazing pirate adventure the likes of which I have yet to see!
This game is set in the golden age of piracy. It borrows heavily from historical figures and accounts while spicing it up just enough to make it a great adventure game.
You play a non-historical pirate who slips into the role of an assassin during the game's introduction. This is very interesting for many reasons. Firstly, it means this pirate game is unlike any other pirate game, because you have much more to do than just plunder, pillage and drink copiuous amounts of rum. Throughout the story, your character fights beside an ancient group of anarchists, but also many historical pirates such as Blackbeard, Hornigold and of course the legendary Bartholomew Roberts.
You start off with a small galleon named "Jackdaw". At first, it barely has enough firepower to threaten a lonely trade ship, and it's hull falls appart if a rock formation looks at it wrong. By the end of the game however, you can upgrade it so much that it can take on fortresses, ships of the line and even legendary ghost ships. This is where I think the fact that this is an AC game truly shines.
All other pirate games that I have played have distinct "game modes" such as "sailing mode", "land exploration mode", "ship combat mode", etc. Not so here! There is no transition from walking around the harbor to sailing your ship. This is because ships like nearly everything else save for sheer cliffs is climbable. So, if you are done on the shore and want to set sail, you climb on board your ship, walk to the helm and grab the wheel and off you go!
This is even more amazing if you board another ship. You will be presented with a series of objectives, but how you complete them is up to you. You can stay on board your ship, fight on the enemy deck or climb around aloft and do air-assassinations on their important fighters from above.
Add to this the great graphics engine that runs smoothly even on my old GTX 780. My GPU is 10 years older than this game, and yet it still looks amazing. This is because they took great care to make the interaction of the environment with your character to seem realistic. Anything from how you swing with a rope during boarding actions to brushing away leaves while strolling through a jungle looks very detailed and believable. I should also mention the water, which is another thing that works much better than most other pirate games I have played. It feels like a real ocean, up to the point where you have to factor it into your line of shooting during ship battles. Waves vary in size and have a direct influence on cannon trajectory. Also, huge waves look really scarey. They are less of a gameplay danger and more of a "holy crap look at that thing!" moment that sent shivers down my spine.
So, graphically, this game blew me away, even compared to newer games with "better graphics". I'd say it was less the technical specs and more the atmosphere and how the world was built. It just feels real!
There are many more things to go into, but one more thing I want to point out are the diving scenes. They are the only thing that are really "seperate", because you have to dive using a diving bell and you have no weapons. Instead of hiding from guards, you have to dodge sharks and sea urchins while searching through forgotted wrecks for lost treasure. Here again we see how much love the designers gave the concept of making the game feel real. It is loads of fun to explore the many caves and wrecks that hide on the ocean floor. There is even one quest that require you to navigate an abandoned mine shaft, take out a guard and then use only the weapons you find to assassinate a target in a cave that has no other access.
There is only one problem I have with this game: Once you complete all the quests, the game is over. Usually, end game content isn't something I need, but this game is so amazingly awesome that I really wish there was some sort of item I could spend 1000 hours grinding for. The crafting system is really cool, especially because you have to hunt down plans for maxing out your ship by opening chests. Having said that, I wish it was more like Skyrim where I could spend weeks or months trying to find ways to make my gear even better.
So basically the only complaint I have is that it is so awesome that I'm sad I beat it.

There's so much missing from this game. The unit workshop we were promised early on was scrapped. The "barbarian" feature had an overhaul that actually made it feel reasonable. By that I mean aliens will leave you alone mostly if you stop attacking them, they can turn angry or docile. A great improvement by far, but overall the game alone lacks originality.  Most of the unit upgrade choices as you progress through "Affinity" are the same for each branch. Virtues remain relatively the same, simple and straight forward but with column and row bonuses. The only other real change from Civ 5 would be the satalite layer.
Also the cities start as outposts instead of actual cities. Now granted you can now make trade vessels now and increase the speed of their growth. Eventually with trade you can eliminate the economic downside of large expansion.
All in all this game feels hollow, like there was so much waiting for it. I have a sad feeling this game was released as a DLC magnet (like The Sims).
You're better off checking out something like Pandora: First Contact.

Very unique, competitive, and fun game. WASD movement, skills are really skillshots, and fast rounds.
For casuals, this game is great, you have daily and weekly quests, and alongside to new players, there's achievements that they can unlock. All of these daily quests, weekly quests, and achievements, you will gain rewards such as cosmetic chests and ingame currency.
Everyone has an equal playing field, no runes or masteries that give you a head start in the game, also no buying items. Instead, at the beginning of each round everybody has an option to chose 1 out of the 3 "battlerites" given to them for their character which allow you to customize your abilities and playstyle.
Combat is really fluid, thanks to WASD and skillshots, every character's kit seems to fit well with the gamestyle. The game is easy to grasp, but hard and rewarding to master.
Every champion is viable, just certain team compositions are not good against other compositions. This game's balance is okay, no character is broken since every character can be countered. Characters are more balanced in 3v3s than in 2v2s, since you have more variety of champions to play with and against. If you're looking for the most balanced game mode, it's going to be 3v3s, but not much people play 3v3s.
Battlerite's playerbase is okay, nothing you need to worry about, there's 2.5k people playing each day, its not going to decline, it's in Early Access, its completely fine.
Nothing wrong with ranked matchmaking during this stage of the game. Only 2.5k players playing the game each day during peak times, you can expect going against the same people a couple times. Yes you will be matched with others higher than you, but if you dont win against them, then you dont deserve to get up to that rank, so don't complain. If you dont want to go against people higher than you, you use "Strict Matchmaking" which sets you to play with others are your rank, but you'll have to compensate for the time to search for players at your rank.
For only $20, for all the champions (including all the future ones), and for 400+ hours I have on it, this game is worth the money. More features are to come, watching this game develop since October, 2016, its a very promising game. I have fun each day playing it.

If you like fighting game, this game is a great change in gameplay. It is a sumo-fighter, like those in the Series Smash Bros series, but it is designed with a competitive mindset in hand. The characters feel both balanced and fleshed out, providing a great experience. I first noticed this game on Humble Bundle, and I was skeptical at first. While, I had played Brawlhallah, it the characters felt empty and unbalanced. The mechanics were also a little unclear, unlike Rivals of Aether. In RoA (Rivals of Aether) exhibition matches are done as a best 2 out of 3, and while both games feature the "sumo" mechanic, where the objective to to knock the opponent out of the ring, RoA's normal gameplay doesn't reward you points for a knock out, but instead penalizes you for getting knocked out. This, in contrast to Brawlhallah's normal scoring system, rewards player for not just knock outs, but kill streaks and kill steals as well. I felt as though it cheapened gameplay, and rewarded those who were good at the latter, but not necessarily completely competent in overall skill. The biggest differences in mechanics, generally speaking, compared to others are that: 1) you cannot grab ledges, but each character is given a wall jump and can use their recovery move once before and after the wall jump; 2) shields do not exist, you can still "perfect shield" like in the Smash series, but it will only activate a "parry" which allows you a brief window to punish your opponents mistakes; 3) it has no grab/throw mechanics, other than Etalus's up air; 4) there are three types of attack buttons, jab/tilt with a normal attack, special attacks, and heavy attacks (like Smash attacks). I feel that, with these mechanics in place, it creates a much different environment and experience than that of other Sumo's, or "Smash-likes."
In summary, I feel that Rivals of Aether offers fun, balanced gameplay with unique, well-developed, and creative characters, all while keeping the game feeling fair and offering a true test of mettle in gameplay. Now I could go on about how greatly unique and fleshed-out each character feels, or how the stages, hazardous or not, are well designed and approached with a competitive mind. Unfortunately, I can't in my right mind do that, because then when you get the game you won't have any surprises left.

Following the roots of Crytek's first game, FarCry 1, Crysis brings the player to an island occupied by North Korean forces. While your purpose there is straightforward at first, a bigger problem unfolds throughout the game that changes the playing field for humanity forever.
First of all, Crysis offers an amazingly fun game experience. The year is 2020, and you are part of the US Army's most elite team. You all wear the latest Nanosuit, a suit capable of cloaking you, increasing your stamina and strength, and makes you temporarily invulnerable to bullets. The nanosuit is of course regulated by its power source which quickly regenerates over time, so you cannot use all abilities at once. Deciding on which to use and how to use them together is the trick, but oh boy is it fun. Since the world is also quite open, it gives the player different opportunities to complete the mission at hand. It is not until later in the game where it become more linear.
The graphics were and still are amazing in the game. For its time, nothing rivaled the graphics of Crysis. Today, Crysis still looks beautiful. With the advancement of GPU's and CPU's since 2007, one shouldn't have a problem to run Crysis on ultra and enjoy the setting.
The story is also quite enjoyable. Not anything fantastic or extraordinary. It's relatively simple and straightforward, but the presentation of the game makes it feel like it's a whole lot more than it really is. The voice acting is quite good, and the overall sounds in the game are great. The soundtrack, on the other hand, is quite lacking and uninspiring, so you may have to listen to something else in the background if you value great music.
The few negatives of the game are the AI, which is ludicrous at times, and some annoying glitches that may appear from time to time, but nothing game breaking.
Crysis should make it to the top of the list for those who have never played it and want to try out a story-based FPS shooter. You definitively won't be disappointed.

This War of Mine is replete with morally taxing decisions.  The entire game can be boiled down to that single sentence. It's a difficult game to play, but for the right reasons. As a game about civilians in a war-torn country trying to survive, the setting is oppressive and the tone dark, but with elements of hope and human kindness.
Yes, it's a game with randomly generated elements; yes, it has crafting; yes, you have to juggle resources; most importantly, everything you do is a choice: do I get the materials to upgrade equipment and make things, or the wood to burn for heat and cooking food and also make things? Do I get the weapon parts in the hopes of building something later, or do I get the sugar and make moonshine to trade for weapons or other goods?
Ultimately, at some point you'll find yourself having to make the decision: do I steal food to keep my survivors alive, do I let them starve? Keep in mind you're stealing food from other survivors, from people who may be homeless or in even worse situations than your own. You may even have to decide between injuring, or even killing, another person to collect the basic necessities. Unlike other games in which you play a character who is amoral, or at best, has a bar that says how "good" or "bad" they are, the characters in This War of Mine behave more like real people who are saddened, even depressed, by things they do and things that happen.
Snitched on your neighbors for stealing supplies? Watch as your characters feel sadness and shame at turning their neighbors in for a few meager supplies. One of your survivors dies? Watch as your characters spiral into depression and mope. However, not all characters have the same moral compass or ethical levels, so while some may react poorly to stealing, others might see it as perfectly acceptable behavior. Others still may be glad it someone else who died and not them and not feel the same sadness of others.
A deceptively simple game, it's difficult to play because the setting and content--fighting in the streets at night preventing you from going to certain areas, updates on the radio about people being killed, notes left by, presumably now-dead, survivors--but it still manages to be fun. The somewhat random nature of the game allows for replayability, but obviously the emotional impact will be felt most strongly in the initial play.
An artistic endeavor can be seen as successful when it causes an emotional response. This War of Mine causes emotional responses, one after another. While that's important, as a video game, the most crucial question is, "Is it fun?" Yes, yes it is. For as difficult as the game can be to play, it's a challenge to survive, but each day your group manages to survive, especially in the face of injury and illness, feels like a small accomplishment.
That was rather high-minded, so here's a few specifics:
-Randomly generated to a degree--starting characters, materials you'll find (maybe?) in zones, supplies traders have, events you'll see.
-A side scroller with crafting, your game day is broken into "day" and "night": during the day, upgrade your home, make water, cook food, greet guests, rest; at night, scavenge war-torn locations as they become available, each with varying degrees of danger, items/resources available, and trading opportunities.
-Must manage food, heat, sickness, and sleep for your survivors. Also, at night you determine who is on guard, who sleeps, and who scavenges--keep in mind any weapons your scavenger takes is unavailable to your guard(s) and weapons are not plentiful (at least early on).
-Plays well in OS X. In fact, I would guess it plays well in Linux, and obviously, plays well in Windows. (As played on a 2010 Mac Pro with a GeForce 680 4GB.)
-Controls are essentially left click, right click, and TAB to switch between characters. As simple as it gets, though combat is a touch clunky (click the icon to shoot/attack which can be inconvenient when trying to run away or duck behind cover--perhaps there's a keyboard key to shoot, but I'm not sure what it is if so) but not bad enough to warrant anything other than a simple note about it.
I highly suggest doing a search for a let's play if you're considering the game as it is somewhat difficult to describe. I watched one and was convinced this was a game for me, buts its highly emotional content may not be for everyone.
Edit: two years later, it's still a heck of a game with expansions, mods, and just as much emotional rollercoastering as ever.
Edit: three years later, it's still just as impactful now as it was on release due to the atrocities taking place in the world. This isn't an "easy" game to play from an emotional standpoint, but it remains one worth experiencing (and it is fun, it's just that it's more than a "fun" game).

Basic concept of a game is "to be fun".

The "fun" aspect was cut out by really unballanced decks. Of course that you HAVE TO PLAY with PREMADE decks in campaign with no sideboard option (devs, ya heard about sideboards?) and no way of checking what was added to your deck in any way but restarting the next duel - which you obviously will, since it takes at least 10 tries to draw a hand that would in some suprising way be a good hand against a sadistic I-am-really-prepared-for-only-your-deck deck. Map builder, Steam supported multiplayer system, mod support, AI that can range from unnaturally stupid to exceedliny smart and challengeing, lots of stats, so many switches/levers, and a bit more. Like most RTS games, matches can last a long time, especially if you're on a large map with multiple star systems. Should you be playing with/against friends and need to call it a night, save away and either of you will be able to rehost the match from where you saved. There is even a bit of humor tucked away here and there.
There are 3 base factions with their own strengths and weaknesses, and they are further divided in half to make a technical total of 6 factions with different playstyles and strategies. Stardock does try to keep mechanics balanced so you should be on relatively even ground when against similarly skilled players.
The graphics and music are great. You can run this game on a weaker machine (I wouldn't recommend hosting a game though) or you can max settings on a big rig for all the lasers and ship detail. An easily togglable Cinematic view mode is even included so you can watch massive conflicts without a bunch of clashing UI elements messing up the view.
If RTS games, celestial bodies, or space ships, are your jam, this would be a fine addition to your collection. It's by no means a perfect game, but the majority of its flaws will be your own personal preference or really minor issues I believe.

Woah boy, where to start? When I first saw this game, I immediately hopped on my bike and bolted to gamestop for a steam card. The music and visuals were absolutely breathtaking, the combat mechanics were simple, yet incredibly well refined and balanced, and it was on sale! Alas, when I got home, the sale was over! All that was left was a -30% on the game+soundtrack bundle. Out of spite more than anything, I nabbed that little sale and got to downloading.
My body was not ready.
Right from the get-go, I was plunged head-first into this expansive and content-packed metroidvania (I didn't even know that term beforehand), and I started to epxlore. It was a little daunting at first, but I quickly discovered that the game rewarded players for their intrigue and investigation. Left and right I'd discover something to that strange set of scaffolding, that shaft of light protruding from the rubble, or so be it. Each area would lead into the next, and yet nothing ever seemed forced. Even the backtracking wasn't too bad, because of the way the user-updated map functions (The chart has a border indicating walls, ceilings, and floors, but there's no border if you haven't poked your head in)
Furthermore, the combat is easy to learn, difficult to master, and impossible to exploit. Even when you encounter mulitples of one enemy (sidenote, there's like almost 150 unique enemies), you'll find what you did you defeat the first doesn't always work on the next. it's not that they have some special learning thingamajig, or that they react differently on a by-case basis (although some do), but because the enemies simply have such a complex way of figuring out how to strike that it takes mulitple enemies to see what they have to offer. On the other side of the coin, you've got your nail and some charms.
Seem underpowered? Well, the game has a way of making sure you're always well-equipped (assuming you find at least some of an area's secrets) for an area's monsters.
Now let's talk about the story...
It'll take a 100% playthrough
to understand it. I reccommend a pilot-G2 pen, a pack of note cards, and some tissues (real men admit when they cried)
Lastly, there seems to be 4 capstone challenges throughout the entire game, capstone being used in place of the word unholy. There're boss, combat, platforming, and exploring, and none are for the faint of heart (I guess I should censor this if you wanna go in blind)
tl;dr: don't buy this game on sale. The price is close to stealing as it is, and the 3-man team (if I have that right) deserves so much more.

In Shelter, you play a mother badger trying to keep her badger cubs alive in a world populated by predatory animals and dangerous natural obstacles.
Now that's a concept you don't see everyday.
I like that the designers chose to take a serious rather than silly approach and thought they did a very good job in realising their vision. The brutality and indifference of nature is well represented, with every loss in your small family being a painful moment; the sense that you must move on quickly for the sake of those cubs who do survive is acute.
The art and music is interesting, creating a unique, understated mood.
On the downside, it's short, offering only an hours' worth of play for a playthrough. Unfortunately, because of the inherent simplicity of the game mechanics, I'm not sure the replay value is very high either.
All in all, it does what it sets out to do, and I rather enjoyed the c. 2hrs I spent with Shelter.
Worth a shot, but be warned that it is a short game.

Like many I got this for free as I already own Bioshock 1, 2 and Infinite.
So, what can I say about this "remaster"?  It's a terrible port, of a port of a port (yup, Console (Xbox 360/PS3) to PC, to console (Xbox One/PS4) back to PC).
The performance is, interesting.  One moment I'm blasting along at almost 600 FPS (no thats not a typo) the next I'm down to 30 FPS, then back up to over 200 FPS.  Wash, rinse, repeat.  No obvious pattern, VERY irritating.
The mouse smoothing - ignoring the manual INI file changes (really?) - when loading a level/area the mouse movements are VERY slow and unresponsive, then they seem to "bounce" back to normal after 5-10 seconds.  There are some serious aliasing and texture popping issues - and make sure you enable frame limiting (nVidia/AMD config) or the game looks like it's going hard core rave with lighting issues!
Thankfully I've not had any crashes...yet.
One good thing though, the original gave me no sound from Windows 8.1 onwards - at least I get sound now.
All in all, a very poor effort.  I thought untested remasters were supposed to be consigned to the days of the Amiga/Spectrum/Commodore - guess these jokers hanker for the bygone days.

First off. Don't listen to what the bad reviews have to say about this game. Just get the game, play some matches and have a great time.
So if you play any other MOBA, whether that be League Of Legends, Dota 2, Smite/etc. Y'know those good♥♥♥♥♥team-fights in the late-game that can win or lose a game? Imagine that, but that's the only part of the game, and you don't die in 1 shot. No armour that you have to take into consideration, no worrying about late-game. You have your damage, and your health. Some characters have more health, some have less.
So that's the main idea of the game, but now instead of items that you get throughout the game. You get buffs to your abilities. (Or, better known as "Battlerites") You get to choose from 3 each round. On the final round (If it's 2-2) You get to upgrade your ultimate ability.
If you play League of Legends (I dunno if this applies to other MOBAs) Imagine your battlerites as buffs to your champion that only last for that game. These Battlerites can be as simple as increasing the damage of one of your abilities, to pulling in all your enemies once you use your ultimate ability. And depending on who you're vsing, and what the enemies play-style is, your choices of your battlerites may change. You're playing a long-range character, the enemy is not bothering to focus you, and they are contesting Mid-Orb well? Get more damage on your "Snipe", or it's the opposite. I have clocked in thousands of hours in the X series, all the way from X2 to X3AP. So believe me when I say I could not be more disappointed with how X-R came to be. 7 years in development, when in reality it was 7 years of Console development, a failed pitch to Microsoft, and a quick cash grab to recoup the costs of their monumentally dumbed down game.
From design decisions based on programmer's personal beliefs (no automation, jump drives, SETA, mind numbingly boring minigames), to decisions that simply boggle the mind (no cancelling of trade orders, your ship carries no cargo, you personally have to drive around and order your ships to trade, literally nothing in the game is 2 button presses to issue an order)
Sure, the space cities look damn pretty. From the outside. Because they had to be, because to even interract with one of these gorgeous space cities, you have to scour the entire external surface with a fine-toothed comb to even dock. And when you do, you'll wish you hadn't. X-R features the most hideous, badly rigged and designed character models I have literally ever seen. The models in X2, a game over 10 years old, looked better. Between that and the mandatory hunting of arbitrary pilots to pilot your ships *for* you (because you will never leave the Skunk for something better), the disgusting 'find the crates' minigame, and the heavily Consolized conversation wheels, you'd wished you stayed outside, and wonder how this ever because a feature.
Next we have the Universe. Something that the X series is pretty well known for; it's huge, sprawling universe that you are but one speck of. Well good look seeing the universe, because the new map system is taken out of a preschoolers scribble book. Not that you would even need a map, because there are only 4 regions to explore. Admittedly, they are divided up into 5 sectors, dozens of zones and plenty more inbetween, but cmon. X3AP had 213 individual sectors, and there was more life in the empty sector of Maelstrom in X3 than there is in 90% of the zones in X-R. There simply is no life. Lots of show and distractions, but peek behind the curtain and you realize that all the NPC ships around you only exist when you're there. Ships in space highways literally do not exist outside of those highways. The flowing traffick that weaves through space cities? This War of Mine is replete with morally taxing decisions.  The entire game can be boiled down to that single sentence. It's a difficult game to play, but for the right reasons. As a game about civilians in a war-torn country trying to survive, the setting is oppressive and the tone dark, but with elements of hope and human kindness.
Yes, it's a game with randomly generated elements; yes, it has crafting; yes, you have to juggle resources; most importantly, everything you do is a choice: do I get the materials to upgrade equipment and make things, or the wood to burn for heat and cooking food and also make things? Do I get the weapon parts in the hopes of building something later, or do I get the sugar and make moonshine to trade for weapons or other goods?
Ultimately, at some point you'll find yourself having to make the decision: do I steal food to keep my survivors alive, do I let them starve? Keep in mind you're stealing food from other survivors, from people who may be homeless or in even worse situations than your own. You may even have to decide between injuring, or even killing, another person to collect the basic necessities. Unlike other games in which you play a character who is amoral, or at best, has a bar that says how "good" or "bad" they are, the characters in This War of Mine behave more like real people who are saddened, even depressed, by things they do and things that happen.
Snitched on your neighbors for stealing supplies? Watch as your characters feel sadness and shame at turning their neighbors in for a few meager supplies. One of your survivors dies? Watch as your characters spiral into depression and mope. However, not all characters have the same moral compass or ethical levels, so while some may react poorly to stealing, others might see it as perfectly acceptable behavior. Others still may be glad it someone else who died and not them and not feel the same sadness of others.
A deceptively simple game, it's difficult to play because the setting and content--fighting in the streets at night preventing you from going to certain areas, updates on the radio about people being killed, notes left by, presumably now-dead, survivors--but it still manages to be fun. The somewhat random nature of the game allows for replayability, but obviously the emotional impact will be felt most strongly in the initial play.
An artistic endeavor can be seen as successful when it causes an emotional response. This War of Mine causes emotional responses, one after another. While that's important, as a video game, the most crucial question is, "Is it fun?" Yes, yes it is. For as difficult as the game can be to play, it's a challenge to survive, but each day your group manages to survive, especially in the face of injury and illness, feels like a small accomplishment.
That was rather high-minded, so here's a few specifics:
-Randomly generated to a degree--starting characters, materials you'll find (maybe?) in zones, supplies traders have, events you'll see.
-A side scroller with crafting, your game day is broken into "day" and "night": during the day, upgrade your home, make water, cook food, greet guests, rest; at night, scavenge war-torn locations as they become available, each with varying degrees of danger, items/resources available, and trading opportunities.
-Must manage food, heat, sickness, and sleep for your survivors. Also, at night you determine who is on guard, who sleeps, and who scavenges--keep in mind any weapons your scavenger takes is unavailable to your guard(s) and weapons are not plentiful (at least early on).
-Plays well in OS X. In fact, I would guess it plays well in Linux, and obviously, plays well in Windows. (As played on a 2010 Mac Pro with a GeForce 680 4GB.)
-Controls are essentially left click, right click, and TAB to switch between characters. As simple as it gets, though combat is a touch clunky (click the icon to shoot/attack which can be inconvenient when trying to run away or duck behind cover--perhaps there's a keyboard key to shoot, but I'm not sure what it is if so) but not bad enough to warrant anything other than a simple note about it.
I highly suggest doing a search for a let's play if you're considering the game as it is somewhat difficult to describe. I watched one and was convinced this was a game for me, buts its highly emotional content may not be for everyone.
Edit: two years later, it's still a heck of a game with expansions, mods, and just as much emotional rollercoastering as ever.
Edit: three years later, it's still just as impactful now as it was on release due to the atrocities taking place in the world. This isn't an "easy" game to play from an emotional standpoint, but it remains one worth experiencing (and it is fun, it's just that it's more than a "fun" game).

Easy there, cowboy. The thumbs up is an "only for a certain kind of gamer" recommendation. While that usually doesn't need to be said, in this case fans of RPGs may find the game's flaws too glaring to forgive. So I strongly recommend researching the ups and downs of Final Fantasy XIII before committing to a purchase. Steam does have a refund policy, but it takes more than two hours of game-time to really see where FF13's design flaws come into play.
Having played through this game on the PlayStation 3, I can say without reservation that I enjoy this game's combat system and that I think the characters are pretty cool in their own ways. Whether that can carry you through a 60 hour RPG is up to your individual tastes. The game can be engaging and pretty but the main draws that players associate with RPGs aren't really here. The storytelling is badly-paced and underdeveloped, often requiring the player to take a break and read in-game Datalog entries to solidify their understanding of the game's concepts. The stage design is almost oppressively linear for the vast majority of the game and does not really open up until close to the end (at which point you are given the opportunity to experience the plains and valleys of Gran Pulse, which introduces the kind of area design that Xenoblade Chronicles on the Wii gave players free reign over from the very moment they took control of Shulk and Reyn in Colony 9). There are no real town exploration sections except for a single mid-game interlude in a theme park which players are not allowed to revisit afterward, either; the game consists almost entirely of traversing enemy-laden wilderness and dungeon areas in a strictly linear progression, making it by far the most monotonous game in the Final Fantasy main series (one could accuse Final Fantasy X of being too linear, but it still had the basic staples of an RPG's adventure progression and the freedom to revisit old areas, two things XIII does not provide).
The negatives are ever-present and all-encompassing: this is a game that is definitely not for everyone, and even having enjoyed my first playthrough of it, I personally have not been compelled to either complete all of the sidequests (which you only gain access to once you reach that late-game Gran Pulse area) or to play through the story a second time. Replay value is at an all-time low here.
If these things do not sound like flaws that will totally break the experience for you, then I encourage you to give Final Fantasy XIII a try. If you're unsure which way you'll swing, I recommend watching some Let's Play videos of the game on YouTube to see for yourself what the game is like--HCBailly in particular is a good bet.
The bottom line is that this isn't a game I can give a single sweeping recommendation for. I could do that for the sequels, which while lacking in story cohesion are just better-designed as videogames; but this first entry in the Final Fantasy XIII trilogy is the hardest recommend to people, even as I can't see it as exactly "bad." If that makes any sense.
If there was an option in between "yes" and "no" I would probably have picked that instead.

In 2007 Turkish-German game developer Crytek released ‘Crysis’, a cryengine-built first person shooter which exceeded the graphical norm at the time more than any other game ever did or would later do. Almost no computer could run it at the time and for many years it would be the ideal game to test new gaming PC’s with, but even disregarding this main strength of the game Crysis is a very decent FPS.
In Crysis you take the role of an American soldier named ‘Nomad’ who is part of an elite squadron of nanosuit-equipped soldiers . You are sent to the Lingshan islands in the pacific to rescue a team of archeologists from North-Korean soldiers who took the place over. Story is not quite the part of the game that deserves closest examination because of that it is quite generic. After all, even back in 2007 there were already quite a few games that had the player kill soldiers while playing as an American soldier himself, but luckily the story takes a bit of a back seat here. It would not be until Crysis 2 that other things than combat would be given some attention. In terms of story delivery there is also nothing new here.
What you would want to play Crysis for, if not the superb graphics, would be its gameplay and it does this quite well. Although it uses pretty standard FPS mechanisms the nanosuit makes for a welcome addition. Basically the suit gives you a choice of four superpowers, which consume from one general energy bar. There is a speed mode, pretty self-explanatory, a cloak mode that makes you largely invisible, a power mode that lets you jump higher and fling heavy objects and an armour mode. Using whatever improvements your power gives you costs energy and generally this system holds up pretty well. It is nice that you are given the choice between stealthing a section with the cloak or fighting through it normally, and if you choose the latter you can also pick different tactics with either the speed or the armour mode.  A nice small addition on the side is that you are at any time able to modify your weapon, which means you can pick your sight, add a suppressor or make other small modifications.
The game also excels in giving the player freedom. Before Crytek set about on making Crysis they made the original Far Cry. Why these developers are so attached to the word ‘cry’ remains a mystery. But anyway, Far Cry was an open world game which was, like Crysis, set on a tropical island and sometimes it seems as if the developers carved a big and wide linear path out of Far Cry’s sandbox to make Crysis because Crysis feels about as unlinear as a linear game can be. The entire game has a structure similar to Half Life 2, in that you are never teleported to a different location but always go there yourself. There are almost no missions that all of a sudden take place somewhere else unless the last mission had you go there by yourself. Some objectives give you entire towns to play around in, a lot of the houses can be smashed up and most objects can be grabbed and thrown as weapons. What also makes this game feel like some fenced-off sandbox is the completely free use of vechiles. When you need to go to the next firefight you can walk there if you want, or you can get in a car which the game just puts outside most villages. Driving mechanics are not very good though, so if you are being shot at you are in more danger in a car than on foot.
Although Crysis is indeed a very good FPS it does have a few minor issues I want to mention. Firstly that would be the story. I understand that a game like this leaves little room for something outrageously good, but they could perhaps have done a little less effort to make the North-Koreans look like jerks because in a game based around so much military excessive force, as showcased in a level where you take part in a big tank offensive, making the enemy seem evil just puts the entire game in a big cliché. Of course in a game with such a simple story you want to have your side as the goodies and the other side to be the baddies, but emphasizing that so much makes it all feel a bit fake. Some enemies come across as silly cartoon villains. My other nibbles mostly restrict to specific sections and mentioning them spoils parts of the game for you, so be warned about the following part. What peeved me a bit about one level that takes place in an alien space ship was that the entire place is extremely disorienting. Although that bit still looks extremely gorgeous graphics-wise, I found myself moving through the same looped corridor about five times before I found the right way by accident and the beauty loses something if it is forced upon you for so long. Another annoying part was one section where your squadmate, ‘Prophet’, has a damaged nanosuit which means you have to escort him and bring him to some kind of heat source every few seconds to prevent him from dying. It is not even hard at all and the combat is not harder with him around, so the entire thing just feels like a silly delay.  On the side, I found the game’s soundtrack to be very unimaginative. It does nothing to increase the atmosphere.
So, in conclusion I would certainly recommend Crysis, even today. Although the graphics don’t excel anymore and the story is pretty rubbish, the gameplay is still very nice and you have plenty of liberty to explore the nanosuits potential, and that certainly outweighs the game’s few issues.

For someone like me who does not want to blow fat wads of cash on real cards and who has real life friends who feel the same way and/or live too far away, Magic Duels Origins is a great game.
Pros:
-Every card in the Origins set and future sets (Battle for Zendikar, for example) is and will be obtainable without paying a dime
-Robust learning system and deck building assistant for newer players
-Easier to earn gold than Hearthstone and no multiples after the max # allowed in decks making obtaining a collection much easier than Hearthstone
-Foiling your cards is much, MUCH less expensive than obtaining "golden" cards in Hearthstone: good for completionists and proud players alike
-2v2 mode is a blast!
-Gold is plentiful: able to be earned by completing tutorials, quests, story campaigns (5 total), battling various levels of AI, battling real players, etc. making pack opeing a common experience!
-Once again, it is MUCH easier to collect in this game over Hearth due to the above mentions and the fact that 20g is earned per ranked game compared to 3.33g in Hearthstone... And you get a bonus 20g for your first ranked win of the day... WOW! EARNING GOLD IS MORE THAN 6 TIMES FASTER! Even with packs costing 150g over 100g, you are still opening packs 4 times as often as in Hearthstone!
Cons:
-Day 1 and 3 server instability lauched the game with a rocky start
-A couple bugs with completing quests to earn gold still unpached as of this writing
Overall: Especially by the end of this week, with the harmless bugs patched out and servers stabilized, this is a very easy game to recommend. Those who gave scalding reviews were salty about the rough start. I stuck through and am still happy to play daily!

Magic Duels: Origins basically does the same mistakes as Duel of the Planeswalkers: It simplifies a game that lives of its complexity.
First for the pro:
- the game is free to play and such easily accesible for new players
- the tutorial is well made and most of the campaign is well balanced to introduce beginners to the game
- all the cards can be optained just by playing
- the game looks kind of nice and the deckbuilding-wizard is a great help to get started
Now the cons:
- the game simplifies many aspects of mtg, losing charm for advanced players
- the campaign is partially really unbalanced which can be really frustrating
- the cardpool is very limited at the moment and it takes ages to afford new boosters
- quests can only be completed with wizarded decks
- the controls are unintuitive
Conclusion:
Duels Origins is a good way for absolute beginners to get into magic, but it lacks way too many features and gameplay aspects to even be remotely interesting for advanced players. But since its free you can still have your fun with the game, playing some wanky cards you'd never play anywhere else.

I've got about an hour into this one. I like it though, and here's why:
I've been a gamer for a lot of years. It all started with games on a Texas Instruments computer back in the early '80s with such gems as Parsec and Hunt the Wumpus (not sarcasm, they WERE gems).
Shortly thereafter Atari showed up along with Windows 3.1 and MS-DOS.
Speaking of MS-DOS, here is where the relevancy to A Matter of Murder comes in.
Back around then, I first played a game that used ASCI graphics called Sleuth. You roam a mansion examining possible weapons and question suspects until you solve it or get killed. This game is very similar to Sleuth except this one has graphics, sound, and music.
You play as a budding detective in a typical British manor type setting with your usual suspects, various lords and ladies, an explorer, a couple foreigners, a veteran of the war, and a maid thrown together. One of them is murdered and it is up to you to point the finger at the culprit and say why it was done and with what weapon.
You have a time limit though and you lose a bit of time whenever you ask a suspect a question or examine a nearby weapon. Once you've ferreted out everyones alibis and motives and have found the weapon, you hit the accuse button and hope you're right.
As the cases get solved the next ones become harder. Alibis become more challenging to figure out, as do motives. You also have to rely on what the suspects say about the wound on the body to figure out the weapon instead of just being told that the poker has blood on it. The logic gets amped up pretty steeply after a few cases so it might help to have your own pen and pad handy as the in game notebook resembles a Clue sheet and doesn't have any space for notes of your own.
If you get tired of the names of the characters, you can change them into friends of yours. That's a nice little feature which Sleuth also had way back then.
This isn't a AAA game by any stretch of the imagination, but it is a fun little time waster for when you only have a little time to waste.

Because there's a lot of misinformation and reactionary reviews to the game's rather poor launch state, I've decided to write a review, covering the game's pros and cons in the most objective fashion possible. No aggressive bashing, no unwarranted praise.
I want to begin with a very simple fact - the game is free. That means that you don't have to spend a dollar (or euro) to try it out and see if it fits you. This fact, of course, does not shield the game from criticism, but it's a thing to remember - as long as you're having fun with it, you got your "money's" worth.
To add to that, the monetization system is super-fair. Unlike other games, where you'll keep opening repeats of cards you already own over and over again, in MDO (Magic Duels: Origins) each pack will contain only cards you don't own a full set of yet. According to some (yes, I'm too lazy to make the calculations, but if you're interested, look it up), this puts the pricetag on the entire set of cards of $70. That is laughably cheap, both compared to it's competitors and "real" Magic. I'll come back to this system further into the review, but the overall impression is extremely positive.
For the list of gameplay pros, we have to start with the obvious - it's Magic the Gathering. One of the best TCG games on the market, going strong for over 21 years. Whether it's THE best, that's up to your opinion, but if you love the game and want to have the option of playing it any time - it's here. If you haven't tried it out yet and are looking for a great introduction - the Duels of the Planeswalkers series (to which this game kinda belongs to) was always an amazing learning tool. And now, it's free.
As an additional bonus, the game features a surprisingly great soundtrack. While it doesn't seem energetic at first, you might quickly find that it puts you in the right kind of magical atmosphere.
Now, for the "controversial one", or the one that's neither an obvious pro or a con, the game only features cards from the newest MTG set - Magic Origins (and also some common cards from other sets, as well as cards from some expansions in story missions). It actually seems to lack some cards from that set as well. Additionally, as you craft your deck, you may only put one of each Mythic-rarity card into it, two of each Rare and three of each Uncommon, instead of the standard maximum of four for each card.
While that may seem like a con - and it definitely is for people who were looking for a 1-to-1 recreation of Magic - I feel like it's just a change. If you ever felt like paper Magic was about slamming the most expensive rares and mythics into your library, well, here you only need a couple of copies and these rare cards have an added downside of being less reliable than common ones. Since everyone sticks to the same rules - your games will be balanced and Magic Origins, as a set, is made a bit like a "new" Magic - the card's balance has been shifted to promote more thoughtful, more strategic play than before.
Now it's time for cons. I'm going to intentionally skip over connection issues and some bugs - if you want to get the full, accurate picture, do your research, as any complaint about them might have been fixed by the time you're reading this or any other review. Also, the game might be developed further, which means that even the complaints I'll post below might get fixed. Again, do your research or just try the game yourself. Developers promised updates with new cards from new sets - it might also extend to Quality of Life improvements and bonus features.
First of all, the UI is not very user-friendly. There are numerous issues with it - it doesn't do a great job of telling you in which part of the turn you are. The button placement is questionable. Once you grab a card, there is no way to back off, you have to play it. Questions about decisions are displayed as huge pop-ups that cover your entire vision, which is annoying if the decision regards stuff that's on the battlefield. Manually tapping lands is broken. The list goes on and you'll probably come up with your own complaints along the way, like having the "skip attack" button appear in the same place, where "continue" button was a second ago - I never had a problem with it, but I saw people that had.
Second of all, there isn't much content in the game yet. The AI fights and the ladder system give you the option of playing "pure" Magic, but the game lacks any fun modes, like Commander or even competitive ones like Draft or Sealed, featuring only barebones two-headed giant. If these two available modes won't suit you, or will just bore you after a while, you might not find anything else in the game to entertain you. However, I'm going to immediately discredit the complaint about the game lacking a chat feature - many competing games also lack it, because even I can sometimes feel the salt coming from my opponent. I don't want to read it as well.
Third of all, and my final complaint, is that the game is overly simplistic with it's rules. While I like the fact that it's made with beginners in mind, it actually doesn't even feature some elements of the turn, like upkeep - a moment between untapping and drawing, where you should be able to cast spells. I don't think that the game's direction will allow for it's inclusion, or any increase in difficulty, unless they'll features something like a "Pro" queue. That said, if you do feel comfortable with the rules, remember to go to the game settings and uncheck all the features that will basically make the game do some decisions for you, like deciding blocking order.
In the end, I'd like to, again, come back to the monetization system. After you finish the campaigns and loot all of the possible gold coins from Skill Quests, you'll gain 5, 10 or 15 gold for a win against AI (depending on it's difficulty), or 20 against a real opponent. A pack containing six cards costs 150 gold, which you'll get after eight won duels online, which, again, is really fair compared to it's competition. There's also a standard quest system, which nets you bonus coins from time to time, although it's pretty broken at the time of writing this review, for instance quests that require you to play with a set archetype only work with decks created using Deck Wizard. Again, the developers claimed to be working on it right now, so check for yourself.
Should you spend real money on it? In the state it is now - no. But if you're reading this two months into the future and at least half of my complaints are fixed - sure, I'll drop a buck. Try it out and see if it fits you.

This game is pretty solid. It is a complex strategy game that can be very large and in depth. I would not recommend it for any amateur strategy gamers. Balancing this game play may be too frustrating if you are just starting out in this kind of game. There are other RTS games that are better suited to start out with. This is in the Sci-Fi genre, which adds quite a bit of fun to what can happen.
There is also a difference between this game and nearly all the other RTS games. This one doesn't really have a story mode. There is no campaign mode that other games have included. There are plenty of pre-built maps ranging from small to very large. All of them including different planet types and stars. There just is no story mode. Some find this to be a set back. But for any just looking for some straight strategy, this is a fun game. Especially once the very large maps are played.
This does have a multiplayer mode. It is very straight forward. You can start wtih alliances already determined, or you can create alliances as the game progresses. This can be very fun especially with an appropriate map. Some notes about the multiplayer: If you start up with 6 players, and someone drops out for any reason and the rest are still playing, the game will assign that player's assets to an AI and play can continue. There will be one player designated as the "server" and if this person drops out, and the rest are still playing, this "server" function will migrate to another person. It is quite handy, except that so far it seems that the player who dropped out is not able to reconnect and continue playing.
It has a great resource infrastructure system in the game. Also a limiter on how many ships a player can have. Which isn't so bad considering how large of a game this really is. It has great effects and imagery though. The camera controls allow you to view an entire galaxy from far out, or zoom all the way in to your smallest fighter as it attacks.
There is a diplomacy function here, which allows you to interact with the other players in the map. It allows you to set up trade pacts, and also some infrastructure bonuses. Which depend on what faction or race you are. There are inherent problems with the way this is set up though. It is difficult to get through, and there are not as many options as there could be to interact in a diplomatic way.
There are a few DLC packs available for this. Which expand the universe a little bit by adding different planet types and also solar events.
This is a sequel of sorts, to itself. The reality is that it isn't very much of a sequel. The Sins games which were released before this are not very different. Which is unfortunate. Hopefully any next version of this franchise can at least get an art refresh. If you have played any of the previous ones, you will notice much of the art is the same. Loading screens, profile thumb screens, and so forth. Even the opening movie hasn't changed very much.

Symploké es un increible esfuerzo de un desarrollador novel con reminiscencias a las antiguas aventuras gráficas de Sierra, en la vena de Space Quest o Las Aventuras de Larry. Incluso el estilo gráfico y edición de sonido recuerdan a esas narrativas de finales de los 80, principios de los 90.
La historia nos transporta al entorno universitario de una España atemporal, donde todo el que ha ido sabe qué es vivir una aventura: Hay que sobrevivir. Y Benito Retamosa encarna perfectamente ese deseo y a través de él, el jugador quiere ver cómo la historia progresa y como Benito se sale con la suya.
La traducción al inglés es magnífica y tan divertida como el propio guión, los NPCs están tan vivos como las voces que los representan y el estilo y la lógica absurda de los puzzles transportan al jugador a un pasado donde las aventuras gráficas eran las reinas.
Un hallazgo increible que más gente debería jugar. Esta es una clase de filosofía de la que no perderás detalle.
¡Viva Gustavo Bueno y viva Symploké!

Hitman: Absolution is a decent stealth game. It may feel limiting at times, and over-whelming at others ( especially that early Chinatown mission), but it also adds some new twists to the stealth genre. In most missions, there are a number of ways to "accidentally" eliminate your targets. And in general, there are usually multiple ways to accomplish a certain objective.
Another neat feature is being able to disguise yourself. It adds a touch of realism to the game. As such, Absolution is not really kind of a classic stealth game where you stick to the shadows or stay hidden from view, and that may throw some people off. While there may be multiple ways to achieve an objective, the levels are mostly very linear as well, and again some might be upset with this.
Visually, the graphics are good. Voice acting is fair. The cutscenes are decent. Story is kind of so-so for me. It serves its purpose, but I wasn't necessarily drawn into it.
On the overall, I liked Hitman: Absolution even though I may not have been blown-away by it. It is a stealth game that brings along a few new innovative features with it. As such, naturally I'd recommend it.

Games like this don't come around very often, which is why you revel in every minute you play them.
The Stanley Parable is really one of those types of games you can't watch on Youtube, you need to expereince it for yourself, because the joy of the game comes in the experiences you have and discover yourself, the little things, the many discoveries for curious minds and the sharing of said discoveries with other curious Stanley Parable players. Even better than playing yourself is giving the controls over to someone who has never seen or played the game themselves and just carrying out your own little experiment.
- How easily manipulated is the gamer?
- Will they follow orders because the narrator says to do so, or will curiousity get the better of them?
- How far will they go if they DO decide to do their own thing?
- Just how defiant / curious can a person be?
There are simply so many things you can discover about a person's personality that this game is more than a game, it's a personality quiz. It's not so much what they do after several playthroughs, but what they do in the first or even second playthrough that makes it so interesting. You could give the game to several people and the interesting thing is how susceptible they are to simple and subtle instructions.
Are we really that easily manipulated? Are we really part of an endless Matrix? Is everything a lie? What happens if I don't conform? How afraid am I to not conform? Am I a leader or a follower?
So much questions...so many thinking.
You owe it to yourself to play this game and if you already know what it's all about, get it anyway and use it as an experiment to identify how those around you think.

I found this title pleasantly engrossing. Engrossing, not challenging. Because Torchlight is not an action game (if defined as a high-stakes button-masher requiring wicked reflexes and spatial awareness). Half the time, I'm not even watching the screen during battles. I'm spamming magic bouncy arrows and monitoring my twin health and mana gauges.
Torchlight is a resource management simulation of a dungeon crawler. You spend most of your time comparing armor and weapon stats, shifting gear from place to place and optimizing loadouts. The dungeon crawling and fighting parts of the game are merely resource harvesting for the ecosystem of destruction that surrounds my Amazon warrior (aka a "Vanquisher").
And perhaps your experience playing the wildly randomized world of Torchlight will be different. As for me, I selected my Vanquisher - a chick who shoots guns, crossbows and bows - on normal difficulty and just started augmenting her native stats and abilities without branching much. A quarter through the game, she was noticeably overpowered. Halfway through the game, and she was a force of nature. My gun one-shot all but the largest monsters, and my pet cat endlessly spawned a hoard of zombies to handle crowd control, aggro and dirty fightin'.
One or two times during a single dungeon level, I paused to load my cat up with gear and send it back to town to sell it at the market. While it's gone, I endured what I jokingly call "hard mode," actually having to carefully draw enemy aggro, aim my weapon at specific targets and flank my foes. I could not WAIT until that damn cat gets back.
You really want to play Torchlight as an action game (otherwise, I would have selected the fighter ... er ... "Destroyer"). The enemies are all pallet-swapped idiots. The dungeons are repetitive. And the bosses are a joke. But the loot, oh my GAWD, the loot. Torchlight strokes that same mental tick as bottom-feeding browser games like Farmville. Just one more shiny thing. Just one more click ...

Great action game with some fun RPG elements.
I loved the ability to play 3 different types of characters, basically hunter, mage or warrior. The characters are available for play only at the beginning of chapters or main areas before you start. AI for characters you are not playing seemed really good even though there were several times they got lost in an area or couldn’t jump down into an area. The pathing needs to be fixed on AI characters for sure.
Story and voice overs were great, I love all the Lord of the Rings stories and this game does an excellent job getting you engrossed into the story and wanting to learn more about the characters. I have never been a super Tolkien Lore master so I can’t tell you if it is true to all the original Tolkien Stories. The game is more about a small group that helps with activities outside of the main storyline with Frodo and company.
Combat with Keyboard and mouse was very responsive and easy to play. Skills are minimal but helpful during battles, especially boss fights. Items and equipment can be found almost everywhere with special sets available and that can be worn for bonuses during game play.
There are NPC's in every story area for purchasing equipment and repairing equipment. Also there are lighted areas before main story battles that allow you to Buy and sell equipment, also gives you the option to travel to previous locations if needed for quest turn ins.
Large map can be used for fast travel by just selecting area, also contains fighting challenges for group to fight waves of enemies.
Only down side of the game other than the AI pathing issues is that there is no manual saving, the game saves automatically at new areas or story starts. When you complete a battle or area you find a glowing point that allows you to proceed to next area and it performs a save. Even though the game didn’t allow manual saves, it saved game enough times that I never had to redo a lot when my party was defeated in battle, since it typically saves just before the major battle or area change.
Overall I would highly recommend this game, especially now that it is within budget price.

I bought this game just to see if a credit card worked.
My sister's jeep broke down in a pretty big way, and we needed a credit card to be able to rent a car while her jeep was being fixed. We scrambled all across the house and dug through everything multiple times, with things going less and less right as the day went on, and her losing her patience with everything very rapidly.
Then I found it. An old card.
Problem was, it might've been a card that she thought she lost a couple years ago, and thus had shut down. She decided that the way to see if this would work, would be to buy a cheap set of note cards or something off Amazon, since she uses those for school. Amazon had different ideas, however, and wouldn't provide a checkout button. We were stumped, as we were both pretty sure that Amazon didn't have a minimum price limit, since it's not like they eat the shipping charge.
Then she remembered Steam was a thing.
We went over to my computer, and I searched for the cheapest game right now, which happened to be this game for a measly 14 cents. Without even looking at anything about it, I threw it into my cart and checked out. The suspense built as Steam processed the card. And then payment went through.
We joked about how this game would be the worst game ever, and looked at the store page to see a very XBLIG-looking game. I booted it up, and played it just a tiny bit...And it was actually a legitimately good game. The graphics aren't exactly pushing my PC to its limits, but it's a fun little game centered around gravity manipulation, and I've spent more on worse. After playing it for a bit, I noticed the game was made by the people making Road Redemption, which is a game I actually really want.
All in all, I'd reccomend this game to people looking for fun little puzzle platformers, or people who need to test out their credit cards quickly. Thank you, Fish Factory Games, for letting my sister rent cars with confidence.

Most war games are all about unlocking new weapons and blowing limbs off of the enemy team, But the thing is, war is more than shooting a gun and getting that '' VICTORY '' text on your screen.
This war of mine comes with a large variety of emotional problems, disease and so on and so on, 95% of war games leaves these parts out , but '' This war of mine '' does not.
This a 2D Survival poInt and click game, it focuses on the horrors of actual war, so of you're seeking for a FPS that takes aim and reaction skill, you're in the wrong place.
Imagine a zombie apocalypse, minus the zombies. I.E disease, struggle for food, coldness , Constant awareness of bandits, Emotional parts of robbing/killing a civilian and so on. That is what this game is about.
The time and place of this game is the city of Pogoren in the country of Graznavia and im guessing its somewhere in the 90's ( based on weaponry and buildings ) The names of both playable characters and traders makes me think this country is based off of somewhere in eastern europe.
The story of the game goes as such : The cities around Graznavia are in constant war between the militairy and government rebels, civilians from all around the country have fled to the capital ( Pogoren ) in hopes of rest. But at some point the war came to Pogoren as well. The Rebels are mostly untrustworthy and psychos that want to have the entierity of the country in their hands and the militairy was from the beginning sent out to stop them, but after a while, the militairy went mad, they took the opportunity of the situation and turned powermad aswell, since they had equipment and weaponry already they were on a good spot, but one thing that they had that the rebels didn't? They were disciplined and united. And now they are as bad, if not even worse than the rebels. And the civilians in the city are the ones who are in the worst spot, they lack food, equipment, weapons and medicine and the struggle to keep holding on is almost overwhelming.
In daytime snipers guard the streets and keeps civilians from leaving their shelters and that's when they have to fortify their home and craft different variesties of useful things, but in the nighttime, thats when the civilians thrive. They spread out looking for supplies in the cover of darkness. and before the night is at an end, they better be back in their settlement, or sniper fire and militairy forces will make it hard to get home.
Depending on your personal thoughts about these types of games, if you like a challenge and dont mind the drawish style of the game , then i'd say its well worth the 19€, If it goes on sale however i do well recommend it to almost anybody.
Now there remains a few questions unanswered, Will the war ever perish? Do you have what it takes to survive? These things are for you to discover.

This War of Mine is a great game that isn't exactly fun.  It doesn't give you a rewarding feeling when you build a new item in your home.  It doesn't give you an exciting feeling when you win a fight with someone.  All it gives you is grim satisfaction when you survive another day.
You see, we're surrounded by other people trying to survive in a civil war.  Some are murderers and soldiers, but most are survivors who got caught up in the same war we did, regular people who are just trying to make it another day with what little supplies they have left.  However, in order to survive, we may have to do unspeakable things.  And these things don't happen without consequence.
Depending on how you play, your story will be wildly different.  I first played as a group of survivors stuck in winter who helped everyone they met and never stole or killed, only to end up sick and dead because they ran out of fuel for the furnace.  My current playthrough is with a group who decided that stealing and the show of force was the way to go.   I have to admit, I didn't feel good about myself when I broke into a home and stole the possessions of its inhabitants, especially when I found out they were two unarmed women and a little girl.  This game makes you seriously consider your actions, and the consequences that come afterwards.
Technically, this game is pretty solid.  There's a few bugs here and there, but I haven't found anything game-breaking.  The controls are simple and easy to get used to.  There's a lack of instructions, but the game isn't that hard to figure out.  I would have liked an explanation of how combat worked, however.  Figuring it out when you're getting attacked for the first time was interesting.
My only real issue with the game is that it only saves at the beginning of every morning.  Meaning that if you need to stop the game for any reason at home or while scavenging, you lose everything you did for that day.  This is actually a good and bad thing, since the decisions you make while scavenging are permanent unless you're willing to go through the entire day again.
All in all, this is definitely a game that will leave an impression on you after you play it.  For that alone, I would recommend it.

I really only bought this game because I was curious about all the internet rage directed against it. I can see where it came from, honestly, so it's an odd game to review. You see, I bought it expecting to play for a couple hours, see that it was as bad as they say, and then chuckle as I turn it off, ready to move on. This didn't happen though, I ended up finishing this one. Why did I finish it? Well...
Objectively speaking, this game checks off every item on the list of elements that draw the hate crowd: drastic changes to an established and venerable game series, confusing and poorly presented story, awkward 'romance' scenes, weird anime character archetypes (looking at you Vanille), and very linear gameplay with a streamlined battle system when compared to ealier games in the series. These problems really are present, and I can see how they annoyed people, especially uber fans who wanted this game to be just as good as they remembered the earlier games (bit of a loaded point there, I'll leave you to interpret it's meaning). Personally, I didn't really mind these problems as I wasn't expecting a masterpiece to begin with. I actually found all these elements entertaining in their own right, especially considering the concept of the story is pretty interesting if you can get past all the weird anime melodrama and the really horrid (at times) dialogue. ("Worst birthday ever!" is exclaimed by a character who is supposed to be the practical level headed uber soldier.)
In addition to the problems that were present in the original console version, the PC port is laughably inept. A game this old should not struggle to maintain 30 frames a second on a PC equipped with a GTX 980 and the surrounding hardware to support it. I've never had a problem adjusting to crap framerate, but if you're the type to get nauseated from the sight of inferior video display, steer clear of this game.
So what did I like about it and why did I finish it? No reasons that were intentional on the part of the developers. As I said, the bad elements are very entertaining and worth playing if you find this kind of thing funny and not intolerable. The battle system starts out infuriatingly simple, but gets better after an excruciating 20 hours of tutorial-like handholding, during which my interest was only sustained by the train wreck of a plot unfolding. When the battle system does open up, however, it's actually fun to experiment with, where the point is to sort of pre-program the party make up and switch between these programs in order to react to changing battle conditions.
Also, Lightning's character design is incredibly attractive so thats okay...

I have played every Civ game to date, and I find B.E. refreshing. The technology tree allows you to take your civilization on a path that is not a race with everyone else's, and that's a nice plus. Things like miasma, the oddly behaving aliens (unlike barbarians, aliens choose if they attack you or not, and it makes a more interesting game) and the trade route system make the game more interactive than just the old Civ tech race, diplomacy and trade through diplomacy screens options. That being said, it needs improvements, and it is lacking some oldies but goodies from the old Civ system. Naval units need improving, the orbital units need clarification, for example, and the health system is a disaster to manage tot he point that I understand that people ignore it, whereas in the old Civ, the happiness level (equivalent of current health) was a mjor component that could cost you the game. We need more ways to make colonists happy, and for that the virtue tree needs a revamp. The wonders are hard to locate and don't seem to play such a major role in this game, I miss that. The new system makes a cultural victory hard in that the tech tree is too spread out for wonders.
The espionage system I find good, with its levels and difficulties. I miss the trade of commodities (not needful resources but the old luxuries, they're gone) and wish you'd bring them back.
