This game has a lot of potential but has 3 glaring (though easy to fix) flaws that prevent me from recommending it righ now.
1) trade routes have to be reassigned so frequently that once you have more than 4 or 5 cities, you are basically spending almost all of your time playing the game just reassigning trade routes over and over and over again.  I think it was Sid Meier who once said a game should give the player interesting choices.  Making the same choice over and over again for the vast majority of the game play is ... not interesting.
2) there needs to be something in the name of the units that tells you what class the unit is.  every upgrade of every unit has a unique, rather arbitrary name, that gives you no indication what type of unit it is, and the graphics are too amorphous to be able to tell half the time.  The unique names are cool, the lack of any feedback on what type of unit that name represents is just tedious and annoying.
3) the tech web, while cool is implemented as an amorphous blob where its not possible to tell which items you are gaining from a given tech are buildings, which are wonders, which are satellites, and which are units which makes picking a tech take 10X the time it needs to.
All of these are easily fixible and it looks like there is probably a good game here hiding under those glaring frustrations. But until those items are fixed, the game is *not* fun to play.
I'll revisit this review once the game is more fun and less frustration and tedium.

Let me begin this review by first clarifying that I'm a big fan of Irrational Games and specifically the bioshock series, and that I was looking forward to the remaster since first hearing of the updated version's inception. However, being a free update as a previous owner and seeing it was more a touch up than an overhaul, I had moderate expectations that the game would both look refined in all the right areas, and play better than the original from a technical standpoint. If you want the short version, go ahead and check out the bottom of the review. If you'd like a detailed analysis of the significant differences between the two titles, please read on.
I'll go ahead and start with the positives being that most of the negatives have been spread around by word of mouth, and the good things that Blind Squirrel have accomplished don't get much light of day. Overall, Blind Squirrel hit all the right marks visually for the game. Admittedly it's a shame that the game didn't receive a more massive overhaul with Unreal Engine 4, knowing I as well as many fans would have loved to see Bioshock through a photorealistic lens and truly appreciate certain environments like Fort Frolic and the game's introduction sequence. At the same time, they keep the original's aesthetic charm and have worked up textures and resolution. This means the icons for ammo types, posters, neon signs and all are much more clear this time around and noticably so. Water looks much better in both dynamic environments as well as set pieces (including a bethesda like ripple in the water as you move through it), and Jack's first person weapon models/arms are all improved.
Interestingly, they
add new animations and models to exterior environments and narrative heavy moments. For example, Jack waves the cigarrete around more elegantly in the introduction, a sea turtle/jelly fish/seaweed have been put into the introduction, and the outside environments sport a higher density of ocean life. (Particularly immobile creatures like star fish, seaweed or jelly fish once again.) This was all a very nice touch, although in the introduction of the game you'll remember the iconic Bouncer Big Daddy growling as it sees the bathosphere travel underneath it, as it presumably is repairing the tunnel. Narratively, this made sense as Big Daddies were initially designed to assist in repairs of Rapture with early renditions of the Big Daddies even sporting specific tools to repair. Here in Bioshock Remastered, you'll notice they've replaced the Bouncer model with a Rosie, and a bugged Rosie at that, as it is missing its Rivet Gun. This seems like nitpicking, but really, it just came off as a very unnecessary change to what is one of gaming's greatest introductions.
The last and surprisingly most pleasant alteration of Bioshock was the addition of challenge rooms, director's commentary, and the museum. The director's commentary I'll touch on first as it's very simply not that in depth, for what I was hoping to be a Valve strategy where the commentary is appropriated to specific moments and areas, it is very much a video series of Geoff Keighley interviewing Ken Levine (creative director) and Shawn Robertson (animation lead). This really wouldn't have been much of an issue, but begrudgingly the game requires you to search for each of the ten videos throughout the physcial landscape of the game, a process felt thrown in to add another element to what is already a somewhat bare remaster. This isn't to say the series isn't informative and worth your time, but unless you are an achievement hunter I would recommend looking the series up online and saving a couple hours of time. To piggyback off of this the museum is also a wonderful addition that is given to you immediately, and contains some neat prototypes/concept art in a 3D environment which is really a shame didn't make it into the final product. (I'm looking at you, rumbler) Finally, the challenge rooms, a portal-esque handful of levels designed to force the player to think outside of the campaign's dynamic and work out slightly complex puzzles to attain a higher score or lower time record. These are a cool addition and give you something extra to scratch that Bioshock itch, furthering the incentive to fire this particular version up again, but as there are only just a couple the novelty is thin. Once you accomplish these rooms the gradual decrease in fun is apparent and it turns into a chore.
Alright, so time to get down to business with all the things they screwed up and the things they didn't unscrew from the original. There's a couple big points, and a few smaller, but all the same there are a handful of in your face issues that dilute what is a fantastic experience. I'd like to point out that if you did not play the original verison on PC there were a ton of issues as well, including lack of sound for half of the game's elements, dipping framerate, and rare launch problems. These have all
been fixed and I applaud Blind Squirrel for that, but this is an eye for an eye situation and I would deal with the first game's issues above the latter anyday. First we will be talking about the crashes and boy let me tell you, there are indeed crashes. To list areas where I've experienced repeated crashes: Manually saving, Big Daddy pathfinding (get stuck and stress on physics crashes game), loading challenge rooms, bathosphere travel, and if you make it through the bathosphere at times it crashed upon walking out. There's really no further explanation for this other than the developer's ineptitude to playtest and polish, as it happened at least every other time I've launched the game and it is absolutely an issue worth noting. Regardless of whether the game is sold as a bargain in The Bioshock Collection or as a free upgrade, this is dare I say disrespectful to an audience that enabled Bioshock as a cultural sensation to gaming and slaps long awaiting fans in the face for waiting years to see Bioshock play well on PC. Outside the gameplay, you'll also find it very difficult to alter any settings as they are barebones and clearly a port from the console iterations. The FOV is increased by default, but there is no option to revert this or even tinker it to a comfortable level. Mouse smoothing is also unfixable in game and you must access the files to adjust, so I highly recommend using a controller as I did.
The AI this time around is also shockingly worse than it was before, albeit only slightly. Specifically in the Medical Pavillion where splicers just couldn't find their way to me after turning a corner, I would often stand waiting for scripted sequences to take place and would have to actually engage the enemies myself. This problem didn't seem too radical past this chapter of the game, however Big Daddies and Splicers would often "forget" I was in the area once I began fighting another enemy, for lack of a better word. Some other issues are unrelenting but much smaller, such as a consistent stutter upon using the Vita Chamber, background music looping, and some visual hiccups like purple boxes on bright environments and screen tearing on flashing lights. Small issues, but when so prevalent it becomes a drag to deal with and gives the player a headache. As a last addition, although not consistent, one audio diary didn't show up in inventory after collecting it. This wouldn't have been a major issue had I not been acquiring them for an achievement and 50% done with the game, but alas this now forces me to replay the game again due to such a small problem.
Ultimately, Bioshock Remastered is worth your time as a previous owner. If you could handle the issues in the original PC version, the trade off here isn't tremendous considering the gain, however if you are considering purchasing, I would hold off as 2K has acknowledged these issues and is looking to address them.

First of all, I'm going to be honest with you guys...
I could write a really big review detailing all the pros and cons of this game, but at this point in time we all know that if you are writing a review during the Autumn Sale, you're doing it for the badge. So yeah, I'm feeling kinda lazy to write a detailed essay about this game. What's the point in writing massive walls of text if no one is going to read it, right?
But looking back at the massive amounts of fun I've had with this game, I feel ashamed that it took me so long to actually write a review about it. I feel ashamed that the only thing that made me write this review was a freaking virtual badge. And I will certainly feel ashamed if I churn out a half-baked review on this game just to get a badge!
This game deserves much more than that. I'm sorry, Hollow Knight... I'll make a decent review about you, even if no one sees this! It's time to put that laziness aside and actually write a good review about this game, whether I get a badge or not!
I'll try to keep this review as spoiler-free as possible, so you will be able to jump into the game blind (kinda), which makes the experience even greater.
Oh my God. This game. I can't tell you guys how much I absolutely adore this game.
I've played Metroidvania-esque type of games all of my life. Who knew Super Metroid III would change my gaming life so much? If you too are a Metroidvania fan, you might have noticed a somewhat long drought in the genre after Metroid Prime 3 had released. If you are like me and love the 2D metroidvanias even more, like the old Metroid and Castlevania games, then that drought was even longer. Sure, there were some recent indie metroidvania games in the past few years. Some of them were good, some of them were great, but personally, I feel like none of them got the formula right...
... Until Hollow Knight showed up, that is.
This game is certainly amazing. It manages to recreate the metroidvania (this is quickly becoming a buzzword in this review) formula perfectly while still managing to feel fresh, innovative and original. I mean, look at the screenshots of this game! Doesn't it look amazing? Did I mention that was all drawn by hand? I'm sure the store page did. And if you already think the game looks amazing, wait until you play it, wait until you
it.
Which brings me to my next point. The art direction in this game is ABSOLUTELY FANTASTIC. Who said that only games with stunning next-gen graphics can be considered eye-candy? This plays a big role in getting you invested into the game. From the very first area, the Forgotten Crossroads to the final boss, you will certainly feel many different emotions, such as awe, surprise, excitement, tension and even fear. This game is a rollercoaster, and its name is "One Hell of a Ride" (feel free to arrest me after being incredibly cheesy in that last line).
And of course, the soundtrack is just as phenomenal as the art direction. And just like the art direction, Christopher Larkin does an excellent job in conveying so many emotions throughout his soundtrack. It fits the game so well that it makes certain moments of the game even more memorable. That wondrous sense of discovering something grand, something amazing (or sometimes, something downright dark, sad, creepy or scary...) is enhanced by Larkin's masterpiece. Each boss fight feels like a different kind of struggle. Sometimes you will feel tense while fighting that insanely hard boss. Sometimes you feel like you're fighting for honor certain bosses. Who knows, you might even fight some bosses with a huge smile on your face (I'm looking at you, Ogrim, you amazing beast), all thanks to the visual and sound feedback.
If you can take one thing for granted in this adventure of a game, it's that it both looks, sounds and feels great to play!
The gameplay sure feels solid and tight. Everytime you die - and trust me, you will die A LOT in this game - feels fair, you know it was your own mistake. The combat in this game is all about timing, really, especially when we are talking about bosses. Getting to know the bosses patterns well is a must. After that, you'll need to know when to dodge, when to strike and when (if you can, that is) to heal. If you happen to be a cyborg with unmatched precision skills, you might even be able to parry some melee attacks from most enemies and certain bosses.
But hey, this is a metroidvania, remember? The game is not just about combat, it's about exploration and platforming too!
Exploration-wise, it's exactly what you'd expect from a great metroidvania. Some areas aren't going to be accessible at all for you until you get a certain upgrade. You will soon find out that every area in the game is unique, filled with secrets and collectibles, some of which are also impossible to reach without said upgrades. For me, this is what makes metroidvanias so amazing to me, this sense of progression that is unrivaled by any other genre feels amazing. And Hollow Knight really nails it in that aspect too.
Regarding the platforming sections in this game, they are incredibly varied. There are a lot of platforming puzzles in this game, each more interesting than the other. And then there's the platforming... challenges (more like nightmares). I don't try to think about them to much, lest I get 'Nam flashbacks and die of a stroke. Remember when I've said earlier that whenever you die you feel like that was completely on you? Yeah. Let's just say you'll grow to hate yourself a lot in certain segments (the same can be said about certain bosses). One segment (by far, the hardest one of the game) comes to mind in particular, which reminds me of Super Meat Boy, especially because it has a lot of moving, rotating saws in it.
Some of these segments aren't necessary for you to finish the game (the ones with saws, for example), but you absolutely need to finish them if you want to get the True Ending.
Hell yeah baby, this game has multiple endings too. Three, to be exact, but obviously you'll want to get the True Ending one first. Trust me!
I really won't say much about the story, except that its phenomenal. The story-telling is also fantastic. And obviously, you can always get to know more about the world of Hallownest by talking to the many NPCs in the game and by finding collectibles. The writing in this game is also amazing. And that's all I'll say about it because I really don't want to spoil much about the game. Just believe me when I say that the world of Hallownest is a memorable one, and so are its denizens.
Performance-wise, I feel that this game is quite optimized. I've even managed to play it on a dying rotten potato laptop I had here with me sometime ago, although I don't remember its specs anymore. Sorry =\
And let me remind you, this is a very hard game. The learning curve in this game is a good one, but oh my GOD is it INSANELY HARD by the end of it.

I certainly enjoyed Civ V and this isn't much more than that. There's a lot of potential, but all of the new ideas, namely the Orbital Layer, Affinities, and cross-the-map upgraded unit types, aren't enough to warrant the switch from your fully DLC'd Civ V to the new Beyond Earth. Other than the three new aspects mentioned before, it's essentially a reskinned Civ V - more like a heavy-duty modification than a whole new game.
I can't help but feel Firaxis held back their best ideas for upcoming DLC's, but that's cynical of me.
I'd like to see floating water cities, full space stations in the Orbital Layer (hell, why have ground-based colonies at all!?), Orbital units and Battles (why limit yourself to a water-based navy in a game that's called "Beyond Earth?) more direction in the Tech Web so by devoting fully to a particular Affinity, you box yourself out of alternative technologies (Ex. Biospheres and Climate Control are mutually exclusive because they're completely different approaches to the issue of the hostile native environment. Each makes the other reduntant. See what I'm saying?)
Ultimately, I love the style but I feel like we've all been suckered. As a sucker, I recommend this game.

Games like this don't come around very often, which is why you revel in every minute you play them.
The Stanley Parable is really one of those types of games you can't watch on Youtube, you need to expereince it for yourself, because the joy of the game comes in the experiences you have and discover yourself, the little things, the many discoveries for curious minds and the sharing of said discoveries with other curious Stanley Parable players. Even better than playing yourself is giving the controls over to someone who has never seen or played the game themselves and just carrying out your own little experiment.
- How easily manipulated is the gamer?
- Will they follow orders because the narrator says to do so, or will curiousity get the better of them?
- How far will they go if they DO decide to do their own thing?
- Just how defiant / curious can a person be?
There are simply so many things you can discover about a person's personality that this game is more than a game, it's a personality quiz. It's not so much what they do after several playthroughs, but what they do in the first or even second playthrough that makes it so interesting. You could give the game to several people and the interesting thing is how susceptible they are to simple and subtle instructions.
Are we really that easily manipulated? Are we really part of an endless Matrix? Is everything a lie? What happens if I don't conform? How afraid am I to not conform? Am I a leader or a follower?
So much questions...so many thinking.
You owe it to yourself to play this game and if you already know what it's all about, get it anyway and use it as an experiment to identify how those around you think.

Very unique, competitive, and fun game. WASD movement, skills are really skillshots, and fast rounds.
For casuals, this game is great, you have daily and weekly quests, and alongside to new players, there's achievements that they can unlock. All of these daily quests, weekly quests, and achievements, you will gain rewards such as cosmetic chests and ingame currency.
Everyone has an equal playing field, no runes or masteries that give you a head start in the game, also no buying items. Instead, at the beginning of each round everybody has an option to chose 1 out of the 3 "battlerites" given to them for their character which allow you to customize your abilities and playstyle.
Combat is really fluid, thanks to WASD and skillshots, every character's kit seems to fit well with the gamestyle. The game is easy to grasp, but hard and rewarding to master.
Every champion is viable, just certain team compositions are not good against other compositions. This game's balance is okay, no character is broken since every character can be countered. Characters are more balanced in 3v3s than in 2v2s, since you have more variety of champions to play with and against. If you're looking for the most balanced game mode, it's going to be 3v3s, but not much people play 3v3s.
Battlerite's playerbase is okay, nothing you need to worry about, there's 2.5k people playing each day, its not going to decline, it's in Early Access, its completely fine.
Nothing wrong with ranked matchmaking during this stage of the game. Only 2.5k players playing the game each day during peak times, you can expect going against the same people a couple times. Yes you will be matched with others higher than you, but if you dont win against them, then you dont deserve to get up to that rank, so don't complain. If you dont want to go against people higher than you, you use "Strict Matchmaking" which sets you to play with others are your rank, but you'll have to compensate for the time to search for players at your rank.
For only $20, for all the champions (including all the future ones), and for 400+ hours I have on it, this game is worth the money. More features are to come, watching this game develop since October, 2016, its a very promising game. I have fun each day playing it.

Unique Character Designs – choose from various champions, such as an assassin or a pyro-loving creature, each with differing playstyles and unique designs.
Fast-Paced Action – players must constantly be ready and on the move in Battlerite. The maps are designed to be like an arena, where action and bloodlust are always present.
Clean 3D Graphics – enjoy clean 3D graphics that clearly depict characters from the environment in smooth models.
Be Awarded for Skill – dominate opponents with skill, as there are no items or such distractions in the arenas of Battlerite.
Spectate – join the crowd to watch champions collide in the arena, learning from master-level players or simply to enjoy the adrenaline rush.

Let's make this review as the game is: short, but juicy.
The obvious +'s of the game are it's lore, background and story. It plays in the original LOTR world, with the original lore, original characters (you will meet the fellowship, Bilbo, etc, albeit only a few have the original voice actors). The plot and quests are believeable and fit nicely into the original LOTR plot.
The graphics are fine. Controls, too, which is a surprise, given it's a console port. Might want to take this as an example for other *coughDScough* games.
The Coop mode is nice and definitely upgrades the game's feeling. If just because the AI is horrible and needs to cheat the rules to actually be remotely useful.
So... it looks nice and has a nice story? You already noticed what's lacking? Jep, the gameplay.
The gameplay itself consists of running through linear levels, picking up loot, chests and secrets along the way, whilst slaugthering pile after pile of enemies with a few 'bosses' in between. Albeit those 'bosses' are often ridicolously weak, with the game's toughest points being the 'defend the gate' style horde attacks.
Which fades right into the next issue: The game is too easy. It comes with two further unlockable difficultys, but actually the game becomes only easier on the 2nd run, given you, by now, have a pretty well-skilled character who (if you know your numbers) is built towards synergizing mass slaughter. (Note that me and my mates got too bored of the game to try a 3rd run on the highest difficulty setting, but I don't expect things to change.)
As you can guess, inbetween nice (but boring once you know them from the first run) dialogues and repetitive slaughter is only boredome or exploring the map for glitches (floating trees are my favourite). The game definitely does not offer a lot of content.
As mentioned above, the AI (at least for your teammates in singleplayer) is lackluster, nuff said.
End result? 6/10
It's fun to play once or twice, short enough for it'S repetitive melee system not to become boring, but not exactly an awesome game by any stretch. If you see it on a cheap sale (5@ and below sounds good) AND have someone to play it with, grab it. Otherwise, not really worth it.

Containing dialogue and a plot  that's both at times ridiculous and super serious, as well as a protagonist and villain shrouded in mystery, this gem of a tactical RPG is not something to be missed out on.
With a fresh approach to turn-based strategy, the combat system utilizes commands broadly, with the player assigning generic actions such as melee/mage/heal to groups of characters, with individual units acting accordingly, using skills from their repertoires pertinent to the current combat situation, producing occasionally surprising results. Quick time events are also present in combat, and upon successful completion of sequences of them, reward the player with the ability to strike before enemies, or have characters reassess their planned action, usually allowing them to attack with more powerful skills.
The party management system will have you planning and continuously analyzing your team makeup, group formations, active skills, and molding character abilities to fill certain roles in combat, and although overwhelming at first, is only as complex as it needs to be.
Packed with side quests galore, a wonderful soundtrack composed by Tsuyoshi Sekito, and boss fights that will have you devising your moves meticulously, The Last Remnant does not dissapoint. A walkthrough should however be utilized for second, and subsequent playthroughs to experience all the game has to offer.

In modern war... you'll die like a dog for no good reason  -Ernest Hemingway
Most war games are all about unlocking new weapons and blowing limbs off of the enemy team, But the thing is, war is more than shooting a gun and getting that '' VICTORY '' text on your screen.
This war of mine comes with a large variety of emotional problems, disease and so on and so on, 95% of war games leaves these parts out , but '' This war of mine '' does not.
This a 2D Survival poInt and click game, it focuses on the horrors of actual war, so of you're seeking for a FPS that takes aim and reaction skill, you're in the wrong place.
Imagine a zombie apocalypse, minus the zombies. I.E disease, struggle for food, coldness , Constant awareness of bandits, Emotional parts of robbing/killing a civilian and so on. That is what this game is about.
The time and place of this game is the city of Pogoren in the country of Graznavia and im guessing its somewhere in the 90's ( based on weaponry and buildings ) The names of both playable characters and traders makes me think this country is based off of somewhere in eastern europe.
The story of the game goes as such : The cities around Graznavia are in constant war between the militairy and government rebels, civilians from all around the country have fled to the capital ( Pogoren ) in hopes of rest. But at some point the war came to Pogoren as well. The Rebels are mostly untrustworthy and psychos that want to have the entierity of the country in their hands and the militairy was from the beginning sent out to stop them, but after a while, the militairy went mad, they took the opportunity of the situation and turned powermad aswell, since they had equipment and weaponry already they were on a good spot, but one thing that they had that the rebels didn't? They were disciplined and united. And now they are as bad, if not even worse than the rebels. And the civilians in the city are the ones who are in the worst spot, they lack food, equipment, weapons and medicine and the struggle to keep holding on is almost overwhelming.
In daytime snipers guard the streets and keeps civilians from leaving their shelters and that's when they have to fortify their home and craft different variesties of useful things, but in the nighttime, thats when the civilians thrive. They spread out looking for supplies in the cover of darkness. and before the night is at an end, they better be back in their settlement, or sniper fire and militairy forces will make it hard to get home.
Depending on your personal thoughts about these types of games, if you like a challenge and dont mind the drawish style of the game , then i'd say its well worth the 19€, If it goes on sale however i do well recommend it to almost anybody.
Now there remains a few questions unanswered, Will the war ever perish? Do you have what it takes to survive? These things are for you to discover.

This War of Mine is a great game that isn't exactly fun.  It doesn't give you a rewarding feeling when you build a new item in your home.  It doesn't give you an exciting feeling when you win a fight with someone.  All it gives you is grim satisfaction when you survive another day.
You see, we're surrounded by other people trying to survive in a civil war.  Some are murderers and soldiers, but most are survivors who got caught up in the same war we did, regular people who are just trying to make it another day with what little supplies they have left.  However, in order to survive, we may have to do unspeakable things.  And these things don't happen without consequence.
Depending on how you play, your story will be wildly different.  I first played as a group of survivors stuck in winter who helped everyone they met and never stole or killed, only to end up sick and dead because they ran out of fuel for the furnace.  My current playthrough is with a group who decided that stealing and the show of force was the way to go.   I have to admit, I didn't feel good about myself when I broke into a home and stole the possessions of its inhabitants, especially when I found out they were two unarmed women and a little girl.  This game makes you seriously consider your actions, and the consequences that come afterwards.
Technically, this game is pretty solid.  There's a few bugs here and there, but I haven't found anything game-breaking.  The controls are simple and easy to get used to.  There's a lack of instructions, but the game isn't that hard to figure out.  I would have liked an explanation of how combat worked, however.  Figuring it out when you're getting attacked for the first time was interesting.
My only real issue with the game is that it only saves at the beginning of every morning.  Meaning that if you need to stop the game for any reason at home or while scavenging, you lose everything you did for that day.  This is actually a good and bad thing, since the decisions you make while scavenging are permanent unless you're willing to go through the entire day again.
All in all, this is definitely a game that will leave an impression on you after you play it.  For that alone, I would recommend it.

This game is a... peculiar one. It's definitely a rather unconventional game but then again what else one would expect from a jRPG ? ;)
More to the point, game features a turn based combat but... everything else is different. Battles happen on a different screen and you have a tactical view of the field. You command units which can hold up to 5 characters (maximum amount of characters you can have is 18) each and order them which enemy unit they have to attack. Depending on the "formation" your unit has and the speed of the characters in that unit, how fast the unit moves on the battle field changes, therefore you have to be mindful about that, since if your unit attacks an enemy unit that was targeting different one they get a bonus to damage and morale boost as well. And yes, there's a morale gauge. They more in your favour, the more damage you do. The more in the favour of the enemy... the more damage you take. The actions which your characters will perform depend on... few factors. First is what arts they can use and have enabled, second which enemy they are targeting (you get different set of commands for different enemy units), third is the morale situation and there's also the class of your unit leader. Oh and lastly there's a bit of RNG involved. Yes, this means you can't directly tell each character what action to perform but at the same time, it does make the command selection faster and forces you to be more flexible with your tactics. It can screw you up if you happen to have bad luck, but that's rather rare. When the untis are performing the commands, you can have a "critical offense" (or defense when they are recipients of an attack) which requires you to press a button at a certain moment. The game will choose between one of two buttons, and those depend on the weapon the character uses. When you perform it successfuly the next ally is automatically boosted in the turn order to perform their action. If there are at least two critical offense before the last character acts and both are successful you get a big damage boost to an art or a free one if one wasn't selected... along with the boost of course :D
Now, when units engage with each other, you have what is called a deadlock. If another unit engages a unit while that is already in a deadlock, you'll engage in a Flank, which boosts the morale and gives a further boost to damage. If you manage to perfom another flank in the same turn, it will change into rear assault, which deals even more damage and grants a bigger boost to morale. And if you do it with yet another unit, you get a massive assault, which is even stronger. However some enemies can deadlock few units at once, so you rarely ever see anything more than a flank. I am yet to see a massive assault performed by my units, although my units having massive assault on them isn't that rare xD
With basics explained, let's move onto the character development... which doesn't exist... on the first glance. You don't have an exp gauge or ability to directly affect the character stats, nor to even change their equipment, but... you can help them decide what to focus on (balance, mystic or combat) which affects what equipment they want to get. That in turn affects what arts they can use in battle, which you can enable or disable if you don't particularly like them. Characters gain stat points from fights (duh!), the longer the fight (aka more turns) the higher chance they gain those and not just one. There's a limit to the turns, so don't go doing 900 turn fights, because it will result in the same gain as from a 30 turn fight :P Also fighting enemies of a higher battle rank than you helps with getting higher stats... and developing the arts faster.
Ahh yes, the arts. Probably the best thing about the game... IMO. The combat arts are purely dependent on the weapon you're using AND how you're holding the weapon. Therefore you have one handed arts, power grip (aka holding one handed weapon with two arms) arts, two-handed arts (weapons that can be held with two hands), dual wield (two weapons) arts, quad wield (yes, 4 weapons) arts, dual power grip arts and... yes you guessed it, dual two handed. The basic ones are very simple, like a quick lunge or a swipe, but the more advanced ones... wheee, now those are some cool looking ones. And then come the weapon arts and special arts, which are basically your "limit breaks" from the Final Fantasy games so to speak. I suppose I should mention the mystic arts, but those are not as complicated as the combat ones. You simply have different categories and using them unlocks more from a given category. Most characters have around 1-2 different mystic categories, mages naturally have 3 or 4. There are also item based arts that revolve around... yes, items. This includes healing, damage dealing, status afflicting and combination of the latter two. Lastly there are summons, which basically add a unit to the field comprised of a single... being.
There's a lot more to explain but I'm just gonna make a short list of the rest:
- You have a world map in the style of FF X, aka literal map on which you point where you want to go.
- Your main character is the only one you have full control over equipment and is the only character that can learn all the arts in the game (apart from some weapon arts).
- Story is half decent, it isn't groundbreaking in any way shape or form, but it's enough to keep you interested playing the game... at least in my case.
- If you like to get everything as soon as possible... prepare for the game to be harder. As funny as it is, the game becomes harder the higher your battle rank is and that rises with the amount of defeated enemies. Your stats on the other hand don't.
- There's a plethora of sidequests to keep you occupied. And there's a New Game + as well, which let's you play in Hard mode and keep all your components along with a lot of money that depends on how many guild quests you did.
That's pretty much it tbh. This is definitely not a game for people who want to be taken by hand with everything or expect an "industry standard" turn battle system. This game is as peculiar as it gets and if you don't want something that doesn't work like any other game out there... don't buy it. But if you're open to such new experiences... you'll definitely like the game... and then hate that you can't choose those damn commands yourself xD
TL;DR;
- incredibly peculiar game with a turn battle system unlike any other game, only for the most open minded people out there
- combat arts look cool
- the game is incredibly simple, yet with a lot of depth to it as well
- the grind and superboss battles can be insane for the completionist types out there
- story is average but enough to keep you in
- New Game + exists... yay \o/
- Hard mode exists... yay?
- critical offense/defense keeps you occupied even when you don't select the orders, makes the game faster paced than it actually is

If you're a fan of the original X series you will be disappointed with this attrocity.  Though it has always been advertised as a revisioned game it is so different from its predecessors that it does not deserve an association with the X series.  What was once an open-world with millions of choices to be made in the style of a simulation has been reduced to one ship you may fly (unfortunately named the Albion Skunk which you cannot change) with anime-inspired graphics, a flight interface which occludes half the view, a virtually non-existent radar/scanner system, and offers no sort of targeting control.  The innovation of the highway system (a replacement to the original gate system which was shut down in the previous game) serves as more of a almost mini-game component and is just a waste of time.  Instead of accessing wares available at a station through a consolidated centralized monitor, you must now dock at the station and search for what you need via a first-person perspetive that incorporates a graphics engine similar to that of the original Duke Nukem 3D (No offense Duke--you're awesome)
Credit can be given to the immersion aspect of the game with the added ability of a first-person exploration of your ship (which, unfortunately, serves no purpose than the ability to say you can do so) and stations (which sounds neat, but quickly becomes more of a hinderance to your mission than it is worth) and the ability to hire crew to manage systems on your ship.
On top of all these stupendous attributes, the game seems like it was highly rushed to the shelf by Egosoft, previously one of my favorite game producers, and is chock full of small bugs that make an already frustrating game that much more unbearable.  My advice, since we cannot expect a game from Egosoft in the style of non-Rebirth X-series games, is, first, to not waste your money on this doorstop (duh), and, second, to follow the following games in hopes that eventually we will have a worthy follow-up to a incredible series of games that has now left a foul taste in my mouth.
Check out these games currently in development:
Star Citizen
Elite Dangerous
Infinity

Hey all, Deadpool here with a review. Now that the obvious is out of the way, let's get to it shall we? Here be the review for Sins of a Solar Empire; Rebellion, a 4X RTS game set in space. Oooooooooo.
Plot
There isn't one. At least not that I can infer. I think. Let me start from the beginning. Rebellion is the first Sins game I have played. As with sequels, you'd usually get a recap, yes? Crysis 3 has a rather long one, the Assassin's Creed games(save for the first) have recaps, and the list goes on. Sins of a Solar Empire; Rebellion does not have one. So me being new to the series, I have absolutely no clue what is going on. The intro video, while stunning and well done, offered little to no info. All I know(and still know because I am too lazy to Google) is that there are humans, some very spiritual alien peeps, and some nano-tech alien things that are running from something. Each race has been split into Loyalists and Rebels. So you have, vaguely, six to choose from.
The Good Stuff
The game is pretty well balanced. The developers seem to have a keen eye for balance between the various ship classes and races that produce the ships. I tried spamming with smaller frigates, but was easily defeated. A balanced fleet is a good one, and the Devs seem to have hit the nail on the head when it came to making sure of it. The Same can be said for the balance between the factions themselves.
Graphics. Wow. The explosions seem legit, and make the camera shake if you zoom in. Which, I love. The level of detail in the game is astounding. Then again, it being a space based game, you'd really hope so. Truly well thought out and beautiful artwork. Same can be said for the sound. Very, very well done and aesthetically pleasing.
Complex, but simple. It is complex enough to thoroughly enjoy and really make you think about your next move, yet simple enough to where there is a minimal learning curve; especially for someone like me who has never played a Sins game before. Little to no micromanaging of your planets and/or colonies, which allows you to truly focus on your fleet, defense, economy, and of course diplomacy.
Now, for diplomacy. The devs offered up something I haven't seen in diplomacy before I played this game. It is complex with your actions affecting not only the intended faction, but rippling through to the other factions in the game. And likewise with their actions. Not only that, but to create alliances and forge pacts, not only do they have to like you, but your people have to like them. I, for one, absolutely love this. It prevents you from going all out and forging alliances just to win an allied victory and truly brings into perspective just how closely and how far the devs went to instill a balance into the game.
Voice acting. It is phenomenal. 'Nuff said. Some of the best I have seen. Or heard, rather.
Diversity. The diversity between the three races, and even their Loyalist and Rebel sub-factions, is outstanding. The research options differ greatly between the three races. The technologies are different, the voices are different, everything is different! Mostly. Each time you play as a different race, it feels and plays completely different from the last.
The Bad Stuff
Campaign. There isn't one. The only mode, aside from multiplayer online, is relative to skirmish mode on Command and Conquer games. That's it. No campaign to play through, nothing. Nothing but a repetitive procession of skirmish after skirmish. Set up, conquer, win. Set up, conquer, win. As amazing as the game looks, it gets old. Unless you're like me and use Galaxy Forge(Comes with the game, program you can use to create your own maps) to play very sadistic games with the AI.
Speaking of AI, it is very finicky. If you have great defenses, they don't attack. Even when you set them on the hardest difficulty, they wont attack. The only good thing about the AI is the diplomacy, and watching them fight between themselves. I once sat for two hours watching five AI's battle it out over 2 different star systems. There was a tug of war, take and lose. The AI's fight each other real well, but if you're too powerful they leave you alone like you have the plague. If you maintain a decent level of awesomeness, they will attack you. They will take what you have and own you. So it is somewhat of a balancing act. Depends on how you want to play it.
Micro Management. I put this in the Bad Stuff section as well because if you're like me and love micro managing, then this game will disappoint. Yeah sure you build things in orbit to advance your culture and spread it, but so what? I want to be able to see who the leaders are, select the political whatevermajiggs, change the funding from research to defense if I wanted, and truly see what my people(ingame people, you know, in my empire) are made of. But no. You get a planet, some aircraft whizzing around it, and city lights if you're on the nighttime side of it. That's it. To me, once you learn the game and how to play it, there is sooooo much room for micromanagement. But, I can see why the Devs didn't do it. It is an RTS game, and sometimes not enough time for micromanagement.
Conclusion
Now that I touched on just a few of the high and low points of the game, here is my condensed review of my review of the game. To be frank, the game is amazing. Excellent mechanics, balance, diplomacy, voice acting, visuals, diversity, and a true pleasure to play. Tutorials are available if you have questions, but in the end you will still be discovering little things here and there that you can do months after the fact. Lack of a campaign makes the endless C&C and Starcraft-like map skirmishes repetitive and give it a lack of long-term playability(Invented that word just for this review). In this game, I feel, the Pros outweigh the Cons and thus I give it a 7 out of 10.

After 20 hours, I like it so far. The decks are weaker again than in the last Duels installation, but to me that doesn't rly matter because everyone is playing with the same cards, anyway. In a way, it makes the game MORE fun, because there's less mythic cards randomly turning the game around.
Another plus is the fact that they included the golden dual-colored lands right from the starts. With this, building dual and even triple-colored decks is possible without spending any gold on booster packs. This way, there's lots of different strategies and combinations.
The server problems seem to be solved by now (first two days, you often got disconnected). A few bugs still plague the game, but I think it's about the same as every Duels game up to now (I've played them starting with 2013). Mostly smaller stuff like unable to use some ability, but stometimes a game freezes up telling you "Waiting for another player to make a decission" indefinitely. I hope they can improve this, but I've had those bugs for years, so I'm not too optimistic in that regard.
For newcomers, this is the IDEAL way to start with magic, hands down. The campaign mode does a fine job explaining the rules on the fly. There's also a deck builder guiding you to build your own pre-themed decks, which is a terrific idea. It both gives you a useable deck and teaches you what to look out for when building your own. Two thumbs up!
To bring this review, to an end, they've also brought back the long-awaited 2headed giant, which was for some unknown reason removed from the last game, causing much strife. There's also daily quests, which making earning gold / booster packs quicker. Considering this is F2P, I was pleasantly surprised by this. Personally, I spent 10$ to get a few additional cards, since I work and don't have that much time to spend on games anymore. :-/ Still, I think if you play this for a while, you'll have all the cards soon enough.

I picked this game up on a whim (and the price) and was completely overwhelmed by the experience I got. I wasn't familiar at all with the Chinese Paladin: Sword and Fairy series before this, but now I'm hoping that the publishers release the other games in the series in English as well.
Overall the game is similar in format to many JRPGs, with the twist of being well rooted in a Chinese Heroic Fantasy / "Wuxia" setting. The systems in the game are adequate, and the combat took a little bit of getting used to, but it was servicable.
The graphics feel a little dated, and the animations repetitive in the many, many, many cutscenes in the game, but none of this really detracted from my enjoyment of the game.
What truly won me over was the music (the game has one of the best soundtracks I've had the pleasure to discover) and the storyline. Translation hiccups aside, the story was well written, and each of the game's 6 main characters were given enough time (and space) to discover themselves, undergo change and learn from their adventures.
There's plenty to enjoy in the game, and those who are tired of the usual fantasy tropes will find a very different story waiting for them here.
Given the sheer amount of enjoyment I've had, and at the price it was going for, I strongly recommend the game to people who are looking for something new for their RPG fix.

A tranquil melancholy rests over Hollow Knight. Its protagonist is a small insect wielding a tiny sword. The world is dying, decaying and decrepit. A well in the center of town beckons and through its winding caverns, a tale of a kingdom lost awaits.
In a world saturated with Metroidvanias to the point where the tag alone is no longer a selling point, along comes Hollow Knight and sets a new bar for the genre. This game is artistically brilliant - the music is damn near perfect, the art and animation is gorgeous and cohesive. The world manages to feel both lush and dying at the same time and for a game about disease eating away at a socity, the world feels surprisingly alive.
But where Hollow Knight truly shines and makes it stand out among its peers is the combat. It is challenging, rhythmic and rewarding. The bosses are some of the most fun fights I've had in  2D game in years, and even the normal enemies remain interesting to fight throughout the game.

It's a nice little game for being free. The only drawback thus far is that it seems easier for me to drive to a friends house and play a game than it is to find an online opponent who'll stay for the match.

Saint's Row: Gat Out of Hell is the newest installment of the Saint's Row Franchise. It is a standalone expansion to Saint's Row IV, and as such shares a lot of similarities with it, mainly the gameplay and superpowers.
Let's get the obvious question out of the way: you do not need to have Saint's Row IV installed to play, although Gat Out of Hell will automatically detect a Saint's Row IV savefile on your system and import your custom Boss into the game for use in cutscenes.
The story begins right where Saint's Row IV leaves off. Having conquered Simulation 31 and taken down the Zin Empire, the Saints are now living aboard their "borrowed" spaceship which now houses the entirety of whats left of the human race.  We are introduced to Kinzie's birthday party, where Matt is getting the Saints to try out a Quija Board. Spoilers aside, this does not go well and a portal straight to Hell opens up and drags the Boss in. Johnny Gat and Kinzie decide to go in after him.
Without spoiling too much more, I will say that this game is still as fun to play as previous Saint's Row titles. You can expect your fair share of awesome weapons, including many themed after the 7 Deadly Sins. My favorite of these are the Diamond Gun that literally shoots diamonds (Greed) and the recliner mounted with a chaingun and rocket launchers (Sloth).
There is a brand-new map with plenty of the usual diversions and activites to participate in aside from the main story. Many of the activites from Saint's Row IV return, but with their own Hellish flair. For example: Trailblazing is now Hellblazing, requiring you to fly through orbs and checkpoints to complete it. Rather than a traditional progression of missions, Gat out of Hell has players completing diversions and causing general chaos in an effort to raise the level of a meter called Satan’s Wrath. Once certain milestones are met on the meter, a cutscene is triggered. The game turns into a musical at times during these scenes, which may be quite enjoyable for some as they are played out in fully-voiced cutscenes with decent dance and lyrics.
Superpowers return from IV, and they’re upgraded by collecting Soul Clusters that are scattered around hell. Most are returning powers (blast, stomp, aura) with some new elemental powers, but Summon is exclusive to Gat out of Hell. Depending on which variant you use, it allows you to recruit imps to your side, make towers explode out of the ground, or produce a giant demonic ally.
All of this is fine and dandy, as the game is such a blast to play, but fans of the franchise may be disappointing in the omission of certain features that have long been established in the series. For one, since you play as either Johnny Gat or Kinzie Kinsington, you are pretty much stuck with the outfit they have by default. There are no clothing stores in hell. Also omitted was the ability to whip out a cell phone and have an ally deliver a vehicle to you. This isn't too big of an issue, as you can at anytime sprout wings and fly wherever you need to go. Flying controls are pretty smooth, with upgrades allowing more refined control while in-flight. And finally, there are no "home bases" to upgrade or radio stations while driving, not even an option to import music from your PC to use in-game.
Gat Out of Hell isn't a long game, and as a standalone expansion I didn't expect it to be. After about 2 hours of play my save completion percentage read a modest 45%. Gat Out of Hell delivers what you'd expect from the Saint's Row franchise, just in a smaller package. Overall, it is worth shelling out the asking price of $19.99, especially if you are a long-time fan.

A sloppy, technically-challenged game that is ultimately redeemed by its quality story and the sheer uniqueness of being one of a very small number of English-translated Chinese RPGs. (Note that this is a preliminary review. I have spent six hours with Sword and Fairy 6 so far. I'll update the review to give my final thoughts when I finish it, or earlier if I hit major issues that are worth mentioning.)
Sword and Fairy 6 is a fairly conventional RPG, mechanically. It follows a typical town, exploration/dungeon, repeat structure. One thing I find interesting is the ability to freely jump. This makes town navigation a lot more interesting than most RPGs thanks to the ability to jump onto roofs and run pretty much anywhere. There are lookout points in difficult-to-reach locations scattered throughout each area that even reward that sort of experimentation. On the flip side, the freedom you have to move anywhere also means it's very easy to hit the edge of an area or even fall through the void at the bottom (which conveniently just resets you to nearby solid ground).
Combat involves controlling a single character while the rest do their own thing, which can be influenced with tactical options on the left and by the skills selected. Each character has two sets of skills, each generally useful for a different situation. For example, one character has one skillset that focuses on DPS and one that focuses on buffs. It feels fairly sloppy to me since you don't really have fine control over everything your characters do. The best tactic is seems to be to manually control the character whose abilities are the most important for that particular situation (like healing or drawing aggro) and hope that everyone else behaves competently. There are also bonuses for defeating all of the enemies within a specified amount of time. I am unsure whether it's simply impossible early in the game or if there's some aspect to the combat that I do not understand, but not once have I managed to get the bonus.
The story is interesting. It starts off with some convenient meetings between characters who are all working towards a fairly simple goal, but it quickly becomes apparent that there's much more going on. Everyone is plagued with their own problems, doubts, and secrets, and I am very much looking forward to seeing how it all plays out. I'm being fairly vague to avoid spoilers, but I do find it neat how some twists are immediately obvious yet others are carefully laid-out yet never telegraphed. The voice acting seems great, not that I can understand much of it.
The localization is mediocre. The introductory video is by far the worst of it - I'm pretty sure it was machine-translated. But the in-game dialogue, while definitely wooden and sloppy (incorrect tenses, odd sentence construction, stray markup tags) is understandable.
The tutorials fare worse by some explaining some aspects but never really divulging why they matter, leaving you to flounder until you realize things through trial and error. The boss of the first dungeon is definitely a wake-up call that demonstrates why provoke, an ability simply mentioned in passing in the tutorial, is a key tool. And lots of things are never explained at all. For instance, NPCs sometimes respond differently (or even not at all) to different characters. If you've clicked on one who has the talk icon but they turned and didn't say anything, it's because they will only respond to a different character. I still do not understand the way the quest board in each town works. Sometimes quests that I cannot take appear on it, yet other quests never appear. It's weird and, again, never explained.
Another problem is the performance. Sword and Fairy 6 simply does not run very well, and looks nowhere near as good as its requirements would suggest. I have a GTX 1080 and the game stutters regularly. Not constantly, but it hitches every minute or two. The art style is fairly nice but areas look quite blocky and are often monochromatic. Animations are extremely stiff and repetitive - I hope you like seeing Yue Jinzhao do a facepalm, because he's going to be doing it a lot and in the exact same way every time.
Ultimately, despite the technical issues and general feeling of sloppiness that pervades many aspects of the game, I am enjoying my time with it and do recommend it. Sword and Fairy 6 is far from the best RPG you can play on PC, but it's still a fascinating journey through a fairly foreign (to Western eyes) world.

I should start by saying that I'm aware that this game isn't perfect. The opening cinematic was translated extremely poorly, and I was nervous about the rest of the game because of this. My fears were unwarranted, because the rest of the game is not only coherent, but I'd say rather well done if we disregard some minor errors here and there. It's not particularly well optimized, although it's certainly playable, even on my low-end gaming laptop.
What I really want to say is that for those who are looking for the polish of a FF title or the next "tales of" game, you might be disapointed, but for those who are looking to experience something genuinely different from the other RPGs you've played in the past, this game really might surpise you. I'm not nearly finished with the game, so I can't comment on the story as a whole, but up until this point I have been engaged and pulled along, despite the aforementioned technical hiccups.
The battle system has a bit of a learning curve, but once you realize that the game has actually given you all the tools to succeed and stop blaming the need to "grind" on all of your problems, the game is not only winnable, it's a lot of fun! Not only have I not grinded at all, I've actively avoided encounters in areas I've already cleared and have only died once during a boss fight on normal. My advice to the newcomer: Always Be Healing!
I've never written a review before, and likely won't ever again, but I felt that it would be an injustice to let this game fall under the radar of any true RPG fan who hasn't experienced a CRPG before. For the record, I'm not the kind of person who  plays super obscure RPGs in my free time, this is my first forray into the wide world of Chinese gaming.
I should also say, reports of extremely long cutscenes are not exaggerated, although the story is so engrossing I have yet to mind.
At a $15 list price, this game is well worth a shot, and on sale even more so. Hope I've convinced at least one wary buyer to give this a shot, I want them to localize the other Chinese Paladin titles!

"I do not believe in destiny, only the blade in my hand and the friends by my side."
Love that exists in the mortal realm can transcend the powers of the heavens. When was the first time you were moved to the core by a fictional work? I still remember encountering the Xianjian Qixia Zhuan series through its first game in my early days, and being shaken and stirred by the tale of Li Xiaoyao, Zhao Ling'er, Lin Yueru, and A'Nu, and their struggles for good in a world threatened by darkness yet filled with hope in every corner. Perhaps Xianjian 6 does not reach the heights achieved by some of its predecessors, but it provides a lovingly crafted narrative comprised of a memorable cast of characters and an intricately written world that evokes a sense of nostalgia of youthful dreams of heroism in longtime fans as well as appeals to new players looking for a fresh gaming experience with traditional storytelling.
While it resembles previous games of the series in most respects, Xianjian 6 also diverges greatly in some aspects.
The combat system of this game is drastically different from all other titles in the series, in that it is real-time rather than turn-based (the format the Chinese RPGs, including the Xianjian series, have followed for decades), and the transition is rough. The combat pacing feels off somehow and execution of actions seem disjointed and hectic, with a camera that is prone to display suboptimal angles (though the "camera" for story cutscenes is always expertly operated). I still prefer the individual speed-based combat system that has one character take action at a time that clearly displays move order on a bar and features casting times and knockback effects, which also involve strategic planning instead of a scramble to input commands before it's too late.
The absence of 2D character portraits during dialogues and cutscenes is also glaring, and follows the precedent set by Xuan-Yuan Sword 6 and the transition to the Unity Engine. I feel that the 3D facial expressions and character model animations are adequate, but not satisfactory replacements for the highly expressive and stylish character portrait art players of the series have gotten used to. Hopefully this will improve by the next game.
Speaking of 3D, the overall graphical quality of the game isn't ideal, and the aesthetics of the environments in-game often do not meet the potentials of their original designs. Certain textures can get gnarly up close, and the game looks slightly more dim than necessary. While the addition of the jumping function (this can use some better animations) expands the vertical exploration elements of the game, it also brings about funky physics and collision-related issues occasionally. Personally, I think that Softstar's strong suit is 2D art, and graphic styles such as those of games like Xianjian 2 and Xuan-Yuan Sword 3: The Scar of the Sky would still find popularity nowadays. The 2D animated cutscenes in place of prerendered 3D animations are also a dramatic departure from series norms, and have their positives and negatives that I won't comment on here. Hopefully, the developers can realize their artistic visions with more experience and skill with future releases.
Plot is where this game truly shines and delivers, with complex webs of relations and events all connecting to lead to a touching and fulfilling conclusion. From the cunning and devoted Yue Jinzhao, the repressed and innocent Yue Qi, the honorable and naive Luo Zhaoyan, the shrewd and laid-back Xianqing, and the conflicted and emotional Ming Xiu, to the meek and aspiring Ju Shifang, all of the main characters will connect with the player in one way or another by the end of the story, and the plethora of supporting characters and places to visit breathe life into the game's fictional setting. The voice acting is top notch for every voiced character, further enhancing the immersive nature of the game.
On the music front, the game does not disappoint, featuring a huge collection of original compositions for cutscenes, battles, explorations segments, etc, as well as four vocal pieces by four different artists. As is always the case with Xianjian games, the soundtrack is used well in the game to support its melancholic scenes and joyous occasions alike, and is superb even on its own. The music playback menu is a neat touch.
The English translation of this release is decent (barring the opening cinematic), but I have noticed that many lines were translated out of context and give off the wrong impressions to the player, which should be addressed.
For its current price, the game provides about 60 hours of content, plus free postgame story DLCs. I highly recommend this game to everyone, despite its flaws. This is not your typical instant gratification kind of game, but a piece of art to be savored at a leisurely pace. It is rare to see a Chinese game of this caliber getting a worldwide release in English, and the success of this game can lead to more to come.

This game seems to be a port from mobile which you should keep in mind when buying it. The graphics are really nice (once you set it to Full HD or higher in the "hidden" settings menu after you start actually playing). And if you have fun ripping on bad dialogue this is another enjoyable part of the game. You also have the choice between different weapons and what parts of ship you upgrade. Weapons and perks are bought with credits which are won through battles and ship systems can be upgraded through skill points which you get by leveling up.
The core gameplay is turnbased combat. In every turn there's a countdown, until it's ended you can do as much as you want so if you're a fast clicker you have an advantage. Every action takes times and has cooldowns. Every ship has the same five systems that allow different actions. If a system is destroyed it's options are unavailable until they are repaired through the reactor system. The hull can't be repaired in combat but will be auto-repaired once the combat is over. Once it reaches zero you loose the battle, when you chose "1 life" at the beginning you end your game here and have to start from the beginning, but if you chose "Normal" you can just retry.
At first the game was frustrating because the first enemy after the tutorial was super hard to beat until I tried to focus on the scanner instead of the weapons, I easily won. So now one could think every ship has his weaknesses and unique specialties. They tried to do that and have your assistant always tell you about it before every battle but you can just ignore everything and win every time by just aiming for the scanner, kill this system and the enemy misses you almost every time. This means no damage on your system his hull and other systems take gradually damage until one turn isn't enough for the enemy to repair everything (which they seem to always try before retaliating).
10/10 would buy again for $.014 to sell trading cards for profit.

This can be a fun and tense game, but the tutorial section and half of the 1st zone REALLY let it down.
You can find 40 minutes of gameplay with commentary here:
StarSmashers is a turn based space combat game. Where you progress through each zone fighting a range of AI starships. So far it has always been 1v1 with the player or AI taking tuns targeting different components of the ship. As I mentioned, when I first played the tutorial I regretted paying for the game, battle with the initial weak ships are uneventful and it is not until half way through the 2nd zone (1st being tutorial) that the game gets interesting.
Where the game shines is the pressure of repairing your ship, targeting components of the enemy ship and taking defensive measures during a very limited turn countdown. Close battles can be very fun, but steamrolling the AI at times has the opposite effect. There is no pause that I found, so you need to finish a section before walking away.
With 5 different components to juggle, 5 weapon types (each with a way to counter or enhance) and the ability to add 2 auxiliary abilities - ship loadout can sometimes matter. I should note that so far I have stuck with the same weapons/abilities, just upgrading them, and have progressed.
The tutorial and second zone took me a bit over an hour to play through, whereas the 3rd zone took me about 35 minutes. It seems the game has 8 zones in total, so I expect about 4 hours of gameplay from this title (depending how often I die).
The game also has 2 game modes - normal - where if you die you can repeat the battle, and 1 life - a semi roguelike - where if you die its game over. This gives it some replay-ability, depending how much you enjoy the initial play through.
The game is easy to play and being able to think and click fast is an advantage, the graphics look nice as its a unity engine game and games where the combat is close can be very fun.
On the downside, the ship explosion animations are simple and the firing animations are repeated. The music - turn it off before you begin. While the menu music is fine, I have found the combat music is short and looped.

Received a friend play code (beta account with six characters) from a friend.
Honestly, this isn't a bad game. It's a very good game, in fact, but I'm giving it a thumbs down.
The reason for that is the unimaginable levels of avarice this game employs. Two weeks to grind for a single hero? THREE Epic grade outfits to pay for just TWO Rare grade ones? Most chests you open contain two portraits and a pose (which, if you don't have, are completely worthless and if you do have, are worth a total of one TENTH of a Rare outfit combined)?
It's sickening.
Gameplay - 9/10
Think about CS:GO without items and top-down, or DotA2 without items and levels and everything is a skillshot and no creeps or towers.
It's a really fun game.
Sadly, I have to take a point off, because there's too many people AFK and not enough done about them. This holds especially true in the Brawl game type, which I've not had a single match to date that did not involve at least one (if not more) player being AFK for the entirety of the match.
Balancing - 7/10
This game is blind picking, with the only two guarantees being you don't have two of the same hero on the same team and you don't have two supports on the same team.
Not the most complex system, but seeing as some heroes counters others so very well, it feels a little... Lacking in player involvement as to whether or not your climb of the ladder will be slowed by an unfortunate match-up or you'll speed through the ranks unhindered.
It's alright, though. Really not the worst thing that could happen. And matches are at least short, so you don't spend 40+ minutes getting to a late-game you know you can't win.
Model quality - 7/10.
"Rook, what are you eating? What? No, put that down, that's not meat, that's a bag of trash."
Seriously, I've seen better models in Fable 1, and that came out in September 2004 (or September 2005 for the PC version). Even taking Sept 2005, that was almost a dozen years ago.
That said, the maps are passable (though there are very few of them and they are all tiny), and the game is top-down so you'll hardly see the models. Some of them are quite hideous, though.
Music, sounds, effects - 5/10
If I was feeling charitable, then I would describe the sounds as "performing their duty in informing the player of the important skills cast reasonably well."
I don't, though, so I'll say that the music is dreadful and the sound design isn't great either.
Texture quality - 5/10
As a hobbyist game modder, the level of pixelation is painful.
This isn't "stylized", it's just low quality and low effort.
Monetization system - 0/10
The greed and open hatred for people that aren't willing to pay real money is glaring and obvious and just plain unpleasant.
Total: 7/10, because the gameplay is still very fun, despite the unpleasant feeling of the monetization system and the dreadful visuals.
-Sleepy

Amazing smash-like, cheaper and with a great community, many good players willing to help, cool pixel graphics and great music.

Shadow Warrior took me by surprise and completely blew me away.
Excellent visuals, amazing & visceral combat.
The sword play is the real strong suit in this title, it's probably the best melee has ever been in first person and it's incredibly satisfying to chop enemies into pieces.
The guns tend to be left forgotten because of this, but the rest of the arsenal does hold it's own.
The story and voice acting is surprisingly good, with large amounts of crude humor.
There's also a good tale to be told and they did a good job combining the laughs with the more serious tones.
It combines new and old in a great fashion.
With skillpoints, weapon upgrades and powers gained by progression yet maintaining the arcade style combat and leveldesign.
There are a couple of bossfights, which are pretty middle of the road. The bosses look amazing but they tend to overstay their welcome and the battles drag out for too long. This is especially true on the higher difficulties.
It's a great reimagining of a classic title and I wholeheartedly recommend picking this up if you enjoy the faster First person shooter titles of the days of old.
Flying Wild Hog has done an excellent job with this one.
Shadow Warrior has proven to truly belong alongside the greats of the genre.

If a slightly more than casual co-op hack 'n' slash set in Middle Earth sounds appealing, then you should buy LOTRTWITN.  (fun acronym, innit?)  If you want something deeper to play by yourself, then you will probably want to look elsewhere.
War in the North is essentially Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance set in Tolkien's universe. By that, I mean you and your AI/co-op partners will hack, combo, loot and sever your way through several chapters of ... who cares.  While the setpieces are faithfully drawn from Peter Jackson's LotR films, the story itself is not that important. Heroes will triumph in the face of seemingly insurmountable odds, and bad guys will deliver gutteral dialogue through the rugged steel spikes of their helmets. If nothing else can be said for the story, it at least gives the eagles an excuse for not simply flying Frodo to Mt. Doom to begin with. (not a specific spoiler, but yes -- there are eagles)
Combat involves stringing combos together and landing stronger attacks when enemies are critical. In a way, that system reminds me of the original Witcher.  (tho very basic)  Leveling up gets you three attribute points and one to invest in skills.  Diabloesque ability trees allow you to play as you desire (to an extent), though melee combat remains relevant for every class. Further Diablo inspiration can be seen in the item "sets" you can combine for cumulative stat bonuses. All three classes have their own gameplay styles and the ability to discover hidden loot. The game is not a simple brawler: some areas and boss fights will require more than button-mashing and spamming skills. For tough foes that can knock you down, the dodge/roll ability is your friend.
Presentation-wise, this game is behind the times. It runs on a souped-up version of a 2001 engine. While Snowblind has added some flourishes to remain relevant, it looks more like an early 360 era ('06) game than something released in 2011. The bland (but passable) visuals hold close enough to the film's art design. Just don't expect anything to write home about. We encountered a few frustrating glitches while playing, but they did not repeat. 360 controller support makes this a nice game to play from a couch, but the keyboard & mouse work fine for those used to already doing so.
General sound design seems fine and supports my 5.1 system, but there seems to be an unresolved issue where the game has a permanently open mic in multiplayer. (so you hear quiet echoes if there's speaking in the room) The music ranges from fine to slightly distracting. I don't know whether it was a licensing issue or creative decision to forgo the musical scoring of the films, but it might have helped give the game a grander feel.
Like many co-op titles, it's best played with friends to be experienced at its fullest potential.  If you have to fly solo, you may find this to be a disappointing experience. Either way, I'd say it's best purchased at sale price.
