The Last Remnant is the best 3D turn based RPG to hit the PC for ages. The union system allows you to control groups of characters by issuing a single command and while it might seem simplistic, the way you arrange your groups and what abilities you select for each character to use in combat makes it much more interesting, and the way your characters evolution isn't directly decided by the player, but rather managed by what you do makes it very immersive. As the player, you will need to pay attention to what a character's actions are in order for them to become stronger. Also the boss fights can resemble alot what an MMORPG boss fight is like, as you should assemble specific groups of characters, such as a group of healers and a tanking group, and getting the right characters to fill in these roles isn't as simple as to pick them up in a store, the player needs to develop the characters in a specific way if they are to become a specific member of the group, as you can't just put anyone doing anything.
The story is interesting enough to keep you going, having it's ups and downs, and the side quests are a nice break and chance to make your characters stronger.
The letdowns are how the item gathering system works, as it isn't always clear where you can get the items you need to craft or upgrade your characters, but a great wiki is present at
which has all the information you will need to help you with this. The main character is simple minded, childish and might not be your prefered one, but he's flexible enough to become strong in anything, so you'll find him useful.
This being said, the game is a great chance for people who have been wanting a deep, fun and challenging turn based RPG, specially on the PC who hasn't had anything like this in a long time.

To preface: I am not an avid fan of the FPS genre.  I can enjoy games when they are well made, but the mechanics of FPS games do not inherently have much appeal to me.
Its really hard to say much about this game.  I'm sure it was an amazing title when it came out but it doesn't age well because the story is thin and not fleshed out.  As such it ends up as just another shooter, maybe a little less boring than the others.
Performance in this game suffers hard.  On my 6850 HD / 2.8ghz *6 / 12GB system on a mix of High/Med visuals the game NEVER got above 35FPS if any action or foliage was on screen.  In the end part of the game impossible slowdown would occur, causing frame dips into the single digits.  Even reducing resolution and graphics options did not remedy this, although some persistence and restarting the game several times helped make it through.  The game did not throw event triggers properly at least four or five times in my playthrough, requiring reloading of earlier saves.  Physics interactions were also problematic, making slowdown from colliding objects and leading to vehicles becoming inescapably stuck.  The graphics quality does seem alright, but since none of the environments have any artistic influence or design aside from the alien area its mostly wasted.
Gameplay does not stray far from the formula, but that is to be expected of AAA games.  Its more or less the same formula as Far Cry down to the letter, with the addition of a stamina meter that also serves as regenerating shield and cloak.  Everything is the same.  Stealth isn't meaningful, the open environments are still actually linear, enemies spot you from a bit farther away than is reasonable (better than far cry at least) and have horrible pathing and AI.  Gun variety is par for the course and more or less feels fine.  Vehicles are still overpowered for their mounted guns, and enemies with mounted guns are still problematic.  Environments are all generic jungle up until the end of the game.  The characters are all stereotypes and completely lack depth.
The game's story is intentionally incomplete, doesn't cohere well, and cuts short at the end in a sequel hook so painful it almost feels insulting.  You have a few moments that don't really mesh.  Enemy nano-suit wearers ambush you once but never appear again.  You have to perform a pseudo escort mission for an ally presumed dead after escaping some aliens and then he just bails for the sequel hook.  The koreans just exist as convenient foreigners for you to shoot at until the aliens appear.  I don't think its strange to want story in an FPS or any other game, but its a different kind of appeal I guess between Deus Ex or Bioshock Infinite or Fallout NV and something more arcadey like this.  Far Cry 1 dragged on forever with its pacing over 15 hours and this game just suddenly ends with no resolution after 10 hours.
There's... nothing special about this game.  Its just solid enough to not be terrible and looks alright.  You're better off spending your money elsewhere, certainly not worth the $20 being asked for today.  No reason to not wait for a sale if you're going to bother at all.

Best shooter of the last 10 years. Not because of all the things it has but for all the things it takes away. Shadow Warrior has all the makings of something totally gratuitous. And if all you do is scratch the surface, that's what you think it is. But instead, it challenges you all the way and makes you feel small and helpless. Usually in these kind of games, the difficulty is up front and when you level up enough, you'll just cheese through the rest. And the story is loaded up front for the lazy release reviews.
In Shadow Warrior, I can guarantee you that the greatest challenges come in the end, when you think you've a grip on all the skills and weapons and your movement. But then the game will squeeze you just that much harder to make you truly master everything. If you take something for granted, the game will take it away and throw you a challenge harder than you've ever faced before. And for the first third of the game, the story hasn't even started yet.
What a masterpiece.

Your playable characters are grouped into parties that will be affected in different ways depending on who is in it. What affects the group? In general, the type of combat preference your characters have, the formation you have the group in (You'll see soon enough in the game once you can recruit multiple members into your parties), and finally how many people are in a party. You can have multiple parties.
Speaking of the story specifically, it is well written, but is by no means a master piece, but as I had said, the story the game brings is fulfulling and is more than enough to please you.
Gameplay specifically, as I had previously mentioned, this game starts out slow and somewhat hard. Grinding is not exactly mandatory in this game, but is somewhat appreciated if you refuse to fight boss battles over and over. The game really wants boss battles in this game to live up to it's name. And in the beginning of the game, boss battles are excepionally harder than most fights you will encounter.
Also, a REALLY IMPORTANT note to make, all boss battles are preceded by a cutscene of varying length, usually more than a minute or more in length. This is important to mention because CUTSCENES ARE UNSKIPPABLE, meaning that if you fail a boss battle, you will have to suffer watching the same cutscene over and over. Hence, grinding is somewhat a real recommendation early on in the game. If you are finding yourself in this loop of a boss battle failing, I reccomend going back and grinding a level or two and consider upgrading your equipment and changing your parties' formations. Also, shift tab is reccomended if you can't stand the cutscenes. This is probably the only problem you will have with this game.
^Tl;dr: Grind if you hate time passing you by without making progress.
Also, another note worth mentioning is that this game has a New Game+, which means that after you beat the game, you can play through it again retaining all your arts you learned as well as components you use to make items in the game.
Although if you plan to play New Game+, you should SPLIT ALL UNNEEDED ITEMS before the final boss. You lose everything in material things but components, you even lose your gold.
*Any gold you get in New Game+'s start is based on how many quests you did.
Although, a perfect thing to be mentioned is that this game might not be for everyone. But with everything in mind, this game is by all means a decent thing to buy, especially consideing its low cost on steam.
*Can skip cutscenes with an xbox controller, only
Also, a note worth mentioning, this game is fully xbox controller compatible, and the game is automatically set to think you are playing with an xbox controller.
Change the controls first thing you get into the game, unless you want to be forced to by invonvenience

I like Magic: The Gathering (I played it constantly from 1994-2003, and then off and on since then) but I did not have fun playing this game.  Here are the main issues:
Just playing through the story mode to get gold for more boosters was frustrating.  After the first set, you are pitted against decks that are better than yours, and you can actually lose incredibly simple matches with very simple decks just because you do not draw as well as the AI.  Your deck's power in incredibly inconsistent because they are poorly designed, slow, and rely on cards you just won't see some games. It is not fun to very slowly lose a game of Magic because you are playing a very weak deck against a slightly stronger deck that randomly drew better cards.  It’s mind-boggling that they would design the initial scenarios that make up the first few hours of gameplay so poorly.
The actual card game simulation (the way you control your cards) is extremely mediocre and annoying--I've definitely played several that were better.  The game is constantly pointing at cards you can play (literally every turn there is a big red arrow pointing to one of the lands you can play).  While you are playing through the first set of story missions, you are constantly being pulled out of the game to play through a simulation explaining some basic game mechanic.
There is a stop button you have a few seconds to hit in order to respond to things but when you have to click it is extremely unintuitive and just generally annoying, especially when you want to do something at the end of your opponent's turn and it skips the second main phase entirely.  Basically, the game alternates between going painfully slow and barely giving you a chance to respond.  I’m sure you could get used to (and even appreciate) the fast parts eventually, but early on they’re a pain and the slow parts will likely only get worse.
The way you are started out in this game is extremely frustrating and the interface is consistently annoying.  At the time of the launch, there have also been problems with disconnects causing you to not get credit for games you won.  Magic is fundamentally a fun game, so obviously these problems could be fixed, but at this time the game will just annoy you, especially if you are a fan of the core game.

I reccomend this game with heavy reservations.
Having dumped 40+ hours in it, I'd say it definitely is still fun.
I had such a hardon for this game, but I was pretty disappointed in the end. The AI is terrible, I played normal in a massive Domination match, and was never attacked even though I played very aggressively and constantly spat in the face of my opposition, allowing me to slowly plow over the massive map over the course of 600 or so turns with little-to-no retaliation. Even mass-scale assaults were met with maybe 1-2 gun ships buzzing my infantry before being shot down.
The spy system is a bit more advanced the previous ones, but it's the only thing the AI is good at countering, making it almost useless, but I haven't played it against a live person.
The aliens, after you upgrade your infantry to level 3, aren't at all a threat, making clearing them a very, very easy task using a single of the mid-to-late game infantry to plow through them. Though, near the start of the game, the aliens can make expansion and resource aquisition extremely difficult, adding to the fun.
In Civ 5, the barbarians leveled with you, making you constantly need to contend with them in heavier force than they had, but the aliens stay a measely 8-16 strength, and you'll have building defences that prevent combat altogether. The Seige worms (equal to a mid-level unit) are either far too aggressive early on, or not at all, leading to a quick death or a slight irritant.
I enjoy the difference in technology routes, using Xenos as allies through Harmony, staying "pure" to humans, or going the cyborg/robot route, and the units aesthetics reflecting as such, but it doesn't really affect gameplay much, the individual perks barely changing between the three factions, as they're all more-or-less the same in combat, save for slight differences in mobility, which play much less of a role in combat than you'd think.
The starting of the game can be an uphill battle, but once you're at the top, it's far too easy and smooth, even on higher difficulties.
But, with some more expansions or mods, I feel this game will be one of the best Civs yet.
Buy it if you've got the money, but I'd reccomend waiting.

A highly addictive game with plenty of room for improvment.
After several days of gameplay you come to see that this isnt just another civ game, there are subtle differences such as aliens instead of barbarians that react to how you treat them. More focus on the strategic resources and three visually different worlds to explore.
However you can see that the developers have some future plans, but could have gone further into the realm of scifi to make this game stand out more than previous titles. There is too much focus, I would say, on the strategic resources with plenty of late game units and city buildings requiring a vast quantity of these three rare minerals. Probably some further ballancing required. The tech web is a nice take on a new form of tech tree, you dont need to have each tech on the web to win, you can focus on what your colony does well, but even I, after some time of playing now have a prefered path through the web.
The game to me is more finely tuned to exploration and an attempt to make each game different and allow you to make the most of the landscape or world you are on are quests, of which many allow you to make slight adjustments to your city buildings to give them some extra resouces.
Dissapointment comes from some minor areas, few unit choices, theres only one aircraft that you can upgrade through the game to suit your needs, but this aircraft is a combined bomber and fighter. The same aliens no matter what 'biome' you see. An AI that can be a little too predictable with diplomacy that doesnt go as far as some fans would like.
Dont get me wrong, I am an Alpha Centauri fan boy but like I have already said, this game had a lot of room for improvement, and the obvious holes are probably going to be patched with DLC or future expansion packs.
Personally I would like to see more diplomacy options, further work on the randomness of the worlds, maybe more alien types each with a slight difference. More choice of units away from the generalised one for all options units. A deeper look into espionage, a couple of more factions as not to have the repeated leaders each time.
For now, this is a great game and one I have been looking forward to since the release of Alpha Centauri. Im actually glad this isnt a clone but rather a close cousin to the game.
Highly recomended and I look forward to what the devs come up with for the future.

So finally they've translated Chinese Paladin 6: Sword and Fairy into English and released it on Steam after 2 years of waiting, with “C-RPGs (Chinese RPGs)” further discussed in the discussions. Honestly there are a number of minor flaws and bugs but it's still bearable. The translation for the 2D opening cinematic is a disaster but the rest of the game is coherent.
There are a large number of cutscenes at the beginning, which may seem boring. However, as I invested more time in the storyline, I found it fascinating and thought-provoking. Nobody is fighting for justice or something like that, and everybody has his or her own goal or ideal. In this version, I found the subtitles sometimes disappear too quickly and the words are just so small. Hope there’s a way to fix it.

The battle system is a little hard for me at the beginning. It’s even hard to beat Yue Jinzhao and Yue Qi in the first battle in the original version. Fortunately the devs did some adjustments in values and the battle experience became smoother than before. If you played FF13 before, you may find the battle system of CP6’s similar to it, but unfortunately, less friendly. Guess they would add controller support later. P.S.: the meridian system is a special system with mysterious Chinese characteristics.

An excellent stealth game from an established series, Absolution made me enjoy the arts of assassination immensely. The tone of the game is slightly different this time, with 47 being on the run from his agency, though the plot isn't particularly interesting or engaging. What it does do is serve as a device to push Agent 47 to some great locations to ply his craft and sneaking through a level to eliminate a target is both familiar and wonderfully realised.
The objectives through each level are hardly revolutionary; get to target, kill target, escape. The pleasure is in the execution, with several different methods of accomplishing each objective. From a mysterious accident, to a poisoned drink, the signature garrotte and more, 47 has a vast array of lethal options at his disposal. You could even go in all guns blazing of you want, though I wouldn't recommend it; the shooting mechanics leave much to be desired; stealth is the focus here.
There are various methods of infiltration, many of which depend on the level. The most obvious options are either via the traditional stealth method, or by using disguises. Unfortunately both of these mechanics leave much to be desired. The stealth option has far too few actions available and consists of being able to crouch behind cover, move on ledges and hide bodies. Similarly, the disguise system is virtually useless as people wearing the same uniform can see through it, rendering the whole thing pointless in most settings.
The layout makes up for things a little and I ended up ignoring the disguises for the most part, preferring to sneak through the excellently set out areas. The level designs are fantastic, from bustling stations to the arid south.
I was genuinely impressed with just how atmospheric the various setting were, even if the strip-club that now seems mandatory in “mature” games felt gratuitous and contrived. I also loved the dry humour present throughout the game. It’s subtle, only really there if you look for it, but I found it hilarious.
The new engine really shines in-game and it looks truly impressive at every step. Areas look simply stunning with excellent lighting, textures and attention to detail. The Chinatown level is particularly impressive, with a staggering amount of NPCs present, each moving independently, that really gives a feeling of stalking your prey through a busy city.
I’ve noticed that truly great stealth games are incredibly rare these days, and I can’t remember the last game that actually demanded patience, thought and exploration. Absolution most certainly has the latter under its belt and whilst it wouldn’t be unfair to say that my recommendation is partly based on the lack of competition, it’s still highly enjoyable and I’d definitely recommend it.
It’s not going to be a classic, but it’s good enough for stealth fans.

Great game if you like battle arena games. Rounds last up to 3 minutes (best of 3, so max ~15 minutes per match).
It's pretty much like League of Legends / DotA; minus the item shop, lanes/turrets, mobs/jungle. Clasically played 2v2 or 3v3 no respawns.

There's a relatively high learning curve when it comes to positioning, awareness (picking targets) and landing skillshots though. But that's never been a bad thing right?
Chests work like in Overwatch, 3 items per chest with 1 guaranteed rare (common-rare-epic-legendary), though there are some chests that have like a guaranteed epic, or even a guaranteed legendary. Any duplicate items you get from chests, you'll get tokens for which you can use to buy an outfit or weapon of your choice. Chests you buy with coins you get from doing your dailies or just playing matches.
Go and get it, if you want all the champions unlocked right away... Or wait a few more months until it releases Free To Play, though you will have a hard time unlocking battlerites as they are quite pricely and you will miss out on buying chests

Lord of the Rings: War in the North is in my opinion a great game.  While the story isn't exactly intriguing and the dialogue can get a bit stale, it has lots of action combined with RPG elements.
Pros:
1: Great coop
This game is absolutely designed for coop.  With three different characters, each with their own abilities and classes, this is a VERY fun game to play with friends.
2: RPG elements
The RPG elements in this game, while not nearly as serious as something like WoW, adds an extra layer of fun to the game.  It gives you incentive to explore and complete sidequests.  You can equip different armor and weapons, and while some of them look the same, I was impressed with the diversity of the appearances of the gear.  There are class exclusive weapons and armor, which you can either sell, or give to your friends to help them out.  The sidequests are quite creative, which is very unique in a game these days.  It's not the standard, kill this many enemies, gather this many herbs.
3: Combat
The combat in this game is very fun at first.  Now, it can get a bit stale and repetitive later on.  But by switching characters, you can alter your whole playstyle.
Cons:
1: Price
While this game is great, it is definitely not worth $20.  I would suggest waiting till a sale to get this game.
2: Story
The story in this game is, well, not great.  While it makes sense and ties in to the books/movies, it just doesn't capture that middle earth feeling.
3: Voice acting
Enough said, right?  The voice acting for the main three characters and some of the secondary characters in this game is just fine.  It's when you come to the characters that were in the books, or more specifically, the movies, that it starts to get a little dicey.  While I can understand not being able to hire the actors, the voices sound completely different.  I feel they aren't even trying to sound like they do in the movies.
Overall, I highly recommend this game.  As for bugs and glitches, I haven't come across a single one in my whole time playing.

I just finished my first playthrough, somehow managing to survive the war with all 3 of my characters, and even recruiting another a week or so into the civil war. The siege of the city lasted 42 days, and in order to survive we had to loot hospitals, steal from the military, trade with our neighbours, run through sniper gunfire, all while trying to maintain our sanity.
My first playthrough of the game lasted 42 in-game days, which equated to just short of 16 real life hours. This is one of the few games that I've actually paid full price for, but after reading a couple of reviews (yet trying to avoid any gameplay videos), I decided I couldn't wait for a sale, and I have to say it was worth every penny.
The gameplay is relatively simple, and everything is controlled simply through mouseclicks, you have limited resources and limited time, and you have to somehow make the most of your situation. Should you spend the daylight hours crafting new equipment for your next scavenge, or spend it napping to recuperate? Two members of your party have gunshot wounds, yet you only have one medical kit, who do you give it to? Your food has just been stolen, and you're on the verge of starvation, do you steal another group's food in order for yours to survive?
I lucked out and had a fireman as part of my starting group, who made an expert scavenger (carrying 15 items). He was my go-to man for night time. Then I had a chef and a fast runner, who spent most of the time alternating shifts between guarding at night and resting. A few days into the siege, a young girl, a musical school graduate, came looking for help, and we took her in. Her joining us allowed the group to have 2 guards at night for security, and while they slept during the day to recuperate, she was able to do the menial chores such as collecting water, crafting, and so on, without interrupting their sleep, at the cost of an extra meal per day.
There were many times in my playthrough where I had to resort to less than humane tactics in order to survive, and often my group was on the verge of death, only saved my the local trademan stopping by in the nick of time to trade food and medicine for a stash of diamonds I was rewarded for saving a man.
You do become attached to your characters, especially when you have to decide who is going to get the last medkit, weighing the advantages and disadvantages of your decision. One thing I didn't realise until far too late was the flashing 'bio' in the corner of the character portrait, which gave helpful insight into your characters' thoughts. I don't know how much they effect gameplay, but they give you a glimpse into the mind of the character. One became so depressed at the sight of his friends wounds, that he remarked in his biography that he would be willing to do anything to get medical equipment. I'm not sure if it does, but if that transferred into the gameplay (reduced morale hit for stealing medical supplies, for example), it would be amazing. It may already work like that, I'm not sure, either way it's a nice touch.
There are a couple of improvements I could see being made; One, is having some kind of randomised safehouse. (different room layouts, different numbers of holes in the walls (which you need to board up to lessen risks of raids), etc. It would also be great to see some strategy being put into the layout, and where you place certain items. Putting your fireplace near beds for warmth, placing armchairs around each other for a morale boost as characters can discuss things while resting, rainwater catchment near the holes in the walls (possibly a choice, safety by boarding them up, or free water by leaving them open and collecting fresh water), and so on. These are only suggestions, the game itself is great as it stands, especially for a new, independent developer.

Experience has usually left me very cautious whenever I see a licensed videogame, particularly when it’s tied in to a film franchise. It seems that virtually every blockbuster in the past 20 years has had an awful accompanying game aimed at cashing in on the hype surrounding the name. I’ve usually felt differently about the Lord of the Rings games because they’ve been pretty good (the tie-ins on the original Xbox were actually pretty great) so I approached this one with rather less cynicism than I’d usually reserve.
It’s immediately obvious that this isn’t a high quality, high budget title. The cast impersonators are the first clue and every member of the original cast that appears in the game has an actor that sounds not-quite like what we’re used to hearing. The crude visuals, basic soundtrack and the sense that they’ve hired one voice actor to cover every other NPC were a little disappointing, though not enough to be off-putting.
So, yet another 3rd person hack ‘n’ slash, this one with the most basic of plots; “that guy is Sauron’s mate, let’s kill him”. Obviously, being a mate of Sauron he’s quite powerful and has many orcs between him and your party, so you’ve got to kill them off first. The plot is as simple as that. On the way you encounter some of the characters shown in the films, as well as some only mentioned in the books, (minor spoilers, though it’s not like the story here is that important!)
Levels are very simple, with three or four stages to each level and a peaceful base every few levels where you can return to repair, buy and sell items and turn in quests at occasional checkpoints. You won’t spend very long there though; the main part of the game is either chopping up orcs or running towards the next lot of orcs to chop up.
Gameplay is very repetitive and, though the combat is very functional, it gets quite dull as you go from one stage to the next doing the same bloody thing over and over. Combat is quite a standard affair, with standard fast and heavy attacks melee attacks, a ranged attack and the options to block and dodge. The controls are functional and work well enough, but everything feels quite floaty and a little detached. Each character has unique abilities that can be unlocked and upgraded as the character levels up, most of which are pretty cool to execute. The problem is in how repetitive it becomes as you take on endless hordes of a very unvaried enemy. I often compare these types of games to God of War, but there’s a reason for that; in those games, there are dozens of various attack types and there’s a huge variety of enemy types, all of which require different tactics to combat. In this case, War in The North has 4 basic enemy types – a melee guy, a ranged guy, a sorcerer and a troll. Sure, there are technically more, with goblins, Uruk Hai and so on, but all they really are is the same thing with better stats – which doesn’t mean anything as they are only encountered later in the game when your own stats have also grown massively. This effectively means that you’re fighting the same group of things in a sequence of different rooms for the entire campaign, broken up by the occasional mediocre boss battle and combat is broken down to a sequence of dodge, attack, dodge, special attack for the entire campaign. Not exactly Ride to Hell, but hardly a prize winning game either.
Visually the game plays it safe, using the same design aesthetic as in the films, although without any of the grand scenery or set pieces that I loved about the trilogy. The settings are familiar and just a little bland, but it does the job. It’s in the graphics that the game shows its limitations, especially in the resolution and framerate. This game looks like a last-gen console port and even running at 1080p it doesn’t look like it’s in HD. Framerate is similar, even though FRAPS showed it running at a solid 60fps it certainly didn’t look like anything approaching that, in fact it felt like 20. I don’t know why everything looked so poor, or why the framerate randomly dropped to 2fps for a few seconds at random, or why the last level is so glitched you have to reinstall 2 year old drivers for your GPU to run the sodding thing, but it’s very poor form and quite infuriating. That these issues haven’t been patched, despite the forums being flooded with various technical issues, is pretty disgraceful.
War in the North is one of those licensed games that get a recommendation because it’s “good enough”. If, like me, you’re a fan of The Lord of the Rings, you’ll probably enjoy going toe-to-toe with a horde of orcs and just being in Middle Earth. The game almost loses my recommendation due to the technical issues and game breaking bugs and if you don’t want to♥♥♥♥♥♥about fixing it yourself then I’d advise you to steer well clear. If you’re fine with that, it’s a pretty decent distraction for a few hours.
It’s a good enough game; quite repetitive, and pretty average combat, but it’s a good amount of fun carving through a mass of orcs.

This War of Mine has an interesting take on survival games by putting the player not against zombies, or the wilderniss, but against human nature. You begin with three survivors in a city under siege during a civil war, supplies are running low and they just arrived at an abandonned building. This will be their holdout for the war.
You will then manage their daily lives, making workbenches, chairs, beds, and everything else they need to get through the war. Of course, with supplies low, you need to prioritise. Do you really need a second bed? Maybe that material can best be spend on something else..
At night, you go out to scavenge supplies. You bring one (Only one per night) of your survivors to a location that you hope has supplies you can use. Once there, you can encounter many things. It could be an abandonned building with nothing there. There could be a friendly (But well armed) trader, there could be civilians like you just trying to survive, or you could be shot on sight by the locals. Or there can be any other event... Or nothing. There is plenty of variation to be had.
Personally, I went to a church, unarmed, as I had nothing yet. The priest told me about how the place was robbed, and asked me not to disturb the refugees under the church. So I went on to the ruined building behind the church. Scavenging up supplies, when I notice there's sound outside the door. It's just standing there, so I creep to the door and look through the keyhole. Just then, a man with a pistol turned around and made for the door. I looked for a place to run and hide and set off, just as he opened the door.
"Oh, Hello there. Don't worry, I'm just looking around"
He seemed pretty friendly. So I just went on my way to pick out some more nails and wood for my own business. It went alright this time. But plenty of people are less friendly than this guy.
Combat, which you will at some point get into, is not explained in any way. So you will likely have to take a bit to learn about it, and stock up on bandages as you do so. At the same time, the stealth system is not explained, but easy enough to understand.
With all this, you are tasked with making your group survive the war. Or at least as long as you can. It can be easy, challenging, or at times nearly impossible. But that's war, and neither the government nor the rebel forces will help you there - You're not their problem.
And once you've gone through the game, you can ask yourself if you really did win. Did you end up stealing from old people to let them starve? Did you rob a priest for fuel? Shanked a doctor for a bandage? You can ask yourself what winning really means in war. And if just surviving is all you should try to do.

THE BELOW REVIEW IS MY ORIGINAL REVIEW, WRITTEN SHORTLY AFTER RELEASE - IT IS NO LONGER MY OPINION OF THIS GAME.
My review has little to do with the bugs in the game - I don't believe bugs should influence the rating of any game in this current generation as they all have them to varying degress and to be honest, I have not experienced the poor performance and all the other bugs people are pointing out - bugs get frixed.   However..........  here's my story and why I rated this game what I did.
I was waiting for this game for what seemed like an eternity, and I was so psyched on the release date... eagerly waiting for the end of my work day so I could jump headfirst back into X.  despite the poor design choices I had heard about - I was still eager to throw myself back into the X universe and exerperience the next evolution of this wonderful series.   I pre-ordered it - this was the first time I truly felt like an idiot for pre-ordering a game that didn't meet my expectations.  Let me explain -
I loved the previous X games, I love the universe and I love the complexity of the enormous sandbox wolrd filled with racial tension, econimic struggles between major corporations, and yes, I even loved the plot.  X3 is a true masterpiece, a work of art,  and despite what the critics say, I did not find the releases past X3: Reunion  to be all that hard to navigate.  The Menu's were not that confusing - I find that people today lack the patience and attention span to pay attention and scan what is in front of them a little before becoming intimidated - the only reason it was intimidating is the sheer number of things you could do and the massive amount of data placed before you.   These are, once you give the games a little while, what you come to love about it.   This is what X was all about.
The boasts that Rebirth would improve upon what you loved about the previous games and streamline it, making it accessable to everyone turned out to be game crippling design choices and do not achieve that which they set out to do.  The menu navigation is more convoluted and time consuming than in any of the previous games, and the information provided to you about "your empire" is far too simplistic to actually allow you to do the things you play an X game to do - that being, whatever you want.  Even simple tasks like trade are a huge chore and it feels more like a job than a game.  Games should not feel like work, I play games to escape from my daily life and live in a universe where I don't HAVE to work.   Rebirth robs hardcore X fans of what they wanted the most and alienates them, while offering the newcomers a sub-par experience at best.  I honestly cannot fathom how the current methodry makes this game more accessible than the previous - I have had a hard time doing ANYTHING in this game and that's a huge let-down bgecause the universe looks simply amazing and I would love to get to the point where I have a fleet of capital ships and fighters going to war with (insert faction/corporation here) - but I honestly do not see myself getting to that point - ever.
I cannot stress enough how much of a disappointment this is - because the game boasts such an impressive uinverse and such depth - it waves it in front of your face, teasing you like a dog with a treat - and then retracts its hands, not giving you that treat you oh-so desire, due to your own inability in-game to get the game to function on such basic levels as to be able to complete a simple, early-game trade mission.    I'm not going to get into the specifics here as you can just go vsiit the forums and read all about these shortcomings and no-doubt the mission I'm referring to in numerous posts.
I can only hope Egosoft does some very serious re-thinking in terms of the design of this game - because as it is, it is quite literally impossible to form a great trade empire and change this seemingly great universe, and bend it to your will, as I have done and thoroughly enjoyed in the previous games in the series.  But the real question in my mind is, can they even patch such fundamental design flaws?  ... as well known as egosoft is for listening to fans and fixing their mistakes, the core of this game seems broken and if you add to that, that you are limited to piloting one single ship as opposed to the massive amount of choices you had in the previous games, I can't help but view it as a step, or perhaps a lot of steps back from their previous installments.
The entire design from the resource management to the gameplay leads me to the assumption that Egosoft were  trying to reach out to the console crowd, becuase this game seems highly tailored for console game play and every single function within is based around using a gamepad to play - sorry, maybe I'm stubborn but a control pad will never be as precise as a mouse and keyboard, nor will it ever offer the customization and flexibility.   I play PC games for a reason - and only a select few games are truly better with a gamepad.   Simulations are not one of these.   I can honestly say I unfortunately never get to experience this seemingly wonderful universe becuase I will never be able to get past the clunky, hard to manage core features of this game.
I'm honestly insulted by this title and I feel betrayed by one of the few gaming companies I stood behind.  They not only alienated their fanbase, they did a mediocre job attracting their new target crowd.   I wish I could say something better about this because I've wanted it for a very long time, but I can't detect a redeeming factor in sight.   Graphics are not enough, guys.... and a sandbox should offer freedom, not just let you know it's there and deny access to it.
I do not recommend paying for this game until egosoft does some SERIOUS patching, if it's even possible at this point - I could get into more and more negatives and make this review pages long, but it's nothing you can't find spending 4 minutes in some forum and repeating it is almost as tedious as the game itself.     At most, I'll keep my eye out for any real improvements but until that fateful day I guess I'll just keep playing Terran Conflict and Albion Prelude.
Egosoft will never get a pre-order from me again, even if they manage to live this one down and remain a game developer.  God damn, what a huge bummer, I didn't expect such a drastic failure....   enjoy my $50, hopefully you do something constructive with it, Egosoft.  This review is liable to change, if down the road I load up this game and I find they really did do something to make it as playable as the previous installments.... but for now -

This game is amazing! The first thing you need to understand is this game is the fixed version. If you look for reveiws online they all talk about the Xbox and Playstation versions that were all a buggy mess. When they ported to the PC they added in all the content from both consoles and fixed the bugs and glitches.
I recommend using a controller for the game as well (though it does work with keyboard and mouse but I found it more enjoyable/easier for me personally to use a controller). I used an Xbox 360 controller (built-in support for it) and had no issues whatsoever.
The difficulty of the game is counter to almost every other JRPG made. The difficulty increases as you grind and level up so you can technically beat the game at lvl1 faster/easier than at lvl99+. The combat is turn based/auto-resolve where the only control over the fights you have is setting up the units in the groups and telling what style you want the group to fight as (attack/assist/defend/etc).
The game part way in unlocks the ability to slow/freeze time to allow you to "tag" enemies so you can chain groups to increase the drop chance of items and increase the xp you get (bonus for the more enemies you fight at once).
There is a New Game+ ****BUT***** it's not your normal New Game+ Mode. Instead of having all the levels, items and units you unlocked before you start over from scratch with only some things carrying over.
Things that carry over as copied from the wiki article
All components
All formations
All magazines
Your current customization levels
All items that unlock arts for Rush. Rush will also begin the new game with the first art of the skills granted to him by the Orbs and Formulas. For example, carrying over the Evocation-enabling Azure Orb will grant Rush the lowest-ranked Evocation, Mystic Missile, at the start of the game.
Mr. Diggs' skill levels and digs count
All area maps
So when you are close to finishing the game (it'll be pretty clear as you'll be able to craft really good items) DON'T CRAFT ANYTHING AND FINISH THE GAME IF YOU PLAN ON PLAYING NEW GAME+!

I write this review with some tepidation. Let me start by giving my history with the Civ games. Civ5 was my first foray into the series and I enjoyed it for its depth but found it could be rather tiring. I have tried Civ4 but found it was not quite as engaging. I enjoyed Civ5 enough to purchase the DLCs and play it with friends, and found the Concept of Civ:BE to be interesting enough to watch for a sale.
First off: This game is not worth the AAA price. In many ways its obviously built off of Civ5 and the high price it expects for the content is a bit surprising. I would recommend waiting for a sale unless you are truly desperate for more Civ5 style gameplay.
The game is fun, don't get me wrong. There is a difference in focus between Civ5 and Civ:BE. Civ5 focused on advancing forward in ages, which resulted in stronger units and city progress. Civ:BE military progress is tied to Affinity, which is a trio of idealisms based on either Harmony with the alien ecology, Purity of the human settlers, or Supremacy through the use of cybernetics. Certain techs advance your Affinity, allowing unit bonuses that apply to all living or created units.
This is sort of a broad focus, as opposed to Civ5's focus on individual unit advancement. I enjoy Civ:BE's version more. Civ5 allowed two visually similar units to have entirely different abilities and stats, depending on what unit they originally were and their combat experience. In Civ:BE units advance automatically as their tech is unlocked and chosen, with combat experience only adding a small modifier bonus (or it can instead be used as a single-use heal which is, in general, not useful.) This takes some of the micromanagement out of unit advancement and I appreciate that, though I can see it being less appealing to some. My main issue with unit advancement is that is can be rather opaque which unit turns into what. I'm not the best at remembering unit names to begin with.. for instance the basic melee unit, the "Soldier" can advance to the "Marine" regardless of affinity bonus, but then it can become either a "Brawler", "Sentinal", or "Disciple", and then later each of there can become either a "Marauder", "Centurion", or "Apostle" (with various modifiers such as "True" or "Pure" besides!) This led to several situations in which I was trying to build military might and was absolutely flummoxed at what the hell I should build. Is the Ambassador or the Redeemer the current name of my tank? Should I build more Executors or Devastators? This is obviously a surmountable problem fixed by going into the upgrade trees and reading unit descriptions, but its far from transparent and can interupt gameflow, which is a big issue during multiplayer.
Returning to Affinities. This is an interesting mechanic. It allows you to keep advancing militarily while focusing on non-military units. Affinity is mainly gained through the tech tree (which is much less linear than in Civ5) though it is also possible to advance using the quest system (covered below.) Since four of the five victory conditions is related to tech advancement (and 3 of those to Affinity advancement) it makes every tech decision important. Affinity gains are in general tucked into techs with unit-unlocks and broad tile upgrades, instead of wonders of buildings. This means you need to balance the progression of your cities against the progression of your Affinity, since allowing either to flounder could cripple the other.
Another new, and in my mind more interesting addition, is the inclusion of "Quests." Quests take several forms in the game. Some are used as pseudo-tutorial elements which allow you to decide your Affinity and unlock basic bonuses that aid progression early on (an early quest gives you a soldier for building a second colony, for example.) The vast majority of quests relate to the various "Buildings" that can be built in your cities. The usual progression is: Finish a Building, wait several turns, get offered a binary progression option (For Example: Building a fence to keep back aliens unlocks a "Quest" where one can choose to either expand the range of the fence or use the fence tech to protect trade units.) These sort of "Binary Choice" quests allow a certain degree of uniqueness to buildings that is useful in customizing your city to suit your terrain. There is also a sort of "Quest Line" that follows your Affinity development. It gives you bonuses to your chosen Affinity and can be useful but becomes repetitive since there is only a certain number of paths it can take. Sort of a "Chose your own adventure" you are required to play every game.
Now for some of the bad. One of my largest issues with Civ5 was the inability to use Mods in conjunction with Multiplayer. This feature was expected to be a dev priority but has, as far as I can tell, still not been addressed. In general I find the Civ devs rather lacking in upkeeping their software and dealing with issues. As such it was not surprising to me that various bugs are still unfixed even after the game has been out since October. These issues include an annoying issue in which if a sea- or air-unit attack an embarked land unit the attack animation for the attacker will loop what appears to be 8-10 times while the embarked unit sits there dumbly whether it has the ability to retaliate or not. While this happens the player is basically forced to watch and wait, effectively stuck. I can't see HOW this sort of a bug made it past BETA, as this is not an uncommon situation. Another bug related to unit Upgrading, in which the unit upgrade preview will shot multiple overlapping units. This appears to relate to having multiple upgrades on the same turn (which is not surprising since a single Affinity level can unlock multiple upgrades AND getting multiple Affinity levels in a single turn is quite possible.) In general these bugs don't make the game unplayable but they are frequent enough to be frustrating reminders that can interfere with gameflow. As I said above this game is priced like a AAA-title and as such I hold it to a standard where these issues should not exist.
So should you buy it? for $50? I wouldn't recommend it at that price. On sale then? Yes, most assuredly. I am definitely getting $30 worth of enjoyment out of it despite the bugs. We will see how the devs manage this project in the future as well. I am looking forward to DLC (Civ5 had fun DLC though some of the mechanic changes were unexpected), and though I have not explored Mods much yet I deeply wish that we will see the ability to both use Mods AND Multiplayer concurrently with this release.

So... how to describe Shelter? Saying it is unique seems too superficial, and it doesn't do the game credit to be honest. In this modern day and age where the market has been oversaturated with many games that can easily be classified as "mindless run, gun & slash" fastfood entertainment, some developers try something different.
Imagine a hybrid of a Bambi/Lion King animal based story, with a clear Circle of Life theme, spiced with loss, altruism and tragedy and an artistic painted storybook look to it. Art and emotion. That's Shelter.
The game, in all it's simplicity and with its limited length and replay value grabs a hold of you and leaves you in equal measure impressed, feeling uneasy and with renewed insight of how fragile life can be, especially in the Wilds as part of the food chain.
As you see, Shelter can't be defined or categorised easily and both topic, style and gameplay might not be for everyone... BUT what it does, it does very well and I can recommend this small but shiny gem to anyone who's up for experiencing "something different".
In short:
Pros:
- Artistic
- Unique
- Experience a painfully clear Circle of Life story
- Appeals to your emotions and has a psychological impact
- Clings to your thoughts long after you stopped playing
Cons:
- Graphic style isn't "photorealistic", even cartoony, and won't appeal to everyone
- Short
- Simple
- Low replay value
- Controls can be a bit cumbersome

As much as I spent nearly a full year complaining about it while playing through it, I still probably liked it more than any of the others since 8. Aside from the UI being garbage (seriously, it's like a masterclass in Function Follows Form), at least most of the weird or frustrating things in the game come from it trying new and different things which sometimes work and sometimes don't, which is better than it being because they did the same thing as usual, just not very well.
For the first time since the pre-FF7/pre-3D days, the story is actually coherent and makes sense for the most part. I wouldn't go so far as to say that I think it or the writing are great overall, but it avoids the usual degeneration into overwhelming nonsense by the end of the game that usually seems to happen, and it has some of the best character moments in the entire series (which sadly don't really end up going anywhere after they happen).
The combat is pretty interesting at first and fairly different from the other games. It removes a lot of the decision-making from the actual fights themselves and moves it to character/party setup outside of battle. However, once you figure out how it works, almost the entire rest of the game can turn into mostly button mashing "auto-attack" for a few dozen hours. Call me weird, but in terms of Squenix games that take away direct control of your characters, I preferred how The Last Remnant did it because I felt more involved there.
And yes, 90% of the game (aside from the post-game content) is strictly linear. It works and it doesn't. I get why they did it from a storytelling point of view, and that's fine, kind of. As a player though, it's kind of fatiguing playing a game for 60 hours when for almost the entire time you're railroaded through non-stop battles and cutscenes with nothing to break them up. Towns and side quests and random exploration in the other games are as much about giving the player a break and a chance to♥♥♥♥♥♥around as they are about anything else.
I'm mostly glad I played it, but it felt overly long. The mechanics got boring long before the game ended, and the story started to drag after a while and felt like it could've been told in a much shorter time. It did not strike me as something that needed a sequel, much less two.

Bioshock is a First Person Shooter set in the 1960's in a fictional underwater City called Rapture, you play as Jack, a plane crash survivor who ends up outside a mysterious Lighthouse, throughout the game you find yourself facing off against various different enemies like the Splicers who are mutated Humanoids addicted to ADAM and Big Daddies, who's purpose is the protect the Little Sisters.
Throughout Bioshock you are given various tasks by Atlas (Greg Baldwin) and are forced to locate Andre Ryan (Armin Shimerman), your main uses of combat are various Guns and Plasmids (Essentially Magic Powers) which require EVE to use.
Later in the game you are tasked with deciding the fate of the Little Sisters by either Harvesting them or Saving them, Harvesting them nets you the highest possible ADAM, but Saving Them grants you with exclusive benefits that can only be obtained by saving 3 Little Sisters, every 3 Little Sisters gains you a reward and a bonus 200 ADAM, Harvesting Little Sisters grants you 160 ADAM and Saving Them grants you 80 ADAM.
The Little Sister are protected by Big Daddies, Big Daddies are re-purposed Rapture Construction Workers tasked with protecting the Little Sisters while they wander around gathering ADAM from dead Corpses, Big Daddies come with various weapons like the Rivet Gun, heavy drill, rocket launcher, or ion laser, Big Daddies are Neutral and only attack if provoked, either accidentally or on purpose, if you get too close to a Little Sister they will assume an aggressive stance in attempt to scare off the the player, Big Daddies have 3 lights to alert the player of their current mood stance, Yellow is Neutral, Red is Aggressive and Green is Hypnotised.
Bioshock Remastered isn't by any means a "Perfect" port, nor is it a terrible one, as of the writing of this review, it is missing a few essential PC options which Blind Squirrel have stated that there is a patch "On the way".
In my experience I only noticed One texture bug and One crash in the 3 Hours that I played, the mouse was fine, could be better, the FPS was brilliant with no FPS drops.
In conclusion: Bioshock Remastered is less of a Remaster and more of a HD Edition, not enough has been done to it to really call it a Remaster, however it is still worth the £13.99 asking price, Bioshock is truly a great game and is worth playing if you're new to the Franchise.
This review is based upon a free copy of Bioshock Remastered so naturally I couldn't hate on the Remaster, if you haven't bought the game yet, I would personally wait for a few patches to flesh out some bugs before purchasing Bioshock Remastered.

Not a horrible game if you have the patience to get through all of the repetitive levels, but also not a great game.
The art style is what drew me in to this game. I remember playing the demo on the console forever ago and somewhat enjoying it, so I thought I'd try it out while it was on sale. The gameplay is exactly what it looks like in the thumbnails. You spend most of the game beating up enemies with a large array of weapons and magical attacks with different properties.
However, this game is very dumbed down and shallow. The lore and quests are not very deep, and the voice acting is over-done and a bit comical in its style—which can be enjoyable, but is not for everyone. The focus of the game is to beat up monsters inside of ruins, which can be pretty fun if you have the patience to get through the game.
As an RPG, this game lacks many customization options. You have a choice of three types of characters—one of which, the meelee character, is basically obsolete—and an option to have either a pet cat or a pet dog. Other than that, even though there are many items in the game, their properties are ultimately meaningless. The only real stragegy to play the game is to sell old items and buy the most powerful new items. The result is that, even if you spend a lot of time considering how you want to approach the game and saving up money to design specialized weapons to fit your play style, you'll end up cycling through weapons as you progress and your old weapons quickly become obselete. If you play this game, it's best not to put too much thought into your weapons and armor, since they will be replaced by better weapons by the time you make it back to the shop.
The game is not very challenging on any difficulties other than the hardest difficulty, and it doesn't allow you to change your difficulty in a save. However, in this game, difficulty is not exactly something that you want, since this game spawns in the same enemies every time you re-enter a dungeon. Not only this, but the levels are very repetitive and not very meaningful. Each level and boss looks very similar to the last, and you'll end up wishing you could get through the repetitive level design a lot sooner.
If you give the game a little patience and little thought about the meta-game, and can bear the quirky art style, you might enjoy this game, but it can get repetitive and annoying as you go along. I wouldn't recommend this game at the full price (as I got it on sale), but I might recommend it to someone is looking for a simple game that doesn't come from a large franchise that requires a lot of playtime and work to get into.

When reviewing a game, the question isn't whether you had fun. I did have fun playing this game, I even feel like I got my money's worth, but I just couldn't reccomend it at the $20 price point. There are a lot of good games at or below that price (most notably, Saint's Row 3 and 4), that will give you a lot more enjoyment for your dollar than will Gat Out Of Hell. There are three places where this installment just doesn't live up to it's price tag: the length of the game, the features in the game, and the scope of the game.
First, this game is really short. It's not terribly short as DLC goes, but like I said above, there are lots of full games for $20 with significantly more content. I had beaten the story missions in about five hours playing at a liesurely pace, taking time to fly around, getting some collectibles, and doing a few challenges. After about 11 hours I have a 99% completion, with just a few of the annoying challenges to go. Again, for DLC that isn't bad, but in context a game like Saint's Row 4 or Red Faction: Guerilla will last for weeks, and these things are the same price.
Second, this game lacks a lot of the features of previous Saint's Row games. There are no radio stations. There are no physical shops to visit. There are no character costumes or weapon skins. There are no cribs. There is no cell phone to call in support. Calling this game a DLC is a little bit misleading, because DLC expands a game you've already bought, and even if Gat Out Of Hell didn't include its own shops and costumes, an actual expansion to the game would have carried these things over from Saint's Row 4. Instead, Gat Out of Hell is actually a stripped down version of Saint's Row 4, with a new area and story, but missing many traditional Saint's Row features. If your idea of Hell is harassing the damned with the Violator, while dressed as a genki girl... well too bad, because you can't do that here.
Finally, this game doesn't accomplish much. The game map is pretty small, and once you get your wings and a couple upgrades it will only take you a minute or two to fly from end to end. The game doesn't really tie up any of the loose ends from Saint's Row 4, nor does it do anything for Johnny's character, as the end is too ambiguous to mean anything for the series long-term (they are also extremely unsatisfying). Neither Johnny or Kinzie grow or change as characters, despite their hellish context, which is a little bit of a let down. Kinzie might be the biggest let-down about this game for me, because I really thought that Hell would be a great place to explore her unique brand of crazy. Unfortunately, she's completely flat as a character, and it's pretty obvious that despite being a playable character, she got very little attention. Johnny is much funnier and fleshed out in this adventure, as well as reacting more authentically to being in Hell.
I got this game for $20, and I thought it was worth it just being big fan of the Saint's Row games and the developer Volition, but I can't really recommend it. If you've played all of the Saint's Row games and you're just itching for more, then you should pick up Gat Out Of Hell. If you haven't played Saint's Row Before, you should pick up Saint's Row 3 and 4 before playing this. There are just too many great games out there for $20 to justify buying this for the story or gameplay.

An absolutely amazing game and a well done sequel to Blood Money. The people at IO Interactive decided to raise the stakes by making Agent 47 fight the Agency itself. As usual, the levels are varied and they were all meticulously designed. 47 traverses through various locales and all this is presented to us beautifully. I remember Blood Money being a beautiful game but Absolution upped all this - this game certainly stands out in its genre.
I expected this considering the companies behind the game. After all, high production value can easily yield the necessary results. However, it is not enough to make a game with an interesting story or gameplay and this is where Absolution excels.
For those of you who are new to the franchise: in Hitman you control an assassin whose job - on each level - is to eliminate someone. Stealth should be the preference as while running and gunning is also an option (but makes the game significantly more difficult) picking the silent run method gives a much higher satisfaction. Enemies' clothing can be picked up and disguise is important to get through various parts of each level.
A change to previous installments is that some sequences are specifically action oriented or more linear. Yet, core and hardcore elements are still there. Also, predicting the routes enemies do can be done with the introduction of the so-called "Instinct Mode". I would say that this Hitman is easier on a normal difficulty than its predecessors but one can always go for the additional challenge by picking another difficulty.
All in all, an excellent follow-up to the franchise and, therefore, highly recommended to the fans as well as to the newcomers.

Giving this a hesitant thumbs-up but the review is more of a PSA. If you're curious as to why this game has such a low rating, I can boil it down for you pretty quick here. It's not a bad game overall - in fact it's essentially the same as every other year - but Wizards has made two pretty aggravating mistakes.
1. This is an online-only game, and the online servers are not very functional. They work *much* better now, but at launch there was simply no playing this.
2. The story mode (which was the main draw for many players, as it fleshes out some lore elements that have been mainly untouched for a couple of years) is pretty awful. You're given a pre-built deck, to fight another pre-built deck, and you do this twenty five times. All "fifty" decks involved (most are variants on eachother) are just bad decks and games routinely run into the 30-45 turn mark, sometimes taking almost an hour apiece to wrap up. Wizards tries to spruce it up by adding matches with a twist (alternate win conditions, the semblance of fighting multiple enemies, even one where you're supposed to lose, which was very frustrating to find out as a player who knows how to track a game and hit "restart" a few turns in advance when a loss is imminent) but I have to stress the fact that the pre-built matchups are exhausting and poorly balanced, so you'll be sitting through a headache.
The rest of the game is fine, it's serviceable as a quick MTG fix but if you're here specifically for the stories, just read some forum materials and the relevant Uncharted Realms content. Take it from a several year Magic player, that's going to be a better way to get the story.

Bosses are great, they are diverse and they give slight notice before attacking so you can react, they aren't unfair. Every area feels way different thanks to great soundtracks: creepy, lively, abondoned, epic, mysterious... Game's music combined with the artwork does wonders.

This game is a must play for any fans of over the top, super gory ninja ultra violence. I loved the original game in the 90s, I never had the full version (I finally did eventually thanks to Steam) but I had the demo (back when those were a common practice for games). Not only does this recapture that same game but it improves it 1000%.
The in-game dialogue is very funny and the random fortune cookies scattered about will guarantee to put atleast one smile on your face. The soundtrack is also fantastic (gotta love a game that starts with Stan Bush playing) and adds to the atmosphere.
Combat is different compared to other FPS, the standard RMB aim down sights isn't there instead the button is used for alternate attacks and optional weapon modes (example: akimbo SMGs or fanning your revolver to make it a semi-auto). The katana when used properly can clear out rooms (can also throw shurikens when wielding the katana, or if you are using a gun that same button does a quick slash with the katana) and it only gets stronger as you progress. Combo attacks can be learned and upgraded that turn you from a standard killer with a blade to a whirling dervish that splatters blood everywhere. Additionally you have magical abilities that can be used and still can attack with equipped weapon (just no alternate attacks) and it does take a little bit to get the hang of using the magic and combos. Certain demon body parts also can be used as weapons.
The enemies can be a pain as the game goes on, however you can still take them out fairly quickly if you aim at the right spot, this allows you to disarm demons (literally they can't wield an axe if the arm is severed)
My only real con about this game is that the debris on the ground seems to be just alot of the same. Seriously if you made a drinking game and drank everytime you saw a VHS tape or cassette tape on the ground you would die from alcohol poisoning before chapter 2.
I can't wait to try Shadow Warrior 2, just gotta be able to afford it first.

A long while ago, I saw The Last Remnant on a sale and picked it up on the cheap.  I think something like $9.99.  There it sat on my hard drive for many months undisturbed.  As I played through other games and completed them, I decided that I would make The Last Remnant my next project (after L.A. Noire).  The main reason behind this was due to the fact that The Last Remnant is something like ~25 gigs installed.
I played through the game, doing about 85% of the optional side quests and optional content.  The game features a sort of mix of classic final fantasy style turn based combat, mixed with some unit management and tactical strategy.  Throw in some RPG elements and standard JRPG writing and you've basically got The Last Remannt.
It's a decent game all in all.  I think I put in around a total of 35 hours of gameplay over the course of several months, putting in 1 hour here or there when I had time.
After beating the game, you do have the option to go back and play "New Game +" which was actually way more fun -- for a time.  It lets you cut all those corners you couldn't before and obliterate your opponents.  It's like easy-mode.  But as I played through New Game + for a few hours, I realized:  I'm not going to get a better ending, and those 25 gigs seem awfully nice to get back.
Bottom Line:  If you like JRPGs and you like Final Fantasy Games, then this might be worth your time.  The learning curve will be easy for someone familiar with the genre.  But I warn you:  Be prepared to throw down your controller (or mouse) in frustration from time to time.  You'll breeze through dungeons, areas, buildings, and castles with no problems -- slaying monsters left and right until your heart is content.  Then you'll run into a boss and have to re-load your save 50 times, changing formations and swapping out soldiers to find the perfect blend to kill him.  I am sure I could have saved myself trouble by following a walkthrough but, that takes the fun out of it, doesn't it?
Good luck!

I spent a long time looking for something new to play and I have to say, I'm quite disappointed. The game has its fans and plenty of decent reviews, but for me, it fails on several fronts. 'Galactic Civilizations', 'Haegmonia:Legions of Iron' or 'Star Wars: Empire at War' will offer a better single player experience. ( I haven't played it multiplayer)
Complex Diplomacy: good & bad
Fleet Management: poor
Planet management: simple
Ship classes and tech tree offer nothing new
The diplomacy is new compared to most games on the market. You have to research new options, use planets/starbases to expand influence or send envoy ships to boost good will. But by the tme you've got round to reseaching all those options chances are you'll already be banging heads with the neighbours.
Fleets battles are not very fluid to control. Ships can be controlled either by grouping 1-9, specific fleet icons in the command bar, or zooming in at low level. But to select individual ships can be difficult and I found the command interface jumps around too much. Again its difficult to check how much health each ship has. Against lower levels of AI even a small fleet of Capital ships will win most battles.
'Homeworld 2', 'Nexus: The Jupiter Incident' or even 'Star Wars: Empire at War' to me, offer better fleet simulators.
Not much of an Empire game when your planet construction is limited to two types of Mining Facilities, Two types of shipyard (frigates and capital) and a trading post. Then a small mix of defences and a titan depot. The research tree handles some benefits, but the planetary shield only defends against super weapon blasts and soon fails against a small group of frigates.
'Galactic Civ' 'SW: Empire at War' and the 'Total War' series can offer a better planet/city management.
The ships range from Corvette, Frigate, Crusier, Capital, Titan (1 max). The amount you can have is limited by 2 reseachable upgrades that boost 'commanders' (needed for capital and titan) and 'supply' that limits you overall fleet size. Titans need 2 commanders and 150 supply, a frigate 0 commanders and 6 supply. Each ship has special abilites, a Torpedo/missile crusier, a heavy hitter, repair.  No stealth abilites though. The capital ships gain experience and unlock extra skills, so you need a mixed bag to win, but similarly just build a lot of big guns and you usually can still win. Coupled with the low survivability and skills of the smaller classes, once you start building big ships, frigates are redundant, and there isn't enough depth to the sytem to micromange the ships properly.

I'm not going to say it has the best story, because it doesn't.  It does have the best graphics for its time (but that also made it practically unplayable back then and still gives my computer an aneurism now) but that's not what makes it so special.  Is it the incredibly clever exo suit system?  While awesome and incredibly challenging tactically, it is not even this gameplay development that makes Crysis so special.  The thing that Crysis does so successfully is give the feeling that you as the player are not only in this world, but completely and totally outgunned making you essentially screwed.  You walk into a situation and feel that there is no way that you are going to walk out alive.  Then you simply out your head down and start fighting anyway.  Then somehow through instinct, skill, reflexes, whatever--you find yourself emerging victorious on the other side of the fight.  Nothing else in any video game will ever make you feel more badass and victorious than overcoming seemingly impossible odds.  Furthermore, Crysis does not give this feeling once, but over and over and over again the entire game.  The stakes are constantly raised even up to the final boss battle.  There is never a chance to truly stop, catch your breath and say: "Ok, I'm safe so I can relax for a bit."  The tension and sense of dread never abate from the first moment to even after the game is finished.  Seriously, even after the credits rolled I was still on edge.  That is a sign of a good video game.
Definitely get this one, let it grad hold and refuse to let go taking you along an adrenaline thrill ride of dread, action, and unequaled reward of overcoming the seemingly impossible.

Let me just say off the bat, the story in this game is garbage.There are some great NPCs that make it bearable, but as it stands, the game's plot and narrative are not that good.Having said that, everything else in this game is incredible.The combat is simply amazing, at first things may appear to be random, but most of the work comes from you building a working party.Your party consists of unions, and your attacks in the battle are determined by who's in that union and what skills they possess.For instance, if you want a union to have the chance to cast mystic arts, you'd use predominantly mystic art users in that union.You can also turn off characters skills, giving you another level of depth to play with.Aesthetically the game is gorgeous, plenty of effects in battle and clean texture work, it's also runs pretty well on lower end PCs.When it comes to audio, this game is damn near perfect.The voice acting is surprisingly well done, save for the main character, but everything else is top notch.The real star of the game though is easily the soundtrack, there is nothing wrong with it, and the quality is probably the best I've seen this generation.In the end, if you can look past the story being so stale, then you have one of the most unique games on the market right now.I thank god Square Enix decided to port this game, it was decent on the consoles, but it really shines on PC.

Absolutely love this game. Controls are a bit a hard to get into if you've never played one of these kinds of games before but that's half the fun (also the strike mode has an easier time). The visuals and audio are amazing (the soundtrack composer also made soundtrack for Homeworld I believe). The strike suit mode is really fun, locking on and firing tons of missiles quickly to destroy tons of enemy fighters in a single volley.
A few things to note. The allied AI / difficulty really infuriated me at times. I would have to singlehandedly stop all enemy torpedos aimed at an allied capital ship while also singlehandedly destroying the enemy capital ship but it was also extremely satisfying when I finally finished the level.
The different "unlockable" weapons are just stronger variants of the previous with more drain or less ammo capacity with exception to missiles. Missiles have a few different purposes. However you will basically only use them to destroy capital ships since the strike suit mode missiles completely destroy fighters and you have a limited supply of normal missiles.
The other pilotable ships basically have absolutely no reason to be used over the strike suit except the bomber. The bomber is basically a mobile artillery platform that can tear up a cruiser much faster than the strike suit (if the torpedos land) but this is a niche use since it can't be used to deal with mass waves of fighters which are pretty much everywhere and completely handled by you.
Warning to achievement hunters, you can not get a perfect game without the DLCs.
I do not believe that these negatives take away from the gameplay as I still enjoyed the game in the end so I would wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone looking for a space fighter sim.

What started with gorgeous, promising trailers of X Rebirth turned into an unfortunate case of developer myopia on release.  It's bad enough to speculate that perhaps their publisher, Deep Silver, strongarmed them into an early release because, come release day, we were given something riddled with enough show-stopping bugs that this is an "Early Access" game without the benefit that title brings as an excuse.
It's possible you might have a little fun here, just scoping out the huge the stations and shooting some things down but, before long, your fun will be soured by nasty performance bugs, broken core systems, and a sorely pointless station interiors.  X Rebirth doesn't just need polish; it needs a massive low-level revision.
If you've already bought the game, I wouldn't bother waiting for incremental patches on this one - come back around April or March '14 and see then if X Rebirth is worth playing.  Also, be sure to check out the community mods.
Until then, I recommend paying no more than $10 for this game, and cross your fingers that the next game in the X series actually remembers what an X game is.  Terran Conflict or Albion Prelude are entirely different games, and remain reasonably worthy purchases.
