The Hitman games are iconic stealth-assassin games. They center around Agent 47, a trained and classy contract killer and this part is no different. I'd never played a Hitman game but saw the appeal of it, so I took advantage of a Steam sale and dove in.
And wow, here's a game that started out promising with great features, but did not do itself -any- favours. The story revolves around Agent 47 going rogue to save a girl that's chemically altered to be a killer or something along those lines. It's filled with one-dimensional characters whom I didn't give a crap about. The big bad guy is generically 'crazy' guy (ugh, can we stop with the crazy/'random' villains?) with a very thin motive to kidnap this girl. The locations, though interesting and varied, also seemed extremely random and detached from each other. I mean... I'm pretty sure I went from a factory to a wrestling match in one mission...
I was initally very impressed with the controls and the gameplay. It went smooth, I liked the disguises mechanic and every major assassination target has several cool ways to kill them off. What I could've lived without was the scoreboard never disappearing from view. At first I thought "Oh cool, this'll motivate me to be the best assassin I can be. To plan my kills, to play as perfectly as possible" but as time went by, I began to see it as a malevolent schoolteacher grading me and marking me for every mistake I made. "Got spotted?" it would ask, "oooh, that's another 1300 points off your scoreboard. :) You're below your friends' scores now." And there is no way to turn it off.
This wouldn't be so annoying if it wasn't for the next thing I want to touch on. I was under the impression the Hitman games were like Dishonored, in that you have a big sandbox in which you can carefully plan out your kill. Hitman: Absolution didn't do this. Instead, Absolution drops you in small maps with increasing amounts of patrolling guards. The game became less about "plan carefully", and more about trial-and-error of trying to navigate through a maze of guards (and civilians who immediately warn guards...). I began desperately trying to avoid a massive shootout (with the high density of guards, when one sees you; you're boned) and constantly hitting Restart from Checkpoint because I got caught which would drop my score, instead of finding enjoyment in the planning and executing of the perfect kill. This, coupled with an increasingly frustrating scoreboard marking me and comparing me to my friends, began so IMMENSELY frustrated.
For a game which motivates you to be the perfect assassin, it sure does a lousy job. Half the time you'll have to restart the mission over from a checkpoint that has scripted guard conversations which you'll have to wait for to move on. Another thing that really bothered me is that it's very unclear when a kill is silent. Strangling someone with a power cord with them going "No! Grkkhk!" is silent, but a silenced pistol shot is not? There's a distance-based delay in guards seeing you while you're disguised , meaning that you can manage to scroll past a few guards in disguise (without using Instinct), but if you bump into one around the corner, you're IMMEDIATELY spotted. Spotted means every guard is warned, and that means a massive shootout.
Even the ending left me completely blank because I didn't care about any of the villains. I didn't care about the girl I was supposed to save because I didn't have a reason to other than the game telling me "CARE ABOUT THIS GIRL D:<" And the very final kill happens in a cutscene... A fittingly frustrating ending to a frustrating game.
The Good: Stealth is unique if nothing else, graphics are tops, disguise mechanic is fun, many different ways to kill someone that do give a sense of victory, lot of potential.
The Bad: Trial-and-error in the worst way possible, story vague and thoroughly uninteresting with no relatable characters at all. And as final bad point; the one mission with the SM-clad battle-nuns. Why the hell does this game have SM-clad battle-nuns?!

I've never been in to Simulator games, From the 90s on i've found them boring as heck! Living in the country surrounded by farm land and from a recommendation from a friend I was enticed in to try this.    It's critical you watch a few videos first to get a understanding of what to do.  I did that before buying this.
I've spend over 50 hours in this game. That's quite a lot for me these days.  While on paper simulators and one about farming sounds boring, I found this to be the most rewarding game in recent years for entertainment value.
If your a solo player like me and want to do one of the bigger maps. You really have to start modding the game so you can harvest and replant a feild in an hours time .
I found it pretty educational as well.  I always wondered why a farm around my way had a massive white tarp with hundreds of tires on top of it. Figured it was used to dry grain.  While driving past it last week I noticed the cover was off and saw dark hay and realized it was Silege, something I didn't know prior to this game.    I can also identify and understand all the farm equipment that drives past my house.
While the game is simple in nature there is something very therapeutic about it and fun.
My only 2 complaints is the size of the equipment later on in the game when you make out well is too taxing with time to manage as a solo player, it can be hard to find the right mode that balances this so it's not too strong and takes the fun of it.
My other complaint is some actions such as bailing hay, mowing grass, and hauling product does not have a autopilot feature. Doesn't sound like a big deal and it's not starting out.  But when your managing a lot of stuff all your time is invested in performing those same exact actions manually and it's no longer enjoyable because your forced to spend all your time doing it.   If they added that I have no doubt I could pick it up again and keep going.
Recommend this game for sure, had a great time.

Sins was a game that honestly had me relatively surprised in a number of aspects. Here's my thoughts:
Graphics: 7/10; For a game made more than a couple years ago, it manages to push a rather impressive resolution, detail and ambience. Everything from massive capitol ships and Titans, to small units such as fighter squadrons are well textured, clearly defined and able to give a good visual experience that's both impressive, and incredibly well optimised. So well in fact even older PC's can handle the game on higher graphics levels. Sadly in large scale games with multiple players the game does tend to putz around a bit with the number of items and commands being issued but thats simply a common feature among RTS games.
Gameplay: 8/10; RTS at its finest, with a bit of micro-RPG elements attatched to each ship, the game is fun to play, flows well, and encourages good strategy as well as economy management. The controls are a bit much to take in all at once, and it like many other games involving a 4 tier RTS, requires a bit of a learning curve. However, once understood the game is able to flow well, it rewards tactics and an understanding of your opponent, and a satisfying feeling of accomplishment.
Sound: 5/10; Its an older game, but the sound effects hold up, and are fairly solid. Listening in on battles is an enjoyable experience and the sound levels are accurate. However some of the more notable abilities used by the Titan units seem unnessecarrily loud, and if listening with headphones can be somewhat deafening if zoomed in close to observe the battle.
Addictiveness and Depth: 4/10; The game suffers from one major flaw. Its absolute lack of a single player campaign. The game has all the makings of what could be a very entertaining single player space domination game, however it is restricted to arena style RTS combat over a set number of worlds against 1 - 7 opponents. The game does have an interactive level up system for Capitol ships, which are allowed to level in a manner you can guide them in by increasing their abilities, and the games heavy amount of depth via a diplomacy system, a working active and live economy, as well as player issued missions, falls by the wayside when faced with the knowledge that the entire games structure is simply a Starship based battle arena.
Overall: 6/10; The games very fun if you can settle into its niche setting. Enjoying well detailed space battles happening in real time is difficult to manage especially with the graphical quality this game manages to provide. However the lack of a single player campaign hits this game hard, and pushes it onto a back burner if you're looking to pick it up. Best to get if you know a friend that plays it as well, or if you enjoy the competition of facing down another player in a 3 Tier RTS game. Only reason this game isnt being reccomended is its heavy reliance on other players for any sort of content.

After 125 hours, far more than anyone can say is reasonable for a game you're not enjoying, I can safely say that Torchlight is not for me and I wouldn't recommend it.
It'd be tempting to nitpick, to try to justify my stance to be some semblance of reasonable, to browbeat others, but that's not what we're here to do.
I can't recommend Torchlight because I don't like the core mechanic of pointing and clicking to direct and attack with a character in realtime combat. That's just a core disconnect that Torchlight is never going to bridge. I didn't realise it going into it, but after 125 hours of unenjoyment I had plenty of time to go over where I went wrong in life.
With that clear, subjective, inescapable bias out of the way:
Torchlight is about descending below the titular Torchlight, through 35 floors with 6 themes to them, various bosses popping up along the way to say hi. It's Diablo but more colourful.
The death-filled dungeon's environments are fairly nice, and provide an appreciable backdrop to endless slaughtering.
Art design has some nice visual density without being cluttered or too generic. The ground being a canvas, combined with enemies not immediately despawning, leaves you knee deep in the dead after every encounter, which always a good look to end on.
Environmental design covers levels that I couldn't tell you are procgen or not. Either they're tilesets or they're copied and pasted to death, but either way it's linear and boring. Your massive levels shouldn't leave me wondering why I even have a map.
Character design fairs less brilliantly. Tends to stray into gaudy Blizzard territory, goofy - sometimes plain ugly - designs combined with giant pauldrons. The works. You've seen it all before, and it's never looked good. Not sure why character only have three fingers, either.
Playing as these ugly characters, weird difficulty spikes abound; even on Very Hard, most of the time you're invincible. Nothing can touch you, doesn't matter what class you play as. Then boom, hitscan beam or elemental attack waterfall of pain that destroys you in a second. Pumping elemental resistance by spamming gems that, even when maxed to Perfect/Flawless, add pitiful bonuses that just encourages the pain.
The Dark Zealot is infamous for a reason. It was less frustrating than just baffling, that things would be balanced like this.
Luckily it's mod-friendly. Extremely, extremely mod-friendly. I'm certain it wants you to mod it.
Mods could probably change how unbalanced the classes are, but in the vanilla state you really want to use Vanquisher. Every class can use every weapon and a good half of the skill tree (side note: every time a game with a skill tree is released without a respec, I commit crimes.) is universal, but it's simple logic:
Ranged weapons have the same DPS as melee. DPS-based skills deal far more damage than flat-damage upgrades and summons are worthless. Your biggest dangers in this game is closing distance to kill high-value targets before they immediately kill you. So the Vanquisher creams where the Destroyer and Alchemist scream. Compared to her, they're almost painful to play.
Postgame activities are in here, you've got the Shadow Vault, which is just running the same tilesets/levels with different enemies in them until you get bored, nary a boss or postgame questline in sight, and you've got fishing, which is worthless.
After 1000 fish I got two permanent fish, so there's your payoff for that. You can probably mod it.
You could make a case for there being a story, but I'm not sure I'd buy it. NPC shows up every now and again, and there's exposition between tilesets, that's about all there is.
So I didn't have fun with, at all, so I couldn't recommend it.
But as for saying whether or not it's good, frankly I don't think I'm qualified. If you like Diablo-likes, then I'm fairly sure you'll like this, but that's all I have to offer.

CivBE feels just liek playing a re-skinned civ 5. Instead of making a game that feels different, they decided to slap on some new graphics and unit names and call it a day.
The entire premise of the game seems flawed to me, since it's predicated on humanity not changing at all as we explore the stars.
For example, why the heck would all (or at least a lot) of the rockets land on the same planet? And then, why are most of the units you can make military? Would the first thing we do on a new world really be start fighting?
Same thing goes for the currency system, where instead of gold you have energy. It feels like a incredibly contrived throwback to the civ series because the devs couldn't come up with some other constraint.
I think that actually sums up the game fairly well: lack of vision. Instead of exploring new frontiers, they settled on the same tried-and-true approach from the past, and it doesn't transfer well.

I have not played other space flight simulators extensively, so I cannot review this game based on how it compares to others in the genre. I can say that the graphics, controls, and level design do deliver on one thing - immersion.
When you're making a hard turn, going upside down to try and flank the ship on your tail, the tension is real, as is the feeling in the back of your mind that you are travelling through endless, empty space. When another computer controlled ship in your squadron swings by and bails you out of something or steals your kill, it feels like a real, chaotic dogfight.
Possibly the most important immersive part of the game is, once you unlock the Strike Suit, how much it really does look and feel like you are piloting a Gundam. When you first get it, with the music playing in the background and all of the swarms of enemy ships, you completely annhilate almost everything you can see. Then, in the next mission, the learning curve picks up, and you start to feel the limitations of this awesome machine. Quickly, because of how powerful the strike suit is, you get thrown into messes that are too much for the ship alone, and you have to knuckle down and enhance your skills to keep up. Meanwhile, the war rages on, and its emotional toll is felt by all.
Doesn't that sound just like the plot of most Gundam shows? I was impressed by how the designers used their game's difficulty curve to reinforce the feel of being that one pilot with the super weapon on whom everything depends. This game is pretty hard, or at least it was for me, and as the best hard games do, it pushed me to get better and really hunker down to get specials from the missions so that I was well equipped enough to handle later ones.
The story is nothing to write home about, and some of the combat scenarios get repetitive, especially since you often have to replay missions to get power ups. But the overall atmosphere of the game? Superb. And that makes playing it a joy, even if part of you is thinking 'torpedos? Again?'

As far as the game dynamic is concerned, there is some promise here.  There are a lot of interesting ideas.  Unfortunately, it feels like someone wanted to make $$$ more than they wanted to release a finished product that people could understand and enjoy.  The ideas that look promising seem half-baked, and the UI is just awful.
The combination of a garish color scheme, and conflicting/overlapping visual indicators, result in a confusing experience.  Even simple mapping concepts were really difficult to make out much of the time.  (Where territory borders lie, which grid areas have resources or other traits, where my units and enemy units are, etc...)  I don't feel like I should have a headache after 10 minutes of playing a game...  I have a difficult time believing that any kind of objective user-studies were performed and acted upon prior to this game being released.
The tech-web and affinity progressions are... interesting.  This is what happens when you put engineers into a room without supervision and tell them to come up with an abilities-tree.  The result is quite complicated and not very fun.  The tree/web itself has a lot of words, but doesn't explain what anything means.  I feel like they threw together the core concept and then forgot the part where they're supposed to make it reasonably understandable.
So yeah... cannot recommend.  I REALLY wanted to like this game, but it is too confusing to be enjoyable.
Also, hard to justify the $$$.

TL;DR
From someone who 100% completed it, this game is short but awesome. Graphics: 7-10 Sound: 9-10 Gameplay: 8-10 Difficulty: Medium, even the hardest challenges can be done in a pretty short amount of time. If this game is on sale for $1 or less, get it. If it's full price and you're considering it, get it. If you don't like this kind of game, it might change your mind. Probably not, but it might.
Review:
If you like puzzle games, games that make you think, games with interesting mechanics, and don't mind failing a few times before finding the solution you will love this game. It started off slowly with easier puzzles to teach you the 3 most important gameplay elements: Gravity Wells, Anti-Gravity Wells, and the Shield. The first two are pretty self-explanatory. The shield makes you immune to any gravity well effects. As the game progressed, it became more difficult. Some challenges require precise timing, some quick reflexes, some both at the same time.
The very end of the game did become slightly frustrating to me. Not really because of the game, but because I wasn't paying close enough attention to what effects the gravity wells would have.
The music is unbelievably good. The graphics have a modernized-retro platformer feel to me. And the character controls pretty well. The game is quite short (100% completed in 3.2 hours). Nothing is randomized, so there isn't a lot of replay value, but it's a cool experience.
I got this game on sale for a ridiculously low price, so low the cards it dropped are worth more than what I bought the game for. And after having played it completely, I would recommend it at full price. Do you have what it takes to become a Gravity Ninja?

Good: Fantastic graphics and music
Bad: Rather linear, although not as bad as some people make it out to be. Other FF games are very linear also, they just give the illusion of choice by allowing you to steal potions out of people's dressers, etc. The linearity here just dispenses with that illusion and keeps you moving forward. But if you're a big fan of side-quests, look elsewhere.
Ok: Battle system is interesting. You get rated after every battle which seems to affect what loot drops. You only control the main character directory but assign roles to the entire party. You then switch these role sets (called 'paradigms') during battle based on whether you want attack, healing, defense, etc. You have to time these shifts correctly, so it's more about having quick reflexes to switch paradigms for an efficient battle than about micromanaging tactics.
Story is good IMO, but pretty complicated. Three different things have similar names which can be confusing. However, there is an extensive story summary available in case you miss something.

It's strange for a Remastered version that still needs fan-fixes to be playable, but since they're easy to find and implement I personally didn't feel it was much of a problem as some others do. So here's a tip 2K: Don't call something a remaster when it's this broken on release. Spend a few more weeks tweaking it so PC users can have the same quality of experience as console users, and have them be able to configure the game to their preferences. If you had done that all these negative reviews wouldn't have been here
SO before you start playing:
-Google 'Bioshock Remastered fix'
-Find the sections about Mouse options, otherwise it's near unplayable.
-And if you like you can change the FOV and graphics for a better experience.
WATCH OUT. If the game crashes, which might happen sometimes, you lose all your preferences. Make sure to put the .ini files on "READ ONLY" after you've done the fan-fixes to largely prevent this problem.
So the remaster is basically a better looking version of the original game. It doesn't make any changes to the combat or interface which some find annoying. Like being unable to use plasmids and guns at the same time, but I believe that would remove some of the challenge. And I personally had no trouble playing the old game as it's supposed to be played. All in all it's still Bioshock. Spend 20-30 minutes to make the game play smoothly for you, then dive into the underwater story of Rapture once again.
Oh and you get some challenges, achevements and a nifty museum to look at old models and other artwork from development which I found pretty neat..

There need to be more co-op RPGs like this.
It might be an easy and short game, but I really, really enjoyed it. If you have two friends you often play games with, then you should definitely check this one out. It's best played like that, with this game only benefiting you from playing co-op. Each character has their own secrets which can open up areas that hide loot, and each character has a race skill which can help the other characters out. The combat is very satisfying, because you can pull off some awesome dismemberments and decapitations, and even do Fellowship strikes or kills when all characters are attacking the same enemy.
At first sight it looks like it offers the typical character selection, being a Mage, a Warrior and a Ranger. But none of these characters HAVE to be played like they usually are. I played as the Ranger, and you would assume he would mainly use his bow in combat. I really only did when there were enemies you could only reach with ranged attacks. The game gave me the option to use two-handed weapons, dual wield two one-handed weapons, or use a one-handed weapon in combination with a shield too. There were plenty of skills which would increase my effectiveness with either of these weapon combinations, as well as skills which would give me new archery abilities or give specific bonuses to me using my race skill.
I feel like this game is a nice combination between an action-based hack-and-slash game, with the looting system of an Action RPG/Dungeon Crawler, and a story and setting which fit right into the LOTR series. I'm not saying the story is interesting enough to make every LOTR fan play this game, but it's also not ruining any part of the lore. It might just be a little more interesting for someone who likes the LOTR story than for someone who doesn't care for it at all.

It kills me to have to write a negative review on a point n click game as they are so rare but here I have no choice.  The list of cons is so long I have to.
CONS
- Only made 7 years ago but it feels and looks like it was made in the early 90s.
- No widescreen, black bars down the side of my screen
- Dreadful voice acting.  Not just bad inclination but somehow actual bad acting. ie actor 1 stops half way through sentence waiting to be interrupted but actor 2 waits a significant time before supposedly interrupting.
- Fay one of two playable characters just looks permanently grumpy I actually wanted her to be killed off along with most other characters.
-And the biggest con was HOW the story was done.  It took an interesting idea; time travel to prevent a catastrophe due to climate change but because of the heavyhanded approach to the story I felt I was being thumped on the head by an extreme environmentalist at the same time listening to a boring lecture on the subject instead of playing a game.  The problem with crusaders of any kind is that they have zero humour and manage to not only suck any joy of anything they touch but actively put you off any interest you had in the subject.
Usually daedalic games aren't written by people like that and have multi subject threads in a story to keep it interesting.  Even games that are dark or serious, if they are good have either fun gameplay or characters done in a way to keep your interest or humour in certain parts of a game.  If only they hadn't been so heavy-handed or had more than one subject that the conversation revolved around this could and should have been easily an interesting gripping story.
Although I felt all joy being sucked out of everything including gameplay, most gameplay was technically good it just felt leaden. It was this devs usual gameplay, not obvious in parts a lot of exploration more old fashioned point n click gameplay.  They had some mini games which were either not easy or not quick.
I had played most of this before at GOG (hence short time here) but couldn't finish it due to cons so picked this up in steam sale as it had achs and it was only that that kept me playing this time.  But at least this time I knew to mute sound, and just FF speed reading all the lectures. I wanted to see if it got better and it did about 3/4 way through, the lectures mostly stopped.  I don't do real spoilers ever on plot or story but if you don't want to know anything about the end then don't read the following spoiler although it is more my general feeling on the writing.
It was so close to being good and could easily have been if above points were addressed, that is what is frustrating about this game.  More storylines, better more balanced writer and editor it could have been good.  If you don't mind being lectured at, can FF the dialogue, play on mute and like harder games to work out then I think you could enjoy this (if you also are tolerant at what people come up re science in games) if not then I'd pass on this one. The biggest problem with Magic Duels is figuring out where to begin your list of what this game does wrong. I think I'll try list form.
1: The UI is ugly as♥♥♥♥♥♥ boring to look at, and seems to be the same UI that's used in every Duel of the Planeswalker
2: Quests give the same amount of gold regardless of what you have to do to complete them. A quest to win 2 games with a BR deck gives 40 gold, just like a quest to win 4 games with a BR deck.
3: Quests can only be completed vs. AI. For some reason it doesn't recognize beating a person as a win.
4: The Deck Wizard is helmet-wearing, mouth-breathing, paste-eating ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and you're forced to use it because only decks made by the Wizard count for quests.
5: In Versus mode, your opponent can and will concede the game if they don't draw a great hand, and instead of you winning, you're forced to play against the AI (losing your own mulligan if you hadn't taken one yet). At best you waste 20 minutes beating the AI, at worse you lose and suffer all the penalties of losing despite your human opponent having quit <1 minute into the game.
6: Fatal Errors, black screens and generally unplayable for people with Intel integrated graphics. Even if you have a badass GPU, the game automatically defaults to running off the integrated graphics, which can't run the game.
7: Complete and total lack of communication from WotC/Stainless. The community manager for the game took launch weekend off, and can't be bothered to answer any questions that people direct towards him.
8: M:TG's stratgic depth is well documented, you can make all kinds of different types of decks in the game, but in Magic Duels your choices are going to be aggro, aggro or aggro because the card pool is so tiny there's not enough tools to run anything but aggro. Imagine Hearthstone but EVERYONE plays Face Hunter or Aggro Paladin every game.
9: The servers are so unstable that you will find yourself playing the Story Quests multiple times, not because you lose, but because after you finish one of the missions, you'll be informed that you can't connect to the servers and thus can't save any progress in the story mode or in any quests. Just barely beat that first Chandra mission? TOO BAD you gotta do it again because for some reason in 2015 game companies still don't properly prepare an infrastructure for their game.
10: A wealth of dumb and random bugs from people not having their quests complete, people not receiving new quests, people finding the gold cap doesn't reset for them, people not receiving rewards from the Story Quest, people not receiving cards from booster packs, cards disappearing from their collection randomly, it's just a big mess.
Ultimately, I give this game a 1.5/10. Most of the story missions are fun to play, though some can be real frustrating due to poor deck design and a very questionable shuffling algorithm that seems determined to starve or flood you. However, as fun as the story missions are, all they do is get you hyped for the rest of the game which makes the massive dissappointment that much worse.
If you're looking for a online card game alternative to Hearthstone, I would recommend Hex over this pile of lazy crap.

You want to have any measure of competent deck to play with in this game? Then you better be prepared to buy booster packs from store (which is expected), because you’ll have a hard time earing them in any reasonable span of time. The way the game expects you to do that (or even learn the game) is by playing the story modes. However, therein lies a few little problems. First, many of the story mode "challenges" are so unfairly stacked against you they soon cease to be a tests of skill, and instead become more of a test of how lucky you are during your current attempt. Second, the required always online component of the game. Lose of connection to the server, server goes down, whatever may happen between your machine and the game’s server. Connection gets dropped, progress in the story cannot continue. Worse (and what happened to me) you could be attempting to finish one of these unfair match-ups against the AI, finally win (after about 3 hours of try after try), then the server goes down and you are not given credit for finishing that match, and have to do it all over again later after the servers come back up. Infuriating, unfair, and ridiculous. Locally saved information is not allowed to upload to the server on successful re-sync? What is this, 2001!?
“Oh, but I’ll just earn my gold for boosters in the vs online mode. Fighting the AI is for chumps.” Really? Well, if you truly wish to take your chances online, enjoy eating loss after loss from either the expert players or the players who don’t mind reaching into their wallet to get an advantage.
All that being said, I do enjoy Magic, and I’m actually looking forward to playing more. Maybe this game will end up being the final push necessary to get me to start collecting the actual cards. But as a piece of software, and a game service, I cannot recommend Magic Duels right now. Give it a week or two, and maybe by then it will have received some more polish, some more content, and its infuriatingly unreliable server issues will be fixed by then.
I look forward to the day I can rate this game with a thumbs up.
Cheers.

One of the best Space RTS games I have ever enjoyed, besides Homeworld. This RTS is what Diablo 2 was for hack and slash. You play it obsessively for awhile and then stop. Then you will find yourself coming back for more down the road.

Story - It doesn't really have one, but I think they are gearing up to create one.
Atmosphere/Music - Whether it be a desperate fight or a steam roll, just sitting watching your empire go about it's day, you'll feel it in the music and in the atmosphere of the game.
Sound - It's great. Giant battles are something else.
Gameplay - Wonderful, maps are always fun and different, all of the ships have a purpose and all of the planets are meaningful.
Overall, this is my personal 10/10 RTS. I love everything about it and will continue to support it until a new version comes out or the company dies out.

Don´t know where all the hate is coming from, but I have to say, I did not play any MTG games before nor did I play the actual card game.
But from what I have heard about the MTG Planeswalker games, they seem to be aweful.
This game however does not force you to buy extra slots for your decks, you also get 20 gold per win against a human opponent (a booster costs 150 and contains 6 cards one of which is a rare or mythic rare). You also earn gold by playing the campaign and skill quest and by playing against the AI. After finishing the campaign you will be able to get around 7 or 8 booster pack.
I did play quite alot of hearthstone and the business model is indeed similar as some reviews here have already stated. But this game is actually less of a cashgrab than hearthstone. For example in hearthstone you will get alot of duplicate cards while opening booster packs, here you will only get as many duplicates as you can use (you can use 4 cards of the same name). Again a hearthstone comparison, golden cards are hard to come by and cost double their dust value, here you can get foil cards for 5 gold per card and it also includes all duplicate of it (if you enchant a card to be the foil version you pay 5 gold and if u have it 4 times all of them are foil now, same for the ones you draw from booster packs).

I picked this up because I'm a huge fan of Ori and the Blind Forest, and heard about it/thought it looked interesting while awaiting Ori's sequel. Hollow Knight is like a combination of Ori and Dark Souls; less platforming, more combat, very dark in tone.
Positives+
***
This game is rock solid all around. The visuals are good, and the soundtrack helps sell the melancholy and dreary nature of the world. The main theme is a chilling piano track and it sets the mood right away.
If you liked Ori, like me, this game is quite a departure away from the platforming/maneuvering focus of Ori. Hollow Knight is built with a greater emphasis on combat, and gives you a lot of tools for that. The game is challenging, especially some of the platforming segments and bosses. Some of the bosses are pretty tough (though the hardest one I faced had an environmental method to make them slightly easier).
This game is DARK, and I don't just mean visually. The more you progress through the story, the more depressing and grim it becomes as you learn more about the setting and the characters.
Some areas may outright make your skin crawl from the aesthetic they set, too. (Do you like bugs!?)
A cool feature of the Charm system (character augment system; limited amount equipped at once, but gain more slots as the game goes on) is that some charms combine in interesting and powerful ways. You can increase the range of your attacks, the power, your ability to gain, manage, and use your Soul (spell resource for damage and healing), how your health functions, and more. Some even unlock new dialogue with other lore characters.
Sequence breaking! You can do things in a fair bit of variance, including some plot events.
Negatives-
***
Sequence breaking... There is missable storyline stuff. While it isn't earth shattering to the story, it is really unfortunate that this can happen in some instances.
There is a great emphasis on exploration. Sometimes too much emphasis, in fact. I was completely lost for a while, and the general advice is to just explore around. However, going back through areas and combing over them multiple times, only for it to dawn on you that you haven't yet unlocked the skills to access some of them and wasted all of that time is a huge downer. I hated wandering around for a while until I unlocked more core abilities for accessing things. And, as I stated, platforming is downplayed a bit, so your ability to rapidly traverse some areas is hindered. After a certain point in the game, one of the main areas loses some of its access points, further increasing your travel time to parts of it that you'll likely need to revisit later. This brings me to my BIGGEST complaint...
Travel. The fast travel system(s) in this game is scarce. This wouldn't be a big deal if many areas I had to return to weren't literally as far as possible from all fast travel locations. I spent an enormous chunk of my initial playthrough running around. There are very few mechanics for getting around rapidly, and especially coughing up precious attack range charms for obnoxious flying and exploding enemies. Some places have shortcuts that can't be unlocked until later, and some shortcuts are completely useless before or even after you get them. This is the worst part of the game to me. Ori rewards skilled maneuvers for getting around, but Hollow Knight doesn't particularly offer any until late in the game, and they have flaws/weaknesses. So get you hiking boots and prepare for a long haul in some stretches of the game if you're not racing through the story.
The double jump mechanism isn't obtained until halfway+ through the game. It also sports an interesting delay, though I think this is more for the aesthetic of how it's used. Overall, it doesn't universally make traveling significantly faster over the Dash and Wall Climb you'll already have by that point.
A small gripe is that collecting the dream fragments from the trees later in the game is REALLY tedious in some areas. Like, oof. Circling back through areas trying to find the one or two you missed was annoying.
-------
I *highly* recommend this game as an action platformer, especially if you like sprawling areas to explore and some combat elements. Nothing ever felt particularly unfair. There's multiple endings and quite a lot to do. This game is easily several magnitudes of length compared to Ori and the Blind Forest (granted, my first play on that game was 7.5 hours, and now I can 100% in less than 3).
I believe this game is a much closer title to Castlevania in feeling. The aesthetic is darker, and there's a stronger emphasis on combat strategy against some enemies, and some bosses will most certainly require you to adapt in different tactics.
This is definitely worth a buy and I will be looking forward to a sequel if there ever is one.

Torchlight is a 3d hack-and-slash modeled after games in the Diablo series. If you’re not familiar with that, it’s basically a lot of left clicking, dungeon roaming, and loads of looting. It’s hard to talk about this game without referencing Diablo, as even the music seems like it was pulled straight from that game and the visuals are reminiscent of the third game with their vibrant colors and auras.
Torchlight adds to the familiar mechanic by giving you a pet that acts as both a defender and pack mule, able to be sent back to town to sell all your loot at a moment’s notice leaving you to continue looting and pillaging. There’s also a fame system that acts as a second “experience” meter and gives you a skill point for every level you gain in addition to skill points given by actual experience levels.
Unfortunately, this game lacks a sense of excitement regarding gear. Frequently on my play-through I would see unique and set items drop, giving me a momentary rush that was quickly extinguished upon identification. It’s sad to say that I ended up simply buying and enchanting the majority of my gear in town, meaning the dungeon crawl was more of a means of gathering gold and experience to fuel my character development topside. It was about 20 or so hours before I finally got my first decent weapon drop…from the game’s final boss. The only use for it then was to do the infinite dungeons the game offers afterwards. Since Torchlight has no multiplayer, there was nobody to show the cool weapon to either.
Some other grievances: the storyline isn’t particularly engaging and the bosses are barely memorable save for the one that caused tremors and the big bad at the end. The game also has an issue with the Z-axis and projectiles in many levels, making your attacks hit stairways and ramps inconsistently, even when you directly target an enemy (this is incredibly annoying). Lack of multiplayer was a serious oversight IMO as the thing I remember the most with the very first Diablo game was hundreds of hours spent playing alongside friends and randoms online.
Torchlight isn’t a terrible game, but it’s not really good enough for me to recommend when there are so many other games around that do the same thing way better.

Fight Jacket One is a game inspired by science fiction classics like Free Space, Homeworld, and some anime I totally never heard of and/or watched. You take control of a fighter craft early on that works just like you would expect a space fighter to work. You can choose from several weapons ranging from the usual cannons to scatter guns, homing missiles, swarm missiles, etc. It's a very competent space-dog fighting game like this with an emphasis on being a small part of a large conflict.
See, while you're tasked with an objective, there are dozens of friendly star fighters roaming around the battlefield in between larger ships that all shoot about as straight as I pee. But it helps in making you feel like you're fighting in an actual war instead of just being a single fighter going from mission to mission.
But there's also Strike Suit's most standout feature!...The uh...The... The Strike Suit.
The Strike Suit kind of turns the game on it's head and makes it feel like a really updated version of those Macross games that used to come out on the PS1. It works as a star fighter, yes, but you can charge a super mode via EXPLOSIONS, once you feel comfortable enough with what you've charged you transform into a mecha style mode and tear up anything in front of you with a complete missile massacre that makes your enemies go "Wow, that's a lot of missiles!"
The Strike Suit itself loses speed, but it makes up for it with a dash as well as overwhelming fire power, it feels great to just unleash hell on everything in front of you with a well timed barrage.

It does miss some of the "soul" or flavorful-story feel of other games but I think given time, patches and expansions it will rival or surpass Civ 5.

Note: This is my impression after playing the base game without DLC or the Director's Cut, depending on the changes in the Director's Cut, some of these complaihnts may have been resolved.
A space game in the vein of games like Star Wars: Rouge Squadron or Star Wars: X-Wing Alliance.  Due to the lack of games in this genre lately, I was greatly looking forward to this when I first heard of it.  Unfortunately, it didn't quite meet the mark.  The story starts out farcical, becomes mediocre, and then decides to be incomplete and farcical again on the final level.  When I first started playing, the controls felt too sensitive for me to fly straight, but this was solved by turning up the blind spot on the controls.  The difficulty spikes a couple times throughout the game, typically due to the targeting system not highlighting the targets you want it to in some levels, the ease of having your vision obstructed by explosions or damage preventing you from visually locating important objectives, or the dense, hyper-accurate turret concentrations on carriers.  The game also leaves you to figure out which weakpoints on large craft are actually important to kill in order to not fail the mission instead of telling you what the symbols mean.  It took me a while to come to the realization that the Strike Suit was mostly useful for its ability to kill massed enemies or bombard targets from beyond your normal range.  Also, collisions deal fixed damage regardless of speed or impact angle, which can frequently result in your instantaneous loss of all your shields from drifting too close to something while trying to kill a target.  Also, I found that it was necessary to rebind most of the weapon control keys to something else in order to not keep hitting the wrong button accidentally.
Strike Suit Zero generally manages to be a game from a dead genre that reminds you that you want more games in the genre, but rarely manages to be even average at what it tries to do.

The easiest way to tell if you will enjoy this game is to take this simple test, stop reading if you answer "no" since this game is not for you. Do you like JRPGs? Do you enjoy a difficult challenge (really stressing the difficult here). Do you enjoy  unique combat systems and large casts of characters, several of which have very detailed backstories. If you have answered yes to the aforemented, buy this game, now. No seriously do it, its one of the most enjoyable and simultaneously frustrating games I've ever played (due to its difficulty). The main selling point in this game for me was the battle system, you fight with large squads in a 3 dimensional battle zone where numerous variables often mean the difference between victory or defeat. With the game having a maximum of 18 player characters in a single battle, in up to 5 squads, its understandable to see how it can be a confusing and complex battle system where sometimes you are not given the options you want when you want them, this can be handled with tweaking abilities before a fight as I learned later on, but it is an incredibly complex battle system which is well beyond anything Square Enix or any developer I'd wager has done. The story is the typical serving from Square Enix, although much more like their older titles (as in focused on single story and world but giving you lots of free reign to explore and expand the story with relevant side missions). The general premise for the game is hard to explain, and for that I'd refer you to the game itself as it is told quite well and it evolves as you progress through the game, one thing leads to another etc. The music is good as are the graphics for this title, with only some details being loaded delayed (could be my end). The voiceacting and dialogue is a mixed bag, with sometimes it being well scripted and logical, while other times it is random and idiotic (sometimes in a good way). In summary I give a full recommendation, its  one of the true JRPGs on steam at this time, if not the only one. It isn't for everyone, however if you are a JRPG fan, and have the time to sit down and dive into the masterpiece which is The Last Remnant, I fully recommend it.

First off, I need to say that I need to spend may more hours playing this game.  Secondly, if you have been playing the Civ games for a long time and win the space victory and then find youself wondering, "Well that was awesome, but now what?"  then this is the game for you.
They have finally gone back to explain to us what happens when the space race happens.  When you select your starting faction, you are in essence selecting who won the space victory in the previous Civ game.  One of the settings is to have the different factions arrive on different turns.  This is genius in my opinion.  Even on the harder difficulties, no one achieves the victory condition at the same time.
That being said, this is not really a new game.  In my opinion and experience I would call this a "stand-alone expansion."  What I mean by that is you can play this game having never heard of any of the Civilization games before.  It will teach you how to play.  But if you have more than 200+ hours on Civ5, you may feel like you waiting a couple years for an expansion.  The graphics are the same, most of the resources are the same, and it plays a lot like a very detailed mod of Civ5.
If you are ok with what was just said, then know that I highly encourage you to buy this game.  I am the guy who has always wondered what happened after you won.  It has inspired me to go back and finish my achievements in Civ5 and then come back to it.
Happy Gaming

If you don't have Smash4 and don't want to set up Faster Melee, I can recommend this.
Otherwise, I prefer Smash Bros personally.
What Rivals of Aether has over Smash Bros is a neat tutorial explaining some advance tactics to Smash gameplay.
What ROA removes is ledge grabbing and grabbing. This is so the gameplay is more simplified and moves quicker without interruption. But the game loses variety because of it. No grab into combos. No advanced edge guarding. The focus of the game is doing a combo to push someone off the stage, and because there's no edge it's more simple to do.
Shielding is also removed, parrying is replaced by it. Now if you play online lets say, everyone who has played the game a lot will know all the cool combos that will spell your death if you get hit even once. So that's where the parry comes in. But to me this system isn't really compelling.
I know there are people who prefer this simplified version of the Smash Bros formula, but if you like grabbing or shielding it ain't gonna be there for yeah.

Jeez, I don't even know where to start. To make things simple, if you can buy this on sale for $5 or less, then I'd say it's probably worth playing if you're into generic hack and slash RPGs. Otherwise, this could have been an awesome reimagining of Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance or Champions of Norrath but falls flat in so many areas.
Combat encounters are loads of fun at first because you're not hindered by the awful AI partners; they can actually kill enemies, revive you, and face groups on their own without your constant babysitting. About 6 hours in (of around 12-14), the beefier enemy types stop reacting to your moves which turns the fun hack and slash combat into a chore of "XXY, roll away or block, XXY, etc," and reviving your AI partners because they don't block or roll. About another 2 hours after that, though, you run into enemies who interrupt your attacks and can stun lock you, so good luck reviving anyone once one of your partners is down unless you're lucky (or play Ranger and abuse his Evasion skill).
There's also no sense of empowerment as you gain new abilities and equipment. Even ignoring the fact that most abilities (for even the Lore-Master/Wizard) are just boring power attacks that have a cooldown, they never end up doing enough damage to make them feel worth while as you progress through the game. New enemies are thrown at you in such a way that by the time you're doing significantly more damage, the enemies have double the health they used to.
I'm not sure how common the technical issues are (seems like more of an AMD thing), but unless you want to downgrade drivers you can probably expect to deal with an inconsistent framerate that BOMBS for seemingly no reason at certain points in the game. Bugs are littered throughout as well, but I didn't run into anything that wasn't solved by quitting and reloading a checkpoint.
I should note I didn't play any coop in the game, so maybe that saves some of the issues with its combat, but it's hard to believe the studio that made the amazing Dark Alliance and Champions of Norrath released this. It could have been so much more.

Rivals of Aether is a 2D fighting game. As is clear from the gameplay and what others have to say about it, this game is very similar to Nintendo's Super Smash Bros. series. It most closely relates to Super Smash Bros. Melee, widely regarded as the most 'competitive' game in the series. This game shares many aspects of Super Smash Bros., and I will be comparing both games frequently.
Firstly, this game is designed to appeal to more competitive players of fighting games. However, this does not mean the game is difficult to play or understand. The basics of the game are as follows: up to four players fight against each other on a stage, each player having a certain amount of 'Stocks'(lives). The objective is to lower your opponent's stocks to 0. The first player to do this wins. Damage works similarly as it does in Smash Bros., where your character starts the game with 0% damage. As you get hit by enemy attacks, your damage percentage will rise. The higher your damage percentage, the easier it is to knock you off the stage. If a player is knocked farther than the edge of the screen(past what is known as the "blast zone"), they will lose a stock, and respawn in the center of the stage.
Every character has numerous attacks and abilities at their disposal. Each character has 5 aerial attacks, 4 strong attacks, and 4 'special' attacks. These moves have a wide variety of effects, and each character has its own unique playstyle. As in other fighting games, moves can be strung together, creating combos.
This game is heavily centered around competitive play, and has a lot of competitive 'techs'(techniques) that can be used by all characters, including Wavedashing, Teching, etc. Many of these techs are derived from Super Smash Bros. Melee. The characters also share many similarities with Melee characters. Many of the characters in Rivals of Aether are culminations of the attacks of different Melee characters. For example, Wrastor, the bird character, is a combination of Marth and Falco from Melee. Likewise, Absa is a combination of Pikachu, Ness, and Mewtwo from Melee.
This game is quite difficult to grasp when you first start(especially if you've never played a Smash Bros game before), but it does a great job of introducing its mechanics and features to the player. For example, the aforementioned 'techs' are all taught to you by the game in the tutorial, including the new mechanics added by the game. The tutorial is very extensive, and does a phenomenal job of teaching new players how to play the game and even how to use some advanced techniques. There are some major differences between Rivals of Aether and Smash Bros. Firstly, the addition of 'parrying'. In Smash Bros, every character can shield enemy attacks for a certain duration, negating any damage done to them until they lower their shield. In Rivals of Aether, characters cannot shield, but instead have to parry. Parrying, like shielding, provides temporary immunity to damage, however you are only immune for a very short time. If an opponent attacks you as you parry, they will be temporarily disabled, meaning that they cannot perform any action. During this time, you are free to attack them. The addition of parrying makes Rivals of Aether a lot more fast-paced, as players can no longer hold their shield button down to block attacks. Instead, it forces players to anticipate enemy attacks and properly time their parry to punish their opponent, further adding to the game's competitive nature.
The game currently features only a couple of gamemodes, including local and online play, however there are new gamemodes in development. Online play is quite entertaining, however the lag can get unbearable at times. Very rarely will you find an online match that doesn't lag even a little bit. I really hope the developers can work on this, as quick response time is imperative for a competitive fighting game such as this. Local play works fine, and the AI is pretty good. You will, however, get to the point where the AI doesn't even stand a chance, making the single player experience a little weaker, although the game is still very fun nonetheless.
As for presentation, this game has brightly-colored, varied stages that are all accompanied by their own music. Each stage is unique, and the music fits the game really well. The character animations are great, and there is a lot of detail on character designs and stages. I should point out the slight customization in this game. Rivals of Aether allows players to create their own color schemes for every character, altering not only the character's color, but the color of some of their moves as well. This might seem like a minor addition, but It's quite fun to design your own color scheme and use it in online games.
In conclusion, Rivals of Aether is a really good fighting game. It is very competitively-oriented, but it does an amazing job of teaching its many mechanics and techniques to newer players. The stages and characters are well-designed, fighting is fun and fast-paced, and the music is amazing too. If you've never played a competitive fighting game, Rivals of Aether is probably the best place to start.
Seeing as how this review is 13 billion words long, I'll summarize.
TL;DR: If you like fighting games, you'll love Rivals of Aether. If you've never played a competitive fighting game, you'll love Rivals of Aether.

I love Magic. It was a fun and cool part of my childhood, and thus, I want to like this game too.
I REALLY tried to like it, but in its current state, I can't do that.
The game has more flaws than interesting things, and it is a really bad experience for newcomers in MTG. It starts all right, with a decent difficulty curve in the first set of quests, lets you buy a few boosters and everything is peachy. You can ALMOST ignore the constant disconnects and the game's mutant superpower of disconnecting right after a game and therefore denying you your gold.
But then, as soon as you go beyond Gideon, there it comes the brick wall. Just as if the game is screaming "HEY WANNA WIN? BUY ME SOME GOLD AND GET YER BOOSTARS!".
AI becomes a nightmare, even in Easy, as it casts things that are nigh impossible to stop with your still-crappy available cards (enemy casting a 6/6 giant with renown 6, for instance) since it looks like every time you use a deck, a perfectly opposite nemesis deck with better cards is matched against you. And all you have is a Frost Lynx. Yey.
All in all, this is what I can see for the moment:
Pros:
-Well designed GUI, easy to learn and pick up.
-Well explained tutorials for every single effect.
-Good background music
-Quickly build a deck and play it, it takes no longer than 5 minutes
-Deck builder contains a quick reference for experienced players, so you can build a working deck with your custom strategy
Cons:
-SERIOUS connectivity issues. You will lose more gold to this than the cheaty AI
-Unfair, really really unfair, once you win the first few games.
-Deck wizard limits your already limited selection of cards, forcing you to adapt your deck to the archetype strategy. This mostly results in a bad mana curve, expensive cards and bad combos.
-Deck builder lets you create your very own personalized deck... that won't count towards most quests since you are forced to use a deck wizard archetype deck for those
-Forced to play colors you don't like and bad, boring decks to accomplish most quests
-Battling friends won't earn you any gold, because of reasons.
-Neither does Two Headed Giant
-*Very limited pool of cards
*This may change in the future, as they add the expansion packs for this base set.
All in all, it's a well designed game with an unfair "you get owned so you spend cash in the store to get better cards" style. It starts great and gets dull, boring and frustrating after a short while.
I'll check it again in some time, and if some issues are adressed I'll change my review to the one I've always wanted it to be since I heard about the development of this game.
IT. SHOULD. BE. A. GOOD. GAME.
But it's not. Yet.

Bioshock Remastered
Action-RPG
2K Boston, 2K Australia, Blind Squirrel
2K
is the remastered version of the 2007 FPS action-RPG. This review will focus on the main additions of the remaster rather than its story and gameplay, which are the same as the original version.
has one of the better stories ever told in a video game: you play as Jack, sole survivor of a plane crash. He finds himself near a lighthouse that houses a bathysphere terminal that takes him to the underwater utopic city of Rapture. The city has turned into a dystopia run by Andrew Ryan, objectivist business magnate, and your goal is to find him and put an end to the chaos that's been going on in the city.
The story takes many interesting twists and turns, and it is worth playing only for it. It rightfully deserves a spot in the pantheon of video game history as an example in storytelling (even though the actual ending is kinda weak).
The graphics have definitely been improved, with updated textures and the lack of fog as the most notable differences. However, there are some problems...
Even though I am not among them, many players are having constant crashes, and I can't not acknowledge this. While performance is always over 60FPS, there is constant frame drops ranging from 100 to 70 (while I don't notice the difference all that much, those who do find it very annoying).
My biggest issue is the lack of graphics options: the original had a lot of different settings that you could enable, while this one only has V-sync, antialiasing (ON or OFF), anisitropic filtering, and Expanded FOV. For a game released in 2016, these settings are truly insulting. But is it enough not to let me recommend the game? Not really.
The game is an FPS with RPG features. You can buy upgrades for your weapons, unlock new plasmids (which are special powers like using electricity, fire, telekinesis), hack turrets and cameras by playing the classic pipe minigame. The shooting feels very outdated, but it still works in this context. Fighting the Bid Daddies in order to either Save or Harvest the Little Sisters ranks amongst the most intense mini-boss fights in modern gaming, and the Metroidvania approach rewards exploration.
The game offers a solid challenge, especially when fighting a Big Daddy. I also recommend playing on Hard mode from the get-go, since there is more fun having normal Splicers give you a solid challenge.
The voice acting and soundtrack are as excellent as before. Again, some players have synchronization problems with the audio, but I had no issue at all.
Other than the campaign and the two different endings, there are 65 Steam achievements to unlock, Challenge Rooms to beat, Director's Commentary to listen to, and a Museum of concept arts to visit.
Overall,
is not the best port out there since many players are having technical issues. For once, I was lucky enough to have a smooth experience, and since this is free for owners of the original version (and you still get the original when buying the Remastered), there is no harm in replaying this quality aRPG.

The problem with not playing these games in order is that they all share the same sci-fi backstory, which is continued from game to game, although the emphasis on this part of the story varies per game. I don't think it's all that great, although there are some very neat moments when the plot of the past and present overlap.
They all have on thing in common: Being outstanding virtual tourism games, since they create a remarkable look into the past, which despite some more or less obvious artistic liberties, feels quite authentic most of the time. Bustling city life and impressive vistas were there right from the start and there hasn't really been another games series yet that managed to pull of something comparable. Chances are, if a particular era you like is represented by an Assassin's Creed game, that representation will be the most appealing rendition of it in a video game.
As others have said, AC II and Black Flag are the best in the series. AC II shines thanks to its fascinating story and setting in Renaissance Italy and Black Flag is just a really enjoyable, gorgeous pirate game.
The original Assassin's Creed has aged significantly, that's true, but it's still a rather impressive looking game with huge cityscapes. At the time of its release, it was one of the best looking games on the market and to many, including myself, it was one of the games that really showcased the power of the last console generation and contemporary PCs. The fact that you can scale any building in the game's vast cities was just unheard of, especially with such smooth and responsive animations and controls (for the time). The first time I climbed a tower and saw that dramatic camera pan around it is one of the most memorable gaming moments of that era, even if it's now a cliché for Ubisoft open world games. Combat is alright, quite graphic, but it can be both too easy and unfair, depending on the situation. While the cities are large and fairly detailed, there isn't really much to do outside of the passable, but repetitive missions. Both future and past story lines are solid, but nothing to write home about. However, if you like conspiracy stories, it might be just the thing for you.
Assassin's Creed II is better than its predecessor in every way. The story is filled with charismatic and interesting characters, the Renaissance Italy is almost overflowing with color compared to the almost monochromatic predecessor, which used strong color correction post-processing to give each location and distinct, but rather dull look. Controls are smoother, combat is much more enjoyable (still dated though - this was too shortly after Arkham Asylum, the game that defined modern third person brawling, after all), mission design is more varied, there's an overabundance of side activities, the modern day plot really takes off. It's a great game, a modern classic. Enjoyable without having played its predecessor, but more enjoyable if you've played it, since experiencing the impressive amount of progress is just remarkable.
The rest of the Ezio trilogy, Brotherhood and Revelations, is best described as more of the same. There are a few minor gameplay additions and modifications, but nothing too major. Most people stayed on board, because they wanted to experience the story of Ezio. They feel somewhat lackluster compared to II, although nobody would deny how competent and polished they are.
Assassin's Creed III is a bit of an odd game. Expectations were high after the end of the Ezio trilogy and many players were hungry for a new scenario, with speculation about ancient Egypt or Medieval Japan being the setting running high. The announcement of it being set during the time of the American Revolution was seen as catering to American schoolchildren, to put it mildly, at least outside of the US. Development was plagued with issues and the game was plagued by bugs upon release, albeit nowhere near as much as a certain later game in the series. With the colonial setting, the large, sprawling cities the series is known for were gone, as there were no major cities in America at the time, and with them much of the city parkours, replaced only partially by lengthy and unwelcome sections in nature. The half-native American protagonist was an odd choice, there were jumps in the storyline as the result of last-minute changes to the game, etc. A complete revamp of the combat system was promised, but it felt very similar and somewhat dated. The modern day story is again quite noticeable and important. Overall, it's by many considered to be one of the weakest entries in the series, but again, if you're interested in seeing a rather pretty rendition of that era, it might have some appeal. One aspect was however well received: Sea battles, which were transformed into a major gamplay element with the next entry.
Black Flag and its standalone DLC Freedom Cry are somewhat of a departure. For the first time, players are not controlling an Assassin. Modern day sections were significantly paired back and now resemble a point and click adventure game. You might almost forget they are there. The writing is sharp, fun and energetic, it looks absolutely stunning at times, especially on the ocean during storms, the soundtrack is probably the best in the series, the map is overflowing with activities. If you are a completionist, then this might be the game that breaks you. There are large cities, caves, jungles, ancient ruins, wrecks, massive boss ships, small islands, treasure maps with corresponding treasures, just so much to do. Ship to ship combat plays a huge role. It's not realistic, but there is a modicum of strategy involved and the final boarding of battered and damaged enemy ships is still one of the most remarkable things I've ever seen in a videogame. You can climb masts and other parts of every ship just like you can climb buildings and as two ships get close enough to each other, the animation and control system elegantly deals with it. Combat is a bit of a mixed back. I really don't see any progress, but it's alright, if too easy most of the time.
Next up, there's Rogue. Basically Black Flag again with a slightly different setting, but interestingly, this is the first time the player is seeing the story pan out from the other side of the conflict. This game was meant to be somewhat of a second prize for the old console generation, which did not receive Unity, the next big entry in the series that was developed at the time, but it turned out to be much better reviewed and was later ported to PC. It's really good. If you're looking for more of Black Flag, Rogue does just that.
Unity was meant to showcase the power of a new engine on new console hardware, but it did not go as planned. Set during the French revolution in a stunning rendition of 18th century Paris, it's easily the most visually impressive game in the series to date, but the visuals and massive crowds (the series was always known for large crowds, but Unity turned it up to 11 with sometimes hundreds of characters on screen) were too much for consoles and PCs of the time. Hideous glitches, instability and other issues quickly ruined its reputation. Going from the open seas and sea battles to a single, albeit pretty, city location was perceived as a downgrade by many. It didn't help that controls were floaty, the writing undecided and gameplay variation lacking. After many patches and on modern hardware, it's perfectly playable now and if you want to explore a beautiful Paris with more detail than pretty much any other open world game, then this is still quite an attractive proposal.

As most reviews say, this is not the Hitman you know, this is very different. The levels are not as big as some of the previous games, but if you ask me, they are way more detailed and more options than the previous Hitman games. You don't get to much of an open world anymore, but more a, get from point A to Point B style. i was skeptical about this at first, but grew to love it, even though it's a From point A to B, you still get alot of diversion and ALOT of choices on how you wanna get there. The new disguise system is 50/50, i love how it adds to the realism. The cop will know you are not one of his colleagues, but how is the civillian to know that you are not a cop? It is a bit to sensitive though, even though you are standing with your back to a guy who is 6-7 meters away he will still notice that you are not one of them, and that is a bit to much. You don't get to choose what weapons and equipment you wanna use anymore at the start of the game though, but i think this adds to the fun, and it works well with the story, this also means that you don't have a pocket filled with thousand coins anymore, instead you gotta find objects around the world, that you can use as distractions/weapons, this is also a welcome change.
The story is also a big part of Absolution, in the previous games. You got your mission and then you executed it, however you felt like and that was that, and that was good, cause that's why you played it.
I felt alot more motivated to keep going in this one, cause of the story and what happend in it, and even though i mostly try to do it stealth with none or a few extra casualties , there was just places where i went in guns blazing cause i didn't think the ones i was up against deserved to live. I also had some really heartpounding moments, cause i was so focused on killing my target for one reason or another and that rarely happens to me.
On that note, it also alot funnier to do fire fights in Absolution: When you empty your 45 cal. UMP magazine into a guy and you see him spasm all over the place as he falls to the ground, feels really awesome.
All in all I will give this game a 9/10 it is a great game, but with a few things i would like tweeked, but these things are so minor that they can be looked through pretty easly. Don't expect the next version of Blood Money, but a deeper more involved game.

Where to begin... actually, I have a good idea.
Quite simply put, this game is unfinished. Beyond the plethora of bugs and performance issues, there aer many, many features that are simply not well implemented or unfinished. THERE IS NO RADAR ON A SPACE SIM GAME. That's something AWFULLY basic to leave out of a space sim.
Trading is another excellent example of this. In order to trade in this game, you have to order your freighters to go around picking up or selling wares which takes ten or twenty minutes depending on the location or god forbid, you run into a bug where your freighter simply sits there and do nothing. However, for some unknown reason, Egosoft decided that a cancel trade order button is not necessary. Really? At this point, I don't even know if this is intentional design or just another checkmark on the growing list of unfinished features.
Beyond key missing features, the state of the game itself feels unfinished as well. The truly awful looking character models look like they are placeholders until something better takes their place, and space scenery, while gorgeous, wavers upon closer examination as you fly up next to ships and stations and see generic, bland, I would say almost placeholder-like low-res textures.
Adding in walk-in stations per requested below. There are only 3-4 presets in every system, which wouldn't be so bad in and of itself if the game did not force you to walk in stations for every other interaction. Picking up missions, dropping off missions, hiring marines, hiring pilots and officers. Couple that with the atrocious looking NPCs and you can see why almost no one likes this aspect of the game. The fact that the most popular mod is to REMOVE the need to walk in stations says volumes in and of itself. That being said, it can be a great platform for future mods, but in its current state, implementation, and restrictions? It is really bad.
