How do you suppose the world is going to end? Here in the thick of 2017 we have more options than ever, but climate change is certainly a popular one. That's the angle that A New Beginning takes, the fight against a ruined future fought in the trenches of environmental science and politics. But it turns out that it's not fracking or carbon that's going to do us in. No, what truly dooms the world are the absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥ people you have to deal with throughout this adventure, people so repugnant that you almost can't help but lie back and wait for everyone to die.
A New Beginning opens in the fjords of Norway with Bent Svensson, a reclusive scientist who gave up his hopes of a green future to grumble about how much he hates his life. A mysterious woman named Fay shows up on his doorstep to recount a mad tale of a future destroyed by climate change and a desperate quest through time to prevent it. While most of the action takes place in flashbacks there are plenty of interludes with Bent and Fay, eventually leading to the actions in the present that will determine the fate of humanity.
There's a chance that all sounds pretty neat, so let's go back to Bent's grumblings real quick. While puttering around in the makeshift prologue tutorial, Bent is going to harangue you constantly about his failures as a scientist, his failures as a father, and his failure to actually do anything about any of it. When Fay shows up, instead of helping kick-start his long-dead motivation, the first thing she does is call him an idiot for accidentally harming a bird. And then later, Bent's therapist calls him and actively discourages him from improving his life in an absolutely INFURIATING dialogue where you are forced to say something stupid and self-harming. I almost quit on the spot, but somehow regrettably soldiered on.
Now let's fast forward to chapter 2 and Fay's efforts to determine the cause of the apocalypse. She's joined by two teammates, one of which is the most hostile, dismissive, and venomous ally I've ever had in a video game. There's not a hint of humor to it, either; he hates Fay, fully thinks her useless, ridicules her (your) efforts to do anything, and twists her accomplishments to his own ends. He's a wholly reprehensible human being, and your other teammate is a depthless doormat who defers to Captain ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in every conflict. At this point, my regret was palpable.
Doesn't that sound like fun? Trying to save the planet with a gaggle of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who resent your successes? Bent is no better, constantly picking apart Fay's stories and belittling her conclusions. And Fay herself vacillates between woman of action and gormless simpleton, plowing through puzzles as you direct her but often being caught off-guard or making terrible, baseless assumptions about anything new. And I'm not even digging into the worst of this compost pile... To progress the plot, Fay will happily sabotage her own allies, and one of said allies will at one point murder an innocent in cold blood.
I cannot stress enough how disgusting the story beats and interactions between these people are. Every one of them is awful in their own way, and their lines come off as entirely divested from reality with ill-timed snark and bizarre exceptions to the strangest things. I'm sure something is being lost in translation here but there's no way that can account for the abject unpleasantness of every person you are forced to interact with. And, AND, this idiocy extends to the over-arching plot which isn't content to just let climate change happen as it's happening, but ties the apocalypse to a baselessly alarmist doomsday scenario involving a nuclear power plant. I suppose I shouldn't be surprised that writers who can't even make people sound like people don't know the first thing about environmental science, but it is shocking just how angry the ignorance on display could make me.
In mechanical terms, A New Beginning is on the lower end of point-and-click competence anyway. The interface is clear enough, and most of the puzzles make sense and provide decent challenges. However, just about every chapter has at least one puzzle or sequence where what you need to do is clear, but the solution requires an extra twist of complexity that only the developers would think of. One example is when you have to power up a hand-held laser drill. There's a whole bit about locating a battery and a power interface that should do the trick, except you ALSO have to change the focusing lens by carving a chunk out of something that the game warns you is rickety and should not be messed with, and can only be interacted with at one tiny corner.
The art isn't bad with its clean items, expansive backdrops, and detailed characters, though the animations have a pretty severe lack of frames. Sound does its job as well, and I admit they got decent voice actors for this, even if their lines and direction are awful. A New Beginning would be a tolerable adventure game if it wasn't filled to the brim with intolerable morons slogging through an equally moronic story. After the prologue got my blood pressure up I stuck it out maybe a third of the way through the game, but not only did the aggravations not let up, they found new ways to infuriate me. Honestly, if playing through A New Beginning were the only way to avert the apocalypse, I'd rather just die and get it over with.

Hollow Knight is the best Metroidvania ever created, and I honestly don't think anyone can top it. It is personally my Game of the Year for 2017. The fact that Team Cherry, a small group of developers from Australia, perfected the Metroidvania genre on their first Try... is really astonishing. Hollow Knight is a game about a kingdom and the bugs inhabiting it. I really don't want to explain the story for spoilers sake, but just know that the game takes inspiration from dark souls unconventional way of story telling, and constructs its own narrative from it. A lot of the story and lore is told through journal entries and the enviroment. The vibe of the game is very dark and derelict, but still manages to have light hearted parts scattered throughout. The soundtrack is also amazing. The ost  has many different tracks that just fit the mood of the game perfectly. From the depressing overtones of dirtmouth to the enchanting melody of Greenpath. The Soundtrack is just one of those things i listen to when im doing my schoolwork. Overall, the presentation is top notch. The   Gameplay, however is where Hollow Knight truly shines. Just like any other Metroidvania, when you first start the game, your moveset is very limited, but as you progress, you become more versetaille. There is something truly satisfying about backtracking to a place you already discovered. and killing all the enemies that used to give you trouble in like a couple hits. Also with your ever expanding moveset, you discover new paths in places you already visited, making you feel like you are evolving with the map. These motifs however, appear in almost every other Metroidvania, the difference with Hollow Knight however, is the level of polish applied to it.  Hollow Knight takes the best ideas from the genre, and perfects them while also bringing a lot of new ideas to the table, and executing them flawlessley. For example, in the game, you can purchase maps of different areas, however the maps aren't filled out, making you be the one to fill it out yourself. It really makes the player feel like an explorer while also opening up a truly open experience that makes other metroidvanias feel  linear in comparison. The enemies and bosses are also incredible as well. There are exactly 144 enemies in the game, with 30 of them being bosses. All of these enemies have their own, design and attack pattern, making the nearly 25 hour campaing never feel repetitive or tiring.  The Combat is amazing, and thats just because of the free range of movement and special attacks you are given. In other Metroidvanias, usually you can't control the characters jump pretty well. Some games like metroid allow little movement when your in the air, while castlevania you just jump in a straight arc. In Hollow knight,  You can adjust the height and distance of your jump, making the bosses and the way you fight your enemies a lot more strategic and engaging.The Gameplay is just pure bliss.
My only Flaw with the game is the degenerate Grey Mourner Mission Which (SPOILERS!) Involves you carrying a flower from one side of the map to the other without getting hit or teleporting. That Sidequest made me want to blow my brains out.

Torchlight, like its sequel, is a quite enjoyable ARPG dungeon-crawler with a lot of loot, fun, and exploration to be had! I've enjoyed this game since 2013, and although I haven't played it in a while, it, along with Torchlight II, are probably my favorite ARPG games!
The game is set in the small mining town of Torchlight, and the town needs help, as its mine is being attacked by monsters. As you continue further and further down the mine, you'll see a vast array of different enemies and environments, and quite a bit of loot to be had!
There are three classes in Torchlight, and each one has different spells and weapon specializations.
The Alchemist is a mage, specializing in staffs and wands, and has elemental spells and attacks. He has the highest MP of the classes.
The Destroyer is a melee-oriented class that is best at using swords, axes, maces, and polearms. He has the largest health pool of the classes.
The Vanquisher is a range-oriented class which has abilities that strengthen her ranged combat. She is best suited for long-range combat.
Torchlight is an enjoyable game to play, and and its visuals nice. Its soundtrack is excellent, as well, and compliments the game quite nicely, giving it its cool style, just like the sequel has a nice style. The environments in the game are pretty fascinating as well, and sometimes quite varied, and there's many places to explore, and some side quests to do too.
I also appreciate how lightweight it is, graphically. I think it still looks pretty good, while at the same time, being able to run even on old machines in my home, including old laptops!
Throughout the game, just like with its sequel, there is a huge variation of armor, weapons, and enchantments that you will find, and you can also transmute items and enchant things at an enchanter. You can also find "ember" to socket items, which gives you various bonuses.
Overall, I have no complaints about Torchlight. Its gameplay is very satisfying and quite fun, and I would certainly recommend this game, as well as its sequel, which introduces multiplayer co-op! Definitely pick both of them up, if you are someone who enjoys ARPGS, Co-op games, and loot games. ^.^

Alright let me start off by saying this game is definitely one I'd recommend giving a shot. It's incredibly powerful, and made me feel like a terrible human being on more than one occassion.
Anyway, my "This War of Mine" story starts off like this:
My three survivors, Pavle, Bruno and Katia, lived together in a bombed shell of a building, but they were happy. Well, as happy as they could be under the circumstances. We had enough food and enough resources to get us by. By Day 7, we had a knock at the door. I had thought it was a trader, like the first few days, but I was wrong. It was a school teacher by the name Cveta, who was asking for a place to stay. She didn't offer much to the group, but I took her in regardless of the fact that our supplies were running low. I couldn't bring myself to say no.
That night, I decided to send Cveta out to see if taking her in wasn't a complete waste. I sent her to a small apartment block to scavenge some supplies. Needless to say, she did quite well. The only issue was that she stole it. My group, and myself, felt quite bad. It wasn't anything to be worried about, but it was a bit of a blow to the groups morale.
The next night, I sent Pavle out to the same apartment block to see if we could scavenge some supplies without robbing the people. As I was traversing the building, one of the residents saw me and went to alert their friend, who was armed with a fully loaded shotgun. I ran downstairs and hid in a dark corridor. By some miracle, he knew where I was and aimed his gun at me. I acted on impulse and clicked, and took him down with one knife stab to the chest. Followed by two more. In my eyes, it was an instant kill. But for Pavle, it was the longest moment ever. I didn't want to kill this man, but it was him or me. Suddenly, his friends (or family, I couldn't know for sure) ran downstairs and tried to attack me, but they were unarmed. Pavle slashed at one of them, cutting the arm. They then began to beg for mercy and cry as they stood around their friend's corpse. I took everything I could find and ran home.
Pavle, and I, for that matter, felt terrible. I actually had to turn the game off for the night and went back to it the next day.
I managed to survive 37 days on my first run without losing any survivors. But Katia died on a scavenging run on the 37th night, and I felt so attacthed to this characters and everything they'd been through, I deleted the save and had to start again.
10/10 would recommend

I only got round to playing Crysis in 2015, although I've been meaning to for years!
From what I'd seen, I was under the impression that you'd play a kind of semi-indestructable super soldier in this game, dashing and jumping around at high speed and slicing through dozens of enemy soldiers with ease, but really it plays more like you're just a fairly standard FPS soldier dude with a few perks. I found myself not bothering with things like the stealth and speed mode very often as they both drain your energy incredibly quickly. On hard difficulty, a few well-placed enemy bullets can still take you down if you're not careful so you don't really feel invulnerable.
The gameplay is fairly standard FPS fare, akin to Call Of Duty or whatever, with open-ish world elements but lots of set pieces. The game world never feels as open as, say, the Far Cry series and you are pretty much railroaded into tackling things in order, though how you approach each set piece is up to you and you do feel that you can take a variety of approaches to solve the obstacles you encounter.
The graphics have really stood the test of time, It didn't feel particularly dated.
My only gripe was that the campaign only took me 10 hours to play through - and I didn't exactly rush through it. If I'm honest, the storyline is also very standard and unengaging, following a rather cliched 'US saves the world from alien invasion that is unwittingly aided by the nasty Asians' formula that's all too familiar by now.
Overall, I'd say that if you're a fan of the FPS genre, you've never played Crysis before and you see if on sale for a few pounds/dollars (like I did) then it's definitely worth picking up! It's an enjoyable, if short, experience.

A fun enough Diablo-like ARPG.
The graphics are fairly lo-fi (even for the time) but the art direction is nice so it works.
Audio design is fine and the soundtrack is pretty amazing in places, but god I can't stand the old man voice telling me when I've finished a quest, levelled up etc, his pretentious fake british accent makes my flesh scream.
The story is as basic as they make them ("something evil is threatening our village, work your way through the dungeon and kill it"), but honestly what would you expect from a hack'n'slash?
As for the most important part, that is, the gameplay:
- The industry standard three classes: tanky melee guy, archer woman and mage. I went with the archer because that's what I always do in this sort of game.
- The four character stats (strength, dexterity, mana and defence) are really straightforward - strength buffs melee, dexterity buffs ranged weapons, mana buffs elemental damage and defence makes you tankier. Items have stat requirements that (unlike in Torchlight II) you HAVE to meet in order to use them.
- Passive and active skills are simply locked by level as opposed to being arranged in a tree you progressively unlock. Active skills usually depend on weapon DPS and they're going to be your primary means of dealing substantial damage. Passives buff your combat abilities, pet, buy/sell prices, money drop rate and various other things.
- Maybe I was doing something wrong but even on Normal difficulty (2nd of the 4 available) enemies were very tanky so I had to spam a lot of attacks, especially on bosses. I'd rather have enemies who are easy to kill but more lethal when you let them attack you.
- The loot system is a little weird, for example I kept using a bow 20 levels lower than my character simply because I hadn't found a better one since. Sockets and enchantments allow you to improve gear but there's the annoying chance of an enchantment attempt disenchanting the item.
- You have a pet who helps in combat (but its role mostly just boils down to aggro tanking) and can run back to town to sell items so you don't have to warp back as often.
- Once you finish the main storyline you unlock a randomly generated dungeon with randomly generated kill/fetch quests, much like the entirety of Fate (the sort-of prequel to Torchlight). It gets repetitive after a while.
So yeah, this is a good ARPG that you should definitely play if you're into the genre at least a little bit. It's not as good as its sequel though, imho.

Some old bugs still plague this release (like the airplanes that never stop attacking). I've had it lock up my whole machine once. I'm into artsy visuals and gameplay, but this game didn't really satisfy me.
It looks great, and the explanation of gameplay mechanics is well done, obviously with the principle "Show, don't tell" in mind. Also the general idea of playing badgers is cute.
I barely got a chance to get emotionally attached to anything in this world. When my poor badger babies were stolen from me by nature's cruel hand, it didn't feel... sad? I was like "Oh man. Damn. Oh well.".
It happened quickly and cheaply every time that it did happen, and neither the badger lady I was playing nor its brethren seemed to care at all.
Basically, next to the cute idea of being a badger and the cute visuals, the game gave me no reason to feel attached to anything, no emotional buildup and all. Which is admittedly hard to do, when your game is as short!
I feel like the lesson this game was trying to teach me was "Look how difficult it is to survive in this hostile and cruel world!". And yeah, sure, that's true. And then what?
Without any emotional impact, there's not too much to take away from this game. The ending was anticlimactic, the gameplay mechanics that were there were really uninteresting - food was absolutely everywhere and felt like it had no impact, hunting the three kinds of other animals there were felt unnecessary and difficult - and most of the little gameplay time I have on this game, I spent waiting for my slow as ♥♥♥♥ badger babies to follow me.
And sure, subpar gameplay can be excused when your game gives you a great story or atmosphere that you can lose yourself in, but I absolutely didn't feel that here. Towards the end of the game, I was ready to accept the walking-simulator-esque if I found some redeeming quality in it. And then the game ended, and there was no redeeming quality left to find.
Unsurprisingly, replayability is close to zero as well. Can't really be arsed to go back and find SOME cute detail that I missed the first time that would make this game worth it.
All in all, I don't think it's worth your time or money. It's not a lot of money, and it's not a lot of time, but personally, I didn't find it fun, and I got nothing out of it, emotionally. You might. Maybe not. Probably not.

This Civ is not Civ 6 nor is it Alpha Centauri 2. If you expect either, you will not get what you want. Think of it as a spin-off of Civ V.
When in doubt there is a Demo you can play.
This part of the Civ franchise tries a few new concepts. Most importanlty it aims for "less is more":
Few well developed cities with rather low population can be more powerfull then a bunch of mega-cities.
The terrain also limits how many forces can be brought to bear on any city, meaning that here too class beats mass.
Truly unique is also the affinity system, wich can have much more impact on the playstyle then the Sponsor selection.
There is mod support for single player, with full Steam Workshop integration.
Culture/Borders, Civ 5 style unhappinies (in form of health), hex grids, One unit per tile and other stuff make a reappearance.
Release specific issues:
It has the usual amounts of bugs and imbalances, with some being able to prevent the game from running (again, the Demo is there).
Also noteable is a strong lack of visualsiation (wonder and victory videos in particular).
Also as with all previous Civ games it does not have everything of the previous Civ game+all it's expansions at release.

Change you character to who you want, select map size as *huge* and then the difficulty on hard. Pick plant settings as "random" and enjoy trying to survive in a realistic scenario.
The game is realistic in a couple of different ways:
Because you were launched at different times, you don't arrive at the same. So *you* may get to your planet in the year 2500AD to discover russias been there since 2490. In my first playthrough, France didn't arrive until 2600(The game starts aat 2500)

Being an avid Civ 5 player (500+ hrs), I had huge hopes for the sequel. However, this game was an utter let down. Civ: Beyond Earth was supposed to be a revolutionary game in the Civ series, but Firaxis really let its players down with this one.
- This is at most a shallow mod for Civ 5 (As they play very similar)
- Affinities were a nice idea but get lost as its really just, "Choose a victory and follow that affinity."
- The Tech web is somewhat boring as every player goes for the core values and then picks up the one or two needed for victory later on.
- The aliens are essentially barbarians that will get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at you
- The planets have a darker, more unconfortable feel than playing the regular Earth-like maps in civ 5
- They're really arent that many units, as Firaxis took like 3-4 base units and reskinned them depening on Affinity.
- The bonuses yeilded from a certain Affinity unit to another are nothing to call home about and haven't made a huge difference in my play style.
- The final Ultimate Units for each affinity are not actually that exceptional on the battlefield.
- Domination is essentially impossible with the new "Health" (Happiness) System, along with grand empires.
- Culture, as common with the rest of the Civ games, has always been promising and then falters. Here is not less as it is lost in the eyes of production and money, even as the culture sponsor.
- There are only 8 Sponsors... which they added a background (albeit shallow) that basically said they comprise all of earth, leaving the idea that Firaxis did not want to create more.
- Picking cargo and passengers for the initial games seemed fun until I realized my friends and myself would always pick relatively the same 3 or 4 things no matter who we played.
I could go on, but really what is comes down to is that this had HUGE potential. But ended up being a HUGE let down. For all the avid Civ fans out there, this would not be a game to be proud of in your library.

The remaster of bioshock generally is more of the same. While enhancing texture resolutions (and supporting higher resolutions) is of some value, the things that would actually be of some benefit to be changed coming back to it ten years later are still as they were in the original.
All of the animation jank from the original is still present here;
-main characters are still represented using enemy models
-prerendered cutscenes use very lossy codecs and have low audio quality
-Still no explanation as to how the player removes an entire big-daddy suit while in a tiny elevator in the final act.
These are a few of the things that could have been fixed when taking the effort to go back and remaster the game, but it feels like the only real difference between this and the original, is the inclusion of developer interviews.
To me, a remaster should do more than increase the maximum resolution of a game, it should try to make the vision of what was attempted, even closer to the dream. Being able to tell whether or not a can on the ground is cat-food or dog-food may make the game look sharper, but where the game was actually lacking was in the animation department, and that is harder to see through screenshots.
All that being said, if you want to play bioshock, this is the version you get. It has everything the original did, for better and worse.

If you're a long time fan of the Final Fantasy series, then you're in for another treat. Although the game is extremely linear, the majority of the game is very enjoyable. Furthermore, no game is without it's fair share of problems. Half the cast of characters that you'll be playing with aren't needed within the games story at all. Instead, they seem to either be an annoyance, or hardly used due to being a weaker overall character compared to others.
The story is fair, nothing that will blow you out of the water but enough to keep you interested and looking to see what happens in the game which if you look around and do a fair amount of battles/training, can see from start to finish of the game, last you 40-50 hours. The music however, is fantastic. Every battle, area, cutscene, has different unique music to it that's very enjoyable and my personal highlight of the game.
Another con for this game is that in my opinion, it has zero replayability to it whatsoever. Unless you're looking to play the game in a few years after completing it, which is completely fine, then replaying the story soon after beating the game isn't probably something you want to do. It's linearity is what condences the game too much which makes it feel very repetitive and not very engaging as if it would be more open.
Finally, one huge complaint that many people seem to have in the framerate in the game. Although a small sample of people don't have any issues, the vast majority of players will experience constant framerate drops throughout the game.  Cutscenes will always hit 60FPS without problem, but there are areas in the game that can see fluctuation in FPS. If you're using the minimap, just disabling it will for whatever reason, will increase the FPS drastically. Enabling the mini-map will drop your frames to 40 in most places, but disabling it will push it back up to a full 60FPS. Additionally, when entering a battle, the frames will even drop to 30FPS. Square Enix could've done a much better job of porting this over to help the FPS issues that many players have and would've made the experience of the game a little better.
The game struggles in certain places, but that doesn't overshadow the other aspects of the game too much. If you're a long time Final Fantasy fan or even a newcommer, I'd say pick it up.

War in the North is the tale of a dwarf, elf and ranger wandering the wastes and plains of Middle Earth away from the main events of J.R.R. Tolkien's book and films.
It's a respectful hack and slash action rpg, with the major gripes being the lack of much ability progression and a lot of the same enemies appearing over and over again. A mildly coherent tale against a relatively unknown antagonist is only brought back from boredom due to the rich lore that has been previously established.

Three characters playing on screen, Each one has their own unique moves, spells, and abilities and you fight against Sauron's minions in the North. One can get involved with alchemy, another with breaking down walls to find treasures, upgradeable weapons, gear armour etc. Other games do everything it offers better. There are a few short appearances from the major LOTR characters in Rivendell but their sudden appearance and disappearance only cements the insignifance of the playable characters. Campaigh is about 10-12 hours long, bit longer I would think on higher difficulties.

A great indie game and a very well-made Smash clone so far. Though there are only 8 characters, all of them are unique and varied in their playstyles, and have so much depth I could never get bored of using just one. My favorite is Orcane, with his slippery...slippery-ness and water abilities, though his recovery isn't always the best.
Gameplay is fast-paced and very focused on offense. There are no shields, so your only forms of defense are well-timed dodges and a new parry mechanic which lets you punish an attack or reflect projectiles, but can be punished if you don't use it correctly. No items, but I don't miss them and the game can get chaotic enough with four characters at once. Stages either have fun gimmicks or can be toggled to be more friendly to the serious player. Online is 1v1 only at this time, but the netcode is great as far as I could tell.
There's some great features of its own as well, like the ability to make your own color schemes for every character, a well-made tutorial that walks you through the basics before covering more advanced techniques and character-specific info, and playtesting controls ON THE CHARACTER SELECT SCREEN. Frankly, every fighting game needs something like this.
Don't get to play it as much as I like though, which is something I need to fix! The game does not seem far off from its full release, so hopefully more people can check it out. I highly recommend it (the music is great too)!

If you had a copy of the original version of this game in your steam account before this remastered update hit, then you're obviously not losing much.  If you're new to the Bioshock series and are thinking about trying it out, then I cannot honestly recommend the remastered edition in its current state and you're definitely safer starting off with the original releases or just wait for them to patch out the issues plaguing the remastered edition if you really want to play those.  As of this writing I'm about two hours into Bioshock remastered - haven't tried Bioshock 2 remastered yet.  I will say the improved graphics are nice when the textures aren't flickering like a CRT monitor.  The definite deal breaker though is that in my multiple playthrough attempts the game has without fail crashed to desktop every time I've picked up the armor piercing bullets in that closet with the turret in it in the Medical Pavilion.  This has happened twice in a row so far and from what I've read, I've been having one of the "better" experiences with this game so far.
Also one other thing I've noticed that I'm not sure is actually a fault with the game or not, but oddly it seems to me that it's a lot harder to hit enemies with the electro-bolt plasmid in the remastered edition.  Even when it looks like my reticule is dead on target, something like two out of three times it'll just miss them by a hair which is immensely frustrating since the "one-two punch" is pretty much your bread and butter in the first couple of levels in this game.  Again though, I don't know if I can pin this on the remastered release or not - it's entirely possible that I'm just bad at hitting people with the electro-bolt, although I don't remember having this problem in the original release.  And I'm only bringing this up because I'm curious if other people have noticed this as well and if they have any advice on the subject.
Anyway, it's looking like there are fixes on the way which is good news.  But until they've been implemented, I can't in good conscience recommend anyone who doesn't already own these games on steam try the remastered editions.
EDIT: I've played completely through both remasters since this review and I am very pleased to say that they've largely fixed the issues I initially had and from my experience they are both in a playable state.  The graphical changes they made really did spruce up the first game quite a bit and an FOV slider is always welcome.  As for the second game, any changes they made graphically are barely noticeable, and between the first two games it probably needed the least improvement anyway as it was already a pretty good looking game. It is nice that the remaster of the second game didn't have the incredibly vexing habit of crashing to desktop without warning like the original release did.

EPIC COMBAT SYSTEM: you don't control just one party, you control several parties at once on a battlefied against multiple groups of enemies. Gone is the traditional micro of turn-based combat; instead you direct each group to focus on magic or combat techniques and which enemy groups to engage - and then watch as both forces charge towards each other, resulting in interceptions, flanking, and morale swings. Late-game, the respawning normal monster combats become tedious, but the boss battles only get more EPIC.
Gorgeous visuals: I was once stuck on a quest wandering around a giant desert for 2hrs or so - and I didn't care, because the sand dunes in every direction just looked so pretty.
Immersive storyline of the kind SquareEnix is known for. Every character has a story.
The only thing I would gripe about is the expensive crafting system. At least your party members will just ask you for any components you have that they could use - you don't micro their equipment upgrades, either.

Daedalic Entertainment is a German developer specialised in point-and-click video games. I started playing
right after I finished
from Wadjet Eye Games. It was a nice transition since both are point-and-click games; Daedalic, however, employs hand-drawn graphics as opposed to Wadjet's pixelated approach.
We have two protagonists in this game. Bent is an inventor - he invented a new type of fuel. His blue algae can be used as a new alternative resource, however, he is not taken seriously. He enjoys his retirement (while his son continues his research) in a secluded area in Norway when a helicopter lands near his home. Fay, our 2nd playable character, claims to be a time traveller from the future who tells Bent how mankind destroyed its world by messing with the climate. In order to reverse the process his blue algae can be useful but they must act quickly otherwise mankind will be doomed by 2050.
We control either Bent or Fay (depending on where we are in the story) throughout 8 chapters (plus a prologue). The game looks great and regular cutscenes (in the form of comic book like storytelling) make the immersion better. I have to admit I really liked the game's soundtrack which often changes once you go to another screen. The journey also has an acceptable length as 10 hours or so will be needed to see our heroes' journey till the very end. Since the game is linear and there are no areas where choices are offered a walkthrough pretty much means no replayability here.
I thoroughly enjoyed the game from start to finish. I only had 2 annoying bits with it - first, there are some typos here and there and sometimes for an action we would like to carry out only the French, Spanish or Russian name pops up (e.g. you'd like to "look at" a window and the action is described as "examina"). The other part adds to the difficulty - it is not always obvious what you need to do. But this was the case with LucasArts games, too. I still remember picking up a dog with Guybrush Threepwood in Monkey Island who casually noted how big his pockets were. Here the issue is with mainly not knowing how to combine and use some items which would probably be obvious for a scientist or an engineer. A "hint" option as an aid would have been useful.
I recommend this game to the fans of the point-and-click genre. It might add to the experience if you are someone who likes games where contemporary issues are dealt with such as global warming in this case.

When i first started playing A New Beginning so many months ago I was very early bored by how hard the game was. No matter where I clicked or walked, I couldn't get further...and this happened early on...
I kept seeing many items and objects, which I clicked on, but nothing really got me further. As I like to complete games without help and walkthroughs, I had a hard time playing for a very long time per session. It got so boring.

...
I changed my way of playing. I found a walkthrough and used it whenever I got stuck for a longer time, and it became much more enjoyable to play. I liked the story, but standing around too long was not something I wanted, as it's a fairly long game.
At some point the game just became really exciting and the thrilling story could continue without any stops or hesitations. I also understood more about how the game worked, and could work out most of it myself, while only using the walkthrough for things I thought didn't sound right.
By the end of the game I played for hours, and after finishing it I wrote this review and now I want to recommend the game to other people aswell. The biggest problem with the game is that there are so many things that are there just for show, and sometimes I did the correct solution, but with the wrong timing. Really frustrating.
So on one hand...it's a really hard game to complete, and it's a pretty serious game too, so not getting further will make it boring, but I'll give it a thumbs up. Maybe not for everyone, but most definitely not a bad game.

First of all a premise: if you cannot stand buggy games don't buy this game UNDER ANY CIRCUMSTANCE! It seems like developers just stopped maintaining this software and let it fell apart on its own. Puzzles are average to good, maybe just a little bit too easy and seldom not that logic. The interface is in my opinion the true weakness of this title, since it is tricky to use and hard to get used to.
Unless what I wrote in the first paragraph made you think that you don't wanna deal with such a buggy thing, I strongly recommend you to buy this, especially if you are a fan of graphic adventures.

Alright let me start off by saying this game is definitely one I'd recommend giving a shot. It's incredibly powerful, and made me feel like a terrible human being on more than one occassion.
Anyway, my "This War of Mine" story starts off like this:
My three survivors, Pavle, Bruno and Katia, lived together in a bombed shell of a building, but they were happy. Well, as happy as they could be under the circumstances. We had enough food and enough resources to get us by. By Day 7, we had a knock at the door. I had thought it was a trader, like the first few days, but I was wrong. It was a school teacher by the name Cveta, who was asking for a place to stay. She didn't offer much to the group, but I took her in regardless of the fact that our supplies were running low. I couldn't bring myself to say no.
That night, I decided to send Cveta out to see if taking her in wasn't a complete waste. I sent her to a small apartment block to scavenge some supplies. Needless to say, she did quite well. The only issue was that she stole it. My group, and myself, felt quite bad. It wasn't anything to be worried about, but it was a bit of a blow to the groups morale.
The next night, I sent Pavle out to the same apartment block to see if we could scavenge some supplies without robbing the people. As I was traversing the building, one of the residents saw me and went to alert their friend, who was armed with a fully loaded shotgun. I ran downstairs and hid in a dark corridor. By some miracle, he knew where I was and aimed his gun at me. I acted on impulse and clicked, and took him down with one knife stab to the chest. Followed by two more. In my eyes, it was an instant kill. But for Pavle, it was the longest moment ever. I didn't want to kill this man, but it was him or me. Suddenly, his friends (or family, I couldn't know for sure) ran downstairs and tried to attack me, but they were unarmed. Pavle slashed at one of them, cutting the arm. They then began to beg for mercy and cry as they stood around their friend's corpse. I took everything I could find and ran home.
Pavle, and I, for that matter, felt terrible. I actually had to turn the game off for the night and went back to it the next day.
I managed to survive 37 days on my first run without losing any survivors. But Katia died on a scavenging run on the 37th night, and I felt so attacthed to this characters and everything they'd been through, I deleted the save and had to start again.
10/10 would recommend

*Note: This review is strictly based off of my opinions and experiences with the following game.*
Shelter is a fairly enjoyable experience - it's the type of game you can curl up to at night and play while you're hidden amongst a mountain of blankets. As a mother badger, you must care for your cubs and journey with them through beautiful environments. While not everybody will enjoy the art style, it's something new and interesting. And while the gameplay can be repetitive, it's entertaining enough for a single run of the game.
However, a single run is most likely all you'll really get - or want - from this game. After you've completed it, there's nothing really extra to go back for. The story doesn't change, there's no choices, no collectables - and it becomes very linear. The paths you'll take will always be the same, you'll always encounter the same prey, and the same events will always take place at the exact same times. Unless you really enjoy the game, you'll probably only play through it once.
Also, the game is rather short - which in this case, isn't a bad thing. I feel like if it would've dragged on, it would've become quite boring to sit through. It makes for something simple and easy to play if you don't have much time to mess around.
I'll also add that I've never encountered a glitch in this game - not a single one. I'm sure that other people have probably encountered a few, but in my case, it ran very smoothly.
So, would I recommend it? Yes, I would. Although it's not a game for everybody, and it isn't the perfect game, it's still something sweet and interesting, and something that deserves a chance.

I devised a lil FAQ review this time around.  Let's have at it:
Is this more Firaxis beta trickery?
Um...yes.  Sid Meier's Civilization: Beyond Earth is Firaxis staying true to form:  fun but incomplete--even buggy--at release, followed by a slow update schedule and an expansion or two that makes the game into what it could have been in the first place.  For example, after two expansions (and a slew of DLC), Civilization V is an outstanding iteration of the Civilization series, although some of the drastic changes have alienated some fans.  When Civ V was first released, however, it was but a shadow of its current self.  Hopefully Beyond Earth will receive at least a single expansion because, even in its early form, it's an entertaining if incomplete game and it deserves improvement.
Should I buy it?
Usually a question I would answer later in a review, but what the hell, I'll answer it now.  I wouldn't pay the $50 or even the $30 or so you can probably find it for this close to the holidays.  I don't regret doing so, I've already put in 80 hours and I've had a good time; however, playing Civ V for another 80 hours would have been a lot more fun.  Buy CIv V instead, if you don't have it, or the excellent Endless Legend.  (I also hear Pandora: First Contact is comparable and, at the moment, better than Beyond Earth.)  By the time Beyond Earth has dropped to $15 or $20, it'll likely be well worth it.
Is this Civ V?
Mostly yes...and a little no.  Beyond Earth, at its core, is very much just a reskinning of Civilization V.  A really good mod, even.  It shares many of the same concepts and gameplay, often just renaming certain similarities (i.e., happiness is now health, money is energy, etc.).  So, if you're expecting an entirely new game on the scale of the changes going from Civ IV to Civ V, well...you're not going to get it.  Beyond Earth is also different in a lot of ways, with lots of options to tweak your civilization, even  before you launch into space, but the core mechanics are the same.
Is this Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri?
Hell no.  The developers avoided calling it a spiritual successor and it's evident Beyond Earth is much more a child of Civilization V than Alpha Centauri.
What's good about it?
It's a pretty game.  Uses the Civ V engine, although it's not quite as colorful as Civ V.  Lots of dark greens and browns beyond Earth, it seems.
The score is outstanding.  It's also free if you sign up for it through the Steam interface.
It still retains the just-one-more-turn quality of the series, even in its incomplete state.  It took me several games to really start seeing what was wrong with it, but even after discovering its inadequacies it still kept me up late.  Still does, and the first patch should be out soon (woot).
It's modular in design.  That may not be the correct word, but what I mean is there are many small decisions that come together to form your direction in the game.  Some of these you make before even leaving Earth, choosing sponsors, spaceship, cargo, etc.
Three interesting affinities to choose from which give bonuses based on their themes as you level each up to the max level of 18.  These are Harmony, Purity and Supremacy.  They offer a different take on the game outside of leader choices and are a big part of winning one of the five different victory types.
It feels different from Civ V.  I've already mentioned the similiarities between the two games when it comes to mechanics, but the planet itself, the atmosphere, is a good bit different.  There's alien miasma all over the place, which causes damage to units.  Alien nests also spawn a variety of alien lifeforms which make the planet feel hostile and new.  They are Beyond Earth's answer to barbarians but still, they make planet feel all the more foreign.
So tell me the bad, yes?
The AI is awful.  Playing a game on Apollo (the highest difficulty) is akin to playing a game on Prince in Civ V (the "normal" difficulty).  This isn't anything new, Civ games have traditionally relied on AI bonuses and player disadvantages to make the game more "difficult".  But it's way out of tune in Beyond Earth.  The AI mostly blunders about the map and when they attack it's usually in a haphazard fashion with no tactical fortitude whatsoever.
The interface needs work.  It's a bit clunky and it lacks some things that should have been fixed in the first round or two of internal testing.  For instance, when you complete a building and click on the notification to go to that city and begin contruction of a new unit or building, there's no way to tell what you just built.  Silliness.  The tech tree, while interesting in a non-linear form (it's more of a tech web, a simplified version of what you'll find in Endless Space), is mostly devoid of color, which would make it much easier to choose new technologies.  Instead the difference between buildings, wonders and such are portrayed with slight differences in icon shape.  And they're all white.  Also, contantly keeping up with your trade routes can be a hassle, too.
On that note, trade routes are overpowered.  They juice up a city in no time and beelining for Trade Posts and Autoplants is a viable strategy.
After building a new type of building for the first time the game will give you a mini-quest of sorts offering two choices for that building.  You can only choose one.  This, in theory, is interesting, but many of the options are no-brainers and you end up choosing the same option every time for some buildings because the other option is just not on par.  For instance, I forget the other option for Autoplants because the best option--+1 trade routes for all cities--is the only one worth choosing.  And, referring back to the interface issues, none of these options are visible in the "Civilopedia" (err, Help menu), or even in the tooltips, so unless you already know in your head or write them all down like I did, it's hard to plan ahead.
Wonders are underwhelming.
The leaders are cardboard nobodies.  Sure, there's a lot of background information in the Help files for the different sponsors (leaders) but every leader says the same thing, portrays their people in the same manner.  They have different attributes, but no different units or buildings, which is a shame.  Not to harp on SMAC, but the factions in Alpha Centauri were so amazing, each with their own obvious goals and natures...coming to Beyond Earth is a big let-down in the personality department.
It feels "samey" way too fast.  Most people who've been playing Civ V for any amount of time have put in hundreds or thousands of hours and are still having a blast with it.  It can be very different every time.  Beyond Earth starts to grow stale all too fast.  Even the achievements seem lackluster in terms of motivating players to replay the game again and again.  Civ V had a plethora of fun achievements for each faction, enough to keep players coming back for a long, long time.  Beyond Earth has 60+ achievements and they are easily accomplished.
Is there a future for Beyond Earth?
I reckon so.  I mean, no expansions have been announced just yet, but I can't imagine Firaxis not putting out at least a single expansion.  After some patching and some added gameplay nuance from a full expansion (or two, which would be great), Beyond Earth should be a great game.  For now, though, it's hollow and incomplete.  But I still dig it enough to recommend it, depending on what you might be willing to pay for a late beta test in its current form.

[This is an extended edition of my Good Game review of Civilization: Beyond Earth]
I've said it before and I'll say it again, Firaxis has been experimenting with new ideas on the old Civilization game. Since 2008 Firaxis breathed fresh life into the idea of its TBS game with Civilization Revolution. The difference in this game is for the first time there's a narrative to the story. While it's not the studio's first science-fiction game, this is their first genuine attempt to expand the classic history game into the possibility of the future, thus becoming a rebuttal to Activision's miscarriage; 'Civilization: Call to Power', their vulgar attempt at parroting the then fledgling franchise. The only other times Firaxis have ever tried science-fiction in their turn-based game were from premade mods and scenarios, such as 'Final Frontier'; a mod for Civilization IV, but it was a game of universal conquest.
In all honesty though I was rather afraid the game might end up the way of Civilization IV: Colonization, a game largely viewed by the fans as a glorified mod. As a member of the CivFanatics forums I got a taste of the pre-release pictures of the game, I couldn't help but spot a few similarities in the city banner and border art and colours; it all seemed a bit too much like a standard mod for Civilization V, only flashy and sci-fi-y. That alone was enough argument for me to determine whether or not to pick it up at all for a week, eventually the unhealthy want to get another Civ game was too much.
So....after getting it and giving it a solid month of playtime I feel...........................quite ambivalent about the game. I'm not really sure how, or indeed what I feel about it. What I can say is don't get me wrong here, I like the game and as a Civilization nutter I'm giving it my approval, but in terms of whether it is a genuine game or not is actually very hard to determine. I'll therefore sit on the fence on this one and leave it up to the reader to decide. For now though some context on the very first Civilization story; in the distant future as Climate Change and the pollution from Industrialization kicks into high gear, the seas rise across Earth and low lying island nations are washed away. As the Pacific Ocean rises a mass exodus from Far East Asia sweeps across the planet as affected peoples resettle in Europe, America and Africa for their survival. The political landscape changes, alliances form and break apart, and in the twilight of the world eight sponsors from all over the world begin their quest to recolonise and resettle on a new world. In the depths of deep space you find a planet to resettle and you land a colony ship onto this new world in the year 2600. And so starts your game.
Right away you can see some changes from the very beginning, in a standard Civilization V game you just pick a civ and you get all its perks and unique stuff. Here you don't just pick your sponsor and get bonuses from it, you can pick a bonus for your starting turn, your cities, even a free unit. As you play you'll discover all the new and very unique mechanics in Beyond Earth; the most impressive and noteworthy of these is the 'technology web', Civilization's first non-linear technology system. Essentially you research a branching origin tech and when you're finished you can either research the next branch or any of the available leaf techs you unlock having researched their root tech. The branches are tiered and unlike former games just about every tech in a tier is connected to one or two others - creating the web structure, and making the old tech tree structure next to impossible to develop for this. Another mechanic with a very unique spin is unit upgrades; normally in order to upgrade your units to their more advanced counterparts you needed to first research the technology needed, bring your unit into your borders and them pay a lump sum gold amount as well as fulfil any resource requirements. In this game Affinities dictate your unit upgrades - I'll go into Affinities further later on. Initially each unit gets one update regardless of which Affinity you get to it, but thereafter each unit can split into three possible units where sticking to one Affinity will upgrade your units down a specific tree.
Affinities are another interesting idea. Affinities are rather like the Ideologies in Civilization V - they add specific bonuses when you add Affinity points by either completing quests or researching certain techs. The Affinity system is designed to be ultimate driving force behind how you play the game because these bonuses affect every aspect of your game; your units, your cities, relations with the aliens. For a reason I don't really understand Affinities even change your leader's, city's and unit's appearances. Which is a bit weird, but I don't really mind.
However, I must now call your attention to the similarities to Civilization V. First and foremost is one I've in fact only just mentioned a moment ago - Affinities are fundamentally Ideologies. In the same way you get bonuses to your civ from the Ideologies, the same can be said for Affinities, they just use a different method in achieving them. In Civilization V you needed to reach specific technological goals to have the ability to play as only one of the Ideologies and reap their benefits, in here you need to reach levels of Affinity in order to freely gain the bonus and you can have them all one at once. Despite these differences it's the same deal. Then there's the Virtue system, which for all intents and purposes is an almost exact copy of the Social Policy system in Civilization V. You have four trees to follow, each with fifteen Virtues to fully unlock broken into three tiers of five each. Apart from the interesting idea of gaining extra perks from progress down a tree as well as synergy between all four trees these numbers and the system itself looks like a cut-and-paste job. Then there's the trivial stuff; Beyond Earth follows the 1UPT rule from Civilization V; 'One Unit Per Tile', the loathsome lump of steaming misery Civ purists spat acid at when Civilization V released. The city borders resemble the strategic map from Civ5, the hills and coast modelling seem to look exactly like it was ripped right out of Civ5.
All of this can culminate into a world of problems for anyone who wants to get away from the Civilization V experience of......well......playing Civilization V. However this will also bug a player who wants to play a game that is different and experimental, only to find a lot of the work is cosmetic. I'm sorry but you just can't replace the Gold yield with something else and expect to get away with it. For me, in terms of the game's uniqueness Firaxis has missed the mark a good deal; it's a bit too derivative of Civilization V to call it an outright new game. But I do love Civilization V, and I'll admit to growing a love for this game, so I will recommend it. It is still a shame that there hasn't been enough to really create the sense that you are in fact playing an entirely new game.

If you had a copy of the original version of this game in your steam account before this remastered update hit, then you're obviously not losing much.  If you're new to the Bioshock series and are thinking about trying it out, then I cannot honestly recommend the remastered edition in its current state and you're definitely safer starting off with the original releases or just wait for them to patch out the issues plaguing the remastered edition if you really want to play those.  As of this writing I'm about two hours into Bioshock remastered - haven't tried Bioshock 2 remastered yet.  I will say the improved graphics are nice when the textures aren't flickering like a CRT monitor.  The definite deal breaker though is that in my multiple playthrough attempts the game has without fail crashed to desktop every time I've picked up the armor piercing bullets in that closet with the turret in it in the Medical Pavilion.  This has happened twice in a row so far and from what I've read, I've been having one of the "better" experiences with this game so far.
Also one other thing I've noticed that I'm not sure is actually a fault with the game or not, but oddly it seems to me that it's a lot harder to hit enemies with the electro-bolt plasmid in the remastered edition.  Even when it looks like my reticule is dead on target, something like two out of three times it'll just miss them by a hair which is immensely frustrating since the "one-two punch" is pretty much your bread and butter in the first couple of levels in this game.  Again though, I don't know if I can pin this on the remastered release or not - it's entirely possible that I'm just bad at hitting people with the electro-bolt, although I don't remember having this problem in the original release.  And I'm only bringing this up because I'm curious if other people have noticed this as well and if they have any advice on the subject.
Anyway, it's looking like there are fixes on the way which is good news.  But until they've been implemented, I can't in good conscience recommend anyone who doesn't already own these games on steam try the remastered editions.
EDIT: I've played completely through both remasters since this review and I am very pleased to say that they've largely fixed the issues I initially had and from my experience they are both in a playable state.  The graphical changes they made really did spruce up the first game quite a bit and an FOV slider is always welcome.  As for the second game, any changes they made graphically are barely noticeable, and between the first two games it probably needed the least improvement anyway as it was already a pretty good looking game. It is nice that the remaster of the second game didn't have the incredibly vexing habit of crashing to desktop without warning like the original release did.

A pretty fun classic point and click adventure game with an interesting story.
The game tells a story of a team of people from the future where climate change did destroy the earth as we know it and the upcoming sun storm is about to destroy the rest of humanity. To prevent that they go back in time to prevent the climate change that destroyed the world we know. In the game you play either as Fay a radio operator from the future - or an older retired scientist from the present - Bent Svenson. They team up in order to show an alternative to the nuclear power - which is supposed to be green algae. The story takes them through quite a few locations around the world.
The story is interesting, a bit educational probably but that did not bother me at all and I had quite fun following it through. Most importantly it makes sense and keeps you wondering what will happen next. Well told.
The levels are varied and well designed. Very well painted as well. The animation of characters is also quite nice, although scaling them to smaller sizes at times shows some problems. Cut scenes are presented through a comic like panels - they fit well within the whole aesthetic and look just good. Every sentence said by any character is spoken which is nice. For the most part the voice acting is descent - they do have some trouble with more expressive emotions but that's not that big of a deal.
I enjoyed the puzzle design very much. Most of them are pretty well designed, make sense and they're well contained. You have to solve them before you'll be able to move forward. There's no jumping between multiple locations looking what to do next. And they make sense - the amount of random clicking everything on everything is quite rare.
Apart from few bugs - a text displayed in wrong language or missing required item (fixable once googled) - the game has no other bigger problems. The are nitpicks that I've had with it. The first being a rare but frustrating plot holes, when something just happens and you're not sure how it came to it. The second being the plot twist at the end - totally didn't see it coming which is good - but the more I think about it things don't add up. It brakes a bit a great story in the end and is hard to let go - more so that the story held up pretty well till the very end.
Overall a very recommendable point and click adventure game.

Ah, where to begin? It's an adventure game, or as I like to call them, sociopathy simulators. Seriously, when did you ever play an adventure game whose protagonist doesn't end up committing countless crimes, wandering around dozens of locations they technically have no business being in except to advance toward some overarching and/or loopy objective... and frequently slide back as far as they've advanced even after solving puzzle after confusing puzzle?
But I digress. A New Beginning is a game with a certain amount of ecological awareness linked to its plot and setting. The problem with eco-themed games is that unless you're already into saving the environment, they probably just annoy you; nobody wants to have someone else's views foisted on them, right? But just in case you're on the fence, well, this could potentially give you a thing or two to think about. I wouldn't expect miracles, but it's a worthy attempt at least.
The voice acting is passable. I'm inclined to say the voice direction, in particular, seems rather poor; as if the actors, at least in the english version, were given their lines to read in a studio with no context, no complete script, and so they have to guess at intonations when in-game you can tell some line are meant to refer to another line, which can be pretty grating, at least to me. It really impedes the establishment of any kind of mood or character chemistry, which is a shame because:
The characters are, at least in a few places, pretty interesting. I was particularly impressed that someone has made a game whose protagonist -or at least one of its two- is a depressed, burnt out, retired middle-aged workaholic scientist who's lost faith in himself. A different sort of underdog, and one I didn't at all mind getting to know over the course of the game. The rest of the cast is a bit less fleshed-out than I'd have liked, but just the aforementioned character alone earns them points for originality in my book.
The puzzles are a bit hit-and-miss. You may well get stuck wondering what to do, but that's what walkthroughs are for... or community guides if you want to keep it all within Steam.
Overall, I'd give it a minor thumbs up - good but not great. As with most things, I'd wait for a sale -Daedalic have had some very major discounts from time to time, and you could probably do worse than a lot of their adventure games. Sorry, meant to say sociopathy sims.

War in the North capably follows in the footsteps of the old LotR action games. While not as tightly constructed as its predecessors, the broadened RPG elements and online functionality safely glides the game into the recommendable category. Each character plays uniquely enough, with three skills trees each to vary things even more. The combat plays similar enough to the aforesaid games, albeit with some Arkham counter-attacks thrown in. Very fun. Very silly.
That said,
.
, something blatantly evident during offline party management. Simply described, there are two inventories: the player's inventory and the AI's inventory. The player's inventory encompasses any currently controlled character (whichever they may be), whether offline or online. But the AI's exists utterly autonomously (as it would with another player).
So say you're playing the ranger when you pick up a nice axe you'd like to use when playing the dwarf. To trade it, you need to save and exit the current game and reenter as the dwarf character. Think of it as logging and relogging between two toons on an MMO, except all of your characters share the same loot bags. Conversely, and this is IMPORTANT, if you just trade the axe to the cpu version of the dwarf, the item will be cast into the nether: the cpu's inventory. You will not get it back. You cannot force the npc to wield it. When you log into the dwarf character, you will not find it.
This extends to leveling up as well. As much as you may enjoy playing a particular character, I highly advise you regularly redo previous missions with whatever characters you've been neglecting. They will not level up or progress their skill branches on their own. They will gain XP, to be fair, but they become increasingly outmatched as the game goes on. So if you rock the first six levels with the dwarf and decide to finally switch things up and finish the game as the elf, prepare to be overwhelmed.

If you haven't played this game yet, I can't recommend it enough. It's beautiful, creative, heartwarming and challenging all at the same time, the whole way through. It's a metroidvania type game, so you continually explore a gradually increasing map as your character develops new ways to traverse it. Lets go through some of the high points.
Movement
For me, games kind of come down to how well the character handles, and the controls for Hollow Knight are tight, responsive and fluid. You uncover a tun of ways to move around the map, not just for getting around better for moments like "i was wondering what was up here".
Combat
The combat alone would be the selling point of the game if it weren't so goddamn beautiful. Turns out it is, so even if you hate the combat, keep going and breathe in this beautiful world. Anyway, the combat is defintiely challenging, but it never feels unfair. Everytime you take damage, you were either too slow, using the wrong loadout or in the wrong spot. The combat is so fast, so natural and so fluid, that I stop playing other games to come back to this game.
Visuals
The game is gorgeous. It's expressive, atmospheric, unique and powerful. You feel the scope of the world you're in, the tone of a new level you've entered almost immediatly. Character and enemy designs are all so cute and cool. I wish i could hang out with some of them. The bosses are all well designed too, not just from a combat perspective, but their actual models. You can tell right away what type of fight you're in for, whether it's someone big and tanky or fast and sneaky.
All in all, if you like challenging combat, immersive environments, fluid movement, fun character designs and open ended storytelling, this game is for you and then some. buy it now. Stop looking at reviews. Get this game and then DM me so we can talk about it.

A New Beginning - Final Cut is a point and click adventure game from Deadalic Entertainment.
You start the game as a retired bioengineer Bent Svensson, trying to live his peaceful life in a shack (well, a more luxurious shack) somewhere in a Norwegian forest. But just as he is going on about his everyday life, a young woman, a time traveler named Fay invades the privacy of his home and tells him the most imaginative story he has ever heard; about a future with no hope, where the clean air and fresh water are hard to find, and the planet is dying (Fallout anyone?).
And Bent is supposed to be the person responsible for the planet salvation, so Fay convices him to go with her to try and stop the exact event that started the process of the extinction of life in the future.
The story is well written and while it may sound cliched, it makes enough interesting twists and turns to never make it seem boring or repetitive. The characters are well done, and have real and believable motives for their actions throughout the game.
From the graphical and accustic standpoint, Deadelic always delivers and this game is no different. Beautifully drawn backgrounds and landscapes, well done comic-like cut-scenes and a great voiceovers accompanied with an atmospheric soundtrack make for a great gaming experience.
The game is not hard, and all the puzzles and actions needed to make progress make sense and should not leave you bashing your head for two hours, trying to figure out what to do next. It took me about 15 hours to finish the game which is a pretty decent length for a p'n'c game.
And now, some negatives. Sometimes the text in the game becomes russian or german for a brief second (for example when inspecting an item) or the characters glitches out and disappears from the screen. On one occasion I couldn't access my inventory so I had to reload the previous game save. Also the bomb defusion puzzle has a bug, where the counter on one of the sides adds an extra +1 so you can't complete the puzzle (again reloading fixes it). So nothing too serious, but it could annoy you, especially if you haven't saved in a while.
Score:
+ beautiful hand drawn backgrounds
+ great voice acting and atmospheric soundtrack
+ decent length for a p'n'c game
+ interesting story line with some cool concepts of the future
- bugs
- sound disappearing at times
A well done adventure game, for old school p'n'c players and anyone willing to give it a go. A solid 8/10.

What a game, what a game.  Probably one of the best all around games I have ever played.  The game is meant to be played at a slower pace to allow for more battle strategy and production and economy tactics to be utilized.  Don't let anyone tell you this game is better when sped up 4x- it's simply not.  That's the reason I love this game actually.  You can change your strategy every game and you have to adjust every game depending on the map, etc.  All teams are balanced (at least in Rebellion), Titans can be a little OP, but they are easy to kill if you practice at it.  Assaulting is made easier than every with anti-building frigates.  Starbases provide a great way to plug up a flank (at least for a while).  Ships all have their uses and every one can be used depending on your strategy.  The 3 factions allow for the accomodation of any strategy.  Your research tree is enourmous, allowing for a huge amount of play styles.  There are two main few things I don't like about this game: Superweapons, the huge difference in computer difficulty between hards and extremes (intenses, whatever).  Superweapons are crazy- especially the TEC Novalith Cannon.  You basically just say f*** you to your opponent by destroying their planets' population from across the galaxy.  The even worse part is that TEC Loyalist now has the cannons at tier 6.. with no pre-requesite research needed.  That's obnoxious.
Please play this game! Give it a chance.  It's quite hard to grasp at first because it is just so in depth and different from other RTS's.  Once you get the hang of it, grab a few friends and teach them.  You will literally sit down with them and play for 8 hours straight without even noticing.

A beautiful game with amazing soundtrack - but don't let this fool you. This ain't no Ori and the Blind Forest. There is a strong focus on skillful combat. Which is definitely much easier to do with a controller than with a keyboard. The dream bosses being even harder when using a keyboard sadly made me lose interest in 100% finishing the story line.
Which leads me to one design/comfort issue I have with the game: Yes, Ori's "mobile" safe spot was an odd, yet brilliant choice.. but my god does it get annoying if you have to travel the same area over and over again. It's not a challenge anymore, its just wasting time. In at least one case, I found myself traveling longer to the boss than actually fighting it. Argh. If the 'respawn' would be faster, I would have kept banging my head at the challenge until it (the challenge) breaks.
The other issue I have with the game is its low story-density. You get bits of lore here and there.. but somehow, things feel strangely disconnected. While I get the impression, the story and the world has more to offer, the game doesn't readily give that knowledge to the player. And so I don't know for sure whether there just isn't 'more' or whether you have to grind through all areas to figure out whats actually going on. This could have been done better and feels like such a missed opportunity.
All in all, its a beautiful and fun dexterity challenge that is worth its money. And my god does it have fun character designs.

If you like strategy games, you will greatly enjoy this game
First off, while sounding like an expansion, it isn't.  You get everything plus three extra sides, the 'rebels', each with their own unique titans.
Now to the meaty bits...
Gameplay:  8-10
If you are used to a strategy game having a campaign mode, you are in for a disapointment.  Other then a cutscene setting the storyline and a tutorial, the 'story' is yours, played out via either single player skirmish modes on a choice of about...50-60 various maps plus whatever you can cook up in the 'galaxy editor'.
The sides themselves each have their own small strengths and weaknesses, the TEC for example being the local turtlers.  There are also plenty of mods out there to boost your fun, adding sides different planet types or even completely converting the game in the case of 'sacrifice of angels' a star trek total conversion mod.
There are some features I think that stardock missed the boat on which other games have proved can work.  The ability to play with your colonies other then just upgrading areas.  The ability for a ground attack minigame like that in galactic civilizations 2 would be a great touch, as would be the ability to customize individual colonies even more (again, like in Galactic civs 2)
Graphics: 9-10
This I can only talk from my own experiences as it may vary upon your setup.  This will be from the POV of almost complete maxed out settings.
The graphics themselves are good...your ships move smoothly through space how you would expect, fighters leave little contrails from their engines and the explosions turn big fights into firework shows.  That said, in later games, the sheer amount of weapon fire and ships can cause even the best gaming PC to chug a little when you are zoomed into the action.
This also becomes more apparent with some mods during the bigger fleet battles.
Modding & expansions potential: 9.5-10
Almost full marks for this.  The mods that can be found are all usually fun, even the beta ones.  Some like the aformentioned 'sacrifice of angels' are fun to play and literally feel ike you are playing a star trek game.  Others, like Maelstrom add a whole new selection of new sides to the game, 6 in total (three sides split into loyalist and rebel, like with the original 3).
That said, this is where it runs into a wall.  Stardock are good about constantly updating with bug fixes and patches via new versions, but these new versions render the collected mods useless until the modders release a new version.  This is also why it does not get a perfect score.  A proper content expansion would be welcomed by fans and myself.  While stardock has added mini-expansions in the form of 'stellar phenomena' and forbidden worlds', all these have added is some new world types to colonise and some random phenomena to spice up the gameplay a little.
A expansion that adds for example, a real NPC threat other then the pirates which can be easily neutralized by the saavy player and even an easy AI would greatly improve the game.
Final verdict: 9-10
This game is a must buy for any fan of the RTS genre and is well worth the price of £30.  As long as you can put up with your mods being constantly shut down by version patches, you wil get hours and hours of fun out of this game.

Firstly, I wish I could give this game a neutral rating.
I'm an avid Civ V fan and I did enjoy Civ BE. But BE is overpriced for the amount of game content, and the multiplayer is too unreliable to be counted upon unless gaming with a known premade group of friends. I have given up on even attempting public mutliplayer at this point in time. Basically don't buy this game if single player isn't enough for you.
BE offers a refinement on Civ V's mechanics in many ways, the tech tree, automatic Civ-wide instant unit upgrades, and the "explorer" mechanic instead of old scouts being three major ones. But other game mechanics just don't exist (yet, I'm sure they will add DLC for them later). Religion, culture wars/tourism, great works, great people, and world congress all do not presently exist in BE and have no replacement mechanics. The number of military units is less than those found in vanilla Civ V as well.
The tech web is probably the greatest concept of BE, but I didn't understand why until I actually used it. It allows players to diversify and focus on wonders other players will never even attempt to go for, and it rewards players that focus on one "branch" of the web as opposed to Civ V where everyone was researching the same techs and fighting over the same wonders all the time. In BE you can research only the branches of the web you want, and games can end long before all of the tech web has been researched.
Unfortunately, the tech web by itself isn't the game. For all the beautiful graphics and (much appreciated) game optimization done, it feels like there is less game content here than there was in the original Civ V at its launch. There's only 8 "civs" but most of the original V AI was carried over with all it's idiosyncracies and inability to win without ignoring all the game rules. The AI itself is not as dangerous either, and presently seems to be bugged so that it will only ever use ~20% of its forces at a given time. Any Civ veteran will be capable of beating the highest Apollo difficulty AI in a straight up normal game on any map 1v1 once they understand BE's mechanics.
Civ BE is a good game in of itself, but I'd suggest waiting for a steep sale or the inevitable steep discount when major DLC gets released. The single-player AI will make for an unsatisfying challenge for Civ V veterans and the multiplayer will only lead to a hopeless waste of many hours per failed game.
