While Crysis' story was never really anything special to begin with, it certainly gets the job done. It takes some unexpected twists and turns along the way, and it does lead to a fairly interesting conclusion, but all in all it's clear that this is a game of gameplay over story. If you want something with a story that will rival franchises like Half-Life or Bioshock, you're looking in the wrong place. The story of all the Crysis games combined serves only one purpose, and that purpose is to give you a reason for going from A to B if wanderlust alone isn't going to cut it.
Now then, how is the gameplay?
The gameplay is great. It's everything you expect in a modern shooter - Decent-to-good AI, a nice selection of satisfying weaponry, explosives and gadgets. The Nano-Suit turns out to be one of the most interesting features in any FPS since the Gravity Gun, and the game is ripe for multiple playthroughs thanks to all of your options and the, at times, huge maps that you can get lost in. Crysis is perhaps the flagship of what a liniear open-world game can be - No, you're never really 'free' but you don't feel like you're being pushed through a bottleneck - because you're not! What Crysis likes to do is to give you a fairly simply objective, a huge map, and then basically leave it up to you as to how you go about completing your mission. You can go in guns blazing, blowing up enemies left, right and center, or you can play it like you would any stealth game, capitalizing on your ability to turn invisible.
Graphically there's not really much to say. You can pick up and play this game today, and you won't be disappointed. Even by our current standards, this game arguably looks better than a lot of new releases. The low pricetag also means that it's going to outclass a lot of otherwise very competent indi-shooters.

When Civilization: Beyond Earth was released it didn’t take many days until I gave in and bought a copy. It is developed by Firaxis and builds on the previous Civilization game series. Civilization:BE also has a “spiritual predecessor” in Alpha Centauri. I haven’t played that game, but I have spend uncountable hours playing the previous versions of Civilization and Colonization. Now, one month and a lot of turns later, I will summarize my experience and thoughts.
You lead colonists that have been sent from Earth to establish a new home for mankind. Your task is to build a civilization on a newfound planet filled with strange aliens and rich in natural resources.
If you have played Civilization you will recognise a lot. You found cities, construct buildings, and explore. Other civilizations will also settle on the planet and you can either work with them or try to conquer them using warfare. I don’t find the civilizations in BE as prone to warfare as they are in for example Civilization V, which makes the game a bit less intense and you can focus more on your plan instead of worrying about what the others do.
The first thing you will notice is that BE is very different from Civilization when it comes to victories. The game is much more story driven and you win by reaching certain conditions (research these technologies, then build this wonder, then do these special actions etc). You have a quest log with missions that you can complete for rewards that is meant to help you get closer to victory. It is a fun change, but after playing through numerous games it tends to be a bit repetitive.
Finishing quests or researching certain technologies allows you to control what type of civilization you should build. This is called affinities and you have three to chose from. They basically can be summed up with: Become more alien, become more technical, or stay true to humanity.
Leveling up your affinity also levels up your units, which is useful. I have always found that managing and upgrading units in Civilization has been tedious, and having them upgraded automatically is a nice change. However, if you don’t focus strongly on one affinity you will find yourself surrounded with much stronger opponent civilizations and become vulnerable to attacks.
Researching technologies in Beyond Earth works slightly different from previous versions of Civilization. Instead of a research tree you have a tech web. This, combined with the new victory conditions, means that in higher difficulties you really have to be certain of what victory you are going for and what you are researching. It is a cause for more difficult decisions and it is sometimes painful choosing what research you have to focus on.
The spy system we are used to in Civilization V has gotten a big upgrade and is much more fun now. Just as before you can place covert ops agents in other cities. The more covert ops activity there is in a city (called intrigue), the more tasks your agents will be able to chose from. When there is low activity you can for example steal gold or science but at higher levels of activity you can start stealing technologies or order alien attacks.
The aliens are also worth mentioning. In Civilization, we are used to barbarians that attack units or pillage lands. On this new world there are roaming aliens. They are not at all as aggressive and a lot dumber. If you start attacking them however, they will understand that you are a threat and become more aggressive towards you. This is a change I really like, as the barbarians had an annoying way of always messing up my plans… :)
As I am a complete sucker for Civilization, Beyond Earth could have been either a complete miss or a complete hit for me. It is definitely different from Civilization in many ways and it is not a replacement or the next version of Civilization but rather another type of game in the same series that has its own tactics and charms. I’m glad to say that Beyond Earth, for me, is a hit.

The satisfaction of progression is very important in games, something a lot of companies have forgotten.

Theme Decks and/or Intro Packs (Which are great to use as a core for your own decks)
Propper 15 card Booster packs (the extra commons will give you a wider choice for your deck building)

With a heavy heart I can not recommend this game and I'll keep this review short.  I dislike ones that are long winded.
First off, I love Magic the Gathering even tho I'm far from running on the pro circuit.
I'll start with the positive:
The game is fun, and a lot of enjoyment for someone that is not playing with $200 decks for paper cards.  There are some good cards in game for the casual player that work well off each other.  If you play Magic on the kitchen table with some friends, then there are fun matches to be had.
The cons:
It's a grind and wasted time.  The booster packs you can buy with coins (in-game money) cost 150 coins and you get only six cards per pack.  I believe the pack break down is three commons, two uncommon and one rare.  Early in the game you can earn some boosters to add to your collection after running through the story mode and the free cards they give, I have only 254 cards.
Once the story mode is completed the main way to earn more coins is playing against other random players and if you win you will earn 20 coins.  I'm fine with that, the game is free so I don't expect to earn coins too quickly.  Here is the kicker, if you lose then you earn nothing.  I've played two matches online and between both of them I spent an over an hour and earned zero coins because I lost.
You can also play against the AI with three difficulty setting easy (5 coins), medium (10 coins) and hard (15 coins).  So this is even a slower way to earn coins.
Lastly there are "quest" to complete.  They are things like "attack with five creatures at a time, five different times" or "counter 20 spells."  for what I've seen they net 20-40 coins each.  But the quest may be for deck you don't enjoy playing, so you may not enjoy the game when running certian quest.
Also you can buy coins for real money and here is the break down in how much money will get you coins to buy a certain amount of packs and the cost of each pack.  That's a hard read but there it goes:
$1.99 = 150 coins = 1 pack = each pack cost $1.99
$4.99 = 500 coins = 3 packs = each pack cost $1.67
$9.99 = 1250 coins = 8 packs = each pack cost $1.25
$24.99 = 3750 coins = 25 packs = each pack cost $1.00
$39.99 = 7500 coins = 50 packs = each pack cost $0.80
And there are no trading or selling of cards in the game.
If  you want to learn Magic, the game does that very well.  If you are a causal player, there is some fun.  If you are an experienced player this will not be the game for you.

When I got this game for console when it first came out, I despised it. But, I kept playing it hoping it would get better after a while. Eventually, I beat the game and walked away dissapointed, enjoying only the naval side of the game. These feelings towards the game actually turned me off from the series, as I had already felt the series was losing its touch since the release of Assassin's Creed III. (Yes, I was an Ezio fanboy and hated to see him go)
Fast forward several years, it goes on sale on steam, and I decide to go ahead and pick it up to give the game another shot. Needless to say, I fell in love with it the second time. The story was much better than I remembered, the characters weren't as dull as I originally thought they were, and I was unable to tear myself from the game this time, whereas I was forcing myself to finish it the first time. At the end of my second playthrough, with 100% completion and 55+ hours logged, I found myself much more satisfied than I originally was. The game was well worth the second purchase.
So, if you were like me and hated the game the first time, give it a second shot if you are thinking about it. You will more than likely find yourself satisfied with another playthrough.

If you like strategy games, you will greatly enjoy this game
First off, while sounding like an expansion, it isn't.  You get everything plus three extra sides, the 'rebels', each with their own unique titans.
Now to the meaty bits...
Gameplay:  8-10
If you are used to a strategy game having a campaign mode, you are in for a disapointment.  Other then a cutscene setting the storyline and a tutorial, the 'story' is yours, played out via either single player skirmish modes on a choice of about...50-60 various maps plus whatever you can cook up in the 'galaxy editor'.
The sides themselves each have their own small strengths and weaknesses, the TEC for example being the local turtlers.  There are also plenty of mods out there to boost your fun, adding sides different planet types or even completely converting the game in the case of 'sacrifice of angels' a star trek total conversion mod.
There are some features I think that stardock missed the boat on which other games have proved can work.  The ability to play with your colonies other then just upgrading areas.  The ability for a ground attack minigame like that in galactic civilizations 2 would be a great touch, as would be the ability to customize individual colonies even more (again, like in Galactic civs 2)
Graphics: 9-10
This I can only talk from my own experiences as it may vary upon your setup.  This will be from the POV of almost complete maxed out settings.
The graphics themselves are good...your ships move smoothly through space how you would expect, fighters leave little contrails from their engines and the explosions turn big fights into firework shows.  That said, in later games, the sheer amount of weapon fire and ships can cause even the best gaming PC to chug a little when you are zoomed into the action.
This also becomes more apparent with some mods during the bigger fleet battles.
Modding & expansions potential: 9.5-10
Almost full marks for this.  The mods that can be found are all usually fun, even the beta ones.  Some like the aformentioned 'sacrifice of angels' are fun to play and literally feel ike you are playing a star trek game.  Others, like Maelstrom add a whole new selection of new sides to the game, 6 in total (three sides split into loyalist and rebel, like with the original 3).
That said, this is where it runs into a wall.  Stardock are good about constantly updating with bug fixes and patches via new versions, but these new versions render the collected mods useless until the modders release a new version.  This is also why it does not get a perfect score.  A proper content expansion would be welcomed by fans and myself.  While stardock has added mini-expansions in the form of 'stellar phenomena' and forbidden worlds', all these have added is some new world types to colonise and some random phenomena to spice up the gameplay a little.
A expansion that adds for example, a real NPC threat other then the pirates which can be easily neutralized by the saavy player and even an easy AI would greatly improve the game.
Final verdict: 9-10
This game is a must buy for any fan of the RTS genre and is well worth the price of £30.  As long as you can put up with your mods being constantly shut down by version patches, you wil get hours and hours of fun out of this game.

I really like The Last Remnant. The PC version anyways. While the inability to micromanage every unit's exact move is not present, I found manipulating the battle system and secondary progression systems around it to be extremely enjoyable.
It's a bit late so I hope this review doesn't become nonsensical.
The battle system involves positioning, unit selection, skill progressions, classes, equipment, a large cast of unique characters with truly unique abilities as well as strengths and weaknesses when it comes to their abilities in battle. You can group up characters in 3 to 5 groups based on whatever criteria you choose, selecting leaders of each group to help direct the given selection of battle commands based on their class and it's a requirement if you want to use their unique ability (and forfeit that of their supporting units). The group formation selection can be used to further a unions strength or cover up a weakness of the composition of the group. A 5 man union packs a stronger punch and is harder to take down in most cases, but more unions give you more flexibility in what you can complete in a given round,
The PC version offers extended control where you can take each and every unit and enable or disable any specific ability for any of them individually, which offers an extent of control not found in the 360 version.
There's a lot of skills in the game, short range magic, long range magic, hexes, item combinations, single or duel wielding or two handed weaponry, even morale type items whose skill type escapes me at the moment. The protagonist can go in whatever direction you desire and all of the rest of the cast will branch out in whichever selection of a given handful you choose for them. There are nearly infinite possibilities to how you form your final 18 man army.
The battles system itself, outside of secondary systems, is also very deep. You can gang up your unions on a single enemy to induce incounterable back attacks and overwhelm them at the cost of leaving your own flank open, or pair friendly and enemy unions up two-by-two and simply win out slowly on all fronts. Knowing when to keep distance and build AP or fall back to provide a heal or a cleanse is also imperative, as well as knowing how to abuse insta-dodges provided by casting a limit break (or whatever they are called).
There's lots of interesting bosses, especially in the PC version that mirrors the 360 dlc, where battles will test your ability to fight on many fronts or clear a high HP single target out in five or fewer turns. Shows how many ways there are to construct a battalion and execute an encounter.
The fact that battles have dynamic ( and awesome) music selections based on the strength/rarity of the enemy and the flow of the battle is just gravy.
The story provides enough motivation to keep you playing, which is all I could ask for from a JRPG. None of the characters are terrible, though few are remarkable. The VA performance is good on average, minus a few characters whose actor didn't seem to give a♥♥♥♥♥♥(Irina.)

This game was my introduction to the world of point and click puzzle games. I had never played this type of game before and I realised during and after that this is probably my preferred and favourite style of game. I tend to get scared/stressed easily when it comes to action based games and if I am confronted with a problem will usually I panic and make a lot of illogical decisions no matter how many times I play the area. I find that this is a more relaxing (while still challenging) experience as it allows me to gain my bearings and make decisions in my own time.
Pros:
- Relatively good story.
- Pretty art.
- I liked the puzzles.
Cons:
- I feel like the English voice actors had potential but it sounds like they were given bits of script with absolutely no context, so their voices seem to rarely reflect the lines they are speaking. I was able to stand it sometimes, other times I kind of wanted to rip my hair out…
- Some sections and puzzles were unsolvable for me (needed the walkthrough in especially tough times). However, if you complete a puzzle or a section of the game completely by yourself there is an amazing sense of accomplishment to be had.
Overall I would definitely recommend this game and other games like it for people who don’t actually work well under pressure or get stressed easily. I got about 21 hours of play out of it, you may get more or less. Since it's a very linear story and there is only one way to play-through it there is not much re-playability, but it was definitely worth the couple of dollars I got it for.

I wanted to like this game very badly. That said, it's a terrible game. It's fundamentally unfun. Virtually every game mechanic can be summed up as "tedious" at best.
Escort missions take 20 minutes of sitting around waiting for something to happen, followed by 5 seconds of combat, followed by 10 more minutes of waiting for the ship being escorted to dock. Travel between sectors takes forever, even when piggybacking on a jump drive capable ship. Of course, if you do piggyback on something, it's guaranteed to die when it inevitably passes through an impossible-to-avoid PMC controlled zone. If instead you just send it through alone, no problem, emerges unscathed, through the miracle of out-of-sector combat!
Trading takes forever, and station-building relies on trading at its core, so that's twice as tedious. Half the materials you need will be obtainable mostly through hijacking freighters. Guess what? Hijacking anything is also tedious with yet another timesink there. And what is the reward for all these timesinks? Cool things to upgrade your ship with? Nope. Awesome new ships you can buy? Haha, no. Maybe some new capability for your stations or something? Get real. Usually it's just "Yay, I got to advance the plot to where it showcases the next horrible game mechanic!" Best part: The ending. I won't spoil it for you. But basically, all of a sudden, the plot just... ends. If the game was amazing, that could maybe have been forgiven as the expansion pack hook, leaving you wanting more. But in this game, it was more a sigh of relief. This stupid thing is finally over.

Another day, another Kickstarter. This time it’s Born Ready Games and their first foray into the space combat genre with single-player-fighter-turns-into-mech game: Strike Suit Zero. Raising $174,804 with the goal of $100,000 and achieving the stretch goal of mod tools, Strike Suit Zero is another shining example of what crowd funding can do for small time developers. Strike Suit Zero—or SSZ—is a space combat game similar to classics like Tie Fighter and the Wing Commander series, but with one big caveat: you can turn your fighter into an anime styled mech.
You take on the role of Adams, a faceless, voiceless pilot who has apparently fallen out of favor with his superiors. You have to earn the trust of your commanders and comrades in order to be allowed to take the helm of a fighter again. You know, a real rebel story, where you’re Starbuck and everyone else is completely incompetent. The story hinges on some cliché elements, like a woman fused with an AI construct, a commander searching for his white whale, and Adams being the chosen one, all of which are totally mismanaged and telegraphed from the get-go.
You spend most of the game with your wingman and commanding officer, Reynolds. She’s a fiery, but effective, leader who will deliver such witty monotone one-liners as, “You know the drill, Adams” and “I’ve got your back.” It’s unfortunate that the voice actor seems as if she’s taken twelve Ambien and just wanted to go sleep instead of offering a moderately appealing performance. That seems par for the course when it comes to all the voice acting in the game. There was plenty of opportunity to use the voice work tactfully, but for some reason the best mechanical use is, “They’re going after Adams.” This line is repeated constantly with no context and sometimes no real reason other than to fill quiet time. It’s unfortunate that Born Ready Games didn’t seize more opportunities to use voice chatter as a mechanic rather than ambiance that breaks immersion and falls flat.
Mechanically, the game is pretty simple: cycle targets, shoot targets, win the game. It’s fun for a while, but becomes repetitive. Missions are long and don’t vary much. You’ve got the typical escort, kill, bombing run, and capital ship battles that are tried and true tropes of the genre. You can unlock new weapons by earning medals and special objectives, but you really don’t need to grind in order to progress. There’s nothing really new or earth shattering, either. The controls work well, but you’ll likely find a flight stick or gamepad better-suited to gameplay than a mouse and keyboard.
The defining disappointment though, is the very thing that separates the game from the rest of the genre. The mech—also known as Strike Suit—is incredibly underwhelming and mostly boring to use. You gain a resource called Flux, which powers the fighter’s Strike Suit mode by dealing damage to enemies, thrusting, or taking damage. Think of it as a rage meter from World of Warcraft. You use Flux each time you shoot or fire rockets from Strike Suit mode. You can gain Flux while meched out, but the amount is reduced greatly in order to get you to use it more strategically. It just feels like the mech could use more unique abilities beyond shooting and firing rockets to make it more appealing.
If there is one thing SSZ does well, it’s visuals. The space-boxes are beautiful and do a great job of immersing you in the universe. You really feel like you’re in space, dog fighting, looping, and bombing. The ships are all nicely rendered and have a distinct visual style inspired by countless space operas and animes.
If you’re into future-tech animes and flight combat games, you should have plenty of fun playing SSZ. If you like the idea of a fighter that transforms into a mech and expect to get something out of that, you’ll be disappointed. Only around one third of the thirteen missions feature the Strike Suit, which you don’t even use in the first couple of hours. There’s about 5-6 hours of content though, so you will get decent bang for your buck. If that’s not enough for you, there’s always Freespace 2 and the mass of mods being made to this very day.
This review was based on a day one retail copy of the PC version of Strike Suit Zero developed by Born Ready Games

This game is an absolute gem of brilliant design.
You lead a group of randomized survivors through a civil war. Not that they are fighting in it, you are not a combatant, you are just trying to get through to the next day and there are plenty of things to trip you up as you go. The game has several distinct phases that will change up what challanges you face as you go. The whole time you have to feed and arm your survivors as well as fortify your base.
You will find yourselve in a variety of precarious moral situations (who gets to eat, do you help your neighbor, do you help a perfect stranger, among MANY more).
This game has a very rogue-like quality as you are balancing several very limited resources every day.
Each day has two parts:
Day - Is  a sort of resource managing survival game where you create the tools you need to survive.
Night - Plays out as a 2D stealth game where you scavange, steal, barter or raid for whatever you can to survive.
By the end of this game you will be limping forward, my playthrough ended with all 4 of my party barely alive.
The difficulty is brutal and mistakes are punished severely, death of a party member can happen in a matter of moments and losing that one party member can cause everything to spiral out of control.
I have exactly one knock on the game, when your base is attacked, it is simulated. I would have loved to have had to defend my base in the 2D combat engine the scavenging uses.
The game has a ton a replay value via random events, party members and resources.
If you like survival games, you will love this game. If you like resource management games, you will love this game. If you like games that make you think about your actions, you will love this game . If you like to feel like a complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, you will love this game.

Every time I play an action RPG I'm reminded of Torchlight. It's not even the first in the genre but I always remember it as one I never got bored with. I played floors the way I take my medicine, one a day. It's interface, challenge and loot always keep me coming back. Even after I finished the main story I still delved deeper into the extra dungeon that opened up if only to test my mettle.
Let's take a look at the story though since I brought it up. You're helping this mild mannered swamp town inhabitants by venturing into a bottomless cave in hopes of uncovering the cause of the blight that has cursed this small mining community. More focused you're helping another adventurer find out what's happened to her friends. While you journey down the mines you read journal entries on what happened to the alchemist you're chasing. It all leads to an epic battle in which you see who's got the bigger magic stick.
Really though, this is one of those games where the journey matters more than the destination.  I like the idea of the three classes as there's lots of ways to take down enemy hoards. You can even take your trusty pet with you. I prefer playing with the alchemist. I find that the best approach to taking on large groups of evil spawn is to summon my own to fight with me. The game is probably easiest with this class and I generally really liked the versatility with weapons and skills to choose from. The vanquisher and destroyer classes both have their strengths and weaknesses but I think the alchemist is more middle ground with the best of both worlds.
There is loot a plenty. Weapons of all shapes and sizes. Many different things you can use to kill. There's also no shortage of quests. The one thing I think I would have liked was to have more towns or diverse number of people you could interact with. You are pretty much stuck with the same citizens of Torchlight throughout your journey but there's all the maps, quests and challenge that makes up for it. Also note that all the shortcomings of this game was made better in Torchlight 2. Though as the original I think it definitely stands the test of time.

2016 RE-review
Like most folks, i was not very thrilled by CIV BE when it came out back in 2014. The initial release was a little bare bones to say the least. Seemingly weird and different 'just' to be different. Yet, with an engine and interface virtually identical to Civ5. It felt like a full price mod or worse a re-skin of Civ5. To be fair, that alone would have in my eyes justified a purchase. But it was not what we expected. Or wanted to pay for. Now, those of us that remember SMAC, are definately remembering it through thoroughly rose tinted glasses. It was seminal, ground breaking, freaking awesome BACK in the day. Now, its still good, just not that good. Beyond Earth is not SMAC 2. And I would argue it doesn't have to be. Its a different game, set in (more or less) the same "place."
Fast forward to Rising Tide, a bunch of patches and sale prices later. 2016. Should you buy it? Yes, no question. the only caveats I would offer to those of you who are very picky eaters. I have replayed it start to finish and have just started another game immediately. i love it! I think you may also. But keep the following in mind:
It has a science fiction feel that you need to embrace on a role playing level. Watched Interstellar? Want to find out whats happens after the ending? THIS is your game!  Read the individual writeups and if you have time, read up online how many are based on actual science/scifi concepts. The various buildings and abilities make the game so much more dynamic, than the Civ5 map-based resource structure. Building an empire on a desolate wasteland is an interesting challenge.
The 'Barbarian' life forms keep the AI in check, especially on large maps, so you get few vast AI empires.  Interesting things happen, even without the added events. The quests are a very nice touch and now have structure/reward, beyond the simple +1 whatever resource of the vanilla game.  Game winning victory devices are built in vulnurable hexes outside your cities, foreshadowing Civ6 city districts. The tech tree is a weird mess, but after a few play throughs you will understand its structure and know how to pick your own path. And over-lapping Affinities really spice up units and abilities.
yes, some parts of the game are STILL a little rough around the edges, but I think that is mainly due to the lack of customer support for the game. Why should Firaxis keep working on a game that was so negatively received?
Buy it for a very enjoyable take on what happens after a Civ science victory. Just don't expect it to be earth shattering.

This game has some merits, which I'm sure you can see just looking at it if it piques your interest, so if you're already interested, I'll tell you why I don't recommend it:
The gameplay is slow. You're really not doing very much. In fact, your only controls are WASD, left mouse button, and shift/ctrl for run/"crouch." All you do is go down a very linear path looking for food for your babies, which is either plants that you just pluck from the ground, or animals that you "attack." I feel like the animal interactions are also bugged, because on one level I missed three frogs despite being right on top of them.
And about those frogs, they were on a "stealth" level. It's a nigh level where the fastest you can go is an incredibly slow crawl (except for some scripted events), and it is so tedious.
The real tedium set in for me when I lost my first cub. It didn't feel like my fault. I gave my babies all of the food I found (except for the animals that "ran" away from me when I was right on top of them), which speeds them up, but one still died somehow. It really broke immersion for me and I stopped caring trying to care for my babies, because they just die anyway.
The really funny thing is that this game is only an hour long. Imagine an hour long game feeling tedious.
Aside from slow, tedious, and uneventful gameplay, it also somehow performs poorly. A 3 year old game that looks like this should not give an RX 390 problems, but it still had some jarring stutter trying to run it at 1080p/144hz. It seemed to stay around 70 FPS and moving the camera made it dip so badly that it disoriented me frequently.
It also looks a lot worse in motion. I think the screenshots look fantastic, but when you're actually playing, the graphics seem less artistic and just feel poor.
If you want a nice relaxing game, just look elsewhere. But honestly, for a dollar, maybe give this game a shot anyway.

Getting attached to little creatures and hoping they live is very common for me, hence why I played this game! But that does not mean I can inherently recommend Shelter to people, or to say that it's exactly worth much.
This is yet another game where Steam really should have more options than just a Yes/No.
The overall experience is still nice (though rough around the edges), and certainly made me want to keep my little creatures alive. But it will take you less than 1 hour to complete. My total gameplay time is actually messing around with things and trying to understand why the visuals of the game are badly done, which I'll get to shortly. (And I don't mean the fact that they chose lots of flat colors.)
You essentially control a mother badger and must take 5 children along with you throughout 5 different chapters/areas, as time passes along as you play. Each area has a different type of obstacle, threatening to take a child away from you. Your goal is simply to keep them safe and to move along a mostly linear path. You find food as you go, and must make sure to feed the proper child badgers, paying attention to whom you've recently fed and who is hungry. The actual difficulty of finding food was non-existent. In fact, there were portions where I was just running past items, and none of the child badgers starved at all.
Besides the above, there really is nothing else to the game. You get to the end, and it's done. You can replay if you want, but it's the same "experience" repeated - unless you're trying to trick yourself into thinking you never played it, and that you'll save more children the next time around.
The visuals of the game are nothing special, in my opinion, and actually made things really difficult to see. For me, the title screen was almost blurred together with similar colors to the point where some text was unreadable (and the same applied when the credits were rolling after I completed the game). And while playing the game, I had to turn my computer's brightness setting down to almost nothing, because the contrast is super high in the game, leaving a bright white layer over-the-top. It was just extremely difficult to see. The game itself definitely needs contrast settings, but none exist in the Options.
There really is not much else to say about Shelter without explicitly talking about the details of the areas, which doesn't make sense for a general review.
As I said above, I don't think the game is bad, but I also don't think it's exactly great or something to recommend. I myself got sad with things happening to the children as I played, so I suppose I would say to try it out if you are drawn to that. But the game itself isn't exactly worth the full price, as most of it is relatively simple in visuals and overall design, without much longevity.

Sure, it looks visually better than the original console version, but that's sort of a given in anything dubbed a "remaster."  Even so, I was almost immediately underwhelmed because of the degree to which everything was exactly the same.  No real gameplay improvements or tweaks, little added graphically beyond improved textures, and somehow, less graphical flexibility than the original port.
Graphics aside, it's as though the only ideas anyone had as to how to remaster the original Bioshock were "better textures" and "nicer lighting."  Oh, also that 30fps physics thing that modders already fixed.  Basically, a really ambitious modder could have pulled this off.
These remasters epitomize how completely tone-deaf a developer can be to the needs and preferences of an entire market, namely PC gamers. This is probably the main reason why the Universal Windows Platform is still even a thing, but I digress.
What I honestly think happened here is that the game was ported to PS4 and XB1 first, then remastered, then ported back to PC.  Since the game runs okay at 1080p and 60fps, no further optimization was done for PC despite there being ample room for it.  Let's hope that the dismal Steam rating I'm about to contribute to inspires them to try harder.
Bioshock Remastered is, as a PC port, basically a cruel satire of PC ports in much the same way that the game itself is a cruel satire of Ayn Rand's objectivist philosophy.  In either case, smart people knowingly did the wrong thing because it was easy or otherwise resulted in personal gain.  Even bad ports make money.

To start out, let me explain that I wanted to like this game, I really did. But I don't. There are a few things in Absolution that I did like, but unfortunately, the cons definitely outweighed the pros. I'm only going to focus on a few rather serious flaws that ruined it for me. These complaints are common, but valid nonetheless.

Gone is the open world from the previous Hitman games with their complex layouts. Now, levels are laid out very basically and divided into mulitple sections. Many of these sections don't even have targets to kill. Most of them are just "Get from Point A to Point B". It's a poor way to add length to the game by making you do a bunch of busywork. A lot of the shorter level sections don't have checkpoints either. If you come across a difficult section and screw something up, you have to restart back at the beginning and do it all over again, which may take multiple attempts, especially on the higher difficulties. In some levels, I just lost my patience with rolling from cover to cover and crushing the Instinct button and just started neutralizing every guard I met. Which leads me to my next complaint...

Previous Hitman games had a proper save/load system, but the one in Absolution sucks. The checkpoints save your position on the level and any disguise you are wearing, but nothing that you've accomplished so far in terms of disposing of guards, dead targets, any other objectives, or your score. This often forces you to backtrack if you have to reload your current game, which is always much more difficult than just restarting. This wastes a great deal of time, stretching mission times out to hours longer than it would take if you could just SAVE THE GAME. The only good thing here is that it also doesn't save the enemy alert level, so the disguise you are wearing isn't "blown" when you reload and enemies aren't actively searching for you.

Previous Hitman games would allow you to wear disguises and move past anyone wearing the same clothes. As long as you didn't linger in front of them, or walk too closely to them, they wouldn't recognize you. In Absolution, if you approach any where near someone wearing the same clothes as you are (within at least 25-30 feet), they will recognize you as an imposter in three to four seconds, unless you have enough instinct to hold down CTRL and walk out of their sight range. This really breaks immersion for me. Mana management in a Hitman game? Otherwise, disguises usually work flawlessly against every other character wearing a different outfit from yours, seemingly regardless of the circumstances. You might just as well be invisible. It's very unrealistic.

Being as level designs are very linear, Absolution is quite limiting in how you can kill your targets, often presenting only a single viable option, unless you want to end up killing half the guards in the area trying anything else. In terms of equipment, or lack thereof, the story is mostly to blame. As 47 is on the run, you are very limited in your equipment and must scavage things you need from the level. You will have your Silverballers and garrote (most of the time), but unlike previous Hitman games, you can't bring anything else from one level to another, not even extra ammunition for your Silverballers.
For those reasons I cannot recommend this game, at least to fans of the Hitman series. New players may find this game fun, and indeed, it does have some truly fun and interesting missions (the cornfield is my favorite). But as far as I am concerned, these gameplay flaws make Absolution the weakest in the Hitman series to date.

First of all: I played this game with a controller, and didn't finish it yet, but there are just two of 13 chapters left, so there isn't much to see except of the end of the story. Also, this my personal view and opinion on the game.. :)
+ Pros:
> Graphics: The game looks just awesome with nice special effects, especially on the cutscenes!
> Setting: A steam-punkish / Sci-Fi game style, that i enjoyed personally, even if some monsters were a bit weird
> Character-Design: Characters with their own individual personality that are not like the old hero-stereotype char, even if they sometimes annoyed me because of all their "what should i do?" moments
> Fight-System: New fresh system, something like the ATB system, which is based on different "classes" which you change during the fights
> Leveling-System:
> Port: Pretty okay, played the game with a controller and everything seems to be okay; sometimes the camera doesn't turn properly while running in one direction though
- Cons:
> Gameplay: Very, very linear (!!) gameplay: Slay down enemies, follow the only path form one cutscene to the other. In between some changing of gear and buying of items, bet except that, nothing you can do "on your own". :P
> Story: The story itself is pretty okay, a classic jrpg story with a modern kind of taste, if i understood right, you have to play FF-XII-2 too, to experience the whole story. So you practically have a half story with this game..
> Story-Telling: Like i said, you just watch the cutscenes for the story part of the game. So its like a semi-interactive  movie which was cut into pieces..
> No classic overworld: There are no cities, no npcs no real sidequests (except the cieth mission at the end of the game), and especially no exploring!! Also you can't get back to old levels, because there isn't something like a open world, its more a kind of journey (like i said: very linear)
> Summons: Cool looks, but too long animation, also often they doesn't help you out thaaat much (i think personally)
> Music: Not from Nobuo Uematsu the genius man, which made many of the popular ff music.. :( Instead there ist just background music, that is quite amtosspheric but in my opinion "Meh" (especially one jpop-like song ._.)
> Weapons & Items: There are many Items that I didn't even use once, the weapons-skilling system is new and okay, if you know how it works (a bit confusion in the beginning). There is no armor, just weapons and accessoires, didn't like it that much..
________
Conclusion: I'm a big fan of Square and the Final Fantasy series, but this one is the first that didn't impressed me. (Have played five FF games yet, six with this one). For instance, FF7 is my favourite one, with much more love for detail and better over-all style, even if the graphics are pretty bad. So I'ld rather wait for FF7 remake or FFV if graphics are important for you. :) So I won't buy FF XIII-2.. :P

As someone who wasn't a huge fan of the older Hitman games Silent Assassin and Blood Money, I really like the improvements in gameplay that Absolution made. Surely, hardcore fans of the older titles may be disappointed with the somewhat more linear structure of this game, but I thought that the superb stealth, shooting, and movement mechanics were exactly what this series needed, and Hitman Absolution delivers big time in the fun factor department. Gorgeous environments that are incredibly lit, fantastic sound mixing, and moody ambience really make Hitman Absolution a title to remember. It's a generous game with a lengthy campaign and a separate Contracts mode if you want to dig deeper into what the community is doing within the game. Rounding things out is a surprisingly cool story with some very memorable characters, including a blood-curdling, redneck villan that you'll never forget. Hitman has always been a hard game to classify, as it has practically become a genre unto itself. But while this title may polarize fans of the older titles, there has never been a better Hitman game for the newcomer to jump into and discover the one-of-a-kind experience that the Hitman franchise offers.

Don't play it..just don't. The video trailers are completely misleading, as were all the hypes and promises made by EgoSoft. The voice acting is terrible, sounding like someone reading (for the first time) off a script with little to no emotion. The NPCs are all static and don't move anywhere around the cut-and-paste station interiors. No matter what the station looks like on the outside, it'll probably look pretty much the same on the inside.
Combat is clunky- the first bit of combat where you fight a couple of drones, your ship maneuvers like a stoned whale, so you can barely hit them, and from what I've seen from others, this doesn't particularly improve.
While the universe, artistically, is gorgeous...the rest, not so much.
If you want to travel from point A to point B, you'll have to fly manually the whole way, often using the weird space-highway system. Having to circle a station for 5-10 minutes to find where you're supposed to dock adds to the frustation.
As does suddenly losing a chance at being liked by an NPC due to some sort of (completely unexplained) conversation minigame coming up and disappearing before you know what's happening.
Your supposed crew members looking after your ships have all the intelligence of a sub-average brick. They have to be told exactly what to do (and sometimes still won't do it) through a maze of menus and submenus. Your co-pilot is worse- she throws random lines out here and there which make no sense whatsoever, her voice acting is terrible and cliched, and she provides no extra purpose to the game beyond being an annoyance.
OVERALL:
While the space-graphics are pretty, and there's a lot to potentially do....the game is fundamentally fubared, with some parts completely ambiguous, others blatantly and utterly broken, and the majority of it frustrating.
Conclusion:
Don't buy it, like I did. I'm really wanting to ask for a refund.

I spent the day playing this game from beginning to end and enjoyed every second of it.
I will admit that I never NOT use walkthroughs when it comes to these puzzles games. There were definitely some puzzles where I needed to check the walkthrough whether because I was too stupid to analyze the situation or because the logic was not really evident.
There are a couple of minigames throughout the game and I've actually managed to solve most of them without skipping them (which you can do by the way) or looking up the whole answer (I took a quick glance on how the puzzle mechanics works).
The puzzles aren't too hard once you get the gist of what you have to do. You may or may not need a quick glance at the walkthrough but managing to complete them with skipping definitely made me feel satisfied about myself, you know, convincing me for a moment that I'm not a complete idiot.
I liked the comic style of the cutscenes but I loved the art style of the environment. It's realistic looking, vibrant, and detailed. I giggled seeing a box with Hello Kitty on it in the water control room at the power plant. There are lots of scenes that wowed me because the charactes whom are kind of cartoonish are so little in this relatively big realistic environment. There were more areas in the game than I expected, which makes the exploration quite fun and the environment more enjoyable.
I can understand how some people did not enjoy the voice acting. Some lines feel a bit forced or lack a bit of emotion. But only some, I really liked the voice acting in general because it really gave the characters personality.
For the subtitles, there are often typos but personally the good voice acting compensates for it.
I don't know what more to say apart that the story is interesting (who doesn't like time travel plots?), the visuals are great, the characters are cool, the music is ambient...
If you don't mind glancing at the walkthrough a few times, I definitely recommend this game even if you don't really enjoy puzzles. However, if you refuse to look at the walkthrough or skipping the mini games, I wish the best of luck.

Of course nothing good lasts and the Colonies eventually want independence from the United Nations of Earth (UNE). Things come to a head with the discovery of alien technology that massively tips the scales in favor of the Colonies. Too bad you play a pilot for the UNE so you’ve got your work cut out for you.
Strike Suit Zero starts off as a space fighter simulator game very similar to Freespace, but with less weapon and ship customization and you’re not the “squad leader” so you can’t order your teammates around or call for support. Your ship has guns and missiles for weapons, and shields + EMP for defense. The EMP is like a flare that you fire off right before a missile hits you to deflect it. Some of your missiles have lock-on capability and are good against fighter craft, while others may be dumb fire and be good for hitting large slow capital ships. Yes, the capital ships have turrets and weak points that you can destroy to keep them from chewing up you and your teammates.
A few levels into the game you gain access to the Strike Suit, a prototype fighter with the ability to transform into a humanoid robot with superior weapons after gathering enough “flux.” You gain flux from killing fighters or shooting turrets off of the larger enemies. Think of it as a kind of hyper meter that you constantly gain and spend by transforming into the strike suit and firing your weapons. In strike mode your main gun becomes like a flak cannon (moderate damage but auto-aiming) and your missile weapon becomes a super-fast lock-on homing missile that can acquire large numbers of targets before firing (with infinite ammo). Basically if you have to wipe out waves of enemy fighters, switch to strike suit mode and just spray them dead.
Pros:
+I like space fighter games where you fight large enemies mounted with large numbers of destructible turrets. With patience and accuracy your fighter can take down corvettes, frigates, cruisers, and even carriers.
+Some nice music to blast your enemies to.
Cons:
-The story is mediocre
-You need to have the game’s DLC to get about half of the game’s steam achievements.
Overall the game is fun and actually less difficult that it seems. I played Strike Suit Infinity first and got my♥♥♥♥♥kicked. I should have started with Strike Suit Zero since this game actually has a story and slowly ramps up the difficulty.

Wait, hear me out.
So, there are two things to look for when designing a competitive game: the degree of
, and the degree of
. When it comes to mainstream games, we associate the former with competitive viability and the latter with "casual" appeal. For example, some might argue that the later Smash games are more "fun" than Melee, even if they're less "challenging."
But there's fun in competitive design, too. Do you enjoy playing Peach vs Puff in Melee? Or even Puff vs Peach, for that matter. I'm a Marth main, and I dislike fighting ICs, even though he's good against them.
There are aspects of Melee's design that make it
. Yes, it's competitive, and it has a high skill ceiling - but Marth vs Fox when the Fox is above 100%? Not fun. Just frustrating.
It only took a few hours of Rivals of Aether to realize that the game rights many of Melee's wrongs. For example, knockback seems to scale more for kill moves than combo moves, so damaging your opponent too much never makes them harder to kill. That's more intuitive than Melee's approach; why should Fox at 150% be more of a threat than Fox at 75%?
RoA is filled with tons of little improvements:
* Horizontal wavedashing makes it easy to get a "max length" wavedash.
* Wavedashing without a directional input gives you a wavedash in place rather than an accidental air dodge.
* More recovery options make gimps harder, but you can still get edgeguarded for days.
* Blast zones are closer to the screen, so there are fewer of those "Samus bomb-jumping back from the corner of Dream Land" situations. Either you're in a fast-paced edgeguard situation, or you're dead.
* No Tournament Winner, thank god.
On top of that, RoA adds its own layers of depth. Parrying is an awesome mechanic, and it'll grow more sophisticated as people get better at the game. Air dodges actually add movement options in neutral, not just recovery - lots more to explore here too.
Honestly, the only thing this game needs is players. Its design is already better than the games that inspired it. It just needs a higher skill ceiling - and I think the potential is there, if we develop the meta. Keep it up, Dan & team!

As a long-term Final Fantasy fan (my favourite games in the series being 6 and 10) I could easily see the design flaws of FF13, but still managed to get quite obsessed with it (as you can see from my play time).
Like so many others I initially disliked the linear nature of the game, but could eventually see past it because I realized what the developers were trying to accomplish. The linear structure keeps the game very focused and story-driven, and I enjoyed many of the cutscenes scattered throughout the game. The pacing of this game is quite good imo. Usually just when you were starting to get bored with the constant forward-running and fighting, there was a beautiful cutscene to move the story forward. The graphics, in a word: GORGEOUS, even though this is already a 5-year-old game.
The story itself is a mixed bag, though. The Fabula Nova Crystallis lore is interesting and detailed, and the plot of FF13 explores it quite thoroughly, especially in the well-written datalog entries. Even still, the dialogue in this game is often bad or so-so, with poorly hidden exposition every once in a while, characters explaining self-evident facts, and being all-around jerks. I cannot count how many times I facepalmed during Snow's "Self-proclaimed hero" -rants. Some of this has to do with the voice acting (which is generally good, though), but a lot of the writing is a bit clumsy and not very clever. On a broader level, the plot of the game was intense and interesting.
The thing that kept me going, though, was the intense, strategic, increasingly rewarding and (imo) absolutely fantastic battle system of FF13. I cannot stress this enough. Without a battle system as good as this, I doubt I would have become so hooked on this game. Characters have different roles to fullfill in battle (physical attacker, mage, medic and so on) and you can freely combine these in different battle paradigms. The "paradigm shift" system, which requires the player to change the roles of each character in your party according to different situations in battle, is pretty much the most intense and fun battle system in the Final Fantasy series, if you take your time to master it. Different characters have different specialities in battle, and combining those specialities in an effective way is the main challenge of this game. Final Fantasy 13 is HARD, especially near the end, and requires you to really explore the battle system and master it to take down some really tough foes (with millions and millions of hit points). Finally taking down an especially tough enemy that you have tried to kill many times before with various different accessory/paradigm setups is an intensely rewarding experience.
Weapon/accessory upgrading is also a nice touch. Hunting the "Treasure hunter" -trophy, which requires you to hold every weapon and accessory available in the game, is tough and most of my gaming hours consist of trying to achieve this trophy...
I have seen some complaints about the optimizing of this game, but it runs very smoothly with only a few fps drops here and there with my 2,6 ghz, 8 gb ram laptop with a Nvidia Geforce 710M card. No complaints there.
To sum it up, if you can look past some of the obvious design flaws, this game is very rewarding, challenging and fun.

The majority of the story in FF XIII happens between the characters that you control and the group of seemingly antagonistic entities known as Fal'Cie. There is quite a bit that happens that would take far too long to detail, but know that this is a pretty story-rich game with decent character development and a satisfying story arc for each character. That said, there isn't a lot of explanation of the backstory for the world, the Fal'Cie, and environments that happens in-game, which leaves the player with questions. There is much, much more information that can be gained by reading the datalogs in the menu, but it can be quite tedious and it's a shame that there wasn't more of this information put in the actual game. Clearly this game asks for a large amount of time from the player, would it have been that much more onerous to explain the inner-workings of the game's world to the user without resorting to datalogs?
The battle system for a FF game is a good one. Similar to FF XII you are only in control of one of your three party members at a time, with the computer taking over for the other two. You can assign "paradigms" to your party, with one of six being active at any one time, with the ability to switch to others mid-battle. This system works well throughout the entire storyline, but can occasionally cause problems when attempting optional late-game content. In some late-game scenarios it would be extremely helpful to have more control over the other two members of your party, and sometimes you might have to retry battles due to computer players making bad decisions.
As stated earlier, there is a point late in the game in which you can explore/grind/take on side missions that really shines. This section of the game really feels more like a final fantasy game than the rest, and if you're a fan of the series then this section will definitely scratch your itch for more FF. If you're not a veteran, than this area still holds some value and interest if you're enjoying the RPG aspects of the game and want to go further. While some people might argue that it was frustrating to leave this section until the later parts of the game, I think it was actually a good idea. Players who only want to experience the story can do so and can completely ignore this section of the game. While others who want the ability to ignore the story for a bit and develop their characters and inventory further can do so without the worry of having missed certain items or content earlier in the game. With all the "missables" of previous FF games being a frustration to completionists (especially FFXII with the Zodiac Spear nonsense), leaving this content until later works out really well. There are plenty of challenging side-missions and achievements to hunt that will satisfy all but the most hardcore of FF fan.

All in all Absolution is a great game in two aspects; one is its polished look and two is the great freedom it gives you.

I wouldn't recommend this game, at least at full price.
To begin, A New Beginning is a point and click adventure that has some decent strong points. It has great music and background set pieces. Oftentimes, it is lighthearted and doesn't take its ridiculous premise that seriously, and there are even some decent introspective moments interspersed throughout. It has a very likable main character in Bent Svensson. Its best points during gameplay come in the form of straightforward puzzles that require heavy critical thinking but do not require you to, in the words of another commenter, 'have a telepathic link with the developer.' A New Beginning is at its strongest when its newest puzzle doesn't require heavy backtracking but still asks you to put in some decent legwork to find the solution.
Still, I wouldn't recomend this for a person looking for a casual, more cinematic experience. This game can get real hard and real specific, sometimes overly so. Sometimes the solution will be hidden in one line of dialogue that can easily be skipped over, or just require you to figure it out with no context. This can get exhausting and frustrating, ending up in lots of unnecessary backtracking and head scratching. The really obscure solutions serve to drag the game down into tedium, and stacked on top of the many non-logic related flaws of the game make it hard to reccomend this game.
The minigames are almost all maddeningly difficult, and they are just purely standalone logic puzzles you'd expect in a puzzle book. They do not require any knowledge of the plot and can be skipped (at the price of foregoing an achievement), but attempting them for full completion can serve to ruin any momentum you've had advancing the game. It doesn't help that some of them offer really no clues to completion. For two of them, the answers were so difficult to figure out I just looked at a walkthrough so I could nab the achievements, which left me a little bit bitter that my wins weren't legitimate.
Then there are the optimization problems, which are the worst aspect of this game. For a game which is mostly sparsely animated 2D sprites walking around static backgrounds sometimes there will be random frame drops and freezeups. The game's coding is heavily unoptimized in the sense you can straight up break the game. During some event sequences, if you click where youre not supposed to it will run another event simultaenously, which can break the whole thing. One time, clicking one thing triggered an event that was supposed to be triggered by another. At one point I think I accidentally triggered an event that caused an object to be drawn onto my character, which locked up the controls and made it impossible to advance. Good thing I had saved.
On top of that, the english voice acting and translation brings issues as well. Often times it is not fully synced to the characters lips, which meant they just slapped the voices on top of the sprite speaking the original language. There are random text and dialogue skips, times where the subtitles are just completely different than what is being said, some actions are untranslated and left in Russian, and the subtitles can lag behind the dialogue. The subtitles cna go haywire in particular if you glitch the game accidentally, and let me emphasize you can glitch the game just by clicking through dialogue. Also, some of the voice acting is a bit awkward, not fitting the situation.
Finally, the story. It makes no attenpt to hide its criticism of free market capitalism and exploitation of the environment, and at some points implies that the end justifies the means in regards to ecoterrorism. Thats the major gist of the story, and when its not lighthearted, it is either ridiculously convoluted or preachy and obnoxious. The other main character is an accomplished radiooperator and can solve complex puzzles but still manages to come off as ditzy (she's still one of the stronger female characters I've come across.) It probably has one of the most abrupt and disappointing endings ever as well.
I wanted to like this game. I put in all the time I could to get 100% completion, and at points I really enjoyed specific aspects of it. Sadly, as a package it fails to deliver.

For an idea, this game is a cross between the space battles of "Star Wars: Empire at War" and "Endless Space". If you haven't played those, another good comparison would be a cross between "Starcraft" and "Civilization".
It's a realtime strategy, 4X game. You explore the galexy, settle planets, and extract resources. At the same time, other civilizations will try to expand their empire and resources beyond yours. There are constant space battles, micromanagement of economics and government influence, diplomacy, bribery, etc. There aren't any game "phases" as there are in most games of this genre. Instead, they are all happening at once, requiring you to switch from view to view.
It's a fantastic, indepth game. My only real complaint is that it takes a VERY long time to finish. It's difficult to get any kind of resolution without playing the same game for days.

When I first saw this game being played by a youtuber, my initial impressions was that it was yet another survival game but man was I wrong. This War of mine combines elements of survival you find in games like Don't Starve with the themes of surviving as a civilian in a city at war.
This game doesn't blow you away with its graphics however what it does exceed at is story-telling and strategy.  You will face many ethical dilemmas such as prioritizing your own well being over others that are trying to survive the war. Early in my first few hours I raided a small apartment killing the guy and girl as a result, only to find a diary indicating that these two were just trying to survive to get by. Although the game technically lasts between 38-42 days, there is high replayability due to the fact that you start with different characters and conditions in each run (e.g. Winter vs Warm conditions).
Elements like that plus some strategy in devising a plan on which resources to create make this game one of my favourite purchases to play this year. No wonder it made back its development costs in two days.
What I've found a bit frustrating is that certain parts of the game are still bugging. E.g. I had a crowbar permenantly equipped on one of my characters, whenever he tried to open cabinets, the icon would freeze in progress and he would stop his action. The crowbar was able to sold in barter but I could never use the crowbar action past that point. I had to abandon that run. There are also instances in which the game generates doors which are barred from one side with no real way of reaching it.
Other than those few major bugs, the game is a definite recommend. I would love to see some DLC for new characters or even an endless mode added to the game, however I don't think that will be happening anytime soon. Nonetheless, a must play for 2014.

This game is alright, but it suffers from quite a few problems relating to the enemy design and the pacing of the game itself. Don't get me wrong, I enjoyed this game for the most part. However, the game suffers from being very repetitive and relies on throwing more enemies at you to provide difficulty. It also has a couple of annoyances that just make it more awkward to play. So where to start?
Ok so you know how much you love using that katana? Here are some enemies that fly high out of your range or stand so far back that you can't hit them with most of your skills. I say "most" because you can throw small damage shurikens or use a ranged horizontal slice (but it's very tricky to hit against flying targets). I understand that this game could be considered an fps but requiring you to switch to another weapon to kill enemies took away a lot of the fun imo. The katana is your main weapon (and the reason this game feels unique) yet the level design doesn't reflect this in a lot of cases.
"I love enemies that quickly approach me and explode for huge amounts of damage!" Said no one ever. Why these things are even in the game I don't know. They're infuriating and only serve to pad out the later levels with areas that you have to take slowly. Shoot them, skill them, slice them or get near them and they blow up. If they get enraged they roll towards you and blow up. You leave them alone, they roll balls at you that blow up. Not to mention the fact they also spawn in with crowds of enemies from time to time too. Very cheap and annoying enemy design.
Again touching upon the point about katana's being ineffective, the tanks of this game are incredibly spongy. The "fodder" type enemies are very fun to cut up and kill yet the bigger enemies completely ruin the fast-paced melee combat. There's tanky and then there's just inflated health. Try using a katana on these guys and you'll be there all day. They don't pose a significant threat alone but when there's other enemies or additional tanks added in, the combat just slows down to a crawl. It feels like a chore to get through the enemies and into the next area which moves me onto my next point...
After getting about halfway through the story I began to realize that there wasn't actually much variation to the combat or enemy spawns. The setting of each mission is divided into separate areas by doors, elevators and other blocked exits.These areas are essentially arenas for whatever enemy spawns in. After killing the enemies, you get to move to the next area and on and on. This is already pretty draining but add in the fact that the enemies attacking you pretty much always spawn in some sort of sequence, and it's just boring. Kill the fodder, tougher guys appear. Kill them, more appear or a tanky enemy spawns. The game tries to change it up by having tanks bust through walls or appear in groups to surprise you but it just doesn't improve the combat. The enemies feel like they are there to prevent your progress in the story and the game, rather than being there for entertainment. Sure, some parts were fun but the vast majority of the combat just feels like it's there to pad out the game's length.
Now I must confess this review is partly down to me venting frustration as I slog my way to the ending, but that doesn't change the point I'm trying to make. The basic gameplay with the katana is enjoyable and made me feel like a badass but it's held back by a tedious and long game. The story, setting and it's characters had me interested but again, this interest was lost as the game continued to drag. I can't recommend this game simply because in my experience, it's drawn out to such an extent that the gameplay there provides little satisfaction. It did show promise though, so maybe you'll enjoy it more than I did. Wang's "humor" and the fortune cookies scattered about gave me plenty of laughs for sure.

I found that the game hits a sweet spot between a simple arcade-style shooter and a complex spaceship sim. As such, it is relatively easy to learn and control but has a fair bit of challenge and you can really feel yourself improving as you play. SSZ is also a highly focused game. Story, graphics, and sound design are all good but not great and it only has a relatively short singleplayer campaign, with no multiplayer or other game modes. However, the core gameplay is definitely strong enough to carry the game and make it worth playing. Flying along an enemy capitol ship and blowing up its turrets and fighters in a space mech is very fun and empowering, even if you end up doing it a lot over the course of the game.
Overall, I'd recommend it to people who like singleplayer space combat sims, especially the Freespace series.

As dungeon crawler RPGs go, Torchlight is a considerably decent entry in that particular category. Created by former staff members and developers of Blizzard, the game serves as an excellent spiritual sequel to the popular Diablo franchise, albeit one that was created prior to the release of "Diablo III".
The game improves upon certain mechanics originally featured in the Diablo series, and brings its own new tricks to the table as well. Examples include the ability to create magical gems using lesser gem fragments picked up in the various dungeons of the game, as well as the ability to send your character's "pet" back to a safe haven to sell any excess loot you pick up, both to earn your character a bit of extra coin, and to help alleviate your character's overburdened inventory.
The further into the depths you go, a new challenge waits to be conquered, a new monster waits for a worthy opponent, and new treasures are eager to be discovered. Equip your gear, grab your pet, and prepare to hack, slash, shoot, and blast your way through level after horrifying level in one of the best top-down RPGs since the release of "Diablo II".

Damn good Smash clone. While it does have a faster pace than Smash 4, it feels like it isn't as fast as melee so the average Smash 4 player can keep up with it. The game also brings in a tutorial mode which goes from the basics to advanced. My one complaint so far is that the tutorial can be a little picky on how it wants you to perform certain actions (down to the exact frame) but even then it is me being nitpicky.

Overall Crysis offers the player a good experience. However, if the player is looking for a smooth transition from beginning to end, they will fall a bit short. Game difficulty moves far too quickly from cakewalk to hell on Earth and back again too quick and far too often. Progressive difficulty is expected with any game. It naturally makes the game imersive so the player doesn't get bored. Finding levels later in game which seem nearly impossible only to move on to levels that are about as difficult as a tutorial is a bit much. Some levels you don't even have a damn clue what you're doing. For instance *spoiler alert!*...you end up in a different world a long time ago in a far away land. For some reason suddenly the gravity turns off. Ok...so I have thrusters. Didn't know that. Why the hell don't they help me jump higher along with the strength ability? Anyways...you'll find yourself inside this thing...we have no clue what it is. Some sort of factory? No clue. Enemies will be flying around you and giant bolts of electricity will be doing the funky chicken along the walls. So you try to figure out what you need to do. More and more bolts of electricity are forming and you start to wonder if the last 5 min you've spent in the area is all for nothing because you can't figure out what you're supposed to do. No...thats not it at all. Its a countdown to a portal that is going to whisk you away. So it turns out its a waiting game. Anyways, *end of spoiler!*
PROS:
-You get an awesome suit with different abilities which are not only fun to play with they are a must to complete missions.
-The learning curve is surprisingly fast.
-Good graphics. Honestly though even for its time...I don't see what all the fuss was about.
-It is one of the better single player FPS experiences out there.
CONS:
-3 main guns until right near the end. At which point you're so happy to pull the trigger of a new gun you nearly have an 0rg@smic moment which can only be bested by finding the 3rd warp whistle in Mario 3 when you're 12.
-On the later guns...(oh yes I'm not done!)...what is described as basically a nuke in a shotgun's body needs a Ph D and 20 yrs experience from Nasa JPL just to figure out how to work the damn thing and figuring out what to aim it at to make it work.
-*spolier alert* Aliens...not just regular aliens like E.T., Jarjar Binks, Predator, or Padme' Ama f'in dala (yes she was an alien...technically...a rather hot one at that,) these aliens are deadly flying around in Zero G. They are deadly (mostly 1 hit kills) on the ground. They blow up when dead. They pilot some serious hardware. Why the hell do they need all this? They can kill Billy King Badass in his super Badass suit with bare hands.
-3 weapons.
-Being invisible doesn't last as long as it should. In many ways it is nearly pointless. More invisible time=more fun.
-Multiplayer is dead.

EARLY ACCESS
Rivals of Aether is a platform fighter in the vain of Super Smash Bros. Melee, that has a strong focus on competitive viability. The game does act as a great jumping off point for those who wish to up their game in Smash, as well as stand alone as it's own platform fighter. Just by changing a few core mechanics, the game is new and it's exciting. Though with all this said, the game is not without flaw, and all the issues I have will be covered later in this reveiw.
If you are unaware of what a platform fighter is, I recommend you do some research first as I will not be explaining every detail. To start, a big departure from games like Smash is the lack of grabbable ledges. The games recovery meta revolves around wall jumping and heavily mixing up your approach back on stage. This game also replaces sheilds with the ability to parry. If timed correctly, parrying an opponents attack will freeze them for a short period of time. These two changes alter not only the core mechanics of platform fighters, but also up the pace of the game. Games are blood pumpingly quick.
The game makes heavy tech skills in Smash like wave dashing and L-Canceling much simpler. The timing for the former is much more forgiving, and everyones wavedash is quite large making it quite versitile. All ariels, with a few exceptions, automatically cancel making for huge combo potential. With all this said, what's easier for you will also be easier for your opponent. Although most pro players stick to ranked mode, you will still get bodied by those who are even more comfortable with the easier controls elsewhere.
The general meta of the game has it's flaws. Most character's tool kits have a very potent dash attack, making it a viable option in almost all combos.I find some characters can get away with dash attack after dash attack at low percents. Not only are they good in combos, but also amazing for starting combos. In Smash, dash attacks are very situational with plenty of ending lag, leaving you open for major punishes if wiffed. Since RoA doesn't have a sheild option, it's much harder to counter a dash attacking opponent (especially online where lag is a factor). To mention one more smaller gripe, the games art style, although very good, makes it difficult to know when to tech.
Rivals of Aether is a step in the right direction when it comes to putting platform fighters on the map. The game is fun, vibrant and captures the style and hype of the genre perfectly. The game does lack features for the casual gamer, but the game is still in Early Access. Rivals still has plenty of time to grow both in balance changes and in features, and I hope we as a community will support it in it's growth.
