I've been playing these Duels of the Planeswalkers games for a few years ago, and as flawed as they are, I think they are an excellent way for players new to Magic to learn the rules of the game and how to play effectively.  Where it always dropped the ball was in perhaps the most important aspect of Magic the Gathering: deck building.
Previous games only gave you specific sets of cards to play with, which were all intro packs more or less.  Most of these decks did not employ a strategy more complicated than "Use a lot of flying creatures" or "I hope you like burn spells" and while playing with these decks would net you related cards for the purpose of augmenting the existing set, it really didn't change much.
Starting in Duels 2015 and continuing with Magic Duels players finally have the opportunity to build their own custom decks and play a true game of Magic the Gathering online!
...It's just too bad they have to do so with a horrible set of cards.
Origins sets you up with a scant offering of basic cards when you begin Magic Duels.  There isn't much variety and you'll be hard pressed to build a deck with much synergy, even while remaining mono colored.  It isn't a good means of getting players interested in the game.
The same holds true, for the most part, in the story mode.  In story mode players embark on several challenges themed around the origin stories of the Planeswalkers featured in the Origins set.  You are provided with a deck themed around the Planeswalker in question but are not provided with a chance to look at it or modify any cards.  Ontop of that, many of these decks are horrible, and do not implement strong synergy.  The sad thing is that this is perhaps the best place for new players to learn it, and Origins, while considerably simpler than the previous Tarkir and Theros set, employs some fun mechanics.  I, in particular, enjoy all the milling that blue can do in this set.  A golden opportunity, squandered.
That isn't to say that there is no enjoyment to be had.  Victories net you coins you can use to buy boosters, containing cards that address all the above issues, as everything stems from a horrible card selection at the onset.
Magic Duels will feel like work before it feels like a game.  The question is, is it worth it?  I can't tell you the answer to that, but I can tell you that it warrants investigation.

I got this game on Black Fridayat Target for 25$, I must say that this was a well spent 25$. This game tends to be get a rather negative review status, so hear me out, and i will explain why I think that this game, in time, will be extrodinarily excellent.
So let's start with the comparison between Civ V and this game. I will admit that I started playing Civ with Civ V, I never played IV or earlier editions soI can't really give an accurate say on those, ut I will say that although I liked Civ V, I never really cmpletely got as much hype for it as others did . I liked the game, but I felt that it became too tedious and annying at points, It always felt the same as I progressed through the eras, and I always fell back on playing one or two specific Civs in order to make it become an enjoyabe experience. I got Brave New World and I enjoyed it, but again, the game really never felt as good to me as it did to others. A main reason I like BE is because it's a futuristic, sci-fi-y turn based strategy game, similar to my favorite gaming franchise, XCOM. (Except for the fps adapments...we don't talk about those) The game itself feels more, intriguing if you will. The idea is great and it was put together pretty well. Looking back this didn't make as much sense, but I hope you were able to gain the basic gist of this.
Secondily, let's discuss some major differences and similarities. Starting with Research. the new Tech Web makes the game feel more diverse and less list-task like. With CIv V, you were forced in a way to research teh same techs, as thsoe were the only techs you were allowed to study. With BE, more techs are available to research and you never really can start with teh same techs, unless under certain conditions. Overall, i like the Web system better. Secondily, the Aliens. Mother of God I love teh aliens. Let's face it, barbarians, sucked. They were annoying, and always just seemed to be an asshat most of the time. With Aliens, this is changed completely. They will stay perfectly passive (except teh worms,♥♥♥♥♥dem worms yo) unless attacked, and their diversity is much better. You can't just go about attacking them, as they are built harder than the barbarians in CIv V. Plus, it actually feels like an accomplishment when you kill them. Words cannot describe the happiness I had when i killed a Siege Worm with 3 Gunner troops, or when I drove back teh great Alien war of 2805 with my lowest ranked city. Overall, BE was able to take a part of Civ V in which I despised and made it one of my favorite features. Let's move onto Quests. Quests are basically optional tasks or decsions that can be made for rewards, I thought they would be annoying as hell, but they are the opposite in contrast. They will always provide you with some sort of benefit, if you chose correctly. So to sum it up, Quests=Good. There are also minor changes, ruins have been changed to resource pods, but still exist in their own way, siege warfare is much improved, and such. But a big change in my opinion was Covert Ops. I'll admit, I never really went too in depth with covert ops in Civ V, but in BE they just feel...more useful. The fact that you can call in a worm strike on an enemy civ is just awesome, and overall, Covert Ops are just awesome. There also are Affinities, but I won't spoil too much with that. Lastly, the major difference and reason why my friends are skeptical of this game are the victories. 1 of them is total conquest, 3/5 of them are research based, and 1 is disocvery based. There is no diplomacy crutch (I call it a crutch cause I lost to that too many times) and the game feels more fast paced and more tech based, wich as I said before, is much harder. Overall, the victories aren't the best thing in the world, but I see nothing outstandingly wrong with them.
To sum everything up, I see nothing horrendously wrong with this game. Diplomacy isn't the greatest, and the sponsers seem redundant from time to time, but the game still hits the right notes. If you're skeptical about this game, I highly reccmond you get it, it's a fun game and keeps me interested. I completely understand why people are skeptical and feel unfufilled, But if you REALLY don't feel comfortable getting it, wait for an expansion. I can guarentee that with time, this game will be jsut as good, or even better than Civ V.

Magic Duels is the latest and final installment in the Planeswalker games. The basic premise of the previous games was $20 Magic game on the computer, which gave you a set of preconstructed decks you could unlock cards for by playing. It was pretty limited, but a low barrier of entry into a normally daunting (and expensive) game. The games were brought down by mediocre UI that was clearly not designed with the PC in mind, netcode which was unreliable at best and a limited number of game modes. Each year we saw much of the same, maybe a new game mode would be added, but ones from last year were oddly absent. New decks were the main draw from year to year, even if many of the basic archetypes and even cards were the same.
With that preamble out of the way, let's dive into the "new" game. The bones of this game are the same tired ones seen in the previous games, bad netcode, unskippable tutorials, a severely limited set of game modes, and user unfriendly UI. The only saving grace of this game and arguably its predecessors is that at its core, it is still Magic the Gathering a wonderfully deep strategy game. That alone almost makes it worth playing, but you are limited to running through the campaign and either grinding out games against the AI for gold to unlock all the cards, or playing against strangers you can't interact with and who might as well be AI. Playing with friends prevents you from gaining gold as does playing 2 headed giant, one of the most popular modes in the series.
So this leaves you with the 2 options, grind out all the card unlocks basically playing single player and then play the modes which give 0 rewards for playing with your friends or pay around $100 to unlock cards which would have cost $20 if this were a regular release in the series. Doesn't make a whole lot of sense as there is no added value in this release compared to previous offerings.
This game had a lot of potential. If they cleaned up the netcode, put together a snazzy UI, included lots of modes (like all the modes in the previous games and EDH), made it possible to play with friends while still progressing (2HG campaign anyone?), it would be worth playing and kicking in some cash. In its current state, it just isn't very fun or interesting or worth your time.

Hitman: Absolution. Let me start off by giving the obvious acknowledgement - yes, it is predictably sexist - the strip clubs, the streetwalkers , the PVC-clad, sexy criminal nun gang (yes, I'm not making it up), the old, abhorrent baddies with their 20 something year old hussies dressed in ridiculously revealing outfits, and so on. I'm not going to harp on about it. It's expected.  So now the boring sh*t is out of the way, I can review the game for its quality as a single player game.
The storyline is an extremely gripping, albeit predictable, action-fuelled chase to save a girl (I know, I know) called Victoria, who some baddies have taken for reasons you'll find out during the game. It's a part stealth, part action game, and I really appreciated the fact that you can choose how to go about achieving your objective in the way you want; be it stealth, going in all guns blazing, or setting traps to distract, kill and remove evidence. The controls are a bit fiddly at first, for example, shooting involves using all your mouse buttons, but you can get used to them quite quickly.
The tasks are varied and fun, and some of them made me genuinely laugh out loud (setting a trap so a guy got electrocuted when he urinated on a live wire is one that springs to mind). Agent 47 is a stereotypical badass - chisel jawed, handy with weapons and has an icy stare - but I couldn't help but like him. He was a man of few words, usually delivered just before he shot someboy between the eyes.
The graphics are top notch and some of the scenery is spectacular. The cutscenes are exciting and immersive and using disguises to go into certain areas or bypass guards was particularly fun (did anybody else dress like a scarecrow, or was that just me?) I liked the fact that you had to scout out a building or room and look for ways to carry out your objective, and it wasn't just clear cut. I liked that this game was sometimes really difficult (and I actually ragequit a few times), rather than being linear and obvious. It was well worth the £3  I paid for it during the sales, and I'd absolutely recommend it, particularly if you enjoy stealth games. If you can overlook the usually unecessary titillation in place for the boys, and the occasional cringeworthy scene, this game is really worth a playthrough or two.

"The Stanley Parable" is a well-produced, fourth-wall smashing, indie game that I would consider to be very incisive and highly relying on the choices made by the player. It is similiar to those Choose-Your-Adventure stories that one would flip to a page if one made a certain decision.
The premise of this game is that the player is a character named Stanley. Stanley has to go to a meeting at work, but finds that everyone is missing and cannot find a trace of human life, etcetera (it expands upon that). You go through a series of different doors, long hallways, and pressing buttons (the Narrator claims that Stanley has almost a fetish with buttons). The "right" way of completing this game is to follow the instruction of the Narrator. Or so it seems.
Well, choose your own story, find out ways you can complete different paths, and enjoy!

For an idea, this game is a cross between the space battles of "Star Wars: Empire at War" and "Endless Space". If you haven't played those, another good comparison would be a cross between "Starcraft" and "Civilization".
It's a realtime strategy, 4X game. You explore the galexy, settle planets, and extract resources. At the same time, other civilizations will try to expand their empire and resources beyond yours. There are constant space battles, micromanagement of economics and government influence, diplomacy, bribery, etc. There aren't any game "phases" as there are in most games of this genre. Instead, they are all happening at once, requiring you to switch from view to view.
It's a fantastic, indepth game. My only real complaint is that it takes a VERY long time to finish. It's difficult to get any kind of resolution without playing the same game for days.

Now, I'll start by saying that this game is really fun and has some very funny lines and moments in it. It has a lot of different choices you can make to have different playthroughs, too, which is great.
However, this game only has so many endings. After a while, you'll go "well, seems like I've done a lot of different choices, and I don't see what else I could do different." and when you search it up, you've done a very large majority of the ending, with only a few remaining that require you to press a button for literally 4 hours (half way through you get a second button, so there's that too.)
Pretty much, once you've completed the endings you can or will, that's pretty much it for the game. This game isn't really worth it, because you can watch a youtube playthough on it and you'll get almost the same overall experience as an actual playthrough.
So heres a little list:
+Fun puzzles
+Amazing and funny dialogue
+Hilarious situations
+Many endings and ways to play through
+Adventure line
-Limited gameplay
-Some endings require 4 hours of the same thing (with a minor change to make it tougher)
-Gets repetetive and annoying at points
-Feels like it tries to be open and welcoming to different ways to play through but doesn't succeed
-Expensive for the gameplay it provides
-Feels empty after you've done most of the endings
-Requires you to either be ridiculously clever or search things up for many of the endings (Not saying I don't like having to be clever, but some of this is just a little absurd how I'm supposed to figure things out and do things in just the right way)
Overall, I can't say I didn't have a good time, but I can't say I would buy it again for the experience. It gives a few good laughs for a little while, but then it just doesn't feel like an amazing game with more to do at the end.

Overall Crysis offers the player a good experience. However, if the player is looking for a smooth transition from beginning to end, they will fall a bit short. Game difficulty moves far too quickly from cakewalk to hell on Earth and back again too quick and far too often. Progressive difficulty is expected with any game. It naturally makes the game imersive so the player doesn't get bored. Finding levels later in game which seem nearly impossible only to move on to levels that are about as difficult as a tutorial is a bit much. Some levels you don't even have a damn clue what you're doing. For instance *spoiler alert!*...you end up in a different world a long time ago in a far away land. For some reason suddenly the gravity turns off. Ok...so I have thrusters. Didn't know that. Why the hell don't they help me jump higher along with the strength ability? Anyways...you'll find yourself inside this thing...we have no clue what it is. Some sort of factory? No clue. Enemies will be flying around you and giant bolts of electricity will be doing the funky chicken along the walls. So you try to figure out what you need to do. More and more bolts of electricity are forming and you start to wonder if the last 5 min you've spent in the area is all for nothing because you can't figure out what you're supposed to do. No...thats not it at all. Its a countdown to a portal that is going to whisk you away. So it turns out its a waiting game. Anyways, *end of spoiler!*
PROS:
-You get an awesome suit with different abilities which are not only fun to play with they are a must to complete missions.
-The learning curve is surprisingly fast.
-Good graphics. Honestly though even for its time...I don't see what all the fuss was about.
-It is one of the better single player FPS experiences out there.
CONS:
-3 main guns until right near the end. At which point you're so happy to pull the trigger of a new gun you nearly have an 0rg@smic moment which can only be bested by finding the 3rd warp whistle in Mario 3 when you're 12.
-On the later guns...(oh yes I'm not done!)...what is described as basically a nuke in a shotgun's body needs a Ph D and 20 yrs experience from Nasa JPL just to figure out how to work the damn thing and figuring out what to aim it at to make it work.
-*spolier alert* Aliens...not just regular aliens like E.T., Jarjar Binks, Predator, or Padme' Ama f'in dala (yes she was an alien...technically...a rather hot one at that,) these aliens are deadly flying around in Zero G. They are deadly (mostly 1 hit kills) on the ground. They blow up when dead. They pilot some serious hardware. Why the hell do they need all this? They can kill Billy King Badass in his super Badass suit with bare hands.
-3 weapons.
-Being invisible doesn't last as long as it should. In many ways it is nearly pointless. More invisible time=more fun.
-Multiplayer is dead.
-3 ♥♥♥♥♥ng guns. RAWR!
-Hot research lady scenes do not contain a lap dance. =)

I played Shadow Warrior back in the day, and I became a fan. I found out that a company went back and released two new Shadow Warrior games, and I told myself, "I got to see this!"
I saw the screenshots of the game and videos showcasing the gameplay, but I also noticed the release date of these games, which in turn, made me quite upset actually. I said to myself, "How the hell did I end up missing this♥♥♥♥♥♥"
I felt a wave of nostalgia hit me, reminding me why I became a fan in the first place, but this feeling was more than just nostalgia. It's been a while since I felt so excited, filled with hope, day dreams, and expectations for the release of a classic game reimagined in more of today's era of videogames.
Here are my thoughts when I played the game, or what I thought about when I was writing this review down:
Movement: In the game, the movements that you make is quite fluent, some may say, "It feels kind of off.", and I would agree with them... at first. Once you start to grow interest into the game, I'd say, It won't be on your mind for very long. You'll probably think, "Even If the movements in the game feels kind of off, I think I can still see myself playing this game.", which turned out to be true for me. Your characters movements can also be seen as a type of defense besides your actual blocks, or powers; try utilizing your movements, consider it a priority to get in a habit of doing so, especially on the harder difficulty settings. It could save your life one of these days.
Weapons: I felt that they definitely aimed for you to use a variety of weapons, because some weapons are fit to handle certain situations better than others. You'll know what I mean once you see the amount of enemies that are in one area or areas, what types of enemies you have to handle, how upgraded are your weapons, which is a thing now, what level enviornment are you in, and♥♥♥♥♥♥like that. So you should get in a habit of assessing your situations, and reacting to those in accordance to your strategy... quick thinking is a plus.
Comedy: Come on guys. If you played the classics then you'll know that Lo Wang, that's the guy you be using, duh, can say some funny♥♥♥♥♥♥from time to time. Sure It's not the same voice actor, but I still think he did his job well. Enjoy the times that he talks and the body gestures that he makes. He's always been the same funny Lo Wang that I knew back in the day, in my book. There's alot more characters that you meet that crack a couple of good jokes, be it with words, or body language. ♥♥♥♥♥ still funny to see and hear; and those fortuna cookies? Oh, they're off the chain! Try to look for them all.
Here are some examples of what I mean. Quotes by the legend himself, Lo Wang:
"You no mess with Lo Wang!"
"Who wants some Wang?"
"You look like a stupid!"
"You are tiny grasshopper."
"Just like Nagasaki."
"Just like Hiroshima."
"Just like Pearl Harbour."
"Ancient chinese secret."
"Oh, must be American made."
"That's no ordinary wang."
"Two wangs are better than one."
"Lo Wang's gonna womit now..."
"Do you want to wash wang? Or do you want to watch Wang wash wang?"
Cinematics: Let me tell you now, Someone had the skills to draw all those pretty drawings that you see during those cinematic cutscenes that happen from time to time again. I really found myself attracted to, well, looking at it.
References: There's a huge nod to the classic Shadow Warrior games in here, but also to some more modern games too! I see what the company did there. I won't spoil it for you, instead, I'll let you play the game and let you see it for yourself.
Gore System: I had to mention this as a way of saluting to the developers that I acknowledge this mechanics existence. If you ever seen the gameplay of Doom 2016, or seen Brutal Wolfenstein, Brutal Doom, Brutal Half-Life, this is pretty much it. I mean don't get me wrong, the gore system in this game is great, but It's not as gory as you would say, like Brutal Doom, but you can't ignore the fact that there are some cool moments that you can witness with this gore system they implemented into the game. Pay attention to it whenever you find yourself attacking the enemies.
Storyline: I wanted to know what the hell was going on throughout the whole game. The game starts by dropping Lo Wang to recover a sword for his Boss, and that's what essentially the game is based about. Lo Wang recovering an ancient, yet legendary swords that can really kick a demons♥♥♥♥♥ It's really enjoyable to know what's next on the agenda, and what's happening in their universe. That's all I'll say, so please play the game if you will.
Powers: I personally haven't used the full extent of my capabilites, but It's definitely something to look into. It can help you out whenever you find yourself in a pinch, such as having the ability to heal yourself. Your on low health and are about to die, but nope, "I can heal myself ♥♥♥♥♥!" Your powers grow as long as you kick majorass. Look around your environments for those sweet juicy items in the secret areas.
Secrets: Yep, definitely a nod to a classic method seen in many games, having secrets in it. If you want the best for Lo Wang then you'll have to search your environments well and find those juicy little morsels, and in return, you'll be kicking more demonass than you ever did before.
Sounds: Sometimes I listen to the sounds of my battles that I have with the demons that I come across, and the environments that I'm in, and the music that plays in those scenarios as well. There's something about it that just really sets you up for some nice, fast pace action situations, or It swoops you into the world that is, Lo Wang's world.
Conclusion: Maybe It's not so much of a bad thing to check this game out yourself after all, but hey, you don't have to take my word for it. I am 11 hours into the game, an unfortunately there are many glaring flaws in this game. I believe most of the technical issues will eventually be resolved, but there are some serious design issues which really drag this game down.
I have long been a fan of the X series and I have been looking forward to this game for months, so my experience might be colored somewhat by my disappointment. I have been plagued with poor performance, constant game crashes which sometimes require a reboot to get out of, and numerous glitches in the trading system and missions that make advancement impossible.
Again, the technical issues will be resolved via patching. What may not be resolved are the design choices that depart from previous X games. To list:
1. You can no longer hop from ship to ship. You can own multiple ships and you can issue them limited orders, but your starting ship will be your ending ship and it will be the only one you pilot.
2. The trading network has been neutered. You can only issue trade commands for your freighters to sell or purchase goods in their system only. You can't set up the elaborate chains that were possible in X:TC.
3. Voice acting: You are chained to another character that has some of the worst voice acting I've heard since Final Fantasy X.
4. Menus, sub menus, sub-sub-menus: You can't just buy a gun or missile while floating in space. You need to dock your ship, walk to the individual merchant, open a conversation, request to see their goods, request to see their missiles, then request to buy them, then tell them how many you want. Seriously, restocking missiles is a 5-minute ordeal after every fight.
I think I see where they wanted to go with this game. They wanted to make it more appealing to the masses that were previously turned off by the massive learning curve the series holds. Unfortunately, instead of streamlining the game mechanics they just hid them behind a poorly-designed and time-consuming interface which is somehow more painful to deal with than the spreadsheets of the older games.
I want to like this game so much, but there are just too many jagged edges to get much actual enjoyment.
+Mods, +Fluid combat, +Cheap, +Three Classes each with three skill branches, +Pets, +Decent loot system, +Character to character item transfer. If you liked Diablo, you will love this. Recommended

Okay, so I've put some pretty good time in to the game. First, don't buy this game if you get frustrated by frequent crashes and bugs. However, if you're willing to try out the different systems and explore a beautiful space universe, this game really is quite fun and addictive. Thus far, I started off by using the Long Range Scanner to pick up random items out in space in Freeplay mode. Apparently Campaign mode is horribly broken (it crashes constantly for me), so I've been learning the systems by trying them out and researching the forums and live streams. After collecting and selling junk, I upgraded my ship to where I felt comfortable attacking a Capital freighter. After many failures, I learned that having a TON of marines help. I began capturing and selling freighters for cash, and attempted to send one out to trade. It was very time consuming and unpleasurable to search for "trade deals". It was, however, fun to ride on the deck of the freighter, standing outside of my ship, while it tore off through space to destinations I commanded it to go. Eventually I decided to try for an Arawn, the biggest baddest Carrier in the game. Somehow after 10-15 tense minutes later, I captured one. I then tested out refueling theh ship for instant Jumps. It took the Arawn almost 2 hours to line up to the fuel dock, and then failed to load anything. At this point, none of my Capitals are able to load Jump fuel. Before I went back to the Dockyard, I saw another Arawn and decided to pounce on it. Three reloads later (due to my ship flying into the structure of it, among other bugs), I was able to capture another one! These sell for 50 mil apiece! My next endeavour is to learn to build my own stations, and continue raids into the Albion system to pilage and plunder freighters and super carriers. Amassing my wealth and building my blood Empire for the day that the game is fixed, playable without near paranoid saves, and as fun as I know it can be. Give it a few months if you're not THAT in to this genre. But if you're starved for the mere experience of exploring in your own ship, and testing some fun systems in the mean time, then I'd recommend picking it up. Hope this helps someone!

Magic Duels is the latest and final installment in the Planeswalker games. The basic premise of the previous games was $20 Magic game on the computer, which gave you a set of preconstructed decks you could unlock cards for by playing. It was pretty limited, but a low barrier of entry into a normally daunting (and expensive) game. The games were brought down by mediocre UI that was clearly not designed with the PC in mind, netcode which was unreliable at best and a limited number of game modes. Each year we saw much of the same, maybe a new game mode would be added, but ones from last year were oddly absent. New decks were the main draw from year to year, even if many of the basic archetypes and even cards were the same.
With that preamble out of the way, let's dive into the "new" game. The bones of this game are the same tired ones seen in the previous games, bad netcode, unskippable tutorials, a severely limited set of game modes, and user unfriendly UI. The only saving grace of this game and arguably its predecessors is that at its core, it is still Magic the Gathering a wonderfully deep strategy game. That alone almost makes it worth playing, but you are limited to running through the campaign and either grinding out games against the AI for gold to unlock all the cards, or playing against strangers you can't interact with and who might as well be AI. Playing with friends prevents you from gaining gold as does playing 2 headed giant, one of the most popular modes in the series.
So this leaves you with the 2 options, grind out all the card unlocks basically playing single player and then play the modes which give 0 rewards for playing with your friends or pay around $100 to unlock cards which would have cost $20 if this were a regular release in the series. Doesn't make a whole lot of sense as there is no added value in this release compared to previous offerings.
This game had a lot of potential. If they cleaned up the netcode, put together a snazzy UI, included lots of modes (like all the modes in the previous games and EDH), made it possible to play with friends while still progressing (2HG campaign anyone?), it would be worth playing and kicking in some cash. In its current state, it just isn't very fun or interesting or worth your time.

First and foremost, let it be said that this game needs some serious work in order for it to really be good, though considering it is Free to Play, I would still recommend it.
Here's a basic breakdown of the game as well as my final thoughts.
Pros:
-It's Magic.
-Pretty generous F2P model.
-You can now fully create your own decks, unlike previous versions of Duels.
-Two Headed Giant is here.
-It does a good job of introducing the basic mechanics of the game for new players.
-The current cardpool is pretty decent, though considering it's based on the Origins set, that's not surprising.
Cons:
-The UI leaves a lot to be desired. You can get used to it, but it'll need a facelift eventually, especially the deck creator.
-Bugs out the wazoo. Although the game works fine mechanically, I have experienced numerous bugs with matchmaking (like my friend and I being put on opposite teams in 2HG) and it crashes pretty consistently when I Alt+Tab out.
-Content is pretty lacking. The cardpool is decent for a starter set (Essentially just the Origins set with a few extras/missing in order to make it easier for beginner decks I think), though there are very few gamemodes. The main story will last you a few hours, though it's pretty dull, and there's currently only 1v1 and Two Headed Giant multiplayer. I would've at least expected a Free for All option, but that's absent.
Those are the major things I've noticed so far.
Ultimately, if you like to play Magic on a regular basis, you should go ahead and give this a try at least. The core gameplay is there and most of the bugs will probably be fixed in the near future. The Content, though currently lacking, will eventually start to trickle in. Maybe we'll even see Commander or Planechase variants one day.
If you're new to Magic or have never played it before, then I might recommend just waiting a few months for it to be a bit  more polished. Even though it does do a good job of introducing new players to the series, the bugs and other quirks might seem a bit overwhelming to them.
Despite the game's flaws, they aren't numerous or severe enough to actually detract from the core gameplay, which is just as fun as ever, and at the end of the day, it is free, so you don't really stand to lose anything other than time.

Shelter is a 2013 game by Might and Delight. You play as a badger, mother of five cubs. Your task is to venture out into the wilderness and watch your little ones grow over the course of the four seasons. To me, it isn't obvious why, because you neither are really searching for a new home (or "Shelter") nor do you lack food in the beginning. Nevertheless it is one very interesting experience.

There are about 5-6 different areas that you have to cross before reaching the ending. All of them contain some kind of threat to your cubs. Except the first one- which is a "light-hearted" introduction to what turns out to be a "heart-breaking" experience. Everything starts out just perfect in summer or spring (I'm not quite sure) and then the environment slowly starts to show its claws- be it through predators, a waterfall, a forest fire, or just the harsh weather in winter.
The levels are quite big and are made to give you an open world-feeling yet everything about the game feels linear. Even when you start loosing some of your cubs, you begin to ask yourself: is this really my fault or is it all scripted? Strange thought, but this makes sure you play the game more than just once. Maybe it is possible to finish with all of the five cubs. Or what will happen if all of them die?
When you finish "story-mode", the so-called "Nurture"-mode is unlocked, where you have to check on your cubs every day in rl to make sure they get something to eat and grow up healthy. A very interesting concept to keep you playing.
The gameplay is very intuitive, though anything but challenging. You only need the typical WASD-scheme, left mouse button to interact, shift to sprint and ctrl to sneak. All you have to do is look for all kinds of food to feed your cubs with. At the beginning you are left alone with looking for things to eat, but as your cubs grow, they start running towards everything they see.
With things you find you can only feed one cub at a time. That is until you decide to try out your hunting skills. Mice are the easiest to catch, but then there are foxes or frogs. When you manage to catch one of these there's a feast for all of your cubs.
One thing that really bothered me however is: How does the mother survive without eating anything? Does she feed on her cubs being content and healthy or have I missed something?
The artstyle is really interesting, but after some time you begin to realise that technically it's well beyond it's possibilities- especially for a game released in 2013. The textures(even for me- someone who normally doesn't really give a s**t about graphics) have very low resolution and the lighting is very dim and colorless.
The soundtrack however is perfect. In every scene (or level) it enhances your experience- by creating a tense atmosphere, winter atmosphere, light atmosphere and so on.
Although the game runs fairly well on my PC without any technical problems whatsoever, after I finished it, it hardly got back into the main menu. The screen just sort of kept popping for a whole 30 secs.
Shelter is a very special experience. Over the course of only 70 minutes it managed to personally engage me into the journey of a group of virtual animals- some would call it a family. Everytime I lost a cub I felt bad- it made me feel as if I was a loser to make that happen. At the end I had only one cub left and it felt like victory to me- with a bittersweet aftertaste- but a victory nonetheless.
It is also a very tedious experience. The visuals aren't as fresh as they should and the pseudo-open-world just hinders the experience as in some closed off areas there is nothing to find except a single carrot. Also the popping menu screen leaves a very bad impression in a technically nearly perfect game.
In general, Shelter is something you have to experience. It isn't the best and it has its problems, but as a whole, it is a gratifying experience. You get to learn that although the world can sometimes be cruel, it has its reasons. It genuinely makes you feel good- although it also makes you think.

The word of Middle-Earth can be regarded as the archetypal high-fantasy setting. Thus, it lends itself very well to games of this type: hack-and-slash fests with some light RPG'ish elements (leveling up, learning skills and upgrading weapons). LotR:WitN goes beyond the known lore of Tolkien though: Snowblind Studio's have put a lot of work in a story that branches from the Ringbearer's one. Most of the time, this works quite nice: a lot of the scenes you'll visit are familiar (Barrow Dows, Mirkwood etc.) but are presented in a fresh way. The game actually offers quite a lot of background to the regular books, which is nice for those who haven't read 'The Silmarillion' etc. (me among them).
As a game, LotR:WitN is quite pleasing: you select one of three characters and smash all sorts of foes to blubber. Each character has it's own strenghts and weaknesses and you can switch in between chapters. One mechanic that didn't work well for me was blocking: I finished the game without using it a single time (mostly playing as a dwarf). Still, I enjoyed it quite a lot for it's story and graphics. All in all I recommend this to those who like LotR and action-games, especially when you can get it at a sale.

Anyone who actually has a halfway decent PC, beware of this poorly executed port. My GTX 980 should more than be able to run this port of a PS3 game, but Square Enix clearly didn't bother to test this port with any modern software or halfway decent graphic cards. In windowed mode at 720p res settings with MSAA at minimum and shadows at a low setting, the game ran consistently at 30 fps in most areas, until a battle or cutscene starts, where the framerate jumps between 60 and 15 in a matter of seconds and continues to fluctuate in this manner, dropping whenever any movement or spell effect occurs. Not only does this make battles impossible to keep track of or even look at without wanting to barf, it causes a slight de sync in cutscenes that can be annoying at times and just awful at others.
Also, the game does not look good. The higher resolutions are okay, but the AA is consistently ugly, even at 16x. Lightning's hair can look very pixelated at times from it and it effects the other characters and the surroundings as well. It's distracting and it makes the PS3 version look like heaven in comparison. And if your performance requires you to lower the shadows, enjoy them. They turn into blocky messes at anything below the two higher settings.
As for the game itself, it's Final Fantasy XIII. Go look at everybody else's opinion. This port just goes even further to highlight what a let-down this game is, as well as Square Enix's performance as of late. My only hope is that Final Fantasy XV gets a better pc release. Or at least that Lightning Returns does.
The game itself is a 7/10. This port is a 4/10, being barely playable for those with high pc gaming and RPG standards.
Note: Some people have no performance issues with their systems and I understand that. But that's some people. The others have a right to know what they're getting into. That's why I'm downvoting it.

I'll recommend the game, but not at full price. Don't buy it for more than 4-5 euros.
The game isn't too hard, but not to easy (as long as you don't skip the puzzles, but who would ?). It demands thinking, logic and memory. The "hard" parts, the puzzle, can be skipped, so if you're just here to live an adventure, it will do.
The drawing are most of the time beautiful, especially landscapes and large pictures. Unfortunately, the animations are sometimes really odd (or totally ♥♥♥♥ed up, but you can't say that on Steam). During the cut scenes, the sound / image / subtitles are way too often no synchronized, so the narration is hardly enjoyable. Moreover, Fay is suffering so hard of scoliosis, I wonder how she still stand.
As for me, I separate the the game in two parts : First part, you discover the plot, the characters, the goals. It's a nice part, well written, with various environment, the year 2050 was particularly nice to go through. The second part, on the other hand, is heavy and not that interesting.
One of the biggest problems I found in this game, is the lack of psychology and deepness in the character. Someone close to you dies ? Ok, nevermind, just go on. You are betrayed by everybody ? Ok, nevermind, just excuse yourself and I'll forget it. Someone who tried to harm you died ? Ho my god, bring the sad music and the cut scene ! That's not making sense at all, even if Fay is used to see dead people, and even if Bent is an old  disillusioned man, there is no way they would react like that. Add this to some cheesy dialogues, and you might want to punch them in the face once in a while.
The scenario is quite good however. Climate change, collective responsibility, how far will people go to save mankind, sounds good to me. Too bad the activists are, once again in a video game, represented as fanatics or stupid hippies, but nevermind, the storytelling is good (if you can pass over the synch problems I spoke before).
I'm a bit frustrated though, because I find the game way too short, and the ending too quick. But it IS a good game, a good point and click where you should think and reason. Even if my review is mostly negative, but it's harder  to me to describe why I enjoyed rather than what I didn't enjoyed in the game, in particular because english isn't my native language.

This game is an odd one.  It's a JRPG complete with animal people, teenaged leading character, and a fairly good story once it gets started but it's got a pretty strange combat system.  It supports mouse/keyboard though it could have supported them better.  It also has a tendency to hide pretty important information on how the game works but there's now an excellent Wikia website that will fill you in on all the details you care to learn.
The combat system is really the make-or-break feature for this game, IMHO, and it's very different from anything I've ever played before or since.  It's turn based but you get to have a lot of characters in your party (up to 18 eventually) so telling each one of them exactly what to do would take way too long.  Instead, you divide your team into squads then give general orders to the squad along the lines of "attack with melee" and "stand back and heal" then the members of the squad use their abilities to carry out those orders.
Not all the possible commands appear every round, though.  The game will pick out four or five of them depending on the situation, who the squad's leader is, and other factors.  That will drive some folks crazy but I found it to be a fun part of the game as it forced me to think about what I could still do even though I didn't get to do exactly what I wanted.  It's a bit like being dealt a hand of cards then figuring out what to do with them instead of picking out the best cards from the deck every time.
You're definitely given a lot of choices in this game.  Simply picking the most expensive commands and attacking whatever is right in front of you with whatever squads you throw together will work OK for a few hours but you'll never make it through the whole game that way.  You're going to need to think about what characters should make up your squads, how many squads you should have, which characters should lead, which characters to hire, which monsters to attack (genocide is NOT the answer), how many to attack at once, whether to send all your squads after one enemy squad or to spread out more, and so on.  You certainly don't need to master every aspect of the game to complete it but you do need to get good at most of them.  (Unfortunately, the game doesn't have a difficulty setting.)
Character skill progression is a learn-by-doing system.  If you want Nora casting Cachexia by the end of the game then you'll need to let her do some poison gas spells instead of pounding everything with her hammer.  Character weapons are a major part of progression, too, which are advanced by finding components for your characters to use.  (The Wikia site is extremely handy for that aspect of the game.  Why the developers thought you would actually remember where you found some necrotic metal or which type of critter dropped a mystic fiend horn I have no idea.)
I see a lot of reviews are complaining about grinding... uhh, yeah, you can ignore those.  This is one of the few JRPGs that will actually PUNISH you if you try to exploit the game by grinding!  You see, most JRPGs have fixed monster levels while the characters that get added to your party as you find them automatically adjust to the player's level.  So some people will sit back in the early parts of the game fighting the same monsters over and over until they are so high level that nothing can stop them.  In this game, the characters you find are fixed level but several of the monsters scale to your party's level.  That means the same tactic in this game will result in hiring weak characters against enemies that only a few members in your party can really fight!
That said, the game CAN turn grindy after you've gotten all the characters you want but it's completely optional.  The game can be completed just fine with no grinding at all.  You won't be able to finish some of the most difficult quests but you won't miss out on any of the story at all.
It's a great game, I love it.

Gameplay: At it's core Hollow Knight is an exploration and combat based game with metroidvania aspects. The combat system focuses of learning enemy attack patterns and striking them at the moment they are vulnerable, without getting too greedy and exposing yourself to a potential follow up attack. With a variety of almost 200 different enemy types, there is no shortage of new enemies to fight. The combat system is supplemented by the charms that allows you to customize your play style. Want more  damage, want allies to aid you, want more powerful magic? All of these play styles are obtainable and offer their own advantages and disadvantages.
Story: The story revolves around the titular character, the hollow knight, exploring the dying world of formerly great kingdom of insects. There is VERY little direct narrative presented to the player. This is easily comparable to the way that information is given to the player in Dark Souls. Most of the story and lore of the world is presented to the player by small dialogue segments with NPC and by reading item description.
Level Design: The amount of detail put into this world is awe inspiring. Each area of the game feel unique and well developed charm (Well... except Kindgom's Edge). Most areas will culminate in a Boss fight that will challenge of test the skills you've learned. Many of the bosses will have an optional, more difficult form.
Sound: The soundtrack consists mainly of string and percussion instruments. Most areas and bosses have a custom music that never made me want to mute it. Look up the theme the Mantis Lords boss fight. I rarely suggest picking up video game OST, but the Hollow Knight - Official Soundtrack is a must have.
Graphics: The artistic direction of this game is a tremendous asset. Rather than focusing on high fidelity graphics, the game focuses on a consistent, beautiful art style . I played most of this game on laptop with a GTX750M GPU and had no problem maintaining 1080P 60FPS.
Overall: This is the best game to come out in 2017. The amount of quality content in a $15 game makes this game feel undervalued. I would gladly have paid upwards to $30 for such a well polished game. The consistent new content the developers have released post launch make Team Cherry a top developer in my book.

I will begin by noting that this is the first Hitman game I have played, but will certainly not be the last. It has definitely made me wish to go back and play some of the older titles in the series. As a result, my review can only be one for Hitman Absolution rather than a comparison with previous Hitman titles.
Hitman Absolution is a good game. It has solid stealth action but seems to feel eerily similar to a Splinter Cell title at times. Since I like the Splinter Cell series I do not consider this a bad thing, and certainly Absolution's 'disguise' mechanic adds more than a little to the stealth gameplay it may have borrowed from Sam Fisher. Nonetheless, despite some rather interesting ways of killing targets, with quite a lengthy campaign at 20 (mostly linear) missions, the game begins to become rather tedious. You kill several targets in the same way, for example. The game seemed rather rushed towards the end. And, as expected, the storyline was pretty much laughably poor. But we don't play Hitman for the storyline...don't expect Metal Gear Solid here.
Although this review seems profoundly negative, I had a lot of fun playing Hitman Absolution and it has a surprising amount of replay value and some rather fun challenges to beat. The graphics are beautiful at times and some of the best I've seen on the previous generation of games. Upping the difficulty can be an interesting and very challenging experience, and competing with friends to see who is the best Hitman is also quite a fun dynamic to the game also.
In sum, Hitman is worth a play. If you like no-nonsense stealth games, this is definitely one for you. 8/10.

This War of Mine is a strategy game about collecting and using resources from multiple locations around your base to construct tools and structures that will further help you, while maintaining the health and happiness of the survivors that live there. The game focuses on moral and conscious decisions. Will you steal from the eldery couple to eat tonight? Will you give the children medicine for their dying mother or will you keep it for if your designated scavenger becomes deathly ill?
The atmosphere of the game is amazing, and you'll find yourself immersed in a bloody war from the moment you start playing, and you'll be forced to make difficult decisions. Make a heater so that you don't become ill from cold tonight, or construct a trap you can use to catch and eat rodents and the other small animals that make their way through your home. Collect the book so that you can forget the horrible tragedies of war, or grab and take home some extra medicine to your dying friend?
No run will definetely ever be the same, with events that you can encounter when going to different scavenging locations (such as encountering friendly looters at the supermarket sometimes). Each new run offers different experiences and ways to play the game, as well as an opportunity to get different starting survivors to play as.
One game (from what I hear) ends after about 45 days, and each run could be different. For instance, a neighbor might come to trade with you, children might come looking for medicine for their mother, or a good samaritan might come to you looking for an extra pair of hands to help dig out the residents of the recently shelled and collapsed apartment building down the street. Each game is full of experiences and things you can do differently, strategies you can come up with and decisions to make.
If you're into challenging decision making in a immersive, depressing war zone, this game is for you. And at it's current price (20$, even less when it's on sale), it's a relatively cheap game to buy considering it's content. Do yourself a favor, give it a try! You might like what you see.

Strike Suit Zero seems like a good game. It has pretty backdrops, some fun and exciting music, and the promise of a robotic mech spaceship to annihilate enemies. But the gameplay is so frustrating that playing it is a chore, and a frustrating one at that.
The basics combat system is good enough. It's fairly easy to get the hang of picking off enemies and sending missiles in every direction. In fact, Strike Suit Zero feels the best when it has you fighting against dozens of enemy fighters, honing in on enemies to build up to the moment where you can transform and unleash hell. But that's a small part of the game. At least 50% of the game is attacking larger stationary ships, taking out cargo, or blowing up turrets, all of which is so boring or frustrating that it brings down the little bit of fun the dogfights provide.
To make matters worse, there is a constant barrage of turrets, cannons, and other non-evadable damage that not only steadily drains health but keeps the screen in a disorienting panic that's less exhilirating than it is confusing. Many missions, especially the incredibly tedious ones that involve picking off every turret from a large cruiser, turned into me going for an attack, then flying aimlessly while my shield recharged before trying again. Rinse lather repeat.
If you're looking for your fill of space dogfighting, I don't think Strike Suit Zero is your best bet. There are many older games, and even some very recent ones that are starting to fill that hole better. If you're dedicated to playing every space game out there, you'll probably have fun with it, but otherwise I'd sit this one out.

Strike Suit Zero is one of the best games that I have had the honor of playing. The graphics are great, the story is interesting, the combat is absolutly fantasic and the music. OOOH the music. But without furthur or do here is the review.
Overall Rating: 8/10
Graphics: The graphics are absolutly fantastic. I don't have to specify why, because if you look at the screen shots, and the trailer you will see why. The effects, and the lights make it feel like your in a fire fight, and the sounds that go along with the graphics are just fantastic. Although since the lights and textures are bright and colorful and they are of abundance so players you are warned.
Combat: The combat is the highlight of this game. The combat goes as followed. You move with the W,A,S,D keys and can use the left shift to use thrusters to boost around the battle field. You have two guns, the Primary which is usually fast fireing and powerful that has unlimited ammunition that uses energy (which regenerates over time). Then there is a various amounts of missles in the game that you can use that have their own speical properties and effectivness in situations. Some times in combat you can have your weapons lock on to the enemy, and the bullets will follow them. Mot of the time I find myself using my primary guns, and to use them effectivly you have to arch your aim so that the enemy flys into it. Fortunatly it gives you a place to fire, so you know where you need to shoot (However you need to be close or the circle will not show up). The primary weapon has unlimited ammunition since it uses the energy of the ship, but the LMG's, and various missles have ammunition and can be depleted fast. There are many different ships you can use, and I personally perfer the Strike Suit. You can switch from Mech to ship with the space button and just like regular primary weapon fire, the Strike suit requires power to be used. How do you do that? By blowing things up! All in all the fighting in this game feels "realistic" so to speak and is very fun and challenging. Although the large amount of enemys in the area of combat can be over whelming, it always pays off to be moving, and to not get to close to the main enemy ships until the fighters are taken care of. In that way its tactical and makes me want to stay with my team.
Music: The mustic brings a tear to my eyes, as its as epic as it is interesting. Many times I find music repeating but I don't mind that very much as it is quite epic and makes me fight harder and get into the heat of the moment.
Pros-
Music
Graphics
Combat
light effects and sounds around the area
story
Cons-
No multiplayer
Gets repetitive
Final Opinon: This game is really good. There are some things that didn't live up to my expectations, not much DLC, no multiplayer, not alot of missions, etc. But on the other hand the dlc isn't a need, the multiplayer would be fun but isn't a thing that needs to happen. The missions are long and increse in difficulty as you go on. The combat, music, and graphics are all in my own opinon great. I bought this game today, and played it for 2 hours. No regrets. If you like Mechs, and the Sci-Fi genres this game is worth the $19.99 and is worth picking up to play.
If you are a good or 'Hardcore' Strategy/ 4X Game Player this game is definetly a optimal choice, to take into review if you wish to but a game of this Genre. Play smart!

I played Shadow Warrior back in the day, and I became a fan. I found out that a company went back and released two new Shadow Warrior games, and I told myself, "I got to see this!"
I saw the screenshots of the game and videos showcasing the gameplay, but I also noticed the release date of these games, which in turn, made me quite upset actually. I said to myself, "How the hell did I end up missing this♥♥♥♥♥♥"
I felt a wave of nostalgia hit me, reminding me why I became a fan in the first place, but this feeling was more than just nostalgia. It's been a while since I felt so excited, filled with hope, day dreams, and expectations for the release of a classic game reimagined in more of today's era of videogames.
Here are my thoughts when I played the game, or what I thought about when I was writing this review down:
Movement: In the game, the movements that you make is quite fluent, some may say, "It feels kind of off.", and I would agree with them... at first. Once you start to grow interest into the game, I'd say, It won't be on your mind for very long. You'll probably think, "Even If the movements in the game feels kind of off, I think I can still see myself playing this game.", which turned out to be true for me. Your characters movements can also be seen as a type of defense besides your actual blocks, or powers; try utilizing your movements, consider it a priority to get in a habit of doing so, especially on the harder difficulty settings. It could save your life one of these days.
Weapons: I felt that they definitely aimed for you to use a variety of weapons, because some weapons are fit to handle certain situations better than others. You'll know what I mean once you see the amount of enemies that are in one area or areas, what types of enemies you have to handle, how upgraded are your weapons, which is a thing now, what level enviornment are you in, and♥♥♥♥♥♥like that. So you should get in a habit of assessing your situations, and reacting to those in accordance to your strategy... quick thinking is a plus.
Comedy: Come on guys. If you played the classics then you'll know that Lo Wang, that's the guy you be using, duh, can say some funny♥♥♥♥♥♥from time to time. Sure It's not the same voice actor, but I still think he did his job well. Enjoy the times that he talks and the body gestures that he makes. He's always been the same funny Lo Wang that I knew back in the day, in my book. There's alot more characters that you meet that crack a couple of good jokes, be it with words, or body language. ♥♥♥♥♥ still funny to see and hear; and those fortuna cookies? Oh, they're off the chain! Try to look for them all.
Here are some examples of what I mean. Quotes by the legend himself, Lo Wang:
"You no mess with Lo Wang!"
"Who wants some Wang?"
"You look like a stupid!"
"You are tiny grasshopper."
"Just like Nagasaki."
"Just like Hiroshima."
"Just like Pearl Harbour."
"Ancient chinese secret."
"Oh, must be American made."
"That's no ordinary wang."
"Two wangs are better than one."
"Lo Wang's gonna womit now..."
"Do you want to wash wang? Or do you want to watch Wang wash wang?"
Cinematics: Let me tell you now, Someone had the skills to draw all those pretty drawings that you see during those cinematic cutscenes that happen from time to time again. I really found myself attracted to, well, looking at it.
References: There's a huge nod to the classic Shadow Warrior games in here, but also to some more modern games too! I see what the company did there. I won't spoil it for you, instead, I'll let you play the game and let you see it for yourself.
Gore System: I had to mention this as a way of saluting to the developers that I acknowledge this mechanics existence. If you ever seen the gameplay of Doom 2016, or seen Brutal Wolfenstein, Brutal Doom, Brutal Half-Life, this is pretty much it. I mean don't get me wrong, the gore system in this game is great, but It's not as gory as you would say, like Brutal Doom, but you can't ignore the fact that there are some cool moments that you can witness with this gore system they implemented into the game. Pay attention to it whenever you find yourself attacking the enemies.
Storyline: I wanted to know what the hell was going on throughout the whole game. The game starts by dropping Lo Wang to recover a sword for his Boss, and that's what essentially the game is based about. Lo Wang recovering an ancient, yet legendary swords that can really kick a demons♥♥♥♥♥ It's really enjoyable to know what's next on the agenda, and what's happening in their universe. That's all I'll say, so please play the game if you will.
Powers: I personally haven't used the full extent of my capabilites, but It's definitely something to look into. It can help you out whenever you find yourself in a pinch, such as having the ability to heal yourself. Your on low health and are about to die, but nope, "I can heal myself ♥♥♥♥♥!" Your powers grow as long as you kick majorass. Look around your environments for those sweet juicy items in the secret areas.
Secrets: Yep, definitely a nod to a classic method seen in many games, having secrets in it. If you want the best for Lo Wang then you'll have to search your environments well and find those juicy little morsels, and in return, you'll be kicking more demonass than you ever did before.
Sounds: Sometimes I listen to the sounds of my battles that I have with the demons that I come across, and the environments that I'm in, and the music that plays in those scenarios as well. There's something about it that just really sets you up for some nice, fast pace action situations, or It swoops you into the world that is, Lo Wang's world.
Conclusion: Maybe It's not so much of a bad thing to check this game out yourself after all, but hey, you don't have to take my word for it. You can either choose to play the game or to wang the game (set it aside). Who knows man. I'm just gonna go ahead and let you guys know this one thing in advance, and that is:
"You mess with the bull, you get the wang."

Shelter came in a Humble Bundle for me eons ago. When I first got it, I fell in love with the graphics immediately. Shelter follows the story of Mother Badger and her five cubs. You have to overcome the challenges of the wild to ensure the survival of your litter. It's a quick game, with about an hour of game play, but a lasting impression.
The game is moreso a moving art piece. The plot progresses slowly, changing only when the chapter shifts. Essentially, you set the pace for the game and you have limited freedom in exploration. Overall, the maps are pretty linear, but you can sniff around.
The mechanics for the game are simple, and it's pretty low stress (apart from wanting to save your cubs). Feed them, feed yourself if you choose, and move forward.
Pros:
- Artistic masterpiece
- Great sound track; super relaxing
- I got pretty attached to all of the badgers
Cons:
- Plot driven, but not a plot heavy game. Thats a pro or a con depending on what type of game you're looking for.
- Pretty short game play. I wish it was just a little longer.
- The flow between chapters appeared choppy at times.
- I got pretty attached to all of the badgers :(

Sigh.
I have fond memories of the previous DotP games. Most of them were unimpressive, sure, and many, particularly last year's iteration, have been complete jank, but there was always the barest shriveled remnant of a soul keeping the game alive. I remember eagerly plowing through the Challenge Mode in Duels 2013, unlocking cards for my favorite decks, playing through archenemy, planechase, 2HG, the long and compelling story campaigns, the revenge campaigns...
All of the DotP games had that -spark-, that soul, even if they were terrible, the work was there. The heart was there. The love was there. What then, is my strongest memory of Magic Duels, the new F2P iteration?
Running through the barebones campaign in an hour and a half, then working up a minimal amount of enthusiasm for like what, two or three multiplayer games? How about playing through my backlog and wondering if I really wanted to muster up the drive to play a multiplayer duel? Or perhaps checking every hour to see if the servers were back up out of curiosity, rather than any real desire to get my cardboard monsters on? Nothing great, apparently.
Magic Duels is jank.
That's the skinny. Magic Duels is not value rares or money mythics. It's not hot trash either. It's jank, those cards that linger in the pack that just arent quite good enough for any format, but you can't help but look at them and want to make them work. You throw em all together in a deck, post 1-3-0 for FNM, then get incessently heckled by your friends about how terrible your deck was and what the hell motivated you to build it, but you know, -you just know- that if you had only drawn that card one turn early in round 2, and if you hadn't had to mulligan into a manascrew in that one game, and you didn't make that one misplay, you could have went 3-0-1. You ignore the rational part of your mind, the part telling you exactly what your friends are telling you, and you hold on to that feeling, even though you know for a fact that you're going to keep posting 1-3-0 with that deck every week, every friday.
Magic Duels is those cards, it is that deck. Magic Duels is that feeling. It is also a videogame.
Where do we even start?
- Magic Duels is based off of Magic Origins, the latest and last core set. It's not a terrible set, but it's not taking the game in a great direction. Remember that old axiom for the game, that anything you cast for four or more mana should win you the game on the spot? Well, Wizards of the Coast has thrown that out the window. Hope you like running nothing but four- and five-drops in your aggro deck. The mana curve has not been pushed so much as violently jostled sideways.
- The starter cards they give you to build noob decks out of? Hot trash. Nothing new right? Well...
- Booster packs are stingy as hell. It takes eight wins against another player to unlock a single booster, and the boosters only come with six cards: three commons, two uncommons, and one rare with a 1:8 chance for the rare to be a mythic. Commons, however, are the backbones of your decks, and because they are the only cards that you can run full playsets of, don't expect to make anything approaching cohesive until you've cracked open a million of these. Oh hey, nice Titan of Erebos, that would be great for a mono-black deck! Good luck pulling the four Read the Bones that you're going to need to get that working though. I'm sorry, but pulling Commons should not be harder and more psychologically taxing than pulling mythics.
- You can do Quests to earn gold as well, but the most common ones, Archetype and Archetype Paragon, don't work. They don't update at all, no matter how many games you win with those decks. Other quests are often quite hard and just as much of a grind as winning, which the majority of quests require you do anyway. The payout for the quests also isn't fantastic, averaging 40 gold for a completion. Nice, four of them will nab me a booster! Too bad you can only do three a day.
- Of course, you could pay real money for these boosters, because that's always awesome, right?
- Because the card pool is abysmal, the metagame is not incredibly varied. Expect to fight White/Red Auras a lot.
- You get nothing for losing. This wouldn't be such a problem if any of the above weren't true, but because of the terrible cards and ridiculous mana curve, games go on for way longer than they have to and playing just feels like a chore. Imagine investing 45 minutes into a single game (not match, game) and walking away with nothing. Think of all the other things you could have done in that 45 minutes. It's infuriating.
- Barebones campaign, no challenge mode, no variants besides 2HG, no free-for-all multiplayer, no sealed or booster draft. I mean sure, you could play 2HG, but you get nothing for it. After the hour or two it takes to do the campaign, multiplayer with randoms is pretty much as deep as it gets.
- No chat, communication, tables, lobbies, or trading. Pretty much as antisocial as you can make MTG. Also, again, no trading. I don't care how you're never going to run that mythic. I don't care how much you need that playset of commons your friend pulled. No trading. Way to take the T out of TCG
- A technical nightmare, but that's kind of par for the course for DotP. Below-average UI, crappy servers, dated graphics. I'm willing to forgive a lot of this one. All of these elements are still way better than they were in Duels 2015, and they probably won't give you motion sickness. On the other hand its like saying raw chicken is alright because it might give you salmonella, but it won't give you Ebola.
The worst part about the game is that it could be good. Hell, it could be great. But it isn't. It's jank. It's held back by a mediocre MTG Set, a bland and cynical F2P model, the technical shackles of previous games, and the curious desire for the yearly release of a notoriously low-budget game from a company that collectively has more money than God. After the horrible critical response of the last game, you'd think they'd have learned, but apparently they only learned all the wrong things. DotP 2015 might have been a wake-up call for Wizards of the Coast, but they must of hit the snooze button when they cranked out this one. Maybe if they improved the business model, fixed the servers, expanded the card pool, maybe one day it might be a fun, playable, and faithful adaptation of everyone's favorite trading card game. But right now, it's not. Right now, it's jank.

- the game is supremely linear, I mean every final fantasy game is linear, but for instance in FFX or FFXII you had this open world kind of thing where you moved around and went as you please. I'm not going to state what's already been stated thousands of times before.  I will talk about the theme of this game instead.
I will start by mentioning that the purpose of the linear gameplay on Cocoon represents society that is isolated away from the rest of the world and the people in Cocoon live in constant fear of Pulse. The linearity of the chapters on Cocoon may represent that this society is very linear, with all its rules and standards, compared to the openess of Gran Pulse. When the player gets to Gran Pulse for the first time, it is a major change from the ten chapters of linear paths that existed on Cocoon.
Cocoon is ruled by a city called Eden, which gives this game a strong Biblical reference, like Final Fantasy VII. Later in the game it is learned that both humans and the Fal'cie were created by a god, called Maker, but this god went away after creating the world. This is Deism, which is the belief that God created the world, but left it in the control of humanity and doesn't interfere in it at all. It turns out that the Fal'cie want to bring back the Maker and to do that, they will sacrifice the humanity that is inside Cocoon by killing the being that controls Eden, called Orphan. The Fal'cie's version of salvation is about destroying the world, which is different to what humans have. This is an obvious reference to the doomsday Christians and their obsession with the world ending violently. This obsession with the world ending is a sign of a very twisted state of mind that is about nothing but negativity and doom. The Fal'cie will do this by creating an apocalypse called Ragnarok using one of the characters who originated on Gran Pulse.

This apocalypse fails because the characters don't allow the Fal'cie to remove their hope and they overcome the plans of the Fal'cie to destroy Cocoon. At the end of the game Cocoon attaches itself by crystal to Gran Pulse and the citizens of Cocoon emerge from that society that has been isolated from Gran Pulse. What happens in a cocoon? Transformation. That is why this society is called Cocoon, the characters and the citizens are being transformed and emerge out of that cocoon into a new world. The very logo of this game shows Cocoon at the end being merged to Gran Pulse. The game logo emphasizes the rebirth of the world and of humanity.
The characters from Cocoon are turned into crystal because they fulfilled their focus, but then are told to wake up and they suddenly emerge from their sleep and find themselves in the new world. This is a very Gnostic theme at the end of the game. The characters spend all their lives in Cocoon, which is about transformation or Alchemy, they resist the will of the Fal'cie and then wake up in the new world, the very idea of Gnostic salvation. The name of the main character is Lightning, as in something that comes from above and lights up the darkness in the world beneath. That is what happens here.
The things I didn't like about this game were the following:
The lack of shops in this game, compared to every other Final Fantasy game. Shops give towns a lot of personality, which was seriously lacking here. You can do all your shopping over the Internet (or whatever they call their Internet), but it lacks character. The shops in Final Fantasy XII were amazing and I want that brought back.
Related to the lack of shops was the lack of towns for the same reasons. On Gran Pulse you feel like you are all alone in the world, except for all the animals that are trying to kill you. The people in the towns and villages give the game a lot of character and atmosphere and that was seriously lacking in this game. Think of every other Final Fantasy, you really felt like you were exploring a new place and were interested in the backstories of the inhabitants.
If you are OCD about completing the hunting side missions, it is long and drawnout. What's worse is that most of the missions are in the one large area of the game, and you get very sick of being in this area. There were times when I was about to throw in the towl and move onto the next game.  The hunting sidequest in Final Fantasy XII was long and drawn out as well, but there was a very wide variety of different places, people and stories; you never felt alone, or bored of the landscape.
The last major problem I had with this game was the amount of levelling up you have to do if you want to fight the harder bosses. This wouldn't be such a big problem if there was a large variety of places to look at, but you get bored of Gran Pulse. The story of the game only takes 60 to finish, so you can just call it quits then and move onto the next Final Fantasy game. You could argue whether playing the game for another 50 hours or more is worth it, when you will get an extra few achievements.

Every once in a while there is a cutscene where the characters mostly follow one of three patterns, or even all three in quick succession: A) blame each other for things that aren't absolutely their fault; B) try to deliver exposition to the player, mostly unsuccessfully due to the absurd quantity of things that are established but not explained; C) get separated by the most unrealistic expedients possible (the most hilarious is when one of the characters is about at shouting distance from the others and they all decide that they don't wanna waste their time waiting for him and move on leaving him alone).
The combat system is certainly innovative, but that doesn't mean it's good: you can have up to three characters in a party but can control only the main one while the other two are handled by the AI and you can only change their behaviour to match pre-determined battle schemes, and even your character is basically controlled by the AI because there is a convenient "Auto-battle" button that you can press to have the game select the best abilities to que up and the enemy to unleash them upon. You can, of course, try to select manually the abilities you want to use, but there really is no point when they all seem the same and the computer already chooses the ones that mostly suit the moment. So the combat mostly feels incredibly boring, and you end up just mashing the "Auto-battle" button for about 90% of the time.

‘Terminator’ meets ‘Captain Planet’ in this point ‘n’ click adventure that may be more preachy in its message than it was supposed to be, but it still tells an interesting story with simple, yet entertaining puzzle mechanics.
It is difficult to write something about saving our planet from pollution without resorting to tired speeches, but ‘A New Beginning’ almost managed to do that. Almost. While it is not just some pro-environmentalist propaganda, and the theme is integrated well into the story, sometimes the message it tries to convey is little more than a PSA after a Saturday morning cartoon.
Said story is an interesting baggage as well, since it likes to switch narrative styles. Initially, it is a time-travel tale set in the apocalyptic future, as presented by the first protagonist, Fay, who went back to 1982 to convince a retired biologist, Bent, to continue his research into clean energy. This leads into a family drama between Bent and his son, which somehow turns into a James Bond movie against an evil energy mogul who hides in his private fortress in the jungle. And finally, the entire plot just ends in a very Shyamalan-like twist.
Gameplay is almost as varied as the storytelling: we start with relying on inventory-related puzzles in the future segments; dialogues, distraction, and some investigations in the initial chapters set in the present; and finally, old-school point ‘n’ click adventure insanity for the conclusion. This variance is refreshing to some degree, and it usually fits well within the current narrative, but it also feels like as if the game struggles to find its own identity and just experiments with whatever the creators just came up with. The result is an enjoyable, but probably too distracting product that can be recommended to adventure game fans only.
