I've been playing Civ games for more than a decade, I'm a hardcore fan of the series.
The nice things about BE are: the completely new look (it's on an alien world after all), the affinity model, the quests and the choices you have to make at the beggining of a new game (options for you civ). Affinity is the coolest new feature, and the fact that your units evolve based on affinity. Really awesome feature.
They tried to innovate and it shows. However, I do feel that a lot of things are missing.
For instance, wonders are there but not longer feel useful or even necessary. Sure they provide nice bonuses to your city or civilization, but I only build a few in a single game so far, and it didn't make any difference overall. That's odd for a civ game.
The complete removal of great people is also odd. The previous Civs linked great people with wonders, they were one of the reason why you built wonders. Remove great people, you don't need wonders any more. I miss them.
Diplomacy hasn't change at all and has no real impact on gameplay. I don't even bother with this aspect of the game.
The AI is not that great either, as opposed to previous Civ game. Experienced players will have to play on higher setting than they had to in previous civ game. The AI don't tech as fast as they should in affinity. So you basically get a big combat advantage on them real fast. Cities are also less resilient than before, which is a nice change. Unfortunately, AI don't defend them properly. Experienced player will know that having a high unit count is the key. If you stick to that strategy, AI won't be able to mount a proper offensive. I never lost a city in BE so far, and I have never built the city defense buildings. That tells you a lot.
Lastly, and I recommend you read the spacesector review, the biggest fail in BE is immersion. The new setting removes a lot of the historical flavor the Civ series created since the beginning: moving through the major period of human history. So basically, it's not a Civ game anymore, and that's the challenge.
At the end, this is a mixed feeling review. Hardcore civ fan will find something for them, but will be left wanting. Unless patch or expansion fixes some of the above, I probably won't play that long in the near future. By opposition, I played Civ 4 for more than 5 years and Civ 5 for at least 3 years.

I will begin by noting that this is the first Hitman game I have played, but will certainly not be the last. It has definitely made me wish to go back and play some of the older titles in the series. As a result, my review can only be one for Hitman Absolution rather than a comparison with previous Hitman titles.
Hitman Absolution is a good game. It has solid stealth action but seems to feel eerily similar to a Splinter Cell title at times. Since I like the Splinter Cell series I do not consider this a bad thing, and certainly Absolution's 'disguise' mechanic adds more than a little to the stealth gameplay it may have borrowed from Sam Fisher. Nonetheless, despite some rather interesting ways of killing targets, with quite a lengthy campaign at 20 (mostly linear) missions, the game begins to become rather tedious. You kill several targets in the same way, for example. The game seemed rather rushed towards the end. And, as expected, the storyline was pretty much laughably poor. But we don't play Hitman for the storyline...don't expect Metal Gear Solid here.
Although this review seems profoundly negative, I had a lot of fun playing Hitman Absolution and it has a surprising amount of replay value and some rather fun challenges to beat. The graphics are beautiful at times and some of the best I've seen on the previous generation of games. Upping the difficulty can be an interesting and very challenging experience, and competing with friends to see who is the best Hitman is also quite a fun dynamic to the game also.
In sum, Hitman is worth a play. If you like no-nonsense stealth games, this is definitely one for you. 8/10.

This game holds up well in the RTS field.  Keeping the review simple:
Strengths
-Scale:  The game can be customized to all sizes, massive or tiny.  Starting criteria such as fleet sizes, economy rates, research rates, and many more can be tweaked.
-Real time combat:  Battles can be long, drawn out, and at such a large scale - very rewarding.  Fleets of hundreds and hundreds of ships can meet each other in battle if you time it correctly.
-Research:  Research differs quite a bit from race to race, with each having strengths and weaknesses.  The research trees are fairly extensive and divided into subgroups (such as economy, military, civilian, defense, etc), so you can choose the path you wish to follow first.  Research isn't fluff, and has a significant impact on gameplay.
-Aesthetics:  The fleet of each race differs greatly once you get into making larger ships, and the graphics are more than passable.  The game also runs very smoothly even during intense combat.
-Diplomacy:  Coming very close to a Masters of Orion style diplomacy, with unlocked teams you can sway your opponents or allies to perform tasks for you or manipulate them in many different ways.  Some research is dedicated solely to diplomacy.
Weaknesses
-Online Play:  Finding a community of players to game with can be difficult.  Often, there are very few people to game with and IronClad online goes down sometimes... this also leads into next weakness.
-AI:  The AI in this game isn't the worst I've seen, but it could be improved.  Because it's hard to find other players, if you want to play you are often stuck with AI.  The biggest difficulty in this is the differences between AI settings.  The AI can be somewhat inconsistent.  Weak to Normal to Strong is a huge jump, and if you crush Normal settings, there's a very good chance you'll get crushed versus Strong settings.  The small bonus to this is that the AI isn't too easy across the board, and if you crank up the difficulty it will mostly likely smash you.
-Planets:  While controlling planets is a primary goal in the game, planet customization is very simple and takes a back seat to fleet research and gameplay in general.
-Endgame:  This game can play out many different ways, but often you know you're going to win well before you wipe out the other factions and the game ends.  Sometimes 20-30 minutes beforehand.  This can lead to very anti-climactic victories.
If you like RTS, you WILL like this game.  Replayabliity level is high if you're a RTS fan.  If you have fond memories of playing Homeworld or Homeworld 2, you should definitely pick up this game.

I want to love this, but I can't, not yet... [POSTED: 11/29/2014 - SUBJECT TO CHANGE]
[PRE-CIV 5 IMPRESSIONS]
...As much fun as I had with it, I couldn't help but feel emptiness inside while playing it, the game just felt incomplete, it felt like I just paid $50, expecting a full game, but instead recieved a closed beta invitation with "Release Date: TBA" on it.
If you didn't catch what I'm hinting at, the game feels extremely incomplete.
There are more bugs than just aliens, if you want to play this in multiplayer, good luck with that.  You'll need it.
If you want to fight a challenging computer, you'd better boost it all the way up because all the difficulties are basicly the same unless you declare war first.
If you wanted to have a deep feeling for the characters you converse with, then I'm sorry.  But there are only about a dozen characters, all of which have the exact same dialogues and everything.  They don't even have backgrounds like they did in Civ 4, they just pop up, wave, post the same text message you got from the past three people for killing aliens instead of living peacefully with them, condem you, shake their fist, then disconnect from chat.  That's not as meaningful the fifth time guys...  First maybe...
Now despite these gripes there are some things I like and want to see improved on.
First off: The tech web.  Yes, I said tech WEB.  I love it so much, I'm glad to see them trying to push liner trees out of the way, a web is so much better.  I am very happy with this (obviously)
Second: The Aliens.  If you're going to play this game, play on frenzied aliens.  You'll feel alone on a planet, desperate to survive while trying to set up on your own.  If you play without frenzied aliens turned on...  Well, then expect the aliens to play the role of wildlife in Civ 4.  Oh no, the lions attacked me, better one-shot them with my most basic unit.
Third: The affinity/quest system.  This allows multiple pathways, buildings are no longer so static as to work exactly as intended, depending on your personal choices your buildings can have various different effects.  You can produce buildings faster, or infantry faster.  And affinity lets you pick your moral alignment towards the aliens...  You have three groups:
Harmony - Live in peace with the aliens, become future-nomads riding the things like dinosaurs as you explore the toxic planets atmosphere, and live as an indigenous species.
Purity - CLEANSE THE ALIEN!  PURGE THE MUTANT!  CARRY THE EMPEROR'S WILL AS YOUR TORCH!  *ahem* sorry don't know what came over me there...  This faction is basicly a group of marines...  in space...  Who feel it's best to kill all aliens, and turn the planet into a second Earth.
Supremacy - Why change the planet (terraformation), or change the wildlife (domestication), when we can change ourselves..? (GLORIOUS EVOLUTION!) This group uses the advanced minerals and resources of the alien planet to transcend the human species to the next step of evolution!  What is this you may ask?  BRAINS IN JARS!  ...and then put the jars in robot suits, think tanks, or simulations.  Just hope you don't find any pesky chosen ones who ruin your fun.
A final note: The quest system while refreshing is also stale, the quests are always the same, always given at the same timers/conditions, always have the same results, and always have an objectively superior answer if you metagame.  "Hmm, do I want +15% city health while defending against aliens who will never attack it?  Orrrrrr do I want +2 more health, that thing you can never get high enough!?"
[POST-CIV 5 IMPRESSIONS]
Yes I know, not playing Civ 5 sooner?  What herasy is this?  Well I was having enough fun with Civ 4, M.A.X., Masters of Magic (don't judge me), etc.
But yeah, having played Civ 5 now, and looking back at Civ BE.  No longer can I call this game a Beta.

This may include taking out turrets, specific ships or guarding one of your own friendlies. As you fight, your teammates will be doing their own thing against the enemy. This is a neat concept but the game didn't go as in-depth as it could have. Essentially, you can change your targeting system to whomever you'd wish at any moment but unless your specifically supposed to take out 7 enemy fighters, you'll have no idea how many enemies are left.
The game controls themselves are okay. The rolling feature is okay but doesn't feel extremely effecting in dodging opponents fire. The flying itself takes a bit of time to get used to. Once you are accustomed to the style, most likely you will excel in the art. There are no cool gimmicks to do loop-to-loops like Star Fox or any crazy barrel rolls. Boost at least was included as well as a feature to "brake". They did add an arsenal of weapons to choose from. The basic weapon given is an energy weapon in which you can choose to shoot it rapidly over time or all in one burst. This weapon needs time to cool down in order to be fired efficiently again. Pressing the D-pad to the right will switch from an energy weapon to a chain-gun/machine gun sort of weapon. I personally like this one as the enemies health can quickly degrade. Missiles are another feature within the game. These can also be changed given what you like most or what you deem important for certain missions. Upon completing a few missions, the player will be given the opportunity to use other ships and even transform their ship into a space mech. The space mech can only be used when the player accumulates enough flux from landing their shots on enemies. Upon pressing A to transform, the mech utilizes it's own special set of weapons and missiles that can literally fire at many targets. This is a high light feature of the game. Overall, the flying experience is pleasurable and the combat experience is mediocre at best.
The visuals are very nice and use somewhat of a luminescent look. The sounds are decent as well as the dialogue. There isn't much variance when it comes to explosions or when weapons are being fired. A cockpit view as well as a ship view is available to choose from which is greatly appreciated!
As I've stated, a few people may find this game exceptional while others may stop playing a few missions in. It is fun, but it can feel like a grind after a while doing the similar missions over and over. I also found the difficulty to sort of jump at times.
RATING : 6.85/10

Very basic Diablo clone with childish graphics and no atmosphere whatsoever that can be fun—for the first few hours anyway.
The first few hours are quite fun due to its basic structure, which is very like the first Diablo (single town with a dungeon under it).  It can be addictive building up your character, and the game provides a decent amount of ways to power up outside of simply gaining levels.  You can attach gems to equipment, try to have equipment enchanted (and risk having all enchantments removed), and buy random equipment that could turn out to be enchanted.
Unfortunately, there are way too many things holding this game back.
First, the graphics and atmosphere.  It was designed to run on netbooks so the graphics are very simple.  That doesn't bother me so much... but the cartoony exaggerated look that couldn't be more generic means you'll be playing this for the mechanics only (more on that later).  The music, composed by the guy who did the music for Diablo 1 & 2, is just alright.  It sounds a lot like Diablo, but not nearly as good as Diablo.
Second, the itemization is poor.  I found my best equipment not even halfway through the game on Hard.  Outside of finding rings that would give me +8 Dex vs +6 Dex, I had basically the same equipment loadout for the last 6 hours or so.  Nothing that dropped even came close to what I already had.
Third, the dungeons are dull and feel way too long.  You have a mine, spooky castle, lava place, spookier castle.  That's about it.  The layouts are randomly assembled from larger pieces, but there is nothing whatsoever interesting.  Other than randomly coming upon merchants and bosses, there is nothing to look forward to or be surprised by as you explore.  Some unique hand-crafted rooms or levels or something would have gone a long way.  You have to go through 35 of these to beat the last boss, and once the item drops got boring so did the rest of the game.
Fourth, the enemy variety is awful.  You typically have 2-3 enemy types per level.  Usually a small fast monster that just charges at you, an archer or wizard hanging back shooting spells, and a big tough monster that slowly comes after you.  That is basically it.  Each type of enemy will have some unique abilities (such as "shoots fire" or "stun resistant") but most of it is window dressing.  The bosses are just HP-inflated monsters that summon minions over and over.
Fifth, the game is way too easy.  Diablo clones need to strike a good balance between being difficult and unfair, and need to give you access to skills and tactics that let you push the odds in your favor.  The only time I had any difficulty here (note: I played on Hard, which I know is code for "Normal" in this game) was in the last couple levels where they would routinely spawn demons that could basically instantly drop a two-hit kill spell on me.  If you die you can resurrect in town with no penalty, resurrect at the start of the level with some gold missing, or resurrect in place with a gold and exp penalty.  So in other words, there is really no penalty for dying, and once I learned that I totally lost interest in the game.
All in all, a skeleton of a decent Diablo clone is here (as Torchlight II would go on to prove), but considering the competition (including the original Diablo which has actually aged remarkably well), Torchlight is a hard game to recommend to nearly anyone.

Food was very scarce. Everyone was hungry. Everyone had the same look in their eyes. They thought this dilapidated building to be their grave. Nearby, there was a building occupied by what I assumed to be bandits. I saw they had sources of food, and decided it was me or them. I scouted the place out, bringing lockpicks with me to make my own entrance. I made my way in through a balcony on the second floor, making sure to peek through the keyhole at the end of the room. There was someone on the other side of the door. I made some noise and hid in the closet.  When the door opened, I clubbed the poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to death with a crowbar. I listened and waited. There were two or three people left.
I made my way to the left, where I knew an armed guard was. He must have been their leader. I snuck up behind him, cracking his skull with the crowbar. He turned around, trying to fend me off with the butt of his rifle. A crushing blow to his ribs, and another to the head and his light was extinguished. The third bandit was running to his aid. I closed the door, arming myself with the fallen bandit's shotgun. A woman burst into the room, running straight for the newly deceased. She knelt on the ground, sobbing and crying for her loved one to come back.
I ended her life as well. When I returned, I was broken-hearted. I sat down on a piece of rubble, looking down at my feet.  I sat there for what seemed like hours. Finally, someone broke the silence. "We're the only two left. Bruno abandoned us during the night, and Katia... Katia is dead." She had died of starvation. I had ended the lives of innocent people, only to return home to my friends dead and gone. We got drunk that night. So drunk that walking was asking the impossible.
That night, two children came to our door. They told us their mother was dying, and they needed medicine. Hoping to atone for my sins, I drunkenly stumbled to our medicine cabinet. It was empty. With a heavy heart, I sent the children home to their dying mother. Was there no good left in this world? Was there even any left in me? Hope is gone.
As I write, I hear someone outside. The sound of a crowbar prying away at planks. I am alone. I am unarmed. I am cold and sick. My face is wet with tears, finding their way through the cracks and crevices of dried blood. I cannot live with what I have done. I welcome the raiders and the everlasting peace they bring with them.

First off, my ideal space game would be the flight and combat mechanics of Evochron Mercenary coupled with the depth and complexity offered in the free form sandbox of the X series. I believe this is the closest thing I've found to date and though it has it's issues and may put people off for now it's certainly one to keep an eye on. Despite the drawbacks which I explain further below I am still happy to have made the purchase and I plan to play often, it's still fun but mostly I want to keep tabs on the fixes and updates before I make serious run at the campaign and building my empire. More conservative space fans might want to wait it out.
The game has a lot of the old systems of the X games but right now they're mostly inaccessible due to bugs and design flaws but they are there and I have no doubt this will become one of my favorite games. It has that much potential but keep in mind that it's potential. I actually appreciate the new direction of the series and think that once the bugs are handled and some optimization is done more and more people will forget about the launch troubles and begin enjoying it themselves. My favorite comment on the design and a great description of what I love about the change was that they wanted to make traveling more fun, much like the GTA series where traveling is an extremely action oriented element of gameplay. I believe they have done that and I love the new travel system with highways and drafting, it's really cool and far more fun to use than gates at NSWE. The controller use in space is great and makes all spaced based elements look and feel more like a sim than a RTS as in previous X games where all the flying was mostly done on drop down menu's except when in a fight for brief periods. Traveling was never fun and took way too long. Make no mistake, X could never get by without menus and they're still around, using the controller is the downfall here as with limited options you have select categories and follow the branches although the menus seem to make things easier to manage and operate like property, market and crew functions even if their navigation is less than perfect. All in all it's a huge change that incorporates a lot of the depth of the X series although not as micro manageable as some seem to prefer it but it's packaged in an action sim which is my dream come true. One of the newest features is the ability to visit and walk in stations which I believe is a great idea and it looks good. It's not amazing by any means but for a feel of actually visiting places by leaving and boarding your ship I like it. There are lockers and chests to raid for loot via Borderlands but mostly it's to make contacts with people to hire on as crew or to peruse their wares as merchants. I haven't found it something that you have to do often if you'd like to avoid it I imagine it would be possible to minimize station visits enough to not be bothered. My problem so far has been the optimization as space looks great stations barely chug along which is disorienting but otherwise acceptable, but only for now. I expect all this to improve. Another feature and what some would consider a drawback is your limitation to only fly one ship from the cockpit. It's a cool ship though which you can walk around, it's small but the views are amazing and I love the HUD. You can upgrade your ship plenty to keep you feeling more powerful and you can still own and remotely fly and manage your fleets, stations and vessels and I feel it was a good tradeoff.
I don't want to say the game is not worth the $50 tag because it is although it is NOT worth that much as it stands right now. Pick it up if you are a diehard fan but prepared for frustration. I would recommend everyone keep a sharp eye on the updates which have already been streaming out regularly. This certainly was a rough launch but anyone who writes off a game for a bad launch isn't much of a fan as this is certainly nothing new and it will continue as games become more complex and demanding and users machine become more diverse. I'm not defending anyone except my passion for great experiences through games and as a disabled combat Veteran I am more grateful for the developers efforts in bringing this amazing world to life than I am upset with them for a substandard release. Everyone benefits if it gets fixed so let's just hope for that. Egosoft didn't launch and run and that tells me these guys like what they do and are as embarassed about the issues as some people are upset by them.

Is your idea of a fun game making difficult and emotionally draining decisions? Then This War of Mine is for you.
In it you play civillians trying to survive and a city ravaged by war. Unlike most games depicting war however, your biggest threat isn't enemy soldiers but rather other civillians who have become so desperate to survive they've turned into violent bandits.
In the daytime you work on your abnormally large home, building beds, workshops, and fixing the massive holes in the walls. Occasionally you will get a visiter, usually to trade, almost always to ask for assitance, and rarely to give you supplies for free. You will also have to work out rationing food and working on ways to achieve sustainability via farms, water collectors, and rat traps.
Night time is where the mistakes are made and games are over. At night you decide which of your civilians scavenges, sleeps, or guards. Unfortunately you can only send out one person to scavenge but maybe that's more of a balance mechanic. Of the places you can scavenge there is a clear trend of "Not Dangerous = Not Worth Scavenging" and "Extreme Danger Land = Everything You Need To Survive Right F***ing Now," although there are easy places to scavenge if you don't mind stealing from defenseless elderly people or killing someone who was just protecting their family.
This game is difficult in more than one sense of the word, losing one of my civilians tends to make me lose my willingness to keep going and just start from scratch or stop playing altogether. However, a game that can draw my attention for so long and get me invested is a game I consider good.

I played a couple of Daedalic Entertainment point&click games, and they are way too simple compared to the old school adventures, in fact, nowadays it's rare to see many classic actions like "Use", "Pull", "Open", "Close", "Push", etc... which are useful to make you think, by increasing the number of possibilities, or in other words, the difficulty; also, this game is not open world, so there is no exploration, nothing to solve in a certain order... you have no choice: time by time, you are forced in small zones with few characters/elements, and the interaction is limited by this excessive simplicity. Furthermore, combining an item in your inventory with another item in your inventory is another inexistent or superficial aspect of this game; most of puzzles are so intuitive that you are almost guided through the solution, so as you see from my playtime, you can easily complete the game in few hours, which is ridiculous if i remember how many years i spent in '80-'90 era, by playing games of the same genre.

Unfortunately, I just can't quite recommend this game. If there were a star rating, I'd give it a pretty neutral rating, but since there's no inbetween option, it gets a no. Here's why:
Cons for the game
- Very little help/ instructions. Almost none at all. This is the single biggest reason for the low rating. After all of the effort put into making this game, you couldn't add an extra couple lines of text? One example, balers. There are 2 types of bales in the game, each made from it's own baler. There is no description as to which kind of bale each machine makes, you just have to know. There are also machines and trailers that interact with these 2 different types of bales. Do these other machines specify which type of bale they work on? Nope! Of course not! Because adding a single line of text, even just a 2 word "xxxx Bale" discription would be too much work. Another example is a harvester, the Mex 5. I bought it when I had a little extra money and tried to figure out what it's for since, again, there was no description saying how to use it. I tried cutting different things and no results. Finally I had to look it up online to get an answer.
-Very "hands on", you can hire workers for some tasks but not many. Alot of the jobs, including what I would consider to be some of the most boring, you cannot hire a worker for. Why? Again, given the scope of the game, would it really be that much harder to implement a feature that you already made on some other duties? Example, you can hire workers for some harvesters but not others. Beet farming looks like it would be the most profitable use of a field, but it takes 10x the work since you cannot hire workers to harvest them until you buy one of the single most expensive machines in the game. Instead you have to sit in the tractor yourself, with one of the narrowest harvester heads in the game. It took half an hour to harvest one of the smallest fields, compared to the under 10 minutes of letting a paid worker do it for me, and I only make about 2x the money. Of course even then beets take up much more room, 3x, so that means 3x the trips from the field to the market where you are selling them.
I suppose those are the only cons that come to mind for me. However, they are nearly game breaking in my opinion. You can *almost* play this as a management game, which I would prefer, but too much of the game requires you to actively control the machinery. Also spending hours, and game money, trying to figure out what the machinery does because they could not be bothered to add a description, is just rediculous.
Pros:
... well I wouldn't say there are any, just some middleground "okay" things. Decent or better graphics, though graphics are pretty low on my scale of what makes a game "good". Some jobs can be given to workers, allowing you to do other things, or even nothing if you want, while they work. Yep, that's about it in the plus columb for me.

Well, all of the women die, The plot throws in a bad twist at the very last minute, and there are far more deaths than are necessary, even for a grim storyline. All of the people treated as bad guys by the narrative are also not white. Coincidence?
The art is good, but I really don't understand why Fay has to swing her hips when she's otherwise always in a strict, disciplined position. It took me out of the puzzles every time. Unfortunately, the art looks creepy when paired with the voice acting, most of which was frighteningly bad. Duve's actor was the best one, and everyone else was either between "Meh" and "oh god make it stop".
The game has this duality in that it's a puzzle game and a story game, and while the puzzles are pretty good and some were real brain-scratchers, the story was so flat, forced, and nonsensical that the whole game suffers.
There are also a lot of glitches. Half of the time I clicked on an item, the selection text would come up in Cryllic letters, or Italian. Some cutscenes never played at all, and the game crashed at least 3 times. This game is not ready to be published, and I'm annoyed that I had to pay money for it. Even if you like the story, I imagine everyone would be annoyed by the glitches.
If the developers want to make another game in the future, I'd say to stick to the puzzle aspect, don't try so hard to make the story so epic, work on the uncanny-valley-ness of the voiceovers and art, fix the glitches, and create women characters who don't have to be sexy every second, because that's super distracting.

I love relaxing games, sometimes you want just sit and relax and this game can be really fun and relaxing, but it suffers from a few problems.
First i want to say that i don‘t dislike this game, but on steam you choose either positive or negative review. I would rate this game a strong 6, so giving it a negative rating doesn‘t mean the game is bad, it‘s just lacks many things. Mainly i‘m giving a negative review for lack of effort from developers while making this game.
The gameplay is the same as in previous game. Except this time there‘s a forestry. Well, i thought so, but you just cut down trees growing on the side of the road and throw them into a pond to receive money. It would be nice to have real forests. The tree cutting physics could be better and more accurate. Sometimes it‘s too difficult to do everything from cutting the tree to throwing it into the pond. Physics are just off a bit. Talking about physics, this game doesn‘t shine in physics department. The tractor handling is very arcadey, the whole game is very arcadey. I want handling and physics to be something like Professional farmer. That game does some things better than Farming simulator, but sadly it‘s too buggy to play and developers abandoned the game and moved on to the next one. Another thing Pro farmer has done better is seasons. In this day and age it would be nice to have such simple feature. Considering the sale numbers this game has, developers should have more than enough money to make this game better.
This game fails at career...again. Career is simply a sandbox mode without any goals. You‘re the only farmer in the village and companies compete with each other who will pay you the most. It‘s just stupid. The map feels very empty. You don‘t have any control over your company, no management, nothing. You can hire a worker, but he appears when you hire him and disappears when you let him go. Your workers doesn‘t walk around doing things, it‘s like they‘re not existent. At least it's good the game has achievements so they will keep you occupied for some time.
Graphics are slightly better than in 2013. The tractors and equipment now gets dirty after some time. Also they look pretty good. But that‘s it. The environments are terrible. Trees are ugly, they don‘t move, leaves are static, grass is low quality too. The worst is the sky. It‘s so bad it‘s ridiculous. People the game is made in 2014! The whole sky is one and the same flat sky texture which changes color depending on the time of day. There's no real lighting, the clouds are static flat textures and they don‘t move, sun is at the same spot all day, but shadows on the ground are still moving. It‘s really horrible and is unacceptable in this day.
Plowing, seeding, harvesting is still fun. It‘s repetitive but relaxing, if you had goals in the game it would be much more fun. After hours of doing the same actions it gets boring.
I would recommend this game if you don‘t own the previous one. You‘ll have some fun, but if own FS2013, this game doesn‘t offer anything new or different, it simply lacks improvements.
I have hope that Cattle&Crops will be a good farming game and it will bring some competition.

I liked this a lot more than I thought I would.  I scored it for free during a promotion for Shadow Warrior 2 and I had the misapprehension that it was designed purely to appeal to nostalgia for the original game, which I had somehow missed.  Instead, it is like a love letter to the early First Person Shooter games such as Duke Nukem 3D, Doom and Quake, and a celebration of the 1980's (witness the glorious trailer, which includes snippets of the cocky protagonist singing along to Stan Bush's The Touch in his hotted up Datsun 240Z (known as the Nissan Fairlady Z and Nissan S30 in other markets), taken from the game's cinematic introduction).  The humour would be ill-advised for a modern game, being kind of lame and not very politically correct, but the self-aware jokes suit the protagonist's personality and help transport the player back in time to an age when heroes openly smoked and scantily clad women could be used to advertise absolutely anything.
Although there are a variety of firearms that are all satisfyingly destructive to use, the game mechanics, which include the use of a variety of supernatural powers, are so well thought out that swordplay is a viable alternative to gunplay throughout the game.  I had also assumed that this would just be a graphical remake of the original Shadow Warrior game, but I remember games of that era demanding a far higher tolerance of frustration from players, something that most contemporary gamers simply no longer have, myself included.  I was pleasantly surprised that the game has been designed to cater for the modern gamer that is accustomed to frequent rewards.  I thought that the graphics were suitably good: not mind blowing, but if they were, I don't think the 1980s nostalgia would have been as effectively rendered.  I only played the DirectX 9 version and I enjoyed it enough that I plan to replay it on a harder difficulty when I have a DirectX 11 compatible graphics card.
This is not a cerebral challenge, it is a straight up gory action game with a lot of bad guys to kill.  The trailer tells you everything you need to know.  If that doesn't appeal to you, you will probably not enjoy this game.  If old-school stylish, albeit somewhat kitch, violence that is not afraid to laugh at itself sounds like fun, you might just love this game.

Final Fantasy XIII is a controversial entry in the long-running JRPG series and the reasons behind the backlash it received have a lot to do with some radical choices the developers made. This is a JRPG that removes almost all the adventure and exploration elements associated with the genre. Instead, it chooses to focus on the story-telling and combat.
The story is told mainly through cut-scenes and the combat is a fast-paced variation on the classic active-time battle system found in older titles like Final Fantasy VII. The cut-scenes are very impressive and the story being told does maintain a strong sense of pacing throughout the entire game. Combat is fluid and intense, with enough variety to keep demanding players interested. However, the absence of "towns" and similar combat-free spaces makes the experience feel somewhat repetitive once it becomes clear that the game is just a long series of battles interrupted with cut-scenes every now and then.
Overall, I feel like this is a good game for what it is, but it is flawed in many ways. The UI doesn't really help the player at all and using the Shops and the Weapon Upgrade System is a chore because you end up having to get in and out of menus numerous times. The end game feels rushed and, the further you go, the more it becomes just a long grind. I gave up on it after realizing the last two special bosses are almost unbeatable without reaching the level cap in all the classes.
If I were to score FFXIII, I'd give it a 4/5. Despite the problems I found, the game's quality is impressive. Graphics and animations look amazing, soundtrack is beautiful, combat is mostly great and the story is actually pretty cool once you understand what the hell is going on.

Game Review
Assassins Creed 4 Black Flag
I understand that I am a few years late, most people who will ever play this game have already played it. I played it, and it was fantastic. Once this adventure got started, it was hard to put the game down.
By far one of the best open-world games I've played in recent memory, and easily the coolest pirate game I have played. The setting was interesting, the visuals were gorgeous, and purchasing all the upgrades for yourself and your ship got addicting.
I only have a couple of complaints about the entire experience. One, the combat seemed a little sluggish. I would often hit the Counter button right before I got hit with a sword, just for my character to stand there motionless and get stabbed. Maybe there was input lag from my controller or something, but it annoyed me a few times. And two, I wish the story was a little more believable and less science fiction. The whole "magical artifacts" seemed out of place in a game that revolved around pirates, politicians, and naval combat. The story was solid, however.
I nearly 100%-ed this game in less than two weeks. I grabbed every collectible and did every side quest. The only thing I didn't technically do were all the optional objectives for the main story missions. So the game says I'm only at 96% game completion which is stupid... But I'm not going to take the time to replay the story missions just to do the optional objectives. In my heart, I know I got 100%.
Overall I loved this game, and couldn't put it down.

I recommend Sins of a Solar Empire to any RTS fan out there...
especially when you are into imperialism in futuristic space settlement flair.
The game is very deep and provides many ways to rule outer space.
You can freely combine your research or specialize in either combat/military (offensive/defensive), culture (spreading your culture/resisting enemy culture), mining, diplomacy, almost everything ...
You can build tactical defense like hangar stations, repair platforms, defense platforms (differ from race to race) or even a mighty space station (more like a really giant fortress).
Why not go for offensive Troops with a large variety of frigattes (small ship classes) and standard battleships, aswell as "Capital Ships" (you could compare them to heroes from other RPGs / RTSes) with special abilities? And if your Capital Ships aren't large enough you can still research your fraction's Titan, which is a giant (really your capital ships are so tiny compared to it) space juggernaut with the power of a big fleet combined in one ship (compare to a legendary hero or boss monster in RPG).
Besides militant ways to spread your empire, there is also the way of spreading your culture all over the system, whi9ch leads to enemies losing control of their planets.
Also you can play from the shadows, giving other players missions to destroy your enemies, or let pirates do the trick.
The game also includes a map designer, which is OK. Only downside is the randomness of the map designer, which almost makes it impossible to create a map just as you'd wish.
In the end I can only say: If you love RTS, buy it.

I bought this game when it was on sale about a year ago and finally started to play it due to my reinterest in the "Hitman" series. I remember my first Hitman game being "Hitman 2: Silent Assassin" back when I had my PS2 when I was younger, so I know a little bit about what the Hitman series is about.
I'll say this: It's a great stealth game. It has all you could want in a stealth game and more. The missions are super fun, there are TONS of ways to execute your assassinations, the music is awesome, the graphics are wonderful, and the gameplay is executed very well, both in presentation and control.
What's NOT so great about this game is that it just isn't a good "Hitman" game. It operates quite differently from the previous titles, not to mention it's a little easier than the others. The game doesn't give you expansive levels to explore with some real-time events added into the texture to highten the tension. Not to mention that it also kinda holds your hand despite how many ways you can assassinate someone, and how much improvisation there can be.
The Hitman series used to be partially based on stealth, but it didn't rely upon it. It was about hiding in plain sight, assassinating your targets, and then leaving with no one being the wiser. Absolution has some of that, but it leans on the "sneak around unseen" aspect so much that it's hard to call it a *true* Hitman game.
If you like the Stealth genre, this is a game for you. If you want to play a Hitman game and it be like the previous installments, then you may want to look somewhere else. However, if you just don't care and want a good game to play, buy it. It's well worth the 20 dollars, but nothing more.
I'm taking off a possible extra 2 points because it just isn't a true Hitman experience. 7/10.

Nearby, there was a building occupied by what I assumed to be bandits. I saw they had sources of food, and decided it was me or them. I scouted the place out, bringing lockpicks with me to make my own entrance. I made my way in through a balcony on the second floor, making sure to peek through the keyhole at the end of the room. There was someone on the other side of the door. I made some noise and hid in the closet.  When the door opened, I clubbed the poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to death with a crowbar. I listened and waited. There were two or three people left.
I made my way to the left, where I knew an armed guard was. He must have been their leader. I snuck up behind him, cracking his skull with the crowbar. He turned around, trying to fend me off with the butt of his rifle. A crushing blow to his ribs, and another to the head and his light was extinguished. The third bandit was running to his aid. I closed the door, arming myself with the fallen bandit's shotgun. A woman burst into the room, running straight for the newly deceased. She knelt on the ground, sobbing and crying for her loved one to come back.
I ended her life as well. When I returned, I was broken-hearted. I sat down on a piece of rubble, looking down at my feet.  I sat there for what seemed like hours. Finally, someone broke the silence. "We're the only two left. Bruno abandoned us during the night, and Katia... Katia is dead." She had died of starvation. I had ended the lives of innocent people, only to return home to my friends dead and gone. We got drunk that night. So drunk that walking was asking the impossible.
That night, two children came to our door. They told us their mother was dying, and they needed medicine. Hoping to atone for my sins, I drunkenly stumbled to our medicine cabinet. It was empty. With a heavy heart, I sent the children home to their dying mother. Was there no good left in this world? Was there even any left in me? Hope is gone.
As I write, I hear someone outside. The sound of a crowbar prying away at planks. I am alone. I am unarmed. I am cold and sick. My face is wet with tears, finding their way through the cracks and crevices of dried blood. I cannot live with what I have done. I welcome the raiders and the everlasting peace they bring with them.

Remember that scene from the first Bioshock, halfway through? That scene after which it sort of felt like the game was actually over, but no one had told the game that? The mission objectives themselves are all generally the same protect-this & destroy-these missions so it can be repetitious.
When it comes to the base gameplay they work and control great. The combat can get pretty intense the more enemies you're up against especially when suddenly your targets are large fleets themselves with guns covering practically every surface its got and the sudden priority is to take out the things that fire back.
Surviving involves you keeping your ship's armor (health) and regenerating shield up and as far as I know there's no way of repairing your ship's armor without reloading a checkpoint or getting it repaired when told in one particular mission. The reload-checkpoint-to-recover-everything deal looked to me like an exploitable mechanic of sorts even though there aren't very many checkpoints throughout the game, especially the later missions with their longer mission times and limited amount of checkpoints.
Each mission has an optional objective you can do that will unlock an upgrade but each one are just shared stat upgrades for all of the ships you have. What you're to do and what you can unlock are shown in the mission select screen upon preparing for the mission chosen. New ships and weapons are unlocked through progress of the missions.
After a few missions you'll eventually unlock the "Strike Suit" ship which basically transforms into a straight-up mech (Strike Mode) if the "Flux" bar it comes with is filled enough through received or given damage. It's able to move more relatively freely in the three dimensions its got, has a very capable auto-locking targeting system on chosen targets within distance, and can target & lock-on to large numbers of targets for use of the barrage of the seeking missiles it can fire. The Flux bar starts to drain upon use of Strike Mode's firing capabilities but if used efficiently the Flux bar can prolong its usage without transforming back to ship mode.
Kind of surprisingly the Strike Suit you use is the only mech in the game. No ally or enemy has anything similar although the mech may as well just be a temporary ship with a few more capabilities.
There's not a whole lot else to this game outside of the well-done space-dogfighting.

Is your idea of a fun game making difficult and emotionally draining decisions? Then This War of Mine is for you.
In it you play civillians trying to survive and a city ravaged by war. Unlike most games depicting war however, your biggest threat isn't enemy soldiers but rather other civillians who have become so desperate to survive they've turned into violent bandits.
In the daytime you work on your abnormally large home, building beds, workshops, and fixing the massive holes in the walls. Occasionally you will get a visiter, usually to trade, almost always to ask for assitance, and rarely to give you supplies for free. You will also have to work out rationing food and working on ways to achieve sustainability via farms, water collectors, and rat traps.
Night time is where the mistakes are made and games are over. At night you decide which of your civilians scavenges, sleeps, or guards. Unfortunately you can only send out one person to scavenge but maybe that's more of a balance mechanic. Of the places you can scavenge there is a clear trend of "Not Dangerous = Not Worth Scavenging" and "Extreme Danger Land = Everything You Need To Survive Right F***ing Now," although there are easy places to scavenge if you don't mind stealing from defenseless elderly people or killing someone who was just protecting their family.
This game is difficult in more than one sense of the word, losing one of my civilians tends to make me lose my willingness to keep going and just start from scratch or stop playing altogether. However, a game that can draw my attention for so long and get me invested is a game I consider good.

But the action is just walking in corridors, killing trash mobs while jungling a litle with the different roles availble for longer combats. The gameplay is actually extremely limited, exploration and secrets are non-existent: your run from one pack of mob to another mindlessly, hit "enter" to trigger the AI auto-attack, and from time to time you hit "tab" to select a medic or support role for the longer fights. And that's it, for hours on, enter, enter, enter, tab, bottom, bottom, enter, enter. The only joy you get is when summoning your eidolon characters to have access to some animations during the fight.
The leveling system with several branches is interesting, but it's not a decision-based RPG levelling. You will have to unlock every single node of every single tree of every single caracter because the game forces you too. You need to advance through the chapters of the story to have access to higher tiers of a role, or to another role to spend points on, and the game is designed so that you will get exactly the XP you need to max out everything that has been made available to you.
You could decide to level a specific role first, knowing that you will have maxed everything at the chapter end boss, but then again you don't even decide what characteristics you develop, HP, strength and magic nodes are scattered evenly accross all roles and are set on an obligatory path. Yes you will need to unlock that +3 strength node while levelling your medic role, even if it's completely unrelated to it.
There is an XP system on weapons. Not on use though, nor on kills, no no. You need to level your items at a shop by sacrificing components into it. Components that you loot on mobs and that you can buy directly at the shop. It's a money sink, and it's entirely unnecesssary for progression.
So long as you keep them going through the fights, you have absolutely no control over what the characters do. The story is narrated without your opinion, the rare PNJ you encounter are just decorum, there are no quests. The world is just one long corridor filled with pack of mobs and interrupted by cutscenes showing the story just alike a beautiful FF movie. But the fight against mobs gets boring, it's just a grind, I'd rather be watching all the cutscenes without any user input.

Defy Gravity.....Hmm what can I say about defy gravity? Well how about this. It is absolutely an amazing 2D platformer. There are so many things done right in this game that an absolute TON of games could learn from. For instance difficulty range....there is none. You simply play the game. It forces you to think on your toes and truly tests your dexterity and reaction time all at the same time IN MID AIR. The title has no time limits and no life counter. However, it also comes at you with absolutely no mercy whatsoever. Below are the explanations.
The shield - The shield mechanics in the game are also something I have personally have never seen before. You press S to toggle your shield or you can press Shift for a quick shield. However, the shield is not always your friend. Sometimes having the shield makes levels far more difficult because of the next mechanic on the list.
Weapon - The weapon mechanic may remind some of you of Portal. However, instead of making portals, this weapon uses magnetic fields I guess you could call them. Left mouse button fires the blue orb which attracts you and anything non static also (including enemies). The right mouse button fires off the orange orb which you guessed it deflects you as well as other non static objects (including enemies).
I strongly suggest picking this title up, in my opinion it is well worth the money. In fact it is worth more money that they are selling it for. Controls are simple, W or Space = Jump, A and D = Walk left or right and S or Shift = Shield.
Pros: Instant Action.

Difficult without being too difficult to be fun.

A true test of skills with a keyboard and mouse.

Mechanics are truly unique, creative and they truly cause you to think of what your doing.
Cons: Music can get a bit annoying especially when talking to friends on Skype, I found myself turning the volume down
through the mixer to the game itself.

Not enough options - I found no way to play in windowed mode or to turn the game audio down in game. I think
these would benefit the player more often than not.
In conclusion: If you are looking for a TRUE platformer title that brings back the good ol' days of hard gaming this is your title. I hope everyone at least gives this game a shot, you will not be dissapointed.

Final Fantasy XIII is an abomination pretending to be an awful lot of things, and failing to be any of them quite badly.  It pretends its a role-playing game, yet has no aspects of role-playing in it (and barely any aspects of gaming in it, for that matter).  Even by the more loose definition of a JRPG, it's not a JRPG.  You don't gain levels, you add points to a perfectly-linear path ala FFX's Sphere Grid, only with even fewer actual choices.  It just turns "leveling" into a chore you take care of every few minutes by holding down a button and watching numbers go up.  The combat does everything it can to take the player out of the equation, while also punishing the player for trying to play the game at all by sabotaging any sort of attempt at taking control with split-second irredeemable reversals of fortune.  FF13 also pretends it has a story, but it does not; there is no consistency in its plot, and new elements introduced regularly contradict those that have already been established.  FF13 pretends to have progression, but all it has is endless hallways for you to walk down in a singular direction forevermore.
I've heard tell that FF13 "gets better" around the 20- to 30-hour mark.  I would argue that you could spend those 20 to 30 hours playing much better games instead.  I certainly decided to do as much after wasting 16 hours in the vain hope of reaching this promised "better" game.  I want my 16 hours back, and I advise you to find better uses for your time than FF13 as well.

A mother badger and her fragile cubs, fighting for survival with a terrible case of the munchies.  This is the premise of the independent game, Shelter.  In the game you play as a mother badger looking out for the welfare of her baby cubs as they leave their home and search for a new one.  This game demands empathy from the player, if not, it’s just a boring washed out badger walking game.  The first emotional tie happens right as you start the game.  You see a faded gray colored badger cub lying limp on the cold floor of your cave.  You walk over and grab some food and feed it to revive it.  From then on you are searching for food on your journey to feed your hungry hungry… badgers.  One mechanic specifically really made me empathetic for my badger cubs.  By left clicking on the mouse you could let out a little bark to which your little cubs would respond by yipping back.  This is extremely cute, but it is also a very effective way to initiate a role call.  The game is played with a third person point of view.  I felt this was very appropriate and effective in establishing perspective.  You get a picture of really how small all the badgers are as you walk under a looming pine tree or get buried in a patch of tall grass. The camera lets you view your cubs quite easily and account for them. It’s quite disheartening as you run upstream to watch your cubs get battered by powerful waves and roll downstream a few feet and yelp.  These mechanics do a very good job of evoking feelings for your babies.  The game helps you build a relationship with your cubs as you traverse through different environments all the while feeding them.  You escort your cubs through grassy meadows, rapid waters, dark night forests, burning forests, and open field where eagles prove mortal threats to your cubs.  After all this bonding and watching your cubs get physically bigger, you helplessly run out into an open field thinking you’re free of the predators.  Much to the demise of momma, an eagle swoops three times wounding you and finally carrying you off to her own baby chicks.  This certainly was disheartening watching your cubs wander off alone (the cubs you managed to save).   But also kind of nice to see the mother provide nourishment for the eagles newly hatched chicks.  I thought this game did a good job of evoking empathetic emotions even though it wasn’t the most fun thing I’ve ever played.

I don't come to JRPGs for open world exploration. I come to them for the story, crazy anime ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, and dramatic stares into the middle distance. And I wasn't disappointed in this game. Sure it took me a very long time to play it, but it was a rewarding experience.

Shelter is a game that is more about the experience than anything else. There is no HUD or other user interface. It's about as immersive of an experience as you can get. The game is driven by the concept of being a mama badger trying to keep your babies alive from a cruel world.
The gameplay is very simple. Move across the forest with your babies, while finding (and hunting) food, for them to keep their energy levels up. While keeping their energy levels up, you avoid environmental hazards, until you reach the end of the game. Saying any more than that would be a spoiler.
If you are looking for something different, this short-and-bittersweet title will fit the bill.

I understand that I am a few years late, most people who will ever play this game have already played it. I played it, and it was fantastic. Once this adventure got started, it was hard to put the game down.
By far one of the best open-world games I've played in recent memory, and easily the coolest pirate game I have played. The setting was interesting, the visuals were gorgeous, and purchasing all the upgrades for yourself and your ship got addicting.
I only have a couple of complaints about the entire experience. One, the combat seemed a little sluggish. I would often hit the Counter button right before I got hit with a sword, just for my character to stand there motionless and get stabbed. Maybe there was input lag from my controller or something, but it annoyed me a few times. And two, I wish the story was a little more believable and less science fiction. The whole "magical artifacts" seemed out of place in a game that revolved around pirates, politicians, and naval combat. The story was solid, however.
I nearly 100%-ed this game in less than two weeks. I grabbed every collectible and did every side quest. The only thing I didn't technically do were all the optional objectives for the main story missions. So the game says I'm only at 96% game completion which is stupid... But I'm not going to take the time to replay the story missions just to do the optional objectives. In my heart, I know I got 100%.
Overall I loved this game, and couldn't put it down.

I am writing this to counter some of the really misleading reviews.
First: This is not Civ5. They decided to make a game that was DIFFERENT but played like a Civ game.
Second: The game has a different pace. Changing the victories has made the game play much faster.
Pros:
-Faster Game: Games take half the time to win compared to Civ5. This makes it MUCH easier to play multiplayer games knowing you are not going to be there all day.
-Victories: The victories are completely different except for domination. The other 4 require a special building built, making it much easier to counter someone winning and makes you work harder to defend it. This makes combat considerably more important.
-Progression- This game has made it easier to pick and choose tech and upgrades that follow your play style. Like the previous civ games, you start to see a lot of different methods people like to win.
Cons:
-Trade routes: The advantage trade routes give are vital, just like in the last civ 5 expansion. Also like the last game, it is exhausting to keep up. You are constantly picking what location to send each vehicle. This process takes up more than half the game time. There is no option to keep it on the same route. I don't want to constantly change it, I found myself rarely changing it. They need to move it to the trade route menu and left you change it from there if you want to. It already clearly displays everything you need to know about the trade routes. Just give it a few turns before it changes cities, like spies.
-6 Difficulties: For most people, 1 and 2 are way too easy. It's just for learning the game. 4 is a bit challenging, 5 much more so, and 6 is very hard. Its a bit steeper of a difficulty curve than Civ5.
-Leader count: Needs more leaders, and not paid ones...
Almost all of peoples complaints of problems exist in Civ5 as well. I love BE, if they fix the trade route problem I may not be able to go back to Civ5.

I didn't even know they were getting "remakes". There are some problems, though. Some are rather glaringly annoying. Others have gone over them, but this might help someone anyways.
Annoyances like how your settings get changed to default if the game crashes. Which will happen... Often. Settings are stored in an .ini file that only get rewritten when you close the game yourself, and for some reason whenever the game crashes it deletes the file altogether. Perhaps a fix is copying this file periodically and re-pasting it into the file folder - That's a lot of trouble for something that shouldn't even be a problem, though...
I set my difficulty on the new hardest mode, Survivor, and after my first crash and two areas later, I noticed I'm on Medium and that Vita Chambers are on, though I had them turned off. I had to re-bind my controls about eight times since then, so perhaps it's my fault for not putting 2 + 2 together and realizing these other things would have changed as well.
The new stuff is okay.
There's a new collectable item called director reels, except you don't actually pick them up - Interacting with them opens a menu saying you unlocked it, and it gives you the option to watch it now or later. They consist of Dorito Pope Geoff Keighley interviewing people about various aspects of the game's development. Each one is about ten minutes long, seems like. You can't seem to pause them, and when they're done you get pushed back into the game immediately, so be careful and make sure you're paying attention so you don't get eaten by something. Or just watch from the main menu. I'm uncertain if you can stop these at any time since it never occurred to me to try.
There are minigames on the main screen now that are silly and fun, but they each have about ten achievements and that's not actually an exaggeration even though both have about 30 minutes of gameplay, so that's a bit interesting. There's one where you save a Little Sister from a ferris wheel, for example. There are others, but you can find them out on your own. They're pretty silly, I like them.
There's also a museum feature as well.
At least I can play the game on my PC now, I suppose. I miss my XP computer. 7's fine, too, though.

It's such a nice idea and so aesthetically pleasing, but the reality of playing it is just frustration. Because there's no UI in the name of immersion, you're constantly left wondering what it is the game wants you to do. For example, at the very beginning, you're in a cave with four live pups and one I assumed to be dead. I wandered around the cave and kept trying to exit but repeatedly hit an invisible wall, utterly confused as to what I was supposed to be doing. Eventually I figured out you're supposed to feet a plant to this "dead" pup to revive it. This would have been far more obvious if they had just given the pup a breathing animation or if it had made pathetic whining noises or something, making it obvious it was in fact alive.
The tutorial is mysteriously patchy and explains little. Certain commands are never introduced in the tutorial, like the bark and the crouch. You have to turn to internet forums to get an explanation as to what they do, or even that they exist. During the nighttime section, the dash command mysteriously disappears for no apparent reason, only to reappear at odd times that seem to have to do with a predator? I lost two pups during this section and I don't even understand what I was supposed to do. What's really boggling is that there are little visual tutorials for other tasks, but not for this section, so you're left completely unsure of what you're supposed to do or what even happened. Maybe this was supposed to be for mood, but it just made me annoyed at the game.
Another frustration is the lack of cursor - doubtless done for immersion, but it causes endless frustration when you're trying to target pups to feed. I ended up picking up and dropping food four or five times each time before I managed to feed the pup I intended to. The umpteenth time you have failed to target something, it gets annoying.
And the most grating thing of all was the constant blocking of the camera by the background elements. Is transparency that hard to implement?
It's a really nice and atmospheric idea that was ruined by frustrating mechanics. I couldn't get into the game because I felt like I just spent the whole time trying to figure out what the stupid game wanted me to do as I dropped turnips over and over. An hour in, I had lost 3/5 pups and realized I wanted the other two to just die so I could stop dealing with them. At this point, I quit. The frustration of the mechanics prevents you from getting attached to the pups at all, which is seemingly the point, here.

Two years ago, I wrote that X:R was released in a very bad shape, more or less unplayable but with a faint glimpse of hope that it could evolve into something better.
It took Egosoft almost two additional years after the original release to make the game actually worth playing.
There remain lots of 'but', though. You are still limited to one single ship and there are not plenty of customization options. Yes, you can chose to sacrifice shield strength for a faster regeneration, but that is basically it. Both player and NPC dialogues are still terribly awkward and the voice acting is in general a huge disappointment. Worse than X3, which was not exactly known for great acting.
However, the game has grown nicely in complexity. Runs without any problems even on (from today's perspective) dated machines in full details and offers some great space panoramas. The many little details you can find outside of stations or other points of interests are simply amazing (Elite Dangerous' stations pale in comparison). The station's inside, however, still suck as they did 2 years ago. Fortunately, the mechanics have changed so you will not need to actually walk inside stations very often. The plot still forces you to do this from time to time, but everything in free play can be done via remote coms.
The AAA price tag is still staggering. In a world, where games on steam usually get a big discount a few months after release, this is a weird thing to do. It is even weirder because at a $10 tag, I would recommend every space fan to giove it a try. But with the current price, while still recommending the game overall, I would suggest to wait for when the game goes on sale next.

I really liked Shelter. It's not a game for everyone. Like an old 60s classic flick, this is a game where you really have to look beyond what is actually presented to the audience. It's a game that is not meant to be "won" or "lost", and while not explicitly stated in the game, you already know what the goal of the game is: Protect your cubs at all costs. It's not action packed, and it's not a complex game, mechanic wise. But instead, it's one of those games that you must connect with and play on an emotional level. It's about nature and how there is nothing around to teach you how nature operates. Everything you need to learn about protecting yourself and your cubs, you better learn fast. The game does nature justice. It's not forgiving and it does not hold your hand.
I loved this game. It's beautiful, gorgeous even. Even though it has a simplistic art, the fact that it is so simple looking does not distract you from the true meaning behind the game, but it's also simple in a way so as to not overwhelm you, and you learn to appreciate the game for what it /really/ is. And I don't want to spoil too much, but it is certainly possible to keep all your cubs 'til the very end. Unfortunately, no matter how careful you are, the ending is, well... let's just say that in contrast to every mistake being in your hands (and your hands actions alone), there is a sudden shift of control in the game where it is utterly relinquished from you and you can't do anything to prevent it, even if you know how it could be prevented. If the ending isn't what you want it to be, you didn't mess up, it's just scripted into the game, and it is punishing (but yet, satisfactory enough if you get to see all your cubs make it). I will say I am disappointed that what happens in the end isn't at all due to your own mistakes.
Still, I dont want to spoil too much. The game is still well worth your money, even if it is a bit short, but I have learned how to appreciate and love the game for what it is really trying to tell me.

Alright... So, Farming simulator 2015 is a farming game (No surprise there) Where you can: Harvest crops, Raise cows and other farming stuff. Its fairly fun... At least, when it works.
The DLC is abundant and extremely overpriced. You may get a couple of vehicles or a couple of attachments. And to be honest the amount you get from each pack is surprisingly low... I would happily pay 75% of retail price for it but for its full price I think its just a money grab.
The multiplayer is utterly terrible. If you have a poor connection it is nearly impossible to steer properly. The client often freezes while moving and will reset your velocity which is very frustrating. And as previously stated makes steering and maneuvering difficult. Loading is extremely annoying. When connecting its really  luck based. Sometimes it may connect but usually it doesn't. And when you actually manage to connect it takes forever to load and once you finish loading you end up with this weird player sync thing that takes ages and the entire server freezes the entire time during this process.
Physics in this game are nearly non existent. When getting out of vehicles you can glitch through walls. Grabbing logs and bales is difficult. Getting bales on and off bale forks can be glichy and difficult. Tools often glitch through the ground when attaching to them and it can be difficult to get them out of the ground. Wheel friction is a little funny and you rarely have proper traction.
As for content I feel this game is lacking without overpriced dlc. There are only two maps and only a couple of vehicle brands. And I feel like certain categories such as road tractors and lowboys are extremely lacking. The maps seem small and the layouts are confusing. It is also difficult to get up the hills with large loads because of the wheel friction. The ai on the roads is just frustrating and isn't programmed well. I have had cars turn into me at an intersection many times.
The modding community is riddled with unfinished, broken, and stolen mods. However there are also many well made and good mods. Another problem that I have found is that mods in multiplayer are extremely annoying. You have to find every mod that is on the server before you can join which can be a tedious and slow process. Other than that mods can add allot of what the dlc does to the game and add alot more variety.
So, In conclusion I bought this game during the christmas sales and I have enjoyed it to an extent. Do I think it is worth the money? No, I personally don't believe that at full retail price this game is worth the cost given all of its problems. Would I buy it on sale? Possibly but now that I have seen its problems I am not so sure.
As for fs 2017? I feel that if I don't see alot of improvement in the netcode and physics I don't plan on purchasing it.
TL: DR Buy something else
Also for those complaining about me having poor specs and how that affects my game... My computer is running a q8400 @2.66 ghz, Gtx 750ti (Manualy overclocked) and 8 gigs of ddr3 ram. Yes, It isn't the best computer but it runs fs at max settings with no lag.

A technically polished, but otherwise soulless, modification to the Civilization V engine.   While it tries to take its cues from 1999's fantastic Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri (SMAC), it lacks all personality and spark that made SMAC special.
It's not a bad game, it just never gets out of second gear.  Dissapointing given Firaxis's history.   Maybe expansions will help the game (as they did with Civ V), but I can't give Beyond Earth a recommendation as-is and at full AAA price.
The good stuff:
- Novel try at a "three dimensional" tech tree.
- An orbital map layer where you can deploy satellites.
- Crisp graphics and inventive alien design.
- A clever new social policy "talent tree" that awards going wide as well as deep.
Underwhelming stuff:
- Very limited unit selection and customization.
- Bland AI whose only difficulty comes from production and gameplay bonuses.
- Diplomatic screens ripped right from Civ V.  They didn't even bother to rewrite the flavor text.
- The affinity system.  It tries to organicly grow your culture in the form of a pure human, cybernetic singularity, or human/alien hybrid civilization.   Unfortunately, you have to commit very early to one of these affinities, so it ends up being a forced and uninteresting choice.
- Uninspiring technology quotes.  You'll miss SMAC's philosophy and witty commentary.

OVER ALL: 9.5/10
OVERVIEW: The Crysis series is one of my all-time favorites. I generally dislike single-player games; I'm a very social person (played WoW for 7 years, lots of Halo multiplayer stuff, CoD multiplayer, etc.) and generally detest campaign-based games. However, after growing up watching my dad play this game back when it was originally released six years ago, I had always had the urge to play it for myself. Last week, I started the series with this game (Crysis) and played through Crysis: Warhead and just finished Crysis 2 about an hour ago. It is a phenomenal series, and I cannot wait to get Crysis 3.
POSITIVES:
*Excellent plotline which seemlessly transitions from killing North Koreans to killing aliens
*Diverse array of weaponry (not just confined to a pistol or shotgun) allows the player freedom to choose whichever weapon he desires on whichever level he desires
*Incredible graphics and audio, even by 2014 industry standards
*Varied suit abilities allow the user to adopt his own unique play style (hit-and-run, tank-and-spank, melee, etc.)
*Gun attachments make for interesting gameplay, especially when you are stripped of your weapons between some levels and are given only what the game provides you
*A perfect learning curve (the game definitely throws you right into the action with some North Koreans that you must kill, but it gets substantially harder as time progresses when aliens are introduced to the mix, which makes it very satisfying to play and rewarding to conquer)
*Sectional nature of the game allows for much-desired reprieves from the action (there are points in the game where you feel like you can put it down and call it a day because you have just passed a few levels of action-packed content and are now faced with a low-key cutscene where someone will help repair your suit or transport you elsewhere)
*Ability to save the game whenever the player desires allows for easy, casual gameplay experience (no "I just need to finish this level" mentality)
*Lengthy campaign (20+ hours of gameplay on normal difficulty) means this game is a solid investment
*Fun vehicles are featured in various levels--you get to drive a gunship, a tank, a gauss Humvee, an armored helicopter, etc.)
NEGATIVES:
*Minor glitches and bugs run amock in this game, sometimes causing the player to lose 5-10 minutes of progress
*Some confusion regarding objectives may arise, especially towards the end of the game--I had to repeat the last level three times because of a common mistake that many players had made before me (lots of community support, though)
*Replayability is almost zero--other than going back to beat the game on higher difficulty settings, a single playthrough leaves the player content and exhausted from the intensity
CONCLUSION:
Whether you're new to the world of first-person shooter gaming or a hardened CoD veteran, Crysis is a fantastic game, and you should get it. A player has the ability to create his own play style, experience an immersive plotline filled with just the right amount of relaxed cutscenes to break up the intensity, and take control of various fun vehicles. Although you may be stuck with some bugs or have trouble getting blown up by North Korean tanks, Crysis has its own Wiki with a friendly community that's there to help. Any questions or struggles you may have will be answered.
