This game managed to deliver something no metroidvanias have delivered since Super Metroid: Incredible exploration without hand-holding or GPS systems aside from a rather rudimentary, yet adequate map system. Not only does it look gorgeous and plays incredibly well, but thanks to that emphasis on exploration is far more immersive than most metroidvanias I've ever played. Story-wise, you can expect a similar style to what we see in the Souls games. A lot of carefully crafted environmental storytelling, legitimately puzzling and quirky characters, and an overwall mood of despair that's incredibly difficult to pull off successfully.
Graphics-wise, I'm a sucker for hand drawn animation. Everything about this game's artwork oozes personality and conveys the undeniable love the artists' working on it have for their craft. It's simply fantastic to look at. The amazing use of color palettes to depict the various areas is simply fantastic.
Sound-wise, it's incredible. the soundtrack is absolutely outstanding, heavily contributing to the already massive immersion factor the game's visuals deliver. It's one of the very few games whose soundrack I'd actually recommend picking, because it's quite a treat on it's own merits. Sound effects are also flawlessly executed. In certain areas where they take prevalence, they manage to successfully build a legitimately creepy ambiance to support the visual design.
Gameplay-wise, controls are tight and simple to pick, but the game also happens to present a really good challenge. Bosses in particular are fantastic, following queues from the souls series about fair, properly tuned encounters that become heavily punishing for the sloppy player. The same sense of respect for the player's ability to learn and adapt we see in souls game is unapologetically present in Hollow Knight. It's a game that won't insult your intelligence or hold your hand, but won't feel unfair at any given time.
If there's anything I'd have to criticize about it, however, is how useless some of the trinkets you'll encounter feel. While the game certainly presents an opportunity to optimize your playstyle around some of them, it's unfortunate at least half of them lack any long term usability past a few niche encounters, which may affect replay value. Other than this, I strongly believe this is one of the best releases I've experienced in 2017. Even at full price, it's definitely worth a purchase for any metroidvania fan.

It took me a while to be fond of this game as I played it years ago and while my rig met the minimum requirements (almost reached the recommended ones) it had a hard time running Crysis on it properly. There were numerous glitches, audio issues and frequent CTDs.
But you know what? Putting the technical difficulties aside this is a damn fine game! You play Nomad, a special forces soldier who wears a so-called nanosuit. The story takes place in the future and the objective is to find out what happened on the island previously seized by Koreans.
While you traverse through the deep jungle and small settlements you notice two things: the game is stunningly beautiful (there was a reason for the high system reqs) and that by hiding-shooting you cannot eliminate your foes. You need to utilise your nanosuit.
You can bring up a special menu and select from various abilities. Speed makes you faster, Strength allows you to melee your foes or throw bigger objects and Stealth makes you invisible. All drain your energy bar (which will refill automatically, but slowly) and I do not have to mention that Stealth is the most exciting and most useful among all. Oh, yes, there's a 4th power enabling you to take more damage.
Enemy AI is great - they respond to the noises, work in squads and will try to find you even if you are invisible. On greater difficulty settings they speak Korean so you do not understand what commands they give to one another.
Occasionally, the game throws in some scripted cutscenes - these look good and also interesting. By looking at the pictures on the store page one can guess what they'll find (and what the army was really looking into), but let's not spoil it here.
Crysis is a stunningly beautiful game (even today considering it's more than 5 years old) and makes for an interesting, action-packed ride.
WARNING: This review is based on playing the game on a 32-bit operating system. As per the feedbacks on the store page and amongst the discussions people detail further issues when it comes to 64-bit systems. I understand there is a workaround which has been tried and found good, still, this is just to let you know that before the purchase you should look into this.
There is lots to be done here but the core game is really tight. Can't wait for more updates from Stunlock Studios.

Please bear in mind, the following is my opinion alone. You may disagree with my opinion.
Sid Meier's Civilization: Beyond Earth.
A slight disappointment.
First off, the game is fantastic; it looks good, the research tree has turned into a web, there are all-new aliens, and being in the future, the devs aren't confined to history to make their game.
However - there are also some bad points. Although it does look good, it's not a terribly big improvement on the Civ V graphics. It also seems so dull and lifeless, despite being a theoretically very fun game, and it looks more vibrant than ever. The game simply isn't different enough from Civ V, despite being set in a completely different time, and a completely different planet.
There also aren't many Civs, but I understand that creating factions which do not already exist is far harder than creating factions based on real-life countries.
And the noises for the quests are REALLY annoying.
I think after a bunch of updates and DLC, the game will be worth the £29.99 I spent on it, but you can never predict the future exactly.
Despite being basically Civ V in the future, it is still a very good game, as Civ V is a very good game. It's simply the value for money which gets me.
RATINGS
Graphics - 7.5/10
Gameplay - 8/10
Story - 1.5/10
Value for Money - 5/10
Replayability - Nearly Infinite
Length - Varies too much to rate
Extra Special Feature - Aliens make early game interesting and challenging, unlike most strategy games I have played
My Final Rating:
6.8/10

This game won't be any fun. But you have to buy it.
Game mechanics are simple, but interesting nevertheless. Explore the city with basic combat and stealth mechanics to procure at night, and spend days crafting and managing resources and items. Sounds typical, right? Yes, because the game isn't about mechanics.
The game's about war. The simplest way to survive is to steal and kill, if neccessary. Good deeds don't pay. You shouldn't trust anyone. How much food do you have? How many supplies? How well can you defend it? It's all that matters. You can get sentimental, of course — if you want to get killed sooner. If you want to live, you'll become a mosnter.
Usually, games help you escape reality, but not this one. It's the opposite kind. There are people that are living like that right now: when I write this review, when you read it. And day by day, we see these pictures in the news, we don't give them much thought. We just register information. But when you play it, when you remember that it's not just fantasy, it's not just a pixel man dying on the screen — there are thousands just like him, slowly rotting, in the real life — then it really kicks you in the gut.
If you're a human being capable of empathy, this game won't be the least bit of fun. It will be excrutiatingly depressing. It will be bad. It will be sad. It will be painful.
Good. That's how it supposed to be. May be next time, when you watch the news about people being killed in a faraway land, you'll give it a little bit more thought.

Strike Suit Zero
Rating: 7/10
Overview: Solid Space Combat with some questionable design decisions.
The Good:
+ Graphics are fantastic, fighting ships in space with explosions everywhere, capital ships firing laser beams and seeing a beautiful planet in the background all look amazing and does a great job of immersing you into the game.
+ Multiple ships and weapons that you can select before each mission, some missions however force you to use the pre-selected ship.
+ The main ship and the premise of the game is that one of the ships can transform into a mech that can easily dispatch enemies. Knowing when and how to use your mech is key to winning a lot of missions.
+ Bonus objectives within each mission allows you to unlock upgrades. You are also awarded medals at the end of each mission depending on how well you did although completing the mission under target time usually gets you the highest medal. These provide good incentives to replay the level.
+ The controls may take a little time getting use to but once you get good you will be tearing apart ships very easily
+ Achievements are not too hard to get and may take a little time, a found them to be the right mix of fun and challenging.
+ Good soundtrack
The Average:
Each mission has a checkpoint system and although its fine in the earlier missions, some of the longer missions could have used a few more checkpoints.
There is a story...it involves you and a ship and other people and things start happening...and.....there are explosions...To be quite honest although I'm sure the overall plot is decent the story just isn't presented all that well. It's so difficult to care about any of the characters or the plot.
The Bad:
- One reason why it's so hard to care about the story is that each mission is very repetitive. Every missions involves the exact same thing....blow up enemy ships..over and over and over again. The only difference between missions is the amount of enemies you have to fight.
- The game has some really odd difficulty spikes. Some missions you will beat very easily only to be stuck in the next mission.

Conclusion:
This is a game that has such strong core mechanics that work well but is held back by some very poor design decisions. I would love to see a sequel that really adds diversity to the levels. You don't have to be a fan of space combat games to enjoy this as I found it to be pretty easy to learn all the mechanics but it does have difficulty holding interest for long periods of time.

Here's the deal. Everyone should play this game. Just not at this price. Skip to the end for the abridged version. Excuse my gushing if you dont.
The game:
Im not saying that this is the greatest game ever made. But I am saying that it touched me in a way that no other game really has. The game really puts you into the character of a badger mom because it gives you NO dialogue or instructions whatsoever. You have no choice but to take the game at face value.
Also, there are two ways to deal with loss in a video game. 1. make it a big deal. scream NOOO to the heavens, play a sad song, penalize the player heavily, maybe even in a game over if the loss is too drastic, etc. 2. DO NOTHING.  this game is so simple. theres so few "things" in it. and when you lose something, the game doesnt penalize you. it doesnt do anything. it just expects you to carry on.
The game treats you the way nature treats itself. by not caring. The game could play sad music, or give you some debuff (maybe the mama moves slower or the babies are harder to control when one dies) but they dont. and somehow, when the game gives you no punishment, thats the worst punishment it can give you. Like your loss doesnt matter. as if no loss matters. and youre left with the staggering thought that it was all your fault.
Its a very interesting game. Because it shows us about the struggle between human nature and the wild, and death, and loss, and rearing children, and a mothers love, through the use of a family of honey badgers and no dialogue whatsoever. Its truely something.
This is really what a indie game is supposed to be. simple, experimental, and made by someone who CLEARLY knew what they were doing.
The Price:
That being said, the game is $10, and you can beat it in an hour if you try, an hour and a half if you dont. I am extremely fortunate that I bought this game when it was on sale for about $1.50. I think knowing how much I enjoyed it, I MIGHT have paid $5 for it. MAYBE. But im a cheapskate, so take that into account. But then again there would be no way I could know what it would mean to me before I bought it. so thats why Im telling you now.
TL;DR
-Game is extremely more philisophical than it seems. it was an emotional ride
-absolutely dont buy this game for $10. put it on your wishlist and wait. buy it for nothing more than $5. its an hour long
-NAME YOUR KIDS AT THE START. makes the game alot more hard hitting

If you’re a space games veteran, you’ll find some things in this game that were taken from other space games. For example, you’ll see the large torpedoes and “no need to dodge” countermeasures from “Starlancer”, you’ll remember the flak cannons and ship beams from “Freespace 2”, and you’ll find a Karan S’jet clone. I believe even the missile types are copied from “FS 2”.
What distinguishes this game from the others of its kind is the ability to turn into a mech and fire spread missiles at multiple targets. If you’re a fan of mecha anime, this will be pretty familiar to you. It takes some time to get used to this system. However, once you master it, you’ll be fighting like a real “Macross/Robotech” ace, transforming between mech and fighter in the middle of dogfights.
You should be warned that this game is also more arcade-like than usual. No power management, no radar, no shield convergence. When you fly a bomber, you have an infinite amount of torpedoes. When you restart from a checkpoint, you get a full ammo reload and hull repair.
The story is pretty basic. Colonials want to destroy Earth and that’s all you know about them. There’s nothing about their ideology or personality. There’s no communications from them whatsoever throughout the game, not even a “Surrender or die!”. Enemy units don’t have names, not even the cruisers and carriers.
Mission design is the game’s biggest flaw. When you’re attacking enemy fighters and your flight leader says “ignore the fighters, focus on your objectives”, what she means is “enemy fighters have infinite waves, so don’t bother”. Sometimes you have to take out flak cannons before the bombers come in, sometimes you don’t. Sometimes the objective is to destroy the cruiser, sometimes you have to protect the bombers which will do that for you and it’s mission failed if they get destroyed by those infinite waves of enemy fighters. You’ll see so many enemy ships throughout the campaign, that you’ll wonder if Earth ever had a chance to win the war in the first place. On defense missions, you’ll learn to love checkpoints.
It’s a fun game. Looks easy at first and it only gets hard when you start fighting the Black Fleet. When you master the strike suit, you’ll love flying it. However, if you played classics like “FS 2” and the X-wing or “Wing Commander” series, it’s likely that you won’t take this game seriously.
For example, when I did the bomber mission and realized I had infinite torpedoes plus a ton of missiles for self-defense, I remembered my experience as a TIE Bomber pilot and the bomber tutorial in “FS 2” and I actually laughed.

An absolutely fantastic game, visually and gameplay wise. Firstly, some of the pros:
- Stunning graphics
- A reasonable amount of realism
- Very well optimized (can run on even some low end systems)
- Plenty of different tasks and jobs to do throughout
- Very moddable
At the start, you are presented with two of the in game maps, one being Westbridge Hills, and the second one Bjonholm. Both maps have their differences, all dependant on what you're wanting to do. Bjonholm would be more idea for those that want to go off and work within the forestry area. Westbridge Hills on the other hand is more based around animal and field work. Throughout both maps, you can easilly put multiple hours in without even noticing.
The game has built in Multiplayer support meaning that you can team up with friends and have a blast of a session together. A very stable multiplayer build too, I must add. Within the Multiplayer platform you also have access to run mods on your own in game session. (Multiplayer sessions can be hosted in game, with a maximum capacity of 4 players. A dedicated server can be rented/ hired, which would allow for a 24 hour operation, and you can choose the amount of players you'd like the server open to.)
The modding community- Now this is where the game really starts to get interesting and exciting for many. This game is massively moddable. In the concept of different tools and machinery such as: Combine Harvesters, Seeders, Plows, Cultivators, etc... The list can go on for minutes. Some of the mods that you can find for this game are visually stunning and perform greatly around the farm. Of course with all mods, some you will find to be slightly buggy, but this is to be expected at times.
Performance- The game runs super smooth, on both high and low end systems. Configuration for graphics settings could not be made any easier than the way that it is configured in this game. You choose from the default presets that are available: low, high, very high. In order to get the highest render distances and maximum detail you're going to need a fairly good system to run it. But most laptop systems should be capable of running between medium and high profile settings.
Overall, I'd strongly recommend this game to anyone that has an interest to agriculture. It looks great, plays great, and is a heap of fun. Definitely a 10/10 from me.

text:
Square Enix have created a fantastic Final Fantasy title that has left fans with mixed feelings, yet again.
As someone that has played the game to completion on both PC and PS3, I find very little to complain about.
New FF titles have always been about pushing the boundaries - this is apparent to us from long development times, sometimes wildly different art styles between consecutive titles, and also the stories behind the characters and gameplay. It's true that to some extent developers should be catering to the customer's needs, but at the same time we don't want a carbon copy of a game that came out three years ago. If you do want a flood of FFVII clones on the market then perhaps you should stick with FFVII.
Thirteen exists on its own and does not require you to have played any other Final Fantasy games to get your head around it. The story starts at a mid-point of sorts, on Day 13. As you progress through the story you discover snippets of what happened on the earlier days, and is cleverly crafted so that some of the bigger questions are left unanswered for the majority of the story.
The story centres on Lightning, an ex-soldier from an artificially created moon, Cocoon, orbiting (geostationary?) above the planet Pulse, and it starts in the thick of action and explosions and cutscenes, which can leave players feeling a bit bewildered. The take-home message? Most of the main characters are out to rescue Serah, Lightning's sister, who has been branded by a magical entity, and both Serah and the entity are enemies of Cocoon.
The plot thickens as all the main characters are eventually branded in the same way, gaining the ability to wield magic, but also acquiring a doom-timer in the form of a task they must fulfil within a certain time period. The characters are true to form, behaving as we might expect given the situation, but also occasionally
as expected. This dichotomy of behaviour is one of the more intriguing aspects of the story, but far from the only one. I do not wish to give too much away.
Insofar as performance on PC goes, I did have some framerate issues, but nothing more than that, and only at specific points in the game. Don't look away in disgust! Having said this, I don't think you'll find it any different on the consoles. I think it could have been optimised better for all the systems it got released on, so if you're thinking of getting it I recommend PC. I had no stuttering issues (as others have claimed) and I'm just running Windows 7 Prof. with a GTX590 card.
More on the gameplay though. As expected, FF13 treats combat very differently from how other, previous titles did. Combat is real-time, but there is a cooldown after actions such as attacking, buffing or healing. I believe items are the only exception. So in a sense it is similar to the ATB (Active Time Battle) system from previous titles. But the similarities stop there. There are six roles to swap between during combat - Medic, Saboteur, Synergist, Commander, Ravager, and Sentinel. Each of these has its own speciality - medic for healing, sentinel for tanking and taking the big hits, commander for physical attacks, ravager for magical attacks, synergist for buffs and saboteur for debuffing or crippling the enemies. Oh, and if you really want to damage enemies, you're going to want to stagger them.
It may seem like a lot to take in, but with a bit of practice you'll find it works pretty well. It's possible to customise your preset 'paradigms' as they're called, so that you can go from straight up assault to full defence at the flick of a button.
FF13 is often criticised for its linearity and lack of side quests, but I value a good story more than how complex the game is laid out. If you need a break from grinding for experience towards role levels, HP, strength and magic, there is also Chocobo Treasure Hunting, unique monster hunts, and farming enemies for parts and gold so that you can upgrade and empower your Ultimate Weapons, of which there is an interesting selection to choose from , including various passive and hidden stats (which you will more than likely need a guide for!)
The art is sometimes breathtaking, vast, and beautiful, but occasionally you might find it a bit monotonous. End game maps such as the Archylte Steppe and the Yaschas Massif are so large and indentical in almost every respect that I'll hazard most players tire of it sooner or later. And yet, the game also boasts some true fantasy imagery - Lake Bresha turned to crystal, walking under frozen waves and churning waters; the awe-inspiring Tesseracts and Orphan's Cradle, where the environment is ever-shifting, ever-changing all around (probably why there's a framerate drop here). I haven't even mentioned some of the gigantic bosses - both mechanical and organic, and even the fabled 'Summons' that have become so much a staple of the FF games.
I find myself playing a large chunk of the soundtrack on an almost daily basis too, for there is some incredible work right there. Empowering, mysterious, emotional, it just
so well with the scenarios you find yourself in that it's hard not to find yourself liking at least some of it.
So what if it's a bit linear? I still enjoyed it, and definitely will again. I consider it 126+ hours well spent, and if you think you're up to trying it I can think of no other RPG I recommend quite as much as I do this one. Pick up a copy today.

Though a good game so far, with definite improvment in graphics and some basic gameplay, along with some minor bugs, this remaster still has a lot to improve on.
Though there is a graphical improvment it still doesn't stand up to todays standards of graphics in many regions, with many props and items not framing properly until you are two feet from it. Ive also noticed some graphical glitches when the camera is aimed at random objects in which a basic red/blue field will cover the area.
Along with that the lack of proper control options (especially mouse sensitivity) is less than pleasing. The mouse either seems to stagger far too much or be inaccurate with the few settings given. Though it is easy enough to get used to (especially by those who have played Bioshock before) it would be nice to see more player options available.
Lastly, though it doesn't often happen, the game can and will crash. Though it was running for about 5 hours straight it can be annoying when you are 2 hours into a level and the game crashes, leaving you only with the autosave at the start of that level (as quicksaves won't remain).
But overall, is it bad? No where near. The nostalgia remains from the original with a little bit of modern charm, the message and presentation is still thrilling, and the gameplay is still exciting (even after the massive gameplay improvements and functions found in the procedding two games).
Add on the inclusion of achievments (something I had been wanting in Bioshock for years), the Orphan Gallery and new trials its still definetly a pick up if you havent already, or a play if you, like me, got it for free with your original version.
TL:DR Has its issues and seems to be a bit of a lazy port, but still bloody fun and nostalgic with the improvements in graphics and add ons making it worth playing over the original.

Civ: BE is either a lackluster full-scale title or an ambitious expansion to Civ 5.  Either way, it's overpriced for what you're getting.
The sci-fi theme is appreciated, though a little bland.  Fantastical technologies come and go with little sense of impact, except for the new Affinities (or, reskinned Religion) which are essentially benign except for giving you a slightly different unit than before (or what leveling of individual units used to be) and a soulless reason for other civilizations to hate you or like you.
Barbarians have been traded out for Aliens, which are exactly the same throughout each play-through.  There's no sense of wonder at each play-through as to how the alien terrain will affect you, and not even the decency of a palate swap.  Miasma is also consistent.  Making alien life and ecosystems a bit random would have added a lot to the replay value, of which there is little currently.
City-States have been neutered to Outposts, which provide trade partners and little else.  Instead, City-State demands have been nebulized into goals, which are often forgotten or not even known of until you mistakenly complete one.  These do not seem to change between play-throughs.
Speaking of trading, the system is horribly annoying and unintelligent.  With a few cities running trade caravans, you'll be pestered every few turns with an update to the routes.  Between such notices, you'll have the Espionage system updating you that you have idle agents.
In the end, the game offers few things to enjoy over Civ 5, and what it does offer in this regard are tepid and bland.  It doesn't offer much to offend, either.  The grand sum of this is a tasteless, inoffensive, and largely unenticing game.  I'm hoping future patches and (reasonably priced) expansions (or, if need be, the modding community) will fix these issues, because I want to like this game.  I really, really want to think "I want to play more Civ: BE" this evening.  But right now, the game is just boring.

The majority of the negative reviews are based on two points.
1) There's so much that's new and different that you actually have to study the game mechanics in order to get really good at it.
2) It's pretty much the exact same as Civ V.
Besides the fact that these are contradictory claims (which is ridiculous), I'd say they're also both false. BE (Beyond Earth) adds a lot of new elements to the Civ series, and is actually quite different from Civ V, and have an overall quite different feel to it. That being said, it is a Civ game, and is going to be very similiar to all past installments, especially Civ V because that's the predecessor.
I think it's amazing that they went out of the box, and did something different with this game. The tech tree is not linear, which is a great improvement. You actually decide what kind of civilization you want to develop. Excellent improvement. To those that are complaining about this, be glad the Civ games switched it up a little bit rather than doing the exact same thing for a fourth time in a row.
A third complaint people have is the aliens. True, they do make the beginning of the game difficult, and true, they are pointless later on in the game. But... who cares? The game is about taming a new and dangerous world, and they really made it feel that way what with the poison gas and giant monsters. I loved it. And yeah, they're pointless later on, but doesn't that just make sense? After you take the world, it's not dangerous anymore, duh!
Overall, it's an incredibly fun game, lives up to the Civ reputation, adds a lot of new concepts, and provides a much different feel. I personally think the ones giving negative reviews are being childish.

I started playing this game with very low expectations. It didn’t seem all that impressive from the trailers so I just said to myself: “Yet another one of EA’s attempts to milk the Lord of the Rings cash cow.”
A couple of hours of hacking orcs with a friend changed my view of the game drastically.
The first and most important thing you should know about the game is this: Do NOT expect a fun solo experience. This game is meant to be played with a friend or if at all possible, two.
It is at its best when you are communicating with your friends in order to take down tough enemy groups and help each other survive difficult encounters.
A lot of people are complaining about the simplicity of its design, but honestly, that’s what makes it work so well. The combat is straightforward and impactful (I suggest a gamepad but mouse and keyboard controls work well also) and the looting is surprisingly fun.
War in the North won’t make you care too much about its story though. It isn’t very memorable or interesting in any way for that matter. This could have been improved upon by having the player actually make meaningful decisions. Unfortunately, the dialogue options seem to be there just to give you a little more information if you really want it.
From a graphical point of view, the game is quite ok. You won’t be amazed by it, but occasionally, you might find yourself nodding to a slow motion decapitation or some other small detail (like how the snow sticks you your armor after you roll through it).
This is indeed the grittiest Lord of the Rings game released and it feels great. If you wanted a more mature and accurate video game based on Tolkien’s books, this might be your thing.
The sound is so and so. The music is great as always but the voice acting really put me to sleep. The greatest thing about it is the built in voice chant. It actually takes into account things like the distance between characters and the environment. For example, if a friend is in a cave and talks to me, his voice will have an echo. (I don’t think I’ve ever encountered a game with a similar feature)
Is it a good game? Hell yeah! If you are a fan of co-op games, it will be hard to be disappointed with War in the North.

This game won't be any fun. But you have to buy it.
Game mechanics are simple, but interesting nevertheless. Explore the city with basic combat and stealth mechanics to procure at night, and spend days crafting and managing resources and items. Sounds typical, right? Yes, because the game isn't about mechanics.
The game's about war. The simplest way to survive is to steal and kill, if neccessary. Good deeds don't pay. You shouldn't trust anyone. How much food do you have? How many supplies? How well can you defend it? It's all that matters. You can get sentimental, of course — if you want to get killed sooner. If you want to live, you'll become a mosnter.
Usually, games help you escape reality, but not this one. It's the opposite kind. There are people that are living like that right now: when I write this review, when you read it. And day by day, we see these pictures in the news, we don't give them much thought. We just register information. But when you play it, when you remember that it's not just fantasy, it's not just a pixel man dying on the screen — there are thousands just like him, slowly rotting, in the real life — then it really kicks you in the gut.
If you're a human being capable of empathy, this game won't be the least bit of fun. It will be excrutiatingly depressing. It will be bad. It will be sad. It will be painful.
Good. That's how it supposed to be. May be next time, when you watch the news about people being killed in a faraway land, you'll give it a little bit more thought.

A terribly dissapointing release that seems to freeze or crash in a different way each time it's played.
In scale it might be compared to Skyrim, with its impressively large playable area, but X Rebirth lacks any significant diversity within that space.  A small handful of NPC models are cut and pasted throughout identical locations.  Even when unique characters are encountered, their dialog is confused and poorly voice-acted.  And without the option of skipping dialog, in any situation, the repeatitiveness of the characters and situations is compounded.
While there is an enjoyable aspect to navigating the bustling space around lovely stations, in beautifully rendered external environments, these potential strengths are mitigated by a horribly muddled UI which includes the claustrophobic and largely non-interactive cockpit of your ship, only a very small portion of which offers any useful information for navigation or combat.
As a whole, X Rebirth is a largely broken, badly designed, low-concept product that could use, at minimum, another year in development and a full UI overhaul.  Fans of the series might find the experience worthwhile, but the rest of the gaming community will likely find time and money better spent in Eve.

I think the expectations have doomed War in the North. Since it's Lord of the Rings title, players and Middle-Earth fans alike anticipated something grand, a game that will finally maximize the potential of LotR in a video game. It didn't happen to the extent everyone expected. Yet it doesn't mean War in the North is an inferior product. Far from it.
You play as one of three available characters - a Ranger, Dwarven fighter and Elven mage. Each have three main skills at their disposal and a handful of minor ones. Even though the trio is a bit bland, they are likeable. The story runs simultanously to the Frodo's quest, which is a nice touch - your actions feel relevant as your party contribute to the greater cause.
The gameplay features a lot of hacking, slashing, shooting and looting. You face the horde of goblins, orcs and trolls under the command of one evil Agandaur, who is neatly tailored as a villan. War in the North offers an abundance of loot - here I would like to mention that the equipment in this game is superbly designed. The details on weapons and armor are fantastic, the overall feel of the equipment you find or buy fits the world perfectly, which is a nod to the coherent Tolkien universe and at the same time a welcome break from all the overdone, tasteless and improper design in most of the modern RPGs (a sexy female warrior with armor covering only her breast and groin area? Yes, practical indeed). On your travels you will visit locations and meet characters well-known from the books and movies (Ian McKellen voices Gandalf).
The game's length is reasonable, around 10 hours for a playthrough, and the replay value is here. War in the North is best enjoyed while playing with your frineds in a co-op mode. It's essantially the same campaign as the single player, but obviously more challanging as the opponents grow in strength with each additional player.
Recommended. I approached War in the North without any expectations and was pleasantly surprised by the overall quality - it's not one of the best games you will ever play, but it's certainly enjoyable.

A game that starts off in a desolate cavern, and later opens up into a huge underground map with many distinct areas to explore.  Team Cherry's presentation is astounding, including gorgeous hand drawn landscapes and characters unlike anything I've encountered before.  My first "Metroidvania" style game, brought to my attention at the end of 2016 where people were already stating it to be contender for Game Of The Year (despite its actual release in Feb '17), its barren night-scape failed to grab me initially and it actually went on the back burner for a couple of months while I ploughed through some short single-player games.
Coming back to it and sinking in about two hours, I got hooked running around the first area you are directed to by NPCs
trying to explore every nook and cranny for Geo (the in-game currency) and a way to get past an armadillo-like bug
with a nasty spitting habit.  After obtaining the necessary skill to beat this creature, I was rewarded with entrance into one of the most beautiful areas in the game
, and its combination of lush greenery, creatures rustling through leaves and an amped up orchestral soundtrack hooked me in.
I do have a few gripes with the game though, mainly centred around pace of progression and Team Cherry's decision to force you about halfway through an area before you have a chance to purchase a map for that very same environment.  Also, there are definitely points where you will wander around aimlessly wishing there was some chatty NPC to give you a hint at where to go.  It was at this point that the game was not fun at all, and this is compounded when some bosses or challenges in the game are very far from a
(in-game save point).  An example would be a boss called
, a challenging and energetic boss that is about five minutes and bunches of enemies away from the nearest
.  I knew I could eventually beat the boss but traversing the expanse between where I'd respawn and where I'd fight this jumping laugh-machine was frankly boring.
For me personally, this game was a lot more fun when I looked up a map for the entire game and gave myself goals to reach certain areas to pick up skills I needed or to quickly get to the map seller for where I was.  Doing this didn't ruin the story of the game at all and I would suggest doing the same thing if you get stuck for more than an hour somewhere.  The combat is simple and totally relies on your own skill and decisions as to what
(equippable buffs for your character) you go with.  I had a few problems using a Wireless XBox One controller, but this maybe due to my use of a Bluetooth transceiver that came with my Motherboard as opposed to using the official dongle offered by Microsoft.
Overall, I would recommend this game to anyone (like me) who is possibly thinking about going for their first Metroidvania game and to purchase in a sale for £7.50/$9.89 and I look forward to Team Cherry's next endeavours.

Shelter is a unique little game where you play as a female badger who must protect her offspring as they journey with her throughout the game's world, which consists of forests, mountains and rivers. You must feed your babies regularly or else they will starve - there are plenty of food items around the world, which is useful, however during more intense moments you'll need to make sure that your offspring aren't going hungry as you spend your time trying to reach a safer area.
Dangers in the world come from other animals such as hawks as well as factors in the environment such as rushing water. These provide the player with a lot of challenge, especially if they want to keep all of their babies alive. Whilst the babies are cute, their AI isn't perfect, and on several life or death situations I've had them prance around a turnip instead of following me to safety. There are also a few glitches with falling fruit, where it falls on top of a baby badger, it will cause the baby to freeze up. This can be solved easily however.
The music and environments are very beautifully-designed, and look like they've just come out of a book. I did encounter a few FPS drops, however, which seemed strange as I have a very powerful PC. The game's soundtrack is also wonderful, and it will also change in composition depending on what action is unfolding on screen, which is very effective, especially during the more tense parts of the game.
My main gripes Shelter are probably the mentioned issues, along with the game itself which is a tad on the short side. However, there is also a nurture mode which I've not played yet, which has a much longer replay value and is a sort of tamagotchi-like mode where you must feed your offspring every real-life day.
Overall, I think Shelter is a great little game, and a good example of a unique game concept that works well.

Rivals of Aether is far from being just another Smash Bros. clone.
It is inherently clear that Super Smash Bros. was the foundation Rivals of Aether was built upon, yet the end result is completely different from anything Nintendo has been able to create and what some may argue 're-create'.
A major difference between Smash Bros and RoA is the absence of shield and grab abilities. While that may sound like a major con, it is actually quite the opposite. The removal of those two basic features really brings out what I believe to be the original intent of the developer. COMBO'S, COMBO'S, and more COMBO'S!
Launching the tutorial mode also brings upon greater insight on just how different this game is from anythings within Super Smash Bros. franchise. Advance techniques such as wave-dashing and wave-landing are now treated as a fundemental part of 'normal' gameplay, rather than some glitch only high-level players found useful. In tutorial mode, you also discover that while the shield mechanic has been removed, it has been replaced with, what I personally believe to be a more technical function; that is of course the parry mechanic.
Overall, I am glad to see the smash genre growing and heading in this direction. Even if this game goes nowhere, I hope that developers pick up where RoA left off. However, I am more than happy with the outcome of RoA in it's current state and anxiously await future updates!

Final Fantasy XIII is a lot like a roller coaster ride. It takes a lot of time to build up the momentum, but once it reaches the peak, it rushes down for a ride of fun.
The gameplay has a unique twist to the Active Time Battle (ATB) system. Each character is given a role specializing in either attacking, casting,  defending, healing, buffing, or debuffing. The roles given to characters change up the way battles are typically fought using strategy rather than using brute force to win fights. Terms used for status ailments are slightly different here with "fog" replacing "silence" and "daze" replacing "sleep". A variety of other spells and abilities are also left out with new ones added in this game, so this will feel like a different kind of Final Fantasy game.
The story tells about a world of corruption and morals to be had. Idealisms, ambitions, fate, destiny, all clash within the plot. It has some interesting points and events throughout the game.
The visual graphics are beautiful. Character models look incredibly realistic, except for perhaps the hands and feet. Background visuals are very colorful and blend together very well. It makes the world feel enormous and immersive.
The sound quality has its ups and downs. The voice acting gives the main cast diverse backgrounds, but whether or not the voice fits each character is debatable. Non-player characters do not sound all that great, and monster cries feel a bit weak. The music, however, is very melodic. Although the majority of the orchestrated instrumentals do not sound catchy nor rhythmic, it really sets the pacing and tone for game world it resides in.
Perhaps the biggest flaw this game has is its pacing. The game starts out really slow, with battles played out straight forward for almost one-quarter of the game time. In addition to that, the paths are very linear with almost no room for exploration. Until your characters are actually able to grow (as in, actually increasing stats and learning abilities) it's mostly "mash the attack button to win."
Final Fantasy XIII is an enjoyable game for those that are patient enough to go with the slow pace. Once the pace starts picking up, players will be in for a wild ride.

DEDICATED playing and modding community - even after being out for several years, many people, myself included still play this game religiously.
Incredible mod support - There are literally thousands of mods for this game. Hundreds of new, GIANT maps. Thousands of guns. Thousands of new unit types. Even entire overhall mods to change it into the Vietnam war or World War 2. Mods exist to change every sound in the game and graphical mods exist to ease the strain on lower end PC's or make the game more beautiful than it already was.
Already expansive game - The game, minus mod support, already contains hundreds of units, vehicles and guns in the case of Combined ops
Maps - 15km by 15km maps, enough said. Maps contain multiple towns and villages, and often 1-3 large cities and/or settlements. There are also large area with beautiful landscapes such as rocky cliffs and washing oceans. Some custom maps can be even bigger. But to put it into perspective, Skyrim's map is about 37 square kilometers, where as the default OA Takistan map is 164 square kilometers (About 12km by 12km corner to corner). Think about that one.
Replayability - I do not mean the story when I talk about this, I talk about the virtually INFINITE ability to create scenarios in the editor. Want a tank battle 20v20? You got yourself a tank battle complete with terrain big enough to house it and FOBs for both sides. Want a small special ops team to assassinate a middle eastern dictator from 1.2 km away with a 50 cal? You got it. Want to fly an attack helicopter or CAS jet into the heat of battle? You get the idea. Infinite.
Graphics - Though this is something that many people would argue with me about, Arma 2 came out in 2009. Even though it was released later, OA's graphics are no better because the game is still from 2009. It's the same engine and the same game, with a different setting. Given the circumstances, I do have a very nice rig, so the graphics look pretty to me. I constantly find myself looking off a cliff while preforming recon on an enemy position and thinking "Wow, look at that view."
Realism - This may be a turn off point for many. I, for one, live for realistic games. I often b!tch to myself about other games not being realistic enough. This game, with the addition of a few mods, can be as close to real life as you want it to be. Mods to check out for added realism are ACE 2, Retexture mods for units to make them up to date and state of the art (Changing the US Army units to Multicam from that dreaded UCP camo comes to mind), and the Zeus AI mod.
Multiplayer - 100 + player games. Nothing else to say.
Now for the cons, these are all the problems that I've found with the game that personally annoy me.
Lag/Desync - This is only an issue with larger servers, usually. It can be annoying but rarely 100% game breaking
Poor Performance - This game is not very well optimized, and if you have a weak computer, you will struggle to run it with more than 10-15 FPS. Even if you have a good rig, it will usually only max out at about 35-50 FPS. Don't let this turn you off though, you really just get used to it.
Ocasional hackers - This happens very infrequently, and it only happens on big servers.
Expensive - For a game as old as it is, it is a bit pricy, I reccomend waiting until a Steam sale comes around to make a purchase in the Armaverse.
Lack of Realism in Some Places - This is more of a pet peeve of mine rather than an actual flaw. It annoys me that all the US Army units use the SCAR L, considering it was rejected by the Army. The light version of the SCAR is just ugly to me, and when I can, I always mod it out of the Army. This will probably not bother 90% of people considering this game, but for those that enjoy absolute realism, check out the RH M4/M16 pack on Armaholic and it's respective replacement packs.
STEEP Learning Curve - Patience is a virtue. You need patience for this game. A lot of it. You will die. A lot. And you'll die some more. Guess what still happens to me regularily. You guessed it. This game is a tactical simulator, if you try to play Call of Duty, you will be swiss cheese every time. The controls can be hard to learn, and I changed them right away so I was more comfortable. Modding the game is not reccomended unless you have experinece modding similar games. Though modding is very simple, things can be screwed up if you delete or put a file in the wrong place.
Time Consuming - Processes in the game take a very long time. Firefights can be anywhere from a few seconds to 30+ minutes. The time it takes moving from place to place ranges widely. If you are on foot, expect about a 35-40 minute walk from one corner of a map to another. By plane or helicopter, you can travel long distances in minutes and seconds.
Frusturating - It feels really bad when you're almost done with a mission or objective, and get killed.
Overall this game is by far my most played and one of my most treasured games of all time. Very few games have the scope of Arma 2 and its many addons.
PS: Arma 3 is much less realistic in terms of units and gameplay, but still has the giant maps and mod support. It does have better graphics, as well. I reccomend getting both if you can afford them.
EDIT: MAKE SURE YOU BUY COMBINED OPERATIONS OR THE GAME WILL SUCK.

Final Fantasy XIII is a main installment in the renowned Final Fantasy series that is praised by some and highly criticized by others.  I first completed the main story of Final Fantasy XIII on the PS3, effectively making this review based on both my prior play through and second play through of the game.
I’ll be honest: the story was confusing on my first play through. However, while playing through my second play through of this game, I understood most of what was going on. Though this doesn’t sound like a bad thing, it shouldn’t take a second play through of the game to understand the story or terms that are used.
The story revolves around three connected entities: the Fal’Cie, L’Cie, and the Ci’eth. Fal’Cie are supernatural beings that are responsible for some mission. For the Sanctum Fal’Cie, that mission is to support and protect the inhabitants of Cocoon, the world of Final Fantasy XIII. For the Pulse Fal’Cie, that mission is to destroy Cocoon and all those that live on the surface. However, the Pulse Fal’Cie cannot do this themselves. Instead, they brand others, usually humans, L’Cie and give them a specific objective, known as a Focus, to aid in the destruction of Cocoon. L’Cie that fail to complete their Focus turn into Ci’eth, which are beings that are adverse against living beings.
You follow the story of Lightning, Sazh, Snow, Hope, Vanille, and Fang, all been branded as L’Cie by a Pulse Fal’Cie, to go against their assumed Focus of destroying Cocoon and instead attempt to save it. From traveling through the varied landscapes of Cocoon to trekking through the wildlands of Gran Pulse, the progression and telling of the story is quite decent; however, the surprises weren’t too unexpected and at some points, parts of story felt like they were overstaying their welcome by trying to explain every single detail.
The graphics of this game are absolutely gorgeous. To highlight some of the best demonstrations of the graphics of this game, enemies are more than just simple retextures of each other and each of the elemental Black Magics were always a thrill to look at. In short, you will definitely not be disappointed at how this aesthetics of this game.
The gameplay consists of controlling the party leader and members through the world speckled with roaming enemies. Running up to enemies initiates a battle, but engaging enemies without their attention causes a preemptive strike, allowing your party a huge advantage during the battle. You have probably heard that this game represents a corridor simulator, effectively saying that it is linear. For the most part, this is true. For the first 20 hours of the story, you are tasked with going through linear areas with one specific objective marked by your map.
Much of linear nature of this game comes from the absence of thriving towns and to coincide with the story. The game opens up upon arrival onto Gran Pulse, allowing you to undertake side objectives, the main objective, or some combination of both.
The battle system in this game is quite exhilarating. This game uses a more refined Active Time Battle (ATB) system that was used in previous installments of the Final Fantasy series. In battle, you only control the party leader while the two party members are controlled by the A.I. Each action takes up a certain number of segments of the entire ATB bar, which gradually gets increased as the story progresses. There are two ways of choosing your actions for your current ATB bar: auto-battling and manual battling.
The staggering mechanic is also used in the battle system of Final Fantasy XIII. An enemy is staggered when it you “chain” enough attacks against it. While chaining attacks against a target, it takes a greater amount of damage for every hit against it until it is either staggered or the “chain” wears off due to uncontrolled chaining of attacks or a prolonged passive battling style. If the target is staggered, chains are easier to establish and specific actions open up. To help with the stagger mechanic, the Paradigm system is also used. Paradigms assign roles to each of three active party members to use in battle and may be shifted at any point during the battle.  Put simply, Commandos stabilize the chain gauge, Ravagers build the chain gauge, Saboteurs debuff the enemy, Synergists buff your party, Sentinels protect the party, and Medics heal the party. Need to chain an enemy in a controlled manner? Use Relentless Assault, a combination of a single Commando and two Ravagers. Need to heal after a nasty attack? Use Combat Clinic where one Sentinel protects the other party members while the two Medics heal up the entire party.
One last aspect of the gameplay is the character growth in this game, the Crystarium system. This system allows your characters increase many of their attributes in battle, such as HP, Strength, and Magic, and learn new abilities. At first, each of character’s main three Paradigm roles can only be upgraded, but later in the game, all roles can be upgraded for each character, allowing some extent of flexibility for Paradigms.
The music in this game is quite breathtaking. To this day, “Blinded by Light”, the game’s main battle theme, is one of my favorite tracks to listen to. The only con that I can really point out is that some of the tracks borrow “Blinded by Light”, using some of its parts for that track.
The amount of postgame content in this game is staggering, both in a good and bad way. One more level of Crystarium growth is added after loading a cleared save, which requires a fair bit of CP grinding to complete, especially for the non-primary Paradigm roles of each character. Ci’eth Stone missions take up a majority of the post-game content, requiring you to traverse through Gran Pulse to aid those that have failed their Focus, which is usually the defeat of some sort of enemy. Though some of the earlier missions are simple, the latter ones require grinding to survive and win the battle.
If you’re looking to complete every single achievement, be prepared to take at least double the amount of time it took to complete the main story. Some of the hardest-to-get achievements are gratifying to complete (such as “L’Cie Paragon”, five-starring all of the Ci’eth Stone mission), but others are just mind-numbingly tedious (such as “Master’s Seal, finishing the Crystarium for all characters).
An Easy Mode has been added to this version, which came from the original Japanese version of this game. Easy Mode slightly reduces the amount of damage enemies inflict and dramatically increases the normal item drop rate. As a consequence, the rare item drop rate decreases greatly. The major benefit to Easy Mode is that it makes (normal) item farming less infuriating and allows Gil to be acquired much more easily and quickly than on the original PS3 (US) version of this game.
The PC version of this game runs quite smoothly on my current desktop configuration, which is pretty dated in this day and age. Most of the time, I get a constant 60 FPS while traveling along the world, but it drops to 30 FPS during a battle sequence. There are a few FPS drops when too much is going on in the battle (such as multiple castings of Ruinga at once), but for the most part, I get no frame drops anywhere else.
+ Exciting battle system utilizing many mechanics
+ Beautiful graphics and gorgeous scenery
+ Incredible soundtrack
+ Addition of Easy Mode
- Confusing story for first-time players
- Can be a deterrent to completionists due to arduous achievements

I rather enjoyed their other point-and-click game arc, Deponia, so I picked this game up and thought I'd give it a try.  While it was entertaining and the storyline was interesting enough (although a little predictable/foreseeable in areas) to keep me interested, what really appealed to me was the animated, comic style cut-scenes.  The puzzles are challenging enough and you have the option to skip them after several minutes, which appeals to both player types.  The point-and-click game play rarely has excessive long-walking-to-interact sequences, as it incorporates quick keys for interactive areas/travel, which is also appealing.  The gameplay graphics themselves are decent enough, probably a tad lower in quality than Deponia.  Replayability is probably minimal.
As with some of their other games, you can tell that English is not the first language for this game.  Unfortunately that does make dialogue a bit painful to listen to as sentences are overly structured and not quite "real".  There are even game play areas where translation was missed, so actions or words that are presented are in a different language.  The audio recordings for the two main characters, oddly, were the most difficult to listen to as it sounded robotic in extended conversations (which may be the case).
All in all, the game provides enough entertainment to justify purchasing and can provide you with a couple nights adventure.

is one of Daedalic Entertainments' "pretty good idea, done nonchalantly" games. Thus, it is a great potential story wrecked with many bugs, bad translation and a half-baked ending. I had really some major expectations from this game, with themes such as time travelling, environmental pollution and mass awareness but... No, it doesn't cut. This is not how it's done. This is not how it should be done. All this tension, all these ominous warnings, all this thrill and this action... and this ending? This is not a climax! Are you mocking me?
Sorry, my annoyance gets the best of me sometimes. It's storytelling time. Here, we have the elderly Norwegian bioengineer Bent Svensson who spent all his life working in the laboratory to produce energy from algae for the production of safe energy in hopes for a better future for the planet. After a breakdown that he suffers due to exhaustion, Bent is sent to retirement - the purgatory of a workaholic. He now lives in a small cabin in Norwegian Fjords, away from work, away from stress and away from responsibility. "Calm down, Bent" says his psychiatrist. "You are not responsible of saving the world".
Oh, she couldn't be more wrong! Bent Svensson's silent misery in retirement is suddenly interrupted by the visit of Fay, an odd young woman who claims that she time travelled from the future to find him. According to Fay, she comes from a future where the mother earth is at her limits and about to perish for good due to years of pollution, violent climate changes and toxicity. As part of an operation called 'the Phoenix Plan' she is sent to the past to prevent a disaster from happening to alter the course of time. "Only you, Bent" says Fay, "Only you can save the world!”
I know I was intrigued after the brief introduction to the game. The environmental theme, financial conspiracies, bioengineering, time travel, ecoterrorism... What else I can expect from a sci-fi environmental adventure? Right? Sadly there is a truckload of bugs and irritable mistakes within this game which will simmer down your enthusiasm. There is a common bug that makes your inventory unreachable, thus unable to complete an action to progress which triggers a couple of times, starting with the end of chapter 2. You should either ask Daedalic support for a save game where the bug isn't triggered, or pray you got plenty of your saves to try again.
The graphics are beautiful, this is already a trademark for Daedalic. Cinematic cut scenes are arranged in a comic-style manner where comic panels are presented with speech bubbles over characters, alongside voice acting. The comic style character artwork is a great idea of presentation, but my issue comes with the translation. As Daedalic being a German firm, I assume for original voice acting and script to be in German. So the English translation is... well, horrible. Word puns and scientific explanations are totally lost. There are many, many spelling errors within texts. The speaking animations do continue long after the voice acting is already stopped. With all these errors, it becomes really hard to get into mood and take either character or the story seriously.
About the gameplay itself, it is your basic point and click adventure. Item combinations do make sense, and nearly always they go along with an engineering view point. Lots of things to fix, physical reactions to mind, machines to manage and operate. Thus, it becomes obscure sometimes for you to be able to think of needed ways to progress. Puzzles themselves are very realistic, to a degree of - yet again, becoming obscure. I am usually very good at solving such puzzles without a walkthrough, but in the case of this specific game, I gave up. I personally think there is no one who would be able to solve all puzzles without the help of a walkthrough for this game.
I do not give up on games with good stories due to bugs, really. If I managed to play
to the end, and enjoyed every single moment of it, I'm positive bugs do not pull me down. My problem was the negligence in story persistency all together. Some characters made a shallow appearance and remain unvisited and unmentioned for the rest of the story, which prevents us from emphasizing with them altogether. Aside the character of Bent Svensson himself maybe, characters aren't more than some pictures with speech bubbles. There is no personality, no cause-effect relationship in their actions, no reasoning to their thoughts or dialogues. There were some character inconsistencies, like a trained radio operative like Fay being borderline clumsy, just to force the storyline in a predetermined course. Every disaster or twist in the storyline is foreseeable and determined, aside from a really anticlimactic ending.
All in all, this is a mediocre game with incredible potential wasted terribly. Am I sorry that I played this? No, not at all. Gave me some thinking to do on the theme itself of course. But nothing I wouldn't get from reading Greenpeace bulletin or National Geographic. On sci-fi terms, I'll keep reading H.G. Wells.

This game has been adding new game objectives, research, ships, orbital structures and planet types for a number of years now and it has turned it into a really great game. Each of the races and now factions within the races (Loyalist/Rebellion) offer higher defensive, offensive, economic or boosts to your culture (culture will overthrow enemy planets non violently) which gives a varying amount of replayability and playstyles. The learning curve for playing this game is low to mid, it doesn't take long to learn how to play.
In this game you'll be able to build up a massive fleet armada or split your fleet in two or three and raid the enemy's core planets after destroying their fleet. You'll be able to build starbases that can halt the advance of armadas until they are dealt with that also protect your trade empire from pirate raiders, jumping away from a starbase before it is destroyed seriously damages ships automatically.
This recent expansion breaks each of the three races into a loyalist and rebel faction. Each group has unique researchable abilities that offer different playstyles (defensive, offensive, culture) and each loyalist and rebel race receives a different Titan ship, a juggernaught of a ship that is 10 times larger than any capitol ship. These Titans can easily throw a pitched battle by special abilities that will either do area effect or very high single target damage, while others are disablement oriented, reducing the damage your fleet takes and reducing the firing rate of the enemy.
General overview of races:
TEC (Trade Emergency Coalition) - An economic powerhouse compared to the other races with quicker access to trade ports and higher research done that gives you extra credits anytime another faction buys something. The ships they field are considerably weaker though at end game research, as they have less fleet support abilities unless you have they loyalist capitol ship in the fleet to help reduce incoming damage. Their ships have high armor and their ultimate weapon is the Novalith Cannon, a weapon that sits in a planet's gravity well and regularly fires shots at enemy planets destroying all life on them and making them temporarily uncolonizable.
Advent - This race, in my opinion, fields the best armadas in the game. Their capitol ships and cruisers offer a lot of support abilities to spread damage to each ship, redirect damage from their own ships back to the enemy, area effect shield recharge all the while fielding a massive amount of fighters and bombers making the need for direct engagement with an enemy fleet purely optional. The flip side to this is they have a really weak economy and the worst ultimate weapon compared to the TEC or Vasari. Their ships have very high shields and their ultimate weapon shoots at enemy planets your planet's culture which is easily countered.
Vasari - A brutal alien race that terrorizes the galaxy thru subjegating and enslaving other races. They get a later start with building up their economy but their economy is pretty great at end game. Their units have a variety of disablement oriented abilities and a area effect hull repair and they tend to have higher hull values than the other races. Further research into missile technology allows you to bypass shields making them excellent against advent in a stand up fight. Their ultimate weapon is the Kostura cannon that will shoot at enemy planets damaging and disabling enemy structures in that planet's gravity well. If an enemy fleet is there, the fleet will be temporarily disabled and be unable to move or attack making it an invaluable tool to use while attacking with your fleet.
If you are a RTS fan or just enjoy viewing space warfare, I'd definetely recommend this game.

Marvel vs. Capcom: Infinite overall is a bit of a disappointment and in many ways feels like a lesser game than its predecessor Marvel vs. Capcom 3. Despite it's shortcomings however it still manages to offer some new things that do improve on the former.
The game straight off has a lack of flair in it's presentation. The UI in particular feels bare bones and lacks the kind of comic book aesthetic that MvC3 had which made it feel like a celebration of these two universes.
Presentation issues extend to the character models themselves which are very hit or miss. It's clear that many of the Marvel character designs are influenced by the MCU. However, some like Cap look particularly absurd. He looks like that bad Rob Liefeld drawing.
Couple that with the disappointing roster and its immediately underwhelming. It just doesn't feel like the Marvel universe is well represented without characters from the X-men (No Wolverine or Deadpool? Seriously?) or Fantastic Four. Even some of the characters on the Capcom side feel like odd choices. Spencer and Frank West could easily have been replaced by other characters like ameratasu from Okami, or maybe Felicia or Jon Talbane from Darksiders? Hell they could have picked one of the recent SSFV characters as well.
So how about the mechanics? Infinite does at least deliver some polished mechanics, though the decision to dial back teams to two on two matches instead of the three on three is probably going to disappoint some longtime fans. The game makes an effort to be accessible and even allows for things like auto combos which isn't a bad idea. A good player is still going to stomp a button masher and if you don't like these you can turn them off.
The story has some fun moments with certain character pairings. Hulk and Ryu offer some fun scenes. Others feel a bit mismatched. The plot itself is pretty limp but it does it's job of stringing together fights between certain characters.
Is MvC:Infinite worth checking out? It depends. If your a longtime fan and love MvC3, you will probably be underwhelmed by the content on offer, especially the roster. If however you just want to have a good time, experience a dumb but otherwise enjoyable single player story, it's worth checking out. The one caveat I would say is to wait for a sale. I bought the game and character pass while on sale for about $60. Otherwise the character pass would have been another $20 or in addition to the base game. Even then, I feel that I probably paid a bit too much.
If your looking to play online, I would caution you even further. I have not played online yet, but among the communities I belong to on Discord, it's said the online player base for MvC:I is dead.
Ultimately I would recommend this game, but do so only half heartedly. If I could give it a Maybe I would choose that.

This game is OK.  The redeeming aspect of it is the gameplay, which is as good as you can find right now for a space sim.  It's fun and engaging, and both fighter and strike suit modes offer different forms of gameplay gratification.  The graphics are pretty good (with exception to their implementation of intergalactic warp speed which is just a tacky visual distortion effect).  Production value on this game is quite limited, but this is an indie game from a small studio with more limited resources, so I can overlook things like poor voice acting and purely text-based mission briefs.  The video demonstrations of your weapon options from the loadout screen is a nice touch though.
Unfortunately, the story is worthless.  It's completely unengaging and doesn't do anything to build out any of the personalities the game tries to expose you to.  The plot and characters are all derivatives of implementations from classic games from this genre, but here they're combined into a rather formless blob that fails to really compel you to care about anything going on in the game's universe.  The missions are all artificially longer than they need to be, and only support checkpoints.  The difficulty is inconsistent from mission to mission, and the controls have a rather substantial learning curve due to them not using any previously established standard for flight controls in favor of developing one of their own.  Team AI also seems to be lacking and all too often it's up to you to destroy the overwhelming majority of enemies in order to ensure mission objectives are completed.
As a game that was inspired by the likes of the Elite series and Freelancer among others, the fact that this game has an exclusively linear mission schedule is a bit disappointing as well.  While overall SSZ has more bad things going on than good ones, by playing the game you actually spend more time engaged with what works in the game than what doesn't.  I feel an apt comparison for this game would be Square's Project Sylpheed, which has nearly identical flaws, but substantially worse flight mechanics.  SSZ would be best described as a better version of that game.

Simply not a good game. It lives off the name. They promised a successor to SM Alpha Centauri, and they did not deliver.
The game is plagued by various issues right now, the biggest one being the same terrible AI that already made Civ 5 unenjoyable in the long run.
This game feels like they wanted to start from Civ 5, but accidentally loaded an old build and started from there instead of the latest BNW build - and no one ever noticed. There's quite a few bugs in the game (such as AI offering you a trade, then rejecting your accepting of their terms due to not being good enough) that were in launch Civ 5 but are eliminated in the latest BNW build.
The AI can't fight 1 UPT. Fighting the AI is sort of a joke. Especially now that ranged units have been nerfed it is easier than ever to destroy even a same tech carpet of doom with a few units because the AI is so utterly incapable of any strategic movement.
The game is hardly balanced. Tier 4 affinity units are so much stronger than their contemporary tech tree parts, rushing these is mandatory in MP if you don't want to get taken out by a battlesuit slingshot by turn 80. Some wonders are god awful, some are incredibly powerful. Trade Routes trivialize the internal economy, the perfect way right now is spamming cities and getting massive production boosts through trade routes, as that allows you to build armies within a few turns. The "balancing penalty" for this is the massive pain of rerouting trade routes every turn.
Since the AI is so bad, any somewhat competitive player has to resort to multiplayer, which feels like 90s Gamespy. It's unstable, it takes forever (190 turn game we did earlier took 10 hours) due to crashes, random reloads and general delay between turns.
There are a few improvements, such as simplifying the unit experience system and Favor trading with the AI, but mostly it's just Civ 5 in space with more bugs and less balance.
This game is not worth a purchase even at a -30% discount. Wait until it goes GOTY or gets some greatly discounted bundle along with the first two expansions (ie wait for Christmas 2016), then it may be worth playing. Not guaranteed, since the two weaknesses (bad MP and bad AI) were not fixed during Civ 5's lifecycle either.
Firaxis is getting a pretty bad track record of releasing bad games, riding out their brand.

This is my second purchase of this game. It isn't a grand RPG of crafting and open world exploration but it has the best visual and immersive experience of Middle-Earth I've experienced in a game outside of LotRO (which suffers in detail due to age and size). There are some 35 - 40 unique named areas from the lore, from The Shire to Mordor, disappointingly only about half of the map locations can actually be visited (the rest only have descriptions and story elements) the ones that can be explored feel very real. The downside being that you can't tell which areas of the map are future locations or lore elements only and it can be very deceiving. If it was explained that not all map icons are future areas it wouldn't be such a shock. You are not playing the story of the novels but playing along with it and bumping into characters and witnessing events throughout. It's extremely well done the way the stories work together. The hubs and areas are populated with characters from the books and films and offer more lore, stories and perspectives than any other media I've seen. Gandalf even addresses the annoying (and obviously rediculous) myth that the Eagles could have carried Frodo to Mount Doom in detail through a lengthy optional conversation which I found amusing. Actually most of the conversations are optional but offer a surprising amount of back story all voiced by competent actors though not the voices from the films. In Rivendell alone conversations with Elrond's sons explained where their mother is and why, Legolas explains where Golem was between the Hobbit and the beginning of LotR and Gloin explains what Gimli was up to while he was taking back The Lonely Mountain with Thoren Oakenshield. I could go on for pages of what was revealed in one stop there alone from the at least 15 characters and they all have something different to say each time you revisit a location which you can chose to do at any point in the story. There is just a ton of very interesting story throughout the game and left up to the player to decide how much or little they experience of it.
The gameplay is action as one of the 3; ranger, dwarf and elf mage / healer each with their own 3 skill trees and about 6 or 8 abilities (once unlocked) beyond simple and strong attacks. The area's are mostly linear and at certain points in each level you may switch out among your 3 characters who level up together. I chose to play through with one character each time as the others can level and equip themselves without needing to worry if you so choose. It's not very technical and it gets repetitive but it's fun and while it can pose a challenge when overwhelmed there's still a very powerful feel to the combat. There is a ton of loot that drops with hidden areas each accessible by one of the 3 which inspires multiple plays. The gear grows at a healthy rate so each piece feels significant and you find quest items that add story and have you returning to NPC's and areas for discovery and accomplishments throughout. The gear also can drop with sockets that can be filled with gems that also drop. Equipment can be bought, repaired and sold at the different hubs and at points in the levels and the degredation rate is slow enough not to be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥while adding a needed money sink.
