TL;DR summary:
Lovely soundtrack
Beautiful 2D graphics
Creative level design
Wide range of characters
Unique atmosphere
A fair amount of lore
Lots of good boss fights
High replay value
More detailed review:
Soundtrack and graphics:
Everyone has his own taste of music and visual preferences, but I truly enjoyed every single tune in this game, I highly recommend getting the OST bundle (you can listen to it somewhere else first and decide for yourself).
I grew up with old consoles and don't mind 2D graphics at all, especially when they are well made.
You can tell the backrounds, sceneries and characters are drawn with love.
Characters and lore:
Some characters are funny ,some are mysterious, some can even be tragic and don't feel generic at all.
The lore is quite shallow at the beginning, but you will get the bigger picture as the story progresses. Hidden places and characters add a lot to the lore and make exploring feel rewarding.
Level design and replay value:
Everyone, who played Metroid/Castlevania aka Metroidvania games, knows why this is a huge factor. The game is not linear and lets you decide how you progress through the game. Once you have collected a special move the game lets you decide your next step. The possible routes keep on growing with every upgrade you find, which makes it feel like your very own adventure. There is a lot of hidden stuff everywhere and you will never feel "stuck".
All of these collectables, achievements and challenges (for example speedrunning the game) guarantee a high replay value and motivate you to start a new run and figure out faster routes, optimal setups for bosses etc.
Boss fights:
Most of the boss fights are pretty fun and feel balanced. There are also a lot of optional bosses, who provide upgrades or alternative routes to beat the game. If you ever get stuck on a boss though, you can always revisit old places, or explore a different area in order to gear up and beat that boss another time.
The ONLY thing I did not like:
The final boss fight was a bit too easy, but I also had all the upgrades.
I guess it will be a lot harder to beat in a speedrun.
Conclusion:
All of the above factors give this game an unique atmosphere and turn it into a gem, which will keep you entertained for a long time.
This is the best Metroidvania in my opinion, a must buy for every fan of the genre.

Strike Suit Zero starts out very strong, and hit me with a major nostalgia bomb when I first started playing it. It reminded me very strongly of several space games I had played over the years, most strongly the combat of Freelancer. The game's presentation is tight, with good visual effects and atmospheric sound design, but is plagued by poor optimization, resulting in increasingly intolerable frame stutter and worse, the video lagging behind my button inputs. In addition, over the course of only a handful of missions in the game total, the difficulty quickly spirals out of hand. The titular Strike Suit is difficult to employ properly, and oftentimes I found myself unable to take full advantage of its multi-target locking missiles. It is not unmanageable for the player to take down numerically superior enemy fighter groups, but multiple times the player is expected to protect flimsy friendly targets, some of which can be destroyed in seconds by withering hails of fire from the aforementioned enemies. If you hate escort missions as much as the average gamer does, as I do, Strike Suit Zero is liable to make you pop a blood vessel. I would be willing to forgive that, since I love space games that much- but here's where things get ugly. The frame stutter ultimately resulted in my being unable to finish the final level, and that's why I give this game a thumbs down. I was unable to finish Megabyte Punch simply because I wasn't good enough at the game, and that's not enough reason for me to dislike it, but the technical problems foisted on me by SSZ are simply unacceptable.

This game does quite a few things right. Mainly, I enjoy the endless fun of feeling superpowered and being able to switch between multiple abilities on the fly to deliver the most tactical and/or efficient beatdown. I think what I enjoy most, however, is the way it handles secondary objectives. In most other games, secondary objectives are either too hidden, or made too explicit. The former gives me an endless gut feeling that I've missed out on something the game has to offer. The latter makes them feel less 'secondary'.  Crysis just throws a green and a yellow blip on the map, letting you know "Hey this exists" without ever making you feel like missing it is really going to screw you over. Lump that philosophy in with the games quasi-sandbox nature, and we have a winner. Granted, the side objectives could afford to have a bit more incentive, but the framework is there, and it's nice. Overall, the game is slightly above average. It remains relevant as a milestone in graphics, but its shooting mechanics are middling. Despite that, it's still fairly easy to have fun, and that's kind of the point.

I'd consider this one of the more underrated Square Enix games. There is some nostalgia for me with this game as it was one of the first JRPG's I ever played and I fell in love. Trying to be as unbiased as possible I'll break down some of the pieces that make up the epic adventure.
The Story: The story is in many regards a typical cliched JRPG game. But it has some very interesting characters and villains as well as a few twists and turns that made it engaging for me.
Combat: The combat on the surface looks like the typical turn based JRPG. Digging deeper you will find that every fight and your entire journey can be played more strategically and on harder difficulties requires more skillful play. The class system has a ridiculous amount of depth and every play through I require a guide handy to know what path to follow for my characters. The BR system is not very friendly to new players and can easily punish you for grinding without understanding the system.
Graphics: The graphics are actually quite good for a game at it's time. Like a lot of JRPG's there are a lot small open areas with not a lot of filled environments. The overall game felt full of life to me so it was not something I noticed until playing many more JRPGs.
Conclusion: I'd give this game a 7/10 it has an incredible amount of depth in it's combat/character progression and crafting. The story was enjoyable and held my interests although it wasn't anything revolutionary, I still loved the characters and I became easily immersed. To be able to relax and enjoy the game for what it has to offer I would only play on easier difficulties as the BR system can be punishing if not played correctly. If you want to take the harder approach I'd recommend looking at guides to understand the BR system and how grinding effects your characters and BR.

If you like Super Smash Bros. Melee for its great number of fast, precise inputs, this game probably isn't for you.
Now that that's out of the way, this is a great game. It's known as a Smash clone, but that's largely because it's part of the same unexplored genre, commonly referred to as a platform fighter. Granted, it is a very specific genre, and one that Smash practically invented, and Rivals of Aether also borrows a few mechanics, but I digress. The game has numerous mechanics that make the game very easy to pick up, including a very well-made tutorial mode where your charming guide Orby explains everything about the game, from the difference between walking and running, to how to properly DI so you don't die to a sourspot back air, and more. However, don't think that you can finish the tutorial and then immediately start climbing the ladder on Ranked mode - the skill ceiling in this game is astonishing, and you can easily discern the difference between a scrub and a veteran. Newbies need not fear, however, as the game's active community, including Reddit and the official North American Discord group, are very welcoming and helpful. Or, if its online mode doesn't attract you, there's always the local mode, where you can play against up to three friends or AI opponents.
TL;DR This is a fun game. Buy it, and play it. Like, now.

It is hard to recommand this game since i gave up on getting through it for now.
I got 15 hours in and lost interest because of the very locked groups.
15 hours in and I am still not allowed to choose which group of characters I want to use, neither am I allowed to use a full team, and from what I gather it will take another 5 hours before I am actually allowed to play the game.
So at this point I am just giving up.
However it was 15 hours of ok fun, so for the price it is I would still recommend it, and who knows maybe I will finish it another time.
So now for how the game is:
Combat is quite well functioning, you control 1 character and the other characters are auto controlled, although you control which roles they should be in, you do this from preset roles you set before combat.
It is actually a good fun system which allows you to feel a lot of nice action while not having too much stress.
The camera however is a plague, it jumps all over the place, is too far zoomed in so you sometime miss important skill clues getting you killed because of it, and you got little control over how your other characters use their skillset in the class, so they don’t always makes the smartest moves.
The game is very linear, for the 15 hours I played I have done nothing but moving in one straight line without any ability to deviate from it.
The story is quite good, but it seems to be Very short for what it is, without all the “wasted time” I think the story could be summarized until now in less then 15 min. even so it is enjoyable, and it is Very awesomely voice acted.
I was quite impressed with the dialog, due to the names “snow, lightning, fang, hope, etc” I was expecting quite childish dialog but they were actually quite good and I found most dialog to be positive experiences ^^
The progression system is sadly leaving much to be desired; there isn’t much progression choice to speak of, again everything is linear and because the cap on each role is so low you max them all out so easily, that there is no choice to be made.
This is far from what we are used too in most ff games, but even so it does not take too much enjoyment away from the game.
So well, this is my experience with the first 15 hours of the game.
I would recommend it for the story and general feel; however, you need to know how linear everything is.

As a long time ArmA and Bohemia Interactive fan (beginning with the origianl Operation Flashpoint), I'd have to say that ArmA II OA is the pinnacle of the series for me. ArmA III is great with tons of innovation, but ArmA II holds a very special place in my heart when it comes to capturing modern military combat in a PC game. Yes it's not a true mil sim as that wouldn't be as much fun to play, but it does a great job of capturing realistic aspects of modern military combat. It is not a shooter on rails as so many big budget/big production military themed games are these days. The sheer variety of choice to accomplish a mission is virtually endless. The out of the box experience is fantastic, but the community added content is the main draw for me as a military game enthusiast. There is no other game series available to my knowledge that allows you to try out the various weapons and vehicles of virtually any modern military force.
Aside from the fantastic modern military mods, there are additional mods that let you fight zombies (DayZ), battle through WWII (still better than any other WWII themed game released thus far), or any number of Sci-Fi themed mods. The ArmA community is bar none the best I've ever encountered and shows no signs of slowing down with each release of the series.
If you love fantastic, emergent and dynamic gameplay with tons of choice and options ArmA 2 OA is where you should put your money.

This is one beautiful game. The people at Wild Hogs managed to pick up the saga and boost it into a higher level.  Lo Wang character development delivered us a much less cliched / parodied hero and offered a true origin story instead, where he makes a transition from being a cocky d*ck (pun intended) to a true warrior with a purpose.
The main story of the game runs in parallel along with a Japanese folkloric legend about the gods family drama, forbidden love and a mythical sword. This is an artistical accomplishment in itself only matched by the stunning visuals even by today's standards. You can enjoy beautiful scenery ranging from traditional temples to industrial settings and dungeons. The game runs on DX11.
Gameplay-wise it's wonderful. The melee system and the special attacks with the katana left me with a feeling only matched by bloodrushing suckers with melee Zero on BL2.  Then there are the guns. A nice variety of them, with alternative fire modes.
Weapons, magic powers and combat skills can be upgraded as you make progress.
The music and sound effects are awesome.
It's a fairly easy game. I would recommend playing it on hard mode the first time (hard is normal / insane is hard) because I think it will feel dull otherwise as soon as you aquire more powers and skills.
Definitely a must play game.

I've since put about 24 hours into it and I've got a much better handle on the quality of the actual game. It's definitely the best AssAss game I have played but I've only played the first, II and III previously. I was not a big fan, to say the least.
This really feels like a departure from the first three games, thematically and mechanically. If you didn't like the bulk of the previous games, the climbing, running, jumping, jumping off high things, the fairly rudimentary combat of Counter, Strike, Counter, Strike, there is still a LOT of that. This time the core AssAss experience is very well broken up by a very interesting, fun and surprisingly well realised naval game about piracy.
You aren't the chosen one, you are a pirate that through his ignorance and tunnel vision ends up embroiled in this existential battle. It's very easy to forget there are Assassins and Templars at all, you are reminded here and there, of course, but you are free to go back out to sea looking for islands and having ship battles.
If you really didn't get on with the other games, everything you didn't like is still present. If you like ships and the sea and piracy and didn't totally despise the AC experience you may or may not have already had, it's definitely worth a go.
Things to keep in mind.
Back up your saves regularly. I lost a good 15 hours of progress to a "damaged save. delete or start new game" which seems to have been fairly common.
The Deluxe and/or Season Pass issue. The basic edition of ACIV on steam is entirely complete if we are talking about genuine content, not piffle. You won't run into a part of the basic game where a DLC should be. The genuine content in the Deluxe and Season pass is unrelated to the main game. Different stories, different characters and started separately from the main menu. So I would say for most people, get the basic version, you aren't missing anything of note.

An unprecedentedly complex strategy game that has sucked an impressive amount of my time into its machinations.
As a fervent player of strategy games, I know more than most about the quality and standard of modern strategy games. Thus, it was to my pleasure to find that the gameplay of this game took me completely by surprise. When I purchased this game (due to a passing recommendation by a friend) I was expecting a mediocre 'annihilate-and-win' type of strategy game. What I found instead was a game that truly catered for just about any type of strategy player. One can win via a multiple of ways spanning from cultural domination to research to the common exterminate victory to name just a few. The cultural element of the game was a particularly impressive feature. As a strategist who prefers to punch my enemies into submission, I realized that the threat posed by a culturally superior race only too late in my first few games, where I believed I was winning the game through annihilation. Hence, unlike most strategy games, those who prefer to fortify and dig into their defences can technically still win the game without firing a single shot into the enemy ranks.
The resource accumilation and the ship upkeep features tends to keep most players in check, ensuring that no particular player can expand so quickly that he should overwhelm a coalition of players teaming up against him. This is a neat feature, as it forces players to think cunningly, lest too many of his enemies turn against him united in hate or paranoia.
Amongst other notable features, I also found the time taken to travel between planets to be a key feature of this game. I had not originally known that travelling between say... 4 planets would take a decent amount of time. This means by the time my main fleet arrives to defend a planet under siege, it has probably already been raised to the ground. Hence, players are forced to pre-empt incoming attacks or opt to divide and conquer.
The multiplayer experience is quite enjoyable as this game seems to have a relatively small but extremely friendly following. I was pleasantly surprised to find there are plenty of new players to the multiplayer experience as well as veterans who can teach a newcomer a thing or two.
Overall, Sins of a Solar Empire ranks very, very highly amongst my favourite strategy games. While the visuals of the game is not entirely awe-inspiring, it is very obvious the developers paid a significant portion of their time working on the mechanics of the game. I am happy to say that personally for me, their hard work has paid off and left a very satisfied player in their wake.
Overall Score: 9/10 - Extremely satisfying to play, would highly recommend.

When it comes to Stealth based Take'em Out Genre, Hitman franchise was always one of my favorites. Among all those favorites Hitman series remains most memorable. It's single player is bound to give you most satisfying single player experience and leaves you with lots of good memories of Assassinations, Be it a takedown on shadowy region with Hitman's proprietary steel wire, may be a stab in dense crowded place or Search and Eliminate each one of them at far away mafia's Mension.
GamePlay is of Classic Hitman theme, You play as a Toxiedo wearing bald guy, Sneaking and Hiding, cover to cover, all the way to your target, Just to take that Target out with varieties of means available to you or if you prefer you can blast through exposed in a lethal way. GamePlay provides both of those option to you. Then there are Traps to set through out your path for your victim. All depends upon what style you pick to play.
Comparing to previous Hitman titles there are good number of addition to gameplay, There are more guns and more pickable item's to carry, be it a statue or a tool or even a axe. you are even given a mission to reclaim your signature silver belles. Game also features tagging enemies for a quick swift takeout. On most easy difficulty Hitman can see the predicted route enemy will follow when searching or roaming, that gives you quite a bit of tactical advantage to plan your game play ahead. although feature is limited by hitman's Instinct level which deplete when you use it and depletes quite fast on higher difficulties.
The Character design of the game is Top class, Characters are almost real life like and have test of level they are in, As for  Hitman there are great number of costumes available to Him as disguise. Great for disppearing.
The Level design of the game is Excellent. There are Hidden air vents and path ways to sneak out, you can climb ladders, hang on ladges, Even water drainage to move undetected. That gives gameplay some degree of unlinearity. Almost all maps feature big beautiful Halls and rooms full of opportunities, However once the level is loaded you wont be seeing any loading screen further.
Game also feature great looking graphics. Gives you lot of Eye candy to see. Refined Engine features upgraded Directx 11 features and so the lighting in the game is superb. When out doors you see beautiful lens flares on days and car lights on nights. There are Darker shadows and flashy bright areas to explore. reflections are also lot nice, not so blocky. Therefore game demands a powerful system to play in.
AI on the characters is good however they wont do any thing apart form searching you out when sniffed and delivering few doubtful dialogues. later in the game you face difficult Swat Teams. They are capable of using cover system and flanking you out. However for most rewarding play sneaking past behind them is better option.
Pros
1] Great Looking graphics and characters
2] More guns and items to use
3] Non Linear gameplay
4] Good controls and Better Gunfights
5] Difficult contracts and pack lot of challenge at higher difficulties
6] Has replayabilty
Con
1] Demands a powerful system to play at max glory
2] Cpu heavy game.
3] Uses PhysX but not much Physics Glory.
Highly Recommended 9/10 Game.

Disappointed really, I’d expected it to have a similar feel to Civ 5, which it has, but its not really added enough to the formula for me.
The main disappointment for me though is the AI, it was pretty bad in Civ5 but I can forgive that as the depth of the game helped and it’s been out a while now too. They have made no improvements to it, in fact because the different factions are basically the same it feels even worse than Civ5.
I find myself not really playing it already, and that’s from someone with thousands of hours of play time invested in Civ games.

Graphics: It has great atmospheric graphics. While the graphic itself is not comparable with Crysis for example, it still is stunning how it all looks. The background, the ships and even the tracers of weapons.
Controls: The controls were really complicated. But after the first 2 missions you get used to it and experience how you can do anything you want. From fast barrel-roll dodging to sprint-dashing to an enemy sentry. You have to get used to the game in general.

Gameplay: It was absolutely lovely. Pure greatness. It's fast space-combat while you're in the middle of massive ships shooting at each other with an army of tiny ships flying around you. A great space dogfight.  I had a lot of fun playing this game, while the missions were quite monotone I still enjoyed every mission as it's kind of a 'kiting' game. Attack, when your armor is low fly away, get back when your armor is replenished. And honestly: It wasn't even boring.
As I got the Strike Suit, the gameplay completely changed! It was still a kiting game, but as soon as I had enough Flux (the power to be the Strike Suit and shoot with it) through my normal ship even as I had low armor I was still offensive with my Strike Suit because you had the opportunity to dash away and had a new fighting system.
I absolutely loved it.
Story: There are 5 different missions with every of them including something for the story.
You're a guy who has been sent in deep in space to join the forces of Earth while they're attempting to intercept the fleet. You're in an interstellar war: Earth's forces (U.N.E, United Nations of Earth) fighting against fearless enemies to protect a planet which is shortly before destruction.
You begin as a low-priority guard near Earth. You have an Apex Ship which can't transform into a Strike Suit yet.
After an attack, Earth's command say that the enemies are intending to end the war with one decisive strike.
They've amassed a colossal fleet and are bringing it to Earth.
The story is ok, it gets you fast into gameplay.
Music: It pumps you up, isn't obviously repetitive and fits with the atmosphere and the art of fighting.
Endings:
The game doesn't get any of it's promised updates, which is annoying and sad.
And all that for 19€. (18€ with the Director's Cut)
I would definetly play it again.
Looking forward on buying "Strike Suit Infinity" (6€) which apparently puts you in waves and waves of the decisive war.

I can't really speak as someone who's experienced with fighting games (I almost exclusively play this genre for the single-player, unintuitive as it may sound), but from a gameplay standpoint, Marvel vs. Capcom: Infinite is a lot of fun, and it runs well, too. There are some good ideas in the story mode, too, like the inclusion of mooks as opponents. And, unlike previous games in the Marvel vs. Capcom series, this game has an actual universal tutorial and a player vs. CPU single match mode.
But it's hard to ignore the game's faults. The art direction is bland and uninspired, especially after the vibrant Marvel vs. Capcom 3, the character interactions in the story mode feel forced, the BS character buffs that plague fighting game single-player modes so often pop up way too earlier, and the game's final boss is just awful. And that's ignoring the elephant in the room of the lack of X-Men and Fantastic Four characters, though they've been rumored to be coming as DLC for quite some time now.
It's a very fun game, but understand that it'll be a letdown some in relatively minor but hard-to-ignore ways.

Civilization: Beyond Earth is basically like a future version of Civ 5 without any expansions. It's quite sad that they couldn't build upon the incredible features of Civ 5 Complete. Instead they stripped a lot of what made Civ 5 incredible so they can add it back into the future expansions.
That being said the game is kind of fun, but it can get confusing. The victory conditions are not visually presented through the tech tree. Even looking through the Civilpedia I could only find a vague explanation for how to achieve a few of the victories. When you do win a game, it feels incredibly underwhelming. They don't show you any stats, scores, or graphs of any kind after you finish out a game so it feels like you win for nothing. However, they do have stats of your past games through the main menu.
The civilizations (or sponsors) are really not anything to get excited about. They all seem to have the same personality. The only thing distinguishing them is their colors and their unique looking leaders. I like the improvements they've done with the diplomatic actions. There is one thing I don't like about diplomatic trading though. When trading your resources for other civs' favors, its obvious that the favors are less valuable than the resources you trade. For Instance, If you give 100 energy (gold) to a civ in exchange for a favor, when you come back to redeem that favor you can only get like 90 energy. That makes no sense economically. If anything they should give you interest for the resources you gave to them.
The game isn't all bad, though. The worlds are fun to explore and the early game proves to be very interesting as you try to weave your way through the vast hordes of aliens. But there were no amazing aha moments. I never got as into my games as I did in civilization 5. Beyond Earth is missing that pizazz that Civ 5 possesses. Sure, you get to explore alien planets with a civilization that you get to customize, but the game is basically a barebones futuristic Civ 5.
If you do not own any Civilization game I recommend buying Civilization 5. The game, along with it's expansions, is incredibly well done and will leave you wanting more after every match you play. Beyond Earth is not the same. At its current state It's fun for awhile, but its replay value is nowhere near that of Civ 5.
Do I recommend this game at it's current price ($50 at the time of this review)? No.
However, if you can find this game at a largely discounted price I think your purchase will be worth it. I just don't think this game justifies $50. After 2 years or so I can see this game being just as fun as its predecessor, but it's unfortunate I'll have to pay an additional $60 for it to be on par with Civ 5.
Note: I think it would be awesome if Civ: Beyond Earth allowed you to continue playing as your civ from Civilization 5 if you got a science victory, kind of like how college sport games allow you to export your character into the professional league games.

I am a huge fan of the LOTR universe, so I got excited when they said that there will be a new game about it. to buy the game and. When I finally aquired the game, I dove into the world of Tolkien once more. And I was fairly happy with the results that I've found.
First of all let me say that the world of LOTR "war in the north" is a delicous a mish mash from many of Tolkiens LOTR's resorces. Like the books, movies, cartoon animations as well as the endless Imagination of snowblind studio. Which makes a woundful effort in blending the game into character with the rest of the other stories without feeling stragnly out of place. The visuals are just amazing and the dialog is heroic and thoughtful.
The events of  LOTR "war in the north" characters were invented, well crafted, and detailed by the grandfather of modern fantasy Tolkien. You play either one of three main characters: the female elf lore master Andriel " the sorceress ", the dwarf warrior Farin "the warrior tank", and a human Dúnedain ranger Eradan "the roge". In the beging the trio are seen walking into the Prancing Pony in  the city of bree, heading to a table were Aragorn is sitting. They inform him that the Shire Guard at San Ford was attacked and that the Rangers have suffered a great loss. After the raid a Ringwraith mets with a man of great malice and power called Agandaur. He tells the Ringwraith that he had done as Sauron commanded and he has started gathering the Orcs of the north at the old ruins of Fornost. Farin questions why the enemy would build up a force against the Shire and Aragorn replies that a hobbit with a great burden is on the move to Bree. He asks them to help him keep the Hobbit safe by thwarting the enemies preparations at Fornost. And so begins your adventure.
The game play is a decent standard type of action RPG . Nothing ground braking INTERSTELLER MECHANICES THAT CHANGES THE GAMING WORLD!!! or anything like that. Nevertheless, still decent.
All three characters have mele and range attacks when battlling the endless hordes of orcs, cave trolls and goblins. There is also a combo system which makes the game more responsive. When a yellow bar shows on an enemy's head you get a chance to do a critical strike chope some heads off and gaining more XP.
The pacing of the game is done well. However, there are too many mounted cressbows sequences
that kinda feels repetitive to a point.
On the other hand the game has a good co-op game play of three players. Which changed the expreance of the game altogether. You and 2 more of your friends can jon forces and lead the attack on the eeevil orc meness. And saving the hobbits for certain dooooooooom.

Overall, the game is a wonderful piece of art that shouldn't be overlooked.

TLR feels like a classic Square RPG between the Final Fantasy 6 and 7 era; at least as far as story and world goes. Take a completely fantastical storyline, a slightly irritating yet identifiable character, a supporting cast of twisted backstories and unusual concepts, and throw in some menu-based face smashing with just enough strategy to keep you scratching your head. It's a game that's 50% story and 50% bursts of strategic challenge in the form of difficult boss fights.
My only complaint is that, like any typical CRPG-like, the grind through the dungeons can get tiring, but the story is well worth it.
The system is unique, favoring macro strategy over micro. Your control over your party is limited to who you attack and how, but the choice of which specific attacks, battle order, and timing comes down to the AI and stats. This sounds boring but is actually engaging and unique
In the end TLR feels like a lovechild of Tactics, Final Fantasy 6 and 7, and Ogre Battle. Not a bad thing.

I love Heathstone and I love the physical Magic. I put money into these games like shoveling coal into a coalfire. I don't regret it because I'm gonna have fun with these games for years to come.
The Duels of the Planeswalker series was meant to be the casual digital alternative to physical Magic. You were given exciting premade decks which you could alter slightly to make them play different everytime. I gladly played every game up until DotP 2014. I didn't mind the technical bugs since the gameplay was solid. DotP 2015 was a aweful disaster which I skipped all together because of the missing 2HG mode.
Magic Duels Origins came out of nowhere and when I heard that they were planning to make the MtG Alternative to Hearthstone I hoped for a long term supported title with solid gameplay. Earning gold and buying boosters with that gold or real money sounded like an acceptable system which also works fine in Hearthstone.
So how is it? At first let's just imagine this game was bug free. No crashes, no disconnects. Because these things will most likely be fixed soon (hopefully).
Campaign:
I'll ignore the campaign since it always was imho the least important feature of DotP games.
The card collection:
Just as in Hearthstone you have a starting card collection which you can increase with boosters over time. I was hoping to see full existing MtG sets like the 10th edition. But instead we get the Origins edition which contains some of the most boring and useless common cards of MtG. So be prepared because your first decks will be very frustrating to play.
The Deckbuilder:
Since you have a pool of cards instead of premade decks you can create any type of decks you like with the deckbuilder. I think this is one of the best new features in the game. It let's you easily filter/sort through your pool of cards. You can also select a custom cover and name your new deck.
The actual gameplay:
The targeting system is very flimsy. It gives you no response if you selected a target or not. This makes selecting multipe targets quite difficult. Also why can't I sort my hand cards by manacost anymore? And where has the chat gone? You can't even chat with your teammate in 2HG! Appart from these issues the basic gameplay is ok. They even improved the UI by making it more compact and using less space.
Conclusion:
Will I invest real money into this game? No, at least not yet. I will wait and see if they fix the major issues in the coming months. The best thing about this game is the fact that you can try it out for free.

Beta Reveiw
Well boys and girls put down your Nintendo controllers and start up your PCs because Smash Brothers is being replaced.
I know what you're thinking.  How can I make such a bold statement? Smash is the best. Espescially Melee! I can agree they are great games but from a competitive veiwpoint let me explain why Rivals even while in beta has more potential.
Blast Zone Fighters as I call them are fighting games that instead of a health bar that must be drained, you must knock your oppent far enough off screen that they reach a Blast Zone losing a Stock or Life. Super Smash Brothers being the first of this style. Now we have Rivals of Aether. I'm going to  cover many  aspects of what makes a these and other fighting games great and/or stand out.
Music- Rivals has a Amazing soundtrack that perfectly matches the high speed gameplay. Every stage being themed after one of the Four elements. Just listen to some of the tracks
Control- Perfect, the only word that will suffice. This game takes some melee movement tec wave dashes and landings and simplifys the imputs so there is not specific timing for every character. You hit jump, parry, and left or right as the same time. So missing a input that messes up your posittioning is very unlikely. Dashing and Dash danceing is very responsive and feels great. The jump arc of every character is very managable and easy to familiarize yourself with. Even when you are hit you have a great deal of control of how you tumble through the air while in hitstun. This is a game that a person can never blame the controls. No  " I missed an L-cancle or my wave dash didnt work"  those comments will not be true in this game.
Level design done right- There are two versions of every stage. Rivals has no stages with unfair elements like transitions or moving platforms when the basic stages are being used.(But now it has 2 with moving plat forms only one being a little annoying :note made 06/09/17) Every stage has a silly more casual version called Aether. Every stage has very different platform placement so none of them feel the same.
The Rivals- Every character in this game has a unique power that their move set is based around. Zetterburn can set you on fire doing damage over time, while also being able to absorb it off of his opponent to strengthen his strong attacks, this games name for smash attacks. Kragg on the other hand can summon a rock pillar to change the stages geometry or grab a boulder to throw at you that will remain on stage if it is not destroyed. Every character has something different they bring to the table and it is fun to experiment.
Whiff lag- If you miss an attack in this game you are subject to more lag or "The amount of time before you can begin a new action or retake full control" This leads to players that just throw out attacks being punished and players who plan out there attacks being rewarded with a True combo or DI (Directional Imput) dependent combo or "String".
I beleive tha Rivals has great potential as a competitve game. The game even has a built in Tournement mode that allows you to ban stages and set the amount of matches in a set. If you love Smash bros. Just pick this game up you won't regret it.
Full release addtions
Online- The online fuctionallity of this game much like many fighting games is not the best. Playing a person out of your reagion is almost pointless due to high pings. Low ping matches have different problem that can only be called stuttering. The match will randomly slowdown for 1 to 3 seconds causing input drops. This means all input. In a game that is DI dependent to survive strong hits this stuttering will be the cause of many deaths. The style of random matchmaking is also not a welcome sight. you will repeatedly meet the same players causing a staleness if the matches are one sided in your favor or the opponents.
Rebalanceing- the characters have mostly been worked out other than, some small changes that I dont care for ( the shrinking of Zetterburn Down Str's 1st hitbox for one example) The character now feel very balanced so I never feel like I lost to a character rather than the player. This is something that comes from experiance so some people may disagree.
Conclusion- One of the strongest entries in fighting games that I have played in a long time base solely on the style, combo structure,match interactions and overall design. As a competitive fighter this gets a 10/10

A terrible, terrible game, and a massive disappointment.
X games are always rough on release, filled with bugs and all kinds of problems. But at the core, they offer a deep and rewarding space sim sandbox experience. The clunky UI and sheer scope of the game overwhelms most first time players. But when you finally overcome all obstacles, you're in for a real treat which might consume most of your social life. With all that in mind, i pre-ordered this game. It was supposed to be a PC exclusive, hardcore space sim. It was made by seasoned developers with years of experience under their belts. And man, look at those graphics! What could go wrong here?
Pretty much everything.
X Rebirth is pretty. The space cities look amazig, they're richly detailed, there's plenty of space ship traffic around them, and the game looks really nice at first glance. The backdrops are simply stunning. Every sector has its own unique look and feel. It's by far the best looking space game to date. And that's the end of the positives.
The interface has been overhauled, supposedly, to be more accessible. In reality, we get something both newcomers and old time veterans will have hard time getting used to. The UI is once again unintuitive and badly thought out. Half of the stuff you could do in previous X games has been thrown out of the window. There's no radar. The world map is unreadable. You can't give out basic orders to ships under your command. You can't tell if they're moving or not. You can't see their destination, speed etc... But if that's not enough, you can't even switch between your targets with the keyboard! In a god damn space sim! You can't rebind most of the keys either. And every time you want to check something on your ship's computer (the main UI window), you're forced to watch an annoying animation.
The game is filled with pointless minigames. There's a minigame for pretty much everything you do. From flying through space highways or walking through space stations (in search for random containers filled with loot and free credits), to gathering collectible points for shop discounts or scanning your nearest vicinity for random junk floating around in space. They're pointless, tedious and repetitive. And they definitely don't belong in a space sim.
You can now walk freely inside the space stations. A nice idea - in theory, but in this case it's just another chore this game didn't need. There are 3 different space station layouts. Do i need to say they get old pretty fast? And they're filled with butt-ugly, lifeless NPCs, which are nothing more than a visual representation of the trading/ship managment UI. The voice acting is as bad as you'd expect from Egosoft, except, it's actually even worse. Prepare to listen to your main protagonist repeat the same lines over and over again, making the infamous Bethesda "arrow in the knee" or "i saw a mudcrab the other day" lines look fresh and original.
The game world is small. That's the cost you have to pay for those pretty graphics. And the persistent, reactive world we were promissed was a lie. Rebirth's world is filled with constant traffic. There are hundreds of ships, large and small, moving through space. But most of them are there just for show. For example, hardly anything leaves of enters the highways. So, in reality, the world is mostly filled with dummy props and cool looking graphical effects.
Oh, and there are bugs. Serious, gamebreaking bugs that make you lose hours of gameplay. The AI behaves in ridiculous ways... when it's not completely idle. That's especially annoying if it happens to one of your ships.
The game is bad, and don't hope it will ever improve. It's broken at its very core. No ammount of patches and mods will undo 7 years of bad design and pointless features. Seriously, if you're a fan, stick to X3 and its expansions, if not, get X3: TC or AP. Don't waste your money on this steaming pile of fertilizer like i did. I bought it so you don't have to.

I can't tell. At some points in this game, I really enjoy it. Now, with Shadows over Innistrad out, I was happy to be able to play with the new cards, not only in that set, but also Oath of the Gatewatch.
However, there were three very notable and re-occuring problems that have made me absolutely livid:
This is probably the least sensical problem.
There have been many times where I'd lose gold after I won a match. Before the match, I had 105 gold. Once I won the match, I earned 15 gold, adding to my previous number of... 45 gold, netting me 60 gold. This happened in the game after that, where, once I won, I had 5 gold, and because I won, my total became 20 gold.
I wasn't able to get a screenshot, unfortunately. I guess you'll have to take my word for it. It also hasn't happened in a couple days, so it may have been a four-time occurance (again, I'm sorry for not having any before/after screenshots).
For the love of god, DO NOT PRESS 'A' WHEN IT ASKS TO GIVE THEM FEEDBACK.
Every time I would want to give feedback, the game would blur out, and nothing would happen. I'd have to shut down the game, and then restart, making sure NOT to press 'A' when it asks for feedback.
This is a problem you may have seen. If you want a great explanation for what the problem is, check out
.
Here's the quick and dirty: the spell priority and auto-phase completion does not function properly.
What happens is the game auto-ends your main phase if you don't have a sorcery-speed spell in your hand (anything that isn't an instant, is a land, or isn't a spell with Flash). This function is probably in the game to speed up turns.
However, multiple times in my games, my main phase would end when I could've done something I'd like to do, particularly with Abbot of Keral Keep's ability. When he enters the battlefield, you exile the top card of your library. You may play that card, but only for this turn. The game does not recognize Abbot's exiled card as part of the game, and if, say, it's the only available spell you can play and it has sorcery-speed, the game goes through your phases, ending your turn without your consent, not allowing you to play that spell.
I lost a game just an hour ago because of this. I was getting pretty beaten by a deck with a lot of elves. I was at 7 life, and they were at 20. However, I was given a gift: I played Abbot, exiling a Languish (all creatures get -4/-4 until end of turn). It was exactly what I needed.
What happened was, because I played my land for the turn AND I didn't have any sorcery-speed spells in my hand, the game went straight to my end phase, EVEN THOUGH I had the mana to play Languish.
Would've I won the game if I played it? Maybe not, but I had a hand full of end-game spells, while they only had a few cards in hand.

I checked it out since I was curious to see what the Final Fantasy series looked like these days, having stopped at the SNES era. I was also curious to see if the bad reviews were founded: I thought that at worst it would a nice "autopilot" pass-time, something to go through without torturing my brain too much for when I'm tired.
... Unfortunately, the negative reviews were founded. I mean, the graphics are great and I was genuinely intrigued to see how the story would end, but that about ends the positive points. The game as a whole is a linear borefest with a combat system that invites you to spam a single button, except for the occasional super-hard fight. The combat and crafting mechanics are intentionally obscured, and the "paradigm shift" mechanic didn't strike me as very fun. Give me back my turn-based FF combat please.
Even the much-touted "part when it opens up and becomes real Final Fantasy" i.e. chapter 11 consists of a green plain with some scattered generic fetch quests. And then the game becomes a corridor again. I distinctly remember having an impression of epic freedom while I roamed the world in an airship in SNES Final Fantasy RPGs, not so in this game.
If only the story was well-delivered. Unfortunately most of the time the party has no clue of where they are going or why, and the characters are not very interesting. In the end I made it to chapter 11 to see if it would get better, and then I was so bored that I decided to watch the rest of the cutscenes on Youtube. I'm glad I did. The end cinematic is pretty cool but not worth slogging through the whole game.
There are two sequels, XIII-2 and XIII-3, but honestly I'm not even interested in watching their stories. I'll go play some actual good classic JRPGs I missed or watch a real movie instead.

This is one beautiful game. The people at Wild Hogs managed to pick up the saga and boost it into a higher level.  Lo Wang character development delivered us a much less cliched / parodied hero and offered a true origin story instead, where he makes a transition from being a cocky d*ck (pun intended) to a true warrior with a purpose.
The main story of the game runs in parallel along with a Japanese folkloric legend about the gods family drama, forbidden love and a mythical sword. This is an artistical accomplishment in itself only matched by the stunning visuals even by today's standards. You can enjoy beautiful scenery ranging from traditional temples to industrial settings and dungeons. The game runs on DX11.
Gameplay-wise it's wonderful. The melee system and the special attacks with the katana left me with a feeling only matched by bloodrushing suckers with melee Zero on BL2.  Then there are the guns. A nice variety of them, with alternative fire modes.
Weapons, magic powers and combat skills can be upgraded as you make progress.
The music and sound effects are awesome.
It's a fairly easy game. I would recommend playing it on hard mode the first time (hard is normal / insane is hard) because I think it will feel dull otherwise as soon as you aquire more powers and skills.
Definitely a must play game.

Yes, this title is everything good you expect from Final Fantasy: Staggering production values, an interesting iteration on the battle system, a final battle against a thingamabob that classes in the "deity" range (that's NOT a spoiler - that's Final Fantasy), "Crowning Moment of Awesome" FMVs...you get the idea.
I mean, you really can't go wrong with having Liara T'Soni leading a ragtag band of adventurers that includes a tougher, tattooed callback to both Yuna and Rinoa.
It's a very good game, but it doesn't cross the threshold of being a great game.
To start with, the soundtrack IS nice, but it's also pretty forgettable. The games scored by Nobuo Uemtasu have all had wonderful melodic themes for different areas and characters, themes that stick with you for over a decade. That tradition seems to have been slipping (quickly) since the days of "Final Fantasy X."
Another thing that seems to be wanting is the handling of the game's emotional core. "Final Fantasy" is about living a story, and for that to be good, you have to be emotionally invested in the characters. While "XIII" is noticeably better than "XII" in the department of characters that naturally develop a story, it still doesn't rise to the very high bars set by "VII," "VIII," and "IX." Part of the problem seems to be the seeping in of melodrama and semi-awkward "motivational speech" monologues. This kind of almost over-the-top characterization is helpful in cartoony or sprite-based games, where the onscreen ability to emote is limited. However, in a much more realistic game, it seems awkward and oversold. Some of the really dramatic moments ARE handled well (and even wrenchingly), but there are plenty of others which get too syrupy.
Lastly, the game suffers from an inconsistency problem. "XIII" establishes very early - through basic gameplay, tutorials, linear level design, and so on - that it's basically holding your hand through everything. The difficulty curve is shallow. You spend a lot of time being able to explicitly see just how far your characters can develop for any given area.
...and then the game opens up, and starts presenting abrupt (and mountainous) difficulty spikes. These spikes don't convey a sense of your party being underdeveloped, because they are intermittent. This is especially bad at the deep endgame, where a party that was basically fine in the face of the increasing difficulty is suddenly inadequate for the (very tough) penultimate battle.
This is all compounded by an equipment upgrade system that is both incredibly vague and very slow: You can buy upgrade items, but money is very hard to come by. You get upgrade items as loot, but loot drops at a slow rate - and most of it is pretty mediocre.
Further aggravating the problem is that "XIII" DOES provide opportunities to get really good equipment and character development, but those opportunities are presented through Cieth Stone missions. The missions occur at the point in the game where your character progression cost goes up exponentially, and they don't telegraph a sense of being all that important. (The missions you're likely to go on are the low-level ones - of which there are plenty - and they mostly amount to a battle against a marginally tougher enemy that results in marginally better rewards.) The problematic message from this is that you're not really gaining anything from doing missions that you wouldn't otherwise, so you might as well move on. As such, you miss out on the real benefits of the mission system. It takes too long to see any real rewards.
You could say that this is also a pacing issue.
The flaws aren't fatal, though. "Final Fantasy XIII" is still pretty dang cool, and easily consumes tens upon tens of hours. Optimizing your battle tactics is a loop that manages to remain engaging most of the time, and the gameworld is intriguingly mysterious. "XIII" isn't the brightest crystal in the series, but it's a very long way from just being some dumb rock.

I will write a more formal review later. (It probably lists this as a review using a key as well. Because I went through the process to get a Steam version of my boxed physical copy of the original game that I bought 6 years ago in order to get B:R for free Thanks Valve for invalidating the opinions of anyone who doesn't buy games in the way that benefits really only you. :Read> More money from the portion of every sale made on Steam)
But let's get a few things straight.
The game doesn't have graphics options, but it doesn't really need the ones the original had. If you could run the original game, which any decent modern card can. Then you won't have an issue running the game. In my experience the game doesn't run catastrophically worse in any way compared to the original in side by side tests.
The graphics options in the original made sense for the time. They really don't today for a game that is largely the same at it's core. You really don't need those options anyway unless you are hurting for performance, which really shouldn't happen with any recent decent GPU. And even if you were, based on how the game looks, turning off shadow maps (Game only had an on/off switch), texture quality,model complexity,or high quality post processing and shaders (This is stuff that would've made a difference on the hardware from the time it came out.) more than likely would not make that huge of a difference in the same way on modern hardware. They were very basic things that were performance intensive in 2009. Not today.
It'd need different options, or just in general better optimization for low end hardware.
The lack of sound channel options and lack of EAX support from in the menu is baffling however. No need to remove those.  (Generally if you are not going to put the option in the menu to change the channel configuration, you need to set it up to detect the config from Windows and set it from there. IE: Windows is set to 7.1 sound. So the game detects that. Sets 7.1)I can understand the disdain for that and the mouse not being improved. The audio in general sounds worse however compared the original game. Interesting considering how much more space the game eats in constrast to original.
Mouse accelleration should've been fixed, but it's there in the original. And it's not like the original isn't buggy as well or known and prone to crash. FFS if you have W7 or later, you can't even boot the game without a newer version of OAL installed that isn't even available from Creative's website or included with any version of the game. Apparently the physics/animation are locked to 30FPS in the original game too, but I don't recall noticing.
Just look at the list of issues with the original release. And those are just the well documented ones.
Really, I have yet to have a single issue in B:R that didn't exist in the original. In my experience it's been less problematic than the original so far aside from having to fix the sound. And it looks visually much much better aside from the very toned down specular lighting component in favor of one less harsh, less aliased and closer to looking more like physically based lighting. The rest of the lighting for the game has been completely rebaked and looks much nicer. The textures have been redone look a lot nicer. Though there are many that werne't retouched and stick out a bit more and doesn't look as nice.
If you have stuttering issues, dont’ use in game vsync. Lock it to 60FPS using RTSS , set pre-rendered frames to 2 and force Vsync externally from drivers. Very few games these days get frame pacing and Vsync totally correct without having to fix it from outside the game.

I tried really hard to give this game a fair shake, but I just can't do it. The stealth/instinct systems are just hilariously broken. Disguises are all but useless because the enemies who have access to the areas you need to get into are the ones who will see right through it. Sometimes there's a janitor disguise that will help, but a lot of the time there isn't. I can see what they were going for with the enemies-you-are-diguised-as-will-spot-you-if-you-come-too-close thing, and it's not actually a bad idea, but they define 'too close' way too ♥♥♥♥ing broadly. You will draw aggro from pretty much every guard who has line-of-sight on you, no matter how far away they are. It should be more like 'arm's length or doing something suspicious'. Their ability to see your face should also be a factor. As-is, there are a lot of areas that are straight-up impossible to get through without using Instinct, and Instinct burns out insanely quickly and opportunities to replenish it are very limited.
On the flip side, if you leave their line of sight before they figure out you're not one of them, they immediately forget you exist, no matter how hilariously suspicious the way you vanished is. In one room, I made my way through under a police officer's watchful eye by ducking behind a piece of cover whenever his suspicion meter grew too high. In previous Hitman games, that kind of weird behavior would have prompted an immediate spike in suspicion. In this game, it causes a complete reset. Likewise, if you're dealing with someone who isn't disguised like you, you're basically invisible unless you draw an inappropriate weapon or otherwise blow your own cover. This is true even when the person in question really should be able to spot a ringer: in the very first level, the anal retentive head of security, who handpicked all of the guards, won't detect you if you disguise yourself as one of the guards. If you disguise yourself as the chef - the only chef anywhere on the property, who is clearly several sizes larger than you - he gets on the radio and demands to know who didn't tell him about the new chef's assistant. It's ridiculous.

I'm generally not a fan of the point-and-click puzzle genre, and this game is a good example of why that is. The user interface is clunky (you have to click-and-hold on everything to get a menu, although the menu often has only one item, or two useless items like "Look at" which causes your character to make a useless comment, or "Use" which often makes the character say something like "nah, I don't want to use that right now".) You constantly have to solve puzzles with non-obvious solutions, even though there might be an obvious solution. Example: you need a paddle for a "boat" at some point. You're not allowed to use the broom that's sitting right there in the background; instead you have to combine a rope with a dustpan in your inventory and then combine dustpan-with-rope with a metal rod. The metal rod itself was part of a stairway's normal-looking metal handrail, and somehow you can rip it off from the rest of the handrail. And, there's a large quantity of really boring dialogue.
It's a pretty good game.

Yet another magestic arrow from Sid Meier in his quiver of genius.  This game, contrary to popular belief, is an absolute joy to play.  Granted, it isn't perfect; Civilization seldom is at first release.  And yes, also granted, DLC will most likely be released to fix the stunts people are so hurt by and said DLC will most likely cost in the region of £10-15 but for a game like this why wouldn't you spend that much on improving it?
I have played through this game, only on the Mac it must be noted, in all manners possible already.  I have played the blood-thirsty tyrant, massacring aliens and colonies alike, I have played the middle path trying to find common ground between alien and human and I have played the evolutionary tactic; embracing the new ways and traditions and becoming something not quite human anymore.  Each one came with new surprises for me, and I'm sure I could play them through exactly the same again and get the same result just through a completely new way.  This is what I love about this game; the choices.  It constantly wants you to be involved, it isn't nagging.  If you don't want to be as involved as it asks of you then, quite simply, don't play this.  The choices are not inconsequential; just because the short term effect may not be felt, +1 health in the long run does plenty good to your Civ, particularly if you're planning on expansion.  The new choices system and upgrade system fixes the costly and wasteful system found in Civ 5, whereby you could invest heavily in an army and then 10 turns later find it completely obsolete unless you spend thousands and thousands of gold in upgrading your army.  The world is fantastic, and the way the world is introduced to you is brilliant.
Diplomacy?  This game isn't about diplomacy.  Granted, the AI could be a little more threatening but this isn't Civ V; in Beyond Earth you are not alone, there is so much more to do than worry about what the AI are doing.  This is a game about exploration; you are new people on a new planet starting again, why would you concentrate on others?  Certainly, besides, by the end the AI are more involved; threatening you for your choice of affinity, accusing you of betraying humanity or comitting injustice on the new, intelligent planet.  This is as it should be; this is as it would be.  If you want a game with diplomacy then 'Democracy 3' is just a search bar away.
Civilization Beyond Earth is something completely new to the franchise, it is not just a Civ V DLC nor does it feel like one.  To play this game you have to feel the situation, not expect to be thrown back in time but to be thrown forward.  With the previous Civilization games you knew what there was to look forward to; "I'm going to nuke you at the next chance", "you wait until I get XCOM Squads!".  In this?  God knows what will happen.  You can't even tell at the beginning what kind of Civilization you're going to build, let alone if it will work.  Beyond Earth is not a race for supremacy, it's a race to find humanity, to find what was lost in all the other Civilization games on the way, to find a new way to pay just £30 and get endless entertainment.  My final advice; ignore the negative reviews.  The key to understanding this game is to not expect a Civilization game like ever before, the key is to expect something that is truly Beyond Earth.

One of my favourite games. Three totally different factions fight endless interstellar war. Normal humans focus on economy, lots of ships and a lot of punch. Aliens have advanced phase technology and they can strip planets bare, fleeing from unknown enemy. Psi-humans focus on lasers, shields and mind over matter.
I've played all factions, but my favourite are Vasari Loyalists. With them I'm able to play Battlestar Galactica style games on highest difficulty, where I'm quickly conquered and remnants of my fleet (VL can survive with no planets as long as you have necessary techs and a Titan-class ship) have to fly from one planet to another to escape their destruction, regroup and crush their enemies.
In some games I was left with only one, badly damaged Vorastra Titan and no other ships and after many hours of mostly running away from my enemies, finally crush them :) With right techs, Vorastra has the ability to "construct" ships in deep space, so as long as you can find resources, you can rebuild your fleet.
Other factions are fun too. Advent with their psi-technology was my favourite faction until Rebellion expansion, which introduced Titan-class ships and Vasari Loyalists enabled BSG-style games. Try to survive.

Heh... Well, it's been nearly a year, and ever since Magic: Origins was the only set available, my opinion of this game has changed quite a bit, so much so that I can't recommend this any longer.
If you want to read my positive review, check the bottom of this. It's in italics. It may be funny to read, especially since I was written in August.
I can't tell. At some points in this game, I really enjoy it. Now, with Shadows over Innistrad out, I was happy to be able to play with the new cards, not only in that set, but also Oath of the Gatewatch.
However, there were three very notable and re-occuring problems that have made me absolutely livid:
This is probably the least sensical problem.
There have been many times where I'd lose gold after I won a match. Before the match, I had 105 gold. Once I won the match, I earned 15 gold, adding to my previous number of... 45 gold, netting me 60 gold. This happened in the game after that, where, once I won, I had 5 gold, and because I won, my total became 20 gold.
I wasn't able to get a screenshot, unfortunately. I guess you'll have to take my word for it. It also hasn't happened in a couple days, so it may have been a four-time occurance (again, I'm sorry for not having any before/after screenshots).
For the love of god, DO NOT PRESS 'A' WHEN IT ASKS TO GIVE THEM FEEDBACK.
Every time I would want to give feedback, the game would blur out, and nothing would happen. I'd have to shut down the game, and then restart, making sure NOT to press 'A' when it asks for feedback.
This is a problem you may have seen. If you want a great explanation for what the problem is, check out
.
Here's the quick and dirty: the spell priority and auto-phase completion does not function properly.
What happens is the game auto-ends your main phase if you don't have a sorcery-speed spell in your hand (anything that isn't an instant, is a land, or isn't a spell with Flash). This function is probably in the game to speed up turns.
However, multiple times in my games, my main phase would end when I could've done something I'd like to do, particularly with Abbot of Keral Keep's ability. When he enters the battlefield, you exile the top card of your library. You may play that card, but only for this turn. The game does not recognize Abbot's exiled card as part of the game, and if, say, it's the only available spell you can play and it has sorcery-speed, the game goes through your phases, ending your turn without your consent, not allowing you to play that spell.
I lost a game just an hour ago because of this. I was getting pretty beaten by a deck with a lot of elves. I was at 7 life, and they were at 20. However, I was given a gift: I played Abbot, exiling a Languish (all creatures get -4/-4 until end of turn). It was exactly what I needed.
What happened was, because I played my land for the turn AND I didn't have any sorcery-speed spells in my hand, the game went straight to my end phase, EVEN THOUGH I had the mana to play Languish.
Would've I won the game if I played it? Maybe not, but I had a hand full of end-game spells, while they only had a few cards in hand.

I hate constantly getting fooled by Stainless. I don't want to insult them, since I don't know what goes into developing video games.
But worst of all, I hate that I have to keep putting on my blinders, forcing myself to think positively, knowing that all the nay-sayers will be proven wrong. Knowing that at some point, WotC and Stainless with finally get their sh*t together, make The Gatherer fully operational again, and make the DotP series an actually functional video game franchise.
But it won't ever happen.
For the love of god, your family, and yourself, do NOT spend one cent on Magic: Duels. The Pokemon online TCG game is significantly better optimized; Hearthstone is significantly better maintained; and every DotP before 2015 is better than this (somehow).

An excellent game, but with some room for improvement.
I'm going to start off by saying that I'm huge, huge fan of Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri. I enjoy all of the Civilization games, but SMAC is among my favourite games ever. I know Beyond Earth has gotten some mixed reviews, but I personally think that it's a worthy successor, both to SMAC and to Civilization V.
There are a number of things that need work, but I think that the gameplay is excellent. It really feels different from that of Civ V, despite reusing a lot of similar mechanics. The tech web is brilliant, and I like how your playstyle evolves over time instead of being fixed from the start, due to mechanics such as virtues, affinities, and quests. These same mechanics also help fuse gameplay and narrative, which I think is excellent.
Alpha Centauri's story and aesthetics were its's strongest points. I love science fiction, but I generally don't care much for science fiction in games - I think SMAC is one of the few SF video games with a story that's as good as a novel. I think world-building is especially important in SF, and SMAC really creates a believable, almost realistic world that's really easy lose yourself in. Beyond Earth's story doesn't quite live up to SMAC, but I think it still does a pretty good job. The civilipedia entries for techs, units, and wonders are well-written, often interesting or clever, and occasionally even thought-provoking. There are a few things about the in-game narrative that feel a little cheesy or corny, but for the most part, it's quite well done.
The art is similarly well done. For the most part, it isn't too over-the-top or cartoonish, which helps with the game's believability. I really dig the lush, fungal, and arid world types - they make each random world feel more unique. I do wish there was a little more diversity in unit and city graphics, however - I'm not a huge fan of every faction's units looking exactly the same in the early game.
In my opionion, the base Civ V isn't really all that great, but Civ V with Gods and Kings and Brave New World is excellent. The added game mechanics from the expansions add a lot of strategic depth that makes the game a lot more fun. I think that the base Beyond Earth is a lot of fun - better than base Civ V, in my book; but I'm really looking forwards to seeing how Firaxis develops Beyond Earth.

This game is too hard. I like hard games, but i like hard games that are fun while they are being hard. This game is not. It's really unfortunate because the graphics are really cool and i haven't played a game that made me feel so much like i was in a space opera since TIE Fighter or Babylon 5: I've Found Her. But this style of game has dated a lot, and Strike Suit Zero emphasizes the worst parts of the genre (combat) while neglecting the parts that made it good (storyline, dialog, wingmen, flying around massive space stations in awe...)
I could overlook the fact that your wingmen shoot blanks and your capital ships just float around waiting to be destroyed by insanely slow-moving torpedoes, if it wasn't for the cheesiness of being tasked to single-handedly take down enemy capital ships in a puny fighter that never stops flying forwards. Nevermind being able to fire thrusters to strafe around your target - you can't even come to a dead stop. It makes the whole game feel like Rebel Assault or some other oldskool rail shooter, except for the fact a turret will take you out in about 0.42 seconds. And if you do manage to somehow waste your target, don't worry, you won't get any time to enjoy the scenery, because the mission will either immediately end, or (more likely) another three capital ships will drop out of warp to blast you back to a checkpoint half an hour ago. Great concept, poor execution.

First of all, its classic MTG. It is surely time tested (20+ years is not a joke), but it the rules are somewhat obsolete (Spellweaver and Hearthstone got rid of mana screw each in a different way) and sets contain only about half cards. It can be said, that is si free-to play game, but with some limitations. Especially after Eldritch moon update. It's relatively easy to complete a set while the next one is still on the way without spending a dime, but quest changes after Eldritch Moon are quite annoying. Weekly quest, that require playing versus battle (PVP) started appearing more often and now most of the daily quests are versus (PVP) - specific, that are hard (if not impossible) to change into other quests. IMO, players have to choose whether they want to play PVP or do not. When developers force players to play PVP, like Hearthstone or, Magic Duels after Eldritch Moon update, for me it means only one thing - they want money and they do not know other methods to keep players interested or do not wish to develop the game. I can understand better rewards for PVP quest, but I cannot understand when almost all quests are PVP specific.
Regarding multiplayer... There are PVP and co-op modes, thought I'm not a multiplayer fan.
There is some PVE content, but not much. Cant praise for great PVE.
One more thing I like is time. 20-30 minutes a day usually is enough to earn your booster, which is fine if you a working guy like me.
There are also annoying self-ads in the game and mana-tapping it seems, which always, raised my brows, seems, got dumber after Eldritch Moon patch.
With Eldritch Moon quest changes, I cant give the game thumb up. It might be your splice of pie but I would recommend trying other games, especially Spellweaver, first, though.

A six card booster pack is 150 coins, or $1.99.  A fifteen real card booster down at the FLGS is four dollars plus tax.  Worse yet, there's no discount for buying boosters in bulk (there is for buying their in game currency, of couse however even buying in $40 lumps a box of real cards is a better per card value).  Combine this with the lack of any ability to trade cards and you're at the whims of the booster system, so good luck ever building a decent deck without pouring money into the RNG bucket.
Just consider that this game is more expensive than actually buying physical booster packs, by buying a box at a time I have enough money left over for gas to get to the local shop and a large pizza.  That is stupid, and it's not even getting into the gameplay issues that the Magic Duels has.
The timer based priority system is frustratingly slow when passing phases, but far too quick to reliably respond to spells and abilities, it's very fun having only a second and a half to read and then respond to a faiths fetters or unsummon.
It's very ambiguous where combat declarations are made and when you can respond.  Triggered abilities have a tendency to not work and the game acts odd when you sacrifice tokens.  There's no sound effects when choosing targets for multi-target spells making it occasionally awkward to tell how many of the 3 points of damage you are trying to spread around are on what you want.
In most respects the 17 year old Microprose Magic: The Gathering game is superior to this 2015 release and for any competitive player the free alternatives or MTGO are vastly superior choices.
Maybe if you're completely new to M:TG Magic Duels Origins offers something worthwhile, but if you've any experience with the game at all it's awkward, poorly designed, and overpriced.

Kung Fury is an example of the new trend we have now towards mocking the goofiness of the earlier generations. Retro games and 80's movies are coming in to the mainstream as an example of when things were good (or at least a different kind of entertainment). This movie does that beautifully.
First, the aesthetic. It feels so goofy and over-the-top, and while you'd think it feels like it's trying too hard, It felt wonderfully executed to me. A good comparison is Far Cry: Blood Dragon, it's quite similar. They manage to go so over-the-top without it feeling forced, and it doesn't ONLY stand on that alone.
The music was electronic-rocky goodness that felt so overly 80's you can't NOT like it. The initial fight scene between Kung Fury and the arcade machine was energetic and goofy as hell, but again it doesn't put you off. Visually, the movie is incredibly well made; It has great editing, great looking bad special effects, and fight scenes that manage to feel like an Anime or Video game, but done in real life. Like the other special effects, they're amazing looking bad special effects, janky and fast in a pleasing way.
The retro trend in our culture is something I'm happy to see as an opposing force to the gritty, overly dark tones of most films who want to be "The Dark Knight" but can't figure out how to do it without depressing the audience. This is a refreshing short film that is well worth your time. In fact, it's free! So, why are you not WATCHING IT? Why are you reading what I'm writing to consider watching a 30 minute film? It probably took you a minute or two to read this, and if you're reading multiple reviews to get a fair opinion of the film then you've likely been here for like 5 minutes. WHY? WATCH IT FOR GOD'S SAKE, IT'S SWEET AND FREE!
Also, I'd like to point out how bizarre it is that this is on Steam. Apparently Steam wants to become the swiss army knife of PCs, which I'm simeltaneously concerned about as a potential monopoly, and excited about because I love Steam. Someone must come to oppose Steam one day, and my money's on GOG's Galaxy or one of the software re-sellers. Or, possibly every software re-seller will fuse with GOG to form a mega-discount videogame marketplace. We shall see what arises in the years to come, but I expect the random assortment of reseller sites and GOG are going to start chipping away at Steam's iron grip on the gaming industry. Though, I will say that no good alternative to Steam is out there in terms of convenience and account-based game ownership, but who knows what program may challenge the mighty Steam? We shall see.
