An excellent RPG from Square Enix. A very rare kind of work on PC, Combining the best elements of RPG, tactictal game and strategies to provide some of the best playing times you could wish for.
Great J-RPG.
The story got some nice elements - there also a few cliché and some of the usual plot twists - but the overall is great.
The game has some tactical and stragegic choice as you not only lv up the member of your team, but you must chose which skill learn for each of them - the more you learn, the slower they progress, so the less action of that skill you learn.
You need to chose for them their behavior (simple A/B/C choice when they grow their weapon) by improving their weapon - which require component to loot (mobs / reward / digging).
But the most important part is the squadron. You have a limited number of characters to deploy on battle - and a maximum number of squad. Up to you to decide the number of character per squad (up to his maximum) as well as the squad formation and where the member are in each squad formation.
As each formation have pro and cons, it's important to know when to use one.
Plus you don't chose your squad action as you like. The actions avaible is a guidline determined by the computer depending on the squad Action point, his member skills, his HP/ buff / debuff (as well as the other's squad) and his position on the map compared to the friend / enemy squad.
Add special "limit break" skill, pincer attack and a gestion of moral squad by squad as well as team by team affection your action and their succes, and battle can get quite interesting.
Sadly, as most JRPG, you got a lot of grinding and hidden quest.
The good point is : the hidden quest (who are often harder than the main quest, especially at the end of the game) are the only one really needing grinding and providing real hard fight. But they gave overpowering reward.
All in all, if you like JRPG, don't miss it (it could do with an HD version by now, true).
If you want an exemple that SE can make a great game without using an already existing licence, don't search futher.
If you want a good RPG making the best of old school turn by turn JRPG - don't search futher.

Updated Impressions:
After the release of Rebirth 2.0 and later, this game has become much more enjoyable. There was something there to like, when it was first released, but there were too many bugs and glitches in the way of liking it.
Now, they have fixed every aspect in the game that I have experienced so far. I am running a few items from the workshop, which refine it a bit more, but the core of the game is now believable.
I have played a lot of space games, and I'm not sure what it is that I'm looking for when I play them, but I often find myself playing this game for hours longer than I intended to, and during the whole time I can feel the attention to detail that went into making it an immersive universe.
Most of the characters in the stations still look like scary dolls, unfortunately, but they actually look a lot more like the pasty spacefaring folk from previous X titles, and less like unfinished character models.
Voice acting has been vastly cleaned up, but there are still some instances of line delivery where the voice actor obviously didn't have any sense of context when they delivered the (sometimes terribly written) lines.
The key aspect for me, though, is immersion. In that sense, X-Rebirth is really becoming something special.

Shelter is a game about the hardships of motherhood, and so the game truly speaks a universal language.
In Shelter you are a mother badger taking care of your cubs, feeding them and defending them from predators. It makes you care so much about your little cubs that you can even think they have very distinguished personalities. Some players have given names to them, and reported interesting emotional responses when one of them died. This game can communicate with a primitive instinct in all of us: the love for the little, the innocent and the frail.
Throughout the game you learn to fear and hate predators as they were monstrously evil. But in the end... They are in the exactly same position you were: trying to feed their loved ones. The threatening predator becomes a loving mother, and vice-versa. And so the game shows how every mother is also a fearsome predator, ready to kill for the most pure and sacred love of all. This alone is powerful.
Great survival game with beautiful graphics and a deep emotional procedural narrative.
Positive points
* Simple and beautiful.
* Triggers emotional reactions.
Negative points
* Not recommend for immature people.

I bought FFXIII during Steam sale and really just paid a few bucks for it, and I am happy about it.
Final Fantasy XIII is a lite RPG that lives solely on the beautifully animated characters and the cutscenes, features that all Final Fantasy parts in the last 10 years offered, but lacks everything else which would make this game a nice role play game experience.
While not in fights, you just walk straight ahead. No secrets, barely any secret ways, at least not in the first 6 hours, no open map, different approaches or something like side quests. Basically you just run from one area to the next, interrupted by a couple of fights (which consist mostly of pressing A) and already mentioned cutscenes. You don't gain experience anymore, there is nothing such as mana, you can just cast your spells as often as you want. After each fight, all characters are completely healed, which makes Final Fantasy XIII a real simple experience.
While other Final Fantasy parts such as Final Fantasy VIII could impress with a twisted and complex story, the story background of Final Fantasy XIII is absolutely lame, hopes of the story developing into something exciting will probably lead to frustration. At last, the graphics, apart from the nice faces, can't really compete with other games with the same age. Even with Anti Aliasing and in FullHD, FFXIII only looks slightly better than a 2006 shooter, there are barely any reflextions which take a lot of the vividness of the world. Considering the almost 60 GB Final Fantasy occupies on the hard drive, I really can't explain the super low resolution textures.
In a conclusion I can say, Final Fantasy XIII is rather an interactive movie with toddler-level fights than a role play game, as it lacks many defining elements of such a game. Compared for example to Skyrim, which came out at about the same time, the only point FFXIII hast over Skyrim is the more attractive main character, but thats it.
I played Final Fantasy since the first part, and while I loved Final Fantasy VI, VII and VIII, to me, Final Fantasy XIII definitely is the weakest part so far and you can carefree save the money for this game. Sorry Eniox.

I'll try to tell you what the Stanley Pararble is about without spoiling to much. This is gonna be long, so bare with me.
The Stanley Parable is a game like no other. You play as Stanley, a man who works in an office and pushes buttons for a living. One day you look up and see that everyone in the office has disappeared...
As you wander around the office, a narrator narrates everthing you do. EVERYTHING.
"Stanley wandered around touching everything the office, but there was nothing to be found"
"Stanley stepped into the broom closet, even though there was nothing there."
"Stanley continued down the hallway even though he knew it would lead to his violent death."
As you come to rooms with multiple paths, the narrator will tell you what path to take. You choose whether to obey him or not. If you continue to disobey him, the narrator becomes angry with you and reacts differently depending on what you have done. The narrator is hilarious when you aggravate him! He breaks the fourth wall many times, stating that he knows he's in a video game.
I also really like how much there is to explore in the game. While it may feel confined, if you truly think outside the box there are tons of things to discover. Hidden rooms, narrator soliloquies, and other secrets are everywhere. Even when you think you glitched the game, the narrator scolds you for trying to break his masterpiece. Not to mention there are about 20 endings to the game to discover. (Some are very hard to find though.)
I think the price is a bit high for the game, so try to get it on sale. I got it for $4 and it is definitely worth a few bucks more than that. (Maybe not $15 though.)
Overall, this game is one of my favorites. It's hilarious and your mind will be blown as you try to wrap your head around some of the paradoxes in it. Highly recommended.

This game is very niched.
What does that mean, you may ask yourself? Well I'll tell you.
After playing the game for 15 minutes, you will have played the entirety for the game. So you know right off the bat if this game is for you or not. The game becomes redundant, the battles become harder at the drop of a hat, requiring you to farm the same things over and over again. There are
many things that have been made better, and more fluid, or just to polish the game off. (The sequels at least made of for that)
Is it worth the $15.99 price tag? Look up a gameplay video that's around 15 minutes long (Excluding the cutscenes. There's a reason the cutscene/movie folder for the download is a hefty 40gigs) and ask yourself if the game is for you. If it is, like it was for me, then you'll sit there and watch the "saltine" characters experience every bi-polar moment in the game right before you, and then you'll be asking yourself "Are these characters that thin? Or are they just developing faster than you could say "Emotional paradigm shift, go!"" But you get used to it. And then they make your way into your heart.
As for the gameplay, it is very... different. The ATB Battle system that SE (Square Enix) made for this game is pretty interesting, and I like the new concept intsead of just the old-and-used combat system of FFVII and others like it. Use a skill too early... and a mob will just walk out of it... So there is a hit-and-miss chance. And if, by some miracle, you learn how to actually control where your main character will go (That's it. You only move the leader of the squad... everyone else is just a peasant and stands there the entire fight.) then you can position yourself away from the tank, and actually live the battle.
Interesting side-note of the battle system is that it can be easily abused for maximum damage out-put, and then end-game, you can just spam Lightning's "Army of One" skill the entire battle simply by changing paradigms at the right moment mid-skill.
So the battle-system has flaws, when it's the companies first-endeavor, can you blame them? I would rather see a company try and miss with a new battle-system then use the old system anyday. It's what lets games grow in the world. Otherwise, we would still be in the ancient "Pong combat system" (Yes that could be considered the first combat system, scary, huh?) The plot is interesting if you're into it, and the characters aren't that bad. They're not as thin as most other people see them as, they just grow and develop much faster than we're used to.
So, in the end, is the game good? Yes and no. If you don't like grinding, then don't bother, or if you don't like punching the same thing in the face for the entire game (you re-fight the same boss 3 times...) Could SE have done a far better job with this game? Most definitely. But that's what the sequals are for.
For me, I definitely recommend this game to those who will appreciate it. If you don't know, then look up a simple video of the combat. Cause like I and many other reviewers' have said... it's the same battle through the entire game.
Cheers.

This game is based in the lord of the rings universe, and the story takes place, at the same time as the first lord of the rings movie.
If you know something about lord of the rings, you would properly like this games story to some extend. The game builds on the lord of the rings universe, and you have to visit locations, that are kind of new to the averige lord of the ring knower.
The game still focuses on main charecters such as the fellowship of the ring, and many more main charecters. Your journy in the game has nothing to do with the fellowship, but focuses on killing Saruns right hand (sorry if I spell some names wrong, but they are not so commen)
Your journy starts at an inn, and then you move on througout the lord of the rings universe. This brings you far around the country, and you get to visit many interesting locations. There is a forrest with spiders, an underground cave with undead, A fortres with orcs just to name a few of the locations.
You can take controle of one of three charecters. Each charecer, has his or hers own thing to do for the team. We have a dwarf, who functions as tank for the team, which mean he will be the first to attack, and the one to take the most damage, but still have enough life to surviev. This character uses heavy weapons and crossbows mostely, but can also use small weapons to channge things up.
The secound charecter is a human, who mainly focuses on range attacks, but can also go into combat with duelweld, or a sword, and a sheild. Since this charecter is mainly focusing on damaging, he is the one to damage enemys, while the tank, takes the beating from all the enemyes. Of couse the dwarf can fight by themselves, and thats why the game is great, becouse you can basicly do whatever you want, when it comes to classes.
The last charecter is an elven mage, who focuses on healing. She uses magicel attacks to attack enemyes, but is the weakest of the three and therefore needs the most protection.
The gameplay is a bit different for each of the three charecters, and therefore you can have a different experince with each charecter. But the goal is the same with all three, kill all the enemyes as a team.
The game is best to play with you friends, and since there is only three classes, you don`t have to hold the big gamer party, in order to have fun with this game. I completed the game with two of my friends and we really enjoyed the game, all the way through. We can say though, the story felt a bid lacky at the end, but I will of couse not spoil it. But if you know your lord of the rings movies, you will know what happens at the end of the first movie, and therefore the ending will not be a huge surprise for you.
The loot and trade system between charecters is a bid odd, but besides that, you can clearly see when your charecter evolves on he`s or her`s equipment througout the game, this gives a really satesfing feeling, which you will know for neally all RPG`s.
Now I want to talk about the ending, that is not about the plot, but more like the events at the ending. In the end of the game you get all kinds of awesome items, and you get all new and great talents. But then you fight an easy end boss, and all that awesome stuff you just got, can`t be used, I know you can play your charecter on another person playthrough, but still, the game is far to short to do all the stuff you want to do.
A note to end on, the AI in this game is good, but only for your enemyes, if you play the game alone, you will see your allies are really bad, and don`t really contebute with anything. This is a problem if the charecter you need is the healer, since the healer won`t. Well, heal at times.
This game is really good, and I highly recommend to play it with you friends to get the full experince of the game. But you can of couse play it by youself, and still have a good time with it. This game get`s a thumps up. 6 out of 10

I remember the times of old when Crysis was used to benchmark everything. It's a game I fondly remember for it's brillant and fun gameplay with gorgeous visuals that put modern games to shame but it's far from perfect.
Graphically, it was easily the most taxing game when it came out. "Can it run Crysis on max?" was a common way to judge a computer's performance, and rightly so, it's a intense game to run. Although released in 2007, it still looks gorgeous. The Lingshan Islands feel like very realistic in it's scope and detail. Texture quality rivals, if not outright better than, modern textures, and lighting effects are done to perfect. All in all, it's visually stunning. Worthy to note is the interactivity of objects in the game. The ability to shoot at enemies in cover and destroy their cover completely is realistic and not to mention being able to break most objects in game. Houses, fences, trees and cars are all destructable and this should be abused to the best of your abilities.
Gameplay wise, it's a sandbox, first person shooter, and arguably the best of it's genre. Guns feel like they have a real kick to them and the shotgun especially feels immensely satifisying to use compared to modern first person shooters. The nanosuit has 4 but all very distinct and useful "modes". All 4 modes use energy, an automatically recharging resource, to power their actions. Power mode allows for steadier aim, stronger melee attacks and higher jumps[/spoiler]. Armor modes allows damage to be absorbed via energy. Speed mode allows for faster movement in every situation including walking, crouched walking, running and even moving up ladders (not to mention a ridiculously fast sprint). Finally Cloak mode allows for limited invisibility. However, being tied to a limit and ever draining resource, there is an art to using the functions of the nanosuit. It's immensely satisfying to cloak into cover behind an enemy, switch to power mode, headshot, and then use speed mode to quickly sprint away into new cover. There's also a bit of depth into the mechanincs of the nanosuit, and the game doesn't hold your hand into it. It never tells you to use power mode when you're trying to snipe at long distances, or to use speed mode sprinting while swimming or
to move rapidly. Guns feature on-the-fly customisation, and you can tailor each gun to each specific circumstance, such as adding a silencer with a sniper scope on your assault rifle to act as a long range sniper, or switch it up with a reflex scope and grenade launcher for drawn out firefights. There are a few vehicles to use including tanks, military jeeps and even VTOLs but they're nothing really special apart from using jeeps in creative ways to kill KPA soldiers in the first half of the game.
Storywise, it's very barebones. You're sent to investigate an island who have american researchers taken hostage by the North Korean military (KPA or Korean People's Army). It then is revealed

The few main characters are lively and full of character, especially your squadmates of Raptor Team. Their voice actors do a terrific job putting so much personality into them, including the voice actors for quite a lot of the characters you'll meet. Although there is an exception. Helena Rosenthal was done by Claudia Black, responsible for Chloe in the Uncharted Series and Morrigan in the DA series. She does an okay job in those, but she is absolutely awful in Crysis. Whenever Helena's voice comes on it's like a nails on a chalk board. Absolutely jarring and breaks your immersion. You really have to think how the production team okayed this, when the other characters like Psycho or Prophet are done so well.
However the game is ultimately flawed in many aspects that take away from the experience. The first half of the game is a brillant open world FPS that allows for creative ways to approach every objective. Abusing Cloak feels cheap, but mastery is difficult to achieve resulting in a rather balanced experience. You can still end up in a terrible position with no energy to absorb hits if you don't position properly which means instant death at the higher difficulties. Enemies can also spot you while cloaked if you move in close proximity to them and even while remaining still if they're in touching range. Personally, I play this like a Predator simulator, and it's immensely satifisying to cloak in and out, while headshotting soldiers undetected and causing an alert to go off while you continute to flank and pick soliders off one by one. Unfortunately once you reach the second half of the game, it becomes a completely different game. After you reach
, it becomes a linear FPS with bullet sponge enemies (The aliens you'll fight, the KPA nanosuit soliders aren't so bad). While this isn't bad on it's own, you have to play a completely different style. You can't stealth kill (as in cloaking and headshotting) and so you are forced to shoot behind cover, ducking to recover your armor. I wouldn't mind this in it's own game, but to lose that sense of freedom and ability to play as you see fit from the first half, is a real shame. The game also suffers from numerous bugs, including odd physics interactions like a fallen tree shaking and walking into it causing instant death, falling into the floor of the
and the infamous bug where you crash upon trying to load a game (which you can fix by deleting the most recent save in your savegame folder).
All in all, it's an immensely fun game to play with multiple ways to play it as you see fit. The visuals are gorgeous and constant screenshot worthy moments. I'll start by saying that I haven't been a civ player for an extremely long time. With 158 hours on Civ5 and roughly 54 hours on CivBE I feel like my opinion is purely objective. I agree with other reviewers saying that this game feels unfinished in the sense that I would have appreciated more from the game in terms of depth, however I do feel that it has satisfied my expectations. Leaving Civ5 at the end of the tech tree with our current modern day tech as well as a tiny bit of future stuff was a cool ending point and beyond earth feels like I have definitely gone "beyond earth". There are aliens (while they may be somewhat more of a simple nuisance they are still cool, they arent barbarians and they are refreshing), affinities that tie you to a belief or way of life that separates you from the rest of the colonies, and really cool military 'upgrades' that change your units completely. Satellites are pretty much the coolest thing ever. Have you ever wanted to teleport your army straight to the fight? Now you can.
In a nutshell I want you to be able to see what you are getting yourself into with this game
Pros
- Starts where you would expect it to after playing civ5
- There are quests that open up with certain buildings, points in time etc that give cool options to really define your nation
- Has Aliens running around messing with your stuff from time to time
- Super cool units that do Super cool things (levitate over canyons)
- Affinities that make you somewhat choose a lore for your people that isnt tied to anything historical
- There are already some decent mods to fix small UI problems that Firaxis should have seen coming
- SATELLITES, TELEPORTERS, GEARS OF WAR DEATH LASER THING, SATELLITES TO MAKE IT RAIN(CASH MONEY)
Cons
- Aliens don't really have a purpose other than messing with your stuff from time to time
- UI problems that are very silly to have been missed for a complete game
- It sometimes feels like you don't know the purpose of your playing the game
- The tech web is unintuitive and takes time to understand
- The game has many paths to take that can lead to confusion in your overall goals
Overall YES I recommend this game, HOWEVER I do feel that you should wait for it to go on sale. The game accomplishes what I want when I purchase a game: fun, replayable, multiplayer and singleplayer that are both satisfying.
Overall YES I recommend this game, HOWEVER I do feel that you should wait for it to go on sale to get a good bang for your buck.

Beginning to understand why the release of this game was so hush hush. Quite frankley, this game was not ready for its release date, they knew it, and it shows. The servers cannot manage the (i believe to be somewhat modest amount) of players and, at least for me, it is impossible to get a game with an online player. I think the game has potential and I can see once the cards are unlocked (and the servers get fixed) that the game will be fun to play. But until then... well, unless you are ok with pulling your hair out with frustration I suggest waiting a month or two.
I also find that being unable to earn gold in offline mode to be extremely frusterating. Especially with the servers constantly crashing it makes the grind to unlock the cards more painful than it already is (because you can only earn gold by 1: a single playthrough of the campaign 2: playing against AI 3: Daily Quests, most of which requires #4 4: online matchmade battle against an opponant). Oh, regarding battling an opponant, you only get the gold if you win the battle.
The fact that you only earn gold by beating your opponant is unfortunate because, quite frankley, the starter cards are pretty bad and it is very difficult to build a functional deck out of them. This leads to an unfortunate snowball effect where the players that have more cards unlocked (through either paying for gold and unwrapping boosters, a good streak of luck with multiplayer, or a really long grind against the AI) are more likely to win and therefor unlock more cards. I hope the company sees the problem with this and adjusts the earnings for multiplayer to something like where the loser earns 10g and the winner 30g or something like that.
I mean, i get it... F2P games need a way for the company to earn money, but so obviously chokeholding the community to cough up cash in order to get the cards just feels poorly thought out. Asthetics changes like foiling cards, special profile pictures, alternate card arts, etc. (basically stuff that looks cool but doesnt give a player a gameplay advantage over the other) that you can only get by paying money would have been a better option for earning money then relying on players purchacing gold to get packs. You will always have people who would rather pay money than grind out the cards, no reason to make it as difficult as it is for everyone else.
tl;dr I DO think the game has potential, and I will recommend the game because of that, but it sure requires work to get there. Give it a few months for the devs to get there heads out of their.... well give it a few months for the devs to work out the kinks of release, expand the card pool in the promised addons, and hopefully listen to the community with regards to making earning gold less constricting.

Strike Suit Zero is an amazing open space dogfighting game. There is no denying this. However, when the last level takes EVERYTHING you have been doing in the former 12 levels (The very open space for movement and maneuvers) and throws it away. Instead, you get one of those precision and closed space levels where your ship is carefully navigating the relics NARROW, LINEAR spaces. Not the open place you have been fighting for all of the game. I would not have minded this if the controls were changed... But they aren't. You play as though you are in that open space. The controls are still either super touchy or not touchy enough in this level.

The corridors are long and the time getting to the core takes up about half the allotted time, more if you are trying to be careful. Bumping the walls WILL immediately drain your shields. You will die a lot. If this level were different, I would have loved every aspect of this game. However, I cannot beat the last level because everything I did in the former levels meant nothing. This game demanded precision in a game where it is not necesary.
If you want to get this game, I recommend you do it... If it's on sale. If you are on PC, I would recommend Strike Suit Infinity if you want a fun game like this one, but without the story.

„Make life-and-death decisions driven by your conscience.“
„During war, there are no good or bad decisions; there is only survival. The sooner you realize that, the better.“
There just aren't any similar games out there, so it was really refreshing to see something like this. But unfortunately, good intentions – in this case, showing the horrors of war – don't automatically make a great game.
The main problem I have with this game is that it's overly simple. You have to survive a number of days, and every day is always the same: In phase one of the day you start in your residence doing necessary stuff (cooking, resting, making tools) and in phase two you go scavenging. There is never a deviation from this. Sometimes little events happen during phase one, like people from the neighborhood (which you never see directly) make a request for help (which you can decide to help at your own cost or turn down), or a trader coming to barter.
Then there is stealing. You can make your life easier by stealing from other civilians, and you see the dilemma here, but it's inconsequential: You can steal from them, but there are no consequences regarding their well-being – they just continue to live on, as if nothing happened. Because of that, I sometimes stole a few things I really needed and had no regrets over this – why feeling bad for it, if they manage to survive without any problems?
Stealing from thugs on the other hand is morally acceptable in the game, but there are absolutely no consequences for you, besides the possibility they could kill you in the process itself. You would think they would reinforce their security after you steal once from them, but they don't. Also, they will never roam your neighborhood looking for you for example, even if you stole completely everything from them – pretty generous thugs, I guess.
And finally, my last gripe: A playthrough can simply get too long for its own good to complete. Like I mentioned before, the days have always the same structure and there are no real events, so after some time it can get really repetitive and suddenly even boring. In my two playthroughs, there was no “climax” which led to the end, so it can be just suddenly be over.
Because despite of all I listed it's not a bad game. On the one hand, there is the refreshing setting and it is polished in what it delivers. On the other hand, you can easily pick it up every now and then, because of the clear structure of the days – and every day takes only 15-30 minutes to complete. It also has rogue-like elements (regarding locations, length of the war, loot, characters you play as), which really adds a lot of replay-value.
It's a good time-waster and you can have fun with it (as much fun as one can have seeing civilians struggling in a war), but just don't expect it to be complex. Buy it if you're okay with the issues it has and if you'd like to support games with unusual themes.

I'm going to come right out and say that I'm biased. The original Bioshock is one of my favorite games of all time. It easily ranks in my top 5, and definitely ranks as my number 1 favorite game of the previous console generation. When I rate Bioshock Remastered, I'm rating it with these facts in mind because when you purchase Bioshock Remastered, you're also receiving the original Bioshock and vice/versa. It wouldn't be fair for me to rate this remaster based on what was remastered on its own, and it especialy wouldn't be all that informative.
First, we'll start with the good:
- It's Bioshock, one of the greatest shooters ever made when viewed as a whole.
- It has graphics that are arguably superior to the original release.
- The included Cut Content Museum and Director's Commentaries are interesting if you're into that sort of thing (which I am).
- Achievements! Woo!
- A wider Field of View than the original provides.
- Physics no longer locked to the framerate (which can cause issues of its own, but is still objectively superior to how it was before).
- New Game +
- Previously Playstation-Exclusive Challenge Rooms and Survivor Mode difficulty.
And now for the bad...
- Essentially 0 bug fixes. If there was a problem in the original, it exists here as well.
- Mouse look is broken, though whenever I originally played a game on console, I usually stick to using a controller when I finally play it on PC, so this doesn't affect me (because I use a controller).
- The game's implementation of v-sync isn't the greatest, it can cause microstutter when the framerate fluctuates between 59-61 frames. It annoys me.
- No Borderless Window support, which would help with the previous issue (though the Borderless Gaming app does indeed work).
- The new Field of View allows you to toggle between the original game's 50 degrees, and the new 75. I'm personally ok with 75, but your mileage may vary. Though the FOV can be increased with ini tweaks.
- There are some strange audio issues. Some report no audio in-game at all, but the only audio issue I've encountered is a noticeable lack of audio occlusion... meaning I can hear splicers and cameras and such through walls on completely different parts of the map.
It may seem like the list of cons outweighs the pros, but I personally don't see it that way. Bioshock is a fantastic game regardless of any issues facing this release. If you haven't played Bioshock before, it's definitely worth purchasing (but only if you're willing to troubleshoot a bug or two along the way). If you've already played Bioshock (on consoles, for instance), it's probably not worth purchasing unless it's on sale. With the exception of some behind-the-scenes videos and a mildly interesting cut content museum, there's really nothing new to see here with the exception of a few shiny (or not so shiny, as it were) new textures and models.
Side note: Confused on whether or not I should check this as "received for free"...

This game can be viewed from two perspectives, loving or downright cynical, of which I chose the latter, and a wall of text to boot. Consider yourself warned.
The gameplay in this game cannot really be related to any other game. It is by definition linear, with movement in one direction at all times (unlesss you're a straight thug, in which case you'll hit a wall you disrespectful ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.). This means that your combat is also limited to certain amounts of enemies. This corridorlike design exists in order to put an emphasis on combat and story, which would have been acceptable if both of those were good. By chapter 5, you most likely will be wondering why you used 50 gigabytes of download space just for a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥movie and a hallway with monsters. Don't get me wrong, I can understand the linear gameplay. However, with a totally linear game, there should at least be a superb plot to compensate. The combat at least is enjoyable (at times). Sometimes it will have you relishing a victory after a hard-fought boss and feeling fulfilled. Most of the time, it will feel like a flashier World of Warcraft grind.
The plot is most definitely the least enjoyable part of this game. The game is linear, and people who praise the game will say it is to "emphasize the plot". The plot spoken about consists of characters about as deep as a kiddie pool. There are so many other games with such deep meanings AND nonlinear, gameplay, yet this game fails to nail either. The game is abssolutely riddled with cutscenes, yet unlike a title like Metal Gear Solid, where the cutscenes tell everything about the plot, you most likely will just find yourself referring to the Autolog, which essentially exists as a TL;DR for the plot to compensate for Square Enix's atrocious writing team. Essentially, Square decided to sacrifice every trace of its characteristic open worlds to emphasize an already boring, monotonous, and predictable story.
Finally, the area where this game truly stands out. While walking through not-so-vast expanses of glorified hallways, temples, and generic sci-fi environments, you are greeted with some of the best 2009 has to offer graphically. To top it all of, the game even supports shoddy 60FPS! In all seriousness, graphically, the game is beautiful. All environments are polished and well done, if not a bit repetitive at times. Although a good portion of this game is prerendered, it still is beautiful. However, the soundtrack is almost entirely forgettable. It is akin to Final Fantasy pop music - forgettable and unremarkable (although they were missing a key composer in the franchise). This game may have a mediocre plot, but those hair physics might just take your mind off it.
This game, while failing in some aspects, shines in others. An emphasized battle system and graphical finesse partially compensate for the game's otherwise boring and shoddy plot. I would reccomend this game to someone looking for a game that gives you a fight, not a reason to do so. For those who desire clothes on their protagonists and compelling characters, I would say to look for another FF game.

This game is nothing but a Disney mandated advertisement for the MCU. The roster is total garbage - you're telling me that Gamora got in of her own merit over other popular, relevant characters like Daredevil or Iron Fist? The Fantastic Four are dead right now across all mediums, but with multiple ongoing X-Men books, why is there no Wolverine or Magneto? Plus the story itself is seriously uninspired - a massive yawn fest made to be very easily digestible for the MCU crowd. Fans of comic books - go and play Injustice 2.
I really can't fault the gameplay too much - mind you I am only a causal fighting game fan so more hardcore, competetive players may have problems compared to earlier games in the series. I quite like the 2 fighter teams as opposed to the three as they give you half a dozen or so different styles to choose from in the way of the Power Stones mechanics.
Having said that, single player content is severely lacking - the bar for casual/single player modes in contemporary fighting games has been set high by NetherRealm Studios in games like Mortal Kombat X/Injustice 2. There is no excuse for the lack of content here, although what should I have expected after Street Fighter V. When you finish arcade mode, there is no character cutscenes, just a lazy 'YOU WIN!'-esque screen (that isn't even personalised beyond just a generic image of the team you used). This is more fogivable in a game like Street Fighter V because of the excellent online scene - the online here was DOA and continues to be. I have yet to find ONE SINGLE ONLINE FIGHT after 16 hours in the game.
To summarise: this is a let down for comic book fans due to really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Disney-ised characters, this is a let down for casual fans of the fighting game genre (like me) because of the lack of single player content, and this is a let down for the hardcore fighting game community because online is dead. I really doubt any of those issues will be fixed: Disney will always want their most popular products front and centre, and Capcom is prioritising fixing Street Fighter V over this. I got this game for a very low price and am still left let-down. Stay away.

Yes, I'm aware that Torchlight is a "Very Positive" game, but that does not make it immune to criticism. I didn't write this review simply to be a contrarian jerk.
Videogames age, some more than others. At times, all it takes is for a game to receive a sequel, in order for its age to become readily apparent. Torchlight II improves on the original in every conceivable way. I'll even go as far as to say that Torchlight has been rendered obsolete. There's literally no reason to play Torchlight 1 over its sequel, or over the great many other loot-heavy action RPGs that have been released over the years.
The absolute biggest problem with this game is the difficulty curve. I played through this game on normal, and for 9/10ths of the game, there wasn't any challenge. However, once I got to the final portion of the game, I started running into Dark Zealots. Dark Zealots have auto-targeting instant lightning. All it takes is a couple crits and I die. I admit that my lightning resistance wasn't up to snuff, but the fact that this attack is completely unavoidable is ridiculous. Once Dark Zealots start appearing, they're bound to show up fairly often throughout the post-game. I was on the 5th floor of the Shadow Vault and a Dark Zealot's lightning brought me from full health to death.
I played through Torchlight II on hard difficulty. A veteran is likely to pop in here and say "That's still way too easy." but hear me out. Torchlight II on hard was more consistent than Torchlight 1 on normal. The game remained fairly challenging (for me) throughout the entirety of the main campaign. I didn't sleepwalk through the game, nor did I suddenly get a heaping helping of horse manure towards the end of it and beyond.
By the way, why does Ordrak have 3 billion HP? Why can he summon countless dragons and skeletons? I'm positively boggled that anyone signed off on this nonsense of a finale. The ludicrousness of the final boss really stands out, when every other boss dies in a minute or two. Torchlight 2 was more consistent when it came to bosses.
Loot. Now I know it's difficult to expect good loot. There is the almighty RNG, and I've never been very lucky. Nevertheless, there is a rhyme and reason to how this system should work, and players should feel like their time is rewarded, especially when they defeat bosses or discover secret rooms. Instead, you're just as likely to get a weapon that's usable for half the game as you are to not find any decent armor upgrades for 3/4s of the game. AGAIN, Torchlight II is more consistent.
Torchlight II also has better quest-design, exploration, map-design, classes, skills, monster-variety, and so on and so forth. It's practically a revelation by comparison.
Now I could download a couple mods to fix the Dark Zealot's insane lightning, or drop Ordrak's HP to something manageable, or improve the myriad of other things that need improving, but that's not my idea of a fun time. Mods are at their best when they add to a game, not just fix its problems. Besides, I already own the sequel. At this point, there really isn't an excuse not to. Torchlight II enjoys sizable discounts during all of the major Steam sales.
On the bright side, when I review Torchlight II (eventually); I won't have to spend the entirety of it discussing why it's a better game than the prequel.

Why play Farming Simulator 15?
I'm sure a lot of us who do play get asked that, or are recieved with blank expressions when we say we play this to our gamer friends.
There are many answers, it's a relaxing, casual, no pressure, excellent sim experience. I hate to even call it a game.
Sure, it can be gamed, by either trying to get the best equipment, become a millionaire, buy all the land in the village, have the best multi-player co-op, ect. None of which I have any interest in whatsoever. So why play?
For me, it's one of the most relaxing offerings on Steam. A lot of times, after a hard day at work, or the morning of a day off, I just want to grab a cup of coffee, and relax. This game is perfect for that.
As a chid I also spent my summers on my grandfather's farms, and to me that was truly the best times of my life. After they died the farmsteads were broken up among their children. Broken up to the point that they were no longer feasible farms.
So in a way playing this is like going back to that moment in time where everything, in my eyes, was perfect Americana.
Why do I play? Because, to me, this isn't really a "game" per se. It's a true life sim for those of us who remember or enjoy just firing up, grabbing a cup of coffee and relax with, even if it's just mowing that empty lot or watch the sun set or rise over a field of waving corn or wheat, the sound of roosters or the gentle heavy breathing of cattle chewing their cud.
If anything, it saddens me when people CAN'T understand the draw and attraction of this "game".

If you are searching for a game full of action and a kind of stealth and assasin play style then Hitman Absolution is the game for you!The game takes place primarily in the United States, more specifically around the city of Chicago.This game introduces an online option to the series, where players can create their own missions for other players to complete. In addition, the game features Instinct Mode which allows Agent 47 which is your main character in this game to predict enemy patrol routes.In the aftermath of Hitman: Blood Money, Diana Burnwood, Agent 47's handler with the International Contract Agency, suddenly goes rogue, carrying out a catastrophic sabotage that includes publicly exposing the Agency. The Agency reforms under Agent Benjamin Travis; Travis assigns 47 to kill Diana and bring Victoria, a teenage girl in her care, to the Agency. Shooting and wounding Diana in her home in Chicago, 47, rather than executing her, comforts the dying Diana, who gives him a letter and asks him to keep Victoria safe from the Agency.47 hides Victoria at a Catholic orphanage somewhere in Chicago and contacts an International Contracts Agency (ICA) informant named Birdie, who asks him to kill a wealthy gangster nicknamed The King of Chinatown, in order for him to play ball. After eliminating him, 47 meets with Birdie, who briefs him about Blake Dexter, the CEO of Dexter Industries, who may have more information on Victoria. As payment, 47 is forced to give his signature Silverballers to Birdie. 47 learns that Dexter is in the "Terminus" hotel and after evading Dexter's henchmen, eavesdrops on him. 47 learns from Dexter's conversation with his secretary Layla that he plans to kidnap and auction Victoria to the highest bidder. 47 attempts to strangle Sanchez, Dexter's enormous bodyguard, who proceeds to knock 47 unconscious. After Dexter discovers who he is, he almost kills him, but decides as he doesn't want that kind of attention. Just then, a hotel maid comes in and discovers 47, thinking he is dead. Dexter kills her, plants the weapon with 47, douses the room in alcohol, ignites it, and leaves with Layla and Sanchez. Framed by Dexter for the murder, 47 escapes the hotel and evades the police.
Now I'm not going to say any more of the story because i realy want you guys to take a look at the game yourselves and as always try not to be detected and stay unnoticed.
Have fun playing Hitman Absolution!

Diablo-inspired isometric hack-n-slash dungeon crawler (or "action-RPG"), with many, so many levels filled with treasures and monsters, under seemingly common and peaceful village.
Those of us who have played Diablo before, will recognize everything immidiately, and will be wandering only with cartoon-animated visual style and with the pet - which is quite nice and useful companion, generally, both in fight and in dealing with the loot (which was quite a problem back in time).
Those of us who saw Fate, however, will not be asking any questions, as the Fate is just the base for the Torchlight, with the same visual style, mild music, and the pet. You may think of Torchlight as of much upgraded towards the more comfortable gameplay version of the Fate... And as of next of kin to Diablo Hellfire. And made by the same people, creators of Diablo and Fate.
Torchlight is not a "Diablo-killer", as it goes with so many projects like Titan Quest, Sacred and so many others. On the contrary, Torchlight is actually made all this race to beat the fame of Diablo 1&2 looking even more out-of-order. As you don't need to be better than somebody else. You just need to be fun and complete all by yourself. And Torchlight is just that kind of game - with satysfying content, challenges, variety of features, and general fun-out-of-the-game.
That I personally liked about Torchlight is the atmosphere, which is both quite reminiscent to the original Diablo, with the nearly same background and music... but much more mild and joyful altogether.
That has frightened me there - is the same thing as with the Fate game - the amount of levels below the surface. Even after you'll beat the main scebario nemesis - you still have a long way down before you, with more and more powerful foes and more of the rarest loot.
And it was namely the loot - along with other possibilities to enhance and empower a character - that frightened me the most. Really, while some people are starting to hate Skyrim for the hundreds of hours of adventures, in Torchlight the biggest blackhole, that has eaten the majority of my playtime - was levelling and redistributing items, perks and other enhancements. Yeah, just the same thing for which so many people love RPG systems in the first place - clear numerical system of your hero's progress - made me sick. For it seems so bottomless, that I've dropped the playing at one moment, realising that for every hour of dugeoning I'm spending 2+ hours just orginizing the stuff and making preparations... I'm not saying the game is like this. Actually, you can play it on the flow, and pauses for changing equipment and distributing stats can be as small as you want them to... It's just the way I'm playing the games and living life in general - if I can tune something to go with that in the field, I usually do that, ad perfectum.
Summarizing. Torchlight is the one very nice and enjoyable hack'n'slash dungeon crawler, which can leave uncomfortable only those who can't play action-RPGs, sicked with cartoon-style animation, or completionsts like myself. One last thing to add is that I suggest to start playing right from the hard difficulty, for "easy" and "normal" settings are somewhat less inspiring. Overall mark is 7.8/10.

Warning, contains mild (Edit: heavy) spoilers.
Never having played the famous Crysis, I thought I'd finally give it a shot and find out what the fuss is all about. Naturally, since I played this in 2014, my perspective on the game will be very different from the one who played it when it came out. But only an hour into the game, I realized why people call it such a revolutionary shooter for its time. I didn't play with any mods, yet I would've never guessed the game I was playing came out in 2007 judging from what it presented to me. This is due to the following reasons:
- The vastness of the world and the graphical fidelity are overwhelmingly impressive for an FPS title this old. You can clearly see that the CryEngine is designed to push the limits on what's possible in terms of looks and scope. I was impressed by how open-world-y the terrain is, yet the missions are unmistakably straightforward... which turns out to be an incredibly fun combination in my opinion. Being dropped on a tropical island where you shoot people in a vast and open area offering multiple ways of approaching your goals is to my mind a great way to design an FPS. The level of detail is stunning to say the least for a 2007 title, I have seen much worse in considerably newer titles.
- The gunplay, gun variety and AI are simply great. Shooting enemies feels fun, feels rewarding and feels challenging since the AI actively tries to hunt you down when you for example sneaked away again using cloak. One of the core mechanics, the exosuit and its accompanying suit powers offer great variety for both people who like to be stealthy or those who love to cause mayhem. I found a mix of these to be the most effective and entertaining. Goddamnit I think I never experienced as much satisfaction as when I blew up a truck with a rocket launcher while crouching in a bush with cloak engaged. The effects are mindblowing, as are the sound assets, just really immersive overall.
- Performance is solid. With CFX 7950/7970 I easily manage 60fps, except for very intense scenes involving lots of explosions and stuff. FoV seems to be exceptionally high, I didn't see a slider for it in the menu, but it's at least 100 by default, which is great. Sadly there's a few bugs involving for example scripted events and cutscenes not triggering correctly when loading from quicksaves amidst a level, nothing game-breaking though. Also, 1920x1080 or higher resolution is not enabled by default, you have to manually adjust it in the config file, which is no big deal though.
- The level design is interesting enough. While most levels feature open tropical island terrain with hilly, foresty areas, there's also a sequence where you are in weightless space, floating around inside a gigantic alien structure; very impressive and intriguing overall. The enemy variety is great too: From your usual infantry of all kind to jeeps, tanks, helicopters, boats to rather pesky flying alien crystalline squids with fast-firing energy weapons to a huge♥♥♥♥♥alien motherfugger in the process of sinking a motherfuggin aircraft carrier. It should be noted that you can drive jeeps, tanks, boats and helicopters yourself which is super fun if you like to shoot up stuff in the most classy way imaginable.
Negative points? I have one major one, but perhaps it's not really valid since the game clearly doesn't focus on that aspect at all and never pretends to:
The story is mindblowingly clichée and superficial: >Technologically augmented super soldier infiltrates fictional island under the control of evil North Koreans, gathers intel, blows up stuff, uncovers archeological project gone overboard, sleeping alien entity that feeds itself off energy awakens, causes major destruction, gruffy American general wants to drop nuke on island to kill off the monstrosity, super-intelligent scientists who always know it better advise against it, alien gets nuked anyway, becomes massively stronger, protagonist has to beat XXL format version of alien monstrosity using lots of missiles and a super secret prototype weapon which had never been field-tested but works like a charm (why wouldn't it?), escapes a sinking aircraft carrier and goes right back into the fight because he's a badass and a superhuman, dutiful soldier-tough-guy who has no fear and throughout the entire game requires no sleep at all.
There, that's the plot in a nutshell for you. Not really intentended in the beginning but hey, these are spontaneous and minimally structured reviews after all so w/e.
So there you go, awesome FPS, don't play it for the story, play it for the mechanics and the looks. This is how every modern military shooter should be. You can make a very linear, bland narrative without sacrificing diversity and creativity in terms of gameplay and mechanics. Crysis taught us this.

Me and a friend bought this together, we got it on sale for like 37 bucks. We both were rather big fans of Civ 5 so we were really looking forward to this one. I can't say it's an improvement yet from Civ 5, but I will say that so far I like where it's heading.
The game gives the game a different spin from previous civs, instead of just updating the previous versions idea of a civ game it tries to create a new kind of civ. It isn't too different though that you would be completely lost, in most ways it just replaces old civ features with newer ones such as health for happiness.
Aliens add a interesting rival to the bane of all early game civ games barbarians. However they try to do so in a way that still makes them relevant atleast into the mid game. They have a bit more variety than barbarians did, in fact enough that you kind of wish there was more. Mods have of course already rectified this, but maybe it will be a good idea for future expansions.
The main criticism I have of the game is that after you get used to all the changes and learn your way through affinities and the tech web the game can feel a little barren when compared to Civ 5. At the moment though, I'm willing to chalk this one up to the fact that Civ 5 has had multiple expansions worth of content added to it. I hope that Beyond Earth gets the same treatment because I think that added some meat to an already promsing framework. I would like to see an expansion in the number of options you have when creating your civ. I guess that technically there is more than previous civs as far as end options but it still feels more could be done with it.
It is still a perfectly playable and enjoyable game unto itself. It shows promise, and interestingly I think it's not really going to replace Civ 5 for me but kind of run along side it, and hopefully eventually meet it in terms of content and complexity. I would say if you enjoyed the previoous civs it's a decent addition, and if I had to make the choice again I'd definitely buy it

MTG has released a huge number of games on steam along with numerous DLC's, and I've found that out of all the CCG games the series has released on steam, I like this one the most.
I have found this game to be extremely beginner-friendly. Right from the start, it takes the player through the tutorials step-by-step, and makes sure that after the player completes the tutorial, they play a game using the mechanics they just taught. It is done a lot better than the previous online MTG games, where they just throw everything you need at you and expect you to do well.
After the tutorial, the deck building guide is very helpful too. One big thing that many new players struggle with is deckbuilding, because it's such an open thing that requires so much learning and so much practice, that many players, online and off, simply resort to playing decks that other people built for them. But this game really takes you through the steps, depending on what concept you want your deck to revolve around, and makes suggestions to cards to add in to build upon that. Obviously, the guide does have its limitations, but it is a very good start for new players and really helps them build their own decks in the future.
The campaign is very well-made, although I can see how it can be found disfavourable by more experienced players. It really forces the player to try out different strategies by limiting the deck you can play to the planeswalker you are playing as. Though that may seem like a limiting factor for some players who would rather not have to play with the monocoloured decks prepared for them, I see it more as a challenge to complete the story as they purposely pit you against stronger decks (although I will say that Liliana starts out with absolute crap in her deck. As much as I hate bashing on cards, because I genuinely enjoy playing with cards like Dementia Bat, Liliana really does start out with complete garbage. And also Nissa's campaign is really hard because she goes against decks that are just absolutely bonkers).
But yeah, the way the campaign is set up is rather refreshing, and definitely good for beginners who are still trying to find how they play best.
The best part about this game, I have found, is that it is free. Even down the coins that can be purchased, the players are allowed to unlock new cards for free as long as they keep on playing, and that is something I feel like should be implemented more in the future as well. Because one of the biggest barriers that have prevented my friends from getting into MTG in general is the fact that just about everything, online or in real life, costs money, and they're a bit iffy about spending money on a series they may or may not like. But this game being free really opens that up for them, so now they can try it out without having to spend a penny.
Overall, I just really like this game. I feel like this is one of the best online MTG games they have released because of its accessibility to new players, allowing me to play this game with friends who haven't gotten into MTG because of money.

World is vast, beutiful and interconnected. Each zone smoothly blends into another and has thematically different looks, set of enemies and lore hidden around if you care to look for it. Often you see item just out of reach, prompting to look around for hidden alternate route or waiting until you unlock a new movement ability. Each of these abilities give not only new ways to explore previous zones or open shortcuts, but also additional edge in combat.
Combat is fluid and with variety of options: basic attacks in 4 directions, 3 unlockable Nail Arts (specific attack moves) and 3 directional spells give you enough ways to deal with enemies up close and far away. Take note, even basic enemies you defeated for 50 times can still deal serious damage if you just mash attack button without adapting to their patterns. There are also plenty of bosses giving you a fair challenge, with several of those having stronger versions to fully test your abilities.
Art, animations and sounds are top quality - everything fits together perfectly. Each zone visuals and background sounds (lush forest, worker mines, haunted caves) give off distinct atmosphere. Bugs encountered (as in, characters) on the way really feel that they belong in that world, each with different personality and worries, each adding a bit of lore about Hallownest.
To sum it all: 10/10. Recommended.

OK, I realise I'm not going to get the full MTG experience on an Atom-powered Windows 8.1 10-inch tablet (despite MTG2015 working quite well), but as far as I can tell this is a backwards step. I'd love to be able to comment on the specifics of how the game plays from a MTG persepctive, but I've not got that far.
Now, I know that some of these issues are because of the limited hardware I'm playing this game on (say, equal to an old iPad in terms of grunt, what with it being one of the later Atoms Intel produced) and some issues are server-based, but it seems like mobile play (on a tablet that's not Apple's) is being punished. Why, if the game runs on an iPad, can't this work on a Windows tablet through Steam, and why can't this be played on Android? I don't want to have to cart a laptop around to enjoy a mobile game of MTG (if I've got a data connection, obviously - can't play without one). The game is hardly cutting edge in terms of graphics and sound, so we should be able to get this running (if slowly) on a portable device.
Last dig - The user interface on Android for MTG2015 was pretty seamless - on Windows it's designed for a mouse and keyboard. You can play it with a controlled, but it's a bit poor. With just a touchscreen as an interface on Windows, it is absolutely rank - you can't exit/concede a duel, you can't zoom in and out of cards, you have to double-tap to do EVERYTHING (which is unreliable, seeing as how unresponsive the game is) and you can't select different ways to pay mana for a card. This is absolutely shocking as an interface. With a BT mouse, this plays better, but hardly a nod to the portable market. If you can get the interface right last year and (presumably) get it right for iOS, why isn't there a baked-in option to work for Windows touchscreen-only devices?
Again, I'm sure that, if I get any response to the messages I've left around for WotC/Stainless, they'll mostly be of the 'not rated for your device' nature, which misses the point: considering the effort that has clearly been made in the past for mobile interfaces, why is this not evident in the Windows version?
There's been a lot of talk on-line, trying to get a reasonable answer from WotC/Stainless re: why they've not released this for Android. Some of the chat is around 'platform fragmentation' - clearly this is affecting the Windows version too.
All told, I wouldn't recommend this game. Not on limited hardware, not with the server issues, and not on any Windows portable device. Shabby work all round. Stainless Games? Hardly.

I was really anticipating to play This War of Mine, but I wasn't hyped and I'm glad that I wasn't. Although I mainly complain in this review, you can see at the end why I still recommend it – I merely think that people should know the obvious flaws to have realistic expectations towards it. My playtime as of writing of this review: 34 hours for two playthroughs.
The setting itself for the game is the main selling point. From the official description:
„This War Of Mine provides an experience of war seen from an entirely new angle.“
„Make life-and-death decisions driven by your conscience.“
„During war, there are no good or bad decisions; there is only survival. The sooner you realize that, the better.“
There just aren't any similar games out there, so it was really refreshing to see something like this. But unfortunately, good intentions – in this case, showing the horrors of war – don't automatically make a great game.
The main problem I have with this game is that it's overly simple. You have to survive a number of days, and every day is always the same: In phase one of the day you start in your residence doing necessary stuff (cooking, resting, making tools) and in phase two you go scavenging. There is never a deviation from this. Sometimes little events happen during phase one, like people from the neighborhood (which you never see directly) make a request for help (which you can decide to help at your own cost or turn down), or a trader coming to barter.
Then there is stealing. You can make your life easier by stealing from other civilians, and you see the dilemma here, but it's inconsequential: You can steal from them, but there are no consequences regarding their well-being – they just continue to live on, as if nothing happened. Because of that, I sometimes stole a few things I really needed and had no regrets over this – why feeling bad for it, if they manage to survive without any problems?
Stealing from thugs on the other hand is morally acceptable in the game, but there are absolutely no consequences for you, besides the possibility they could kill you in the process itself. You would think they would reinforce their security after you steal once from them, but they don't. Also, they will never roam your neighborhood looking for you for example, even if you stole completely everything from them – pretty generous thugs, I guess.
And finally, my last gripe: A playthrough can simply get too long for its own good to complete. Like I mentioned before, the days have always the same structure and there are no real events, so after some time it can get really repetitive and suddenly even boring. In my two playthroughs, there was no “climax” which led to the end, so it can be just suddenly be over.
Because despite of all I listed it's not a bad game. On the one hand, there is the refreshing setting and it is polished in what it delivers. On the other hand, you can easily pick it up every now and then, because of the clear structure of the days – and every day takes only 15-30 minutes to complete. It also has rogue-like elements (regarding locations, length of the war, loot, characters you play as), which really adds a lot of replay-value.
It's a good time-waster and you can have fun with it (as much fun as one can have seeing civilians struggling in a war), but just don't expect it to be complex. Buy it if you're okay with the issues it has and if you'd like to support games with unusual themes.

If you're a fan of the serries like I am, there is one word to describe this latest installment: disappointment.
The game launched with more bugs than it has features. Added to these bugs are performance issues - but what is really disturbing with this latter is why it's there to begin with: The game is built on directx 9,  and a quick look into the config files, etc shows XBOX 360 commands all around.
Yes, the best way to explain why this game turns out to be so disappointing can simply be understood from that: it's a revamped down X game made having consoles in mind. The menus and controls reflect this (seriously, you don't even have keyboard shortcuts for targetting) and it takes out most of what made the X series what they were.
But it doesn't end there. You pilot one ship throughout the game (yes, only one) and if you have additional ships in your fleet, they can't even be in a different sector than you. So long for massive space empires. Given the AI is next to nothing, these ships stand and look pretty most of the time instead of firing their turrets or trading.
Ah yes, trading. Gone are the days you could dock at a station and trade directly. You have to assign a frigate you can't pilot yourself to do that and wait half and hour for it to dock and do it (you don't have seta). So when the lack of AI and major bugs get in the way, you curse having lost that half an hour and start editing the save file just for the game to keep running on.
Well, you would expect dogfights to be good since you have one ship - it would be optimized you'd think. No chance. Dogfights are sitting duck shoots whether you're fighting a cap ship or a small fighter. Again, it's an AI problem.
The big thing with this X game that we all were excited about was to walk around stations ... guess, how it turned out? Yes. a disaster. All stations have almost the same interior where all walking around adds to the game is to open crates and get minor items. Most war games focus on the heroism of a soldier that you are inevitable playing as. Not this one.
In This War of Mine, you follow a group of civillians who's lives have been shattered by the onset of a civil war. Every day is a struggle just to get food and supplies.
I originally went into this with the same mindset that I have when I play Fallout, another game that I get emotionally invested in. Big mistake. There are real consequences to your actions in this game. Rather than, as Total Biscuit put it, "press F to feel", you end up making choices that may save your group of survivors, but doom another group living in another part of the city.
On day 11, my survivors were starving. We had no food left and we can't exactly pop down to the corner store for a burger. I had to make a choice. Either allow my people to starve or take from other groups that are trying to survive the hellhole that their home had become. That night, I sent a scavenger out to a home that I hoped was abandoned, but still had supplies. Instead, I found two old people trying to just get by and live out the conflict.
I felt like a complete arsehat afterward. I had nothing to trade with them for food. My people needed to eat. Surely taking a little food won't hurt them? So I thought, as I picked the lock on their cupboard. I came back the next night, to scout the place again, make sure they weren't in deep♥♥♥♥♥♥from my actions the previous night.
They were dead.
The scavenger I sent out there blamed himself for it. He, and I, felt like a complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
This game emotionally invests you in it. It's not about the heroism and glory of war. It's about getting by and moving on.
Everything from the pencil shaded background, to the amazing sound design of the game immerses you in it terrifically.
If you are thinking of buying this game, do it. It is an amazing and terrifying experience.
8/10

So I really feel the need to leave a positive review for this game here to offset the negative, and to be honest, generally usless reviews that consists almost entirely of "the graphics are bad" or "no X-Men, no buy". Certainly, both of those are valid issues to be levied agaisnt the game, but ultimately Marvel vs Capcom Infinite is a good game that you should purchase if you enjoy Marvel, Capcom, or fighting games.
While the graphics are not as unique or even as objectively good looking as the style of Marvel 3, they are in my opinion, servicable. Some characters look better than others, and some look fantastic (Venom). If, however, you do find them unappealing then you should know there are some very easy tweaks that you can make to the game's .ini file to make the game look a bit nicer.
As far as the roster is considered, it is a mixed bag. On one hand, the roster is worse than MvC3 because some fan favorite characters like Wesker and Vergil are MIA, and of course, as are the Xmen. With that said, the roster is also stronger in some ways because we don't have characters like MODOK, Shuma Gorath, and Hsien Ko that many people did not like or understand their inclusion. The roster that we do have in the vanilla game is solid, with great characters to enjoy on both sides and the only questionable inclusions being Firebrand, Arthur, Spencer and Nemesis (in so far that Wesker would have been better from both a gameplay and thematic sense, as he is a direct antagonist to Chris).  The addition of the DLC characters makes the roster significantly better, with Sigma, Black Panther, and Monster Hunter all being great additions and Venom looks to be one of the best. With that said, I would not necessarily recommend the character pass at full price.
The gameplay itself is some of the best in the series, providing a distint experience from Mv3 that is both easier to learn and more fulfilling to master. I will criticize the lack of modes, with your only options being Story, Arcade (with no character endings), Missions, Practice (with a decent tutorial), and Online. The lack of character endings and any additional modes like survival, time, or even something like Heroes and Heralds is disappointing. With that said, Arcade is very enjoyable and there are enough people playing to find online competition (as long as you do so through the practice mode and enable match finding).
TL;DR, a good game with some flaws that you should get and probably will enjoy (so long as you aren't sworn to the Xmen)

I've recommended this game to a lot of people despite (still) not having finished it, I feel now I maybe shouldn't have.
I'm still enjoying it, there's enough Hitman going on for it to be a valid entry in the series, but there's also some stuff that's quite obviously Japanese-y as a result of the game being published by Square; this becomes more evident in act ii.
The level design really is the major failure of this game, once you get used to it and adjust appropriately its not a problem, but it cowers in Blood Money's shadow, and its sad that some of the Blood Money mechanics didn't make it into this game.  There have been levels in past games, also, that had no target, and the objective was mostly just to get to the end of the level; and those levels SUCKED, and they pretty much suck in this game (not as badly though honestly, its only prevalent if you're being a pacifist). Also, ♥♥♥♥ checkpoints, this is a stealth game which means lots of trial and error; if you screw up in this game and want to redo something, have fun replaying entire stretches in between checkpoints, which gets old really, really fast.  If you're willing to accept that some levels won't have an actual target, there's the setup and the escape for most missions that take place before and after the hit, then its mostly okay, works like any other stealth game really.
There are however a lot of little quality of life things that this game got better than even Blood Money did.  First off, you don't have to take someone as a human shield in order to non-lethally eliminate a person; in past games, you had a limited use sedative for such purposes, or in Blood Money there's the aforemenetioned human shield/pistol whip combo.  In Absolution, you have the option of putting someone in a chokehold and either knocking them out or breaking their neck - which you would think eliminates the need for the fiber wire, but garroting a target is faster and you are immediately dragging the body after strangling them, making it a useful tool where timing is of the essence. There are quite a few improvements along these lines.
All in all, I still find this to be a good game, and still would recommend it, but it isn't the hgh point of the series, that would be Blood Money - which you would think is a matter of opinion, but honestly anyone I've talked to that's played numerous Hitman games whole-heartedly agrees with that sentiment. But, if you're feeling the itch to be a top-notch assassin, this game can fill your needs as well as any Hitman game can, in my opinion.

To be honest, I originally wanted this game to fill the void of Diablo, and it did that, somewhat, but I just can't process some of the absurdly streamlined mechanics, or the way that a single drop can leave you overpowered for the majority of the game.... Torchlight torchlight torchlight. I remember when this game first came out. Remember too? The graphics were just plain ugly even back then.
Torchlight's history in short is that most of the Dev team worked on Diablo 1, 2 and every expansion in between. And that is exactly what makes Torchlight a complete failure.
From the very first second I played it, I didn't like anything. The style, the visuals, the setting.... It feels rushed and unfinished. Normally I do a Pro v Con list but there are no Pros here, so here are just the worst things about Torchlight.
- Linear Gameplay: I can't stress this enough, It may very well be the only thing that's absolutely wrong with this game but it's a big one. Ever played a 2D platformer, like Mario? Well that's just about as linear as you can get. Just go from start to finish, no deviation in between. To have something like that in a 3D game is...
Why? But that's what Torchlight is, constantly. You go down and then you follow the path, follow it, kill every enemy you see and keep following the path.
- Music: Well the town music is very similar if not the same as in Diablo 1 and 2. Because they hired the same guy to make the soundtrack. It shows, it isn't good. They probably thought that it'd be nice to have music that sounds the same as a far superior game. But by doing so, they hit the same note when an awful movie refers to a better movie during the movie.
- Classes: Three character classes...? This is an RPG right? What kind of RPG only has 3 classes? Maybe Torchlight isn't the only one, but it should be. There really isn't an excuse for that, most RPGs already have the same classes over and over. But Torchlight takes the most generic 3 classes too, Melee Ranged and Wizard/Summoner
None of which are any fun while running towards the next level down.
- Graphics: I'm not a graphic freak, I honestly don't care about them, choppy framerate? I'm probably the last person to notice, but these GFX?! No! Just no, why is everything squareish? Was the Dev team all like "We need something round but a dodecahedron is easier to draw." I don't think so, don't like it
Final verdict, Torchlight is nothing more than a Diablo clone. But I've played several clones in my day, this is by far the worst one. Torchlight feels like an empty vessel, like a game without a soul. It has no identity other than the one it tries to be. I heard that the sequel is far better.

Per below, the developer probably does not deserve the support for how this title was managed. You certainly should not pay more than $2-3 for it and it is old enough that you can probably find newer, better space mecha combat titles in the same price range.
1) Strike Suit Zero and Strike Suit Infinity are respectively the campaign and skirmish mode of one game, split up to sell on steam as two different titles. It isn't very obvious unless you have both, but once you understand that this was done, you may feel a little ripped off. Also, Infinity has slightly more replayability than Zero. Once you finish the campaign, the only thing to do in Zero is replay the same missions using slightly different loadouts. There are not enough options to really add any replayability there.
2) Both games have been abandoned with unpatched bugs by the developer, which changed its company name and went to work on the F2P Fractured Space.
3) Zero received a so-called 'Director's Cut' as a paid update which improved graphics at the expense of breaking shadows and also granted one armor ported from Infinity and one new armor design. Zero's Director's Cut had its own bugs and was also abandoned without them being fixed.
4) No mission editor. While Strike Suit Zero technically has a Steam Workshop, only a few mods are on it and the modding community for this game has long since been dead.
