This is a game/series that I always return to when I'm feeling stressed and need relaxing. It is a perfect combination of management(if you want to hire out help) and escalation as you build from a small farm up to one busting at the seams. The name explains most of the game, I don't really need to go into detail.  The only caution I would state is that for farmers, the game simplifies things. For example, the vanilla game has no reason to not drive on crops and makes planting as simple as following the combine with a planter as there are no seasons and no soil quality.
Don't see those as negatives though, the simplification is nice and makes the game a relaxing tractor driving game. It is all about farming and forrestry (if that's your thing) and while it isn't a true simulation, it is fun by itself.
While I would still buy the game by itself, it has a wonderful mod community and this is where the game really shines.
I was turned off from mods for a long time because I couldn't find any good ones. Trusted websites that have very good QA like
are few and far between.
is the only one I know of that tests every mod in depth for errors and glitches and makes that report publicly visible.  I highly recommend only using mods from either that website, or from a trusted modder that routinely puts out good work. There are many unrealistic/glitchy mods that are not worth the time and it can be frustrating to sift through them.  When new to the game, it can be overwhelminly depressing.
I recommend starting at FS-UK if you are new, and branching out from there.  It is also an active community with a wonderful suggestion forum for finding quality work not featured on that website.  Sorry if it seems a plug for FS-UK, but just trying to save those new to the hobby some trouble. There are many great mods outside of FS-UK, but I didn't find FS-UK until I'd been playing for years, so wanted to save new players the same frustration I had.

Magic Duels is a free-to-play Magic: The Gathering, which is always nice. You can spent money on micro-transactions if you want to. The platform is supposed to be the last Duels they release, and they will just update and add content to it. But the game's release hasn't been a glorious one.
This game had potential, yet it is held back by lack of quality and thought put into it. Wizard of the Coast wanted to promote this as the best Magic: The Gathering -video game till date. However, the game's marketing was a little confusing. I find it weird that they are going to release a game on different platforms, yet I at least didn't find a dedicated page for the game until the release date. How people are going to play your game if they don't know it's coming or even there? It's a minor issue, but it's still there.
One of the biggest problems are the servers. The game saves your progression and your coins to the cloud server, which you can only access if you are connected to the internet and the server. The problem lies in that the server after the release have been unstable.
Magic: The Gatherings magic is deckbuilding and gameplay. Those are what they did well, kind of. The gameplay itself hasn't changed much since the first Duels of the Planeswalkers in 2009. The best feature in the game is that you can freely customize your own deck from the cards you have. You can play that deck in Battle Mode to face AI bots or human opponents. The deckbuilding is only held back by lack of cards from which you can build your deck. The cardpool has most of the cards from the Origins set, since they left out some of the cards for reasons unknown (for example mana producing creatures). The starter pack that is given is a nice add but the some of the cards inside are generic and uninnovative, but they act as a nice starting point for the new decks.  Good thing is that you get Dual Lands and some decent cards for some strategies, but that's about it. When you play the game you are going to see lot's of similar decks and cards over and over again. Some cards from the Story Mode can't be seen in the main game at all, which is weird since they took the time to program them into the game.
Only way to get more cards is to buy boosters, which are buyed with coins you win from winning games. However you can only earn limited amount of coins per day, and it has been reported to bug as well, as with some of the cases the coin cap doesn't reset after the day. The boosters, which cost 150 ingame coin, has 6 cards inside, which is not much. The coin earnage is slow, and you can earn them only if you play against AI opponent or random opponent over the internet. Daily quests are nice touch and helps you get the coins faster but you get only 1 quest per day, and the coin amount you get isn't that much. Other option is to use micro-transactions, where you pay real money for those coins. It is a nice and welcome change to the game series. The game can still feel a little too grindy if you choose to earn everything without spending any money at times.
The new addition the game is the Skill Quests, that act as the game's tutorial. They popup when something new happens in the game for the first time. Then you can play a small tutorial mission to learn the game's interface, rules and get some coins by doing so. Good thing for a new player to learn the tricks. For the veterans, they are unnecessery. The skill quests appear at random times and sometimes at obnoxius times, or they might not even appear at all. Luckily you can access them in the options menu if you missed them or they didn't launch.
In Battle Mode you can play against computer opponents of your choses difficulty. The difficulty is mainly seen in the cards AI plays. AI makes random mistekes even on hardest difficulty, for example Hard AI attaches Infectios Bloodlust on my 0/2 Gatekeeper Vine... which has to attack every turn after that...if it wasn't a defender creature that can't attack anyway... The game generates a random deck against you each time you play, which adds some challange and versitility to the game.
The story mode was supposed to be the game's selling point. You play through the 5 planeswalkers origins story as you play as them. Lorewise it is enjoyble, for a short time. However, the pre-constructed decks for each of their missions makes it uninteresting, as the decks they are using are plainly said, uneffective. They propably wanted to add some difficulty and puzzle element to the game. However,  at times you may find yourself in a unfair situation where you are drawing bad spells and lands while you are trampeled by opponent that is nowhere near hard difficulty. The decks get upgraded after each mission, which basically just means few extra cards gets added to the deck. After you beat the Story Mode it has no replay value, as you get the rewards from the missions only once, after you beat them the first time.
In time, this game might get better. Wizard of the Coast has stated that when a new set is released they also add a new set of cards accordingly to the Magic Duels. The amount is limited and monitored, and the amount will be about 80% of the set, as it was with Origins-set. The planeswalker, the cards players have wanted to the game, are finally ingame. I just hope more planeswalkers gets added. More cards, more deckbuilding options, more different strategies and more fun. That being said, this game has potential, but it needs serious fixing. The AI is broken, and gameplay is very limited. Two-Headed Giant was a welcome addition, but Free-For-All multiplayer is missing, and that's what breaks my heart. I enjoy the multiplayer element of the game, the social aspect is very important in the real MtG, why it shouldn't be here as well.
I love Magic:The Gathering very much, and I wouln't want to do this. However, this game at it's current state is not a good representation of the legendary card game. But, behind all of it's pros and cons, there is a enjoyable game that needs polishing. That is why my review is mixed.

What I like most about this game is that each shot counts.  If you are even slightly injured, that injury doesn't just go away by replenishing your HP, you have to bandage the wound and have that person rest so it can heal.
Each death counts, if you kill someone else, it is a big deal, your characters become depressed and won't forget it.
Even stealing can leave you feeling bad for those electronic characters.
This game can really draw you in if you let it.  An example of what can happen, I sent Katia (one of the characters) to a supermarket, where she witnessed a soldier♥♥♥♥♥♥a woman.  After that she went from the optimist of the group to depressed.  Several days later I sent her to the bombed out school where she got caught looking through a homeless man's few possessions.  The man attacked her, but she had a knife, and in self-defense she killed him.  The next day she spiraled out of control and committed suicide.
About a week later a man named Anton stopped by.  He was a mathematician before.  Somehow he had been seriously wounded.  I let him into my group, gave him my only bandage, and let him sleep on the bed.  All my characters were sick, since it was the middle of winter at the time and I had no wood left and burned my last book, but I sent Arica to a military base with a bag full of moonshine and cigarettes to trade for food and medicine, she was shot dead.  Several days later, after Anton had recovered, he stole all our supplies and left.
By the end of winter my original three survivors were no longer surviving, I was down to an older lady and a mechanic, both of whom joined my group late game.  Every night raiders were successful at stealing from me, while my scavenging missions were less and less successful.  I briefly considered restarting the game there, both of my characters were sick, one was wounded and all I had left were two coffee beans, a lock pick and some electrical parts, but I realized their story had to end, even if they all died.  So I used that lock pick to open a dresser in a nice family's house where I found all their cans of food, components and medicine and I almost cried in real life, that was enough to get me by for the last several days.
Finally, around day 45, the war ended and I had two survivors.  Then the game played a montage of every good and bad thing I had done.  I was a little ashamed of some of the things I did, such as stealing from a defenseless old couple in the middle of winter.
Overall it was a great game, sure there was an occasional glitch and some game play aspects seemed clunky.  But no game has ever gotten me so involved in the story as This War of Mine.  I would definitely suggest it to anyone.

I was planning my moves for the next day before I fell asleep each night. I was taking notes. I spent an hour talking to a buddy about strategy.
I started looking at my neighbors houses, thinking about what kind of supplies might be in there.
I checked my own pantry to see what kind of canned foods we had in case if emergency.
This game invaded my life.
Playing This War is Mine really made me feel each decision.  I could see how stealing affected my survivors, how desperate I had to be to take a life, and how the psychological effects of my actions had real impact. When my last survivor committed suicide, It affected me in real life. I was actually upset.  I never emotionally connect with a game like this.
It is rare that I pay full price for a game. I feel this was worth the full price.
It is rare I tell other people to purchase a game. I convinced at least 3 other people to buy this game.
This War of Mine is crazy challenging, beautifully designed, artfully crafted, and a ton of fun to play. I have never felt such accomplishment when finishing a game as I did with this. (and I waited until I finished it before posting this review). I didn't even know IF there was an end. And I didn't care. I just wanted to survive.

If you love point-and-click adventure games enough to forgive the rough edges, you might like this one.
The best part of this game is definitely the artwork. The story is quite good as well. The environmentalist themes, although present throughout the plot, never get too preachy, and in the end the game comes across as a tale of personal redemption.
The puzzles are pretty solid. None of them are super far-fetched (I, for one, didn't feel the need to use a guide) but don't expect any huge moments of "A-ha!" either.
I would go as far as say the sound design is lacklustre. The soundtrack is held-back and sparse, there are sections with no ambience whatsoever, and some of the sound effects are, frankly, awful (the car engine sound, for example). The English acting simply doesn't work at all, playing with subtitles over the original German cast is recommended.
The game, although finishable, is buggy. Some translations are not tagged properly in the data files, occasionally showing bits of text in foreign languages (e.g. Russian). Also, I'm almost certain that a few hotspots don't show up and work 100% consistently.

X-Rebirth or "How to blow your franchise reputation in one release"... Well, the game is full of bugs and crashes, under resolution. But what hurt is beneath. As almost unanimously reported, X fans still don't understand why the devs went so wrong and so far from the original soul of the game. People was therefore welcoming the change of the UI, to something a bit more fancy and open.But to that ! To summarize :
- Great, a cockpit ! WHY Can't we see out of it !
- Awesome ! Bars and stations to land on ! WHY only 3 models ? Why so few interaction ? Why stupidly looting the same space suits and entertainment consoles ?
- Nice, lot of space craft traffick ! WHY just to queue and kill your frame rate ?
- Smart, the highways ! WHERE are the crafts appearing and disappearing from on it ?
- interesting, cockpit HUD - but where is the radar, the clear map, the command bindings ?
- One ship to fly with ONLY ? Cannot buy & sell goods at one central place ? Market place looks like a dead stock market with 2 lost guys on it ?
- 5 weapons (including mining laser) ? 3 missiles types ? so few upgrades for your ship !
X Rebirth is the best example of the long awaited game that comes totally out of purpose. Like they didn't tested it, like there was no Beta to get the awful feedback of the players. And this even more cause everyone was so looking forward to it.
Game updates will fix the crashes, but won't resolve the game lacks & faults. A huge rescript could, but I doubt the game will even allow it. That's a lost occasion to release THE space sim. Guess we can only hope now on the First (and probably best) one, Elite serie. Check out for Elite Dangerous, under dev and hopefully planned for 2014.
Let's hope Egosoft will learn from their mistake, stop thinking they can release a popular space sim to be sold on next gen consoles and just do what they know to do. Deep, complex, highly customizable and rich space sim.

It's real time now, and forces you to make use of each character's different roles efficiently and appropriately in order to defeat bosses. Roles and skill progression are interesting and makes combat a little more fun to play around with.
The story is decent, but the gameplay is very repetitive for most of the game: run, fight, cutscene. Rinse and repeat. With the exception of one chapter late in the game, there are no side missions, no chocobos, no open world or areas to explore, no mini-games, no story-altering choices. You just run in a hallway and fight and watch beautiful cutscenes.
Overall, the game feels stale after a while because you're just doing the same thing for 50 hours. Don't buy this game if you can't stand running in an enclosed hallway the whole game. The combat dynamics is the most interesting thing in this game, and really, the only thing you look forward to is the next boss and the next cutscene.

The title is something many of us have heard. Hell, its probably something that many players thought when they first came across Farming Simulator. This, however, is a fantastic game which I wholeheartedly recommend.
Having not played previous iterations of this series, I cannot really compare how far Farming Simulator 15 has come compared to its predecessors. FS15 however is an excellent, fun, relaxing game, in which you run most aspects of a farm from planting/harvesting fields to selling crops and raising farm animals.
The game mechanics work well, although the driving is perhaps a little clunky. Aside from this, I have not encountered any major problems with the way the game works - everything seems to work as intended, or at least nothing seems to significantly hinder my enjoyment of the game.
The game is further enhanced by a wide range of farming tools and vehicles that you can buy, and by a solid economy model which allows you to pick different ways to make money as a farmer. You are entirely free to do whatever you want at any given time - there are no clear objectives, and no timers unless you count plant withering and the missions you can take on in the game. This is farming sandbox at its purest.
The game takes on a new dimension when playing with friends. Online play works well, and allows players to come together to work on the same far. Many a time I decided to play "a bit" of farming simulator with a friend, before realising that I'd spent the past 5 or 6 hours harvesting corn fields.
Although I have little experience of it, the game seems to have an active modding community, which offers new maps, new trucks and game enhancements to refresh the game should you start finding it boring. Many of the mods seem alright in terms of quality, so do check them out if you buy this game.
A surprisingly fun game in which you might end up spending countless hours after having sneered at the concept. This is a solid, well designed game, which allows you to experience a wide range of aspects of farming life. The game is further enhanced by a wide range of tools/vehicles available and a solid, but perhaps basic, economic model which allows you to make money in whatever way you prefer. With no clear objectives/timers, this is a fine farming sandbox. Buy it.

I did not bother with the story. It appears you are just a pilot that is participating in a war and you act on mission objectives given, there is nothing more than that.
You control an array of planes depending on the given mission and you shoot down enemy units in a dog fight. You have 2 sets of weapons: The main gun and missiles. The main gun does consistent damage on the enemy while missiles does large amount of damage but needs time for them to reach their target. There are additional variations of weapons for the 2 main set of weapons. In my opinion, the weapon balance seems okay as every weapon has its pros and cons.
The controls are easy to learn but hard to master, easy in the sense where you can get used to the controls fast but difficult to completely avoid evenmy fire through evasive manuvures.
This game is playable with a mouse and keyboard.However, there is one major annoyance over the control is the fact that the mouse sensitivity of every machine you use is different, so everytime when i am required to use another plane in a new mission, the first thing i had to do is to go to the settings and adjust them. What should have been done was either to make sure that mouse sensitivity is consistent in every unit or make seperate options for each units.
Engaging in an epic fight in space was an awesome experience especially in the first 3 missions. In fact those were the best times i had in my entire playthorugh. I loved the shooting projectiles of the main gun, i loved the cluster missile movement and i loved how enemy interceptors get shot down.
Switching into strike mode is also amazing because they deal a ton of damage and the firing of rockets at multiple targets is very satisfying. The best part is that you can instantly dodge missiles and projectiles by just double tapping to do a short dash.
While i loved the experience of shooting down enemies, i really hated the mission layouts to the core. After enjoying sweet dog fighting in the first 3 missions, the rest of the game was essentially a speed run and I hate them in general. You have to complete your mission within a time limit before your capital ship explodes and you fail your mission. More than half of the play time clocked were spent retrying the mission only to fail again. I don't mind failing a mission because I got shot down, but failling a mission over something that you have little or no control over really pisses me off.
Another thing that I am extremely upset about is that the target system in this game is inflexible. They only target on the objective and completely ignores all other targets. This completely defeats the purpose of having ' target nearest enemy'   button when it continues to target a carrrier miles away when I was flying right beside enemy torpedoes. Due to that, an attempt to even delay the destruction of the capital ship was impossible.
A game that was initially enjoyable suddenly became stressful and irritating to play to the point that I took months break twice from the game.
To me, the game experience is mixed, while I loved one thing, I hated other things even more. Therefore, I feel that this game worth nowhere near $20.

Magic Duels is a free-to-play Magic: The Gathering, which is always nice. You can spent money on micro-transactions if you want to. The platform is supposed to be the last Duels they release, and they will just update and add content to it. But the game's release hasn't been a glorious one.
This game had potential, yet it is held back by lack of quality and thought put into it. Wizard of the Coast wanted to promote this as the best Magic: The Gathering -video game till date. However, the game's marketing was a little confusing. I find it weird that they are going to release a game on different platforms, yet I at least didn't find a dedicated page for the game until the release date. How people are going to play your game if they don't know it's coming or even there? It's a minor issue, but it's still there.
One of the biggest problems are the servers. The game saves your progression and your coins to the cloud server, which you can only access if you are connected to the internet and the server. The problem lies in that the server after the release have been unstable.
Magic: The Gatherings magic is deckbuilding and gameplay. Those are what they did well, kind of. The gameplay itself hasn't changed much since the first Duels of the Planeswalkers in 2009. The best feature in the game is that you can freely customize your own deck from the cards you have. You can play that deck in Battle Mode to face AI bots or human opponents. The deckbuilding is only held back by lack of cards from which you can build your deck. The cardpool has most of the cards from the Origins set, since they left out some of the cards for reasons unknown (for example mana producing creatures). The starter pack that is given is a nice add but the some of the cards inside are generic and uninnovative, but they act as a nice starting point for the new decks.  Good thing is that you get Dual Lands and some decent cards for some strategies, but that's about it. When you play the game you are going to see lot's of similar decks and cards over and over again. Some cards from the Story Mode can't be seen in the main game at all, which is weird since they took the time to program them into the game.
Only way to get more cards is to buy boosters, which are buyed with coins you win from winning games. However you can only earn limited amount of coins per day, and it has been reported to bug as well, as with some of the cases the coin cap doesn't reset after the day. The boosters, which cost 150 ingame coin, has 6 cards inside, which is not much. The coin earnage is slow, and you can earn them only if you play against AI opponent or random opponent over the internet. Daily quests are nice touch and helps you get the coins faster but you get only 1 quest per day, and the coin amount you get isn't that much. Other option is to use micro-transactions, where you pay real money for those coins. It is a nice and welcome change to the game series. The game can still feel a little too grindy if you choose to earn everything without spending any money at times.
The new addition the game is the Skill Quests, that act as the game's tutorial. They popup when something new happens in the game for the first time. Then you can play a small tutorial mission to learn the game's interface, rules and get some coins by doing so. Good thing for a new player to learn the tricks. For the veterans, they are unnecessery. The skill quests appear at random times and sometimes at obnoxius times, or they might not even appear at all. Luckily you can access them in the options menu if you missed them or they didn't launch.
In Battle Mode you can play against computer opponents of your choses difficulty. The difficulty is mainly seen in the cards AI plays. AI makes random mistekes even on hardest difficulty, for example Hard AI attaches Infectios Bloodlust on my 0/2 Gatekeeper Vine... which has to attack every turn after that...if it wasn't a defender creature that can't attack anyway... The game generates a random deck against you each time you play, which adds some challange and versitility to the game.
The story mode was supposed to be the game's selling point. You play through the 5 planeswalkers origins story as you play as them. Lorewise it is enjoyble, for a short time. However, the pre-constructed decks for each of their missions makes it uninteresting, as the decks they are using are plainly said, uneffective. They propably wanted to add some difficulty and puzzle element to the game. However,  at times you may find yourself in a unfair situation where you are drawing bad spells and lands while you are trampeled by opponent that is nowhere near hard difficulty. The decks get upgraded after each mission, which basically just means few extra cards gets added to the deck. After you beat the Story Mode it has no replay value, as you get the rewards from the missions only once, after you beat them the first time.
In time, this game might get better. Wizard of the Coast has stated that when a new set is released they also add a new set of cards accordingly to the Magic Duels. The amount is limited and monitored, and the amount will be about 80% of the set, as it was with Origins-set. The planeswalker, the cards players have wanted to the game, are finally ingame. I just hope more planeswalkers gets added. More cards, more deckbuilding options, more different strategies and more fun. That being said, this game has potential, but it needs serious fixing. The AI is broken, and gameplay is very limited. Two-Headed Giant was a welcome addition, but Free-For-All multiplayer is missing, and that's what breaks my heart. I enjoy the multiplayer element of the game, the social aspect is very important in the real MtG, why it shouldn't be here as well.
I love Magic:The Gathering very much, and I wouln't want to do this. However, this game at it's current state is not a good representation of the legendary card game. But, behind all of it's pros and cons, there is a enjoyable game that needs polishing. That is why my review is mixed.

This is an amazing game. It's great for playing with your friends, and for skirmishes with the AI. Unfortunately that's all there is to this game. Multi-Player and Skirmishes. There is no campaign, and that in itself is very disappointing. But don't let that put you off from buying it. It's gorgeous, challenging, entertaining, and loads of fun (albeit a bit difficult at times). Unlike Endless Space and Galactic Civilizations, Sins is real time. So every split second decision counts. The AI is a juggernaut of difficulty no matter what setting you have it on, so every little plan makes the difference of success or failure. Unless you're a master of strategy, this game will frustrate you at times. One moment you're blasting away at the galaxy, the next moment there are Titans coming at you from every angle.
There are lots of different research topics for each and every civ you choose, and each one is vastly different than the others. Ship options are quite large, and every ship has it's own abilities and strategic usefulness. The buildings have a build limit, until you start to expand your empire. Each new planet adds new resource bonuses, building caps, tech options, etc.
Unlike games like Age of Empires, Sins sort of forces you to expand and explore, otherwise you won't get the necessary amount of buildings certain research items require, the resources needed to build massive fleets, and so on. You also can't just sit around and let your stockpiles grow, build a battalion of ships, and expect to win in one attack. You'll soon learn that the enemy has already colonized 4 planets, each with it's own armada, and enough spare ships on it's way to wipe out your home planet.
Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion is an awesome experience, and a very challenging one. If you like that sort of thing, you will absolutely love this game. The only disappointing thing about this game is the lack of a campaign. Everything else is a work of genius, a real masterpiece. I highly recommend any RTS lover to buy this game right away.

Look at all these negative reviews and assume usual day-one MMO server faults. Now, neglect these reviews as irrelevant, because the game itself is beautiful, well-polished, fascinating MtG experience.
=
Stainless really got the hang of it through previous iterations (see "Duels of the Planeswalkers" series) and delivered finished product.
Interface is slickier than ever, every inch of your screen is used wisely. Fonts are sharp, lines are thin and curvy, cards are beautiful (as always).
Gameplay-wise there's new tutorial-like experience right inside your usual match, when you see some new mechanics and have a choice to launch voice-narrated practical tutorial for it. You get 2 regular quests (e.g. "win 4 duels with green-white deck - get 40 gold") and 1 community wide (for now it's "complete Liliana Vess campaign 35000 times", which is close to completion btw). You get gold for every single duel/battle so buying booster packs without spending RM is not a problem.

PS. Yes, there are still server side outages from time to time but it's getting better every hour in my experience. Instead of crying about (temporary) connection issues like everyone else, I'm going to try and give an objective review. I'm also going to be comparing the model itself to Hearthstone, as it's clear that this is intended to be a competitor.
This game is clearly an attempt to compete with Blizzard's Hearthstone. This is good, considering that if you look at pure numbers, Hearthstone is a terrible TCG. As far as digital TCGs go, this is a fantastic attempt. There are a few things that it's missing, mainly an ability to work towards specific cards. Hearthstone's mechanic of "disenchanting" cards to craft new ones is fantastic, and allows for you to weed out the abolute trash you will more than likely get out of a booster and turn it into something useful. In my limited MTG experience, I've found I prefer certain colors, and the ability to turn multiple cards of one color into a specific card of another color, for example, would be welcome. I haven't run into a situation where I have more than four of one specific card, mainly because I haven't been able to play for that long due to issues connecting to the servers, but I feel like buying boosters and ending up with more than four of a card could end up being a serious problem and make booster purchases less exciting than they could be.
As far as the gameplay goes, It's MTG. same as it's been for every other yearly release. Nothing to really discuss there. The gameplay tutorial may annoy folks who already know how the game works, but it's a tiny time investment (maybe two hours) that you won't have to repeat. It's particularly nice for new players, as it literally spells out how the game functions without you needing to read long tutorials or look up mechanics constantly. The biggest difference is the ability to earn gold while playing, which you can then spend on boosters. The issue is that there is a cap to the amount of gold you can earn per-day, essentially stunting your progress. Understandably, however, they want to keep people who have less time to sink into the game on a level playing field with people who have nothing better to do. This is fair.
Moving on to card selection, I really don't have anything to say, since I've only been playing MTG (casually) for the last three or so years, so I don't know about potential gamebreakers. There are cards that I've used before that it would be nice to see, but they're balancing the game around being a standalone digital TCG.
Here's a list for people who have no interest in reading:
PROS:
+It's MTG
+It's competing with Hearthstone
+The game functions as it should mechanically
+Deck Builder works great in comparison to the pre-set decks of the other yearly releases
+Music
CONS:
-(temporary) Server problems
-Gold Cap is annoying
-Card Selection is a bit small

Whenever I see a classic franchise turned into a game, I jump at the chance to get it. However, this game has made me question that policy, as it was disappointing in more than one aspect.
For one, the gameplay was painfully repetitive. You hack at enemies with staggering melee chains to deplete their tediously large amounts of health, and eventually score a "critical" slow-motion kill, with all such finishers being seen in the first five minutes. This would be all well and good if not for the waves upon waves of the same enemies in every battle, and reskins of the same enemies in every area. Virtually every enemy melee attack is slow enough that dodge-rolling out of them becomes literally half the game. Spells deal slightly above-average damage, yet they're incumbent upon leveling, are very few, have cooldowns, and can only be cast through the non-configurable and inconvenient number row.
The game is apparently intended almost exclusively for co-op, as your ally NPCs' AIs are complete crap. They focus in on one enemy and proceed to totally ignore everything else happening around them; This makes stealth impossible, and leaves the large bulk of the fighting solely to you. One of the only ways to heal is waiting for your mage ally to cast a protective field that very slowly regenerates health - this can be annoying if there are many enemies with high-power attacks chasing you, plus the field can apparently be broken by a strong melee area-attack, which quite a few enemies in each battle possess.
Additionally, although it may at first seem nice to have a semi-instant revive system, your allies are very stupid about using it: They will both run up to you regardless of how many enemies are in your vicinity, and proceed to get themselves mob-murdered, plus the revive will stop mid-way whenever they are hit by an area-attack, or by practically any projectile - making dying in a fight with a troll, a boss, or a few archers essentially irrecoverable. And even though your allies can remain in a near-death state infinitely, waddling about on their knees at random (making finding them at times annoying), you cannot, and game-over in a manner of seconds.
The equip system is also laughably level-based. You can fight three trolls and scores of enemies to retrieve a legendary bow, and in the very next area, find a cracked shortbow in a barrel with 2x better stats. On account of this, wasting hard-earned gold on buying anything other than health potions is a wasted investment, and it's basically pointless to slot elf-stones (item enhancements) until the end-game, when you've finally stopped switching out your entire armor every area. Your inventory is also constantly getting bogged down with what the game deems 'unessential items', which are literally that, and have no secret or quest purpose whatsoever beyond getting in the way of useful equipment.
The story is perhaps the only compelling thing about the game, but interacts badly with the mainline LOTR plot. For instance, when your party asks why you can't be part of the Fellowship, Elrond explains that the members must be stealthy and not necessarily powerful - when Aragorn, Legolas, and Gimli are basically the most badass warriors in the entire LOTR universe. The dialogue seems pretty forced as well, and can be difficult to follow unless you are versed in LOTR canon.
Beating the game unlocks the next highest tier difficulty to play on, but the game has so little replay value that it's hardly worth it. War in the North lacks substance mostly because of its absence of variety and configurability, and I can't say I'd recommend it to any sincere LOTR fan.

So I don't usually play point and click-adventures, neither am I a big fan of Daedalic's games. But this was on sale and since it's story seemed interesting, I gave it a shot.
The story starts out with an incredibly interesting situation and holds it's tension for the first half of the game - just to then completly fall off. Like seriously, how can they put such an mediocre ending to that beginning? And then end it with such a cliffhanger, even though the game most likely won't get a sequel?
The characters you meet are quite different, although most have no real depth to them and don't get much atttention on the long run. The puzzles are mostly easy, and can be skipped. The general interactions are very limited and sometimes obscure, as there is no highlighting for usable elements in the world.
And then there's bugs. Not many, but some so severe that you need to restart a whole chapter (which vary vastly in size btw).
The game cannot be configured and the drawn world is upscaled in fullscreen, but it's not scalable in windowed mode.
I'll give this game a thumbs down, not because I could not enjoy it, but because I'm sure there would have been better games as an intro for the genre. And because of the mentioned bugs, which shouldn't exist in a game of this size.
So should you buy this game? I'd say it depends.
+ Definitely, if you are a fan of the classical P&C genre and/or like Daedalic's stuff.
~ Yes, if it's on sale and you want a short and simple game with other than the typical "Good guy hunts bad guy"-story.
- No, if you are used to getting guided by games and/or prefer a story with more (visual) action. You should then rather watch out for some Telltale games on sale.

I bought this game upon it's initial 360 release and didn't really care for it. I must admit to you that I did make it to the end of the game but lost interest in completing it (saved and stopped just before the final boss). I simply was not invested in the game. So why recommend this game? I restarted playing from steam's sale. This time around I am invested and took more time to appreciate the story and character  development. Just as with most people saying, the game has a "hallway" feel until you reach a particular chapter. Being invested now, it makes sense. It simply follows the script and story nicely. It's not meant to be a race which is what I think most people wanted that rated down because of the "hallway" feel instead of being able to have an open world sooner. Had it been an open world, the story would not have worked. Being attacked by a WORLD's army or demigods... you don't have time to 'explore' when you should escape--which is what we're doing in the beginning. Taking my time, following the character development made me realize this game is amazing. FFXIII has it's flaws in battle and other areas but the "hallway" is done with intent for the betterment of the game experience, character development, story development and makes it more realistic--pulling you into the story. Hypothetical example of more realistic: "We need to escape before we're surrounded by an army". That does not interpret go grind 10hrs worth of levels. SE prevents this type of RPG mentality. MUCH appreciated!
Good:
+Story development
+Character development for ALL playable characters
+Personalizing characters to your play style
+Variety of character personalities
+Graphics are solid today
+Difficulty level--some bosses are extreme spikes to challenge your skill (ie.Juggernaut upon initial availability)

Bad:
- NPC AI is not consistent in battle (healer hip-to-hip on tank taking AoE damage: "MOOOOOVE, Hope, GTFO!" I wish I could pimp slap him at times)
- Paradigm shift animation needs to stop, just stop. Especially when 2 of 3 party members are NOT shifting. This has caused a few deaths on hard bosses (Juggernaut with spiked difficulty)
- Very few things in this game is easy to come by and at times it's unforgiving. (It's a double-edged sword)
In short, if you're rushing, you're doing it wrong.

I will start with the game looking very nice. Monsters look evil, levels are nicely laid out, blood and gore is everywhere. The secrets are very enjoyable, though the retro levels are visually painful and are more of a nostalgia than addition to the game. Overall though, this game makes some very poor decisions in regards to gameplay.
Insta-death falls are never fun and almost never add to gameplay in a positive manner. They weren't fun in Sonic, they weren't really fun in mario, they generally just aren't very fun, especially in games that take forever to revive the game tempo like this one. Fall damage goes along the same lines, especially when dashing down five feet of stairs can lead to the most halarious but stupid insta-death I have personally experienced. In a game that's susposted to be about fast paced crazy dash dodging while slicing, dicing, and putting holes in things it destroys any hype for the game I have when insta-death from a badly portrayed 3 foot fall.
Hitboxes feel wonky as heck. Flying monsters bodies are almost impossible to consistantly hit, but you know what is consistant: their feet! Lower imps have this slow lazy dodge roll that the bullets just seem to disapear through them. The reticle is more a sugestion rather than an indicator. It almost feels like this game was thinking about having ironsights and full tactical aiming, but then remembered that it was susposted to be emulating the classic shadow warrior and threw that to the side.
And while I like the take on the story to explain why the demons are there, the gameplay is just kinda there. If I wanted enjoyable paced crazy then I can play wolfenstein the new order. Shadow Warrior Remake just doesn't quite reach that level of fun, it just feels like a chore to me.

The funnest flight/space sim I've played since Rogue Squadron on the N64—similar structure too.
You'll get the basic patrol mission stuff to start, then you're slowly introduced to combat. The missions are relatively straightforward to begin with. Like Rogue Squadron, eventually the missions start evolving halfway through—simple missions become heated dog fights as enemy reinforcements arrive.
The learning curve is a bit steeper than something like Rogue Squadron though; there are a lot of dynamics involved that the game trains you in at a good pace. This is how it's supposed to work.
I definitely recommend a gamepad. I'm a keyboard user, but this is the sort of thing gamepads are built for. By the last missions, you'll be twitching and flicking buttons without hesitation or thought.
One more thing that makes this fantastic: the soundtrack. The blend of synthetica, ambients and old school woodwinds gives you something along the lines of space-age maritime music. I can't quite nail it down, but they definitely nailed the mood. Cruising towards the black fleet to the harrowing tune of a clarinet (oboe?) doesn't seem awesome on paper, but it is.

Ok so I was a complete noob with 4X (and RTS) games, and picked this up on the Steam sale over GalCiv2 and Endless Space purely because it seemed to have features from both but better graphics and real time features.
And boy am I glad I decided to get it!!! It is a great game - deep and engaging and a deep experience compared to the mindless "go here, kill everything" that permeates the RPG and FPS genres these days.
You can play this on your own against a very well written AI (with only one or several opponents of varying skill levels) or you can play online. It is real time, but you can also pause the game to take your time and issue orders after thinking about your next move. You can micro manage your units or you can leave them on "auto" to do their own thing without bogged down on details (although this will get you smashed by the AI on even normal difficulty settings!).
Maps can be huge or small, auto-generated or pre-defined and it is always a blast flying into the unknown searching for and colonising planets. The UI interaction is great and very well implemented.
To get the most of it however, I strongly suggest dedicating some time reading the wiki, and watching some tutorials on YouTube (there are good series by TzuCraft and GetDaved). They will really make you enjoy it a lot more.

Don't waste your money on this game. It's already discounted for 33% off because of poor sales; but if you want the full game you'll need to drop a ridiculous amount of money on DLC anyway, so what the discount actually saves you is closer to 2%.
Gameplay:
The game is actually pretty fun. They dumbed down some of the controls from previous installments, but it adds a new instant tag out system and still boasts an extraordinary amount of depth. Unfortunately, not all of the new inclusions are as fun in higher level play.
The instant tag out system makes it so you're always safe no matter what you do, and playing against strategies that abuse this (every strategy) can be really frustrating. Push blocking is extremely important in this game, as every team can put you in infinite block-strings, and perform infinite mixups without ever giving you a chance to punish.
Some pro games seemingly consist almost exclusively of mashing the tag out button. This isn't very fun to play or watch in my opinion.
I'm certainly not a pro player so take the above with a grain of salt; it's just my experience with the game and watching a few tournaments.
Story Mode:
The "story mode" is a joke. It's bad fanfiction at best. It lasts a few hours, and 80% of that time is either watching garbage cut-scenes or playing against rinse and repeat "ultron bots" or "corrupted asgardians." On top of that, just to mess with us, you can plainly see the finished DLC character models in story cut-scenes that you'll need to spend another $40 to actually unlock.
Online:
The online mode is mediocre, and barely anyone has the game, so finding a match can take anywhere from a few minutes to a few dozen minutes. It has decent netcode, but disconnects make you wait 2-3 minutes staring at a frozen screen, and then treat the game as though it didn't happen. This really gets frustrating as people have DC'd right before losing in around 10 of my matches thus far (That's around 30 minutes of doing nothing). The "ranking" system is also terrible. It goes from 15 to 1. There are no meaningful rewards.
Mission/ Practice Mode:
Mission mode is there and offers 10 missions per character. It's not bad, but around half of the missions involve tag combos, sometimes teaching you nothing about your character. The practice mode is there and it has what you'd expect; you can queue for online while in practice mode.
DLC:
No surprise here; content is blatantly ripped out of the core game so they can sell it to us as character/costume packs for ridiculous prices at a later date. They really have absolutely no respect for their customers at all.
Voice acting/ Character models/ Game presentation:
Some of the character models in this game are disgusting. The game itself looks like it belongs on mobile. The voice acting makes playing certain characters impossible (Monster Hunter). Animations are recycled from previous games, but instead of recycling quality voice acting, they hire a bunch of homeless people to redo it.
Pros:
- Fun game
- Decent online netcode
Cons:
- Mechanics are easily abusable
- Everything else about online sucks
- Nobody plays the game
- It's overpriced
- DLC ripped out of base game
- Half the character models look like trash
- Most of the voice acting is terrible
- Bad story mode

*Update*
I've been playing Magic: Duels for a bit since it's release. The game now  consistantly connects to servers without fail. Since the initial problems have been fixed, I am changing my recommendation from negative to positive. The building blocks of a good card game are here. People can now dive in with no issues.
________________________________________________________________________________
Original Review
I have played Magic PC games since 2013. I cannot recommend this edition to anyone. The game tracks a player progress and awards them in-game currency. The problem is that most of the time the game cannot connect to Magic servers. This forces the player to decide between playing without any in-game benefit or turning off the game and waiting for the servers to be fixed. A game that has such a heavy reliance on online connectivity should not have servers that are offline more than they are online. As of the time I am reviewing it, Magic Duels is a broken game that is not ready for players.
There are good points to this game. Deck building is accessable for beginners and experts. There are optional skill quests for players to utilize. The one-on-one battles are fun. There are interesting story quests that give backstory to familiar characters. Everything that players like about "Magic The Gathering" is here.
As a fan of the series, I wish I could recommend this to other fans. During it's release weekend, there have been multiple times that I loaded the game and turned it off because the servers were offline. It is impossible to recommend a game when it's "always on" component is so often not functioning. Hopefully this will be fixed soon.

Pros: Graphics, Sound, Gameplay
Cons: Story, Controls, Multiplayer, Bugs
From the reflections in the rippling water to the slow-moving fog that crawls atop the jungle, Crysis' graphics are not only incredible but easily enjoyed on high to very high on most new computers.  The music and sound is equally impressive, with 5.1 surround sound.  Crysis offers many refreshing ways of tackling its missions in the first half.
However, the story gives little time to interact with any other characters, let alone care for them.  An abrupt twist in both the plot and gameplay leaves more to be desired.  The controls are good in many ways, but clunky in many others, for example, toggle aim but no hold-down, hold-down sprint but no toggle.  Unfortunately, multiplayer has been shut down and a number of bugs will never be patched.
Lacking both story and multiplayer, Crysis offers very little that newer shooters can't.

Anyone who has heard of Crysis knows it is still heralded to this day as a benchmark for graphics. Based on the Cry Engine 2, even now it is absolutely stunning.
But more importantly its actually a brilliant game all round. The story is pretty standard, you are a special force operative kitted out with a "Nano Suit" which allows you to perform as a super soldier, whilst on mission you discover an Alien species which are plotting to invade the world (or so it seems). Voice acting is pretty good, the facial mapping is OUTSTANDING!
But the key point that won this game for me was the true freedom it provides you in how you play. The map is very open, leaving it up to the player how you approach each objective. You can switch your suit to max armour and plow straight through the next check point murdering people left right and centre... you could turn on your optic camoflage and sneak through without a soul knowing, you could buff your strength, pick up an explosive barrel, hurl it at the building and watch the Crytek physics bring the roof down upon your foes. It really gives you the freedom to play it in a way that suits you and that is why I would recommend Crysis.

Playing this game locally is very fun, and I have done so on many occasions with friends. However, the big issue I have with this game right now is with its ranking system online. If you're just an average player, you'll either be matched with someone who is ranked significantly lower than you are or you will be matched with someone who is ranked significantly higher. I have rarely been paired with another player whose ranking deviated from mine by 30 ELO points or less. So needless to say you'll either be bored playing someone who doesn't have a ranking comparable to yours or you'll be frustrated by getting destroyed by someone who is light years ahead of you in ranking and overall skill. Furthermore, the community is fairly small so don't count on getting a lot of lag-free matches if you're outside the U.S., especially if you live in Asia or Australia.
The gameplay on its own is fantastic and takes me back to when I first got interested in Smash Bros. Melee. But there are just so many glaring issues with Online gameplay that I can't say that the game is worth it right now. If you aren't prepared to spend several hours a day getting better at this game, don't bother or wait until issues such as the ranking system have been fixed because the way ranking is structured now, newbies will be obliterated. The game may look bright and colorful and welcoming but to say that this game is newbie friendly (particularly online) is an absolute misnomer. Like all Early Access Games, proceed with caution on this one. Rivals of Aether has so much potential and I will change this review if it starts to live up to that potential, but right now I can't recommend it.

Tail Mission, The Game
After a promising start, by chapter 8 the game disintegrates into a hodgepodge of bad level design and listless characters.
I think I played 9 tail missions in a row before I rage-quitted just now. And it's all the same nonesense: you follow a group of characters, skirting the bushes, and trying to avoid enemy soldiers. At some point the game draws a circle around them and you have to stay inside of it. A few seconds away from it and you die and have to restart from an earlier checkpoint. The circle is for "eavesdropping", but you don't really get a chance to listen in because you're distracted.
The fighting is another infuriating mechanic: it's a button mashing marathon and RNGeezus decides how fast you kill. You might walk up and shank two guys, instantly killing them, or you might twirl like a moron for half a minute. Seriously, one time I mashed an UNARMED guy with my two swords for nearly a minute before he finally died. Stupid.
You can rake corpses for bullets, but not during ship boarding. You can also rake for them during fortress capture, but not after you killed the couple of guys you're meant to kill. You can hold your breath for minutes in underwater salvage missions, but not while sneaking around in water. It's open world! But you constantly ram into "area unavailable" walls, because you didn't play some mission yet. You can climb buildings and hide in the bushes, but you can't walk through invisible wall between two trees during a tail mission. GRRRR! The tail missions! Lazy.
This is what this game is: lazy and rushed. All just to churn out yet another Asscreed game. Throw in some enemy soldiers, make two models walk a path, record 30 seconds of pointless dialog, and you got yourself a tail mission. Tail Mission, The Game.
Don't waste your money.
(P.S.: you can leave your game open round the clock and Steam will still count the hours as "played"; I'll be damned if I'd wasted 300+ hours on this turd, it was a lot less)

is a Point & Click adventure game. At the turn of the 26th century, mankind is about to be extinct as the last few hundred left won't survive the next solar flare. Sent back in time to prevent a climate catastrophy, Radio-operator Fay approaches Bent Svensson, a retired physicist, in hopes that his work an algae-based power source could save the world.
The story is interesting, having a slightly dark tone to it. You alternate between characters, viewing the story through their eyes, or through the way they tell their story. All cut-scenes are comicbook-styled boxes and text bubbles, while the gameplay scenes all appears hand-drawn in the most classical fashion of Point & Click games, topped with often dramatic tone-setting music. You must regularly interact with the environment and/or your inventory to solve puzzles, while standalone single-screen puzzles may be skipped after a few attempts, for those who want to.
The immersion is totally broken by the bad voice acting. The voices themselves would portray the characters fine for the most part while other times it's just silly, but the lack of any conviction in the way the dialog is so blatantly read directly off the script is what kills it. There are sync problems with the cutscenes, with reading pauses when the text changes line, sometimes even in mid sentence! There are a few translation glitches in some subtitles or interactions, and in a variety of languages, too (I saw some French and I believe some Russian, while playing the English version). The sprite animation is very frame-by-frame and not very smooth.
★★★☆☆ - It's up to you
I may have been harsh on the game's technical and audio flaws, but I nevertheless enjoyed my ride through the story. Sometimes optimistic, sometimes bitter, the game really made me wonder whether it would have a happy ending or not. In the end, I do recommend this game to anyone who wants to find out for themselves.

I originally bought X Rebirth because it looked like a new direction for the series, and I am generally a fan of open world sandbox type games.  So, despite not liking the series prior to this, I decided to give Rebirth a shot.  If you haven't figured it out by now given that my opinion on this game aligns with the majority, that was a mistake.  X Rebirth is an absolutely terrible game.
Normally I would present the good things about the game first, but it's late as I write this, and I feel compelled to warn people away from this game so they don't waste their time or money.  So, the bad stuff:
*Terrible character models - The character models are easily one of the worst features of the game; something I would've considered passable 10 or so years ago.  For today's technology, they're absolutely unacceptable.
*Bad (limited) dialogue - I would normally say that the voice acting is bad, but I don't think it's (usually) the fault of the actors.  It seems like they only recorded a few lines, then Egosoft used them over and over (and over) again, which removes any hint of depth from the world and constantly reminds you that you're playing a game, not taking part in a story or immersing yourself in another world.
*Confusing UI - The game's interface is a mess.  In combat, target arrows hover around the edge of your ship's windshield, and are small enough that they're easily lost if you're in a crowded area.  Out of combat, trying to buy or sell anything was a pain as well, as the sliders you need to use are flipped - you have to slide it to the left to buy and to the right to sell.
*Bad mission design - Missions sometimes give you indicators that don't really indicate where you need to go.  The absolute worst case of this was in part of the story mission.  The mission indicator had me flying clear to the other side of the galaxy when I needed to stay where I was and buy something first.
*Bad world design - In a game that gives you a whole world to play in, having vendors that are procedurally there or not is a terrible idea when you're trying to find something.
*Broken systems - Hiring an engineer and having him/her work aboard your ship is supposed to enable that NPC to repair your ship on the fly.  That doesn't happen.  You still need to find an engineer in a base and dock.
It's fair to say by now that I could go on and list even more failings found in this game, but I think that's sufficient bashing.  Now for the good points:
*Moddability - This is the sole reason I have not uninstalled this game already - it can be modded.  They've already made a mod to shut the co-pilot up, so there's one step in the right direction.
*Interesting concepts - The idea of a highway in space is interesting, even though it would be impossible in real life (orbital mechanics would prevent structured travel channels like that from working).
*Stations - I may be alone on this, but I actually like the idea of getting out of your ship and walking around.  It's more immersive (or it would be if the character models weren't so terrible).
*Combat - Despite only being able to fly one ship, I didn't hate the combat.  It felt smooth; not too easy and not too hard.
*Space art - Stations were appropriately large and interesting to look at.
*Potential - The idea of taking control of part of the galaxy, building your own space stations and amassing a navy is very tempting.  Supposedly these things are all possible, but I have yet to see any of them for myself.
So, that's pretty much it.  Still, if you really want to try it, WAIT a few weeks.  The price will undoubtedly drop pretty soon, and that way your wallet won't hurt as much as mine does.  If you're at all on the fence, though, I CANNOT STRESS HOW *VERY* STRONGLY I recommend avoiding this game until you can try it at a friend's house (or until they release a demo, if they do at all).  See what I mean?  I put that last bit in all caps and asterisks.  I'm that serious about it.

I played this game for longer than I probably should have.  Strangely engaging for a while but this game has no surprises at all.  It's exactly what it looks like, exactly what you think it is.  Here are some good things:
* Realistic looking equipment.  I wouldn't know how accurate this stuff is, but it's how I imagine this stuff would look.  Very fine details.
* Time destroyer.  If you have too much free time on your hands, you can waste quite a lot of it here.
*  A wide range of farming and farming related equipment to admire.
Now for my many gripes:
* The AI gets stuck on anything and everything.  They can't figure out how to back up and go around stuff even a little.  You really need them though, so you spend a good bit of time baby sitting them.
*  Buggy trees.  The logging is a cool part of the game, but often very frustrating.  Making my wheel loader flip 50 feet into the air was pretty funny though.  Really the whole process of logging could have used some fine tuning, or just a way to feed stuff into the chipper automatically.
* Cryptic.  The tutorials don't explain much and you are left to walk alone.  The store menu is pretty pathetic, they should have included more info on each piece of machinery and explained them a little better.
*Speaking of purchases, this game has a lot of DLC.  I can't find any mods on Steam, but there is sure a  lot of DLC.  Considering that buying new equipment is the ENTIRETY of the goal in this game, I feel that this DLC is especially terrible and stupid.
*Everything.  The "career" mode isn't a career mode at all, the missions are a joke.  It' s a sandbox with no goals of any kind.  I really wasn't looking for much in this area, but there is just nothing.  Once you've bought the best equipment there is no incentive to actually use any of it.  The game is over at that point.
This game is close.  It's so close to being actually fun to play, but I just can't recommend it.  Needs just a pinch of endgame, or plot, or something to keep it interesting.   Basically, if you really like looking at tractors, this is the game for you.  If you like grinding for hours toward a goal that is increasingly ethereal and pointless, here you go.

Runic Games pushes the boundaries of RPG genre by providing a unique dungeon generation experience. Torchlight uses standard mechanisms for character development, but combines them in a unique experience that provides a fun and dynamic game.
In the relatively small town of Torchlight a mysterious element has caused a bundle of trouble. A special mineral known as Ember, popular for its unique traits, has been corrupted by a dastardly foe. A giant monstrosity has released his evil across the land and has corrupted the Alchemist known as Alric. It is up to you to fight through the layers of the mine and free the town of Torchlight from the evil daemon Ordrak who is forged from the ember the mine withholds.
Torchlight provides a relatively linear campaign filled with irrelevant quests that essentially provide a long-winded grind. The main story consists of 35-floors of a mine where each floor generally resembles the next with minor changes to the environment and foes held within. As you battle through the floors the enemies’ levels do not scale with the player; although, they do maintain a good consistency with the player’s level.
To help separate the campaign each group of floors are bundled into segments that have portals connecting them: Orden Mines, Necropolis, Estherian Ruins, Tu’Tara Caverns, Molten Prison, Lost Fortress, Black Palace, and Lair.
Each segment of the campaign contains a main boss which provides a unique battle experience that tests the player’s fortitude and skill.
Torchlight offers a unique mixture of gaming by providing a generated dungeon element similar to Spelunky with a combat system such as Diablo the game provides a unique experience with each champion play through. In my personal opinion the campaign has little to no replay value when playing the same champion twice as the generated dungeons, although different are relatively the same.
Similar to a standard RPG Torchlight provides classes that offer different combat styles: Alchemist, Destroyer, and Vanquisher. The Alchemist is your standard mage class and plays off magic attribute. The Destroyer is your standard fighting class and plays off strength. The Vanquisher is your standard hunter class and plays off dexterity.
The gameplay elements are rather cumbersome and can be infuriating at times. There will be more times you will perish because of poor game mechanics than difficult curve. The player is required to move and fight by left-clicking with the mouse. This causes a lot of times where the players champion will run into battle when you actually just want to shoot from distance, this can also be annoying especially with fast moving and smaller enemies.
I played Torchlight after beating Torchlight II – this game is fun, but some elements are missing which cause the campaign to drain rather than provide enjoyment. The campaign is formatted in a way that seems like a grind rather than progression. The levels offer very little dynamics, meaning one portion of the campaigns play through is relatively similar to the next. Overall this game is relatively fun, and provides a good bit of enjoyment. It is a single player game and I’d really recommend getting Torchlight II over Torchlight, but if you are interested I’d say try to get this game when it’s on sale.
Pros:
+Lots of gameplay – estimated 40+ hours.
+Unique character class with dungeon generation which causes acceptable multi-play through.
+Pet which provides decent dynamics and intelligent character building.
+Once the main campaign is completed the game goes on.
+Two types of leveling: Fame and Experience. Fame gives you points to level your special abilities, while experience gives you points to level both special abilities and character states.
+Amazing item diversity and item building. Enchanting items allows them to become stronger which makes key items very powerful and effective for building a highly custom character.
Cons:
-Poor controls moving and attacking utilize the same button.
-No multiplayer
-Pets stats are relatively low making them not entirely tank or damage.
-Limited tutorial, this isn’t really that bad unless you are not averse to gaming.

The game is very fun at places, but has lots of boring bullet sponge enemies that either enrage more minor enemies to berserk you or revive those minor enemies. Sometimes those two types of bulelt sponges team up. Is running around in circles for two to five minutes firing your weapons at a big bad guy while about 20 little bad guys run at you fun? I don't think so.
The worst culmination of this design philosophy for me was the second major boss fights in or after chapter 11: You have this impressive titan of a boss that could be fun to fight but it has been made the most tedious thing it could be. First you stand on one of three seals for a minute while it deactivates, while the titan is standing far away shooting generic light balls and chained together light balls at you. You dodge, go back to the seal, stand, then dodge. Next you have to shoot the titan in its glowing chest for a minute or so, after which he reveals his weakspot to you forabout  10 seconds. You have to get in place in the right angle in that time, do what damage you can, then go back to chest shooting (while you dodge some light orbs and occasional spear charges).
Once you whittle down the health of the weakspot, you go stand on another, dodge some light balls, you know the drill. Then you shoot him in the chest, try to get to his weakspot. It's the same stuff as phase one, and the first phase alone takes what feels like a loooooong time. With phase two though, the titan gets a spear attack that has the exact same animation as a spear swing in the first phase, but this time it's more accurate and kills you from 80% health (max you can heal to without med packs) in one hit. Once you die, you go back to phase one. Now, I was playing on hard, and I don't mind sudden deaths on hard for me being careless, but being punished by having to repeat a long stretch of tedium just isn't fun.
The game is riddled with similar weird, old fashioned and for-good-reason-abandoned design choices, like generic green explosive ball that you have to destroy one by one while traversing a hall way. They don't add anything to the universe, they don't add anything to the gameplay (just keep your eyes open, aim, shoot, wait for the explosion, move on, repeat), the only thing they do is slow down progres in a game that actually excells in fast paced combat.
Oh, and the humor in the game is positively gringe worthy, but I know some people like that sort of thing.

More than half a decade has passed, but Crysis still impresses with its gameplay and graphics, though the it stumbles in its second half. In Crysis, you play as a soldier equipped with a nanosuit that lets you switch between 4 powers (Armour, Speed, Strength and Cloak) which, when combined with technically linear yet impressively large and open levels, provides many ways to approach situations. Throw in vehicles (which aren't that nice to control but are still fun to drive and blow up), destructible environments and ragdolling and you have a wonderful FPS experience... for the first half of the game. The second half of the game replaces the North Koreans with aliens as the main enemy and abruptly replaces its large levels with standard linear fare. It's pretty decent at first, but uninteresting alien combat and generic missions soon dull the experience. If that wasn't enough, an annoying escort mission, a potentially engaging VTOL sequence marred by crappy controls and an underwhelming final level pop up to turn an average second half into a tiring and fustrating experience that sits at odds with the not quite perfect but still sublime first half. Despite all these issues, the first half alone make Crysis worth the purchase, if not as a standalone product then at least in the Maximum Edition bundle, which includes Crysis Warhead.

I originally bought X Rebirth because it looked like a new direction for the series, and I am generally a fan of open world sandbox type games.  So, despite not liking the series prior to this, I decided to give Rebirth a shot.  If you haven't figured it out by now given that my opinion on this game aligns with the majority, that was a mistake.  X Rebirth is an absolutely terrible game.
Normally I would present the good things about the game first, but it's late as I write this, and I feel compelled to warn people away from this game so they don't waste their time or money.  So, the bad stuff:
*Terrible character models - The character models are easily one of the worst features of the game; something I would've considered passable 10 or so years ago.  For today's technology, they're absolutely unacceptable.
*Bad (limited) dialogue - I would normally say that the voice acting is bad, but I don't think it's (usually) the fault of the actors.  It seems like they only recorded a few lines, then Egosoft used them over and over (and over) again, which removes any hint of depth from the world and constantly reminds you that you're playing a game, not taking part in a story or immersing yourself in another world.
*Confusing UI - The game's interface is a mess.  In combat, target arrows hover around the edge of your ship's windshield, and are small enough that they're easily lost if you're in a crowded area.  Out of combat, trying to buy or sell anything was a pain as well, as the sliders you need to use are flipped - you have to slide it to the left to buy and to the right to sell.
*Bad mission design - Missions sometimes give you indicators that don't really indicate where you need to go.  The absolute worst case of this was in part of the story mission.  The mission indicator had me flying clear to the other side of the galaxy when I needed to stay where I was and buy something first.
*Bad world design - In a game that gives you a whole world to play in, having vendors that are procedurally there or not is a terrible idea when you're trying to find something.
*Broken systems - Hiring an engineer and having him/her work aboard your ship is supposed to enable that NPC to repair your ship on the fly.  That doesn't happen.  You still need to find an engineer in a base and dock.
It's fair to say by now that I could go on and list even more failings found in this game, but I think that's sufficient bashing.  Now for the good points:
*Moddability - This is the sole reason I have not uninstalled this game already - it can be modded.  They've already made a mod to shut the co-pilot up, so there's one step in the right direction.
*Interesting concepts - The idea of a highway in space is interesting, even though it would be impossible in real life (orbital mechanics would prevent structured travel channels like that from working).
*Stations - I may be alone on this, but I actually like the idea of getting out of your ship and walking around.  It's more immersive (or it would be if the character models weren't so terrible).
*Combat - Despite only being able to fly one ship, I didn't hate the combat.  It felt smooth; not too easy and not too hard.
*Space art - Stations were appropriately large and interesting to look at.
*Potential - The idea of taking control of part of the galaxy, building your own space stations and amassing a navy is very tempting.  Supposedly these things are all possible, but I have yet to see any of them for myself.
So, that's pretty much it.  Still, if you really want to try it, WAIT a few weeks.  The price will undoubtedly drop pretty soon, and that way your wallet won't hurt as much as mine does.  If you're at all on the fence, though, I CANNOT STRESS HOW *VERY* STRONGLY I recommend avoiding this game until you can try it at a friend's house (or until they release a demo, if they do at all).  See what I mean?  I put that last bit in all caps and asterisks.  I'm that serious about it.
