It's always been a little odd to me that an idea as freaking cool as mecha has be so minimally explored in games.
I guess the easy answer for that would be because making a quality mecha game is a lot harder than it sounds, which Strike Suit Zero exemplifies even as it comes possibly closer than anyone to pulling it off. In the same breath it also attempts to revitalize space combat shooters, again succeeding to a commendable degree yet still failing to shake the nagging issues that quickly present themselves. Strike Suit Zero's potential and ambition never wanes, but that doesn't stop its aspirations to come crashing down when they collide with reality.
Strike Suit Zero as stated before, is a merging of large scale space fighter-pilot combat and screen filling mecha insanity, by way of the titular Strike Suit which can transform between a fast, maneuverable ship and the extremely power mecha form. The dynamic of swooping around picking off stray fighters and then switching forms to annihilate larger enemies is strategic but also just super cool, making you feel like the all-powerful terror your enemies supposedly see you as and gives developer Born Ready Games an excuse to blow the particle effects out during massive space battles that if nothing else are incredible to look at.
There's a weight to your ship that feels powerful, but without the limited mobility that often comes with higher firepower. It's balanced by requiring you to charge up your ship by killing enemies before you can transformed, and this limited fuel makes combat fast and frantic, as you chain together attacks to keep your meter full while trying to keep track of the situation. Strike Suit Zero excels at making you feel like just one small part of the giant battles going on around you, but still one capable of destroying giant cruisers and chasing down fighters.
Unfortunately Born Ready Games has flown a little too close to the sun as the scale of the game quickly seems to get away from them, and the experience as a whole suffers quite a bit for it. Pacing is on of Strike Suit Zero's biggest opponents, and a concept it's fairly unconcerned with. Early missions are plodding, slow excursions as stiff bombing ships before you're given the Strike Suit, but even after missions have a tendency to stretch on and on as they continue to pile on new objectives which look very much like the last. Mission variety is virtually nonexistent, giving you largely the exact same scenarios each mission but ratcheting up the difficulty to uncomfortable levels.
These difficulty spikes and the unequaled number of checkpoints intensifies the lack of mission variation, which may have gone unnoticed for awhile but becomes hard to ignore when you already had to complete said objective dozens of times do to some untimely deaths. The vagueness with which objectives are explains only makes things worse, often overwhelming me with different tasks to where I didn't even know how to start or simply saying one thing while expecting me to infer the actual objective myself, usually by watching my ship explode and then reloading to hopefully get it the second time. Or the third. Or the forth. That's if I'm lucky.
Much of this difficulty could likely be the result of having missed upgrades the game expected me to have, as each is tied to a specific optional mission objective which are typically much harder to achieve than the original scenario. You can likely see the problem with a system like this, as it rewards skilled play but leaves everyone else in a state of incapable inferiority. The only option then is to replay old missions attempting to unlock the necessary upgrade or pray you can somehow scrape through anyway, which in my case usually involved copious amounts of perseverance and luck.
If not for the constant interruption of a cutscene I'd have likely forgotten there was a narrative here at all, one note and vague on details, delivered with monotone voiceovers telling of events you don't care about and characters you can't remember. There's the basis of something really interesting here, but it waits until the last moment to tell you any of it and by then it's too late to salvage much of anything from a story which for all intents and purposes is just you blowing up countless enemies that for some reason hate your guts.
The moments when Strike Suit Zero opens up, when the pieces click into place and its firing on all cylinders, are amazing and what kept me playing despite them being perpetuated with frustration and monotony. Born Ready Games has so entirely nailed the feel of the game they wanted to create, if only the scenarios you were placed in could keep up or give you any reason to want to continue on with them.

While this "Remastered" release of the original Bioshock offers features such as developer commentary and a small "museum" that offers a quick peek at some of the concepts thrown around during development, the game itself is poorly optimized for PC. Somes issues already noted include surround sound being unavailable (and the sound overall being very poor with audio files being played at improper levels or areas relative to where the player is), mouse acceleration being janky and unreliable, and graphical issues abound. Worse yet is a large number of crashes which may result in settings being reset to default, prematurely ending any difficulty run one may be having, and potentially erasing any number of save files one had made. While one may avoid a certain number of these issues by playing on a gamepad as I myself do, you will still face the possibility of ingame crashes, save file deletion and a host of issues that, while may not prevent you from completing the game, are disappointing to see in what is considered a "remastered" version of the first game.
While somes issues persist from the original release of Bioshock, the reliance most PC'ers have on tinkering with the ini file of ports is theorized to only further increase the possibility of the game crashing.
Keep in mind that this is a "Remastering" of an already released game, it is hard to judge this product based on features already present in the original and harder not to judge the game based on what was or was not improved over the original. This game does very little to alter the experience of the original Bioshock, and on top of featuring several issues that were in the version released several years ago, this new edition brings several more issues of its own.
Because of this, I feel people should at least be aware of these issues before making a purchase, if this is your first time playing Bioshock, I would recommend at least considering simply sticking with the original until this game is patched. Because this is a "remastering" of an already released game and not a new game itself, I will have to give it a thumbs down as I see little reason to play this over the older version available on the store. You will miss out on no gameplay content by avoiding this version.
I have no issue with Bioshock or the developers of this "remastering". I will be playing the game regardless of its flaws and am grateful that I did not have to purchase this for owning the original version of the game. However, price does not erase flaws, and those who might feel it 'petty' to criticize a game that one obtained for free should understand that developers are not children that need to be coddled. Anyone that truly puts time, effort and care into a product, would not want it to be anything but the best that it could potentially be. That is not to say, that this, or any other review are gods gift to earth, but feedback, helpful or not, is always worthwhile and should not be shied away from.

Absolutely, unquestionably, the worst attempt at a "AAA" game that I've seen in a very long time. It's so incredibly bad, that I got the distinct feeling of being swindled. Like, old-timey swindled, by a man wearing a stolen coat, selling a bottle of cure-all on the corner of two dirt roads, with a pet monkey napping on the hood of his dusty car.
I'm serious. It's so bad, that they had to know it was bad. They knew it was bad, and put it up for pre-order and release, knowing they'd rake in a rather large sum of money before the game was playable.
How is it bad - there is no single way in which it is good. The voice acting is worse than the most pathetic attempt at game-making by students. Junior High School students. The graphics look as though they were brought here from 2004. The storyline is all but non-existent. The writing is about on-par with that of a 3rd grader. The character design is something you'd see in the back of a homework folder on that weird kid's desk in High School - you know, the one who thinks he's an artist, but can't draw. The ship, there's only one by the way, is all of 3 rooms, only two which can you walk in, and there is zero interactability within those rooms.
The pilot interface is awful. The entire game interface is awful. It's very clearly made as a console port, except they never said a word about consoles and released to PC first. The game is riddled with so many crippling bugs, that it's literally unplayable. After only 20 minutes, I was forced to restart, because a game-breaking bug halted any progress that could made.
The music, for which they attempted to sell pre-release soundtracks, is mediocre at best, and only by a 2004 standard. The interior of space stations is the same, in every station. The NPC speech is apalling, they say hello, then immediatley say something rude to you, and cut off speech. There basically isn't any reason to speak to any of them. In fact, there isn't any reason to *do* anything at all. They touted the game to be so many things, but in the end, it isn't even playable.
Do not waste your money on this game.

RoA was an attempt to get back into the mechanics I loved, but maybe this time I wouldn't hate the game by the end of it. And you know what? It succeeded. I'll talk more about this later.
Rivals of Aether delivers all the depth and complexity of a Smash game with only 8 characters. Every moment of the game you're making a conscious decision in an attempt to counter whatever you predict the enemy will do. If they're going to attack, parry. If they're going to parry, wait a bit, then attack. If they're going to wait a bit, just attack. It maintains the rock-paper-scissors quality of other fighting games while increasing the pace and the satisfaction of reading your opponent correctly.
Every character is drastically different in how they play, accomadating for each playstyle, so you'll usually find yourself really just maining one character. If you're the fast offensive custom combo type who personally prefers the air, Wrastor has you covered. If you're the heavy hitter who wants to fill your opponent with shame every time you land a hit, Etalus is your character. If you want to♥♥♥♥♥♥off your opponent to the point where they can't think straight, well, actually every character does that
The interesting thing about this game is that every character has some quality about them that you can shift the blame to if you lose as them or against them. If he launches you offstage, Etalus can create armor for himself that allows him to take one hit without taking any knockback or flinching. Forsburn has that ♥♥♥♥ing smoke that he can create at will and basically prevent you from seeing him. Even the stage design has sense of cheapness to it, especially in the stages with high platforms that you can pretty much just camp on to stay safe most of the time. It's really easy to shift the blame onto a broken character or stupid weakness your character has, which might be good or bad depending on your personal viewpoints. I like it though.
One major complaint I have about this game is how unpopulated the game is. Seriously, I'll be waiting minutes just for a match in ranked. Which is why you have to get this game, I'm serious, if what I've said about this game has gotten you interested, buy this game and go on ranked right now so my chance of being able to face someone increases. Please, you'll do the whole community a favor.
All in all, this game is just really fun. It's exactly what I want from a fighting game, and if you're like me, looking for a fresh new start, get this game.

Very decent point&click adventure with a message and morale.
You control Fay, a woman from the future on a quest back in time to save the planet as its dying in her world, and the man she meets, Bent Svensson, a scientist, whom Fay believes can save the world.
The sound and music is decent there is definitely some flaws in the voice acting, particularly with main character Fay. Others also seem to 'overact'. Fays posture is also terrible, nobody can stand like that with a normally shaped spine.
Anyways; the rest of the game is decent, but you will probably need a guide at some of the puzzles. There is normally a reset button, on only one puzzles (water pumps) it's possible to ♥♥♥♥up so you need to reload. Note that the game does not autosave outside of remembering where you are, so you must save in order to get around this one puzzle if you want the achievement for playing all minigames. I also had Fay get stuck at one point, forcing be to reload from a save.
It also has some weird bugs; for example a rock/plank puzzle I was obviously supposed to walk over the plank, then  pick it up and put it towards the next rock, but when I clicked to pick up the plank, Fay would walk over to the rock I was on before, then pick it up. She did this three times before she finally decided to pick it up on the rock she was supposed to be on. Had it not been such an obvious solution I would have thought I did something wrong and backtracked/messed about other things for a long time. I assume the puzzle requires perfect positioning or something.
Also 2 times in the game were the 'use item' options in Russian and near the end at an important scene the subtitles is in German with no English voiceacting. Very annoying.
Some of the achievements are also mutually exclusive, so a save must be made before some puzzles/encounters to make life easier.
The story is about saving the world from environmental disaster, so yes, there is quite a lot of talk about saving the environment and all life is precious etc. It did not bother me much as it was part of the story.
The story is long, 12 hours+ without skipping anything and the ending was imo very interesting.
Recommended; but be aware of possible bugs, lacking voice acting, and environmental talks. Save often in many slots, and keep a guide at hand for the most complicated puzzles.

I've put about 18 hours into the game and have absolutely loved it.  Visually, the game is stunning, and the gameplay runs smoothly with few glitches.  WATCH OUT - a few spoilers below, but it's meant to give you a sense of the game/gameplay mechanics:  The only glitches I have experienced are as follows: 1) the distillery just stopped working, that is, I couldn't click it, so I had to build another (a waste of those precious resources); 2) even with an axe I could not break down any furniture (annoying when wood and kindling for fires are a necessity).  Success in this game seems to be primarily based upon how lucky you are at the beginning in regards to which 3 (or 4) characters you start with, and how successful one is at creating a surplus of resources during the first 10 turns or so.  I believe I have encountered 6 unique playable characters, although their could possibly be more.  It would be nice if you could pick your three characters from the start, rather than them being pre-selected randomly for you, however, I know which three I would pick, and I think it would make the game too easy.  After 3 or 4 restarts I completed the game in 42 days (roughly 7-8 hours of gameplay would be my estimate - I assume this is the norm, but I haven't played all the way through a second time so I'm uncertain).  Major obstacles within the game happen at fairly consistent time-frames, around 10 days you're more likely to be robbed nightly for several nights in a row (a check on the security measures you've taken to that point), and around 20 days you will have to struggle with extremely cold temperatures (a check on key resource surplus - water, wood, fuel).  Other than that the game is fairly easy going, resources tend to become scarce in the last 10 days or so, which I believe is meant to force the player into more dangerous territories on the nightly scavenging map; up until the last 10 days I've found it is best to stay away from dangerous areas, unless you have gone a more militarized route and are equipped with a helmet, bullet-proof vest, and a decent gun with lots of ammo.  All-in-all a great indy strategy game (8/10 at least) that is well polished, with only the minor glitch here or there. I would definitely say it's worth the $20.00, and the developors seem keen on tweaking the game now and again (they just released an update - the most important fix seemed to be npc aggro, which was admittedly I little ridiculous when the game was first released).  Best of luck, surviving the war!

A different kind of final fantasy, it's long, it's linear, and a lot of people hate it. Personally I love this game, despite it's ungodly length, i've played through this three times, twice were on the PS3. That characters have some of the most cringeworthy lines, but if you can look past that, you will find them to be pretty decent, and the story and world is very very facinating, although it will require you to do a lot of reading in the datalog.
The game has very limited freedom when it comes to places to go and explore, but at least I can say the combat is good. Most people will dismiss it as mash "A" to win, but there is so much more to it then that, sadly it takes many many hours for it to ramp up to that point. The difficulty curve is as slow as it can possibly be, but when you get there (Around chapter 9), you really begin to feel where this battle system's complexity lies. Anyone who tells you this game is easy and requires no effort or prebattle preparation, has never truely made it to the endgame. I assure you this game will hand you your♥♥♥♥♥at some point, and luckily it's very forgiving on game overs. It was clearly designed to encourage you to experiment and find the best way to deal with certain threats.
And on to the best part of this game, the visuals. This is one of the best looking games you will see. Even years later it still beats out pretty much any other game I've come across. The animations, the effects, they are all spectacular. Playing this game is like watching a really long and pretty movie, at least until the endgame where it demands your full attention to win fights. All of this is at a cost however, this game is very demanding on your system, stay far away from this game if your computer is lower end.
tl:dr It's a pretty, linear, and action packed RPG that strays a lot from other final fantasies. Do some research before you pick it up, liking final fantasy doesn't garantee you will like this game. And if you have a low end computer, don't bother with it.

FF XIII's biggest flaw is its script. It's a mess. It's convoluted, confused, inconcistent, has major pacing issues, and is ultimately nonsensical. How nonsensical? The game's overall arc, and all of the conversations between the main characters & the big bad, boils down to the following exchange (Spoilers!):
BIG BAD: "You will do my will, and destroy me & because that's what I want to happen and it will trigger the creation of a new world."
CHARACTERS: "No! We have free will, and will never do what you want! We'll fight you & kill you instead!"
BIG BAD: "…That's literally exactly what I wanted you to do."
As a result, the story kind of doesn't make any sense at all, and the problems with it are apparent at every turn. It's a shame, because the core themes of fate & free will are interesting ones. Aside from the major problem of having an arc that is self-contradictory nonsense, the script also fails in smaller ways at almost every turn. It's just bad.
While FF XIII's linearity is the complaint that is at the top of most people's reasons for not liking this game, I actually don't think that's a big problem with the game. Yes, it's very linear but, really, all FF games have linear stories: the difference is that in most FF games you can decide to ignore the story for a while & go grind or just explore. The lack of a big open map does sometimes make the world feel a bit hollow, but I can understand why they decided to go in that direction, and design-wise I admit I'm a fan of an RPG that makes grinding almost impossible for most of the game and, therefore, unnecessary.
The game's brightest spot is probably the combat system. it seems simplistic when you're first getting introduced to it, but as the game proceeds it opens up a lot of depth. At first I wanted to go back to the old days of specifying exact actions of every character at every turn of combat, but the combat is so much more fast paced in this iteration that I can see that wouldn't have worked. The role system enables a bunch of different strategies, and the crystarium leveling system is an interesting way of mapping XP directly to specific stat/ability changes.
Ultimately, if you're a huge FF fan you may very well enjoy this game. I'm not saying it's an awful game, because it's not: it can be fun. But in the end I don't think it's worth the time you have to put into it to finish it.

A game series usually known for being overdramatic with the story and intensity of the plot/progression, this adaptation brings out difference into the series. Following the standard FF guidelines set by 6-8, This is a game that shocked people on its official release. The game itself features different playable characters and many different arcs to get you situated into the story.
Most people would complain because of the time it would take you to beat this game, or because of one of the characters. But I am looking aside for that. Everyone knows now that if you wanted to play a Final Fantasy game for the sake of playing a video game, then you shouldn't play anything past 6. (The MMO's are an exception, but I do not count those)
To start it off, the game play is very simple. It is a linear story with some nonlinear features later on in the game. You play as a few different characters that all have the same goal in mind when they come together. Movement is very fluent in this game, though where you interact with certain things is always set.
About the combat sequences, where most people seem to have trouble. The original Final Fantasy was a turn based strategy combat style. With this in mind, I think this brings about a much faster pace in the battles, letting enemies attack while you are planning your moves, or vice versa. This style of combat does stray a bit from the turn based you would have seen in 7-10.
The gameplay itself is just moving from objective to objective, or finding objective, to complete an arc in the story. Most people would find this a bit tedious, so prepare yourself for an overextended playtime.
Everyone knows that when you review a FF game, you must talk about characters.
Lightning is the soul main character in the game. (Excluding FFXIII-X2)
You will play as her for a majority of the game, so most of you people would have to really get used to her. She is a very monotone character, but sexy and intruiging. She keeps you interested with her morals and ways of keeping her team in tact.
Hope is a character that most people can say they dislike. But I will say he is not close to being as bad as Limel from Star Ocean. Cmon, he isn't.
Hope is a character you will find to be much more useful in the later stages of the game, but he will♥♥♥♥♥♥you off in the beginning. His unreliable combat phases and silly dialogue choice is very bad for you at the beginning.
Of course these are not the only 2 main characters, there are 3 others you will constantly play with, but I do not want to spoil anything.
There is not much to say here, other than the battle theme is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing!
This soundtrack for this game is of course, a masterpeice. There are not many games you can say that you have played that present and Operatic style of progressive classical music.
Overall, I recommend this game because it was a thrill to play, and the story is what will capture your heart!
(Also, the graphics on this game are amazing for when it came out! Please do check it out!)

THE BAD: FInal Fantasy has always been about deep and rich story telling, this game falls a little short of that expectation. The story does grab you from the word "go", but it leads you forward with little in the way of background information on the common enemy of the game, and when you have an enemy that has played a log lasting role like this one, you need that history to better soidify the events of the story. It requires you to plan ahead and to quikly react with more agresive monsters while still keeping the gameplay itself on a casual level. Items and weapons equiped are a big part of the battling process, along with the usable items that you keep on hand. The shopping system is brand new to this game. The shops can be accsessed at any of the save points. The shops themselves are obtained in battle by progressing in the story but there are a few secret shops that are not linked to the stroy missions. This game also brings back monster hunting missions that are optional but are also fun and can be quite the challenge. the leveling process is also a newer feature to Final Fantasy that features a growth tree of roles that you add ponits to to increases the character and the roles effects in battle. On a graphics level that game itself is one big piece of eye candy. From the scenery to the battle ground the screen is filled with collor and life that never getts dull to look at.

If you are an old school FF fan, do not buy this game. It will disappoint you.
If you are an FF XII fan, do not buy this game. It is nowhere near as good as that game.
If you are new to FF, do not make this one your first.
As many reviews have said, it's "on rails," much like an arcade FPS like House of the Dead back in the day. For an RPG, this is about the worst game design choice you could make. I know a lot of newer RPG fans (i.e. idiots) think that a role-playing game is all about story and boring cutscenes, but it is really about the battle system, crafting, classes, and exploration of a huge world. Final Fantasy XIII fails on most of these, although the battle sysem is great in my opinion. Instead of specific commands, you focus more on paradigm shifting, changing classes on the fly. It's fast-paced, fun, and strategic. I didn't like the Retry option at first as a purist, but you really need to use it because there is no "save anywhere" function and any battle can wipe you out in seconds, if you are not really careful.
The first half of the game is all story, no exploration. I began to dread the cutscenes that popped up every two battles or so. If you thought the second half of Xenogears was bad, have the cyanide pills ready for this one. Eventually you get to Pulse, and it opens up a bit, but the sour taste is already in your mouth and it doesn't leave.
As a port of a console game, it also fails, mainly because the console version is better. Even with more than the recommended specs, the camera is floaty, the framerate skippy. I had to lower the resolution so it looks bad and use a third-party app.
If you want to play a decent Square RPG on Steam, I recommend The Last Remnant. It doesn't have the optimization problems, the world is much more open to explore, and the battle system is good in that one too, although different. It's strategic again, and you can't control your team individually (you can't in FF XIII either.) It is a cool system though, and keeps ATB alive.

Single-player Diablo-like game (action role-playing dungeon crawler, isometric clicky clicky with randomized loot drops) that came out in 2009. The world was still waiting for Blizzard to deliver the next Diablo, and so, this was well-timed.  (Runic went on to release Torchlight2 at around the same time that Diablo3 came out.) It also has a pretty deep mod community, though I'll admit that I played the game vanilla on my playthrough.
The game is polished: graphics aged fine, clean audio helps the game feel immersive and responsive, and the game runs smoothly on my high-end gaming rig. Did not try it on anything else, but I suspect it'll run just fine. The story is nothing new, but then again -- you're not really playing this game for the story. It's a game where you diablo diablo diablo til you diablo diablo diablo, while you diablo diablo diablo... diablo. In that aspect, the game entertained me 'til the end. According to the in-game panel, that was about 12 hours.
One point of emphasis: the game difficulty runs easy. If you want a challenging game in which you engage all the mechanics, I'd highly suggest you nudge the difficulty up. In my playthrough, I didn't touch any of the optional map-fragment dungeons; simply the main dungeon and the ones that Hatch opens for you, in his Quest For Many Things. My character's levels almost always matched the number of the main dungeon floor I was on. Though I do have a habit of clearing each floor completely, I shouldn't have been overleveled for any part of the game. And yet, I never had to use a mana potion or any of the various mana shrines. Didn't touch a health potion until L25, and even then rarely. Never had to fiddle with my pet's form -- simply used him as a carryall back to town to sell my items. (So, that took the need to fish right out of the picture.) I had no real use for my currency. (Game only has one -- gold.) I was one-shotting enemies with the gear I found on the ground. I cannot imagine the devs intended for you to three-shot their bosses. At some point toward the end, I just decided to put 100k gold into enchanting a single item, you know, for funsies. I suspect the devs had intended for the enchantment system to work as a gold sink, but I simply didn't need the stat boosts to make the game less challenging. I'm afraid it would have become boring.
I never once used any spells. I also didn't bother learning any non-passive class skills outside of the first available frost shot. Once I learned that, that's what I left my secondary attack on.
Perhaps it was simply because I'd built up a ranged, spike character and the dungeons are designed with bottlenecks galore (hallways and corners everywhere, weeee), but giving the ranged player a NPC tank, a single-target spike, AND a piercing crowd-control projectile so very early in the game may have been overkill.
Even if you haven't played a Diablo before, turn the difficulty up a bit.
Other small notes:
Pet pathing. I realize this is sticky for many devs to get right, but boy -- my pet did not know how to go up stairs when the stairs were perhaps seven feet away from him. It's a small irritant, of course, since I could simply spend the 5 seconds moving around to manipulate his pathing algorithm.
Replayability. Once you beat the game with any class, a new "Shadow Dungeon" opens up. I fully admit that I will not be playing the game again (I have far too many other things to get to!) but that along with being able to "retire" a character to pass along a heirloom makes it seem as though the replayability is solid. And again, there's a pretty decent mod community.

First off, this review is also based on playing Magic back in the 90's to present day.
For any player new to the Magic scene, this is a great game. It has good tutorials, is more patient than I am and the storymode helps get the newbie hardwired in to the gameplay basics for future P vs P matches. I really liked the filter for deck building and the ability to build my own deck or just let the comp generate one for me.
Some of the transitions from phase to phase seem tedious and time consuming, but can somewhat be tweaked in the settings. I have a few issues with how instants and interrupts are played, as well as activating abilities. If you're not quick with the timer or utilize it properly, you can lose out on using those things that can make or break your strategy.
I like the chance to earn gold to go towards booster packs, I just hope they incorporate more options to do so, especially during  P vs P duels. The quests help out, but with all the bugginess going on at the moment, it makes it hard to give a more detailed account of them.
Overall, great game for the newbie wanting to venture in to the actual card game and helps clear up issues with some of the veterans that wondered " can I do that?". For now, I do recommend the game...... for now.... get some Raid and clear out those bugs!!!

Disclaimer: I came to this game from the Super Smash Bros series, I learned and mastered most of the advanced techniques from Melee and I learned fundamentals and spacing and making reads from Smash 4. I have no idea what this game is like to new players, or to casual players who don't constantly try to up their game, so I'm not going to speak for them.
I mainly came to Rivals of Aether because I needed a fresh new start. Playing Smash was getting self destructive, to the point where I would cry after every loss. RoA was an attempt to get back into the mechanics I loved, but maybe this time I wouldn't hate the game by the end of it. And you know what? It succeeded. I'll talk more about this later.
Rivals of Aether delivers all the depth and complexity of a Smash game with only 8 characters. Every moment of the game you're making a conscious decision in an attempt to counter whatever you predict the enemy will do. If they're going to attack, parry. If they're going to parry, wait a bit, then attack. If they're going to wait a bit, just attack. It maintains the rock-paper-scissors quality of other fighting games while increasing the pace and the satisfaction of reading your opponent correctly.
Every character is drastically different in how they play, accomadating for each playstyle, so you'll usually find yourself really just maining one character. If you're the fast offensive custom combo type who personally prefers the air, Wrastor has you covered. If you're the heavy hitter who wants to fill your opponent with shame every time you land a hit, Etalus is your character. If you want to♥♥♥♥♥♥off your opponent to the point where they can't think straight, well, actually every character does that
The interesting thing about this game is that every character has some quality about them that you can shift the blame to if you lose as them or against them. If he launches you offstage, Etalus can create armor for himself that allows him to take one hit without taking any knockback or flinching. Forsburn has that ♥♥♥♥ing smoke that he can create at will and basically prevent you from seeing him. Even the stage design has sense of cheapness to it, especially in the stages with high platforms that you can pretty much just camp on to stay safe most of the time. It's really easy to shift the blame onto a broken character or stupid weakness your character has, which might be good or bad depending on your personal viewpoints. I like it though.
One major complaint I have about this game is how unpopulated the game is. Seriously, I'll be waiting minutes just for a match in ranked. Which is why you have to get this game, I'm serious, if what I've said about this game has gotten you interested, buy this game and go on ranked right now so my chance of being able to face someone increases. Please, you'll do the whole community a favor.
All in all, this game is just really fun. It's exactly what I want from a fighting game, and if you're like me, looking for a fresh new start, get this game.

i wanted to give this game a chance. It's pretty cool in concept, but the execution was shaky. I've had to rewrite my review multiple times because I'm not sure how to feel about this game.
-random difficulty spikes to the point where the game is just cluttered with unnecessary bullets and explosions (and they don't pull off the "crowded battle scene" that often, but when they do, it's pretty cool)
-controls are awkward, but thankfully are rebindable
-the strike suit, which is the draw of the whole game, is a gimmick that only lasts 10 seconds, and has a pretty poor targeting system, which means you'll be darting about not hitting anything, though once you unlock a few upgrades, it becomes decent
-might just be my computer, but I experienced insane slowdown even on the lowest graphics settings. I won't consider this a point against the game, because I've had slowdown issues before
-battles are luck based, depending on if you hit the tiny area that you're supposed to, when fighting a bigger ship. Apparently you need to hit weakspots which may or may not be marked for your convenience, but shooting the turrets does some damage. Targeting system is also broken, as in you normally have the option to aim towards the closest enemy, or a mission objective enemy. Thing is, you can't just target them. You have to cycle your targets until you hopefully get the one you want, like the cruisers and carriers. It's a gambit, so you take what you get.
-game is 90% escort missions, and your friendlies are thin as paper,
-last mission is a pain in the port, and I won't even spoil it.
If you have to try this, get it on sale. I'm talking less than 5 bucks. I still recommend it against my previous criticisms because it tried to be a cool mech game and gave us something to remember, and I was thoroughly challenged. After all, it's better to deal with a challenging game than one that holds your hand the whole way. As long as you get it on sale, you won't regret it, because the game does deliver to an extent. Had I paid full price, however, I wouldn't be as forgiving. Especially once I got that darn last level. If you play through this game, and/or you already played through it, you'll know exactly what I mean.

Hitman: Absolution Review by ScallyWolf: 8/10
Pros:
-Solid stealth/action gameplay
-Tons of replayability
-Interesting, well paced story
-Cinematic atmosphere
-Excellent graphical quality
-Interactive environments
-Excellent gateway game for franchise
-Cosplay
Cons:
-Short story mode (8 hours on Normal)
-Occasionally unpredictable AI
-Abusable stealth situations
Now, before I begin, let me state that this is the first Hitman title I have ever played. I enjoyed the film that released a few years ago, but couldn't get around to playing any of the games until recently. I'm to understand that Hitman: Absolution recieved mixed reviews for it's step away from the staples of previous games in the series. I'm also under the impression that this is the most "casual" approach to the franchise to date. Many felt that the game is too easy when compared to literally every other installment. As for my experience, I found this game to be a very enjoyable mixture of stealth and action. I've played through the game on normal and felt challenged, but rewarded for my achievements. Virtually every kill felt gritty and impactful. The stealth elements are solid, and though not without flaw, usually reward patience and punish mistakes. Even though I never intended to complete any achievements, I found that I was challenging myself to stay hidden and avoid using disguises as much as possible. This ended up extending the time needed to complete the campaign on normal by a few hours. Also, while the campaign only clocks in at about 8 hours, there is a ton of replay value here. Each contract can be handled in a number of different ways, and there are a wealth of weapons to implement. I have yet to even explore the "contracts" function that allows players to create and challenge others with custom missions. All in all, if you enjoy stealth games, replayability, cosplay, or are just looking for a gateway into the Hitman franchise, this is an excellent place to start.

Each level is scored, and each action you take either adds to or subtracts from that score. Kills a civilian? There go some points. In truth I rarely pay attention to rating system like this, but here you need to at least pay a little attention to it because the more points you get as you go along, the more skills you unlock, such as faster reload times. So mind your score a bit so that you can become more powerful.

I actually found a solution to the problem. Here is what happened.
UPLAY and Steam where located on my C:/ Drive in the default settings location. My 4TB Hardrive( E:/ ) is where I moved Steam to. After completing steam installation on the E:/ drive I launched AC4 BF. However despite the saves remaining in the spot indicated by UPLAY(C:\Program Files (x86)\Ubisoft\Ubisoft Game Launcher\savegames/...) the game was not picking up the files and was telling me that I would have to start anew.
As it would turn out I found out that if you install UPLAY on the same drive as the game( E:/) and copy and paste your saves correctly, it fixed the problem.

I've put about 18 hours into the game and have absolutely loved it.  Visually, the game is stunning, and the gameplay runs smoothly with few glitches.  WATCH OUT - a few spoilers below, but it's meant to give you a sense of the game/gameplay mechanics:  The only glitches I have experienced are as follows: 1) the distillery just stopped working, that is, I couldn't click it, so I had to build another (a waste of those precious resources); 2) even with an axe I could not break down any furniture (annoying when wood and kindling for fires are a necessity).  Success in this game seems to be primarily based upon how lucky you are at the beginning in regards to which 3 (or 4) characters you start with, and how successful one is at creating a surplus of resources during the first 10 turns or so.  I believe I have encountered 6 unique playable characters, although their could possibly be more.  It would be nice if you could pick your three characters from the start, rather than them being pre-selected randomly for you, however, I know which three I would pick, and I think it would make the game too easy.  After 3 or 4 restarts I completed the game in 42 days (roughly 7-8 hours of gameplay would be my estimate - I assume this is the norm, but I haven't played all the way through a second time so I'm uncertain).  Major obstacles within the game happen at fairly consistent time-frames, around 10 days you're more likely to be robbed nightly for several nights in a row (a check on the security measures you've taken to that point), and around 20 days you will have to struggle with extremely cold temperatures (a check on key resource surplus - water, wood, fuel).  Other than that the game is fairly easy going, resources tend to become scarce in the last 10 days or so, which I believe is meant to force the player into more dangerous territories on the nightly scavenging map; up until the last 10 days I've found it is best to stay away from dangerous areas, unless you have gone a more militarized route and are equipped with a helmet, bullet-proof vest, and a decent gun with lots of ammo.  All-in-all a great indy strategy game (8/10 at least) that is well polished, with only the minor glitch here or there. I would definitely say it's worth the $20.00, and the developors seem keen on tweaking the game now and again (they just released an update - the most important fix seemed to be npc aggro, which was admittedly I little ridiculous when the game was first released).  Best of luck, surviving the war!

10 out of 10
I have played the first 5 Assassins Creed (AC) games and think Black Flag (BF) is the best of them all (AC4 = BF even though it is the 5th iteration).  BF is a combination of the typical AC elements, sneaking, killing and swordplay, with a pirate adventure incorporating ship-to-ship fights, ship deck fights, diving and harpooning.
The good:
1. BF has fantastic high detail locations, like all AC games.  It is not as spectacular as Renaissance Italy (AC2 and ACB), but still excellent.
2. The ship-to-ship and ship deck fights are great new game elements (S-t-S was also in AC3, but not as extensive).  The other elements we have seen before; BF doesn't do anything new to them, but those elements are still good.
3. The main character, Edward Kenway, is someone you can like for all his faults.  He is no saint, and very enjoyable to follow.
4. The side characters are really good, even though you do not see them a lot.  Much thought has gone into them and how their characters evolve.
5. The music, specifically the shanties - singing on the ship deck is outstanding.  What shall we do with a drunken sailor?
6. The game is very well optimised.  At maximum settings, my laptop did not overheat once as tends to happen with such games.
The bad:
7. The game is too long.  I spent about 100 hours on it.  It could have done without 25 hours of generic content such as Kenway's Fleet and the generic Assassins Missions.
8. The game can be frustrating when you die repeatedly die due to level design and / or imprecise controls.  This is an old AC problem.
9. The game can be frustrating during mass brawls as the camera angle leaves some enemies out of sight even if they stand right in front of you.  The game is not good at locking on to targets either.  These are more old AC problems.
10. The game needed an explicit climbing button.  You climb onto things if you run too close past them, even if you didn't intend to.  An explicit climb button would have solved that issue.  This is another recurring problem in AC games.
11. The game makes no noticeable progress on the modern AC storyline.
The ugly:
12. The morality of this game is terrible, as with all AC games.  I killed more than a 1000 people in this game, yet only about 25 are bad people.  The game should not have accepted you killing innocent guards.  It should have had more ways to incapacitate these generic characters without killing them.  Edward Kenway loses no sleep even though he is one of history's greatest mass murderers.  Clearly he is a psychopath.

Shelter is a charming and quite moving game with a striking art style. It suffers from a number of minor bugs, and slightly awkward controls and camera, but nothing that significantly diminishes the overall experiences. That said, it's worth pointing out that the game has a playtime of only just over an hour and lacks the variety between playthroughs to merit many replays, so bear that in mind.
I would recommend this game for anyone into more arty games, or who is looking for an emotionally powerful game with more gameplay and mechanics than you find in other genres like walking simulators. Further, this is a good example of a "short and sweet" game that won't waste your time, so if you're time poor and looking to fill an evening, this is a good choice. In addition, if you're considering whether to buy this or Shelter 2, I would say this is the superior experience and would recommend you try it (even if you think lynxes are cooler than badgers).

Hello,
First of all: yes I know AC is a massproduction series and I also know that the titles seem repetitive at first.
But...
I would totally recommend you buying this. I never played the first AC but apart from that I can say that this is my favorite game from the series. It is in most ways still in the tradition and it breaks new ground in others. They basically kept the best parts form the previous games (trading, Villa building, Armor/weapons upgrades, hidden items, etc.) and combined them with the new sailing and naval warfare mechanic. The Naval action here is basically my favorite part, if you are in anyway inspired by pirates and ships this game is awesome. The sailing around feels very immersive but there's fast travel for when you had enough of it and the ship combat feels very immersive as well. Shooting down stronger ships and taking on whole fleets could make for a standalone game and if an opponent ship is too strong, you can just swim over and stealth takeout all crew abord. If you know AC, this is basically the classic with this extra of Carribean ship combat. I personally spent most of the game jsut upgrading my ship to a totally ustoppable warmaschine but you can play it as you like.
now the cons
- sadly, because of Ubisoft competence and mass production this game suffers a bit:
- the game has a fair amount of visual glitches for an official titel. I head a lot of complaints about bugs but my own game limited itself to tansforming my ship into a submarine after loading in sometimes. All the crew would float on the surface and the ship would sink below waterlevel for some minutes and inhibit your vision if you were on it. This is a major bug but also cool in some way so the bethesda logic seems to apply here (gamer: is this a bug or a feature ? Bethesda: yes)
Also, I have a major complaint about Ubisoft here. I bought the game via steam and played about 80% of the story. I the stopped for a while playing. Before I came back to the game, I realized that I had an old copy of AC 2 on my Ubisoft account so I linked it with steam and Black flag to be able to play it. When I got back to black flag to continue the last missions, the whole progress and all other save content was lost so I'd advise you to link your account before you spent a great deal of time ingame. But then again, everybody knows Ubisoft so what did I expect ?
The last but minor complaint, is that the game can become repetitve if you play like me. I prefer to jsut spend tons of time doing the things in game that I like the most ex: upgrade the ship half through the game so that in all further missions naval activities became boring. Or doing so many sidequests that it got boring to do the main quests where you had to tail people. I think the game could be improved if they included some new ways to design story missions as they can become repetitive (tailing people for the 10th time in a row)
Overall a great game with some minor flaws that should be expected from Ubisoft.

First of all things to consider is : are you a X3 or X2 or even X veteran ? If not, you can enjoy the game as it is right now (consider though there are still bugs, some of them are game breaking. Egosoft is working on them, so yeah, bugged, but not unfixable).
If you are a X veteran, then this is more difficult to tell. I'm an X veteran, and I'm hugely disappointed with this X Rebirth. I guess I was expecting X4 (don't shout about "they told it it wasn't x4"). I was expecting X4. I was expecting a new way to play, with a rich universe, filled with all the possibilities I had in X3AP or TC. It's not there at all.
Here are though some of my thoughts about the game :
- The graphics are beautiful (in space, in station I find them ugly, but once again, this is solely my opinion).
- The universe is big, but I don't feel like I'm in space (understand space, where there are a few station and lots of empty space). Stations are huge, I like that idea, but it feels like big cities now.
- The highways are a new neat way to move. It's a shame they block your view with a minigame (you drift behind vehicles to go faster. I would have prefered the neat view with no vehicles in front of me).
- They promised "every ship in the game has a reason to exist. It does its thing". While I can't argue this might be true for most of the big ships, I must say this isn't true at all for the ships that spawns in the highways, making it impossible to spy on other ships, see their venues and find what their routes are.
- There is only 1 playable ship (understand in which you can jump). You can control other ships, but it's really limited (against what X3 offered us).
- There are only 4 weapons for your ship.
- Only 4 regions, which are not truly dedicated to a faction. In X3, sectors were belonging to a faction. Here, the factions are mixed everywhere, making the game for the factions disappear.
- This Rebirth is more dedicated towards fighting. Of course you can mine, you can (try) making the economic play (very difficult, there is no real economy, it's more places where you can buy and sell more than a logical economy balanced by the player), or kill the pirates. But this game is more action packed then the X3AP was.
- Even if the idea of walking in station is nice, going inside stations and searching for the right guy is kinda weird for an x veteran. I need to ask the other ships in the game where I can find this man, rather than having a nice list of what you scanned as in X3.
These are in very short some things I think and feel about X Rebirth. I loved the game at start, and then when I saw there were no such possibilities as in X3, I felt I had the wrong game bought. But once again, this is my opinion on it.
I don't want to say this game is bad. A friend of mine is playing it, he never went in the X Universe, and he loves it. He hardly understand why I don't like it. So will you like this game ? I don't know. Read, and watch some gameplay about it on twitch, or youtube, make you see the game, and decide for yourself.

Where do I begin? This game has not lived up to my expectations as an entrant into the X Universe. First off, on release day the game was so chocked full of bugs that I found it largely unplayable. Oh, the basic flight controls and interactions worked (mostly), but you couldn't stop a trade order given to a ship without going into the save file and doing some xml editing to clear out the "stuck" command. The main interface menu in the cockpit would randomly stop working, requiring either saving and then reloading to clear it, or jumping back&forth between the back of the ship and cockpit. Neither were 100% certain to clear that particular issue at any given time.
As for much of the other problems, they seriously dumbed down many of the foundational aspects of the X Universe. Remember the encyclopedia? That handy little in-game list of pretty much everything you've seen? That included things like where a certain ware was found to be sold? Gone. Oh, not all of it. It's still there, but the only things you see are the ware type, volume per unit, container type, and a brief "flavor" blurb to read/listen to the computer spew at you. Remember the map system that allowed you to pan around the map, select targets from the list for interaction, etc? Gone. Replaced with a very inflexible top-down-only view, no pan/zoom, and very limited list-based interaction. Remember targeting controls? Also gone. Replaced with a single mouse-click type/center reticle selection. Oh, the game also likes to forget your target randomly. Remember being able to tell your owned ships what to do? Yup, also severly stripped down. Remember trade goods/wares that NPC stations actually needed? Yeah, half of the classic ware list is "junk loot" now, to be sold to in-station NPCs, carried aboard your own ship, with a seemingly infinite cargo space.
Speaking of NPCs and the game's "Artificial Life." It's on life-support. Most of the ships you'll ever see on screen, just fly aimlessly in circles around huge stations. Most never even display a target icon unless you target them specifically. Only a few will, and those are the only "real" npc ships you'll see, aside from the cap ships.
Remember building massive, multi-station complexes wherever you pleased? Yup, gone. Replaced with location-based build sites. Remember building up a squadron of fighters? Last I had played, only the cap-ship merchants worked. Oh, there were docking platforms for "civilian ships," complete with icon, but no ship-builder NPC. That was as of 1.14, by the way.
I could really go on, but I think by now you get the idea. In the end, I really wish I hadn't spent my money on this game. I had pre-ordered. And while doubtful I'll ever see it, I am indeed asking for my money back, or a refund. Save yourself the headache, and just pass this game over.

Shadow Warrior has a lot of problems built into it. The biggest problem is that the "super enemies" are way too tanky, and they break the flow of hacking through hordes of enemies and watching limbs fly. The falling damage is also broken and buggy as ♥♥♥♥, and some of the levels aren't anything special.
However, that doesn't mean that the game isn't good. When you get into the flow of hacking through hordes of enemies and watch limbs fly, change into your shotgun or Uzi in the middle of it, land a couple of headshots, it feels awesome. The swordplay, while not mechanically too special, feels really really good. That alone saves the game from mediocrity to good. The story is also suprisingly good and had some effort built into it, though you still don't want to play the game for the story (as you never should). The wacky humor was also A++.
All in all, a pretty good game.

Before I start on Rebellion, Some things need to be said about Sins of a Solar Empire in general:
1. SoaSE is a pretty old game.
2. The original was really limited.
3. And certain things were really broken.
Oh, and 4. None of that matters.
For people who skip the intro cutscenes (because that's literally all the story you get), the Vasari, hyper-advanced aliens, have been fleeing from something they created for a loooong time. And now they've stumbled into human, peaceful space. Oh, and this long-forgotten cult called the Advent has apparently decided NOW is a good time to take revenge on the humans for something.
The humans quickly reorganize into the Trader Emergency Coalition, or TEC. by this point, however, much of the human space has been gobbled up by the Vasari and Advent.
Gamewise, the races play very different. The TEC are still industrial titans, so you'll be losing ships quicker than the Advent or Vasari, but rebuilding much quicker and cheaper. The Vasari are mondo expensive on all their ships, but that expense meens even the scouts can operate as main flight forces. And the Advent are all about subversion and abilities, so they primarily employ drone swarms mixed with capitol ships.
Of course, that was only the FIRST iteration of Sins. Entrenchment, the first expansion, added large starbases that operate essentially the same as a WW2 machine gun emplacement: throw enough firepower into the enemy and they don't follow that line. Diplomacy, the second expansion, made allies out of staunch enemies, and actually gave some depth to the computer controlled empires.
So now, we are in Rebellion. The races have been fighting for so long that divisions in them have formed. Each race now has a Loyalist and Rebel facton, and they are not the same at all. Oh, and now, we have these things called Titans. Think like if you took the starbases I talked about earlier, and added more guns, and made them mobile.
TL;DR, if your looking for a strategy game with crazy strategy, give Sins: Rebellion a chance. There is enough content in this wonderful little jewel to make any strategy fan extremely happy. Oh, and with mods, you can play in almost any universe you can think off.

Aah~~ FFXIII.....the game everyone either loves or hates.
This game is definitely not for everyone, however you should still enjoy it if you're a huge FF fan.
The game is hugely linear,especially the first 20~30 hours,however the game does open up a little towards the end,though not by much. If you know you're not the kind of person that can handle linearity, do not pick up this title. The game has 13 Chapters, however the game only opens up at Chapter 11. Chapter 1~10 is all about getting used to the battle system and all about the storytelling.The world is really greatly thought out with some really great visuals. Masahi Hamauzu also did a great job with the soundtracks, following in the footsteps of Nobuo Uematsu.The soundtrack is simply awesome.
The story and characters are basically FF. Many people say the story is too convoluted, however if you follow the game's pacing everything will be handed on a plate, overall not a bad storyline.The characters are quite interesting and there are rooms for character development.
The battle system is quite different in a way it is really fast and frantic. It would seem like full-on buttle mashing but it has a lot of interesting approaches to a battle.The battle system is still a love or hate relationship, if you're considering this title, check up some gameplay on the Internet first.
Overall, I do enjoy this title and will recommend it to diehard FF fans. For gamers new to the series however, I strongly advise you to do extensive research before picking up. The game is still great but it may not be your taste. You have been warned.

Early review at 30 hours of play—I will update it as I go.
To the Point:
Maybe buy it if it’s on sale--otherwise, wait for it to go on sale, watch it on youtube/twitch, or pass it up. As far as FF games go, this is a 3.5 out of 10.
Longer review/rant:
Story (no spoilers):
The story is the weakest aspect of this game and perhaps the weakest of all final fantasies I’ve played; haven’t plated FF8 or 13-2. I’ve tried so hard to like any of the characters, but so far they’re so flawed with little hope of redemption I’ve been pushing through the story and vague, fluctuating plot, hoping any of the main characters will find enlightenment or a reasonable goal I can cheer them on for as I play. It’s felt like I’ve been on a long painful car trip, the car slowly breaking down and I question if the destination will be worth the pretty but irritating journey.
Art/Style:
The art for the game is great; one of the stronger points of this game. The character designs aren’t bad, even if the character’s decisions and/or dialog are bad; if not awful. Environments are well designed even if the “dungeons” maps are at times boring. The CG cut scenes are top notch but honestly expected of them because of the last handful of Final Fantasy title’s CG cut scenes. The chocobo look good, the moogles look like bulbous ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and all of the summons make Final “Fantasy” look mostly Final “Sci-fi.” Don’t get me wrong, FF 7, 8, 10 have plenty of sci-fi too, but at least FF 6 and 7 felt like equal parts fantasy and sci-fi, 8, 10(2) and 13(2) (15?) feel more sci-fi than fantasy and the only recent original fantasy FF games are their MMOs like 11 or 13 and that’s a whole can of worms I don’t want to open here. A shame and I hope if there’s a FF 16, it’s a strong “fantasy” title.
Gameplay:
The short answer is, meh? Sometimes it feels fun when the AI characters choose their skills well and the “staggering” system--that allows your characters to do more (and sometimes necessary to win) damage to the enemy--works well. What’s been most irritating is that Square-enix should know that most of its players know what “strategy” and “tactics” are but they designed it so you have to play select characters separately as a pair or their chosen group of three; you can’t pick your party until about 25-30 hours into the game, depending on your pace of play. Although you feel like you could put a decent group together earlier in the game, the “plot” forces you to play certain characters and half the time they work well together, but the other half of the time it feels like you’re going through the motions, forced to play how they’ve planned you to; and if you don’t, the battles will take twice as long or you’ll lose. For a “role” playing game, you’re given a pretty small role in how you’d like to play through countless hours of play.
Honestly, I could go on about gameplay, but I feel like some might be able to get through it while others will find it mostly unrewarding or irritating like me.
Graphics:
This is about the strongest point of the game. The environments, characters and just about everything look good if you have a good graphics card. That said, if you don’t, it’s okay with a decent card but will be nearly unplayable with a minimum card. It’s one of the few things getting me through this frustrating game.
Final thoughts thus far:
I bought this game on sale and knew it wasn’t one of their stronger titles, but I love the original final fantasies so much that I couldn’t help but give their newer titles a try. Recently, I’ve been playing Final Fantasy Record Keeper on my iPhone/iPad and it’s been far and away more fun to play than this game and I haven’t spent one penny on FFRK. You collect a lot of characters in the mobile game and it made me want to try this title and afterward I will try FF8 for the same reason. And while there’s a few notable characters in FF13, the game and its story have been a real let down. Almost all of the FF games from 7 on down are amazing for various reasons, since then, they’ve been sacrificing story, fantasy and good JRPG mechanics for graphics and voice acting (the english for 13 is passable at best). I hope Square-enix go back to their roots and give us back our mages and knights, dragoons and ninjas. There’s a lot more to FF games than adding chocobos, moogles and crystals.
FF 13 so far, a depressing addition that makes me appreciate the classics more. I only hope there’s some light at the end of this tunnel.

Sins has been my first look into a 4X game, it's definitely not going to be my last.
The game is a standalone expansion to the original "Sins of a Solar Empire" which previous to Rebellion came in a Trinity pack. The game is highly addictive and takes a lot of time to get into the swing of things but you won't notice, you will be too busy exploring Feros, while defending Gateway and sending an envoy to Lexmada at the same time! The game plays much like a space orientated RTS with a top-down camera as default, you can change the visuals in a fullly flexible camera and the zoom can be looking at a shole solar system or a single planet.
The game itself features 3x factions, split into 2x subfactions each. There are a variety of ships & buildings available, several research trees per faction and hours of gameplay just there alone. You can chose to conquer your system with diplomacy as you explore and develop your planets or simply wage war on everyone, choice is yours. The gameplay is quite slow but can be adjusted in realtime.
Some of the achievements are time consuming but keep some replayability in the game, the online multiplayer requires an Ironclad Online account but you can organsie a match in the chat room and the players there will usually stick throughout the whole session. There are ~400 active players at any given time.
Some drawbacks are the games engine, it isn't optimised well for modern hardware so no matter what you're playing on, if you're waging war in a system with 100+ planets, after some time the game will beging to stutter - if you have low / modest hardware you will see this much sooner. It doesn't have an overall negative impact on the game but should be taken into account. Personally, I wouldn't let it spoil the overall experience that is Sins, this is a game that holds hours of play and while it looks very complicated the tutorials will hold your hand through the basics and from there the game takes no time to get involved with.
A secondary gripe is the lack of a single player story, the intro video looks like it is geared for one but it is not present in this game. I'd still recommend it any day.

I'm not going to metion the bugs or the connection issues. The card pool itself is extremly disappointing.
The moment they announced the majority of the cards will come from Magic Origin, I know this will happen. I don’t like playing draft or sealed in paper magic. I don’t like the very idea of “limited”. Why would I want myself be limited in the first place? I do play draft and prerelease occasionally because that’s the only time buying booster packs worth it.
The whole experience of MDO feels like playing sealed even with every card unlocked. The majority of the cards came from Magic Origin means this game has far less cards than a standard game. The power level of cards in this game is downright appalling by comparison with previous DOTP games. Even though previous DOTP game have a card pool of similar size, they have some of the most synergetic or powerful cards from various sets.
Let’s just make some comparison: Comparing the B/G deck with the B/G Sepulchral Strength from DOTP 2013, what we are missing? Are there any cards from this set that are close in power level to Spiritmonger, Pernicious Deed, Greater Good, Maelstrom Pulse. There are not even good commons and uncommons like Blood Artist or Yavimaya Elder.
Compare the best elves tribal deck this set can make to the elves tribal deck Sylvan Might from DOTP2014. What MDO can offer can compete with Joraga Warcaller, Ezuri, Renegade Leader, Immaculate Magistrate? For commons and uncommons, what can replace Taunting Elf, Essence Warden, Wellwisher and Imperious Perfect?
By comparing with standard legal elves deck, we are missing Obelisk of Urd and Sylvan Messenger. MDO doesn’t even have Sylvan Messenger, a card previously included in DOTP2014 and reprinted in the very Magic Origin. For goblins the same thing happens to Goblin Piledriver. Again, reprinted in Magic Origin, just not going to let you play. Not mentioning Goblin Warchief, Goblin Chieftain Warren Instigator Krenko , Mob boss and Siege-Gang Commander.
Magic Origin is an enchantment focused set right? What we have in DOTP2013 and 2014 for enchantment? In addition to Sigil of empty throne we had : Daybreak Coronet, Kor Spiritdancer, Pariah+ Indestructibility, Angelic Density, Celestial Mantle. What we have now? Divine Favorand Nimbus Wings for crying out loud.
The mono green Garruk deck in previous iteration had Primordial Hydra, Genesis wave, Avenger of Zendikar and Primeval Titan. Now in MDO, people are considering Outland Colossus OP, Terra Stomper and Gaea's Revenge are the biggest threat green can offer.
MDO is horrendous in card’s quality. The power level of decks are no higher than the decks built using starter toolkit. It is as if they think you don’t deserve good cards. For $15 I can buy any DOTP game+ expansion which have far better cards than MDO, a game require constant investment.
I can't recommend this game to my friends who may or maynot have played magic before becasue it has no charm of MTG at all. It has been polished more like a tablet game than MTG.

More an action game with RPG elements than an action-RPG, this is nonetheless an enjoyable ride for fans of the LOTR movie trilogy. Gameplay is entirely centered around the action combat, which is relatively simple but satisfying. The skill tree provides a good sense of power progression and allows some customisation of each character. Aesthetically the game clearly follows the movies, but thanks to the story that intersects but doesn't otherwise follow the LOTR story, there are plenty of new locations to see and new events to play through. There are plenty of hat-tips to Tolkiens lore ( a few goof-ups too, but not too bad) and a decent amount of expositional dialogue. Unfortunately there is little depth to the characters in your party, so they will remain somewhat bland in spite of the 20-30 hours you will spend fighting at their sides.
The single-save system is a bit of an annoyance, and so is the limited control and interaction with the AI controlled party members if you play this solo. Technically it was fairly solid otherwise, but the german voiceovers were sometimes assigned to the wrong scenes. An unfixed glitch (imho) is that you can't give shields or potions to your companions.
Overall I'd recommend this game to people interested in a LOTR game, that do not mind to have a somewhat constrained visit to middle earth pesented through linear stories and levels and lots of action combat.

Rivals of Aether is considered by many to be a love letter to Super Smash Bros. However, it's actually the product of hardcore fans looking at all the games within the series and declaring, "Hey, we could do better."
Upon seeing this on Steam one fateful day, I just KNEW that I had to make a purchase. Combining the combo potential of 64, the speed, competitiveness, and meta of Melee (intentionally; wavedashing isn't a glitch in this game), the accessibility of Brawl and the fine-tuning of Sm4sh, as well as adding some unique flavor, some fans would even dare say that this game is superior to any Super Smash Bros game before it.
Rivals of Aether currently has all eight characters, a VS mode, a plethora of tutorials for newcomers and hardcore fans alike, about eight stages, controller support, and an online mode. The online is rather primitive, only allowing 1v1 battles as of the time of this writing, but ranked battles have recently been added.
What truly makes this game stand out are the fighters. Based after various animals, each character can control some aspect of nature; fire, smoke, water, ice, air, thunder, rocky earth, and plants. There are no "clone" characters in this game, as each contestant stands out as their own.
The only thing I dislike is the fact that some characters (read: most) rely on some sort of central gimmick; Orcane relies on his puddles to teleport around the stage and attack, Absa uses her thundercloud to zone, and Forsburn uses his smoke to charge his attacks, as well as generally be sneaky. These character rely on this central aspect to succeed, which can make it difficult for new players who might think that all the attacks are disparate in nature.
The full version will have a Story Mode (complete with unlockable "aether stories" which act as codex entries), an Abyss Mode that functions as an endless gauntlet, and assumedly a fuller online experience. Currently, the devs have no plans for future characters, although they are open to suggestions on their website forums, which suggests that they simply don't have any more ideas for character designs.
Beyond that, there isn't much else. As this is an indie title, they are focusing on gameplay rather than content, especially since it is a fighting game.
This game is made by dedicated fans of Smash. They already have all eight planned characters. All they need now are the Story and Abyss modes, an updated online mode that runs smoother and has a four player mode and a casual mode (perhaps combined into one), and some further character balancing. I think it is safe to say that the devs are halfway done.
They have a website where they post updates to the game, and the latest update focused on fine tuning the online mode and adding tutorials for all skill levels. Updates move along at a consistent pace now, usually one every one or two months. There are no signs of abandonment so far, and I think it's safe to say that they will complete this game by the end of the year.
If you have an itch for local multiplayer, want some online action, or if you're one of those weirdos who can spend up to an hour in VS mode fighting the CPU (like me) then I suggest it. As far as fighting action goes, I think there is enough content for potential ROA fans to get their feet wet. If you're a Smash Bros fan who just wants to try something a little new, I'd also suggest buying. Dedicated devs, an active community, and a unique spin on the Smash formula make this worth trying out.

While Lord of the Rings: War in the North does not bring anything new to the genre, it is still quite well executed and be sure to provide you with a dozen or so hours of entertainment. Specially so if you are a LotR fan. The story follows the battles that took place in the North of Middle Earth while the Fellowship of the Ring marched on South towards the destruction of Sauron and I found it to be quite well integrated.
I did not play the multiplayer version of the game so I cannot comment on that but I found that the singleplayer experience was solid and relatively bug-free. Besides some graphical glitches on some snow levels (which I cannot say were not due to my hardware) and some rare ragdoll quirks, the game looked and behaved quite nicely.
You have 3 characters at your disposal and I imagine that a playthrough with each character gives you a different perspective of the story (albeit with the same levels) so that might give you some replayability value. You also have some challenge levels that might keep you busy for a little while longer. Equipment is varied and scales well (do not bother giving equipment to your party though, they'll equip themselves).
Pros:
+ Truthfull to the Tolkien lore.
+ Stable and entertaining single player.
+ Good graphics.
+ Above average skill trees and gameplay.
+ Good voice acting and overall sound ambiance.
+ Excellent controller support.
Cons:
- Some graphical glitches on snow levels.
- Very linear, you won't be able to explore a lot.
- While you get some gameplay variety at certain keypoints of the game, the time in between is almost pure button and skill spamming.

I admit, Hollow Knight does not really innovate on the "Metroidvania" genre of games, but it does everything else really well.
The art direction is nice, with a more "simplistic" designs for the characters and enemies, while going for more detailed for the environments. This works rather nicely, since there is a contrast between the characters and the environment they're fighting in, making it fairly easy to tell what is going on for the most part.
Combat is simple, but I do feel it gets much more interesting as enemies get more different attack patterns and your arsenal of charms and abilites grow. Charms, especially, give you nice options for varying playstyles once you get a decent number of notches unlocked. Some of them even directly combo with eachother as well.
The story kinda gives me Dark Souls vibe, in a sense that for some bits you may have to refer to other characters, reading the text of some of your items, or other means. The story itself is pretty nice though, especially when you finally do learn the meaning of being the "hollow knight".
The only real problems I have was when the game stutters for a second. That being said, I RARELY died in game because of it.
If you are fan of metroidvania-style games, then I would strongly advise Hollow Knight!
