Where do I begin? This game has not lived up to my expectations as an entrant into the X Universe. First off, on release day the game was so chocked full of bugs that I found it largely unplayable. Oh, the basic flight controls and interactions worked (mostly), but you couldn't stop a trade order given to a ship without going into the save file and doing some xml editing to clear out the "stuck" command. The main interface menu in the cockpit would randomly stop working, requiring either saving and then reloading to clear it, or jumping back&forth between the back of the ship and cockpit. Neither were 100% certain to clear that particular issue at any given time.
As for much of the other problems, they seriously dumbed down many of the foundational aspects of the X Universe. Remember the encyclopedia? That handy little in-game list of pretty much everything you've seen? That included things like where a certain ware was found to be sold? Gone. Oh, not all of it. It's still there, but the only things you see are the ware type, volume per unit, container type, and a brief "flavor" blurb to read/listen to the computer spew at you. Remember the map system that allowed you to pan around the map, select targets from the list for interaction, etc? Gone. Replaced with a very inflexible top-down-only view, no pan/zoom, and very limited list-based interaction. Remember targeting controls? Also gone. Replaced with a single mouse-click type/center reticle selection. Oh, the game also likes to forget your target randomly. Remember being able to tell your owned ships what to do? Yup, also severly stripped down. Remember trade goods/wares that NPC stations actually needed? Yeah, half of the classic ware list is "junk loot" now, to be sold to in-station NPCs, carried aboard your own ship, with a seemingly infinite cargo space.
Speaking of NPCs and the game's "Artificial Life." It's on life-support. Most of the ships you'll ever see on screen, just fly aimlessly in circles around huge stations. Most never even display a target icon unless you target them specifically. Only a few will, and those are the only "real" npc ships you'll see, aside from the cap ships.
Remember building massive, multi-station complexes wherever you pleased? Yup, gone. Replaced with location-based build sites. Remember building up a squadron of fighters? Last I had played, only the cap-ship merchants worked. Oh, there were docking platforms for "civilian ships," complete with icon, but no ship-builder NPC. That was as of 1.14, by the way.
I could really go on, but I think by now you get the idea. In the end, I really wish I hadn't spent my money on this game. I had pre-ordered. And while doubtful I'll ever see it, I am indeed asking for my money back, or a refund. Save yourself the headache, and just pass this game over.

A dissapointing mess of a game. Bugs and performances issues aside (they can be patched out), there are design choices that hurt this game on a fundamental level. Walking around on space stations and talking to NPCs may sound like fun on paper, but in practice it's tedious and ultimately pointless. The interface is cumbersome, apparently designed for Gamepads, making it much harder to get anything done than in previous X titles. The new sector/system maps are so clumsy as to be practically useless. The characters are all poorly designed and badly animated, and the dialogue and voice acting is embarassingly bad.
The inability to fly anything other than the starter ship, or create a player character other than the one named, human male the game throws at you, means that there's no possibility of pursuing your space-faring fantasy. No Han Solo or Malcom Reynolds for you, you are who the game says you are.
Despite some improvements in terms of visuals and the ability to move about faster (via highways and a faster boost), this game is a huge step backwards for the series and not worth paying full price for.

I had originally purchased X Rebirth in hopes that it would be a nice introduction to the X series. Unfortunately, that is not the case. The interface is clunky, the controls are confusing and unintuitive and the game does a poor job introducing the player to them. All throughout playing, I had a problem where the mouse steering centered in the lower right third of the screen instead of the center. This made it difficult to pitch down or yaw right at any meaningful pace.
The action isn't that much better. The fastest means of travel is tailgating ships in congested space highways. When piloting your ship, you will find that the gigantic and painfully useless displays obstruct your view and make it very difficult to track targets and orient yourself.
Finally, the voice acting is deplorable. Every single line of dialogue is dripping with, what feels like, feigned enthusiasm. On top of that, the atrocious writing caused me to sprain my eyes from rolling them so hard.
A more fitting name for this game would be: X Buyer's Remorse.

I admit it, I only got this because it was on sale and I already loved Torchlight 2.  Even so, I heartily recommend it for anyone who loves games like FATE.  Or horses.  (I mean in the Mr. Ed sense, not in the sense of riding one: "Gazing into the horse's eyes, you feel on the verge of understanding a deep mystery.")   If you understand the difference between rogue, roguelike and roguelite then you probably already own this game, and if you don't, you will still enjoy it.
Simply put, this is an enjoyable dungeon crawler game with no downside.  You pick one of 3 classes, akin to a tank, wizard, or ranger, and you go dungeon crawling to improve your gear and items so you can go deeper and deeper.  That's it.  Everything (grinding, levels, shared stash, socketed items, color-coded gear) here is fun and familiar if you've played any Blizzard game ever in the last 12 years.
Do try all three classes for each character, or at least as many as you like, until you find the one you like best.  (Though if you do it like I did, with everyone at once, then you'll find inventory management to be a mini-game all its own.)   You can adjust the difficutly setting and whether it's hardcore so you can tailor the game to be as hard or casual as you like.  And if the price bothers you, wait for one of the ever-present Steam bundle sales and get it at half off!
I recommend this game.  Every time I play it, I feel like I'm on the verge of understanding a deep mystery.  About horses.

I was so turned off by it that I was going to give up after an hour.  I did find that I was able to continue by switching the language back to German.  While not perfect, they at least tried to emote and it synced up with the mouth animations on the panel scenes given that it was the native language of the game.  Just go into it as if it's a foreign subtitled game.  I know that turns a lot you off, but it's still better than the English voice track.
that said...
A rather disappointing outing from Daedalic.  I tried harder than I usually would to give it a fair chance to impress but it never actually came through.
Screens/Backgrounds are well done.  The biggest compliment I can give here.
Story was lacking in my opinion.  Written too loosely and eco-preachy to the point of borderline annoyance.
Characters were weak and two dimentional.  Many of them so unlikable (looking at you Bent) that it was hard to care or empathise with them enough to desire any kind of resolution on my end other than soon forgetting them.
Puzzles are challenging, but fair.  To be honest, I was so tired of it all by the third act that I power FAQ'd.
It's currently $2.  Hard to say "Don't Buy" at a price that low, but I sure wouldn't recommend paying more.  I'll remain a longtime Daedalic fan for what they've done to reintroduce and support P&C genre adventures in recent years, but this  is an effort that can easily be swept under the rug.

If you love action / hack'n'slash RPGs (and are old enough to remember) and prefer Diablo I to Diablo II and want some new thrill - don't skip Torchlight. Many games have tried and all have failed to extract the essence but Torchlight could successfully become the spiritual breed of Diablo. Among an ample of cool things in game mechanics, balance and combat system that is newly oldish, having just the perfect balance, you will find one of the key elements that Diablo I and II had but III did not: master composer Matt Uelmen who single handedly created the atmosphere here with his amazing tracks. Not as if GFX were on the weak side, they are just a little easy, cartoony and cheery for Matt's heavy and dark sonic texture - but that's just me, you can't go wrong with the game itself, it feels, plays and looks cool. It is like a little ninja among the 10+GB sized games: nimble, tiny (600MB or so installed) and very stabile. I played it on XP32, XP64 W7 and W8 and it worked perfectly on all the systems, not a single freeze, glitch or hiccup whatsoever. I guess, developers put an extra emphasis on bugfree coding. It plays extremely solid.
Alsolutely recommended.

Alright, let's start with the good things.
+ Nice graphics
+ Good combat with nice flow
+ Option to choose weither to use english or japanese voice actors (thankfully, the english version is horrible).
+ There's a beautiful cutscene at one point in the game when one of the characters cry.
+ The end-game badasses are pretty hard.
+ Achievements
+ Trading cards
+ Never crashed
Now for what I believe are the bad things.
- Corridors, the game is one really long corridor. It's not disguised as having options. You literally walk on corridor-like platforms in a straight line for almost the entire game.
- You can't talk to people.
- There is almost nothing to explore.
- The vast majority of item drops are "XP"-gain items that are sacrificed to level up equipment. Sounds good? It's not. There's like a hundred different ones, give or take most of them do the same as the next with a very minor difference. Could easily remove 90-95% of them from the game without it having an impact whatsoever.
- An all-time-access shop (well, on save points but they're everywhere pretty much) that has EVERYTHING.
- There's no cash, just item drops (remember the XP-gain items?) from monsters. Drop rates are very low and selling things give close to nothing unless you got a rare drop from one of the end-game monsters (who are harder than every other boss in the game). Still, you need that cash to get the end-game items from the shop.
- Very few secrets to be found.
---------------------------------
I love the genre, both FF and JRPG but I can't recommend this game. It became decent in chapter 13 because after a very loooooong corridor I finally got to run around in a little park instead.
All in all, if you're a must-have-em-all then go for it, when it's on a sale and you already got every other FF game while being ready for a huge disappointment.

OK, let me start off by saying that I've played final fantasy 1-10, 12 and now 13. I really didn't want to give 13 a try mainly because I hated 12 so much and was upset they changed the fighting system. I had also heard a lot of negative things about 13. Alright, so the game is good. I really do like it. The fighting system is easy enough to get used to and to be honest, not that bad. I don't like how you don't level up normally and I don't like how you cant physically control each of your characters. That being said, I think its kinda cool how you can change your fighting style during battle.
OH, and this game was by far the easiest final fantasy game ever. Seriously. I never once ran out of items. You NEVER run out of mp so can constantly use your magic and abilities. The only "hard" (and kind of annoying) thing is that you have to level up your weapons and armor. This is a bit hard because so far, you have to FIND money. You cant pick it up after battle.
The story line is OK. I certainly do NOT think its the best final fantasy game. But, I am glad I gave it a shot and I honestly do not regret it.

The Magic TCG is one of the greatest experiences in gaming. That doesn't change here, but unfortunately some of the digital aspects of the game need a lot of work:
Unlocking all of the cards without spending money is one hell of a grind. Worse than any of the DoTP games. (however, their business model is much better than DoTP 2015, which isn't saying much).
The decks you can build with the starter pack of cards are all terrible. Better cards are unlocked, but it takes time or money.
Servers are frequently down. Progress cannot be made towards unlocking cards while servers are down. This may change in the future.
Deck builder is missing some key functionality such as sorting cards by keyword.
The card pool is based on the current set of paper magic cards, Magic Origins, a set which, compared both to other paper Magic card sets and the DoTP games is terribly lackluster. This may change when the new set comes out in a few months and the card pool is updated.
However, the game still gets a positive review from me since you can easily get many enjoyable hours of gameplay out of it without spending a cent.

Few games evoke such a complex range of emotional responses from me such as Hollow Knight did. It is at once a beautiful and haunting work of art and one of the most relentlessly frustrating excercises in boss pattern memorization I've experienced outside Bloodborne. It was more enjoyable then Cave Story, but perhaps less so then Axiom Verge.
You are a nameless bug knight, wielding nought but a sharpened nail, who has come upon the fallen remains of Hollownest- the last and only kingdom in a world where only ash lies to the west and a yawning chasm to the east. Wanderers come from far and wide to plumb the crumbling caverns and hallowed halls below you in search of wealth and glory, but few return, for a terrible power is sealed within that corrupts all it touches.
I heard about the game from a friend whose background in platformers and melee-focused games left him better suited to the experience. As someone who never excelled at either, something about Hollow Knight's gameplay continued to rub me the wrong way from start to finish. Nonetheless, the game was made with such obvious love and care that to simply ragequit it would have been a disservice to myself and to its developers. It is not a game for everyone, but I am glad that it exists.
Aesthetically, I rank the game among the highest I've played. The hand-drawn artwork, stark colors, excellent musical score and sound design, themes of purpose, lost glory and the power of dreams, and meloncholic atmosphere all struck a chord with me. It has a wondrous array of environments- spider caverns, an overflowing garden, a fiercely-guarded beehive, a fungal maze, and more, and a curious cast of bug-people who have a great deal to say- even more if you plumb their minds using the Dream Nail item, an interesting first in a series of free updates.
Gameplay wise, describing it as a Metroidvania is quite accurate, maybe more so then most, as it shares more in common with Symphony of the Knight then many titles that bear that moniker. However, it also much like Dark Souls- and far more so then you might believe, as that comparison tends to get thrown at any game with above-average difficulty. Scattered throughout the world are Benches to sit on that behave like the bonfires of Souls, restoring health and respawning certain defeated enemies. Also, upon death you leave a shade behind that has all your money, called "Geo." Failure to find and defeat this shade before dying again results in the loss of all your Geo- though, this is much easier to avoid then in Souls. However, as it lacks cooperative play, it is in its way much more difficult. Where in Symphony of the Night you are also predominantly a melee fighter, it is the case in that game, and indeed in Metroid, Shadow Complex, Axiom Verge and many other titles it is possible to acquire so many upgrades, either through exploration or leveling up, that you can circumvent any skill gap that might impede your progress. This is was even how I beat Bloodborne, after a fashion- if your raise your damage high enough, you only need to dodge so many attacks.
In Hollow Knight upgrades are few and far between, and in the case of the Charms, you are limited even in how many you can use at once. Your health bar caps at a measly nine hits, and an admittedly rare few attacks can shave off two of those. In addition, your only projectile attack shares a single mana bar, called "Soul", with your other spells- including your ability to heal, which forces you to stand still. All of this means you are often forced close in with enemies and specifically bosses that can potentially kill you in seconds and may not actually leave you any openings to recover health. There's nothing that will kill you outright as in Souls, but it still creates a high-tension combat dynamic where you will almost always die to a boss for the first few attempts- and as this is a 2D game, you have even less room for error. I can't argue that there's anything inherently wrong with this type of design, but it strikes me as antiquated and unecessarily frustrating in this day and age. And to paraphrase the Angry Video Game Nerd, in some way the worst part of it its the merciful save system- the game autosaves frequently and aside from having to retrieve your Geo, death merely sends you back to the last Bench at which you rested. This means you have little option but to hurl yourself at the same boss again and again until you learn how to beat it, and this wasn't something I could do without taking breaks to collect myself. I find myself jittering slightly even as I write this. I admit I found myself genuinely surprised to win some fights- especially the true final boss, which I am convinced I only defeated due to a particularly cheesy combination of Charms. There's also a bizarre, Super Meat Boy-esque sawblade-addled hazard course near the end that was both felt both vexing and out of place.
After repeating this process for thirty-some-odd hours, the end result of this was a game that frequently annoyed me but left me with enough fleeting moments of satisfaction and wonder that I cannot call it a bad game. But it is by no means an easy one, or even particularly fair. If you believe you can handle that, Hollow Knight is definately worth playing. I am also looking forward to the promised Hornet mode update, an alternate character campaign that was one of the game's Kickstarter stretch goals.

Despite my massive backlog, I had decided to pick up This War of Mine because the premise really, really intrigued me - I absolutely love survival games. To emphasize this, I had purchased The Long Dark, then Eternal Winter, then This War of Mine. Although the first two games were a lot of fun, they were still fairly barebones due to early-access status.
I played This War of Mine for 7 hours straight when I first tried it - 3 playthroughs. I love this game so much that I will be adding
. As an avid reviewer, I play A LOT of games in a short amount of time, and this is easily one of my favorite ones.
If you like grim survival gameplay in a war-torn country, deep immersion potential, testing the limits of your emotions, dark atmospheric themes, and elements from the rogue-like genres, then you will thoroughly enjoy this wonderful, macabre game. I was extremely impressed that an indie game was able to capture the essence of the brutalities and ugliness of war on such an artistic scale.
The aesthetics are fantastic! If you've played the atmospheric platformer Deadlight, you will notice some similarities in the side-scrolling environments. The level of detail in the areas and character models are great, however, I wish there was an option of changing your characters' clothing and appearance (not a big deal). A pencil-shading effect (similar to grain-filter effect seen in games like Mass Effect) adds a very nice touch to the dark and sombre atmosphere - you can adjust this to be soft or more obvious. The music and sounds are great and suit the theme of the game very well. You can also build a radio and leave one of two stations on - one classical and the other more of a general music genre. There is no voice-acting, which I found to flow well with the playstyle.
The game is point-and-click based, so the controls are fairly easy to familiarize yourself with. The learning curve is moderate to difficult, your experience with survival games and how to plan your actions will really affect how successful you may be - keep in mind that the game strongly encourages a pacifist (excluding self-defence) approach. When you start the game, there is no tutorial - you are immediately thrown right into your safehouse. You start off with (usually) 3 survivors randomly chosen from the grand survivor pool - each with a specific skill and weakness (or vice). For example, Arica has a much higher stealth rating and likes to smoke to calm down. You also start in a random season (usually NOT winter). The loot is randomized in each area, however, the layout of each location you can visit remains static.
The game operates on a day/night cycle (you can fast forward to night) - during the day, you will be in your safehouse and do things like build structures, eat, sleep, etc. During the night, you will give your group members different orders: have some sleep, guard, or scavenge (only one may visit an area per night). The areas you can visit are randomized each playthrough, and will sometimes be inaccessible if the civil war leaks over into certain areas. Something I just found out today was that, after

As you progress through the game, traders and recruit-able survivors will periodically visit your safehouse (limited to one event per day). Various neighbours will also come and ask for your help -
Each character needs to eat and sleep - being deprived of either for too long may result in their death or desertion. When you kill, or if a group member is injured/killed, remaining group members will usually experience a blow to morale. Morale falls from "sad" -> "depressed" -> "broken." When a character is broken (and sometimes depressed), they will be unresponsive to your commands - you will have to have other characters deliver food and medication to them. They will also be unusable as scavengers. To combat this, you can have any of your group members talk to the broken character - you can also try having two characters drink together to alleviate some stress.
Building and crafting is a major element of this game, and you will really have to plan out your build and scavenge routes to maximize your time. Trying to simply rush to the highest craft tier will most likely result in your quick death. On the city map, each visit-able location will have a list of items available to scavenge. Items do not respawn or restock in the different areas, and it is generally a bad idea to rely on randomness if you are in dire need of a specific item, like medicine for example. There are many areas where you can trade/steal from others, however, be advised that (at least early) violent/aggressive playstyles make the game exceedingly difficult if you are unprepared. Killing even one person damages group morale significantly, and it is very easy to find yourself with a group of mostly depressed/broken individuals.
The game adds amazing immersion in the character cards - the different members will record their opinions on what's happening. For example: if the group is starving, but Pavle has eaten, then he will have a comment saying something like: I must find my friends food since I am not hungry. The reactions when someone has committed murder or died are very interesting to see as well.
Overall, This War of Mine paints what I would expect an accurate, emotion-driven picture of what life would be like for unfortunate individuals caught in a war, and the tribulations they have to face to simply survive. If you are interested in war simulation and/or survival elements at all, then I implore you to try this game. You will not come out feeling good after playing it (more of an anti-catharsis), but you will not be disappointed.
ABSOLUTELY RECOMMEND!
Cheers,
DJSF

Impressions & Score:
Story: 9 out of 10
A shooter with a story, and a good story. Well that was something rare to see back in 2007. Of course, Half-Life 2 remains the shooter with one of the best stories that I've played, but Crysis isn't far from that. Crysis's story doesn't provide you with many answers regarding the alien race that you'll encounter or the characters, but it gives you just enough to make it realistic and immersive. The story is focused on a Special Ops  soldier, codename Nomad who goes on a rescue mission wearing an advanced nanosuit. The action takes place on a fictive island in the Philippines, where the North Korean army have invaded and taken control of an excavation site, taking all the researchers as hostages. Later you discover in the excavation site, a huge alien structure that comes alive when the North Korean army detonates bombs nearby.  The aliens have advanced technology (zero gravity environement, sub-zero ice sphere etc.) but they behave a bit like animals (from what I've noticed). Anyway, I don't want to give too many details, the story is awesome and it makes you wanna play to discover more.
Graphics: 10 out of 10
When Crysis came out back in 2007 it was game-breaking, due to it's awesome graphics and honestly it still looks amazing in 2014. There are many games out there that have recently been released and they don't look not even half as good as Crysis. If you compare it with modern day games, you'll find flaws in the graphics, but if you compare it with games from 2007, it looks incredible. I was really impressed by the details and by some of the innovative features.
Gameplay: 9 out of 10
First of all, I would like to suggest that you play this game on hard difficulty at least, just to get a bit of realism. Easy and Normal difficulty contain some stupid features that take away from the game's realism, like driving and firing turret at the same time, grenade warning, koreans that speak english etc. I played the game on the max difficulty and I assure you that it isn't too hard or too frustrating to play on this difficulty like in other games, it actually makes you use the different nanosuit abilities more often, which for me it's great.
There are only 2 features that I want to complain regarding the gameplay: 1. The enemies  have way too much armor  on delta difficulty (and I'm refering here only to the korean army, not the aliens, because aliens with high armor seem realistic to me), I sometimes shot over 50-60 bullets in a single korean soldier without killing him, but the good part is that headshots still cause instant kill 2. There are some stupid bugs where objects like barrels or other stuff can instantly kill you (and I'm no talking about explosive barrels). The game has great physics, you'll be able to destroy entire buildings and aliens can freeze you, most of the objects in the game can move and this sometimes can cause the bug that I mentioned earlier where you can get killed by a falling plastic barrel. Anyway the bugs don't happen often so the gameplay is great.
Audio: 10 out of 10
The audio is cool, you can hear animals during nightime or plants moving in the jungle, voice  acting is also well done and koreans speak korean (at least on delta difficulty). I'm not an audio guy but I will give it a 10, because I didn't found anything annoying or badly done.
AI Behavior: 9 out of 10
The AI of KPA soldiers is a bit bad, especially when you shoot them from behind , since they don't realise at all from which direction they are shot if you are far away.  Sometimes their collision system is funny, for example when a large group of KPA soldiers hears a sound, they'll try to hide and they will start colliding with each other and fall down, and you can just throw a grenade in the middle to finish them all at once. On delta difficulty they have very high accuracy, meaning that when they spot you, they will shot very well, however using your cloaking ability will make them lose your track, but be carefull not to cloak right in front of the enemy because they already know you are in front of them, so it won't work, this feature gives a bit of realism to the game.
The AI of aliens is nicely done, I mean they behave like a normal animal will do (a bit strange to see that  aliens with so advanced technology, they programmed their dronnes to have a animal behavior with low accuracy). The aliens have good damage but low accuracy, but what I like most about them is their behavior, which is mostly random. Of course they do the same circle around you and attack, but because they are flying, you don't know from where they might attack so you get this impression of random behavior. This is one of the best AI that I've encountered in a game, so I'm quite impressed.
Multiplayer: not tested
I bought the game in 2014, 7 years after it's release, so in the meantime the multiplayer servers have been shut down. I red online that the multiplayer lacked some variety regarding match types, but contained more weapons. I would have probably given an 8 or a 9.
Overall: 9.4 out 10
One of the best shooters on the market with a lot of innovative features and with amazing graphics. If you want to play multiplayer you'll be disappointed because it was deactivated, but nonetheless there are more recent versions of  Crysis (2 and 3) that have even better graphics and features where you can play in multiplayer. But even without the multiplayer this game still deserves to be bought, because it's  not only a good game,  it represents a game-breaking classic, that raised up the level for how future games should be made. This game is just awesome and I definitly recommend full price (14 99 EUR on Steam) or reduced price ( I've paid less than 5 EUR for Crysis, Crysis Warhead and Crysis 2 Max edition, all together), the choice is yours.
PS: I forgot to mention the fact that the game give you some feeling of liberty, even though is linear, mostly because of the size of the maps which is huge.

I have to admit from the start: I am an adventure fanatic. I love point and click games and the adventure genre is probably the only one that can immerse me fully in the story, it feels at times like I am directing my own movie based on a very strict script. I have been playing a few titles from Daedalic lately and find them all to be pretty good, especially on the artwork side of things.
A New Beginning is simply put: gorgeous! The sceneries are beautifully drawn and the comic book style cutscenes are beautiful, engaging and quite unique, I haven't seen them done in any other game so far. The only issue with the graphics side of things that I can find is the actual characters. They feel extremely out of place in some of the scenes, they difference in detail is quite striking at times and their placement in the scene looks off from time to time. A little more attention to animation and placement would have been nice to see. The interface is minimalistic and easy to access, there's no extra buttons to be pressed, a right click on the mouse and you can easily toggle the inventory.
The soundtrack is also great, the composed songs really fit the game and its circumstances so it also scores high points for sound design. The only issue that I can find with this game is voice acting. Seriously, this could have been a perfect game if not for the lousy voice acting. It really sounds like the actors read line after line without putting them into context, more like a monologue than a dialogue which sounds extremely silly at times and quite unprofessional. And speaking of lines, the script is quite poorly written. You get the feeling that the characters are either uneducated or plain ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Don't get me wrong, I don't expect people in a game to speak like a Literature PhD, but definitely not like someone who barely finished high school.
Speaking of the script I should also address the story. It's a little cliche if you ask me, the kind of story that reminds you of those 90's television-made movies that try to blend action with drama, but also convey a strong message and meaning while not bothering the viewer with questions and instead putting any answers straight on the table. A New Beginning also tries to send a message but it does poorly and scarcely and only focuses on this aspect by the end of the game. It also tries to do it via the aforementioned poor voice acting leaving you rather facepalmed and laughing out loud that deeply moved and touched. It does, however, make up for it in the final scene, which unfortunately appears right at the end of the credits which can be skipped so most of the players will definitely miss this one.
All in all this was a great game to play with an immersive story, great sound design and loads of puzzles ranging from moderate to hard and many actions that require out-of-the box thinking so it can be both challenging and frustrating at times. The game also has a seamless auto-save feature so if your game happens to crash just hit continue on the main screen (the autosave is not visible in the load menu).
I give this one a 8.5/10

I liked it. Time to nitpick.
The sailing is dull, you're on a boat in samy looking waters doing bugger all until one of three different types of ships decide to invade your personal space for whatever reason and you either blow them the heck out, or do nothing - mostly the latter because it really doesn't affect anything at all, you'll have plenty of gold to upgrade your ship just by doing main quest line and the rest is aesthetics and upgrades for the water levels - oh yeah, it has underwater levels, because that's what audiences have been wishing for since Ocarina of Time: More underwater levels.
Somebody employed at Ubisoft still thinks that escorting a character while he/she explains and sets up the plot for the next boat ride to another darn boat battle is "good storytelling".
The amount of stabby you get to do is incredibly limited and the game is just too damn long by being artificially inflated by sailing about.
I started out by being a good pirate and finding that one special set of armour that's in every assassin's creed game, and it's unlocked by killing some scrubs. Then you show up and you talk to some pleb and the plebs act like they've known you for bloody ages even though you've never met them before, and there's one of them you don't even meet in the main quest even though these guys are pretty important.
Then you do the stabbing - it's okay I guess, pretty unremarkable really, but at least it's not sailing unless you count the ages of sailing to get to the islands to get to the people to get to their throats to get to the key to get to the suit.
Finally I got the suit, but it has no hood and good ol' Kenway still does the "putting hood on" animation in every cutscene, as though he's tipping his imaginary fedora.
The best part of the game is when you come to a city and they expect you, so it feels like Assassin's Creed - the first one. Makes you feel like you're an actual threat as opposed to some arbitrary pleb.
Had to climb up some building to kill the last guy contextually in stead of shooting him with my gun because he had plot armour out of nowhere.
Basically the stabbing is sparse, the locations are, as thinly populated areas with something like 4 sheds tend to be, not well suited for assassinations, the animation bugs are stupid but not "Unity" stupid, the storytelling is garbage but at least it's not AC3-level, Kenway being able to do the things that a highly trained assassin can do is breaking the suspension of disbelief, the areas all look identical and there's just too much water.
Now take what I said, and remove every complaint about how much the sailing sucked, because I've heard it's a really great pirate game, I'm just not that into that kind of thing it seems.
All in all:
6/10, a pirate game in the flavour of Assassin's Creed because the title sells well.

The game itself is fantastic. I run it at the highest graphics settings because I can, so maybe I'm jaded in that respect. However, upon entering the game, I was asked to make a stardock account. Im not a fan of games that dont directly link to my steam account, but this one seemed (and is) worth it. I did the tutorials, which I see no problem with. As with any in-depth strategy game, the tutorials are only there so you aren't saying "what does this button do?" later. Once youre done with those, do yourself a favor and set up a small map with an easy AI. Thats the real tutorial. I have played Civ 5 almost religously (I bring it up because it seems to be the most common comparison) and yes, its tutorial teaches you more in a shorter time frame. HOWEVER Civ 5 was also dumbed down quite a bit from its predecessor, if you know your civ. While I admit to not having played enough to get a feel for the power balance among the 6 different factions you can play as, they seem to creatively offer different playstyles, most related to war. An in-game simplistic map creator and adjustable settings of almost anything in the game (victory speeds, quick starts, team locks, ect.) score big points. Mods are endless, Star Wars comes to mind almost immediately. The ONLY MAJOR CON I HAVE ENCOUNTERED is the multiplayer system. Accross PC and console gaming I have never seen a lobby/host/chat system as confusing as SINS. There is a seperate tab for a hosting test, which has a single check box for alloy. I have no idea what alloy is, and still dont after reading multiple stardock FAQs. It says it is used to identify the IP address of your computer to allow hosting. I honestly have no idea what that means, and I personally feel as though it scares away players with little to no knowledge in that area. If it doesnt, the technical guides will. I tried reading the help sections, and posted were comments rich in IT language and computer terms I wasn't familiar with, and most certainly wasn't comfortable with changing on my computer, especially when one of the few words I understand in those comments is "firewall". From the number of commenters and views, a great many other people are having the same problems. I would like to be able to host a multiplayer game, just as easily as I can in any other game, such as Civ 5. I do NOT want to have to become an IT guy to play a 1v1 with a friend. I reccomend the game, and should multiplayer become clearer to me I will edit or respond to this review. However, potential buyers YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED. Multiplayer is confusing and complicated and appears to me as though it cannot do what other games can. I would like to see improvements from the DEV team in the future, if only in its coherency. Love the look. But when setting up a game with other people is harder than learning a real-time, in-depth stategy game, it kills most of the fun. 7/10 from me. For now

First things first: it's a bad port. There are very few options and it doesn't run well. Compared to, say, the Valkyria Chronicles pc port it's embarrassing. Kb/m controls are glitchy. We had to make threads on steam and wait months just to get above 720p resolution and graphical options, which are still very limited. That's how bad a port this is.
Now, the game itself. It looks very good. The cutscenes look amazing, the story is kind of interesting, and, if it's the sort of thing you look for in a game, the female characters are done very well imo, except for Vanille, she's kind of annoying. The battle system takes a while to get the hang of but when you do, it's quite good. Until then, you will be just spamming the A button. The story focuses on a group of unlucky individuals who have been cursed - 'l'cie' (some of the names in this game are silly, and it throws a bunch of nouns at you  immediately which you won't understand) They struggle with their fate - which for me is one of the more interesting parts of the story. A good part of the game is just them coming together as a group, and figuring out their destiny, which makes the dynamic of the group strong and interesting.
The game is very linear. This wouldn't be a problem if the game wasn't so repetitive. There is nothing to do besides walk forwards, fight, cutscene. The game desperately needed some variation, some more puzzle solving, or something. It's too long, too. Be prepared to walk, battle, cutscene for 100 hours+. There are no towns, and very little people to actually interact with in the world, which makes me question why this is even a game at all, and not a film/tv series/ anime. When the game finally opens up all you get are quests, go here kill this monster, but at this point the thought of doing any more battles felt like such a chore I skipped most of them. The upgrade system is a complete gamble and you end up wasting so much money through being inefficient at what's essentially a guessing game. The crystarium levelling system is a perfect metaphor for the game: looks flashy, but in fact is very linear with few branching paths. I am seriously failing to understand what the logic behind some of these design decisions were, unless they thought 'It's final fantasy, we can do no wrong.' Well, they did wrong. I remember the devs talking about streamlining the game to make it more accessible. Well, that was a bad idea, because nobody who doesn't already play total grindfests will want to spend more than a few hours playing this.
I tried to enjoy this game, I really did. I tried to persevere through the repetition to find out what happens in the end. But it's just too much. They should have made this game 15-20 hours, cut most of the flashy yet ultimately linear and boring levels and told a much tighter, more varied story through more than just the cutscenes. It feels like a bunch of grinding attached to an admittedly very stylish and good looking collection of cut-scenes which tell an interesting story. It's just a shame that the actual game couldn't have been better.

Marvel vs Capcom has always been a series I've had quite a fondness for. The gameplay is hectic but simple to get to grips with which means a semi casual like me can have fun without dedicating hours and hours to mastering it. At the same time, there's enough depth in the combo system to allow for more hardcore players to create complex and optimised combos.
Infinite follows that same ethos but there's one glaring problem right now: the playerbase is so small that casual players who can barely string together a combo are matched up against players who can take 75% of your health away in a combo from one hit. It's incredibly frustrating to play for someone like me who is willing to put time in to get better but there's no one really on my lower skill level to play against.
Part of that problem is because the game - unlike Street Fighter V - doesn't have Cross Play between PS4 and PC. Cross Play would have been to the benefit of both playerbases but it's unfortunately absent here.
I would say that this is a strong argument against buying this game on PC but that would do nothing to solve my biggest issue with it. The game needs more players.
And the game doesn't do the best job of training new players. You have a mission mode which teaches you basic controls and basic to complex combos for all characters, but not how to execute those combos properly or how to utilise them in a real game. You could be able to execute the most complex combos in the game but unless you know how to get in on your opponent and confirm your hits, it's all for nothing.
The sad part is that the core game is good. The gameplay is fun - the new tag system makes a nice change from the craziness of assists in Marvel vs Capcom 2 and 3 and opens up a lot more potential synergy between characters.
The infinity stones are something I'm a little on the fence about. I find the vast majority of the infinity surges lackluster which is why a lot of players gravitate towards the homing projectile of the reality stone which is far easier to get value out of. The infinity storms for all of the stones sound pretty useful but without changes to the surges, they will rarely be utilised.
The graphics need a major overhaul. The character models are rough for the most part. The character faces just seem... off. The UI is fairly basic and visually unappealing. And there's this haze to the game which makes everything look blurry. Compared to the heavily shaded comic book style of Marvel vs. Capcom 3, it's a major downgrade for a game with a lot more graphics power at its disposal.
The story mode seems like a wasted investment. I understand that story modes are big in fighting games at the moment but really, most people will play them once and then never touch them again. The mode is alright in Infinite but when you look at the lack of other single player content (like a more fleshed out arcade mode,) it does make you a bit resentful towards it.
The game controversially has also omitted any X-Men and Fantastic Four characters. Given that the characters - especially Wolverine and Magneto - are synonymous with the series, their absence leaves a rather large hole in the character roster. The roster currently comprises of mostly cut and copies from Marvel vs Capcom 3 with a few tweaks and additions to moves here are there, with only six of the characters from the base game being new additions. The available DLC characters are all newcomers but that does little to entice anyone to make that initial purchase.
Marvel vs Capcom Infinite is a fun, solid game with a lot of potential in a very unattractive and underwhelming package. It's almost like playing a game which is in beta, only I paid £40 for it and will need to keep paying to experience new content.
As it stands, I wouldn't suggest buying this game unless it's on sale for a decent price. I do hope the developers work to address some of the main complaints because the core of the game is great. A lot of work went into improving Street Fighter V post-launch. Let's see if Infinite will get the same treatment.

I\'ve put a bit of time into this game and Brawlhalla as well, and because they are contantly in conversations together I will continue that trend and mention that game as I speak about this one.
Rivals of aether is an fun and amazing game very similar to the original smash bros. The game is complex but interesting and have a fair amount of character diversity to make the experience enjoyable. Compared to brawlhalla this game has the better formula, but it suffers from some major lag issues. Make sure to play this game with an ethernet cable at all times and if you play online watch the ping of the other player. If their ping isn\'t yellow don\'t bother playing them or else your match will be plagued with input lag.
Aethetically, the game isn\'t too pleasing and seems like an retro game (guess this appeals to some people), but if you\'re willing to overlook the oldschool graphics you have a whirlwind of fun coming at you. It is obvious this game isn\'t in full release which is evident in the limited online play. Currently, online is limited to only one vs. one as opposed to brawlhalla\'s typical four to eight player free for all. Hopefully the devs can fix the lag issue and improve the game\'s net code.
If you compare this game\'s characters to that of brawlhalla, brawlhalla has the larger roster. ROA\'s character roster may be smaller but every character feels unique and have their own unique move-sets. On the otherhand Brawlhalla\'s character slection is based a select seof weapons and every character have similar move-sets.
With all that being said, this game is exetremely promising and it\'s your go to game to get your fighting-game-fix. I recommend the game, but be warned that the game definately feels incomplete in its current form.

So I finally pushed myself to play more of this game. Do I recommend it? No.
Now, hear me out. The game is a decent action/stealth game. But it is a terrible Hitman game.
About the game:
Avoidma-- I mean, Hitman is about the Assassin only known by his codename: 47. (Spoilers from previous games ahead and minor spoilers of Hitman Absolution story) The game follows up on the previous games. Diana, 47's handler, has betrayed the agency. Because of her, countless agents are dead. So her name was put on the hitlist and 47 was sent to kill her. Which he does. With her dying breath, she explains that she did it to protect this girl who was being raised just like 47, to become a hitwoman. But Diana wanted to protect her. Diana asks 47 to go get this girl named Victoria and protect her, and just like that, the Agency's loyal lapdog (Honestly, 47 is nothing but a lapdog in the first mission, killing his only friend) betrayes the Agency as well and goes after the girl. From that point on, you get a simple story filled with innocent women getting shot quite gruesomly. (Is that a theme lately in games? Sure, why is it okay to see a innocent man getting slaughtered, but not a woman? Well, I like women. >.<) So don't expect a great story, though if you are used to the older Hitman games, then you can expect a great story, because the previous hitman games never really followed a story, and it never had to.
The story is mostly "You almost get it, then you fall into a Deus Ex Machima trap, and you can start all over till you finally get it, or do you? Play the game to find out.
So about the game itself. It's very frustrating. It looks pretty nice (though the cutscenes look worse then Blood Money's cutscenes if you ask me.. But that could be because its really low rez on the PC.) and it plays well enough. But the levels. They try to look like Hitman worthy levels, but its just short fragments of the same with a nice Hitman-ribbon around it. But once you unwrap it, its just really small. For examply, there are levels you can just walz through in a couple of minutes. Level completed. And not talking about the little story levels that only shows 47 getting a new suit.
The levels are like this. Instead of one big level like in Hitman: Blood Money, you get 3 or 4 smaller ones you have to play through. You can get through it stealthy, but because the parts are so small, there really is just one way, maybe two at times. As opposed to Blood Money's levels where you can take 7 or 8 different approaches. That doesn't mean the level's aren't challenging. They are far more challenging then anything a Hitman game ever threw at you. One because they messed up the Disguise system, and two, because they put SO MANY enemies in a level, it will take you many tries to get through it without getting seen. Oh, and there is no quicksafe, so you will replay a level from the beginning often. And there kicks in the frustration. Now, there are checkpoints in the game you can activate. Once you do, you can restart from there, but all the NPC's (Uncluding unkilled targets) will have resetted to their original starting point, so prepare to wait again. Wait again. Waaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaait again.
As mentioned above, the disguise system, one of Hitman's most fun systems, is faulty. You can dress up, but ANY ONE wearing the same outfit as you, will suspect you, and fast. Because in Absolution, every thug, cop, soldier, swat member, gang member, chemist, etc knows EVERYONE by face and can spot that from 50 feet away. Even if you are turned around and are wearing a hood. They can even see you through bushes. In the dark. And still recognise you. Yes, that sounds fair.
The targets you have to kill are chosen at random at times. You get in a spot where there is some mad doctor testing mines, you automatically get that character as a target. Why? Because... er... THAT'S WHY! Makes sense.
Not very optimistic yet about Avoidman, but it has some good things. The voice acting is great, the gritty style is fun, the story is just interesting enough to make you want to follow it through and the shooting is also more fun. And because the levels are broken down in smaller fragments, you can easily replay a part of a level to improve your score and compete against friends in your Steam friends list.
More often then once though, I just shot everything in sight out of frustration to just get through one of those damn hard levels, because after replaying it 5 times and having to wait 5 minutes for some guard/target to move to the right place gets so frustrating that you either just run through the level to the next part, or just shoot everything, just so you can continue the story.
And it happens a liiiitle to much that when there finally is something interesting happening, you have you play through boring enemy filled levels, waiting your move, just to get some more story, and it takes forever to continue.
Sure, it's a new sort of Hitman game, one with more story and emotion. I can accept that. There was a lot of emotion running during some levels where the thugs did something so bad, you just wanted to stalk them all down and kill them, and it felt good. (The ones who played this game know what level I am talking about.) But most levels were just to boring and felt pointless. Some were brilliant, like one where you had to escape from the cops. Yes, it feels very un-hitman like, but it was an AWESOME level. And I wouldn't have minded more of those. They were intense, the camera play was excelent, and it kept you on the edge of your seat. Quicksafe is a must for games like there, or better checkpoints. there is nothing so frustrating as when you spent 15 to 30 minutes in one part, and by one mistake, one thug you haven't seen, or because of the damn disguise system flaw, you have to start ALL over again. I agree it adds more challenge, but save that sort of♥♥♥♥♥♥for the hardcore mode, not the normal mode where players want to enjoy the game, not wanting to throw their controller/mouse towards the screen.
Verdict?
To me a Hitman game is about the puzzle, the planning, the blending into the crowd and finding the most "fun" way to kill your target. To replay a level 10 times, completing your objective differently every time. It is about exploring a big area, seeing the oppertunities to complete your mission as your plan just clicks into palce. (Absolution has a couple of these moments, but just a couple of times in the entire game while in previous hitman games, you had those moments a couple of times in every level.) This is just not a Hitman game, but more like a more actionfilled spinoff starring our favorite Hitman: 47. I give this game a 4 out of 10 when you look at the title. It's a very poor Hitman game. If I won't look at the title and the previous games, I give it a 6 out of 10. It's a fun action/stealth game. Especially for only €19,99. I just can't recommend this game to Hitman fans.

Despite my massive backlog, I had decided to pick up This War of Mine because the premise really, really intrigued me - I absolutely love survival games. To emphasize this, I had purchased The Long Dark, then Eternal Winter, then This War of Mine. Although the first two games were a lot of fun, they were still fairly barebones due to early-access status.
I played This War of Mine for 7 hours straight when I first tried it - 3 playthroughs. I love this game so much that I will be adding
. As an avid reviewer, I play A LOT of games in a short amount of time, and this is easily one of my favorite ones.
If you like grim survival gameplay in a war-torn country, deep immersion potential, testing the limits of your emotions, dark atmospheric themes, and elements from the rogue-like genres, then you will thoroughly enjoy this wonderful, macabre game. I was extremely impressed that an indie game was able to capture the essence of the brutalities and ugliness of war on such an artistic scale.
The aesthetics are fantastic! If you've played the atmospheric platformer Deadlight, you will notice some similarities in the side-scrolling environments. The level of detail in the areas and character models are great, however, I wish there was an option of changing your characters' clothing and appearance (not a big deal). A pencil-shading effect (similar to grain-filter effect seen in games like Mass Effect) adds a very nice touch to the dark and sombre atmosphere - you can adjust this to be soft or more obvious. The music and sounds are great and suit the theme of the game very well. You can also build a radio and leave one of two stations on - one classical and the other more of a general music genre. There is no voice-acting, which I found to flow well with the playstyle.
The game is point-and-click based, so the controls are fairly easy to familiarize yourself with. The learning curve is moderate to difficult, your experience with survival games and how to plan your actions will really affect how successful you may be - keep in mind that the game strongly encourages a pacifist (excluding self-defence) approach. When you start the game, there is no tutorial - you are immediately thrown right into your safehouse. You start off with (usually) 3 survivors randomly chosen from the grand survivor pool - each with a specific skill and weakness (or vice). For example, Arica has a much higher stealth rating and likes to smoke to calm down. You also start in a random season (usually NOT winter). The loot is randomized in each area, however, the layout of each location you can visit remains static.
The game operates on a day/night cycle (you can fast forward to night) - during the day, you will be in your safehouse and do things like build structures, eat, sleep, etc. During the night, you will give your group members different orders: have some sleep, guard, or scavenge (only one may visit an area per night). The areas you can visit are randomized each playthrough, and will sometimes be inaccessible if the civil war leaks over into certain areas. Something I just found out today was that, after

As you progress through the game, traders and recruit-able survivors will periodically visit your safehouse (limited to one event per day). Various neighbours will also come and ask for your help -
Each character needs to eat and sleep - being deprived of either for too long may result in their death or desertion. When you kill, or if a group member is injured/killed, remaining group members will usually experience a blow to morale. Morale falls from "sad" -> "depressed" -> "broken." When a character is broken (and sometimes depressed), they will be unresponsive to your commands - you will have to have other characters deliver food and medication to them. They will also be unusable as scavengers. To combat this, you can have any of your group members talk to the broken character - you can also try having two characters drink together to alleviate some stress.
Building and crafting is a major element of this game, and you will really have to plan out your build and scavenge routes to maximize your time. Trying to simply rush to the highest craft tier will most likely result in your quick death. On the city map, each visit-able location will have a list of items available to scavenge. Items do not respawn or restock in the different areas, and it is generally a bad idea to rely on randomness if you are in dire need of a specific item, like medicine for example. There are many areas where you can trade/steal from others, however, be advised that (at least early) violent/aggressive playstyles make the game exceedingly difficult if you are unprepared. Killing even one person damages group morale significantly, and it is very easy to find yourself with a group of mostly depressed/broken individuals.
The game adds amazing immersion in the character cards - the different members will record their opinions on what's happening. For example: if the group is starving, but Pavle has eaten, then he will have a comment saying something like: I must find my friends food since I am not hungry. The reactions when someone has committed murder or died are very interesting to see as well.
Overall, This War of Mine paints what I would expect an accurate, emotion-driven picture of what life would be like for unfortunate individuals caught in a war, and the tribulations they have to face to simply survive. If you are interested in war simulation and/or survival elements at all, then I implore you to try this game. You will not come out feeling good after playing it (more of an anti-catharsis), but you will not be disappointed.
ABSOLUTELY RECOMMEND!

*NOTE* Review is for ArmA 2 vanilla, not for Op. Arrowhead, as I can't paste the review there for some reason.
ArmA 2, the spiritual successor of Operation Flashpoint and the direct successor to ArmA: Combat Operations. A hardcore open world tactical shooter with lots of mission making and modding possibilities. It's now slightly aged in the face of ArmA 3, the latest entry in the series, but still offers lots of content while running better on lower end machines. The "Chernarus" terrain was made with lots of attention to detail and is quite faithful to the real deal (part of Czech Republic). The realism in the game is still quite high, especially compared to some more popular shooters out there that eschew realism in favour of accessible "run and gun" gameplay. Perhaps one downside to this realism is that, at times, the game can feel a bit "clunky", but with tweaked controls and mods, we can customize it to our flavour. One important thing to note, though, is that this version here does *not* work online as the MP browser is still tied to GameSpy, a service that went down years ago. This means that you will need the standalone expansion, Operation Arrowhead, too in order to play online. So unless you just want to play offline, I suggest you grab ArmA 2 Combined Ops which includes Op. Arrowhead too (and yes, you'll need that to play Day-Z). On a discount, this title is still very worth grabbing, especially for those with slightly dated hardware (make sure you have a fast CPU though, as the ArmA games are known to be CPU-hogs).

I'm the type of person that will get the wrong meal at McDonalds and not bother turning around, or get charged twice for a pack of gun and be too lazy to wait in line again. Yet, even I attempted to contact the developers of X Rebirth seeking a refund for my purchase.
The trading system? Annoying. Maybe it's just the bugs, but I found the process extremely tedious.
Combat? Imagine playing Halo with your 5-year-old nephew. Now make him wear oven mitts. The combat is not difficult unless the odds are 8:1 or greater in the enemies favor. I specifically sought out "Very Hard" missions when I started, because they were all against capital ships. Why? Because all I had to do was get right behind them. Wrap a rubber band around the trigger and just occasionally tap the throttle so you stay in close. Note that getting that close is not remotely difficult, either.
Customizing your ship? You can choose from a small selection of guns. Most are fairly repetitive with the same effect when everything is said and done.
The ability to board stations? I'm fairly certain the individual in charge of these level designs has since been diagnosed with carpal tunnel due to excessive use of CTRL+V.
All in all, don't waste your time on this for at least a couple more years. By then, hopefully the modding community will have completely rebuilt the game from ground zero.

Instead I’ll focus on explaining to anyone that might be interested, why someone like me has put hundreds of hours in a game so fundamentally broken as this.
The short answer for that is in the focus of all early advertisement, what Egosoft called a “real world economy”.
I’m a Builder, and as many others like me I love games like Factorio, Civilisation, Minecraft, etc.
While in Civilisation like games you are building towards a specific purpose, running against the computer, in Minecraft like games you are left with tools to sculpt whatever you like in a huge world made of building blocks. In one, you have a complex finite game that can be repeated and replayed endlessly, but with a very limited variation, while in the other you have an infinite game with countless possibility in a world so simple that it is uncappable to accompany the player.
What I found in X Rebirth is a game that conceptually falls somehow in between those two styles. It’s an infinite game in a complex world, where you can build complex variations that in turn interact and influence the environment.

The first thing you'll notice about this game is that the art style is hugely inconsistent, and I don't mean inconsistent in the way that half of the fighters are from different videogames with varying graphic styles. Many of the characters look like their models were ripped right out of UMVC:3, and this lack of care is especially apparent on the Capcom side. It's almost as if Marvel held them to a higher standard, or that Capcom knew that certain characters were less popular, so they adopted a "that'll do" attitude to the quality of their models.
Having said that, even the characters who have obviously had a lot of artist time devoted to them look strange. Captain America does not look human; he has an enormous wrestler neck bulge and incredibly broad shoulders. It's obvious that he's heavily stylised, but when you place him down with the other 'regular non-anime' humans, he just doesn't fit in. Nobody does. Surely if you're adapting several characters from comic books, those characters should look like they're from the same world? Cap looks like he was breastfed protein shake and raised on a planet inhabited by stretch armstrong figures.
Even if you can look past the jarring visual style, the loading times will send you to sleep. I can only assume that this is because of the Denuvo DRM. I will admit straight away that I don't know how it works, and maybe that's not what causes the
delay between fights, but if not that, then what is causing it? Some people on the user forums suggested that hard drive disk speed was the culprit, and to really experience the game, purchase of an SSD was a must. My only reponse to these people is why? The game has a fairly simple battle arena, no transitions or interactable environment props to load (unlike Netherrealm fighting games), and the visuals are nothing too special.
But let's say that you're a fan of the series, and like me, you're willing to overlook what other people consider to be poor visuals and performance problems because you think the game looks alright and will run well on your system. What about the combat, and the roster?
Well as you are probably aware, this game features a much more spartan roster than previous titles. This is both because Marvel is still dumping on the X-Men and the Fantastic Four due to them not wanting to promote a property that they don't have the movie rights to, and also because Capcom, like all publishers these days, would like it if you paid £40 for their game, but would like it more if you paid £65. So there's a £25 charge on unlocking all of the characters to play.
If that's still fine with you, then enjoy, but don't plan on unlocking alternate costumes for the characters, like you could in the previous game, because there's a £25 charge on that as well. That's the only way to get them.
On a final note about the combat, it is fun, and a lot more accessible than previous titles, but in a bizarre way. They basically added this 'auto-combo' system, where combos are initiated without you having to enter the button combinations yourself. In my experience, it was like the game was playing itself and I felt a little too disconnected. You can literally 'combo' by repeatedly pressing one button, for example. Personally I've never been good at MVC, but I think this system is not the way to fix the accessibility of the title.

(Without spoilers)
The game introduces you with a cutscenes which are beautifully made by the way. My first reaction was "It looks epic". It tells about the usual good vs evil but with a twist. The story really submerges you into the FF world, the athmosphere, music, sound, everything helps with making you feel submerged.
The game has
which all have their own story. FF does a great job on combining them so they all have their own and their shared story.
The cut scenes are a welcoming thing. I am actually excited when one appears. Normally I feel like skipping but with this game its like watching a movie.
The combat is just like (from what I know) the other FF games: Turn based.
Only everything continues simultaneously, so in other words: If you dont tell your character which attacks to use the character will get attacked but wont attack unless you tell it too. You control one character per battle and the others in your party will auto-attack based on what attacking scheme you use.
Fighting schemes decide which classes what characters use.
For example you can have a scheme where you would have one Attacker, tank and a medic. If you would control the character who is the attacker the tank will try to take the hits and obviously the medic will try to heal.
You can switch schemes at any time in a battle and I recommend you do so.
The battle begins as you walk towards an enemy and they notice you, But you can also try to sneak up from behind to try and land a sneak attack. With a sneak attack the enemies stagger bar is already filled so when you hit an attack the enemy will be staggered and take extra damage.
Now what is staggering? When you chain up attacks on a specific target their stagger bar will be filled and when it's full your next attack will stagger it so the enemy will take more damage and be stunned for the first hit.
You fight with a max of 3 people from what I have seen till now.
Is pretty basic, A skill tree based on the classes so for example: Char 1 -> Choose which of the classes you want to upgrade the skills of.-> Upgrade skill -> Earn more xp with battles ^
I am pretty happy with the skill system, its basic but it works good. Feel comfortable and not weird.
You can customize what kind of weapons your characters have and what kind of boosters etc. By the time I am writing this it is not that important in the game yet.

Down my past/new experience(s) with the franchise.
Let's start with the fact I began playing this series with marvel vs capcom 2, at ruckers when I was a kid, a couple of the things that drew me in were the characters, as well as the fast-paced action, flashing lights,♥♥♥♥♥♥flying everywhere with recognizable 2d sprites from previous games, as well as a few new ones all plated on gorgeous 3d backgrounds? and the seemingly perpetual pool of people floating around the machine, the music. Everything.
Along comes UMvC3, wow, what an artstyle. Agressive shading and stylizing really made everything pop and look great, and the roster... oh sweet jesus the roster... they could have called this game "Marvel vs Capcom: A love letter to fans" it became even more expansive and the gameplay became... let's say... mind numbing/kind of hard to watch if you didn't know what you were looking at. Admittedly I played the least of this one due to the fact there was just too much♥♥♥♥♥♥happening at once but it still looked great, and the roster/gameplay was always fun to watch at fighting game competiton and events.
Enter MvCI.
Stone system from the first game, active tag system, two character combat. I was hype. Unfortunately there are some absolutely glaring issues with Marvel vs Capcom Infinite It's hard not too get bothered by. I feel the game needed another year in development to really polish the style they were going for, as well as expand the roster a little. The roster is one of the biggest problems with most of the characters being return characters from UMvC3, which would be fine if they didn't use the exact same specials and animations (for the most part) as the previous game, it just doesn't feel or look very fresh.(If you have ever played Marvel's "Contest of Champions" for mobile, the art style reminds me of that everytime I play it.)
The stone system needs a rebalance, as most people will just use Soul or Reality, A few use Space and Power, and you'll rarely see time or mind. Especiall mind.
The gameplay, is fantastic however. It's the most fun I've had with the franchise thus far, I just wish the roster wasn't so scarce, I'm not even upset about the exclusion of X-men characters, I'm over that already. They could have just made so many better choices, even if they were trying to include the MCU. As I said before most of the roster is returning characters with the same stuff. Some characters need some balancing or the rest of the roster needs buffs as a few characters absolutely dominate the rest of the roster and have all the tools while some characters have none.
TL;DR: Game plays great, roster sucks, art style sucks.

EDIT: This is an updated review concerning RT. I initially gave the (base) game a cautious recommendation but now I am a bit more inclined to recommend it.
Pros that reflect problems fixed:
-  More affinity quests and diverse storylines.
- Prosperity nerfed
- Improved diplomacy; agreements; alliances with AI have greater incentive; AI behaviour much more predictable but (see cons that reflect new problems)
- Affinity victories delayed, but (see cons that reflect unfixed problems)
- Stations blocking expansion not as bad as before
- Apollo no longer too easy, at least I see it that way.
- improvements to perks and building quests, less one-sided choices.
Pros that reflect new content:
- Hybrid affinities, more diverse combat styles
- Traits, which add further customization for your colony
- Sea cities, more space to expand, but...(see cons that reflect new content)
- More diverse aliens
- Better expeditions, with artifacts.
- Marvels
- Some AI will actually try and stop you from winning at a certain level regardless of relationship.
- New wonders and also some nice changes to old ones, but (see cons that reflect new problems)
- Some funny and crazy build combos, like ARC + subtle + spy operation speed artifact + quick speed. Spies carry out operations even 2-3 turns.
- planes are buffed.
Cons that reflect unfixed problems:
- Affinity victories left unchanged, emancipation and transcendence victories still too easy.
- Game now favours wide empires even further.
- Science penalty per city still too small. In considering this with the above 2 points, one common strat you'll see in MP is that people just settle cities everywhere like crazy and then rush down harmony for transcendence victory.
- link between affinity and tech still too strong. The affinity XP threshold per level needs to grow faster per levelup, potentially including hybrids too.
- Some unit perks and building quests are still too one-sided, like the ultrasonic fence quest.
Cons that reflect new problems:
- Sea cities seem a bit underwhelming and their low combat defence is very irritating. Moreover, if you're a sea sponsor, it's preferable that you don't anger the aliens until you can fight off the krakens. Even the sea dragons will put you on edge when expanding. Add hydracoral to that and it's quite frustrating.
- The pace of the game is now quicker than before and with hybrid affinities and on quick speed, it's possible to get tier 4 hybrid units by turn 100. In turn, you can just steamroll your opponents. While the hybrid affinities do make early or mid-game domination victory more viable, you can still snowball easily.
- Concerning diplomacy in SP, it has become too attached to a player's overall performance. There is no character in the AI, and they all see things through a realist perspective. If you perform weakly, the AI will mock you and then attack you. Making peace with them is pointless unless you develop and become better than them in some way. If you snowball early, you don't have to worry about AIs attacking you at all until you are getting close to winning the game. This is because the AI respects you if you respond to their trait criticisms positively and it fears you if you build a large enough army. So in turn, you can game the AI on diplomacy simply by being really good at developing your colony in the early game.
- Some traits are so♥♥♥♥♥♥weak I do not even know why they're there. They're either too situational or easily replaced by a virtue wonder or build, despite stacking possibilities. Some of them also have very situational agreements.
- While the wonders mostly have very nice bonuses, they require distant techs, with limited xp incentive. They are just not worth beelining for.
- Polystralia too strong with trade routes, which is a major snowball mechanism.
Conclusion:
The game certainly has more favour and storyline with the quests. Early game is definitely a bit more exciting than it used to be. The hybrids and traits add more style to the game. The cons that I place greater emphasis on are the unfixed ones because they reflect the core mechanics of the game more so than the new problems. Some of the new cons concern player skill, so it's open to debate as to whether they are really cons to the game. They could be necessary challenges the game needs.
There is still some improvement, but the expansion should have come with the base game. I would recommend buying the game with RT. I increase my rating from 7/10 to 8/10.
