Pros:
-its free to play. Takes like 76 boosters with 6 cards per booster to finish collecting all the cards atm. They said they will be adding more cards every 3 months. Boosters will not give repeats which is a plus. Even though playing against players with a more fleshed out deck could be a little more challenging there is no reason you can't win with this starting pool.
Ppl say u can't manually select the lands, they are wrong u can select them. Also there is an option to turn off auto blocking. All this they would know if they have completed the story properly.
There are 5 campaigns for story mode with 5 missions per campaign. You get 150 gold total from ea campaign.  During the campaign you'll be given the option to do skill quests which teach you the intricates of the game and also award you with ~15 gold. So total of 750 + 250~ = 1000~ gold which you can buy boosters with where ea booster is 150 gold. So around 6-8 boosters.
-Good learning curve for beginners of magic. Yes ppl say the campaign ai  has pre built flavorful decks and even some veterans find it difficult to overcome. That is the whole point of story mode. It is there to teach new players how some tactics can be overcome, and it also sheds more light on how a lot of the mechanics can be used differently. If it was easy, beginners would come out of story mode fighting veterans of the magic community not even having a clue how they were defeated and blame the balance on a small starting pool. Expect to lose and retry a lot in the story mode. You don't need to finish it for veteran players, you just need to finish the first campaign to start building your own deck.
-Deck building. Utter free reign on your deck building as opposed to previous planewalker installments. You can use a deck building wizard or do it manually.
-UI. I just want to touch upon this since I read a lot of the negative reviews are from this category. Yes after like 3-4 iterations of this game the ui should be polished. I haven't experience any of the problems they have touched upon in the negative reviews( like black screens and unresponsiveness), but I'm also using a more up to date pc compared to what some ppl are using, The game when it came out had a lot of server issues disconnecting which could of infuriated a lot of the players, it most certainly♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off when I finally defeated lilliana's campaign after 3 times beating her just to find that I have been disconnected and the results haven't been recorded. But I didn't let that affect my review which a lot of ppl were mostly complaining about. It is around launch so I'll give them the benefit of the doubt.
I'll list the cons of the ui in the cons section, but atm I have no problems with the visibility of the UI and it's responsiveless, with only a few gripes on the available options.
-earning boosters. Vs hard ai for 15gold, probably the fastest way since ai's don't need to think and make you wait. With a good deck you can prob knock off an ai every 10 mins~. Vs human you get 20 gold.
A lot of ppl complain about the coding of this game not being done properly, but I find it decently well programmed since I have been through programming courses, when fighting the ai and looking at how a lot of cards demand a lot of what if and what not commands I find that the programmers have done very well in all the special situations that all the cards demand. Not to mention the ai are actually hard, they will fall for some more complex human tactics but often then not if you let your guard down they will kill you. A lot of times I find myself beating the opponent human to find him rage and replaced by ai just to get beaten by the ai later on. I have only seen one or two coding errors within my 40~ hrs of play time, when using a destroy target artifact enchantment spell I removed the creature along with the enchantment aura it had, and when an opponenet killed my creature with an enchantment aura that gave me life, my opponent got the life boost too when it was already used.
-Don't want to look like a nerd while playing the paper version in public? You can be a nerd at home.
Cons
-UI, they have removed chat from the ui. There's no voice communication either. This goes right up there in ways to ruin a great a game.
The skip atk phase button is in the same position as the continue button so after spamming continue because you have nothing to do on main phase but you want to atk on atk phase you can screw urself over.
The option to skip when human player quits in the middle. But most of the time I would welcome the free gold, but there should be a quality of life option to leave the game as well.
Taking the time to think on main phase but running out of time automatically skips you through atk phase and 2nd main phase after atk phase. There should be some sort of flashy mechanic to draw ur attention when ur about to run out of time and also to not skip thru all ur phases.

2 headed dragon doesn't reward gold. To me this is very weird. Hollow Knight is a jam-packed game with a compelling storyline and tight, clean gameplay. The game has an exceptional soundtrack and stunning hand-drawn characters that help immerse you in the story. The map is HUGE and there is an unbelieveable amount of content in every zone. However, the sheer size of the map can make backtracking a pain, with only select fast travel locations and relatively few save benches in the map. The devs added some improved fast travel options you can find later in the game, and backtracking opens up a lot of new secrets and routes that you can use new movement abilites to get to, but you'll still be walking for a fair bit. This can get annoying in earlier sections of the game where you have to walk all the way back to a boss every single time and don't have any fast travel options.
Gameplay is fun and tight controls reward your reflexes. There are 150+ different enemies in the game, including unique and exciting boss fights that really test your skill and keep each new encounter fresh and interesting. The enemies, especially bosses, are difficult but fair, and you can keep at it with a ton of equipable charms and moves.
The money system is also pretty iffy, and you end up strapped for cash in the first half of the game and wiping with $100 bills in the second half.
The story is exceptional as well, told from the perspective of the other NPCs in the game. Every time you visit a new area, you learn another piece of the puzzle which entices you to explore even more and dive deeper into the kingdom of the bugs. The NPCs help by making the world feel more alive and interesting, and they all feel unique, making you want to talk to them and learn more.
Overall, Hollow Knight is a great experience and I'd highly reccommend it to anyone. This was my first metroidvania game and I was blown out of the water by it. There's always something new to discover, and the story entices you to keep exploring and keep having a great time. 10/10 for me, easily my best game of 2017.

This game was worth getting my hands on for prerelease. However if you're wanting a full smash experience, I recommend waiting until the game is complete.

It's a really weird casualized linear Hitman that also manages to be brokenly difficult.
As in, the stealth just feels really non functioning. Often time I'd sneak past a guard only for him to notice me through a wall. Or I'd have a disguise on that'd make  sense contextually for me to be in the area, but because of the game's instinct mechanic, I'd have nothing I could do to avoid detection.
It's possible to shoot the place up, which was extremely difficult to do in previous Hitman games. The game's snap-to-execution move allows you to take out any enemies you tag in slow motion, which lets you slaughter cops and guards. There's setpieces straight out of a shooter. (You get chased by a helicopter spraying bullets in the game's 3rd level.)
The feel and tone of previous games in the series is just gone. Instead we get a shooter trying it's best to be a stealth game, but coming short in execution.
The story isn't very good either.  The game's antagonists come across as really over the top mannquins, and the just unrealistic character models on them make the game come across as really cheesy. Good ol' stereotypes like the BIG DUMB ETHINC BODY GUARD and nagging rophy wife are just really compelling characters.
Just go pick up Blood Money instead.

Other than serving as a PC enthusiast's benchmark for graphics rendering, this game does have a well imagined open world environment, albeit with a fairly linear storyline and objectives.
That said, I've spent more than my share of time playing through the game, with the freedom to run and gun or sneak past guards with tactical darts to put them to sleep. It isn't your typical run-of-the-mill shooter, and gets a thumbs up from me.

Torchlight is a classic action RPG developed by Runic Games. It features Diablo-esque gameplay with a cartoonish art style.
There is not much to say about the story: Torchlight is a mining town where a magic mineral called Ember is stored. Alric, once an adventurer like you*, has been corrupted by the
tainted Ember and
went rogue. You are to enter the depths of the underworld and track him down. The gameplay is solid and focuses on going deeper down while completing quests and eviscerating thousands of nasty creatures. The setting is an interesting mix of medieval fantasy and steampunk: magic and swords meet robots and firearms. One should not be surprised to see a robot bard who gives monster contracts.
There is a classic trinity: a warrior (Destroyer, male), a rogue (Vanquisher, female), and a sorcerer (Alchemist, male). Each of the classes have 3 skill trees which provide a player with a variety of playstyles. Unlike in Diablo, some skills are shared among the classes (e.g. passive skills which provide an xp boost, dual wielding damage bonus, etc.). What is also unique is that every character can learn to use various spells (up to four at a time). Wanna be a dual axe wielding Destroyer who can also cast fireballs on demand? No problem!
The art style is pretty much timeless: the graphics are decent even now (there are texture mods should anyone be interested). Even though there is not much freedom to explore, randomly generated dungeons are diverse enough to keep one entertained for hours. Moreover, the game is paced just about right – the "just one more level" phenomenon is real. Speaking of art, the soundtrack is just astounding which is hardly a surprise. It was composed by Matt Uelmen, the author of Diablo's soundtrack.
It is a shame that there is no multiplayer, as gathering a group and venturing forth is a staple for action RPGs. The only companion a player will go with is a pet: either a cat or a dog. Pets can support you in a fight, cast spells (up to two at a time), and go to town to sell your items. The player can also feed them fish which make them change into different creatures. Speaking of downsides, there is no character customisation.
In conclusion, Torchlight is a marvellous action RPG which can provide hours and hours of highly enjoyable gameplay. One should do themselves a favour and play this gem.

Nature is both beautiful and brutal, and so is Shelter. Between predators, starvation, and environmental hazards, being responsible for the survival of five little badger cubs is a terrifying proposition. By the end of the first 'level', there's so much built up tension and dread that the end simply can't come soon enough. Every second is a risk, the next threat could come out of nowhere - a fear which is doubled by the lack of a real saving system. The tragic death of one of the cubs can't be reversed without returning to start of the area and accepting the same risk all over again. Every death feels as if it could have been prevented, despite being unable to control the cubs directly, increasing the guilt of any loss.
Leaving room for feelings is Shelter's strong suit. Every part of the game is made so simply - the controls consist of movement, a way to quicken that movement, and a single action key; the music is an uncomplicated guitar strumming which becomes more hectic as danger approaches, and the visual style is made up of only a handful of textures repeated over blocky frames. Nothing's left standing in the way of the player's own grand adventure, constructed from a very basic premise: survive and keep your children safe.

My Take: An okay point and click adventure with a nonsensical plot about climate change. It's fairly short, if you're dedicated to playing it, then it shouldn't take more than about 6 hours. The puzzles are dull and convoluted at times.
Graphics: The art is fairly well done, but the animations can be a little jittery at times. While the resolution can be set to widescreen, the game is played in 4:3; so you've got pillarboxing and unnecessary screen scrolling.
Sound: Voice acting is wooden and mostly boring. Not too much happening in the sound effects department. Prepare to hear a lot of clicks.
Music: Enjoyable enough to make this game a less arduous task.
Controls: Not really a fan of the “left click to bring up options wheel” scheme when left click is also move. Right click opens/closes your inventory.
Did I Finish It: Yes.
Will I Play it Again: If I really am bored and want to grab the four remaining achievements, maybe. I doubt that'll be any time soon though.
Should You Buy It: If you really wanted to play every point and click adventure on Steam, you could probably do worse than this.

I'm about halfway through the game, which I feel is enough to formulate an opinion sufficient for a review.
Pros:
- Vivid comic book style graphics.
- Eco friendly social commentary.
- A nice story with a beginning that does well to draw you in.
Cons:
- A mix of bad translation and sometimes no translation at all for item interactions.
- A large amount of names for simple things like "computer screen" seem to be replaced with a roughly translated word that can often make little sense within dialogue.
- The voice acting seems to be read by people that don't know what is actually going on. The emotions are unstable and chaotic, fluctuating between too intense and frustratingly bland.
- The female protagonist is clearly made by men. No further comment.
- The puzzles involve a level of creativity I cannot seem to manifest within myself. Most item combinations require you to think far outside the box.
Overall, I would recommend the game if you are a casual gamer that doesn't mind looking up help online. I don't recommend this game for anyone that wants a deep experience and immersive story.

Do you like playing games on a laptop out in the sun? Then you'll love this game. Through the miracle of bad art design, this game will make you feel just like it even when playing in a dark room!
This game also manages to both annoy me for the lack of tutorials and annoy me for exesive use of tutorials. You start off in a burrow as a badger where you can walk around with your badger-kids following you. As you explore you'll find some rocks, some sort of beetroot and an exit with an invisible wall. After reading a walkthroug i found out that one of the rocks is actually one of your hungry badger-kids. This was so obvious that the developers decided to not include any hint or tutorial. After that is done the invisible wall is suddenly gone when you try to exit once again. As you walk throgh the narrow passage, your camera will clip through much of the terrain and hanging roots. When you finally get out of the contrastless booring darkness, what should have been a cool contrast between the darkness of the cave and the refreshing light cast by the sun, is instead more grey eye-straining fullbright. You are immediately taunted buy several tutorials saying:
- "Oh you were smart enough to get out of the cave? Better remind you that you should gather food with the use key!"
and
- "This tree has a bright red apple in it. It's really easy to see as all the other colors are grey. Any idiot could probably realize that you can sprint into it so that the apple falls down, but we are going to spoil that for you anyway."
After that there is more gathering of food through a forest closed on both sides. How hungry are the badger-kids? There is so much food that you don't really have the time to find out because you'll soon lose any interest in the game. Im sure there's more beyond that point, but it was too long until the next step so I just stopped after a while.

It's a really weird casualized linear Hitman that also manages to be brokenly difficult.
As in, the stealth just feels really non functioning. Often time I'd sneak past a guard only for him to notice me through a wall. Or I'd have a disguise on that'd make  sense contextually for me to be in the area, but because of the game's instinct mechanic, I'd have nothing I could do to avoid detection.
It's possible to shoot the place up, which was extremely difficult to do in previous Hitman games. The game's snap-to-execution move allows you to take out any enemies you tag in slow motion, which lets you slaughter cops and guards. There's setpieces straight out of a shooter. (You get chased by a helicopter spraying bullets in the game's 3rd level.)
The feel and tone of previous games in the series is just gone. Instead we get a shooter trying it's best to be a stealth game, but coming short in execution.
The story isn't very good either.  The game's antagonists come across as really over the top mannquins, and the just unrealistic character models on them make the game come across as really cheesy. Good ol' stereotypes like the BIG DUMB ETHINC BODY GUARD and nagging rophy wife are just really compelling characters.
Just go pick up Blood Money instead.

The game itself is fun, the characters feels pretty unique, the tag combo system and the gem system are a breath of fresh air for the series, but we can't overlook the flaws in here. The art style of the game is ugly, not just the characters, but the whole concept of the game, to the menus and the UI, it feels uninspired and bland, although it looks better when in motion, you often find yourself looking at the ugly menu screens and the victory screen and saying "eww". Sound-wise the game is also lacking, a lot of good themes were just dubstepped to hell, specially Capcom side, which IMHO is not my kind of music, but others might find it to their taste. The hit-sound is also boring, a punch is the same sound as a slash from a blade, and that's just wrong, it's a minor detail, sure, but breaks immersion. My biggest problem with the game is related to the cast; I don't judge the small roster, after all, DLC is the new type of business in the game industry, but it's just dead wrong to lock content behind a really expensive paywall, why not have a in-game currency which you can buy characters and select skins/backgrounds, much like SFV? Overall, the game has a fun gameplay, but goes down the hill with a series of wrong decisions during development.
Talking about the so promised Campaign mode: I finished it just for the achievements, the history mode feels pretty bland and boring, and has ton of lost opportunities in it. If you wanted a good history mode, with cool moments, sorry to say, but you won't find it here, it was clear that MvC I was done ground up on the Multiplayer competitive scene in mind.
As my final say, heed this: If you're looking for a good fighting game, with cool characters and combat, with a really good and fast pace (not chaotic like UMvC3 was), you will enjoy your time with this game, specially if both Capcom and Marvel decide to patch this up for good. If you want a good story mode, or graphics are your reality, you better off to other titles in the market.

Look, I'm going to be frank. I couldn't care less what Capcom does with DLC. I don't care about the faces because I barely see them, I'm too busy playing the game, where everything is going to blindingly fast that if you're *really* spending that much time focusing on faces, you're probably just going to get whipped into next week, then compain here that the game is hard.
I care about the gameplay. Is the game fun? Do I enjoy playing this game? The answer to both of these questions is yes. The system is somehow simultaneously simple and insanely complex with the tag any time mechanic allowing for disgusting setups and completely unblockable situations ALONGSIDE some free cheese that new players can drop out of nowhere. So based on the sytem, what can I say about this game?
Pros:
Outstanding Gameplay
Each character feels unique and powerful in their own way
The various infinity stones lead to VASTLY different play experiences
An absolute joy to play
Quality netcode
Nice lobby system
Buttery smooth gameplay
60 Frames consistently on my low power machine
Cons:
Rather pointless story mode which I did not enjoy
Poor handling of DLC (which I honestly couldn't care less about)
Reality stone is a tiny bit omnipotent.
With all of this said, I can happily report that this game plays *like a dream.* If you want to spend $60 on a fighting game, I honeslty think this is a good contender. If you wish to wait for DBFZ then I can't hold that against you. But I think this is a very nice, complex alternative to that game.

I own all of the X games. Rebirth was the most "attractive one" for me. New interface (let's face it, the old one was terrible -> keeping it complex doesn't mean that it should also be inaccessible), station interiors, a story line that will suck us in and so.
Well, first of all, the cockpit design was good, at least as an idea. Being able to wander around in your ship is also good. As an idea.
What Rebirth did wrong is that, all the ideas that would elevate the gameplay were implemented so bad that, they actually hurt the title.
The interface causes more issues than fun. Yeah, every space sim fan loves to wander around in their ship, experiencing the roleplay of a space farer. However, when that cockpit causes you to loose your tradeships, fail your missions, limit you from using other angles to see your ship, etc. it becomes a burden. Come on, Privateer had multiple angles and camera views AND a cockpit view. A game that came out two decades ago!
The story, it could've been interesting, even if being a total cliché. However, the voice acting KILLS the atmosphere. God, the voice acting is SO bad that, you will IMMEDIATELY want to turn the audio speech off. The dialogue scripts are also terrible. It is as if a kid wrote the whole script. You meet with the remnants of a long time enemy, in two sentences, you decide to help them fix their base. They are not surprised to see you, you are not surprised to see them etc.
The interiors are all the same, with little to zero difference. The station dialogue stuff is basically trading menus while staring at an NPC, a very badly modeled one to be exact. The "dialogue like" menu is also completely useless. It looks like a pre-alpha stage Mass Effect dialogue tree used for a menu system.
The co-pilot you get in game as a part of the story is also completely useless. Whenever you are occupied with something else, she just... well, she just "exists" that is all. No autopilot, no anything.
The dialogues with other NPCs are also terrible.
The only thing I liked about the game was the graphics. They weren't on today's high end standards and the game crashes or stalls more than a player can bear, but they were still good.
However, gameplay elements of the game were poor at best in every sense and in every department that, it would be disrespectful to recommend this game as a part of a genre where you can find titles like Privateer, Freelancer (in all its flaws), IWar, DarkStar One (even that one is better) and worse, other X games. Heck, even playing back the very old classics like Elite would be much more fun, while you await for the upcoming Star Citizen and Elite 4 as a fan of the genre.
I was really hopeful about this game, even pre-ordering it.
Such a shame... So much potential down the drain.

Solid Space RTS - lacks bells and whistles.
I bought this game based on the trailers showing a big overarching story for a space RTS. Had I found the successor to the Master of Orion series? No.
This game is fun as a straight RTS, but it has no campaign or any other game modes. Think of it as a blend between Starcraft and Master of Orion series.
Regarding the UI you will either love or hate it. Since it is not turn based, everything happens while you are inside any menu. I'm guessing that is why some of the menu interfaces are so ugly. Diplomacy is literally a few buttons on a tab. On the flipside of that, the way the game tracks your fleet and planetary resources is messy. Tiny, tiny icons on the left side of the screen are your quick select options. You can hotkey groups  of ships, but good luck finding all your ships in a large map. The "make fleet" option groups ships together and forms a unit, while this seemed to have a hard time selecting my capital ships as the head of the fleet, the auto-add feature of it worked well (a ship comes to the planet you have your fleet in, it becomes part of the fleet).
Combat is nice, ships move smoothly and fire all their weapons without having to be told. As your capital ship turns around to flee, it continues to blast away at anything in range. Some units, particularly the larger ships have special abilities with energy bars, which allows for some more skill based gameplay.
Overall the game is solid choice (on sale). If you are particular about your UI's or want a story look elsewhere.

I have come to my conclusions based on my experiences alone, not on what others have posted based on their opinions.
Game Rating:  0/10            ( I cannot give a rating on a game that is simply put, "NOT FINISHED!" )
I am an experienced Video Game Beta Tester, QA Member and I am of the opinion that this game is still in its Alpha Stage.
There are too many game stoping bugs, crashes, plot breaking bugs and poor performance issues on a huge array of different spec computers (Low, Mid and High End PC's).  The developer has stated on their website that the game has NEVER been optimized for any High End PC's or SLI / Crossfire setups. Yet during their prelaunch developer videos "Bernd", the head honcho at Egosoft states to the viewers the game Scales Great across all computer specs because it was developed to do so. If you have 2 core, 3 core, 4 core or 8 core the game will use it all to the maximum it can. This is obviously not true as it contradicts his latest statement that its never been optimized for High End PC's.
The AI under your control (Ships, Stations and Personnel like Captains, Engineers, Defence Officers, Managers etc.) do NOT have enough commands in their menus to complete actions properly in the game. Such as Targeting an Enemy with a HOTKEY, commanding one of your Ships to attack someone or even order ship "A" to Protect ship "B". I would wager 80% to 90% of those awesome command abilities we had in the previous X-Games are no longer in game! Those types of commands and the few commands you currently Can give do NOT work most of the time.
Graphics: 8/10
I love the graphics in this game! The stations, the Sectors, Nebulas and Ships all look incredible to me. I am also a HUGE fan of the cockpit in this game. Breath Taking comes to my mind as I fly around and admire the amazing job the Art Team did on this game. However, there is one down side to the graphics in the game and that would be the characters and how they are animated. They look like they were stolen from a video game created in 1998. Just bad!
Trade: 0/10
(Game is to broken with bugs and missing commands to even try trading in my opinion).
Fight: 7/10
Great when it works (Such as the ships you own actually fighting back against who ever is attacking them!) with other ships that you own which at the moment they do NOT, unless you download mods but I have found it still to be very buggy. The other problem is that the capitol ships seem to clip through each other and stations when they are in battle. Fighting with your ship vs others though is fun and actually better in most cases then the previous X Games!
THINK: 0/10 (With trade not working properly and lack of commands this is in my opinion NOT FINISHED! Still in the Alpha Stage of development)
BUILD: 0/10  (With trade not working properly and lack of commands this is in my opinion NOT FINISHED! Still in the Alpha Stage of development) Not enjoyable in my opinion with out Trade working properly and having more commands available.
SHOULD I GET THIS GAME?  Yes or NO    (I will leave that decision up to you. I would like to inform you that even though this game is currently not at an acceptable level for release as a finished game it will eventually be an AWESOME game! Egosoft has made a mistake in releasing the game at its current level of development BUT they will continue to support it by fixing all the bugs and adding new content/features. Over the course of the next few months the bugs will be fixed, new features will be added and the modding community will knock out some of the Best Mods out there in the gaming universe!
I Purchased the game and I am glad I did! Egosoft has a fantastic reputation for Fixing Bugs found in its games and for Supporting their games for Years later with New Features and Content that was given to its playerbase for free!
Cheers

„In war… not everyone is a soldier.“
In this brilliant game where you play with randomly chosen characters and the amount can differ. I started with three, once with four people. They all are civilians and no “up to the teeth armed soldiers”. There is an old man, a cook, a European football player, a principle, a music student and so on. At the beginning you start in you shelter, search for parts, medicine and food, build a bed a  place to cook, maybe your first tool and recognize that you need much more and to prepare it against looters.
It’s too dangerous to go outside by day in cause of snipers and soldiers  / rebels so you decide to prepare for the night. Who is going to scavenge, who is hurt or ill and should sleep, who shall guard?
When you scavenge you have to chose wisely what you will carry with you. Everything will block space in your backpack, otherwise a shovel or a crowbar can become very handy.
Sometimes I could be that you met other people, rebels who want to kill you, other harmless people who become aggressive only if you try to steal from them. Everything you do will have consequences. Will you really rob an old couple if they are defenseless? What will the other people of your group think about if you kill someone just for the loot? Will you get food and medicine at all price? Can you trust everyone in your group? Neighbors knocking at your, needing your help or your medicine. Are you willing to spare them?
I highly recommend this game, it’s a game about war from a completely different view and full of difficult decisions.
The game is not very easy, contains permadeath and only autosaves every new morning, but I survived the war and going to play again, hopefully can make other decisions and not making the same mistakes again to get out of the war still as a human being and not a monster.

Torchlight is a good game.  That being said, Torchlight exists in a world where it is overshadowed and outperformed by its sequel.  The original Torchlight game has a a very small world, and the game/ progress is incredibly linear.  Basically there's a single town and a solitary dungeon with numerous levels leading down that you work through.  That's it.  In addition, the story is pretty much an afterthought.  What the game does get right though, is the actual gameplay.  Combat is a joy, and honestly you rarely mind grinding through the same early stages as you try to progress deeper down into the dungeon.  My typical play session stretched to several hours and I think I burned through this game in two weeks, so that gives you an idea of how addicting the combat is.  Multiple classes, a great concept of a helper pet, and bright visuals make for a fun time.  If you can only pick up one game though, I would recommend the vastly superior sequel.  In addition, if you've already played the sequel then this game feels like a step down after that.  A solid game, but others (including the sequel) do it better.  7/10 for this one.

X: Rebirth looks to be an immersive game, but ultimately the gameplay is neither fun nor even engrossing.
As a massive fan of space games and someone who loved X3:TC and X3:AP (51 hrs and 59 hrs), I was eagerly anticipating the X: Rebirth launch as a chance to reengage in the space genre, but this time as a freelancer pilot in an exciting universe.  Unfortunately, X: Rebirth is not that game.
Ultimately, the game may be fun at some point, but there are far too many constant gameplay aspects that try to be immersive and accessible at the expense of true immersion and fun.  It feels as though the game was not properly play-tested by players, and the experience suffers.  That being said, I’m sure examples would help.  This is not an exhaustive list, but here are some highlights.
1.	In order to trade larger trade goods, you must fly and find trading points to setup the order.  While that means you need to travel, this doesn’t make sense in context of being “in the future.”  How is there not a global listing for known trade hubs/markets/etc?  I understand wanting people to fly to these locations to make them more real, but ultimately this feels forced and unrealistic.
2.	In order to trade smaller goods, you must dock at a station point and then run inside the station to get to individual traders.  This is not realistic nor immersive. I have drones, warp-speed and ‘advanced’ computer systems, but I can’t make transactions via my ship?  It’s like the trade system was designed for a medieval RPG.
3.	Exploration consists of sending out a radar-like beacon and flying to hits.  I really liked this initially, but unfortunately it’s mostly just random items in cans and I have no way to distinguish junk from large ships or hidden nuggets (if they exist).  Once I retrieve these goods, I have to walk in a station to trade said good.  This doesn’t make me feel immersed, this makes me feel like I’m playing a poorly designed game.
4.	I’m only able to fly in my one cockpit view.  It’s neat how I move to my seat and can move around the ship, but the display is far too obstructive.  ~30% of the viewing space is taken up by cockpit walls/dashboard.  It is incredibly restrictive, and ultimately doesn’t make sense.  When I’m in a car, the top of the windshield isn’t 15% of my field of view so why would a spacecraft be the same way.
5.	GUI and map interface are atrocious.  Yes, the game was designed for console players, but unfortunately things are just archaic feeling.  Why can’t I zoom in/out of the map?  If I can, why isn’t there a button on the map to press?  Why do I need to use a Mass Effect style convo bar to access menu items that could easily be accessed by a sidebar or escape menu?
I really wanted to enjoy this game, but it’s not really a game and more of a chore.  If you enjoyed the world immersion of X3:TC or X3:AP, look somewhere else.  Maybe EVE Online for the truly immersive world.  Forcing someone to walk around like a character in a medieval RPG is not actual immersion, it’s only a narrow-minded developer opinion of true immersion.

What do I have to say about this game... well, it's an old school first person shooter, and because of that fact, you really need to like old school shooters in order to enjoy this one.
There are some levels which remind me of Serious Sam 3 a lot, but even on Heroic difficulty - which is the Insane difficulty with the added "bonus" that you're not allowed to save, so if you die you will be forced to restart the whole level - it isn't as hard as Serious Sam, but it tries to be. Once you know how to play it and start getting the necessary powers and skills to survive, most levels are quite easy, and the challenging difficulty adds to the fun. At least in my case, because I enjoy difficult first person shooters (except for the boss fights, which are unnecessarily quirky and annoying).
Speaking of not being allowed to save, there is a bug with chapter 12, and if you encounter it, you will have to play the Windows XP version of the game for a bit. I've talked about that on my blog. You will need to do as I describe here, because otherwise it's impossible to finish the game on Heroic, or maybe even on Insane somestimes.

Needless to say, the game has a dialog humor also in the style of other old school shooters like Serious Sam and Duke Nukem Forever, with lots of nerdy and sometimes racial jokes and refernces, and I honestly wouldn't have it any other way. Even though I've fulfilled my desire to finish this game on Heroic, I still can't put it down, and I've started a new game for the third time. It's fun!
I give it 10 out of 10!
PS: One more thing. If you're playing on Heroic and you've made it to the infamous Chapter 16, I have only one advice: NEVER go somewhere where you're cornered.
As long as you can keep moving, you'll do just fine. I always died on the first wave just because I have a big problem when there are multiple Berserkers around, but other than that it was actually not that hard to survive. This was one of the two games that got me into PC gaming. It's a fun hack-n-slash game that's vibrant in colors and art style but lacking in the story department. However, once you complete the game there isn't much else to do, considering the levels are limited to the small town and the different levels of the mines. However, it's good for about 30 hours of gameplay. With hundreds of weapons,
Pros:
- Art style. The game is colorful and beautiful to look at. It is a bit cartoony, but that's what makes it fun. The UI is nice and clean, which helps when there's a lot of things happening.
- Gameplay. While you do have your mouse buttons for attacks, you also have the number buttons which allow for spells and other interesting enchantments.
- Companions. The pet companion is perhaps one of the best features in the game. It acts like a second person following you. It'll help you attack enemies and even cast spells. It'll also go back to town and sell your unwanted items, which makes it a lot more convenient instead of going all the way back and selling your items directly.
- Optimization. The game runs as smooth as butter. I never experienced any sort of frame drops or bugs/crashes at all.
- Item custimization. There are endless amounts of armor and weapons that you can get which you can either sell or use for yourself.
Cons:
- Story. The story is kind of barebones at times. While the main premise of the game isn't the story, it's not something I can go without saying. It's extremely basic and predictable at times.
While it won't change your mind about these ARPG's it's still a fun addition to the genre and I recommend you check it out.

Takeaway:  An interesting game that explores a lot of cool sci-fi concepts and is fun, but it lacks any soul and does not live up to the hype of being Alpha Centauri 2
I was pretty excited about this game because I enjoyed the predecessor Alpha Centauri a lot when I was younger.  I guess there's no real way to avoid comparing it to Alpha Centauri, so I'll be talking about that a bit.  But also from the point of view of just playing and enjoying the game.
The premise is that your sponsor has put together a mission and sent it off to colonise another planet.  Ahead lie the challenges that this will mean, but you're not the only faction trying to do so, as other missions start touching down.
The game is interesting because you have to play as an alien species touching down on virgin soil on the planet.  The planet has a developed ecosystem and so it doesn't like you.  You can't breathe, you the wildlife tries to kill you and things get nasty.  From an Alpha Centauri point of view, it's not as awesome as the whole fungus/mindworms phenomenon, but it's good enough, and there's also a phenomenon called miasma to deal with that blocks squares and slowly kills your units.
From here, you start to survive and there are three broad paths to deal with the alien menace: learn to live in Harmony with the aliens and adapt yourself to the planet, use technology to push humanity further and to survive or terraform the planet by killing everything on it and building a new Earth.  These affinities form the base of the game and they control how each faction reacts to other factions.
In terms of gameplay, aliens spawn from nest sites and these infinite aliens make life difficult, along with siege worms which are too powerful to be dealt with early game.  In terms of play it's a lot like the Fall From Heaven mod for Civ4, where the environment is the biggest first threat, never mind the other Civs, and just surviving is a challenge.  This can be fun and engrossing, but it also gets tiring.
The mid game involves interacting with your Civ partners.  Initially, you're all happy to be with each other because you're human and the planet isn't, but as competition for resources, approaches to dealing with planet life and your humanity start to diverge, everything starts coming to a head.  Trade is vitally important to staying friends with your neighbours as well as boosting your resources massively through lucrative trade routes.  Keeping trading ships safe from alien mance takes a lot of work, but its worth it and adds an interesting mechanic for those not wanting to go to war.
The combat system is both better and worse than Alpha Centauri.  The artillery which was introduced then now works properly and in a fun way.  But there is no unit designer.  You want drop colony pods, well, sorry.  Instead, units get upgraded based on affinity.  I think the war style seems to change based on your affinity.  Harmony certainly lends itself to raiders with big bonuses for lonely units and the ability to retreat into miasma and heal, but I haven't played the others.  It's a bit underwhelming, but you can see the experience of Civ here tumping Alpha Centauri, but only because so many years have passed.
The game has lots of fun base management strategies and a lot of the worker improvements are a much needed improvement over Alpha Centauri.  Again, the Civ4 getting rid of riots works and health becomes a crucial factor.  The global nature of health prevents infinite city sprawl while many improvements cost energy to meaintain, as well as giving it, making the decision about what to do with your workers interesting and engrossing.  However, there's no feel your workers contribute to the global environment, as they did in Alpha Centauri.
However, the game falls down on what I can only call soul.  In Alpha Centauri, the plot was amazing, the faction profiles and their leader characters amazing and the quotes read out when technologies or buildings were built were pretty good.  Many have stayed with me and, to judge, with other people too "It is every citizen's final duty to go into the tanks...".  The technology tree is still something I pour over and go "oh, so that's what was about" as bits are happening right now in the real world and I start to get what some of the crazy named techs were about.  The story behind the environment was also fresh, justifying an interesting and bizarre ecosystem that initially made no sense, but grew into a "wait, the planet is what?" moment, which made the science victory truly epic.
In this game, the leaders lack soul.  The different factions based on national blocks are, well, bland.  The affinity they gain matters more in the long run.  The technology web is generally meaningless and confusing and doesn't seem to have the same feel to it as the Alpha Techs did.  The quotes are all read out by one person and aren't very good anyway.  The game lacks narrative.  The wonders have meaningless names, random and underwhelming effects and only a quote with no video to indicate that thing you struggled for 48 turns to complete has actually been completed.  I have no real clue what they're supposed to be, just that getting them is a good idea sometimes.
Even the victories are pretty meaningless.  I won a transcendance victory but there was none of the build-up as there was in Alpha Centauri to make it exciting and fresh.  It's pretty much, "research this, research that, then this, now build wonder and wait 38 turns, done".
Overall, it's a good game, but it's not a great game, like Alpha Centauri was, and the lack of narrative and soul at its heart is why.  This isn't a story about mankind's attempt to colonise space and What Might Happen, which you'd expect from a proper sci-fi game, but more Civ in Space.  You play, you win and you shrug.  You don't go off and think though, and that's its great crime.  Potentially, a lot of its flaws could be fixed or overcome through mods, but it's still a shame.

There is where I really need a "meh" review option.  Final Fantasy XIII is kind of a mess...yet I was still compelled to finished it.
The first half of the game is linear to a fault, this would be fine if the battles were interesting at that point, but they aren't.  So you're looking at 20-30 hours of hitting the A button until you get to the next very pretty cutscene.
Then it opens up and becomes more engaging in the gameplay department for a while, until you realize at that point it has just become a grindy, fairly boring JRPG of yore.
The story is fairly close to being complete nonsense and the characters are hard to relate to when they're trying to get their overwrought anime drama-on in a universe that's built on pillars of gobbledegook.  That said, I somewhat begrudgingly grew to like the characters -- only a little mind you, but that's more than I thought I would based on what they were like in the beginning.
And yet in spite of many flaws...I still finished it.  I guess because once you put the battles on easy difficultly (highly recommended if you value your time) it's fairly inoffensive to play and nonsense though it may be, I was still interested in seeing the story brought to its conclusion.

I played this game for thee first time this year. I'm was pleasantly surprised at how good it was. Despite it being a really old game, it better than many "new" games in many aspects.
PROS
The graphics are very good. They aren't as good Medal of Honor: War Fighter (most games aren't) but it holds its very well by today's standards. The lighting great and the special effects are superb. I can only imagine how good they seemed in 2008!
The weapons are not too complicated. The developers weren't ridiculous in their weapons. Everything is space aged but modern at the same time.
The story will keep you playing. It is very well-written, allowing few if any, noticebale plot holes.
CONS
The enemy AI isn't that great sometimes. You can literally hide under the same building and snipe away at bad guys without fear of retaliation. Just shoot, disappear, and wait for them to go back to normal in a matter of seconds.
The graphics are great but some people still cannot play it on max settings. However, this is not a problem with development. This a problem for cheapskates. Go by a decent graphics card, jeez!
If you don't play at fast pace, the pace slows down. There is no consequence for standing around and waiting all day. Enemies should do a better job of searching for you. Then again, that goes back to poor AI.
SUMMARY
Crisis was fantastic! I recommend playing this first and playing the rest in sequence. I give it 7 / 10 as compared to today's games.

Bioshock was the first PC game I ever played. Up until that time I had only played on my gameboy advance or DS so when my friend told me that I should try out Bioshock on my laptop I was sceptical. So there I went: setting up steam onto my rickety little HP laptop, purchasing and downloading Bioshock and booting it up as soon as it finished downloading. The next two hours were rather… disappointing. It took me about three months to get around to beating the game--which I only did because I am a completionist. I’ll admit I wasn’t impressed--this game was lauded for it's story and yet it's twist left little impact with me seeing as my actual play style was largely unaffected. In a meta sense Bioshock ironically tries to give its players as much freedom as it can to tackle rather linear level design and a deterministic premise. I had guessed the outcomes in plot well before the story got to them because of the multitude of in game foreshadow devices (aka the tape recorders) and I wasn’t a fan of the dank, drearily light corridors. Regardless of my friend’s enthusiasm for the game I remained largely apathetic.
It wasn't until many years later, in my final minutes of Bioshock Infinite, taken back to the opening level of Bioshock, did I become nostalgic. All of the sudden I had a longing to play in the rapidly flooding art deco interiors, in an environment so carefully crafted as to feel simultaneously freeing and confining. It took Bioshock Infinite’s loose handling of the tonics for me to understand how beautifully crafted the plasmid/ADAM system of Bioshock was. Rapture as a setting just makes sense in a way that Columbia never did to me. Rapture was at once a city that was livable and dying; where the hostile actions of the citizenry made complete sense in the objectivist hell they found themselves in. When I learned that the Bioshock series was getting re-released with a Remastered edition I was excited. Maybe I would finally get around to replaying the original Bioshock with my now expanded understanding of console and PC gaming?
Jokes on me then for how barely functional this Remaster has been. Most of the reviews mention the limited graphics settings menus and mouse smoothing when talking about how poorly optimized this game has been for PC. My experience has been so much more fundamentally frustrating to me. I could deal with the strangely lurching quality of the mouse sensitivity in the game (an especially difficult thing to forgive when you get to the damn hacking mini-game--I spend about half the time just trying to get my mouse under control) and I could give two ♥♥♥♥♥ about controlling all my graphics settings (partially thanks to my completely ridiculous PC I have now). What I can’t forgive is the constant. Crashing. I play in non-windowed mode usually and anytime I have to switch out of the game when I attempt to alt-tab back in I am met with a black-then-gray-then-black screen. I can hear the sounds of the game but see nothing. The only way I can fix this is force closing the game then going through the long process of starting it back up. Usually my last two saves have been completely deleted and I have to go back through a large portion of the level. This has happened to me four times and I have only played the game for six hours.
The first five times I started the game it would start in small window on my screen (1280x720 for my 1920x1080 screen) rather than keep whatever my previous settings were. The contrast also doesn’t change in-game for me. Any time I want to change the contrast I need to slide the bar on the usual set-up page (the contrast does not change no matter where I slide the bar), guess where the scroll bar might be, apply changes, exit the game, and restart it with the hope that I have found a workable contrast level. I’ve finally gotten the contrast levels down but periodically whenever I start the game it will start in a small window rather than my full screen.
Furthermore, often while I am in the menus the game will completely switch over to Xbox controllers even though I have not plugged mine into the computer since starting the game. The only thing I can do to reset the game to the original keyboard input is quit the game and restart it.
Are you starting to notice a pattern here?
Many reviews I’ve read have mentioned that the original Bioshock glitches remain glitches in Bioshock Remastered. I can’t say whether the issues I’m running into are the same I might have ran into in the original Bioshock but I will say my ♥♥♥♥♥ly little HP laptop never had issues running Bioshock, and that computer was six months from dying by the time I played Bioshock on it.
In order to write this review I visited
Bioshock page to see average finishing times for the game. 69.88% of the reporting players reported completion on PC rather than any of the consoles. That means that many of these players will now have this free Remastered version on their computers. I understand that even in the original Bioshock release 2K wanted to create a console-based RPG shooter and since in the Remaster releases the majority of PC users will get it for free in contrast to the paying customers of PlayStations or Xbox there is (and always has been) less of an incentive to make a quality product for PC gamers. Generally people on consoles have said the remaster is worth playing. I wish I could say the same but that’s hard to say when the game literally prevents me from playing more than 20 minutes at a time. Even with all of this focus towards consoles the lazy♥♥♥♥♥PC porting of this Remaster is both insulting and frustrating--I understand where the anger from other players is coming from entirely. We were given a free Remaster to a game we already owned and wanted to play that original game with at least slightly better graphics and improved all around function. We only got one of those things.
Still, though, I can’t help but think that this completely free product sucking is exactly what Andrew Ryan would have wanted. You win again, free market.

This review is intended for those who have interest in the game but are nervous due to negative comments.
So you've probably heard the tirades about how bad this game is... In part, they are right.  Compared to previous entries in the series, and most other fighting games out there, the production value of the game isn't great.   I, too, had heard these and thought, "That's fine, all that REALLY matters is the gameplay.  And they can't be that bad."  Well, they can be THAT bad.
As opposed to MvC 3, the cool comic book effects are replaced with still screens that basically do't change as the UI swaps depending on th screen.  Some of the characters truly do look pretty dumb and contrast in detail compared to most of the cast.  The low-point is probably Ghost Rider's Penance Stare where you get a still frame of is fiery face for about 8 seconds.
The sound is boring and a lot of the great songs developed for characters over the series have been replaced with standard, unrecognizable orchestra.  Hulk's song changed from a song that sounds like a monster tearing things apart.  Now it sounds like the song from a nature show as a helicopter flies over New Zealand.  Lost, but not least, some of the voices are really bad (Spencer sounds like a whiny teenager).
Pretty much all of the complaints you've heard are validated.  The cast is kind of dull (insert X-Men comment), the story is only OK, etc.
However!  The gameplay, in my opinion, is what really matters.  And it's great!  It's everything you've loved from previous entries in the series with a few improvements and adjustments.  Assist moves are gone and one character removed from your team, but now you can swap almost whenever you want between characters.  This means you can go from a combo to Tatsumaki, switch mid-action and to a launch to Spinning Bird Kick, spike down then swap into a Shoryuken. You can do pretty much anything that seems like it should work, making way for crazy combos, mix-ups and fun!  Yet, with all of this craziness, it seems much less one-hit-to-death-combo than MvC 3.  The result is a strong mix of positioning, movement and combos that I see myself playing for a long time.
Yes, there are things that are unforgivable about the game, but I still find myself placing it at a solid 2nd place in my list of fighters!  If you can allow yourself to get past the ugly stuff, you will love this game.
P.S. I do think releasing DLC characters a month after the game came out is kind of cheap.  Another tick against the game and a point for critics to slam, I suppose.

Personally I have not played any other Assassin's Creed titles, so the only real experience I have is from this game, and this was the most recommended among friends and reviews so I decided to check it out.
I had a blast playing this game. Being able to play as a pirate in a truly realistic(ish) game is quite a bit of fun. The graphics, most of the parkour, stealth and combat mechanics, and the music are all fantastic. Additionally having some deep and moving characterization for the main cast is something good to see in a game mostly centered around a cult of assassins. They aren't just cold-blooded murderers; they are people as well. My favorite parts of the game hands down are either parkouring around the cities or simply roaming the Caribbean. Many of the hours I've spent in this game have just been from capturing ships, hunting wildlife, searching for treasure, diving into the sea, or attacking naval forts. So much free time can be spent in the open sea of this game.
For as much fun as the open world can be for the game, there are a few problems it has.
The real issues have to do with AI and some of the stealth mechanics. Now, I have played many hours of Payday 2 in stealth, but those guards have absolutely NO set pathing, and have completely random patrolling patterns. In this game, they have set paths, but often times trying to perform a double takedown will fail if one guard decides to move at just the moment you attempt, therefore exposing yourself. The gunner AI also is a little ridiculous, with dead-eye accuracy (the realistic musket reload time is a nice touch though), and quickscope speed.
Secondly with the stealth mechanics; why in the hell does a game all about stealthy takedowns not have a crouch? Yes I get you can hide in foliage or crops to obstruct the enemy view. Since it isn't an FPS it can't go the Far Cry route of combining a crouch and vision obstruction, just having vision obstruction. Not to mention takedowns from a hidden area half the time draw a guard to you that you can't assassinate instantly. Just a few gripes of the gameplay.
While stealth in games is an easy way to call "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t" when the AI turns on you and you don't even realize it before you are already shot, this is an amazing game. Many of the praise-worthy aspects I've already mentioned. Definitely a game to check out, sometimes will have some issues with stealth but it is rather forgiving for the kind of game it is.
I'll give it a 9/10.

I have over 100 hours into this game, and here's my thoughts if you're thinking of getting it.
Your gameplay experience will evolve in real time from starting on your home planet, scouting nearby worlds/asteroids/gas giants/etc, and gradually expand your empire.  Most of your fleets will consist of one to a few capital ships (basically your hero units that can level up) supported by anything from light attack frigates to carriers to support ships with unique abilities.  You'll quickly come into contact with other races, and you can try to work with or against them.  You'll start working on your tech tree and focus on unlocking new ships, defensive structures, or diplomatic measures.  All items can be researched, but you'll probably focus on a few core areas. Routes into your empire can be fortified, or you can spend that money on another fleet and attack.  It's really it up to you how you dictate the flow of the game, and that's a strong part of it.
There's communities you can join if multiplayer is your scene, but I would approach this as being a single player game.  There's no story or campaign though, just various maps you can adjust to play on.  There's an editor to create your own maps, or you can find ones made by others online and play theirs.
If you enjoy space based games, you'll love this.  The visuals work well together, and the music adds to the ambiance.  There's lots of pew pew laser/missle/drone/cannon/etc battles you can zoom in and watch, while directing your various armadas.  There's ships that range in size from recon to destroyer of worlds.  I've tried other similar genre 4x space games, but after playing this, I can't get into them.
The easiest comparison I could make is to Civ V, but both games are different.  Sins Rebellion has the 3 main races, and these are divided into two groups, giving 6 different "empires" to play with.  They all have different strategies and styles.
Tech, trade, diplomacy, war, both offense and defense, culture, or combonations of strategies are viable (against the AI).
There are two mini DLC's available, and they both add slight depth, but not essential to the experience.  You can always get them later on, and I do reccommend them.
Cons - Space battles can feel like they can drag on at times.  They game time itself can be hours long, anywhere from 2-6, depending on how aggressive you are and largely on the map size.  If you want a quick game, this may not be for you.  I would really like to see more fluff or story built into the game, but the game experience itself isn't lacking because of that.

Torchlight: a dull glow
I played Torchlight way back when it first came out, circa 2009. I enjoyed it, but there were some things that just nagged at me while I played it. Unfortunately, the more I played it, the less I liked it. Going further and further into the game did not increase my enjoyment. And I ultimately stopped playing.
Sadly that perfectly describes my most recent experience with Torchlight.
I’ve tried to figure out just what it is that I don’t like, but every time I formulate my thoughts I come up with the same conclusion:
The game feels hollow and generic.
It doesn’t seem to have it’s own identity or stand out as unique from other games in the ARPG genre. Hell, Torchlight is essentially an “HD remake” of Diablo from 1996… without the “Hell.” The game follows the same basic progression and is, in many ways the same game, but with less of an edge.
I feel that really hurts Torchlight.
Plenty of games can be fun without a cool in-game world or a “gritty” story hook to pull you in. It’s gameplay that matters in the end, right? Sadly I think that Torchlight also falls flat here as well.
Torchlight is pretty a pretty shallow game, to its detriment. Killing monsters is fun in its own right, but only for so long. Other ARPGs alleviate this by giving you things to work for: new more powerful items, more powerful skills, harder challenges, etc. Torchlight does have all of these things… they’re just not interesting. So although the game does have the “carrot on a stick” incentive to continue playing… I’m, sadly, not interested in the carrot.
I found the gameplay to be rather lackluster and boring. Torchlight’s art style does not appeal to me. The environments lacked feeling, and ultimately felt sterile. The items in the game were shallow, and only the “unique” items had any flavor. The various character skills weren’t very impressive, and didn’t feel very powerful.
But let’s break down the individual pieces of Torchlight and critique it against the five points I mentioned previously.
Atmosphere and Story
Atmosphere
the pervading tone or mood of a place, situation, or work of art.
Torchlight has little to no atmosphere. Certain areas in the game look pretty darn cool, but carry absolutely no feeling.
My favorite areas are a necropolis found underneath the mines beneath Torchlight (Yes, that’s the name of the town) and the underground jungle-temple ruins beneath the necropolis. Why I like these two areas over all the others? Probably because they have the most ‘flavor’. But even then it’s spread pretty thin.
There isn’t much to be said about the game’s various locales other than that they don’t make much sense and require a bit too much suspension of disbelief for my taste.
Story
an account of imaginary or real people and events told for entertainment.
I consider story to be tied very closely with atmosphere, and like Torchlight’s atmosphere, there isn’t really much to be said about the story. It’s pretty generic and could be summarized in two sentences: “Torchlight was built over a corrupted source of magic caused by an ancient evil deep within the Earth. Go kill it.”
More accurately: The town of Torchlight is mining a substance called Ember, which allows for the various forms of magic in the world, but it turns out the Ember under Torchlight is corrupt and will turn anyone who comes into contact with it evil! This is because the Ember Vein runs over an ancient evil, later revealed to be a dragon. You are called to Torchlight to help the mining operation, which is being attacked by monsters, but are promptly betrayed by the man who summoned you. As it turns out he wants to revive the dragon sleeping beneath Torchlight. And you, the hero, have to stop him by traveling deeper and deeper into the Earth uncovering older and older civilizations that fell to the corrupting allure of the Ember.
Pretty good ideas! Not going to lie, there’s definitely a cool story in there. But it’s really only used as an occasional spur to remind you to continue murdering monsters as you travel what seems like miles into the earth. A shame, really.
There is very little involvement in the story, and to be honest the voice acting is pretty hammy. If you like that sort of thing, then good on ya! I had to skip most of it.
But hey, atleast you can skip it! Actually all of it! Which is nice.
Enemies
the persons who are actively opposed or hostile to someone or something.
Unfortunately, the enemies in torchlight are boring. There isn’t any way around it. I don’t like their designs, and none of them really seem to have any interesting mechanics to differentiate them. They’re all just bigger and bigger punching bags. Some will revive their comrades, and some will leave noxious fumes after death. But by and large, the majority of them are meat sacks that fling their bodies against your weapons.
It doesn’t help that the enemies have massive spikes in difficulty towards the end of the game. There is a LARGE increase in enemy health and damage in the last area. And every time I’ve played, it has come as a shock.
I’ll be doing just fine, then I’ll walk into the last section of the game and be murdered. Only to find that I’m unable to deal significant damage to the enemies. Their scaling seems to be off, and it’s just not fun.
Your Character
the representation or expression of something in a tangible or visible form.
Torchlight utilizes the typical stat system. Your RPG standards are all present: Strength, Dexterity, Magic, Life, and Defense. Every time you level, the game gives you five points to allocate to each of these different parameters. Unfortunately it seems like the various stat points are really just a way of directing your progression. It didn’t seem as though loading a bunch of points into Magic made my Alchemist’s magic any more powerful, despite it being his main damage stat. It seemed as though it was just a holdover from previous games. “Diablo had them, so Torchlight will too.”
Really the stats just felt like numbers I had to inflate in order to put on different armor. My character’s power seemed to be located in the weapons and armor he was wearing rather than the character himself.
Skills
skill or expertise in a particular activity or field
Torchlight also follows a rather traditional skill tree format, present in almost every ARPG. Ever.
That’s perfectly fine. Skill trees are used so commonly because they work. Sadly, the skills in Torchlight are boring. Plain and simple. The coolest spells I got for my Alchemist were Chain Lightning and a laser. Everything else rather boring.
I think that is was a major contributing factor to why Torchlight felt boring to me. The three different classes all had pretty boring skills. Nothing really stands out, and everything felt pretty lame.
Itemization
the balance and distribution of items, their types, and the various effects, powers, and statistics attached to them
Last but not least, the items. Again, there isn’t a lot to say. Torchlight’s items were rather lacking. Most items are of the, “+10 fire damage,” “+20 lightning damage,” “+5% attack speed” variety. Nothing to write home about.
This is probably the one aspect of the game where Torchlight tried its hardest to please me.
I received about 7 unique items before reaching level 15. Unique items are Torchlight’s highest rarity item, apparently. They were all decent, and some of the unique wands I found had cool effects that altered combat, like shots bouncing and releasing arcs of electricity on the ground. But they were little more than more powerful versions of the base items. Not particularly exciting.
Boring skills, boring monsters, boring items, boring combat.
Very sad indeed.

I don't really play games like
. The style of action RPG proliferated by titles like
never really interested me. It's mostly just a repetitive slog of killing and looting identical enemies who changed only statistically, becoming incrementally more difficult so as to retain the same amount of effort required for their deaths. While
is all that and more, it managed to keep me entertained for quite some time through diverse enemy types, artistic direction and engaging skill trees.
The gameplay hardly needs explaining - it's like
. You control most everything in the game using the mouse and some hotkeys. I chose to play as the 'vanquisher' class, focusing on ranged weaponry and magic related to it. The abilities of this class mostly serve to complement her ranged weapons, and I managed to completely finish the game without even equipping a melee weapon. I did find that the class benefited significantly from having summoning spells, allowing players to fire powerful ranged spells at enemies while minions keep them at bay. A lot of the more powerful weapons felt great to use, and I was impressed by the game's lenience toward players interested in multiple gameplay styles--nothing stopped me from summoning an army of skeletons, even though I didn't choose the class focused on that at the start of the game.
's balancing feels fine, though later levels do feature some enemies with huge damage output that were a pain to get past. I really liked the way the game's entire story takes place in a single dungeon, with the player's gradual descent into the earth beneath the titular town slowly revealing different fortresses and ancient ruins all lying beneath the ground. The game begins with entry into the mine upon which Torchlight's economy is reliant upon, but before the game's end you'll see a sprawling necropolis, colourful, flooded ruins and a fiery dwarven fortress. The graphical diversity keeps things interesting, and everything's quite pretty too. I liked the cartoony art style, but I found it quite curious how many enemies were simply recoloured, buffed up a bit and reused.
On release, some criticised
for it's lack of any form of multiplayer component. I personally found this to be a good decision, as a single-player game tends to be more focused.
, despite the admirable streamlining of UI and gameplay still contains a large amount of engaging content, even after the final boss. I just don't know if
will be one of those games that the average player can get a huge amount of mileage out of--while I found the content to be sufficient, it certainly does get old after a certain point.

There are some levels which remind me of Serious Sam 3 a lot, but even on Heroic difficulty - which is the Insane difficulty with the added "bonus" that you're not allowed to save, so if you die you will be forced to restart the whole level - it isn't as hard as Serious Sam, but it tries to be. Once you know how to play it and start getting the necessary powers and skills to survive, most levels are quite easy, and the challenging difficulty adds to the fun. At least in my case, because I enjoy difficult first person shooters (except for the boss fights, which are unnecessarily quirky and annoying).
Speaking of not being allowed to save, there is a bug with chapter 12, and if you encounter it, you will have to play the Windows XP version of the game for a bit. I've talked about that on my blog. You will need to do as I describe here, because otherwise it's impossible to finish the game on Heroic, or maybe even on Insane somestimes.

Needless to say, the game has a dialog humor also in the style of other old school shooters like Serious Sam and Duke Nukem Forever, with lots of nerdy and sometimes racial jokes and refernces, and I honestly wouldn't have it any other way. Even though I've fulfilled my desire to finish this game on Heroic, I still can't put it down, and I've started a new game for the third time. It's fun!
I give it 10 out of 10!
PS: One more thing. If you're playing on Heroic and you've made it to the infamous Chapter 16, I have only one advice: NEVER go somewhere where you're cornered.
As long as you can keep moving, you'll do just fine. I always died on the first wave just because I have a big problem when there are multiple Berserkers around, but other than that it was actually not that hard to survive. Oh, and don't forget to get the "Soul Hunger" skill by then. That goes without saying. You will need it, I promise you that.

This installment of Assassin's Creed feels like it is only half Assassin's Creed, and half something else. I have enjoyed it a lot though and I like the characters/storyline. I completely reccomend playing this game but I should warn you of two major disappointments I have.
The combat, as usual, looks cool but gets repetitive and there are only about 4 different enemy types whether on the seas or on foot. Also, metal. ♥♥♥♥ING METAL. It can take so ♥♥♥♥ing long to upgrade your ship towards the ladder half of the game because most advanced upgrades require at least 300 metal. Each source of metal will only give you 50-100 in quantity and it takes about a half hour just to hunt down two or three ships that carry some. This particular issue combined with the mundane combat really bogs down the game for me. I am not a fan of RPG's where you have to tediously grind for hours just to advance in the game and this problem irks me the same way. ESPECIALLY because it is supposed to be an action game where you are always moving around and doing different stuff. Spending hours sailing around in circles searching for metal-carrying ships is not my idea of an action game.

Slaughter bad guys by the thousands! Wade ankle-deep in blood! Blast away with tons of pew pew! Experience a rich story!
These are things you won't see in this game. Honestly, trying to farm with the beginning equipment puts my brain to sleep which makes driving in straight lines very hard. But it scratches an itch. And for what it is, it is very well done.
There's enough reality to make it immersive (graphics are great, models are highly realistic, physics make sense) but enough game to not make it painful (crops grow in about a day, your vehicles never take damage, implements tell you what their current capacity is, seeds magically change right in your tank, camera views let you see what's going on from any angle).
I would strongly recommend potential players go check the guides/forums. In particular SELL ALL YOUR STARTING VEHICLES. Seriously. Get rid of them. They have horrendous maintenance costs and can be replaced with much more capabable and cheaper versions. I'd also recommend harvesting lumber rather than farming to start with. Much more lucrative and non-mind numbing.
Although I realize this isn't GTA, it would be nice if the pedestrians would at least acknowledge the tractor running them over (or actually, just running through them as there's no collision detection). The cars stop if you get in the way, but they don't swerve or anything. At least all the vehicles have a horn. I'd be a terrible neighbor.
One final note is this game seriously needs a radio in the vehicles. Listening to the constant hum of engines doesn't help the aforementioned falling asleep. So you may want to bring your own tunes.
All that said, I feel like I have had a real farming experience and appreciation for my food. I'm sure it's not really a real farming experience, but I did say "feel."

It's good because...
+ Fast-paced battle system once you figure out how it works and have a full team.
+ Cool lore, and some good characters (Well, Lightning and Sazh, so two).
+ Some good voice acting, and there is an option for Japanese w/ Subtitles which is a MAJOR plus in my book.
+ High Tech, sci-fi setting, with some big ideas.
But...
- The first and second quarter are a linear, frustrating slog while you feel constantly hamstringed by having your team members swapped in and out over and over.
- Almost no NPCs, all towns/cities are in the background while you run along your track.
- No exploration. Also no sidequests until the third quarter.
- While the lore is awesome, the story and writing are abysmal.
- All conversations between characters look like they were done with motion capture in front of a plain green screen with no props. Every time they stop to talk they just walk back and forth in a box, saying poorly written lines and waving their arms.
-  Music may get repetitive.
Overall:
Recommended if you enjoy more cinematic, linear gaming, and are interested in the sequels, which are a massive improvement in my opinion.
Not Recommended if you're looking for a large amount of character customization or... choices. Or exploration.

Everyone who says "the game is rubbish", "it isn't Final Fantasy" and even those who say "it only gets good after 10 hours", in my opinion, are wrong. I enjoyed the game from the start. I've not played FF since FFX cameout and although things have changed it still has all the components I expect of a Final Fantasy game. I ESPECIALLY don't get the complaints that it is too linear as FF has always been relatively linear, with most freedom of choice having no real impact on the game. Even one of my favoutie games ever, FFVII, is pretty linear in my opinion.
If you are looking for an epic, cinematic, JRPG then you will probably enjoy it. Some of the characters are a bit annoying or "teenagery" but that is often the case with JRPGs and Final Fantasy in my expereience, sometimes it is endearing but more often an annoyance that can easily be overlooked.
As with most FF games the game is beautiful (not the best graphics but the artstyle itself is gorgeous) and great music. I also really like the animations and movement in the turn based battles, makes them more interesting to watch than in the older games.
The setting and story are pretty interesting. I really like the setting and the story is quite good.
Is it the best Final Fantasy in the series? No, not at all. Does it feel like Final Fantasy? Yes. And I was happy with the price I paid for it in the sale. I would recommend to a fan of the series but point someone new to FFVII or IX (my favourites of the PS1-onward era of FF games).
I really feel like many of these reviews saying it is not-final fantasy like because it is linear must come from people who have clouded memorys, have became used to Western action RPGs or are just crazy.
I have experienced none of the graphical or FPS issues reported by some users. I have a quite good but not super PC.
