This game is all about your experience and you know when those types of games work best? When you don't know what to expect. With Shelter that wasn't the case - without knowing any spoilers, just by going through game description and few screenshots, I pretty much knew how it is going to be.
... And it turns out to be worse than I expected.
Good things?
Very interesting, very different, really good.
At least for the first part. Game does a pretty good job in making you care for your little badger family, but sadly that isn't enough to call it a satisfying experience.
Bad things?
After you get used to the mechanics, you expect something to happen, but for the long time there is absolutely nothing going on. It gets boring really quickly.

I expected that I will be playing this in fear of the family of badgers, but truly, there wasn't any real sense of threat. There are far more dangers waiting for animals that just the few rare ones that we encountered here. And they aren't very well done.
You keep doing the same things over and over again. And things like getting food or avoid danger are not even remotely hard.
Sometimes camera gets stuck on the tree and you can't see anything that's going on. It's not only annoying, it may actually cause you to make some mistake.
In short - unique idea, but pretty disappointing game.

The Lord of the Rings: War in the north is action role-playing game. The game takes place in Middle-earth, the same timeline as the fellowship of the ring, except you're not going to be with the fellowship here, not even you're going to join the battle of Helm's Deep or the Siege of Minas Tirith. You have your own battle here in the northern part of Middle-earth. You will be able to explore Rivendell or you may call it Imladris, the town of Bree, Mirkwood and more. You can choose 3 different characters, each from different race, different abilities and different secrets to found throughout the game. Choose Eradan, a human rangers from Dunedain, Andriel, an elf lore-master from Imladris or Farin, a dwarf from Erebor. Any characters you choose, the rest will become your AI companion.
The game has good and decent gameplay. It's basic hack and slash game but each characters can also use different ranged attack such as crossbow. The story of the game is linear which makes the level also very linear. Items are vary in this game, and items with better quality can be found as the characters level progress and playing more harder difficulty. Once you beat a difficulty, you can continue playing from the start point on the next difficulty level but retaining your characters level and items. You can also play cooperative with your friends here.
The Lord of the Rings: War in the North has good graphics. Each level and stages in the game have great detail on the environment, which makes Rivendell have really beautiful scenery and the enemy castle a very bad place to see. Animation is also good, though sometimes there is a small animation glitch when an orcs dies.
But I also will tell you that this game has downside too. Unfixed bugs and glitches are common here, you may see a sword thrown up without reason, the AI companion is somewhat foolish too, using ability when their foe is already dead, or sometimes they even will become your problem. The acting is also not that good, even the voice acting too. But this game is still recommended from me.
+ Gameplay
+ Cooperative
+ Storyline
+ Graphics
+ Replayable
- Bad AI
- Bugs
- Glitches
Rating 8/10

I didn't even get through the "tutorial" area as the controls threw me off. The jump button has to be held for a split second before it even registers the input - this leads to constantly falling into pits (which either contain spikes, enemies, or a passage to another area, with loading in-between, which just adds to the frustration). Some of the pits are also nearly invisible and don't stand out from the background enough for me to notice them the first time around.
Combat is also really hard to get used to - the attack animation hides the enemy and the movement required to manouver to a knocked back enemy to hit it again is really specific. Also, there's no dash ability (or maybe there is but the game tells you nothing about
it), so learning the 1st boss's
attack patterns is a must. Aerial combat requires really precise movement and with the unresponsive jump button it's nearly impossible to get right. This leads to frequently getting knocked back and falling 3 stories down, only to have to jump up on tiny platforms (again, with very precise input). Add really cheap stalactites falling from the ceiling and the punishment for getting hit being often falling into spikes - so losing 2hp and getting reset to the beginning of the room - and you have a recipe for not a really fun time.
I'm sorry I failed you, "git gud" community, I couldn't persevere. The art style is pretty cool though.

TLDR: Buy and play the original version of the game, not the remaster.
If you have never played BioShock before, the game itself (the original) is a masterpiece. It is well worth a playthrough if you have never experienced it... HOWEVER you should play the original version and not the Remaster.
The "remastered" version of the game, of which this is a review for, has some slight (very slight) graphical improvements, but it also has all the bugs the original had and more. Yes, the remastered actually is buggier than the original. Even after you spend time researching fixes for bugs and things like mouse accelleration and audio (the original had 5.1 audio while the remastered has only stereo) your game will crash... a lot. And not only will it crash, but every time it crashes your settings will be reset and you will most likely lose your save. Sounds great right?
People saying that the negative reviews are from "whiny pc kids" who complain about getting a free game are delusional. I personally purchased Bioshock 1 and 2 again on steam in anticipation for the remastered versions, and anyone looking at this page for reviews and is debating buying the remastered needs to now to stay away from this and buy the original Bioshock instead (which has Overwhelmingly positive reviews atm). Even if the game was free for everyone, that does not mean you should excuse very poor development and a shoddy pc port. Being complacent in games coming out that are clearly not ready to come out, whether remastered or new games, will ultimately make games worse for everyone.

Rivals of Aether is a very decent Smash clone - or rather, I should say would be, if an attention to the details were to be made.
Either the in-game hurtbox/hitbox visualizers are broken, or the hurtboxes/hitboxes themselves. You will constantly see moves with no visual representation of a hit (i.e. Wrastor's wing during his fair not touching the opponet, but them still receiving damage+knockback). This leads to a frustrating amount of moments in which someone made the correct play, spaced a move the way it SHOULD be spaced, but still gets hit.
Riding on the coat-tails of the broken boxes is the absurd amount of trading moves in this game. A "trade" is when two players throw out moves without clanking (when two moves hit each other, make a "clank" noise, and nullify each other) but both players taken damage+knockback. There are some situations where trades make sense - you throw out a move that touches the opponets hurtbox without touching the hitbox of his move and vice versa. You will encounter, however, many more situations that just leave you scratching your head saying "That's actually physically impossible."
If Dan, the creator, spent half the time fine-tuning details of the game engine itself instead of pandering to a community that every month finds a character to crucify and raining nerfs from the heavens like some holy manna, this could be a really good game. In its current state, I would pass.

I'll start off by pointing out I've been playing Marvel vs. Capcom since the "first" one. (Marvel Super Heroes vs. Street Fighter and everything before I didn't really touch, is what I mean.)
Frankly, if you like Marvel vs. Capcom and you're not a blind Capcom fanboy, know that this game does not, in any way shape or form, care about you. You don't matter. All the classic Marvel character themes? Gone, replaced by generic cinematic garbage that is easily forgettable. The X-Men, who started the entire Marvel vs. Capcom franchise? Well, their movies are made by Fox, so Marvel would prefer you forget about them. But don't worry! Captain Marvel has a tri-dash so she's the same function as Magneto! That's all you care about, right?
This game's PR has been an absolute trainwreck, with everyone involved saying the exact wrong thing at any given moment. I feel like the only people working on this game who actually even REMOTELY cared about the final product are the people who worked on the gameplay. It is, in fact, a pretty fun game. I have a blast with it. However, I would never recommend that anyone shell out $60 for this. And I CERTAINLY wouldn't tell anyone to spend an additional $30 on DLC characters, and then ANOTHER $30 on costumes. And don't expect that to stop either, this game sold horribly from what I'm aware, so the only way Capcom is getting any money out of this is bleeding the people who are still loyal to them for some reason dry with DLC costumes and characters out the wazoo.
If you don't care about -ANYTHING- but the gameplay, and I do mean that literally since everything else is awful, I'd say wait for it to inevitably go on sale and pick it up then. And even then, you should probably get it on PS4, since the online for that is bound to be more alive than the Steam version. But then again, you can mod the music in the Steam version to be not awful, so if you're getting it to play offline with your friends and you don't care much for online, by ALL MEANS pick up the Steam version. Just, you know. Wait for a sale. This isn't worth $60.

Strike Suit Zero is a intense and frantic game with a lot of significant flaws. Controls can feel complex and cumbersome, often akin to patting your head and rubbing your belly as you constantly shift between various weapons systems to chew through energy shields or armor more efficiently, time your EMP to throw off enemy missiles, manage weapon and thruster energy so as not to be left vulnerable while also keeping tabs on numerous objectives, enemy types, and friendlies that need more protection than Slippy ever did. Flipping into 'Strike' mode (AKA Mech mode) is only a temporary respite, cutting your maneuverability and boasting a whole different set of controls that must be mastered to maximize it's enormous firepower. It's overwhelming at times all of the stuff that needs to be kept track of, and the cluttered, boring missions don't help. However, when the game is firing on all cylinders and you get into a stride, there's absolutely nothing like SSZ in the genre that makes you feel like an ace pilot. The climax of one mission, for example, sees you screaming into combat as an outgunned allied battleship is melted, corkscrewing through a swarm of enemy fighters blasting at everything to build up flux in time. From there, you flip smoothly into Strike mode, strafing along the broadside of a massive enemy cruiser mashing turrets and hoping to god your shields can hold on for just a few milliseconds longer before shifting back to fighter mode and wheeling out for another run, eyes constantly watching the armor melting off your allied ship. Moments like these will be among the most memorable moments you can have with this game. Unfortunately, they'll also be peppered with hatred for the accursed bomber missions, long missions of "kill this group of enemies, move, repeat ad nauseam".
The Director's Cut improves pacing and voice acting, adds much of the original game's DLC, as well as provides a visual upgrade. However, it is much more demanding on systems and ditches the (rarely used) Steam Workshop support. You're probably better off getting the Director's Cut as a new player, but veterans of the original probably don't need to double-dip.

I'm a huge fan of survival and rogue-like games. Challenge and realism is what I look for in a good survival game.
Now, before I buy a game, I always look at the bad reviews first (which this game only had a couple in relation to the reverse amount of positive reviews) and make a decision. Most of the bad reviews, from what I can tell, are people who were expecting a game that it wasn't. They blame the stealth system or the repetitivness or that they can't explore more than what the devs wrote into the game. While some of this I can see validity and give them some credit, most of the bad reviews taste a little like "rage-quit".
Seeing how I was already interested just from the video (and the music with it right?) I decided to buy it and play it for myself... I was NOT disappointed.
The game does indeed, in my opinion, lack content. But don't let that deter you! This game is really fun and addicting. The devs had a great idea and made it into something that could have a great sequel or some good DLC. The graphics are perfect for giving you that feeling of depression. Every decision I made in the game was a drastic one. But when I finally got one of the two ending achievments, i've never felt so accomplished. Took numerous playthroughs but the feeling of surviving is great. I can now say I am in the 1% of people who have that achievment.
So I'll go over some quick pros and cons before I close out.
Pros:
- Great ambience and graphics (music, art, sounds)
- Balanced, yet challenging loot and crafting system
- Great character and story development
Cons:
- Its a little high priced for how much content there is. (but you won't NOT have fun, I promise)
- The stealth system IS in fact a little flawed. But I don't want to hear any excuses. Surving in real life would be harder than beating this game, so suck it up. I did it in 24 total hours and only got ONE of the two endings.
All-in-all I had a really good time with this game. I'd like to see some DLC or a sequel sometime though. I'd definitely buy them. Remeber, if you don't like survival or rogue-like games, this game is NOT for you.
Happy gaming!

Strike Suit Zero is an interesting space Mecha game. Although the Mecha designation might not be the best here. First of all you are the only who can transform from a normal space ship fighter to a mecha which is much more powerful, however also more stationary. And there is only ship capable of transforming and you don't even have access to it all of the time. Most importantly perhaps is that your time in the Mech mode is limited, you can transform as soon as you gather a little bit of energy (which you can do automatically and very slowly over time, or quickly by destroying enemies), but you also quickly expend that energy simply by firing on your opponents. It seems that the only way they managed to balance the game is by limiting how long you can stay in the more fun Mech mode.
The targeting system also isn't very helpful, and there is no overview of what kind of enemies you're fighting. So the only way for you to get an overview of the situation is by actually looking around. That becomes very problematic in the later missions when you're tasked with protecting your fleet and you've got multiple enemy cruisers coming down on them, with your main objective being to destroy the beam cannons which do massive damage to your fleet. However as there is no overview there is no good way to be sure that you've actually neutralized the biggest threats. Unless you know for a fact how many of each ship is out there, which of course you'll only learn once you've failed the mission and that is simply not good game design.
Background music for the game is very nice, however it can become quite repetitive as there isn't much variety there.
The story itself is very generic, but still passable and kept my attention to the end (which comes quite quickly though), which is more than most other similar games can do.
All in all, the game isn't anything special but it's fun to play, at least through its short campaign.

I played the game for a couple chapters, but eventually decided that I wasn't having nearly enough fun to justify spending any more time on it -- nor, for that matter, to justify taking up 4 gigs of space on my hard drive. It's a point-and-click puzzle game, but the puzzles are seldom of the "reasonable challenge" variety; they're either painfully obvious, or painfully obtuse where you only stumble across them by trying absolutely every way to be wrong (e.g., boosting a laser's power by adding a lens cut away from the plastic cover for a neon sign, which you may recognize as a technique that wouldn't work). This is often magnified by the puzzles having perfectly logical solutions that the game ignores in favor of going around in circles and repeating the same action several times until it finally gives a different result. (It even gives an achievement for putting up with the "Quickie" computer character that embodies one of these moments.)
I grew up with the puzzle games from Sierra and LucasArts; I get that lateral thinking is a large part of the genre, and that it's easy for developers to miss the mark and come up with a "solution" that can only be seen in hindsight. But those games balanced it out by making it worthwhile with good stories. This game does not. It's an extremely heavy-handed story about climate change, bearing a strong resemblance to the film
in its "We're all doomed RIGHT NOW" approach. It's not that I object to the message itself; it's that the message isn't entertaining, which is the one and only possible purpose of a video game. I'm not really geared up to spend several hours lecturing myself. Coupled with protagonists who are utterly unlikeable (one terminally depressed, one aggressively arrogant, both humorless), and there's simply nothing to make me want to play much past the beginning of
.

A New Beginning - Final Cut has everything you want in a point and click adventure game, good story, compelling characters, imaginative enviroments, and challenging but not too hard of puzzles. However, the english version of the game has some pretty poor voice acting/english dialogue. Also, the gameplay was very linear in how you could solve the puzzles.
Pros - Great enviroments; the most memorable part of the game is at the beginning of the game in a post-apocalypse sci-fi enviroment. The art is beautiful. The story was gripping (until the end). There was also talk about philosophy, morality, and ethics. A good message at the end. I also enjoyed many of the characters, even a few which only appeared for a short amount of time. And, I enjoyed many of the puzzles in the game except that I thought some of them were a bit too straight forward. I like the self-awarness that the game had. For example, there is this part when you make this sci-fi antenna which had a frustrating yet satisfying part with the cubes. For the rest of the game the cubes were mentioned as being stupidly difficult.
Cons - People just don't talk like they do in the game. I suspect that the dialogue was originally written in a different language and translated to english. When I heard a character say something in a strange way, it took me out of the game momentarily. Also, the ending kind of rubbed me the wrong way. The game seemed to be building up to something but then the ending was predictable and implausible. Actually, several times during the game, there were details which were implausible even in the context of the sci-fi story. Also, some of the characters were very one-dimensional, like the main villan.
Over all, I recommend the game if you enjoy adventure games with an interesting message and a good amount of attention paid to deatil.

Man, I really wish I could give a thumbs-up to the game-play, but a thumbs-down to the story. As a game, I really enjoyed the puzzle-solving aspect and the beautiful, hand-drawn backgrounds (though the character animation leaves a little to be desired - Fay's posture and walk are perplexing, to say the least). Like many good point-and-click adventure games, the puzzles involve thoroughly searching your surroundings to find needed objects, and then figuring out where and how to use them. Other times, making certain dialogue choices when interacting with other characters will lead you to your goals. I got stumped quite often - sometimes I'd just fumble into the right solution, and other times I'd work it out logically - but in the case of the latter, there were many times when I'd think I was on the right track, only to find I was still several steps away from the solution. While there are harder adventure and puzzle games out there, at least this one can be enjoyable for people who are both fans of the genre and newcomers.
What may make the game less palatable is the story - if the heavy-handed, sometimes unintentionally-funny preaching about global warming doesn't put off even the environmentally-conscience, then the ending that seems to go against everything the rest of the game stood for probably will. The game's plot doesn't stay focused on one reason for mankind's destruction, shifting from global warming to a more catastrophic event, and then there's something about a solar flare which is going to wipe out everyone, anyway, no matter what they do to the environment. (Seriously, pick one disaster and go with it!) And the ending kind of makes you feel like it was all for nothing, along with leaving several questions unanswered.
The voice acting is mediocre - I've seen some pretty harsh criticisms of it, but I've heard worse, so I wasn't terribly bothered by it. Sometimes it doesn't match the onscreen text or gets details confused. Examples: "Chrome Dome" is said in one scene where the words "Bald Pate" are clearly spelled out, and at another point, the dialogue can't decide if it's DH54 algae or DH45 algae. Also, use the knife on Bent in the final puzzle if you want to see Fay mouth two lines of text in German (the game's original language) with no voiceover. These issues, plus weird glitches like dialogue cutting off at the end of a sentence and poorly matched lip-synching give the impression of a lack of polish for the English translation.
Oh yes, the world's savior is named Bent Svensson. Yeah, I know, maybe it's a legit Norwegian name, or maybe it's short for Bentley. It still sounds hilarious to English-speaking audiences.
Rating: 2.5/5

Story lines are the most important (arguably) thing about an adventure game, I will keep this review as spoiler free as possible however there are a few locations that I am going to talk about as well as some things that get established quite early on. If that is unacceptable stop reading now, I shall quickly summarize here: this game should be a 7/10 but is quite buggy so unfortunately I can only reward it a 5 or 6. So my quest to play all and review my games library finally got to A. Unfortunately my magpie sense tingled and I recently purchased another bundle which has set me back onto the numbers. Also steam recently reclassified this game into N which I suppose makes sense but its irked me a bit. Mind that is a issue I need to take with steam and not this game.
So this is a point and click 2d game, and a pretty competent one at that. You play as one of two characters that you change between during the story, Bent, an Eco scientist, and Fay who is a time traveler from a despotic future ruined by climate change. They are trying to create a green fuel and make it the primary power source for the world as to prevent the future. I ended up enjoying the characters I was playing as. They both seem to have well thought out personalities, there isn't tonnes of back story for them though, and they do focus a lot on the environment. I have a friend who has played this game who says that they found it very preachy and there is a little bit of that, but it is to be expected. They both have dedicated their lives to this working out after all.
The game has 2 main sections, one is your traditional 2d point and clicking, inventory puzzles and dialogue trees etc. the second is a single screen puzzle that you have to solve.
A big problem I have seen with modern point and click games is that the difficulty level is much reduced. This is to encompass the casual tablet crowd as the lowest common denominator reaches the biggest market, and as a nerdy amiga/dosbox owning girl, I like my old school point and clicks. This game has a really nice feature which is rather than making all the interactive items stand out it keeps them plain in the background, however, holding down space will light them up. Also in the single screen puzzles which can take a while to figure out there is a skip button. I didn't use space or skip any of the puzzles but it is nice to see that they are optional. I do find the skip button a bit annoying as I feel that if you can't beat a game then you need to suck it up rather than whining to the developers to make it easier and easier however I do prefer it to them simplifying it even more. Modern point and click can be very bittersweet but this one is much more sweet than some of the rubbish on my friend's ipad.
There is one place that this game seriously falls down though, and thats in the Quality Assurance. I understand that English is not the first language of the developers, and I do want to take it easy on them, but it is a taint that makes what would be an adept example of the genre unfortunately adequate. It's a shame too, because a thorough testing session should have picked these up and it comes off feeling a bit lazy and sloppy, but the rest of the game wasn't. I really do feel for the developers and I hope that people don't criticise them too hard for this.
The game has numerous spelling errors but as I say, not a first language. However often the dialogue on the screen and the vocal speech are different and using completely different, albeit similar words. I found that the on screen text tended to be a bit more detailed than the dialogue so I treated that as canon. There was also an instance where a character was saying dialogue choice one when he should have been saying choice two. There are a few parts in the game where you can click to move your character into a spot where they shouldn't go, and they wander off getting smaller and smaller until they are but a pixel. Again, this is not the fault of the programmers. Character scaling while walking off into the distance is a good thing, these are boundaries that QA should be pointing out. Another time I got stuck in a bar, I could not get him out no matter how hard I tried, luckily an exit was just in view and I could double click to fast travel him out. Late in chapter 6 clicking on an inventory item was giving me dialogue all the way back from chapter 2. I'm sure if I was willing to give it a second play through I could find more bugs now that I know some of the triggers.
It is a shame it is so buggy but please don't let that put you off. If you like the genre there is nothing wrong with this game at all, just maybe think about waiting for a sale.

While Civilization 5 plus G&K and BNW is definately a more worthwhile experience, I do still believe that Beyond Earth is a good fun game.
So what do I like about Civ: BE over Civ V? Well, I am a fan of sci-fi/future settings, so I liked all the advanced technology and the alien world, I also believe that aliens are better and are more interesting than barbarians. While the only purpose of barbarians were to annoy you by capturing your workers, killing your scouts and pilaging your tiles, aliens are not aggressive by default (with the exception of siege worms, because screw them) and will only become hostile if you step too close to one of their nests or you show hostility towards them. You can even become friendly with the aliens which is indicated by their unit markers turning blue.
I do also like the idea behind a tech web rather than the tree, though at first, it is extremely confusing and if there's something in particular you want, you'll have to look through every branch and leaf to find the one technology you want. i can remember taking about three minutes to find the technology that allowed me to build solar collectors. The affinity system is also nice, these function similarly to the ideologies in Civ V, except here you can upgrade all 3 of them rather than choosing one. Eventually, you will have a dominant affinity which influences what others think of you. Each affinity has cool unique units. The purity affinity has the battlesuit, aegis, LEV tank and LEV destroyer which are all powerful and versatile units, the harmory affinity has the xeno swarm, xeno cavalry, rocktopus and xeno titan which are all alein-based units that are also powerful and last but not least, the supremacy affinity has the CDNR, the CARVR, the SABR and the Angel, all are robotic-based units and once again, very powerful.
So what's bad? Well, the diplomacy is as poor as usual. There's nothing really more to say, i believe diplomacy is not as good as Civ V which didn't have great diplomacy to begin with. There's nothing you can really do other than trade, become partners or declare war. I also believe the balance is pretty off. Early on and even later on, siege units have little purpose, as ranged units can level a city with roughly the same amount of power except no set-up time and actually passable defences. Later on, siege units become more effective thanks to boosts to city damage but even then, ranged units have superior defences which allows them to be more easily deployed, not to mention that i believe units such as the purity aegis do a far better job than either of these two types of unit. Additionally, since cavalry units have no resource cost anymore, you'll find that most armies use tanks as their main unit as they have better attack and defence than standard units, as well as increased speed with their only real disadvantage being that they cost more production.
Overall, Civilization: Beyond Earth is still a pretty good game at it's core. I have had a lot of fun playing it and I do recommend it, but if you're on the edge about it, i'd say wait for a sale or wait for the first DLC.
Honestly, if you're looking into getting into the Civilization francise, i'd say buy Civ V complete edition. Regardless, Beyond Earth is still a fun game. At least try the demo, then make your decision.

So far, I have played three games on what I think is the equivalent of Emperor setting (2 settings above "normal").  My initial impressions are favorable. The obvious inclination is to compare to it Civ5, but in doing so, it is a bit unfair since Civ 5 has had years of patches and two full expansions, so the amount of content is much greater for Civ 5.  Beyond Earth adds or changes things from Civ 5 enough that it really does feel like a new game, but it keeps enough things in common that it is easy to make the transition.
The things I really like about Beyond Earth are the Affinity system and how the tech tree is now more of a tech web.  What I do not like, are the reduction in unit types (there is no naval mele unit, and for aircraft, there is just a fighter, no bomber for example), and the lack of great persons.  The factions that replace civilizations also seem to lack personality. It might be that I just have not played enough games, but I have not noticed any clear patterns in AI behavior.
I think adding more personality to the AI players and adding great persosn, unique units, and unique buildings for the factions would make a good game even better.  As it stands though, it is still a better game than Civ 5 was before it got the Gods and Kings expansion, and I recommend it to any Civ player.

At last a great platform fighter (i.e. Smash clone) on PC. I’m somewhere between beginner and intermediate, so I can’t comment on how the game is played at high level. I’ll share my experience and thoughts as a casual player.
The controls have an elegant simplicity that grants the game its appeal and low skill floor. Simply input a direction and one of the attack buttons simultaneously to perform an attack in that direction. There are three attack buttons corresponding to tilts, strong attacks and special attacks. The same controls apply universally to all characters and they all share quite similar tilts and strong attacks, so that once you learned to play with one character, you can find your bearings with any of them.
There are only 8 characters but each has a pretty unique moveset with some specific quirks, especially when it comes to special attacks. This can be both great and somehow bothering at the same time. Great because every character has a distinct playstyle and everyone is guaranteed to find at least a few tailored to them among this small but varied cast. Bothering because it steepens the learning curve for two reasons when compared to Smash. First, it slightly gets in the way of skill transfer from character to character. Secondly, matchups knowledge becomes more important.
By no means I want to give the impression that this is an actual issue and that the game is in fact hard to learn, it is still very easy to pick up, it only makes it harder to master. And yet, RoA brings some of its own simplicity to the genre. It pares down the mechanics and trims the formula to its essential components by removing grabs, edge grabbing, L-cancelling, shields (replaced with parries), … What remains at the core is a streamlined gameplay that prominently features exhilarating kickass combos.
The result is a mechanically tight game with a low skill floor, high skill ceiling, and a learning curve sloped to quickly and comfortably project players towards the more fast paced, technical and competitive side of platform fighters.
I absolutely recommend this game to anyone who prefers Melee to other Smash games. This is the closest you will get on PC. It manages to capture both the simplicity and depth that I enjoyed in Melee while still having its own flavor and charm.
Although it isn’t a party game and is definitely positioned towards the competitive end of the spectrum, I also strongly recommend it to newcomers. I mostly play casually with friends at my skill level, and even so I enjoy it much more than the few other alternatives on PC. The action is fast paced, the combos you can pull off even as a beginner are really awesome, and it’s overall extremely fun.

TLDR:
"Those who violently cut themselves straight out of Omelas even as they suffer from severe self inflicted amnesia -the game."
:P
Actual discussion on the game:
Shadow Warrior is a modern iteration on the older school of shooters, back from the era where cover and loadouts remained uninvented in favor of lots of guns and enemies scrambling to fill the screen with their after effects. If you think of the old DOOM (or for that matter old Shadow Warrior) you are on the right track, and if you think of the modern reimagining of DOOM Bethesda released, you are very much still on it.
SW, being an older release than the aforementioned example, is hardly as smooth or even fast paced as the Sci-fi demon-fest that is Doom, and can't help but feel a bit clunky when compared directly to it. But even so, as the years pile on, SW still has a couple of tricks up its sleave that it can pull to remain relevant.
First of all, for all its shooting and guns and whatnot, most of SW see you pilot the katana, rather than stare down a sight.  Guns are plentiful, albeit somewhat generic, but against a host of mainly melee-based enemies it is nice to be able to forego backpedaling for more agressive engagements. Magic is also a feature, and comes in both spell- as well as special sword move variety. These features has seen SW's gameplay remain different to the resurgent old school shooter genre thus far, and is the main thing that sets it apart from its peers. Aside from swordplay and magic, cash can be used to upgrade weapons, and a -for its genre- deep leveling systems lets you customize the protagonist Lo Wang, whose name very niftily allows for a segway into talking about themes and humor.
If you have seen any media at all about this game, you have most likely already noticed how the name of our protagonist is very much played for laughs. In general the entire game follow the same tounge-in-cheek humor with deconstructions of pop-culture-orientalist -not asian, but orientalist! The distinction is important :) - tropes smattered througout. Fortune cookies with wierd quips, as well as a self aware serving of clichés in terms of locations and enemies, makes for a game that knows it's camp and just goes with it. Chucklef*ck tendencies aside the story is -again, for the genre- actually fairly well written, and the actors do a good job selling the serious bits between fights. In short the story goes; Mercenary Lo Wang needs to get a magical sword from his old boss, to help a demon who keeps secret why this is important. To say anything else is spoilery, but hey, maybe the TLDR gave it away :P. While the story is good, production value is however a bit low, and sometimes this is noticeable where the voice actors are a lot more emotive than the models they puppet. All in all though, the story and themes mesh well, leaving you invested enough to push on between fights.
The gameplay, as mentioned before has suffered somewhat from the passing of time. While on the whole very good, it retroactively commits some sins modern games have learned to avoid, and sometimes this makes for a diminished experience.
The game has about three flaws that remain an issue throughout; Pacing, floatiness and what i can only describe as katana control.
The pacing one is easy to describe. Game slow! Modern brain used to fast game! Even going into this knowing about what to expect, I still found myself sighing in frustration running from point A to point B just to traverse empty levels. The game is not badly designed per se, and actually have very good levels with logical paths for players to follow. But! It has filled these levels with secrets and easter eggs, encouraging mucking about in them. Hardly a sin in its own right, but when secrets are placed, not in clever locations, but in backtracky ones, you are for all intents and purposes wasting the player's time. Too bad, but not really a dealbreaker. It mostly gets better later on. Mostly... LOOKING AT YOU INTERNAL RAILWAY SYSTEM!
The second issue is that Lo Wang's movements are kinda floaty, like he is made of helium. This is not a problem on flat ground, where it actually makes him faster, but on vertical levels it makes jumps hard and precision movements more difficult. This was common in games back when, and modern protagonists have taken off the ice skates, but Wang still sports a pair, and sometimes they get him killed.
Lastly and perhaps most damningly, the melee system suffer again from more of that retroactive clunk. Blocking is nonexistant and the rebuke from hitting a shield or wall is juust slow enough to peeve me. Don't get me worng, the gun/swordplay is good, but as you grow used to modern solutions and quality of life mechanics, stuff like this become noticeable, even when they were not considered earlier in a game's life as issues at all. I suppose one could say that throughout your experience, you never really lose the feeling that you are, for better or worse, playing an old game, and for people experiencing SW for the first time, there is no nostalgia to alleviate these issues.
But I've crapped on the game long enough, and for all its faults I'd never have bothered writing anything about it if it was not such a wholesome and enjoyable experience. It is cathartic to mash the cut-button and watch slices come off foes like confetti at a parade! It is cool to get enough money to unlock the alternative fire for your favorite gun and just ♥♥♥♥ up their day with it! It is bloody bombastic to slowly swing your sword in a slo-mo arc and behead four dudes that tried to swarm you from all sides! When this came out it was the BOMB, and whatever faults it has are splinters we don't have to pick out of our fingers playing new Doom today, or stuff we did not even know were bad until the current gen just didn't do them!
If you want to play one of the games that helped revialize the splatter-shooter, and took some of the steps (and subsequent bullets) towards its current lovely state of budding modernization, you'll want some of this Wang! But if you are uninterested in genre or game history, or just want to plow through the newest and best game of this kind, you are probably better off getting new Doom instead.

I've had people tell me to play Guilty Gear because ArcSys aren't as bad as Capcom but if you look at how much each version costs and then the DLC characters, they don't look much different.
I would recommend this game if you like fast paced fighting games with a touch of madness involved.

It's honestly with a heavy heart that I do not recommend X: Rebirth.
First some backstory.
I first got into the X series with X3: Terran Conflict.  It was intimidating and daunting, but I got it during a sale, and I figured that I should at least invest some time into it.  While it was a rocky start at first, I managed to learn the ropes and have myself a good time with space combat and trading.  Excited, I bought Albion Prelude, and got even more enjoyment due to the improvements upon the systems.  The addition of the stock market, for example, was very much appreciated.
Soon after playing Albion Prelude, I heard about the development of X: Rebirth.  Promising to be more accessible but just as deep, I became incredibly excited.  Bohemia Interactive had promised something similar with ARMA3 and they delivered on their promise.  I expected just the same from Egosoft- and why not?  They had been working on the X series for more than 10 years- they knew what their fans wanted and expected.
At least... They should've known.
But X: Rebirth put my faith into Egosoft into doubt.
X: Rebirth is nothing short of a mess.
First off, the game is poorly optimized, with framerate drops quite abundant in the earlier areas and very apparent across the campaign.  Some areas are not quite as bad, but it's very clear that there was minimal QA done.  The computer I use is very powerful but even then it chugs with Rebirth.
Secondly, things are buggy.  Ships under your command behave strangely, trading sometimes does not carry out, and orders can be backed up with no way to cancel them.  Saying that it is a test of patience would give too much credit to the game- it is downright broken.  Patches have fixed some of the problems, but many still hang around.
Thirdly, the elements Egosoft touted for immersion are of poor quality.  From the number of character models to the interiors to the voice acting...  The detail is not even up to 2008 standard, much less a game being released in 2013.  This could be forgiven somewhat if it wasn't for the fact of how repetitious many of these elements were.  There's probably only about five or so voice actors across the entire game, all with equally wooden delivery.  Ren Otani's VA is the best, but that's best in the sense of "Of all the moldy sandwiches in the fridge, this one has the least amount of mold."
Minigames have been put in place, but they feel incredibly out of place in a game meant to be a space trading simulator.  Tapping buttons to time "convince" meters for small-talk or zipping behind ships to speed through the highways are elements intended for action-focused games, not simulators.
But perhaps most heartbreaking of all, the game is missing so many features that made the past X games great.  The radar system is now gone, as well as readouts for speed and distance.  Combat has been given more of a focus but it has lost its complexity and tactical thought.  The elements that should help with establishing a gian trade empire are gone, such as trade automation.
This is not the X game that we were promised.
There ARE some things in X: Rebirth that are worthwhile.  The detail put into the universe is nothing short of incredible.  The low texture resolution can be forgiven as there is now a true sense of scale to the world- the highways, one of the most impressive elements in X: Rebirth, zip you from sector to sector, which can range from stations located in the center of a broken planet to derelict but surviving facilities only tens of thousands of miles away from a star.  It's awe-inspiring, flying around in space.
The base of X: Rebirth is not terrible.  It has given us a more moddable engine capable of a very detailed universe.  But sadly, it should've been more.  Knowing Egosoft, they will work tirelessly to patch and fix the game, but the damage has been done- I've lost a lot of my trust in them.  After being so enthusiastic about a game, I honestly feel betrayed.
Perhaps in a few months, the game may become what I expected.  When that time comes, I'll revisit this review.

PROS:

- Easy to pick up difficult to master
- Game is very cheap on CD-Keys For the PC.
CONS:
- Story Mode is too short and too samey throughout
- ALL the xmen removed
- DLC actually costs more than what i paid for the game. I paid £17 for the game, DLC costs £24.99
- Some character models are awful: Thor, Spencer, Captain Marvel, Chun Li, Gamorra, Morrigan and Dante all look like ps3 imports and are horrible to look at
- Most character themes are awful to listen too, particular Dante's theme
- Music in general is poor
- Lip syncing is mostly out in pre fight cut scenes
- No story mode or comic story mode in arcade mode
- Computer is cheap and uses cheap fighting tactics on hardest setting
- The infinity stone system is broken
- THe Omega Ultron Boss is a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥and is stupidly hard to reduce health even on easy, needs replacing with a better end game fight particular for acrade tbh: like Thanos for example (with his infinity gauntlet on )
- Graphics are substandard and not good enough for a next gen or PC game, even in 4k it looks dated.
- Minor Patches are 7.8GIG each that is ridiculous for updates, way too big and should be condensed, not everyone has unlimited internet or hard-drive space.

Strike Suit Zero (SSZ) is a frustatingly beautiful game; the personification of a game with excellent gameplay marred by horrible enemy variation and an outlandish story. You are a pilot of a fleet taking off to exterminate an alien threat. The game's namesake ship however isn't even obtainable until the third mission - and even then you are charged with taking other ships such as the interceptor (a variation on the starting ship) and a bomber (which was actually pretty cool to operate). The aspect of the game that makes it most difficult is the combat: I want frentic warfare - not a jumbled mess. The dogfights are engaging if only for a moment; taking down capitol ships is an exercise in bullet/missle-sponges; and using the strike suit is like drunkingly blasting ships. Plus it leaves you more vulnerable to attacks - which makes no sense because you have to garner flux to use it and equipping (transforming) the suit should make you more of a bad♥♥♥♥♥ Instead it makes you a sitting duck that relies on wobbly shooting (granted, lock-on firing is available). The story actually has a good conclusion but everything before it is wonky. At some random point there is a grand coupe de tat that is massively overlooked because you are too busy trying to master the controls to even pay attention to the dialogue.
The game's greatest weakness is that it doesn't flaunt the suit! Let me free fly with this piece of machinery. Make it more controllable. Make it worth garnering flux! Sadly, the game falls flat for me, and beating it was a months-long mission whose only vincidation of knocking off one more game off my protruberent Steam library.

- Great character and story development
Cons:

All-in-all I had a really good time with this game. I'd like to see some DLC or a sequel sometime though. I'd definitely buy them. Remeber, if you don't like survival or rogue-like games, this game is NOT for you.

A huge galaxy. Hundreds or even thousands of fighters, frigates, cruisers and capital ships. And, suddenly, 24 hours is not too much for a day.
That's the sensation of playing Sins. Despite my low playing hours at my account, I'm a veteran of the series since its birth, owning other titles on another platforms.
Here, we have got a game from a relative small producer, Stardock, that attends expectations for a 4X - Explore, Expand, Exploit and Exterminate. You have huge maps to explore, with plenty of planetary traits, with anomalies and all that stuff precious to Sci-Fi fans like me. Then, you must expand your initial holding to a full-fledged empire, not only in name, but also in extension. Technological pursuits on a large tech-tree are helpful ate this time. Exploit resource markets, bribe pirates and expect to battle an AI just "smart enough" on the higher difficulties. Exterminate entire planets with sound visual effects of a nuclear rampage. That is the "sinful" part of game. =)
Rebellion is a nice package that has all other expansions in it, and it's worth its price. You got might starbases, shadow diplomacy and nasty rebels in just one bunch.
It may be hard to understand at first, and you may get a sensation of being overwhelmed with a huge amount of information, but thankfully the interface is well suited to it, with a nice and customizable "empire-tree" that pins your ships and planets on the top left corner. Despites being a 2007 game, its graphics still will make you just sit down and admire the stars sometimes, despite all that carnage happening.
Be prepared to a REALLY long play-time. Even a tiny solar system with a couple of planets may consume four hours straight of your day, without your notice. Because of this, multiplayer is hard to finish. On the end-game, you may be counting just on numbers for your victory, sending massive fleet after massive fleet to the same chokepoint. But expects the AI to do the same to you! It "kind of" "kills" real strategy on late-game at first view, but it's just a question of micromanage your assets.
Because of its uniqueness on a genre relatively abandoned (starfaring games), it's a must buy for the sci-fi fan, and also for the strategy game lover, with its mix of "turn" (for the long time and big picture) and "real-time" (the battles). Some units may appear to be too much strong or, on the other hand, useless, but give a try to different approaches and you may get surprised. The AI being smart is really a plus on a time of dumbed-down games.
Bottom line: 9.3/10

Replaybility: 10
Stability: 10
Controls and Interface: 10
Music and SoundFX: 9
Graphics and System Requirements: 8
Value range (price, average price of direct competitors) divided by (expected playing time): $ (lower is better)

Fun Factor: =) =) =)

A great game that offers more ways to achieve victory than Civ 5 thanks to the sci-fi theme. The highlight on the game is on the Affinity and the Tech Web, where Affinity basically defines not only the ideology of your civilization but also your perks, objectives and even your leader and unit appearance. The Tech Web is vast and complex, and it isn't as straightforward as Tech in Civ 5, and you might need the search function the first few times you play. With so many options it becomes less about researching more techs than other civilizations and more about picking technologies to help your cities become balanced. Often you will have shortage in one or more aspects (e.g. health, energy) if you try to force your way in the Tech Web without much planning.
Overall it is a good game, but $50 is a bit too much for a campaign-less game. Best to wait for at least 33% off before buying it.

This game has a lot of potential, and could turn out amazing if the devs listen to the feedback that the fans have! For now though, I suggest skipping this game and picking up one of the other magic games on steam despite this one being free.
Pros:
-Great Deckbuilding! It is really awesome and you can build a deck from scratch with whatever cards you acquire!
-Lots of new cards not in the previous games, but also some returning ones that I couldn't live without.
-Two headed giant is a lot of fun to play. I love the teamwork based strategies that you need to use.
-It's still magic. And magic is... well... magical. Play it if you haven't before.
Cons:
-Matchmaking/server issues. This is a gamebreaker right here for me. The servers are extremely unreliable, which I wouldn't even mind if I could play the campaign while they were down! But you can't. That's right it blocks your progress and gold you made in the campaign if you can't connect to their servers. So that Liliana duel you've spent ten hours on trying to beat and then finally beat it, might just count for nothing if you randomly get disconnected from their servers. *Pro TIp* you will.
- Extremely small amount of gold earned outside of the campaign. Yeah I get that this game is F2P and they need to make their money somehow, but at least let us earn gold in two headed giant, and make the gold gained based on how long your duel takes. Because getting 20 gold for both an hour long duel and a 5 minute duel seems a little unbalanced.
-No chat function. At all. Like seriously. Where is it? How am I supposed to tell my scrub-lord teammates not to sacrifice all of our creatures now. Or even applaud them and give them super high fives when they do something so awesome that helps us win the game? It's definitely not as fun without chat. Magic is a social game... why take out the social aspect of it?!
-UI. The UI is okay but needs to be polished up a lot. I keep seeing cards upside down, damage and defense numbers sideways and floating off the card so I can't see them, and even a couple of errors in the game where cards do not do what they're supposed to do.
-Damage animations. Half the time I spend dueling people online is spent waiting for them to finish watching the damage animations. Please disable them for online play.
-Not necessarily a con but being able to customize your playing field with different backgrounds would be very nice and add some much needed variety into the playing field.
Summary: How long have they been making magic video games now? 4 years? I'm suprised they haven't figured out how to improve on their last games yet. It almost feels like they went backwards with this one. If they fix the little bugs and server issues this game will be very fun for a long time. It would be really great to see them continue updates for this and always be adding new cards/game modes/ etc. My final verdict on this game is to play it if you've never played magic before because it's free, and you can't really go wrong with a free game if you're just trying it out. But if you have played magic before and you're a fan of the series, stick to one of the old ones.

TLDR:
"Those who violently cut themselves straight out of Omelas even as they suffer from severe self inflicted amnesia -the game."
:P
Actual discussion on the game:
Shadow Warrior is a modern iteration on the older school of shooters, back from the era where cover and loadouts remained uninvented in favor of lots of guns and enemies scrambling to fill the screen with their after effects. If you think of the old DOOM (or for that matter old Shadow Warrior) you are on the right track, and if you think of the modern reimagining of DOOM Bethesda released, you are very much still on it.
SW, being an older release than the aforementioned example, is hardly as smooth or even fast paced as the Sci-fi demon-fest that is Doom, and can't help but feel a bit clunky when compared directly to it. But even so, as the years pile on, SW still has a couple of tricks up its sleave that it can pull to remain relevant.
First of all, for all its shooting and guns and whatnot, most of SW see you pilot the katana, rather than stare down a sight.  Guns are plentiful, albeit somewhat generic, but against a host of mainly melee-based enemies it is nice to be able to forego backpedaling for more agressive engagements. Magic is also a feature, and comes in both spell- as well as special sword move variety. These features has seen SW's gameplay remain different to the resurgent old school shooter genre thus far, and is the main thing that sets it apart from its peers. Aside from swordplay and magic, cash can be used to upgrade weapons, and a -for its genre- deep leveling systems lets you customize the protagonist Lo Wang, whose name very niftily allows for a segway into talking about themes and humor.
If you have seen any media at all about this game, you have most likely already noticed how the name of our protagonist is very much played for laughs. In general the entire game follow the same tounge-in-cheek humor with deconstructions of pop-culture-orientalist -not asian, but orientalist! The distinction is important :) - tropes smattered througout. Fortune cookies with wierd quips, as well as a self aware serving of clichés in terms of locations and enemies, makes for a game that knows it's camp and just goes with it. Chucklef*ck tendencies aside the story is -again, for the genre- actually fairly well written, and the actors do a good job selling the serious bits between fights. In short the story goes; Mercenary Lo Wang needs to get a magical sword from his old boss, to help a demon who keeps secret why this is important. To say anything else is spoilery, but hey, maybe the TLDR gave it away :P. While the story is good, production value is however a bit low, and sometimes this is noticeable where the voice actors are a lot more emotive than the models they puppet. All in all though, the story and themes mesh well, leaving you invested enough to push on between fights.
The gameplay, as mentioned before has suffered somewhat from the passing of time. While on the whole very good, it retroactively commits some sins modern games have learned to avoid, and sometimes this makes for a diminished experience.
The game has about three flaws that remain an issue throughout; Pacing, floatiness and what i can only describe as katana control.
The pacing one is easy to describe. Game slow! Modern brain used to fast game! Even going into this knowing about what to expect, I still found myself sighing in frustration running from point A to point B just to traverse empty levels. The game is not badly designed per se, and actually have very good levels with logical paths for players to follow. But! It has filled these levels with secrets and easter eggs, encouraging mucking about in them. Hardly a sin in its own right, but when secrets are placed, not in clever locations, but in backtracky ones, you are for all intents and purposes wasting the player's time. Too bad, but not really a dealbreaker. It mostly gets better later on. Mostly... LOOKING AT YOU INTERNAL RAILWAY SYSTEM!
The second issue is that Lo Wang's movements are kinda floaty, like he is made of helium. This is not a problem on flat ground, where it actually makes him faster, but on vertical levels it makes jumps hard and precision movements more difficult. This was common in games back when, and modern protagonists have taken off the ice skates, but Wang still sports a pair, and sometimes they get him killed.
Lastly and perhaps most damningly, the melee system suffer again from more of that retroactive clunk. Blocking is nonexistant and the rebuke from hitting a shield or wall is juust slow enough to peeve me. Don't get me worng, the gun/swordplay is good, but as you grow used to modern solutions and quality of life mechanics, stuff like this become noticeable, even when they were not considered earlier in a game's life as issues at all. I suppose one could say that throughout your experience, you never really lose the feeling that you are, for better or worse, playing an old game, and for people experiencing SW for the first time, there is no nostalgia to alleviate these issues.
But I've crapped on the game long enough, and for all its faults I'd never have bothered writing anything about it if it was not such a wholesome and enjoyable experience. It is cathartic to mash the cut-button and watch slices come off foes like confetti at a parade! It is cool to get enough money to unlock the alternative fire for your favorite gun and just ♥♥♥♥ up their day with it! It is bloody bombastic to slowly swing your sword in a slo-mo arc and behead four dudes that tried to swarm you from all sides! When this came out it was the BOMB, and whatever faults it has are splinters we don't have to pick out of our fingers playing new Doom today, or stuff we did not even know were bad until the current gen just didn't do them!
If you want to play one of the games that helped revialize the splatter-shooter, and took some of the steps (and subsequent bullets) towards its current lovely state of budding modernization, you'll want some of this Wang! But if you are uninterested in genre or game history, or just want to plow through the newest and best game of this kind, you are probably better off getting new Doom instead.

I'll be upfront: I went into this game expecting, essentially, an upgraded, spotlessly polished, prettified Blood Money. For me, Blood Money was the epitome of Hitman. Why would they change what was the ultimate expression of the sandbox assassination? There are lots of reasons I could speculate on, but for anyone considering this game, know this: It is
like Blood Money. Further disclaimer: I suck at this game. Sorry about that. So, this review is from the point of view of Easy and Normal modes.
That said, on to the actual review, then. Wall of text incoming, I take this fairly seriously, because well hey, everyone needs a hobby.
I'm going to look at this game two ways: as a generic stealth game, and as a Hitman game.
As a
, it's above average, good even. The usual illogical fallicies aside (i.e. hiding behind/rolling between cover in a disguise is the most effective means of transversing an area, despite it's suspicious as hell), it's still satisfying. In comparison to Blood Money where disguises were the be-all-end-all, IO revised the disguise system to where enemies who are dressed like you are will see through the disguise (they supposedly know who they work with, after all), while other people will simply assume you're supposed to be there (provided you have the appropraite disguise). For me, this was at first annoying, and then I realized its brilliance and logic, and adjusted accordingly. It does, however, need tuning rather badly, but it is most certainly workable. The biggest issue I have with the stealth system as a whole is the "Instinct" resource. It's consumed to blend in with your chosen disguise (and use a "mark and execute"-style ability in combat), and replenished when you kill someone. This means you CAN recover from mistakes at a cost (since Silent Assassins don't touch the world around them), but in the end it's a rather shoehorned system; I didn't feel it should have been used in this fashion, as it doesn't really make sense, but that probably comes down to the diguise system tuning I mentioned, so your milage may vary. However, Instinct is also used in "Instinct Mode", a vision mode that gives you x-ray vision, highlights useful/interactive things, and shows you NPC pathing. This was an interesting way of doing things, which I mostly found acceptable, if overpowered (seeing NPC pathing was a little much). It felt like a good way to show that 47 is beyond merely human in his abilities, which despite being a cornerstone of his character, is often glossed over or ignored.
As a
, however, Absolution is woefully bad. Levels are linear, with targets conveniently in your path to the exit. Sometimes, you don't even get to assassinate the target yourself; it's all done in a cutscene, or a forced psuedo-Quick Time Event. Other times, the game literally makes you fail, in the name of plot. Furthermore, gone is the personalized, sandbox approach to dealing with targets: you start with whatever equipment the game decides to give you, and you have no access to anything other than what the level designers have decided is a viable option, and deigned to leave in the level for you. Granted, finding these various ways the level designers want you to finish the mission CAN be interesting, it would have been a more complete exprience were this "find the method" combined with "bring your own toys"... much like Blood Money. That aside, the plot is laughably bad as usual, only this time the story is the center focus... making much of the game a cringe-fest. A further tragedy of the plot-driven gameplay is that, as mentioned, you are at times
to fail in a cutscene. This has the added effect of not only throwing your hard work of, say, Silent Assassin-ing it up to that point, but also makes 47 look like an idiot. Lastly, the game has a weird habit of trying to force you into out and out firefights, but punishing you for trying to meet those apparent expectations (the mission involving The Saints comes to mind).
However, the game world is amazingly alive, nearly on par with Deus Ex: HR, which is the most "living/real" game world I've ever had the pleasure of participating in. Conversations between NPCs are involved and varied, and delivered in an excellent manner (voice actor quality is unusually high for the throwaway NPCs). That being said, it's odd that most of the storyline characters and cutscenes aren't very memorable or impressive. A great deal of effort and money (
) was put into making the cutscenes realistic and impressive, but I found that effort wasted on me; the story wasn't good to begin with, no amount of presentation is going to change that.
I will, however, praise the visuals and effort of the IO art team; the game looks
. All animations except for 47's aiming animation (it's weird, no one aims like that) are very well done.
Since I'm out of space, closing thoughts (
): It's a decent, even good, stealth game; but also, a disappointing failure of a Hitman game. Go into it expecting Splinter Cell Conviction with a viable Ghost approach, and you'll probably like it.
Score out of 10:
7/10 Stealth Game
3/10 Hitman Game

CONS:

- Most character themes are awful to listen too, particular Dante's theme

Re-Review of the game as of 1.24.  Skipping introductions, you can read what I think of the game below from initial impressions to patch 1.17.  The following things have not changed:
1. Trade is still hosed but does respond better.  Stations in entire sectors run dry sometimes.
2. No radar/gravidar for the skunk
3. Limited weapons and everything costs so much that you need to go scanning to get any money.
4. No easy way to repair rep other than the missions that take you close to enemy stations.
5. Performance on high end rigs like mine still sucks.
6. Game is still 50 dollars when it should be 15 for an "early access" since its still a pre-beta
7. NPCs are still annoying and ugly
8. Starting off still sucks since you don't even start with a container ship to at least get trading.
9. Skunk cannot hold cargo like a rahanas can, so at least you can get started trading.
10. Crappy user interface still exists.
Nothing, and I mean nothing has really been fixed without causing more problems.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The core game in itself is a great idea.  The fact that this game was in development for seven years should have thrown a big red flag to me but I am a huge fan of sci-fi space themes.  In it's current state (1.17) the game is so unbelievably worthless it isn't even close to worth $50.00.  This is more of a fleshed out alpha that is close to beta with so many game breaking bugs it is rediculous.
The core game, where you fly around, shoot, hail, trade, and upgrade your equipment is nice.  Building your own space station is nice too.  The problem is, bugs get in the way of almost all of this. The controls for the game are wonky other than the standard space and first person controls.  Menu systems are rediculous where you have to search for what you want and even then, some basic things arn't included like transfering cargo from the Albion to one of your ships.  Why was this left out?  The "It will be there eventually isn't an acceptable answer as it should be in the game since it was considered a "full" release and not a early access.
Graphics are great in space but the minute you hit the stations, it turns into a game from 2007.  Think Borderlands 1 here, that is the scale we are talking about.  Also, if you have crossfire/SLI like I do, disable it or you are gong to go from a standard 120 fps in most games to a dismal 20 or less on board the stations where nothing is going on.  Finally, all stations are cut and paste.  Nothing is unique as they are all practically the same basic 3 layouts minus a few other systems that have something different to offer.  Even those however, are cut and paste within that system.
Sound is annoying, the "Shut up Betty" from Yisha gets old, the same old lines over and over is just boring.  How can a game this long in development be so limited in basic features? The space sound effects are satsifactory but I get tired of hearing the same highway music over and over.  How about some variety?
Other issues such as no radar, again the "It is coming in a patch" was spout off again.  What?  Why?  The year is 29XX and there is no radar?  The map you access is fine but the on screen "No Signal" crap in the cockpit is stupid.  The only time you see a map there is when you come out of a jumpgate or highlight a gate.  The state of the economy is "We are out of everything, go get us stuff".  Don't waste your time trying to build ships, just go take them over since building them will never happen.
Overall, the game could have been great and still can be.  They need to put the features advertised in the game.  Sure, trading is possible, but it is so buggy is isn't even worth the time.  Creating space stations takes forever since the only viable way to get credits is long range scanning.  So many issues and not enough game.  Refunds by Steam should not be issued since we were the ones that bought into the game before we saw the reviews and other input.  No one forced us to buy this game.  Still, I have been consumed with this game for many hours and will continue to play it if for anything, to get my money's worth.

Well, here we are, the hyped BioShock remaster finally came but, sadly, this is not how a proper remaster should be done on the PC.
For starters, the same problems and issues encountered in the original release from 2007 are present, literally all of them; BioShock is a game that was made using Unreal Engine 2.5, the same engine that powered the emblematic Unreal Tournament 2004, one of the best shooters of all time, and an exemplary PC title that showed us back in 2004 that Unreal Engine was meant to be a PC gaming engine like no other. That game has no flaws when it comes to controls, mouse sensitivity, etc., but on the other hand BioShock and BioShock Remaster DO have issues, and I wonder why...
Well, the thing is, today consoles play a big role in the gaming industry, even more than a decade ago, and multi-platform releases are more prominent now than before, therefore it seems some problems will arise then it comes to making "ports" of these games into the PC but...was there such a need to make this version of the game for the PC right now, ignoring all the issues the original one had? No, there wasn't and I, as may other people, though this remaster was going to actually FIX all the issues that plague the original one up to this day (they can be fixed, most of them, to some extent) but instead, by some unknown reason, the game still has those issues in its remastered form.
Since this review is for the Remaster, not for the original, I cannot give a recommendation for it as of right now...this may change after the game is patched, some day -if they ever do that- but right now, whether you got this game for free because you already owned the original (like I did) or you decide to buy the remaster (you also get the original for free then), it's not a proper remaster that I can recommend, and this opinion of mine is for the remaster as I said, Bioshock is still an amazing game every PC gamer needs to play, that hasn't changed at all.
Anyway, it's obvious that the PC version of this remaster suffers from poor keybind / controls implementation, there're issues related to having a gamepad connected, messing with how the keyboard and mouse controls act in game; there're issues when using extra mouse buttons like mouse 4 or 5, the game will crash when using keybinds to those buttons and a help / tutorial tip is going to be displayed....and a crash will make your settings revert to default values, too.
Some people are reporting loss of game saves too, caused by random crashes, others are getting black screens when launching the game, or simply not being able to start the game at all.
The list goes on, but I think this is enough, as a PC gamer with a Steam account from 2004, it's sad to see that the developers of this remaster failed to accomplish even the most basic standards when it comes to PC gaming and, even though the game is still the good old BioShock we all know and love, this remaster shouldn't be labeled as such.
I still hope that some patches will eventually fix this game and all these negative reviews can be switched for positive ones, BioShock deserves that much and if the players are giving this game bad reviews it's simply because we care about PC gaming, we all make PC gaming great by buying quality games and we want it to stay this way.

Egosoft. Whether or not it was intentional, I think you know that what you have released was not as advertised.
I am an avid PC gamer, and have been playing PC games since they began. I'm also an avid space sim gamer, and have enjoyed all manner of space games from back in the first Elite days. My immediate reaction is - any amount of playtesting would surely have shown some of these very basic game breaking issues - why didn't you take care of these gigantic issues *before release*? Beyond the game breaking issues, there are so many changes that would be necessary to make this a game that doesn't seem to be some sort of weird retro alpha project stuck in the mid-90s, that I don't feel right about paying you with my hard earned money to attempt a belated fix for something that, frankly, may simply need to be scrapped and redone to even approach a mediocre product. Alot of people are blaming Capcom, but Marvel studios had just as big a hand (if not bigger) in the poor design.  Outside of the game being rushed and spending too much time on the story mode, the roster itself is enough of a turn off for alot of people.  I've already seen several people (including myself) having a hard time picking two characters to main, which shouldn't be difficult with a 30 character roster (which isn't that much smaller than Vanilla Marvel 3's Roster).
Only six new characters, with the rest being reused from Marvel 3, which don't even include fan favorite characters like Pheonix Wright, Viewtiful Joe, and Wesker  (not even mentioning the lack of X-men and Doctor Doom because of Disney's Pettiness).  Apparently they thought Firebrand, Spencer, and Nemesis were better choices.  The Marvel side is also exclusively MCU characters (either being in movies, tv shows, or movies-in-production), including the new characters, and 3 marvel dlc characters you get with the deluxe edition once they come out.  Marvel also got 4 of the six new characters in the base roster, and 4 of the first 6 dlc characters, which is extremely concerning, especially since one of the two DLC capcom characters is one of the main villains of the story mode.  It just doesn't make sense to me since Capcom took advantage of the chance to make new characters and (excluding Sigma) picked characters people had been asking for.  Monster Hunter DOES have a new game coming out though so I guess she's just as much advertisement as the entire marvel side.  It especially doesn't help that between Chris Redfield, Frank West, Gamora, Hawkeye, Rocket Raccoon, Winter Soldier, and Black Widow (the last two being DLC), there's alot of "dudes who just happen to carry guns, or arrows, or whatever" characters, not even mentioning Spencer and his boring kit revolving around a grappling hand.
The story mode is....an attempt at having some characters bounce off each other, but there isn't really enough interesting here to recommend either, except to unlock stages.  out of the 39 fights, 20 are against generic jobber characters, there's a fair number of fights that are 2v1 or 1v1, Thanos (not the main villain) is made to look like he's a super cool bad guy in an attempt to advertise the movies (even fighting the main villain in a one on one fight and doing better than everyone else did fighting one at the same time), you play as Captain America six times but don't play Zero at all (you play Zero, Zero times), it takes to the last hour before you can any infinity stones (the game's main gimmick besides Active Switch) and there's zero fights that are a two vs two fight where both sides have a stone (which is how all matches in the rest of the game, including arcade mode that has no character endings, are played).  It's not even worth looking up online.  You'd be better off looking at Project X Zone's story and you might get a laugh there.
Anyone who is playing this game are either lucky enough to have their mains on the roster, or enjoy the gameplay immensely.  Alot of people have been having fun with the game with how open ended comboing is with the tagging, but even with easy comboes and hypers, you'll have a better time if you are a bigger fighting game fan just so you can experiment a bit more, plus its hard for me to get into just because I don't have people I want to devote my time into.  It doesn't help the DLC is going to be 8 bucks a character (meaning the first 3 will be 24 bucks together, and the first 6 is more than half the price of the game).  It doesn't help this game has been hacked already and (so I've heard) you'll see people playing doubles of the same character or playing the boss character (Ultron Sigma) online.
I would not recommend getting this game at full price at all, especially if you aren't a fan of fighting games.  Wait and see if it goes on sale, and only get it if the gameplay looks really interesting to you, and if the roster has been improved massively somehow through cheaper dlc or the like.  You'll have a better time playing older Marvel vs Capcom games.  I don't think this game will get an "Ultimate version" but this is the only game I've ever seen where people are going "man, I hope they re-release this game in 8 months with a bunch of new characters".
