No I wouldn't recommend this game to anyone unless they were looking for exactly this type of game.  It can be fun, but it's one of those games you have to repeatedly start over on until you figure out the basics that should have been explained in the tutorial level.
Couple of things you might wanna know before hand.
The default harvester only works on wheat, barley and canola.  Everything else requires EXPENSIVE items that you can't afford from the shop.  No one will warn you against planting other things, but you can do it just as easily as anything else.
The '8' key speeds up time, the '7' key slows down time.  Note that construction will not happen faster if you do this.  It will only make the crops grow faster and animals produce faster.
You don't have to buy any animal pastures, you own them all by default on every map.  To buy animals go to the shop which can be found on the map when you hit the '9' key.  The animals are hidden away in the far right of the shop's menu.
Try not to sell any crops until their prices have gone up.  Only keep an above negative budget in the meantime.
buy chickens as soon as possible.  They're a nice easy source of income early in the game.  Apparently, you don't actually see all the chickens you purchased in the coop but they're there.  They produce more eggs as a result of there being more of them.  Even though you can't see more chickens...

I'm a huge fan of survival and rogue-like games. Challenge and realism is what I look for in a good survival game.
Now, before I buy a game, I always look at the bad reviews first (which this game only had a couple in relation to the reverse amount of positive reviews) and make a decision. Most of the bad reviews, from what I can tell, are people who were expecting a game that it wasn't. They blame the stealth system or the repetitivness or that they can't explore more than what the devs wrote into the game. While some of this I can see validity and give them some credit, most of the bad reviews taste a little like "rage-quit".
Seeing how I was already interested just from the video (and the music with it right?) I decided to buy it and play it for myself... I was NOT disappointed.
The game does indeed, in my opinion, lack content. But don't let that deter you! This game is really fun and addicting. The devs had a great idea and made it into something that could have a great sequel or some good DLC. The graphics are perfect for giving you that feeling of depression. Every decision I made in the game was a drastic one. But when I finally got one of the two ending achievments, i've never felt so accomplished. Took numerous playthroughs but the feeling of surviving is great. I can now say I am in the 1% of people who have that achievment.
So I'll go over some quick pros and cons before I close out.
Pros:
- Great ambience and graphics (music, art, sounds)
- Balanced, yet challenging loot and crafting system
- Great character and story development
Cons:
- Its a little high priced for how much content there is. (but you won't NOT have fun, I promise)
- The stealth system IS in fact a little flawed. But I don't want to hear any excuses. Surving in real life would be harder than beating this game, so suck it up. I did it in 24 total hours and only got ONE of the two endings.
All-in-all I had a really good time with this game. I'd like to see some DLC or a sequel sometime though. I'd definitely buy them. Remeber, if you don't like survival or rogue-like games, this game is NOT for you.
Happy gaming!

A New Beginning is one of my least favorite point-and-click adventure games I've played so far.  Here is why:
I went into this game with fairly high expectations... I grew up with Lucasarts classics like Indiana Jones & the Fate of Atlantis, Sam & Max: Hit the Road, Full Throttle, Day of the Tentacle, and others.  I want to make it clear though, that I'm not saying all adventure games should be like a Lucasarts title in order to satisfy me... for example two of the more recent ones I've played are called "Lost Horizon" and "Primordia" which I thought were both very well executed too.
The first reason I don't recommend this particular game is because it felt unpolished to me.  There were numerous spelling errors in the speech captions, and in some cases the captions appeared in a different language entirely!  When this happened it was sometimes linked to missing audio dialogue too (I played this game in English) where the character would keep moving their mouth but it would just be silent.  These seem like things that are simple to catch and fix through a single round of QA testing.  Since the missing speech only happened a couple of times, this is a relatively minor problem I guess... but still left me thinking "really, guys??"
The main reason I didn't like the game, and this is going to be more subjective of course, is due to the story and interface.  A lot of the interactive items in the game were not particularly intuitive to find.  This made me feel frustrated in my inability to pass certain areas just because I forgot to move my mouse over a particular part of the screen at some point.  Yes, I know this is how point-and-click adventure style games work... but a little more intuitiveness in the solutions is always nice.  Unlike progressing to the next area, the actual interactive puzzles (e.g. rewiring a console) can all be skipped if you can't figure them out, and those I actually found much more enjoyable!  I just wish there were more than a half dozen of them in the whole game.
Story-wise, I found the narrative to be intruging and interesting for most of the game, but then right at the end there is a twist that is very baffling and left me wondering if everything I'd heard up until that point was even true at all, or all part of some confusing web of lies.  Sadly, this twist is not explained in the least bit, the game just ends with a short cutscene.  (Speaking of cutscenes, the animation in them was very oddly edited so the pacing just felt kinda off and "slowed down" even in very dramatic moments.)  Now, I'm okay with endings that are semi-good and semi-bad... but this one just felt like it was leading me along by a leash in a big circle only to get back to the beginning and say "just kidding, we weren't really going anywhere after all!"  Needless to say, I was disappointed.
At the time of writing this review, I have still yet to play the Deponia series that comes from the same game developer as A New Beginning, so I'm hoping those titles are a bit more enjoyable.
Things I enjoyed about A New Beginning:  the artwork, the interactive puzzles, and the story (at least up until the confusing ending).

over all a solid game from a mechanical point of view. the only mechanical draw back "if you want to call it a drawback" is while each faction does have a personality the basic mechanics beyond a few key points are identical to the other factions, the basic ship, the siege ship, the carrier ship etc etc all work the same way.
compare to say other rts games like starcraft each faction and their units are unique in how they approach a function or role in combat. in Sins you have the same core mechanics and approach to roles uniform across the board. This makes the game easier to transition from faction to faction with only a general style change with a few key talents to take into account however it does reduce replay appeal.
the game does have a cool lore but lacks a single player story driven campaign which to some will be a drawback.

GIMME SHELTER
-You are the mother of a group of badger pups. It's your job--nay, DUTY--to keep these babies alive. You have to feed them and protect them from the elements and an evil bird of prey.
-The main game is very short, about an hour, and it features a linear narrative. The badger family goes through danger after danger. Not everyone necessarily makes it in one piece, either. Yes, the pups can die.
-This is true survival horror.
-The story lacks any words and uses cutscenes very minimalistically, yet it tells a very compelling story. Survival is a key theme here, but it goes beyond this in ways I probably shouldn't reveal. It speaks for itself. It's a simple, yet mentally satisfying story.
-The music sets a peaceful ambience when it needs to, but also knows how to keep you on your toes for the more thrilling sections. Great soundtrack.
-After you beat the game there is an optional mode called "Nurture." I did not play it myself, but evidently it's a more arcade version of the main game. Instead of following a story, you focus entirely on feeding the pups for an unknown number of days.
FINAL VERDICT
-I don't know if it's really worth the asking price, but I would certainly recommend it on sale. Just make sure you know what you're getting into before purchasing. The story is the meat of this game and it's only about an hour long. Sure, there is a bonus mode you could play for hours, but I don't think the gameplay itself warrants continued play. While the controls are fine--minimal, but satisfying enough--they aren't enough for me to want to play the non-story variant. I would love to play more if there was another story involved, but otherwise I can't see myself coming back to this one. If you want to explore a good example of minimalistic storytelling in video games, I would recommend Shelter.

Very exciting team-based gameplay. Major emphasis on action/reaction. It's a good brawler, with lots of outplay potential, a very high skill ceiling, and a moderate skill floor. I have a lot of fun with it. There are a multitude of playstyles that are enhanced through Battlerites, and the development team have been actively balancing and rebalancing as required. There are ranked and unranked modes, and the developers have been toying with secondary game modes, such as the Easter event of Bakko's Egg Brawl.
Battlerites are modifications to your abilities, three choices presented per round; these can be as simple as making an ability do a little more damage, or adding a new mechanic to one of your existing skills, or introducing a debuff to another ability. Some Battlerites are a bit underwhelming on their respective tiers, but are overall well balanced to allow the player to make dynamic choices on a round-by-round basis. Sometimes you need control, sometimes you need utility, and sometimes you can do it with a bit more damage.
As the game is in Early Access, the balance sometimes shifts in directions that I don't personally agree with, but overall, it's a fun, competitive game. You can most certainly play it alone or with friends, and I enjoy playing it fairly casually (in the Casual queue).
It is a MOBA in the truest sense; Multiplayer Online Battle Arena. It's not a Dotalike.

This game gets my vote for the most disappointing game of 2014. This was supposed to be the spritual successor to Alpha Centarui. What we got was a Civilization V beta with a sci-fi mod and trade route simulator. It's like Firaxis chose to ignore everything that distinguished Alpha Centauri from Civilization.
Being able to mod your units with newly discovered technology? Gone. Replaced by upgrades via affinities (your philisophical path to conquest). That's extremely lazy game design. Diplomacy? Just as useless and barebones as it was in Civ V when it was launched. Even worse. The other faction leaders are just cardboard cutouts without unique personalities. Yet another step backwards from Alpha Centauri. And be prepared to hear about something you did that another faction leader didn't like for at least a couple hundred turns as you promise yet again that you won't attack anymore trade stations, for the tenth time. And did I mention trade routes? Yeah, have fun managing them all. Culture doesn't serve any strategic purpose other than to learn virtues. The tech web isn't at all intuitive and seems fairly directionless and the wonders are confusing to distinguish from the techs and gained abilities at first. I'm all for new gameplay concepts, except for when they're poorly implemented.
Furthermore, you'll be browsing the mods list and wondering to yourself, "Why weren't these included in the game?" I'm sure like Civ V, the issues will be ironed out with the expansion packs, but that's hardly the point. To take a storied, classic franchise like Civilization and turn it into a glorified crowd-funding project is just shameful. If you must own this game, hold off for the inevitable "Gold Version" which will include the base game and expansion pack(s).
You're better off playing the original. It's more likely to run correctly.

Do not buy this... abomination. It will be months, maybe even years before all of the glitches, bugs, Artificial Intelligence, framerate, and interface issues get resolved, if ever. Bugs can be patched, AI can be fixed, but even then, the game still might not be salvagable. It is the core design choices built into the game itself that is the real problem.
1) The entire UI needs to be completely scrapped and redone from the ground up. It is just that bad.
2) The System:Sector:Zone map scheme is absurdly frustrating, to say the least.
3) Nearly all of the gameplay elements Egosoft has spent years introducing, refining, and polishing in the X series have been scrapped. No more SETA to speed up tedious portions, no more jumpdrive in the ship you actually pilot, no more autopilot, no more sector/universal traders, no more realtime monitoring of commodity prices using a satellite network, no more customizable keybinding, no more hotkeys to cycle through targets (you literally have to click on a ship w/ your cursor to highlight them and get aim-assist).
As many others have said before me, this simply isn't an 'X' game. They should have called it 'Y'. As in Y the hell would anyone play this?
It pains me to write this. I know Egosoft is comprised a a dedicated bunch who have a long history of commitment to thier customers. Few companies come to mind that are as noble as Egosoft when it comes to taking thier fanbase seriously. I want to extend them every benefit of the doubt, but good intentions will only go so far. This game, right now, as of November 25, 2013, is complete garbage. Complete garbage produced over a 7 year period a team with years of experience designing space-sims who really really REALLY should have known better.
Here's to hoping the modding community can fix what Egosoft has broken. My heart.

I highly recommend this game for those who enjoy indie games for the same reason I do: a unique experience. I think it would be a mistake to view this game purely as a game, and not also as a (I imagine) realistic simulation of civilian life in a war-torn city. I found it evoking emotion in a way that few games do. Where most games are about twitch-speed timing and driving up adrenalin, this one is about tense survival and moral choices. The graphics are grimly beautiful, the gameplay intuitive, and the mechanics of the game fit the scenario very well.
Who would want to buy it: Those for whom story is more important than winning, since if you are immersed in this game you won't think of it as trying to win but as trying to survive. By the end of it you may very well walk away with a changed view of war and public policy.
Those who may not like it: The game is heavy on atmosphere, and it seems to me it tries to be more of a simulator than a game, which may annoy gamers looking for the best angle to win. The random elements can throw off min-maxing, which may add to the frustration.
Bottom line: My first game took about 6 hours, I lasted 49 days. By the end, I was stunned; I felt I had known the 8 people who had lived and died under my control. If I never played the game again I would feel I more than got my money's worth. I think this game is a work of art.

A New Beginning tries to share a positive message about climate change, our future, and our resistance to change, but the execution leaves a lot to be desired. The game is not terrible: it has its good points, and if you've ever wanted to play a dimwitted token female with a seemingly quite severe case of scoliosis who wears a sweater that covers only her boobs, then this definitely is your game.
Pros:
+Good message
+The art is quite nice
+The ruined future setting that occurs near the start of the game is very compelling
+The support team answered my emails quickly and were very helpful when I encountered a game-breaking bug
Cons:
-The English voice acting is atrocious. If you want to play the game, set the sound the German with English subtitles - the German voice acting isn't too bad.
-The English translation is not very good. There are a lot of grammatical errors and problems with colloquialisms that really should have been caught by a native English speaking proofreader before the game was published.
-There are a lot of bugs. Mainly I encountered translation bugs: various items popping up in Russian or Spanish. I also found a game-breaking bug, however, which required a replacement save file from the support team to get past.
-Everyone moves so slowly that I found myself screaming at the monitor a few times. Quickly, we must hit that switch before the facility explodes! Now, let me just take a leisurely stroll across the room. Wouldn't want to work up a sweat.
-The game is extremely resource-heavy, and I can't figure out why. My computer heats up while running this game as much as it does while playing a modern shooter.
-Many of the puzzles are absurd. Several of them require knowledge that the average person just wouldn't have. I needed a walkthrough to get through most of it, and many times I realized I would never in a million years have thought to try the thing that ended up being necessary. There's also a fair amount of pixel-hunting for tiny items that blend in.
-Between the slow movement speed of the characters and the seemingly never-ending cutscenes and dialog, by the time I was 1/3 of the way through the game I just wanted it to end.
-The ending isn't nearly as clever as it's trying to be, and felt rather anti-climactic after all those hours of listening to people talk and watching them crawl across the screen to the sound of suspenseful music.
If you can get the game cheap, enjoy ridiculous puzzles, and have a lot of patience for slow movement and long cutscenes, then feel free to give this one a try. If you're used a faster pace or just want something you feel you can solve without a walkthrough, I'd pass this one over.

Finding a new favorite band with a wide-ranging catalogue often presents the early works question. What to do and say about the things the band recorded before finding their own style and making a breakthrough? Listening to that may present new perspectives on their best work but is that reason enough to actually try and enjoy it on its own merits? This is the question I thought often during my hours with A New Beginning, one of the first titles from my recent favorite, Daedalic Entertainment.
Many key strengths presented later are already here, particularly those related to craftsmanship. The whole of the story is well laid out and plotted, with twists all in place and the whole progressing logically throughout with interesting puzzles challenging the brain. Another trademark is the orchestral soundtrack covering a wide range of moods and emotions. And finally comes of course the hand-made art showing once again that no tesselations can ever replace the human touch.
Making parts and assembling them is one thing but then breathing life into the result is another and this is where the game sadly does not succeed. The eco-conscious bent of the story is laudable but the tone is too educational and the contrasts are simply much too black-and-white. There was no room to disagree about anything or anyone or make alternative interpretations to what the writing told me. Consequently there was an airless quality to the entire experience. No characters had enough detail to give them life beyond caricatures with calculated positions in the story (and the message). Dialogue contained many odd phrases that smack of poor translation. A grim security officer shuts off doubt with "Fiddlesticks!" and in more than one life-threatening situation "Good grief" gets used too.
These lecture-like qualities are made even drier by problems in presentation. The voice acting was of very poor quality throughout, there is simply no way around it. The entire cast managed to sound colorless as if concentrating on clear pronunciation and nothing else. The worst offender was perhaps the female lead who sounded so shrill and robotically cheerful I yearned for Lydia for the first time in my life. And while the artists did their best with the milieus there is only so much anyone can do with oil rigs and conference halls from 1982 where most of the action take place. The date makes sense from the thematic perspective but wastes the promise in the strong first chapter in the game, which happens in the future and has an interesting storytelling idea that was thrown out for the rest of the game. It is also unfortunate that while the places in this eco-thriller include Norway and Brazil the natural sights are not shown, unlike helicopter interiors or pump rooms. Overall the aesthetics are best described as having a metallic, inorganic quality to them which contrasts completely with the other Daedalic adventures I have seen so far.
Serving as the final coffin nail were many technical flaws and issues. First off, this is a game from 2010 -- without widescreen support. I had to set my screen resolution to 1024 x 768 before starting the game to avoid the black borders. Granted, the game did look good then but it was an odd thing to do regardless. The game is also littered with typos and words from other languages, including Spanish and Russian. "Grapeseed oil" without the G was the most unintentionally chilling typo I have seen in quite some time.
I wanted to like A New Beginning and it actually feels a bit unfair to lay out so much criticism to an indie adventure made with very limited resources. But no matter what the comparison, the genre classics, contemporary games from other studios or other Daedalic adventures, A New Beginning falls short and cannot truly be enjoyed on its own either. I gained more insight than pleasure from my gametime and would recommend others interested in the genre to look at other options instead. Early demos or shaky debuts from good and great bands may find their way into record collections on the strength on their other albums but cannot truly be recommended to those without fan powers.

Even though there is a huge amount of bad opinions for this game, I still decided to buy it, and play it. I finished it without getting all achievements because I'm sure I'll play the game again one day. Here are my thoughts on overall quality of Final Fantasy XIII:
When I first started playing this game, I felt just the same confusion as with every other game in the series. I had no idea what it's all about, and I only knew that I'm controlling Lightning, and a black dude with a chicken is following me. Just like all FF titles before, FF13 revealed the plot much later, and assembled a gallery of very interesting characters. A couple of plot-holes here and there are something Final Fantasy players are already used to, so I can't say everything is perfect. If you have ever played (and liked) any of the Final Fantasy games' stories, you'll like this one as well.
The graphics are awesome, and beautiful. The wide variety of monsters, enemies and bosses is great, and the main characters, as well as all others, are well designed and interesting.
I've read a lot about stuttering and graphics-related problems online, but I had no such problems while playing in 1080p maxed out.
Music is not as spectacular as a FF-fan would expect, but it's still not bad. It just seems a little... poor.
On the upside, voice acting is great, so we can easily forget about weird and awkward scenes like the HAHAHAHA scene form Final Fantasy X!
If you like using a controller, you'll hate the game in the first couple of hours. It doesn't support many controllers, so the mappings are a little weird, but you can easily get used to them. A big con is that the game didn't any re-mapping options. It's okay, but I can imagine many players get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥as hell because of this.
So, to come to the conclusion:
Final Fantasy XIII is a wonderful game, with lots of gameplay, missions, interesting characters, mediocre music, and bad gamepad-controls. Whoever said it's a bad game, or a bad port should stick to Call of Duty, because this is no game for them.
Personally, I liked it, and I'll most definitely play it again.

This game totally caught me by surprise. It started with a cliche about saving the world and I thought it was going to be one of those dull sci-fi plots but as the story progressed, a lot of issues were explored with regards to that theme. The costs and consequences of our actions on the environment, the triggers needed to make us change our habits, and the ethos of different minded-individuals were questioned. The dramatics were well played out; the soundtrack compliments each scene perfectly, the build-ups to climatic events were exciting, and the graphics were outstanding in their details -- the images used had the right angles and impacts on the viewer. The game mechanics are simple, based on interactions with the environment through point-and-click. The challenging part of the game is more of its mental aspect. You have to use a bit of logic and maintain a lot of awareness of your environment or else you will miss out items or tasks integral to the story's progress. What I really like about this visual novel is its comic-styled graphics. It's like seeing a comic book played out in motion to you during its cut scenes and it places you in the comic book world when you are playing the game. Aside from a few subtitle errors and delays as well as frustrations that come with figuring things out, this game is a great puzzle action game. Also, it helps that you can skip some of the mind-boggling puzzles. You can get Steam achievements out of succeeding them as well as skipping them. Is it replayable? If you are an achievement-♥♥♥♥♥, then yes, there are things to play for so make multiple saves at various points if you do not wish to go back to the beginning all over again. If not, once is enough, which is about the only other discouragement from getting the game.

I don't get what other people were seeing in this. I don't hate it, I just don't recommend it to others.
Shelter is a game where you are a mother badger escorting 5 smaller badgers to a different part of the forest. But Oh No! There are foxes, hawks, fires, floods, and more along the journey.
The game begins with only 4 cubs and a grey one that appears dead on the floor. Without tutorial, you're supposed to know that to proceed you need to feed the baby badger a root. This never comes up again and it feels needless.
After that, you proceed to learn how to get food (which you already did), how to hide, how to bark, and why you should hide.
The problem is that's about it. The entire game is basically the tutorial portion repeated a few times.
You'll find yourself in several hawk chase scenes and they just don't feel tense after the first one because its just the same scenerio over and over. The hawk squaks ever time you walk out of the grass, regardless of where it's shadow is and you "just" make it every time.
My other problem with this game is that for a baby escort game, there's a lot of times where you'll find yourself saying "Why did my baby die this time?"
Additionally, the gamma here is horrendous. Everything looks like your screen's blacklight is malfunctioning, but there's no way to change the visual settings. On top of that, there's a number of graphical glitches, such as floating trees and the camera constantly clipping or otherwise being annoying.
I didn't even feel particularly sad when my baby badgers died because at first I thought it was scripted and since I'm not controling them, I have no ability to stop them from getting ?eaten by an owl? or swooped up by a hawk. For that reason, I don't even understand the "crying into a pillow" meme that litters the positive review section.

Many LotR fans might expect a slow-paced, narrative-heavy, immersive experience. War in the North however just gives you a middle-earthy vignette or a short stay in a very stripped down Bree, Imladris, etc. to provide you with weapon repairs, a shop, and an excuse to leave said location after ten minutes or less. Thus the equipped, we meet the meat of the game, a very linear romp through dungeons, moors, forests etc. where our job is to whack everything we meet. That's it. It's actually quite fun, but in a "a drink and a laugh" (ideally with up to two mates in co-op mode) way more than in a "curled up with a book and an unending sense of wonder" way, if that makes any sense. The game feels extremely arcade-y, from graphics to linearity to gameplay. (To actually put it in a real arcade, they'd have to turn the RPG-y clickable dialogs into cut scenes, and that'd be it.)
Mechanics: The game has three main characters (dwarven "warrior", human "ranger", elven "wizard"), of which the latter is a woman. Each character has their own skill tree. Characters that don't have a human player are controller by the AI (so if you play solo, you'll play in a group of three with two computer-controlled characters). The looks of your avatar can be edited (if you manage to find a mirror in-game, of which there are at least two), but the editor is very basic (a handful of attributes with six or so values each (hair color, face shape, eye color, hairdo -- in fact, that may be it already).
The game caters to the casual gamer. The combat system provides for some token variation without being complicated, and it's nigh impossible to get lost in the levels. If you only get to play once a  week, no problem, it's not like you could forget the current quest ("follow the path, kill everything"). The player characters are never really fleshed out in terms of backstory, so that's another thing you can't forget, and the story is pretty straight forward. Easy mode actually is easy. The game works nicely with a 360 controller. I can't speak to the other two classes, but the "loremaster" (wizard) skill tree had a sufficient amount of sane options.
Gameplay for the most part is quite fluid, though confusingly, WitN introduces a variety of game elements early on (while you're still learning the ropes and what to expect from the world; there is no out-and-out tutorial level) that are never picked up again later -- there's a side-quest that will timeout and fail if you do too many other things before completing that quest, but it seems to be the only one that does that. There are "mines" in the very first location that we're taught can be used to break large structures in the environment, except that we never see the mines again later on, and there's pretty much 0 interaction with the superstructure for the rest of the game. Another early level has a "find the key to progress through this door" situation, but again, it's the only time that happens in the entire game. (To add insult to injury, this happens after we've been taught for a good while what chests look like in the game -- only for the key to be in the sole chest in the game that looks different. Specifically, it looks like a slab of stone or a sarcophagus or what not. Also, it's in the darkest part of the dungeon, so, good luck not running past it.) Mind, those things are not so much a nuisance as they are puzzling. Had they planned to have more content to that effect? Was QC asleep? What was going on? :)
Long story short, if you like fantasy and would like to solo or co-op through linear levels of a fantasy world that happens to nominally be MiddleEarth (it's much easier to believe the Middle-Earth part during the interludes; the action/arcade sequences feel like they could be anything), go for it. It's a nice, uncomplicated, casual game. If you're more the RPG/adventure type or expect deep immersion or generally feel like Tolkien is serious business, you may wish to give this game a pass.
Bought for $1.99 or so during Steam Sale, which, seeing as I completed the game, made it an excellent buy. Buy at $4.99 or better. It may only be worth full price to big LotR fans -- ones who are OK with the premise of an arcade-y game, and one where you don't play a character from the books.

This is the sixth iteration of the Duels of the Planeswalkers (DOTP) franchise produced by stainless. It's a port of the Magic the Gathering (MtG) card game which has been going strong for over 20 yrs with its tactical complexity and constant reinvention.
Previous versions of DOTP were excellent ways to teach new players the game and had a prettier, reasonably intutiive interface than the other way to play online magic (magic the gathering online). The game assumes no prior MtG experience and launches you straight into tutorial mode that takes well over an hour. Unfortunately for people who may already have a basic grasp of the rules, the tutorial campaign is unskippable and for me seemed like a grind/ waste of this time.
The single player campaign is a bit hit and miss. Basically there are 5 planeswalkers, each with their own 'campaign' mode of 5 matches with an evolving deck of cards. What determines the quality of the matches is the quality of the decks provided. The first campaign is the tutorial. Jace and Nyssa's campaigns are as dull as ditchwater. Chandra and Lilliana's campaigns are interesting in the way the play but are very short. In fact the single player aspect of this game can be completed in less than 4hours. After this you will spend time customising your decks (think of each card of 60 as an individual weapon in your arsenal) to take online against other people and duel.
From the start of the duels franchise, there have been minor bugs mainly revolving around netcode, internet lobbies for online matches and matchmaking. Stainless rewrote some of the code in the last 2 yrs for mobile platforms such as iOS and rather than addressing previous issues, FUBARed multiplayer for PC users. This new version is no different - on release, the game needs to be 'always on' (connected to the internet servers) to progress and let the game keep track of cards you've acquired. Except the servers have dropped out at least 6 times in the last few hrs, denying the ability to save progress for me.
Matchmaking remains poor - they've gotten rid of the internet lobby, relying solely on 'quick match.' Except the game tries to connect you to games which are already full. It can take 5 mins of clicking just to find a game to play. Given that MtG is meant to be a challenging, competitive deck building game, the ability to duel online is meant to be the biggest draw. Poor exection leads me to warn people away from this version despite dedicating hours to the paper version.
After taking a play mode out of the last version, 2-headed giant mode makes a return (effectively 2 teams of 2 play against each other). I've enjoyed previous versions of this as it let me play with people such as my brother in a coop manner. Except that when joining with a friend and then trying to find a game against 2 random opponents, the game keeps dropping out with multiple errors. It's not just me- in its current state it appears that it is near impossible to team up with a friend and have an online game in 2HG which is a major step back from duels 2013/duels 2014. Removing the chat also defeats the object of teamplay
The elephant in the room also needs to be pointed out. 2 yrs ago, Blizzard released Hearthstone which is also a 'free to play' online card game. It was designed as a computer game with the bells and wistles of animations, sounds and interactive elements on the board. It may not have quite the depth of MtG but it's visually more appealing and doesn't have anyway near the number bugs or issues with matchmaking that Magic Duels has. An unfortunate disappointment.
Broken & Buggy:
While some elements have been streamlined and are more fun than previous entries in the franchise (combat, maneuvering, traveling), the amount of commonly reproduced game-breaking bugs stop that. Launch bugs are to be expected, but this is equivalent to an early beta/access game - which this is not identified as. Required tutorial story line missions are stuck in a broken state that can't progress. Saving the game sometimes crashes and destroys progress. Basic issues that should have been caught haven't been - walk in front of a scripted robot cleaning the wall? Get pushed through the wall. Stand in front of a vent and open it? The grate lifts you, sticks you to the wall above it, and disables you from closing it. Sometimes, while looking at the ship's in-cockpit UI, the UI becomes non-interactive and can't be left.
Awkward:
Even for a game in the X franchise, this has the poorest usability of the series. Somehow, the focus on immersion lost out to having a decent, playable game. Having to wait for length animations for basic functionality that a player would do often adds to the tedium for the sake of immersion. Despite being in-space, navigation involves entering an animation where the character pushes back, rotates his seat, and waits for a display to activate. During this, the game world is active, so don't count on quickly breaking from navigation to defend your self. Accept a mission to pick up and transport a passenger? Dock and hoof it through repetitive hallways to that duplicated, shoddy model of the passenger, talk to them (without skipping dialogue), wait through their boarding cutscene, then hoof it or teleport to your ship. Want to ask an NPC for directions to a drone trader? Talk to them, press a dozen keys to navigate through multi-level, multi-paged sets of dialogue options in a Mass Effect style dialogue wheel, 6 at a time (4 + "More" + "Back"), until you find Drone Trader, so that NPCs can randomly decline to inform you *after* you've went through 20 - 30 seconds of this UI to hear a snide rejecting remark. The cut for entering the cockpit of your ship teleports from one side of the ship to the next with no fade - akward and unpolished. While entering the seat, the seat animation seems to be mirrored for your copilot so that she flails and rotates in an inhuman fashion. All of this you must bear each and every time you do so and there is no option to skip.
Really wanted to love this - played previous entries in the franchise, played Eve-Online, played Freelancer, played Strike Suit Zero, supporting Star Citizen - but this is a very poor release and very, very poorly designed for any target audience. What would be immersive is just tedious, distracting, and counters any immersion with glaring flaws.

Pros:
+Subtle approach to story telling, TWoM can envoke emotional responses without lengthy cut-scenes or tedious dialog exchanges.
+ Randomization, the characters, loot, locations, events, and even temperature will be slightly* different on subsequent playthroughs.
+ Difficulty, keeping your characters alive requires alot, balancing hunger, sickness, wounds and depression is difficult and often you will be forced to make sacrifices.
Cons:
- Poor PC Controls, the game was certainly made for touch screens and the PC version relies heavily on emulating the touch controls.  This is very akward in combat, when the mouse is used make the character move, take cover, and attack.
- Lazy save system, the game autosaves every morning and there's no way to save during the day or night, if you quit any time before completing the nightly scavenging you will have to replay the entire day.  There is also only one save slot, starting a new game overwrites the existing one.
- Economy balance, TWoM features a fluctuating economy, item values go up and down based on events, it's meant to work a bit like the stock market (buy low, sell high).  But attempting to play the market this way is fruitless, vendors hardly care about an item's market value, instead many vendors have an unrealisticly strong desire for specific items (one piece of wood can get you almost anything from the priest, one moonshine will get anything at the hotel, etc.).
- *Predictable, while the randomization seperates TWoM from the typical scripted and linear games, it's still a bit shallow.  Most locations have 1 or 2 variants (often a variant with friendly NPCs, and one with hostile NPCs), there are about a dozen playable characters of which 3 are randomly chosen at the start, but their stats are always the same (Bruno is always a cook and a smoker, Katia is always good at bargaining and drinks coffee, etc.).  This is enough to make each playthrough slightly different, but hardly surprising.
Summary: The concept and story telling are fantastic, but the mechanics lack polish.  Given the price and replayablity I would recomend this to fans of survival and resource managment games.

Since I'm not a big fan of Diablo, I usually tend to ignore hack-n-slash games. I decided to play Torchlight however after I got it for free with a gaming magazine and it really took me by surprise.
The game has a great artistic direction and a cartoonish design as well as a great soundtrack that adds a lot to the fairytale feeling.
It features 3 classes (Alchemist/Destroyer/Vanquisher) and a gameplay very similar to the one we've seen in Diablo I / II, with a few interesting additions. Among those, one that I found very helpful is the fact that every hero has it's own pet that can sell/buy things for you, as well as the possibility to teach your pet spells and use rings, amulets and collars to give it different abilities.
The game also allows you to learn spells and to fish (normal fishing as well as dynamite fishing). Every fish has special properties and it can be used to transform your pet into various creatures with different abilities.
And if the standard game is no good for you, you can use interesting mods to make it the way you like.
Unfortunately it has a big downside: Torchlight seams to be a game designed for co-op but without co-op.

I'm very sad to have to say this, but as it stands, Beyond Earth is a bland version of Civ 5 with a better tech tree and differently skinned barbarians (aka aliens).  It lacks any of the historical connection that Civ 5 has, which means the technologies are very generic.  I've never been faced with such a disconnected choice, like, do I want the generic +1 health or the +1 power building.  And half the Wonders I could not even tell what they were supposed to be at all, other than their stats.  The units suffer from an excessivly generic issue, as well.  In an attempt to simplify the various unit types, you upgrade existing units throughout the game.  Unfortunately, this leads to questions like "What was the Arbiter again?  Was that a boat, a melee infantry, or rocket artillery?"
As many have said, they retained so much of Civ 5 game that it feels like a reskin of the base game.  While that is not in of itself a bad thing (Civ 5 is great, afterall), they kept too much and what they did change, they made only modest advencements, leaving us with a overpriced, bland, generic sci-fi reskin of a popular game.

Finally Wizards of the Coast finding the right mix between building your own deck from the scratch, a good variety of cards and a fair rewardsystem.
The business model is the same like Hearthstone. You have a free trading card game with a nice tutorial and campaign (the campaign is pretty short but nice for a free-to-play game). After that you spend your time playing against AI or real players - for every win you get around 15-20gold. Plus you have daily quests that give you an extra 40 gold. Every 150 gold you can buy a booster with 6 new cards.
The possibilities to create various decks are really nice. Much better than in Magic 2015! Because everyone becomes different powerfull cards from the boosters and builds his/her deck around that cards you play against many different decks (till now I didnt find a overpowered combination that dominates the meta - but this can change in the future). You also have a season rank system, so new players are not matched with more experience ones.
The only thing Wizards of the Coast has to do now is releasing more new cards, so you get more and more combinations and new decks with the time. And maybe giving more gold for quests (but then no one would buy the boosters for real money^^).
So after all - this might be the best game of the duals of the planeswalkers game series!

And then I actually played it... for an hour... then I went back to Civ V and I haven't touched this game since.
Right off the bat, Beyond Earth simply doesn't feel as polished as the last game and it really pains me to say so. The menu screens are confusing and hard to explore, the environments are bland and relatively dull, and the leader's of the other civilizations you encounter are about as charismatic as Gordon Brown. The whole thing feels like a massive step-back in the franchise with the only positive point I can award it is the introduction of the "Affinity" system.
I know I haven't got to see and indulge in everything it has to offer, but loading this game up feels like a chore. I feel as if I'm going to have to drag myself through the campaign just for the sake of beating it at least once, and I probably will do that some day soon... but the game is just so disengaging and uninviting I can't find the energy to do it right now.
Perhaps when some DLC comes out it may be worth playing, as for now I'm sticking to Civ V.

*Please note that this review was written a few days after launch*
I had high hopes for this game. I really did.
I used to play magic a lot a few years back, but after moving I sorta fell out of it. For the last few months I've been an avid hearthstone player, so when I heard that wizards was introducing their own free to play online MTG game, I got really excited - I saw it as my chance to catch up and get back into the game without having to spend an arm and a leg.
Maybe I should have though.
The lower levels are filled with players who've dumped real cash on building their perfect decks - no way they've acquired collections like this so early into the games launch - which basically turns versus mode into an ordeal even at the very lowest rank. That is if you even get into a game -  90% of the time you're going to get an error message when you try to find an opponent, and will have to try again.
Oh, and also, your connection to the servers can best be described as "fleeting". Oftentimes you'll have to repeatedly try to reconnect to get back on (you're able to play offline, but if you do so you'll get no gold, which is required to get new cards), and you'll probably lose it after the next game you play (oh, and you'll want to hammer reconnect after this happens too - if you win a match and then get disconnected, you'll lose that gold unless you reconnect before going back to the main menu).
There's also issues with the timers. The amount of time the stop timer gives you to press it is WAY too short, and sometimes it simply -doesn't actually work-. I've lost games because I wasn't able to play my instant at the appropriate time because I wasn't able to actually stop play to use it.
Similar to hearthstone, the game offers you daily quests. So far all of my dailies have been "Archetype" quests, where you have to create a deck using the deck wizard (a tool that helps you build a deck from a template, as opposed to building one from scratch) to create one of two decks and then win so many games with it. The problem is, the deck wizard forces you to pick among set groups of cards and has NO idea how to build a good deck. Using it I often find myself begging it to just let me throw in this card or that, but the wizard simply doesn't give you the option, so I end up having to pick a card I don't want to run. These decks are very rarely good enough to be played against another human being - luckily you can at least complete these archetype quests against the AI.
The encouraging thing is occasionally there's a glimmer of hope. Sometimes I get matched with an opponent who's actually along my skill level, things don't break, and we can play a really interesting game. When this happens the game actually feels really fun, and you're reminded why the underlying game that duels is based on is so great. Maybe once they start fixing things there'll be more of these moments and less of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
If you've been considering playing this one, I recommend you wait it out for at least a few weeks, then check in again to see if they've fixed some of the problems with this game. As it is now, I honestly couldn't recommend it - I honestly feel like they've done a pretty poor job with this game's launch and the few fun moments aren't enough to justify all of the aggrevation.

An unfortunate disappointment.
Broken & Buggy:
While some elements have been streamlined and are more fun than previous entries in the franchise (combat, maneuvering, traveling), the amount of commonly reproduced game-breaking bugs stop that. Launch bugs are to be expected, but this is equivalent to an early beta/access game - which this is not identified as. Required tutorial story line missions are stuck in a broken state that can't progress. Saving the game sometimes crashes and destroys progress. Basic issues that should have been caught haven't been - walk in front of a scripted robot cleaning the wall? Get pushed through the wall. Stand in front of a vent and open it? The grate lifts you, sticks you to the wall above it, and disables you from closing it. Sometimes, while looking at the ship's in-cockpit UI, the UI becomes non-interactive and can't be left.
Awkward:
Even for a game in the X franchise, this has the poorest usability of the series. Somehow, the focus on immersion lost out to having a decent, playable game. Having to wait for length animations for basic functionality that a player would do often adds to the tedium for the sake of immersion. Despite being in-space, navigation involves entering an animation where the character pushes back, rotates his seat, and waits for a display to activate. During this, the game world is active, so don't count on quickly breaking from navigation to defend your self. Accept a mission to pick up and transport a passenger? Dock and hoof it through repetitive hallways to that duplicated, shoddy model of the passenger, talk to them (without skipping dialogue), wait through their boarding cutscene, then hoof it or teleport to your ship. Want to ask an NPC for directions to a drone trader? Talk to them, press a dozen keys to navigate through multi-level, multi-paged sets of dialogue options in a Mass Effect style dialogue wheel, 6 at a time (4 + "More" + "Back"), until you find Drone Trader, so that NPCs can randomly decline to inform you *after* you've went through 20 - 30 seconds of this UI to hear a snide rejecting remark. The cut for entering the cockpit of your ship teleports from one side of the ship to the next with no fade - akward and unpolished. While entering the seat, the seat animation seems to be mirrored for your copilot so that she flails and rotates in an inhuman fashion. All of this you must bear each and every time you do so and there is no option to skip.
Really wanted to love this - played previous entries in the franchise, played Eve-Online, played Freelancer, played Strike Suit Zero, supporting Star Citizen - but this is a very poor release and very, very poorly designed for any target audience. What would be immersive is just tedious, distracting, and counters any immersion with glaring flaws.

I really did enjoy this game. I love the Tolkein universe and I think the idea of the story running parallel to the story from the Lord of the Rings Trilogy worked well here. Do not expect an RPG experience, this is much more of a hack and slash, and there are many moments that break the 'immersion' of an RPG game (randomly buying items, mid level, from a floating pool of light, etc.).
Story/Presentation: 6/10
Agandaur, a high ranking commander of Sauron's forces is marching to destroy the north, and you must stop him. That is the meat of the story. Whilst this is nothing original, and there are no plot twists and things to keep you guessing, it serves its job well enough. The story is fleshed out with characters from the Original LOTR story (Gandalf, Aragorn etc.) and it works well to keep to the original lore (from what I know). There
side quests, but they are sparse and sometimes hard to give a crap about. I finished many of them without even realising (found an item from killing an orc, turns out a dwarf wanted it for a quest).
I say 6/10 because as stories go, it is hard to go wrong when Tolkein has done the bulk of the work! The thing that brings this score down to me is how bland the playable characters are. There are many characters in this game that have quite interesting personas, the playable characters are not among them.
Gameplay: 5.5/10
Nothing inventive here. I played the ranger all the way through, and although the abilities that you learn (from a talent tree similar to world of warcraft), I found that most of the time you'll be mashing the attack button from start to finish. There are some AI problems, if your allies (who were clearly designed to be played by friends) see a ranged unit, they will walk slowly towards them, shooting at them, whilst melee heroes hack them to pieces. Other than that the AI is actually quite fine. I will also note here that you can 'switch character', but you lose all items from your first character unless you switch back again, so I really don't see the point. It seems like a big design flaw to me, but I had no need to change my character anyway. 5.5/10 because it serves its purpose fine, and there's a lot of gore and fun to be had, but at the end of the day its too repetitive.
Visuals: 8/10
Whilst the graphics are nothing to rave about, they are really quite good. The linearity of the game means that the surrounding environments look quite beautiful, and there has been quite a lot of effort clearly put in to the design of the scenes. I am also going to mention the gore as well, it is nice to see a bit of blood and severred limbs that is startlingly absent in almost all Lord of the Rings games. The hack and slash gameplay IS quite repetitive, but lopping heads and arms off never really gets old.
Replayability 6/10
Whilst I doubt I will play through the game again, there is the option to do so with a higher difficulty, and naturally with another player character. I think this is a nice idea, but personally I would have rather put the difficulty higher on my first playthrough, than be forced to wait until I've completed the game once. That being said, it's a nice option, and I think many will enjoy playing through again with a second character.
Conclusion: 6/10
A fun game, nothing special, but worth a play through. I don't think this game is worth a full price purchase, but if you see it on offer definitely give it a go. X: Rebirth was meant to reboot the franchise in order for it to appeal to a greater amount of players.  Egosoft meant to accomplish this by removing, fixing or adding features and streamlining them to be more accessible.  Egosoft's promises, however, proved void.
The 'X' series have always been beloved because it is virtually the only franchise that offers a complete sandbox experience in a singleplayer environment.  A massive universe with a plethora of ships to fly and opportunities to pursue made the 'X' series a behemoth in space sandboxing.  However, all this sandboxing always came with a price - a clunky, inaccessible game with a learn curve akin to a 90 degree angled wall sunked in grease and other lubricants, unfortunately doing away with most people giving the franchise a try.  Again Egosoft promised it would tackle these problems.
Hence, considering their past 15 years of experience, Egosoft was trusted that it could release the biggest, best and most accessible 'X' game to date.  Unfortunately, they couldn't have been more wrong.
In it's current state, Rebirth is an unplayable mess.  Severe lack of optimisation, horrendous UI, atrocious character models, abysmal story, game breaking bugs, feature incomplete, frequent crashes and whatnot.  If anything Rebirth is the epitome od unfinished products released to meet publisher enforced deadlines.  It's amazing (give or take) seven years Egosoft brought a very promising and well-established franchise to its knees and even more amazing is how little they achieved with Rebirth.  Not one design goal that was mentioned in their first announcement has been completed.  Trading is utterly broken and even corrupts save game files, controlling AI ships has never been more tedious - regardless of what game we're looking at - horrendous performance on high-end systems show little to no interest in the PC market.
If you have a midrange computer at your disposal most of the performance issues will not apply to you, however.
While Egosoft has done everything it can to continously patch the game and we have seen a barrage of patches come our way, this game is not worth a purchase at all.  Unfortunate as it might be and as pretty as the screenshots may be, the game is an utter and complete mess.
For those coming back as veterans of the series, Rebirth has nothing to offer but instead is a step down from the sandbox that is X2/X3.  For those coming to take a peek at the 'X' series, Rebirth could have been an excellent starting point to ease into the series, if it didn't come with so many bugs, glitches and crashes.  If anything Rebirth is not your harbour if you are coming back or if you are just starting which is unfortunate, because when and if Rebirth works it's an absolutely gorgeous game (in space) and has a lot going for it.  It's a step up from games such as Freelancer in both offering a sandbox and complete experience.  It just turned out the be not the game Egosoft or its fans were hoping it'd be.

So. Yet another survival game eh? No. Not just another survival simulation. This War of Mine takes a different approach to the survival genre, TWoM tries to convey the psychological aspect of living in a war ravaged city, you still need to collect resources, upgrade things and do all those fun OCD like things you love in this type of game, but it has a very real effect on the characters well being. Listening to a baby cry while you break down a door and steal a families food. This type of thing has an effect on your average person, and so it does in This War of Mine.
Your little band of survivors still get hungry, hurt, ill and so on, but now their actions affect group moral too. For example, i sent Katia out to do some essential looting, food, since they were all starving, so she begins looting a small house. The house belonged to an old couple who pleaded me not to rob them, but having little choice, i did so anyway, leaving a little for them. Katia returned that night and felt bad for robbing them, a couple of others felt the same way, whilst the rest thought it was a necessary evil. However 2 weeks of ingame time later, i returned to the house, due to desperate need, only to find the occupants now dead. Actually, Katia found them. So now she's feeling sad and depressed. Sleeping a lot. She blames herself for their deaths? (...Is that a twinge of empathy for a computer game character i just felt?)
This game is good at eliciting emotional responses from you. If you let it. I suggest you do, it's great at drawing you in and is more than a game, it's an experience. Excuse me, must go check and make sure Katia hasn't done anything silly. Yep. that's in there too.

I highly recommend this innovative game. It has very simple mechanics, but gets challenging fast. I really like that it as a kind of “anti-war wargame” in that the focus is on the misery of ordinary people trying to stay alive in a war-zone. The responses of the characters make you feel for their plight (if you have empathy)! You can follow your group's back-stories and root for them and even be sad if they don't make it. That appeals to a different side of gamers that is rarely tapped into. But, if you wish, you can still play it as a (very tough) stealth violence game, as inevitably many will. Just watch out for the karmic retribution if you just rob and kill indiscriminately! Though, I'd have to say the game is much tougher if you try to be a “good” person always, and it's an interesting twist that if so, your resolve to do no harm will get severely tested as conditions for your survivors get more desperate, and the temptation to steal when all else fails is a huge one. It's a very replayable game (I've “won” 3 times by surviving the war, but I'm still playing as there's lots of randomness and game content I haven't experienced yet). 10/10.

Pros:
+Subtle approach to story telling, TWoM can envoke emotional responses without lengthy cut-scenes or tedious dialog exchanges.
+ Randomization, the characters, loot, locations, events, and even temperature will be slightly* different on subsequent playthroughs.
+ Difficulty, keeping your characters alive requires alot, balancing hunger, sickness, wounds and depression is difficult and often you will be forced to make sacrifices.
Cons:
- Poor PC Controls, the game was certainly made for touch screens and the PC version relies heavily on emulating the touch controls.  This is very akward in combat, when the mouse is used make the character move, take cover, and attack.
- Lazy save system, the game autosaves every morning and there's no way to save during the day or night, if you quit any time before completing the nightly scavenging you will have to replay the entire day.  There is also only one save slot, starting a new game overwrites the existing one.
- Economy balance, TWoM features a fluctuating economy, item values go up and down based on events, it's meant to work a bit like the stock market (buy low, sell high).  But attempting to play the market this way is fruitless, vendors hardly care about an item's market value, instead many vendors have an unrealisticly strong desire for specific items (one piece of wood can get you almost anything from the priest, one moonshine will get anything at the hotel, etc.).
- *Predictable, while the randomization seperates TWoM from the typical scripted and linear games, it's still a bit shallow.  Most locations have 1 or 2 variants (often a variant with friendly NPCs, and one with hostile NPCs), there are about a dozen playable characters of which 3 are randomly chosen at the start, but their stats are always the same (Bruno is always a cook and a smoker, Katia is always good at bargaining and drinks coffee, etc.).  This is enough to make each playthrough slightly different, but hardly surprising.
Summary: The concept and story telling are fantastic, but the mechanics lack polish.  Given the price and replayablity I would recomend this to fans of survival and resource managment games.

At first, i was very much taken in. There aren't many space games anymore so it was nice to have one. The presentation of the game was nice, with voice acting for important characters, and the combat was decent (even though the controls are extremely clunky).
However, after a few hours of fun, you start noticing the many problems this game has :
- Dogfighting is almost inexistant. It's so hard to aim, you're better off using homing missiles to blast small ships.
- Since small ships are not much more than flies, you keep encountering middle-sized or big ships to make it an actual game, but the number of different ships is very limited, so the game soon gets very repetitive, blasting one big ship after another one.
- Also, the arcade gameplay means you can crash into a space station of a big ship, and you will only lose your shield, which soon regenerates. I don't ask for a strict simulation, but this is too much on the arcade side. You have no fear of big ships or close fly by, because the worst that can happen  is losing your shield temporarily
- The HUD is a complete mess. All enemies icons are the exact same red. A big ships can have 10 or even 20 icons on her, because there is one icon per gun. So unless you get way too close, you usually are never sure what the heck you're actually shooting at. You can't even make out the difference between a fighter and a gun of a capital ship.
- The sound effects are highly annoyings. Low health ? You get a constant beeping sound. Being targetted by missile ? another slightly different beeping sound. You locking-in on another target ? ANOTHER beeping. And you have to listen to theses constant beeps very closely because you have to notice the "being targetted by a missile" sound (you have to use your EMP at the right moment to avoid it). That constant beeping is driving me nuts.
- And finally, the checkpoints. Born Read Games said they wanted the game to be difficult. Well, spacing out checkpoints, while reloading all ammo (making it easy to choose the low ammo, high damage weapons), and refilling all health wasn't the way to go. Especially when all checkpoints are in the "dead" moments of the gameplay. Usually reloading a checkpoint means you have to suffer through 2-5 min of nothing much happening, before finally getting to the part that is actually giving you problem. More checkpoints, but no health/ammo reloads would have made the game much more enjoyable, and maybe even more difficult.
I will stop that list here. There are other smaller issues, but i don't want to flog the dead horse again and again. Especially since i wanted to like this game, and actually enjoyed the first few hours on it.
On the whole, Born Ready Games had good intentions, and i know they had a limited budget, so they probably couldn't do everything they wanted with the game. However, there are way too many small things that make the game annoying, repetitive, and just a chore to finish on any difficulty except easy (which is way too easy).

In a word: forgettable.
Ship unlocks don't carry forward to new missions, only previous missions - and there's no real reason to replay them.
Side objectives - which are your sole source of basic upgrades (armor, shields, etc) - are only gained from completing side objectives, but with no radar, it's hard to pick out side objectives from the swarm of angry arrows swirling around the edge of your screen - nevermind that you must cycle target priorities until what you want pops up. This is especially agonizing as many side objectives are "stop all the torpedoes"; there are no audio or visual warnings for when torpedoes are launched, so unless you are constantly mashing 'F' to see if any are in-flight, you have absolutely no way to tell - and if even one hits, the side objective is failed...but it gets even worse! When you fail a torpedo side objective, you don't even receive a notification - so you don't even know you failed it until you've sunk ~15 - 20 minutes into a mission and see the results screen. On top of that, on every single mission that has a "torpedoes" side objective, you are required to constantly monitor corvettes, capital ships, and fighters - which you cannot really find unless you set your target priority to each in sequence by tapping 'T'...but since there's no warning when torpedoes are fired, you have to constantly cycle target priorities and mash 'F'...and then you find out 20 minutes later when you've cleared the mission (hopefully) that one single torpedo must have snuck past ya - no unlock for you!
At one point I was boosting away from an enemy cruiser to let my shields recharge - note that this was a good 14 minutes into a mission - and I was abruptly greeted by a "MISSION FAILED. YOU WENT AWOL. EVERYTHING BLEW UP. EARTH BLEW UP. ALL THE PUPPIES DIED. GAME OVER." screen. There was no warning, no audio or visual queue that I was getting close to the edge of the zone like a better game would do, NO - it just springs a "GAME OVER" on you.
Your AI allies are comparitively crippled, dealing significantly less damage and having less hull/shields than enemies. They also pretty much suck at covering you when you're in a slower craft, like the bomber you are required to fly in a few missions.
While the ship agility is fine for open space where there aren't really any obstacles, the last stage will have you smashing your face through your screen trying to guide your ship through 9 minutes of obstacles inside a tunnel.
Altogether it's not a terrible game, it's just underwhelmingly 'meh'. I plowed through it in probably < 8 hours on normal and do not care to play it any further. The issues mentioned above are pretty darn pervasive and aggravating throughout the course of the campaign.

. I don't write reviews. I write opinion and impressions pieces, meaning the detalization may vary from just general feelings about a game to indepth critique of particular game mechanics. I am a fan of classic point & click adventure games. And as a fan of adventure games, I want to really like A New Beginning, but I can’t. Which is sad, because the story really intrigues me, but there’s just too many flaws that accumulate and are hard to look past by in a title of this genre.
The interface is very laggy. To interact with objects, you hold the mouse button, a wheel appears, and you select the action from that wheel by moving the mouse around and then releasing it. In theory that’s a nice system, but in practice the way it’s implemented in A New Beginning is very annoying. It takes like half a second to a second for the game to realize that you’re holding the mouse, and then there’s a half a second to a second animation of the wheel appearing. And this really messes with the game flow. You interact with a lot of objects in an adventure game, and check what contextual actions are available, so in a minute of gameplay approximately 15 seconds are just waiting for the wheel to appear.
And speaking of actions, the wheel doesn’t have a set amount of them, it depends on the object itself. Which is why it’s so annoying when there’s a ‘Take’ action on an object which exists for the character to say that he doesn’t need it (the fact that you’ve spent a whole second or two initiating the action doesn’t help). And you get this feeling that maybe in the future you’ll have to backtrack to take this object and you’re gonna be angry on the character for not taking it in the first place (I actually can’t confirm this, since after the location with this example we go to a flashback of the second main character, but if we won’t ever have to use a fishing rod and a fishing net in the game, I’ll be angry). And you know, an argument can be applied that it was an attempt to remove the ‘adventure game logic’, when you take everything with you and possibly solve puzzles before they appear, but considering that in a later section I’ve recharged a battery before knowing why I need it, I’m not sure that applies (also I still don’t know what certain objects in my inventory in later part of the game are for, I took them just because).
When it comes to ‘adventure game logic’, I think that gameplay flow should be a bigger priority than having everything make perfect chronological sense. Speaking of sense, there was a moment in the prologue when I needed to ask a second character for help. I had to ask her to hold a shutter so nothing would fall out from the fogger. But I couldn’t. I knew I had to ask her because as I failed to close the shutter and looked at it, my character said that he needs a second person to hold it before turning the fogger on, but the actual topic of the conversation with said person doesn’t appear until I actually try turning the fogger on (which leads to the exact same thought line, by the way). These kind of specific things in an adventure game are very detrimental to the experience.
Adventure games are usually very story heavy. And dialogue heavy. And most of them are quite linear. This problem is usually tackled in two ways. In adventure games with linear dialogue (without ability to choose topics), conversations are usually relatively short and to the point, so you can continue exploring and figuring things out rather quickly. And in adventure with non-linear dialogue, there’s, well, there’s all the topics to choose from, and you don’t have to go through them all, you might want to just select only the important ones if you feel like it (so even though overall you’re more passive in an adventure game, you’re still active). But there was only just one (and a half-ish) non-linear conversation during the parts that I’ve played. Everything else was just comic-style cutscenes which also really slowed down the pace – you had to wait for the panels to appear in a cool way before a line was spoken. Each panel animation is not too long in and on its own, but, again, it adds up. So A New Beginning felt more like watching a visual novel rather than playing an adventure game. And even then, the conversations are slow due to a considerable delay between each line.
And there’s also the fact that English voice acting is so monotone and boring that I would recommend to just switch to the original German (or maybe other translation that is actually good) immediately.
But what A New Beginning has really got going for it is the beautiful art style (although, admittedly, the quality of animations may vary from action to action) and a story that has managed to intrigue me, and I want to know how it all turns out in the end. This may seem like a very short point, but it’s actually huge, and plays a lot to the game’s favor. It will have to wait though, until I don’t really have anything else to play. Sadly, I don’t think A New Beginning is well designed as a point & click adventure game. There’s too much passivity, and gameplay doesn’t flow well at all. Maybe I’m missing out. Maybe further down the road things get better. And if they do, I’ll make another post. But as it stands, this particular adventure game wouldn’t be on the top of my recommend list.

9/10 A little gem. Beautiful art, simple but well-designed game mechanics. The chief merit of this game is how it challenges the typical narrative frames within which most games operate to provide a truly compelling--emotionally compelling--gaming experience. Sounds silly, but as a mother badger, you get very emotionally invested in keeping your little cubs alive.
I've done my fair share of "escort quests" in MMO's, but this--whether because of how utterly dependent the cubs are or how unstoppable some of the predators are--really stirs your protective instincts. Not sure whether non-parent players will experience the same thing. That moment when you look behind you and you only see four cubs where there were five a moment ago is truly disheartening.
I confess I didn't do so well on my first play-through (which took less than an hour). So I tried again, armed with my knowledge of the maps and mechanics--and did a little better. The ending of this little narrative is powerful.
The only thing that knocks this down to 9/10 is that it crashed on Mac (a QA misstep acknowledged by the studio), forcing me to replay almost an entire level.
Hats off to Johannes Wadin and Might & Delight. I confess I was a little disappointed to see they have made a sequel. A major appeal of this game is how one-of-a-kind it is. I'm not sure what a sequel can add.

This game has no right to be as fun as it is.
MvC:I was allegedly developed on half of SFV's DLC-Budget, and it shows. The game looks... pretty bad, with lifeless character models, lots of recycled animations and a soundtrack that's - let's just say I switched to Spotify after about 30 minutes of playing. Infinite is now tied to the MCU instead of the Comic universe (most likely due to Marvel/Disney wanting to cross-promote the crap out of this game) so now we have exclusive skins that you can only get by purchasing the new spiderman-movie and other fun stuff.
And yeah, also no X-Men because licensing. Thanks lads.
By the end of it's development cycle, nobody cared, nobody was exited, nobody really wanted to play Marvel vs Capcom: Infinite.
Holy Fudge this game is fun.
First things first: Infinite really doesn't play like a traditional Team Fighting Game in that you have Assists that pop in to throw a fireball every now and again and then GTFO. Instead, you can switch between your two Characters at ANY TIME at NO COST and pretty much do whatever you god-damn please. This makes it that you think of your team less as two individual characters and more as a single unit, much like choosing an Arcana in the Aracana Heart-Series. Combos will have you frequently switch between characters to pick people up from the ground or set up Shop while your enemy is being grilled by a long Hyper Combo. At the cost of two Bars, you can even switch in while you're being comboed to save your teammate.
Movement is incredibly fluid, moreso than even most Anime-Fighters. Between Wavedashing, Walljumps, 8-Way-Airdashes or even the occasional Time Stone, every character has a number ways to cross the screen. Hell, you can even cancel Super Jumps for some dirty Instant Overhead-shenanigans. Everything is very momentum-based, which makes moving around feel liberatingly freeform compared to almost any other fighting game.
Personally, I was sceptical of how much the Infinity Stones could fill the gap of not having a 3rd character but they do their job really well. Every Stone feels powerful and distinct. You can use a stone to offset your team's weakness or further amplify their strengths. Stones have such a profound impact on the metagame that two identical teams holding different stones could result in completely different approaches.
If you can stomach the visuals, the bland, uninspired Interface, the shameless cross-promotions and the terrible BGMs, PLEASE do yourself a favour. Someone poured his heart and soul into MvC:I. Some Developers sat down and said "You know what? We're gonna make this game amazing, despite everything sourrounding it". And they did.
