What can I say, this is literally a game that was designed to be released on the XBox, but released on the PC. It has many features missing, many game breaking bugs, and many systems in place that do nothing but try and ruin the game for you.
They force you to go through stations in order to get crew for your ship, and upgrade. The stations are mostly cut and paste between less than 5 models, and are meant for you to go blindly through and rob it blind. Character models look like something from the 90's, and there is no variation in communication.
In space, nobody can hear you scream as your trade ships lock up. Your combat ships might as well be ornaments since you can't tell them to attack, and unless it's a capital ship, it's dead before it can attack back. As of writing this, you can't buy small ships to outfit your fleet or small trade ships to embark on cheap trading.
If you get far enough from station, you can no longer access trades that were previously there. Stations are not able to be freely placed, and if you don't pay careful attention, they don't function.
The save files are uncompressed XML files, meaning if you have access to notepad, you can cheat your way to achievments by editing them to your hearts content. The install is laden with files that are meant to be used on XBox. Regular controls for computer such as the keyboard/mouse/joystick don't function as well as a computer game should run. XBox controller has full support though.
This is an alpha port, the developers are patching every day or two to fix issues. When it finally fixes enough issues to be a full release, I'll ammend this.

7 Years later, I still can't run Crysis on maximum specs.
In fact, I run almost everything (from model detail to physics FX) on "High"-- intsead of "Very High", and what's not on "High" is set to medium. Even so, the environments from this 2007 game look gorgeous. The way the jungle reacts to gunfights is still rare to find in most modern shooters nowadays.
I've played a glimpse of Crysis 2, and none of 3, so my review is based purely upon the first game. I've yet to check out the expansion--which I surely will when I complete Crysis 1.
So with all of the exposition about how purely "good" the game looks out of the way, the gameplay holds up just as well. With the game taking place on a vast island with many routes to your relative destination. Weapons feel powerful and feasible, and whether youre taking dudes out all stealth-like or via an all-out firefight, the controls feel solid and reliable.
So, I haven't beat it yet. I'm also not writing a review for an official news outlet. But I'd say this game is  a definitive recommendation and deserves to be checked out by FPS fans. It bleeds nothing but quality througout everything I've seen.
I'm still baffled as to how a seven year old game feels so modern. It's a testament to Crysis' fantastic game design.

Promising sequel of the great X series, it's resulted flawed by many bugs and, most important, terrible, terrible, design decisions.
-
: the ships, the effects, the stations and the sky is/are simply amazing;
- Most of the core
of the previous X games are imported here (like owning many ships/stations, complex economic system, boarding system, etc..);
-
: they made the sectors both wide and easy to travel in a very nice way
-
: the stations feels (and are) alive, with many ships that docks and leave anytime while security patrols keeps things safe
-
: the fact that you can target specific subsystems was a very requested improvement, glad they added it
:
-
. Such complexity was handled in all the previous games with many (but simply) buttons and tables on the hud, now all you have is a small (and dark) multi-level radial menu. That means that most of the options are hidden on sub-levels, and even if you know where to look, it will takes 4-5 inputs before your action will be performed.
The radial menu is great for chatting alternatives (and such) on rpgs, but it's awful if you want to submit orders and visualize the status of your ship;
-
. You can still submit orders to other ships, but instead a single table, you have to "speak" with the person you hired to work on that ship (see radial menu concerns above).
Actually this can be a minor issue, since the ship is highly moddable and the drone system somewhat mitigate the problem, but forget to jump into your newly conquered ship. Those times are gone, egosoft declared;
-
: It's not about the 10-years old models/textures of the interior; It's not about the awful "thief-like" minigame inside it; It's not about the time lost in the search of a specific guy to hire in order to use the extra ship you got (a thing that was simple&free in the previous X games). It's about all of that, and much more.
At this state, it's just an ugly and useless feature that should be re-designed, if not removed alltogether.
-
. The lack of basilar stuff like the gravidar and the targeting controls (both presents on the previous X) makes the fighting somewhat problematic;
-
: from the start menu to the last ship that comes your way, if you want to perform a mouse action on an item, you need to double click it. Forget the "mouseOver" events, do you want to make a new game? one click to select "new game" button, and one click to confirm. Do you want to modify a setting? double click there. and so on..
Not a real trouble, but very, very, annoying on the long run..
-
: The FoV cap. The GUI size (and usability). The low-res textures. The small (aka ultra-compressed) data size. The "xbox" references all over the code. All of these details (and even more) points out to just one direction -> console port.
How a game never release on console can be so consol-ish?
.
-
: Many people got a very low framerate even on high end machines. Others suffers of crashes and many other bugs.
This might not be a big issue if they will fix them, but at this state of the game, the point stands.
My opinion is to stick with X3:AP which is the best out of the series, and enjoy the X world until the Egosoft will address to all these issues or, more likely, will give us the real X4

Very exciting team-based gameplay. Major emphasis on action/reaction. It's a good brawler, with lots of outplay potential, a very high skill ceiling, and a moderate skill floor. I have a lot of fun with it. There are a multitude of playstyles that are enhanced through Battlerites, and the development team have been actively balancing and rebalancing as required. There are ranked and unranked modes, and the developers have been toying with secondary game modes, such as the Easter event of Bakko's Egg Brawl.
Battlerites are modifications to your abilities, three choices presented per round; these can be as simple as making an ability do a little more damage, or adding a new mechanic to one of your existing skills, or introducing a debuff to another ability. Some Battlerites are a bit underwhelming on their respective tiers, but are overall well balanced to allow the player to make dynamic choices on a round-by-round basis. Sometimes you need control, sometimes you need utility, and sometimes you can do it with a bit more damage.
As the game is in Early Access, the balance sometimes shifts in directions that I don't personally agree with, but overall, it's a fun, competitive game. You can most certainly play it alone or with friends, and I enjoy playing it fairly casually (in the Casual queue).
It is a MOBA in the truest sense; Multiplayer Online Battle Arena. It's not a Dotalike.

Beautiful graphical style combines with a relatively simple, but working gameplay mechanics to portray war in a more emotionally powerful manner than any other game I've ever played.
Surely we've witnessed emotional moments in war games before, like brothers in arms dying in a cutscene, but after a few seconds we're back in the business of killing. In This War of Mine, the emotional depth is not limited into a single cutscene. The impact of your decisions haunts your characters day and night, and should haunt you, too.
In terms of gameplay, This War of Mine is divided into two separate sections. During the day the game feels very much like playing The Sims, only in a wartime environment: you're tasked with taking care of your survivors and maintaining your shelter. Occasionally there'll be random events and you're left to decide whether to participate or not. When the night comes, you'll get a chance to scavenge one of the locations in the city. There are dangers, trade opportunities and occasionally some location specific events. Both day and night, you're left pondering moral dilemmas: to help or not to help, to kill or not to kill, what should I prioritize, should I really think there are good and evil people and act based on that, or does your current situation justify all means of survival.
The soundtrack adds beautifully to the haunting atmosphere to deliver you a game we all should play at least once.

I love farming simulator 15 and have played this game since FS2009 came out (back in mid 2008 I think); I play lots of other farming simulator games too, (like the old John-Deere-Farmer and Agricultural-Simulator series); I started playing farming-sim games even before the FS series came out. (In this series there was FS09, FS11, FS13 and now FS15 and I have them all).
The game survives because of the modding community that surrounds it, you can even get the Giants Software Game Editor, (some people call it the map-editor), where you can design your own maps and stuff like that. My fav of all time was FS11 mainly because I have the most mods for that particular game, (and I still play it from time to time).
I even have some old FS09 maps that I like to delve back into.  If you are a GTA, BF or COD nut like me, I can say that you probably won't like this game, but I am a games geek and I like a change of pace. Most GTA and Cod players will say  this is a boring game, (and I'd agree with them if they don't have the correct mods installed). If you have a few specific mods, the game becomes a strategy game.
No farmer would spend a $350,000- or more; on a harvester and then have it standing idle. (There is a mod to allow you to play as a services company providing the farms with your machinery and your services to harvest the field).  But by far the best mods to have are (in this order), CoursePlay and the Follow Me Mod. The idea is to create courses to and from fields and more complex courses to empty harvesters to your grain silos, or put manure or slurry onto a field. etc.
Instead of driving every vehicle yourself everytime, 'YOU MANAGE' your farm, by recording and setting up courses to reply when you want. It is just a case of cycling through your vehicles and keeping everything running. (And, that reminds me of another mod you need); You should get the Vehicle Selector mod too, it's called the 'Vehicle Switcher' (Or grouper mod is another). You can hold left CTRL to the press a number on the keyboard to select any vehicle in the 1 to 10 slots - and it can manage up to 40 vehicles. L-CTRL+No. L-Shift+No. R-CTRL+No. R-Shift+No. It beats Tabbing through 40 vehicles!
If you get really good at playing this game and want a real challenge, then adding the soil-mod will raise the game difficulty! Depending upon for you treat your field, just like a real farmer has to; you will gain more crops (yield), from the crops harvest cycle of the field. It takes more time to play though!
You can also add more realism by adding the 'Damage the crops mod' which just means if you drive over your crops, you flatten and crush them just like in real life. I see this fault all the time in 'Let's Play' videos on YT. where virtual farmers are driving on the wrong side of their harvester to empty it. (The wrong side being the side where the crops are still growing).
If you want to know more, go see my blog. ( I am Farmer-George at
where I talk about lots of farming sims games).

~Overview~
STORY: 1/5
DIFFICULTY: 1/5
GAMEPLAY: 2/5
GRAPHIC: 3/5
REPLAYABILITY: 0/5
~My Personal Progress~
Story: 100% [beat the game once]
Time played: 6h55m total [ca. 4h30m story + ca. 2h25m savegame reloading for achievements]
Achievements: 100% [28/28 ACMs]
~Review~
I personally enjoy Point&Click-Adventures such as the "Black Mirror"-Series that really was one of the first games I played on my own computer (ohmy, seems like ages ago ^^"). But unfortunately "A New Beginnig - Final Cut" couldn't convince me at all.
First, the story (in my opinion the most important part about a P&C): at the start the plot sounded quite interesting: a myserious woman from the future asks you to help her save the world but while I was waiting for a mindblowing story to evolve, I was disappointed by a rigmarole that didn't take any step forward until the end of the game when a "sudden" turning point tried to save my day ... in vain. Not only was the story's outcome in my opinion totally obvious, it also turned into an annoying preaching and made the last cutscene seem to take forever.
The difficulty is quite low. I can understand that no one wants to search each and every pixel to find necessary items. That's why I decided to rather evaluate the mini-game-difficulty, and that is really poor: little puzzles in P&Cs are ment to let you enjoy a little, fresh breeze because searching for clickables can be awefully teasing. But "A New Beginning" doesn't offer any good or original ideas in this case; within seconds you can master all of the riddles and so they just contribute to lengthening the game time without increasing the fun.
The gameplay is solid, but all animations take too much time and simply turn out to be frustrating when you're forced to backtrack or simply can't find the essential piece that's missing. Moving-Animations are not of the best quality, they look clunky and sometimes over-stylized (e.g. character postures) so that they almost appear unrealistic and ridiciulous. This might be a possible design-decision that comes along with the cartoonish graphic-style, that - in general - is rather mediocre (dreary color-set, unimpressive location-design, no high-resolution). But even if, I would state that this design-decision was a bad one, because it brakes the sympathy for the protagonists.
The replayability is in my honest opinion practically zero. I personally didn't use any guides for the achievements but still it was easy-going to earn all of them in "one playthrough": I simply saved before every special interaction and when I unlocked one of the badges I went back to see if I could get an alternative answer/question/interaction. Unfortunately, all of the alternatives don't contribute to the story, at all.
~Conclusion~
"A New Beginning - Final Cut" is - in my opinion - one of the suboptimal Point&Click-Adventures. It rather confirms some people's opinion that this genre is boring and has no challenges, at all. Additionally, it can't even convince with its story or characters. I personally really disliked the female protagonist, who took a lot of wrong decisions that simply made her look stupid, impertinent and immature; and none of this contributed to the plot in a positive way. If you're looking for a good P&C you should rather consider buying another game that is able to build up tension with a really compelling mystery that keeps you going because you want to know the secret behind the curtain (not because you want to grind achievements :P).
But at least one positive thing has to be added: the game worked without any bugs or losses for me; savegames loaded and saved as intended, no glitches were found or other similar broken game-parts that let you crash or get stuck. No technical issues, at all.

Strike Suit Zero is a fairly pretty but poorly executed game. Little thought was put into what makes a game fun rather than frustrating. You will most likely spend half of the game trying to accommodate its awkward control layout and the other half regenerating your shields.
The controls aren't at all natural. It will take a few levels until you learn to adjust to the clumsiness of it all. Once you do you'll immediately be hit with a completely different control scheme as the "Strike Suit" mechanic comes into play, turning your space ship into a powerful mech warrior. The transition between control schemes is jarring and hard to get used to, I'm not sure I'll ever really be comfortable with the switch.
There will be times when the enemy A.I. will play dirty and seemingly cheat. They are incredibly accurate and agile, with the ability to stay directly out of your line of sight no matter how fast you turn. They can manage to fire directly at you at a 90 degree angle from hundreds of metres away and hit every shot. They will also often fly in groups, sometimes four or five abreast, in order to take you down. Meanwhile your team mates are miles away fighting their own one-on-one battles.
When the time comes that a mission requires you to carry an extremely valuable payload with a disadvantaged vehicle, you will often have to "lone wolf" the entire mission. On the other hand, when you're in a capable enough vehicle, you're often tasked with protecting similar ships in similar circumstances. For some reason when it's your turn there is no one around to help which is incredibly unfair as you're left to pick off the enemy one by one with a less than capable ship when it shouldn't have to be your job.

An impressive and lenghty fantasy-dystopian semi-realtime JRPG with an interesting story, some nice characters and great lore.
The (up until halfway through and near the end) lack of free exploration is criticized by some, but that's actually one of the strengths of this game. The story, drama and lore is rather strong for guiding down the player an often narrow path. More open RPGs would lose themselves in trivialities instead. Those who feel dulled and aimless in let's say Skyrim will feel much better with a game such as FFXIII. People who may have been used to different ways in previous FF installments could see this as a disappointment, but those who understand the value of this design will know to appreciate it.
Sometimes things get very cheesy though with the characters more often than once - despite being in a hurry to merely save an entire planet - babbling (after overcoming initial conflicts and misunderstandings) about their wonderful friendships and lecturing the player on equally cheesy life themes like to take responsibility and to trust others and yourself and whatnot. I read some compare the characters to Shonen fighting anime which is funny but has some truth to it: They have their interesting sides but also some looks, habits or thoughts which can feel artificial or forced for the sake of drama or conflict or to highlight certain points they make for those players who perhaps wouldn't get it if it were more subtle. I couldn't resist rolling my eyes at times or thinking "Yeah, yeah, I know, get on with it."
The fighting system is interesting. I think I still prefer traditional round-based JRPGs over this semi-realtime thing but it's fun nevertheless. On my difficulty setting - "Easy" - I could for many parts basically keep pushing the "auto-attack" button and let the A.I. decide what attacks to use while certain other enemies and bosses fell out of line and actually required me to use my own brains. Shifting the paradigms back and forth - skill presets used by the A.I. defining the role of your three combatants in the field (like tank, healer, buffer, damage-dealer), pounding the enemies with magic to "stagger" them (putting them into a specifically vulnerable state) and then do regular high-damage attacks to finish them off is a fun pattern to follow even if it can feel messy at times.
What has it's good and bad is how the roles play out in conjunction with the personalities of the characters and their individual stories, and how the combat situations are designed alongside.
For like the first half of the game you have up to two or three characters out of 7 or so go different story paths, meet different enemies and have different paradigms (roles) for them to choose from at a time. The strong confident character X has a guardian and damage-dealer role at first, the shy and indecisive boy is about magical buffing and staggering, the little cheerful shamanic girl can do healing and staggering and so on. As the story progresse more characters find their way into your party pool and more roles unlock until the very end when everyone can have all roles, even atypical ones, at the cost of increased XP points needed to level up the corresponding skill trees.
However this role-play also makes things a little predictable. For all the drama along the way one can tell that the characters eventually will have to group up towards the end in order for it all to make sense, to have these mechanics unlock their full potential. This is where the otherwise great story and immersion themselves are staggering a little.
The leveling and crafting sometimes feels a little dumb and like eye-candy. Per paradigm (combat role) each character has this huge tree of mostly passive stats and some active skills to go through but it could very well be displayed in a more simplified way instead and as such is a bit artificially glorified like it is in Path of Exile or Child of Light.
The crafting is minimalistic. You level up gear by infusing (?) raw components into it gained from mobs or bought through equally minimalistically presented "online" shops. Different components eventually give the item an XP boost when infusing (which I never understood, looked all rather random to me). You level stuff up until it can't go any higher and then keep the item or (which only works for some it seems) transform it into a higher-tier version which can be leveled further again. It's very unspectacular, just a bar filling and some names and values changing. Weapons do look differently when wielded by the characters in combat but sadly you can't properly examine the weapon models and some paradigms (magical ones) have your fighters use their bare hands and not their tools of trade. I never really became much interested in the crafting, I basically started with it only halfway through in the hopes that some bosses wouldn't be as tough to beat. Completionists and those who want to flesh out their characters fully may dabble with it more.

This game is a point and click game by Daedalic.
I love point and click games, and I love the storytellers Daedalic, so it is no surprise I give this game a thumps up, but I will still talk about the game and it`s strong and weak sides.
The games story is about Ben who had to give up his project of making algae fuel, then he is visited by a girl named Fey, who claims to be from the futher.
Ben is skeptic about her story, but when she reveials that a nuclear powerplant will blow up in the future,and therefore make the earth uninhabitable Ben changes he`s mind, and start to work together with the girl.
Now at the same time, the son of Ben is trying to sell the algae project, to the person who owns the powerplant. He has of couse no intention of using the algae for fuel, but will insteed destroy the algae, so that nuclear power looks to be the only good way to stop pollution.
Ben and Fey are both great charecters, and they show a lot of potentiol in the game, I have a problem with the voiceacting thoe.
Normally I can accept that voiceactors can be hard to come by, and don`t missunderstand me, it`s one of the hardest forms of acting, but in a point and click game, the voices and personas of the charecters in the game is so important, becouse the gameplay part is not a new invention or anything. The gameplay is a bit slow as you would expect, becouse it`s a point and click game. It is driven by the story, and this games story is great to follow, and some of the twists in the story is really well thought out.
Eventhough there is some bad voiceacting here and there (looking at you Fey) the story is great, and the overall experience is very good for a point and click game.
One minor thing to end on. I have troubles understanding why you can skip puzzels in the game. Now and again there will be puzzels in the game, and they are at times easy and other times hard. So why did they inclued a skip button? I mean don`t remove all the gameplay, let people think things out (or look it up, I know the gaming comunity to well by now).

Well here we are with another game staring our favorite Bald-Headed killer! This game took me by surprise becouse I really didn't expect another Hitman game,especially a story driven one! YES you read it right,STORY-DRIVEN! Unlike it's predecessors,Absolution isn't just a "RUN 'N' GUN" game,where you could kill anyone who got in your way without penalty.Oh no,now there is a score rating system,where it gives you:-less OR bonus points for the actions you do.Let's say a guard is in your way,and well you think you have to kill him...Welllllll...YOU'RE WRONG! Now you'll get a penalty for every Non-Target casualty.That's why you now have an option to either: Kill or Subdue/Knock out the person who's in your way! (Pssst! Subduing somebody will result in a lesser score rating penalty).Players can use these scores to compete,challenge and to see who's the best Hitman.Now I don't want to spoil the story for you,so I'll talk about the things given to me,to work with.So,in this new installment of the "Hitman" series,we got lots of new and different features,but apart from the In-Game features,we got a new game mode called "Contracts" where the player completes different mission created by other players,and the contract locations take place in the Main-Story locations that you visit trough-out the game (WARNING:This can spoil the main story as some of the targets can be the targets from the Story!!!).The only real shame is that there isn't a Black Market to buy weapons,equipment etc...You're basically left with a gun and the fiber wire trough-out the whole game.And you'll find out what I'm talking about once you play the game.Final thought:Hitman Absolution is a game that really steps up from the previous ones,it's a game that Die-Hard Hitman fans know and love with alot of improvements but still maintains the core shell of a Hitman game,that even newcomers are goig to love! The verdicts for Hitman Absolution are:
-Story 9/10
-Features 9/10
-Graphics 10/10
With the final verdict: 9/10-A fantastic Game!

I originally gave this game a negative review. However, after putting some more time into it, I feel that if you get this game on a heafty discout (as I did), you will definitely feel satisfied after the experience. However, I highly recommend you only buy this game if you either a) plan to play with friends, or b) have a high tolerance for frustrating games (see below).
Here are a few things I think you should be aware of before you purcahse this game:
- The UI is terrible. It is cleary optimized for console/controller use. Even then, it's full of nonsense. Also, be aware of the fact that unless you're using a Microsoft Xbox360 controller, you'll run into problems (I have a Steelseries 3GC, a PDP Afterglow Xbox360 controller, and a MS Xbox360 controller).
- The AI is stupid. Your AI teammates are of little help, and tend to get in your way. If you play as the Loremaster, you'll spend a fair amount of time trying to heal them. If you play as one of the other two classes, you'll find you're doing most of the work yourself and reviving your AI teammates often.
- The interface is terrible. The Keymapping makes little sense, is not customizable and is frustrating when dealing with 'Skill 4' and summoning Eagles (they're mapped to the same key and I have not found a way to change that).
- The inventory system is a nightmare. Your inventory is only accessable on your current character, meaning you cannot equip your AI teammates. The AI is left to auto equip whatever inventory you're not currently using and thus makes managing it quite difficult. In multiplayer, some traded items would just disappear.
- You cannot switch characters in game. This makes it a chore to keep your teammates up-to-date with stats. Often you'll find yourself three levels ahead of your teammates in terms of equipped skills before you get the chance to sort them out.
- The save system is out dated. It's based off of a checkpoint system which is poorly thought out.
- Finally, this game is poorly optimized. It is filled with bugs that may not be game breaking, but are certaintly frustrating and annoying. Including a particular graphic bug which causes a transparent white flashing throughout and entire level. I could not find a solution for this problem, and after searching the internet, I can confirm it is not my graphics card as many are plagued with the problem.
In the end, if you can get this game on a great sale and have a craving to play a Lord of the Rings themed video game - and you're willing to tolerate some frustration - this is worth it. I would also suggest Lego: Lord of the Rings. The voice acting and music comes straight from the three movies; it's very well done.
As a fan of J.R.R. Tolkien's works, I think it is worth it to mention that this follows Peter Jackson's movie version, sadly. Although, it is to be expected from a WB published game.

Short summary:
Give it a go if you haven't played before and are curious, or if you just feel like killing a few hours with some MTG. Otherwise, or if you're a veteran of the game at all, probably best to stay away and stick to the cardboard.
Pros:
- Free.
- Easy matchmaking (although buggy atm) to allow you to play a game whenever you want from home. Convenient.
- Not heavily Pay to Win. Feels a lot like Limited with a new Cube.
- It's Magic (...buut, read on.)
Cons:
- Game loves to help you out, by skipping steps when it sees you can't play anything in your hand, and not skipping when you can. This telegraphs that you do or do not have something to the opponent.
- Game loves to help you out, by assuming that the sometimes-critical upkeep step is for♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and skips it entirely unless there's something already on the board that has to be done.
- Each step gets the same amount of "response time" regardless what's happening. Play a tapped land on turn one: Takes just as long to progress as when your opponent plays a boardwipe when you have a counter. Now you can pause whenever, but you have to be on your toes or you might miss it (A real-time reaction speed "skill" that should never be present in MTG). Amounts to anything from a boring nuisance that you can't go faster to a real kick in the nuts when you lose the game because you're not lightning fast with a mouse.
- Lack of any priority whatsoever. You want priority? Click faster than your opponent.
- Artificial card limit restrictions based on rarity that appear nowhere in any regular formats of the game.
- No chat.
- If an opponent concedes, you don't win yet. You have to waste your time playing against an AI. If you happen to then lose, both of you end up losing rank and nobody wins in-game currency.
- Card pool consists of a static starter box and the non-overlapping origins set that you get through money/playing. Static start results in a lot of similar decks and some rigidity to customization.
- 2HG sometimes puts your friends on the other team. Doesn't really matter though because unless you're connected with another program, you can't chat anyway as already mentioned.
- No FFA or other multiplayer modes beyond 2HG.
-  Rank system appears to be a linear win/loss counter. That's alright though because there's no way to view leaderboards anyway.
- Bugs and connectivity issues. Hopefully these won't be a long-term thing.

I will say this, Rivals of Aether is my favorite Steam game as of right now. And the fact that it’s still in early access speaks for itself. With 195 hours logged in, as well as a decently high ranking on the NA PR, I decided that it’s finally time that I write a review.
For those of you that don’t know, Rivals of Aether is a platform-based fighter, similar to that of Super Smash Bros. However, each character has something ridiculous about them that totally wouldn't fly in your average Smash game. Certain gameplay mechanics such as parrying instead of shields, the lack of ledges and the lack of grabs allow for a much more aggresive playstyle than that of Smash. Some people aren’t a huge fan of this, which I can understand. Personally, I like going ham, and this game can definitely support that.
Probably my favorite thing about this game is the characters. Each character provides a very different, unique playstyle, which is way more than I can say for Smash. Besides that, as I said before each character has something ridiculous about them. However, the characters are very balanced, and every character is viable. This allows for a very interesting play on the battlefield.
In terms of stages, they are all very well done. Each play a different role in counter-picking, and should definitely be worth considering. Speaking of counter-picking, it’s worth mentioning that the local play mode has a striking system similar to that of Project M. So this allows for a better counter-picking system when participating in tournaments.
My only complaint is actually about that striking system. I have no complaints about it, except that it’s only in the local play mode. I would like it if this was in the online mode as well, or to be more exact, when playing online with friends. This allows for better practice on certain stages during friendlies, and allows for counter-picks during online tournaments.
Last but not least, a word for Dan. KEEP IT UP! This game is incredible, and I’m sure that you will do good for the game with every patch. And although I’m sure you’ve already got a plan for the 8th stage, I think it would be cool if we had a stage with no platforms, considering that’s something that every character has relied on in some way possible. If you’re already doing that, then good on you!
As for the reader, thanks for reading! This is definitely a game you should put on your wishlist at the very least, but keep in mind that once this game is out of early access, the price will rise! This is most likely the cheapest time that you’ll be able to get the game, so I’d try to get it ASAP. With that, I bid you farewell, and good luck on the battlefield!

This game can best be described as controlled chaos. Look past the facade of all of the over-the-top effects taking place and you'll find the basic fighting game mechanics are intact and very well done.
What I like best about the game is that there are so many options to open your opponent up. However, there are also great defensive and zoning options as well. The combo system feels very open to creativity but scaling and excessive-repeat rules prevent this from being too much of a wait your turn game.
What I like second best is the tagging system. Tagging can be so frequent that I've heard it described as broken. I agree. I also LOVE it. There's something rewarding about punishing someone abusing the tagging system when both their characters are out and just emptying your meter on them.
I'm pretty awful at the game because I'm learning the series here, but I certainly recommend it because it's very fun.

Beautiful graphical style combines with a relatively simple, but working gameplay mechanics to portray war in a more emotionally powerful manner than any other game I've ever played.
Surely we've witnessed emotional moments in war games before, like brothers in arms dying in a cutscene, but after a few seconds we're back in the business of killing. In This War of Mine, the emotional depth is not limited into a single cutscene. The impact of your decisions haunts your characters day and night, and should haunt you, too.
In terms of gameplay, This War of Mine is divided into two separate sections. During the day the game feels very much like playing The Sims, only in a wartime environment: you're tasked with taking care of your survivors and maintaining your shelter. Occasionally there'll be random events and you're left to decide whether to participate or not. When the night comes, you'll get a chance to scavenge one of the locations in the city. There are dangers, trade opportunities and occasionally some location specific events. Both day and night, you're left pondering moral dilemmas: to help or not to help, to kill or not to kill, what should I prioritize, should I really think there are good and evil people and act based on that, or does your current situation justify all means of survival.
The soundtrack adds beautifully to the haunting atmosphere to deliver you a game we all should play at least once.

Where to start... well lets just place the BLUF (Bottom line up Front)
The game is more like the red headed step chield of Civ predecessors.
Not saying this game is bad, but I have basicly the same grips with this game as there was in Pandora.  Another recent Space 4x.
Lets break this down into the basic 3 catigories that all 4x games have
1) Empire management
2) Militeristic Dominance
3) Diplomatic Actions
I still have not yet found that game that can make me keep coming back for more and this game is just like every 4x game since Civ3 too easy AI with a bad/simple code that alows you to win the game in any way you see fit.  Difficulty is so basic in this game (like civ5) where they have the same AI programing and just give them more buffs (aka cheating AI).  To me that's just lazy programming, but what do I know I'm just a gamer.
1) Empire management - This is split into groups such as health, food, production, culture, science and energy  You can specialize your civilization to excel at one thing, but only if you dont negate the others.  ultimately you can even wonder hord in a city.  Never understood the fact that I could place 50 wonders in a city, wish it would limit those.  Then even if you where doing great in science and production you would have to have a vast empire to build them all.  It plays out like anyone would know, and since civ 4 the auto city placement is more then enough to meet your basic needs, and just prioitizing can give you what you would manually get anyways unless you are going to split up your gains.  All in all the Empire management is what I was especting in a 4x game, nothing special and the same basic systems I know with new names and math.
2) Military Domination -  Would have to say this was a vast improvement on the former titles.  Instead of science giving more advanced units you have to ballance your afinity level to have better troops.  one of the best parts of this system was that it forces you to keep up with the other players if you wish to keep yourself defended, down side is like in most 4x games since civ3 the computer is too passive and lack unit tactics beyond trying to go after weeker units  plus I have yet to see the AI buy units in wartime, would love to see that if they had the coin (energy this game).  Also rarely see other AI try to stop wars or prevent non war wins with war.  Miss the days I built a science victory (space craft usually) and the whole world gos to war to prevent it.  All in all the military afinity is great but everything else is too passive for my tastes for such a short game
3)Diplomatic Actions - Yes I do place Covert Ops here, and would have to say I love how they work in this game, only wish the lower 2 max level building wasn't spamable for every city.  Not only that, but it is granted rather early after spycraft.  giving you little time to maxamize your subterfuge though spycraft.  Once those buildings are in play you basicly only take science and money or switch to your civ bonuses like +health.  You can trade now for favors or even science per turn, which I love, but too many times I see the AI bride me to stop a war and next turn they will try to get there energy back for a few favors.  I also have them tell me to stop having toops near my nation or that I have an afinity they dont like but dont have that option myself, WTF!  Would love to just rub an AI's face into the dirt telling him to switch his afinity or that he needs to keep his troops away from my stations.  All in all they did readd a few things from old games they took out, and that favor system was great in theory but bad in practice.
I still love the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of this game, great to play with other people hot seat that you like to hang out with, but as with almost all 4x players I play the game vs AI more, and would have to say it is lacking in more ways then one.  Well... at least it looks better then Civ3 and I don't have to worry about a stack of 40 units defending a city. which was even worse then just one.  would love to have like 3 or so, or even that civ 5 mechanic where you can populate a city and give it more str.
well if you like 4x and civ, beware.  since it will probably dissapoint, but for those that want a good stand alone 4x game that wont take alot of time to play, and has interesting mechanics you never seen much.  pick it up and enjoy

There are many metaphrical connotations within The Stanley Parable. Each player may find their "Stanley"s in his/her life and gameplay while there might be no "gameplay" in this game.
Most of modern videogames are following a certain narrative structure, whether they are lineal or not. These fixed patterns are not born with the videogames. They are reflections of Western social issues, modern popular culture and the hidden mechanism within the great drama, literature and cinema. Videogame, as most of us, was created (or imposed) through the social construction of reality.
Stanley Parable perhaps intend to challenge the routine play and penetrate into the constructed relationship btwn players and programs. The trial is not completely successful. But we have to appreciate these independant programmers who are able to check what they are doing like the art.
Intrisically, we'd like to play a videogame because we want to play a role, or read paculiar fiction, or encounter the very experience out of the dream. We win a game as we answer a curtain call, we fail in a level as we repeate a chapter of novel, we have to "Game Over" as we have to wake up--That's not the only way games can be. Stanley Parable, to some extent, remind all of us: you can win a game, but you can never beat a game.
When you are playing games, games are playing with you, too.
I expect for more game productions like The Stanley Parable.

A New Beginning is a classic point-and-click adventure made by Daedalic Entertainment in 2010. I've recently played and completed it and I wanted to share my thoughts about it with you. Also, it's currently on a week-long sale on Steam so you can save some money if you decide to get it.
The story of A New Beginning is set in the future where Earth is devastated by climate changes and human kind is facing extinction. A group of scientists sets up a team, provides them with a time travelling device and gives them a mission: go back in time and prevent the disaster! Their goal is Bent Svensson, an eco-scientist who "invented" blue-green algae that can supply enough energy to power the entire world... but is unfortunate enough to live in the time where money is everything and is impossible to fight the nuclear energy tycoons who pull all the strings. That time is late 20th century. During the game you will be playing with two characters: Fay, a radio-operator from the future and Bent Svensson, the scientist I mentioned before. You don't get to pick a character to control, instead the game switches from one to the other as the story progresses.
As I said, it's a typical point-and-click adventure with an incredibly simple interface and controls - right mouse button brings up the inventory on the bottom of the screen, while left mouse button moves your character and offers actions for highlighted objects. That's it - simple and easy. The puzzles in the game range from super easy to normal, they are rather logical and there are never too many available rooms in the same time, so getting stuck is nearly impossible. The only problem may be caused by the infamous pixel hunting, but it's far from annoying as in some other adventures. If I remember right, I only had problems with two items I couldn't see and one was at the very beginning.
Voice acting is average. Some lines are rather good, but most are plain average. Same goes with graphics - it's just average. Cut scenes are made in a comic book fashion with "low frame rate" and the rest... well, look at the screenshots I posted. However, this being an adventure game, neither the sound nor graphics are all that important!
It took me about 9 hours to complete the game and if it wasn't for a bug I encountered I may have been even quicker. The bug I mentioned was at the very end when I had to connect some wires to get specific numbers, but after about 45 minutes of futile reconfiguring, I gave up and looked up the solution online. I was puzzled when I saw the solution because I already tried it and it didn't work. It did, after a reload. The other bugs are mainly language errors: when you click on an object you might get possible actions in a language different than the one you chose, but it really is a minor thing.
Overall, it's a fun game. It has its flaws, but its simplicity makes it fun. The story progresses fast enough to make you want to see what comes next and that's what's really important. Steam version has 28 achievements and they are all rather easy to get if you don't skip mini games and explore everything on the screen.

Defined by many as a Stealth-Action game, I always thought this was more of a puzzle game than anything else, Trying to find the best way to maintain a silent assassin score is the real challenge of Absolution. The story is linear, in a sense of game design. Some of the levels have small playgrounds to move around in, and every level has numerous ways to complete objectives, assassinate targets and meet goals.
The strong silent type will probably find the easier difficulties of this game laughable, Instinct is a limited crutch that tells you where to go, what items in the world are important, and how to avoid enemies, but it can be turned off.
Agent 47 has adopted a lot more "mainstream" features in this game, perhaps to appeal to a wider audience, His movement is a lot more fluid, the cover system is a lot better than the older titles, and can carry a lot more weaponry, (3-4 guns, no need for a sniper rifle case..) without arousing suspicious guards. Costume system is flawed, certain characters know you are in disguise or not, a lack of logic. It is entirely possible to play this game as a third person shooter, when necessary, even if it will leave you with a terrible score. if you wish to play it that way/
Some of the levels are huge, with hundreds of moving NPCs on screen at once, a technical feat all in itself. The dark humour has always been a signature component of the Hitman series, and more than once through the game did I chuckle at the devious ways of killing unsuspecting NPCs.
Memorable Moment: Throwing a poor victim of the Fibre Wire into a vat of Pig entrails to hide his body.
Contracts is there as a fair subsitute for any sense of playground fun in the games 20 levels that may have been lost in this fairly placed story. You can set up your own assassinations with any of the NPCs, using any of the levels items/traps/weapons etc and as long as you can complete it then it can go online for others to compete for the best score.
Absolution is a success. Game looks great with a powerful graphics engine.  Voice acting is distinctive, but there is a few assasinations that feel out of place or forced on you. (killing a number of leather clad nun assassins for example).
Worth getting.

A new beginning is a cartoonish point-&-click adventure about climate change and energy production around 2050. To prevent an environmental catastrophe to happen, a group of organised survivors (I didn't know how to put the status of that group into suited words ;) ) time-travels back to the past to find a scandinavian scientist who might solve the problems leading to the catastrophe.
As a fan of the genre, you might like
- the new environmental setting of the story (which makes the game "special", at least a bit)
- a ten hour campaign
- well-elaborated characters
- beautiful hand-drawn locations, such as an oil-rig
Depending on what you expect from a p&c adventure, you might dislike
- easy-to-solve puzzles
- pretty predictable course of the main story
- inconvenient controls (mostly concerning the puzzles)
To give a resumé: A new beginning is not a milestone of the genre, but you get a solid adventure with a round and unspent story, nice graphics and plausible characters.

Strike Suit Zero is a great indie title. I am sorry I waited so long to play this game. I bought it as a bundle and the game sat on my inventory collecting cyber dust for several months. It is a great standard space shooter. If you just want to get better at dog-fighting, this is your game. If you are looking more of a space sim with trading and stuff, this is NOT your game. However, the game is very good at what is does. The battles go from easy to hard in the blink of an eye. You will find yourself fleeing away from enemy fleet laser cannons and turrets quiet often.  Contrary to popular belief, I found the controls of this game to be very good and responsive. I can see how people who are not very good at dog fighting can argue that the controls are bad. Don't listen to them. The game is fast pace and YOU need to be fast, YOU need to be responsive. I found myself switching between weapons and third/first person mode CONSTANTLY, just so I could get the shot I wanted for the easy kill.  The game has bright colors, great music, and explosions...lots of them!!
Strike Mode
I loved the concept of Strike mode. Basically, as you progress along you get a new ship that’s has the ability to transform into a mean robot looking beast that takes out everything is its path. The best thing about it is that if you are not into that sort of thing, you don't have to use it. Simple!
In short: The game is very good at space combat. It is hard (hard=good) with good controls and I'm yet to see a bug or crash.
Once again, great Indie space title. Play it!

Shelter is a game where you play as a badger mother caring for her five children. That's what makes the game so unique for most people, and why some decied to buy and play it. When you first play Shelter, most people think that their cub is dead, even though they're just hungry. So you just start up the game, and it's already making you sad and scared for your cubs. Now that, is pretty amazing.
There are five levels to play in total. Each level has it's own dangers, food, and lay-out. From eagles to forest fires, there's plenty of dangers to your cubs, and each one makes you check behide mother badger every few seconds to make sure each one of your cubs is still following, and looking for food almost every second of game play out of fear your cubs will starve to death. It's amazing how much fear a simple game can give someone.
Shelter is a game that plenty of people enjoy. It's a truely amazing game to sit down and play for an hour or two. If someone is tired of playing the game over and over, they can go to the extra menu and play nurture mode. In said mode they can spend about 5-9 minutes daily to take care of new-born cubs to grown adult badgers, for about a month.  I think that, if some people gave it a chance, they'd realize just how much it's worth it's price.

At first people think it's amazing and I also thought so but after around 30 hours you start to realize the game's issues. Bad mechanics, extremely bad character design and weird stages. Wouldn't recommend to anyone.
It DOES feel like a good game at first, don't get me wrong. But once you realize it's weaknesses you'll regret buying it and probably go back to Smash as soon as possible.
Okay, I can elaborate.
Bad mechanics:
Parry: Parry is a fighting game mechanic and it's good in some games such as Street Fighter series or Pokken, where it actually works. In a platform fighter like RoA however, it doesn't work. It's basically powershield but worse because smallest mistake can lead to a 0-death combo. If you're playing Smash 4, you know Bayonetta has a similar move called Witch Time which is essentially RoA parry. You know what happened when they added that move to Smash 4? Everyone got crazy over it and now they're considering actually banning Bayonetta because she has a parry. That's how BAD parry is in a platform fighter game. In these kind of games(RoA, Smash 4 etc.) there are moves which are high risk high reward, and low risk low reward. In Smash games, there are shields and if you commit to a low reward move, you'd expect to get punished lightly. But if you commit to a high reward move and get shielded, you'd expect to get punished heavily. In RoA, parry completely ♥♥♥♥♥ on this balance and makes every move high risk, because parrystun is the same even if the move is a high risk move, or a low risk move. This essentially makes the game extremely defensive, to the point where whoever hits first might get punished too heavily so both players would have to play too carefully. I don't see a high-level future for this game simply because of this mechanic.
Random meteor hitboxes: For the sake of making some characters go for crazy hype  meteors and stuff, all hitboxes that goes downwards were given a meteor hitbox. This makes characters like Zetterburn(up-b) or Kragg(nair) meteor the other characters randomly for no reason. Completely unintentionally too. This isn't too much of a big deal but I'd expect a fighting game to be a little more consistent. I like examples of games where you do things and those things work as you meant. In RoA that isn't the case.
Bad character design:

Absa and Orcane:The developer seems to be confused about how the game should be played. He makes zoning heavy characters that punishes approaches, then realizes these characters slows down the game and nerfs them. Shuts down what they have and makes them unusable in high level play. Absa got nerfed twice, and Orcane got nerfed three times. Their zoning tools got nerfed heavily, for no reason. These characters' movesets and designs all compliment to a zone-heavy defensive gameplan. Then he weakens them and buffs other tools they have to make them play more offensively. It doesn't make sense. Very bad design choices by dan fornace. (They should've stood the way they were)

By some miracle of ineptitude, Magic Duels somehow manages to be worse than DotP 2015 across the board. In terms of game design, gameplay content, the cash shop, and even down to the card selection, this is by far the worst work by Stainless Games yet. Wizards need to seriously re-evaluate their digital presence and either needs to find a new studio to work on these games or stop making them altogether.
Gone are the extra game modes, challenges, and even campaign deck construction of previous years. Instead, we have a 20 mission campaign (with unadjustable difficulty) with tutorials sprinkled throughout that can only be played with uneditable decks that get "upgraded" after completing missions. How are they upgraded? It's hard to tell, since most of them are very bad from the start and the game doesn't tell you what changes it makes to your deck. Gideon's deck is the most playable and even that is just dumping your hand and turning everything sideways. I get the feeling that they thought that cramming the challenges of old DotP games into this game's campaign would be a good idea but it really doesn't work. This campaign is (once again!) a terrible introduction to MTG for new players since it ignores deck construction, has a locked difficulty, and has many purposefully unbalanced fights.
Once you finish the very short singleplayer content, you have the incredibly deep and rewarding online play to look forward to. 2-Headed Giant is back! ...But you can't get coin rewards from it. There's a ladder system and matchmaking system finally! ...But server/game crashes and disconnects will give you no rewards. You can quickly play games through Steam invites with your friends! ...But there's no rewards. Playing MTG is fun and all but its frustrating when everyone is playing with the same trash and new boosters are hard to come by because of the stingy cash shop system. Even if you do decide to sink some cash into this game, you're only getting SIX cards per booster! Physical MTG boosters, while in all honesty are meant to be played in Sealed or Draft and not solely to be cracked for value, at least have 15 cards in them for a MSRP of $4. At the worst conversion rate, you're looking at spending $2 for a six card booster. At $39.99 for 7500 coins, you're spending roughly $0.80 per six card booster... but at this point why not spend your $40 on actual MTG cards (or a new video game)? The worst part about this is that even if you do get the most bang for your buck with the coins, you are still gambling on boosters and aren't guaranteed to unlock every card.
Opening overpriced boosters might be acceptable if they had anything worth playing inside of them. Origins is the worst core set I have ever played with, full of worse version of old cards that are purposefully designed to be weaker and/or bad. This set has the format design of MM2015 (which was also terrible to actually play with and people just rare drafted it) and the mechanics design of Theros (Renown is an obvious leftover from Theros's crap keywords). Do not waste your money on physical or digital boosters of this product.
It amazes me why Wizards hates money so much. I understand they want people to dump their money into either physical product or the digital variants available on MTGO, but then why release a barebones mobile game every YEAR then? These games make the MTG brand look bad (because MTGO is poorly advertised) and with every annual release, the DotP series is on the front of everyone's desks. Did reviewers see the improvements to MTGO's UI and layout during its last upgrade? Not really, because MTGO has been out for 13 years. Did reviewers see Stainless drop a complete turd the past two years, with more content stripped from each annual release and with more cash grab attempts built in? Even if reviewers haven't, the playerbase sure has noticed it judging by Steam reviews.
Wizards needs to wake up and find a new dev to work on these games. Stainless has been dragging their♥♥♥♥♥since the beginning of the DotP series; releasing cookie-cutter annual rehashes with slightly different cards every year, and with recent years actually removing content. Even with being a free2play CCG, this isn't worth your time because of the cut content, lack of polish, always-online connectivity, and incredibly stingy rewards for online play.

This game is a disaster, avoid at all costs.
X Rebirth is marketed in big bold letters as a trading game with a vibrant, reactive economy and NPC ships that go on trade runs simulating real economies. This is actually a load of tosh. More than 99% of ships (this is not an exaggeration) circle around stations in an endless loop, all caught up in a slow moving pointless traffic jam. They aren't going anywhere, have no goals and just keep doing this loop forever. The other ~1% seem to spawn next to stations then despawn when they are leaving them, never actually travelling to/from anywhere. It's all window dressing.
Not that it matters anyway, since trading doesn't even work. You'll have to do some really pointless trades (deliver 100 units of food when you can afford/store 100,000? What's the point?), and when you do you quickly find that the entire trading interface and ship control is totally buggy and doesn't work. Half the time player owned ships don't actually move when giving orders, and there's no way to view/delete the orders of ships in game. If your order bugs out you have to manually edit the xml files of your save game before trying again. If you eventually get them to move they frequently reach their destination then either get stuck staring at a station, or ram into it endlessly due to awful pathfinding.
Combat is really, really dull. You only ever get 1 ship, it can carry every type of weapon, but can only ever shoot one at a time and has no turrets or other hardpoints. EVERYTHING in this game is done manually. You can't automate anything.
Walking around stations is... rubbish. It's full of copy pasted stations - which you'll notice by station 3 - and NPCs that only have 4 sets of dialogue and just repeat them over and over again. You're going to get incredibly sick of talking to random people about why they're all a bunch of racists, or why VR holodancers are sexy but not real. It's incredibly unengaging content and somewhat alarming how so much of the development time and focus of the game is on a feature that is not fun from the start.
A lot of people have been saying this game 'has promise'. That 'it'll be fixed in patches'. It won't. This game is defective by design. You can't just fix core fundamental game mechanics with patches. Even if they manage to fix the bugs it won't change the fact that everything in the game is completely lifeless and window dressed, rather than engaging or purposeful.
If there's any one good thing to say about this game, it's that at least it's beautiful. The game is gorgeous, and that's really the only thing going for it.

I was very skeptical and critical of this game leading up to it's release. To be honest I wasn't even intending to get the game what with the lack of X-Men characters and the fact almost the entire cast is reused from Marvel vs Capcom 3 and UMVC3. However I found out it was actually Disney that was responsible for it and not Capcom do to the fact they stated that it would apparently give free publicity to X-Men movies which are owned by Fox currently, showing the depths of Disney's greed.
The Season Pass DLC garbage didn't help any either. Though this isn't just a Capcom problem, it's a problem with a lot of big gaming companies these days to churn out overpriced DLC and Season Pass junk. We need to boycott these practices. These triple A developers shouldn't be allowed to be so lazy when they have a huge team to work on a game, where as a smaller indie game can do everything they do and more with nowhere near the budget. Though to be honest I feel Capcom isn't a bad company overall, they seem to mean well at times, but they make terrible mistakes. They're stupid but not overly malicious... I think that title easily goes to Konami.
Anyways, back on topic about the game. I decided to eventually get the game to try it out, and I was surprised at how much fun I'm having with it. The gameplay is a whole lot of fun with a surprising amount of depth to the combat while also being easy for beginners to grasp. I was upset at the lack of 3v3, but with the Infinity Stone system and the Active Tag system it works incredibly well. The amount of variations you can do with combos and playstyles is really impressive. Each of the six stones have a power you can use, and can lead to different ways of playing. The variety is really incredible, you can pull off all sorts of flashy and unique combos and the way the system works allows for lots of different ways to approach.
I think the 2v2 system works well for this game, given that this isn't called MVC4. Plus the original MVC was a 2v2 fighter as well, and there was also an older game made by Capcom about Marvel involving the Infinity Stones and Thanos as well. It's nice to see a throwback to these older games. Despite the roster being more or less mostly UMVC3 with a few things sprinkled in, the characters all play very well. Older characters from MVC3 have different moves and ways to fight. Zero has some new moves and actions that give him much more depth then he did in MVC3 for example.
The graphics are a mixed bag, while some characters look fantastic, like Jedah for example, others look really outdated and nowhere near what current hardware is capable of. It seems like they had a strict budget, and the graphics can show sometimes when you look at them close, but in-game everything looks nice. The music itself is decent as well, with some good songs standing out, like X having the Intro Stage music from Mega Man X1. Some of the songs are hit and miss, though I wouldn't say they're terrible at all. Overall despite being rough around the edges at times, its solid enough to not be too distracting.
There are a decent amount of content for a fighter in this, though I do think more fighting games need to incorporate deeper single player content. The Story Mode is actually really enjoyable and worth playing through. There's also a classic Arcade Mode where you can just go through some fights and fight the boss at the end for some quick fun. There's of course an online mode as well as missions where you can get familiarized with characters and a decent tutorial as well. All in all I'd say the single player content is okay, but could use some more additions such as a survival mode like in SFV possibly and a score based mode.
I think what really hurt this game was bad publicity and marketing. People are tired of DLC nonsense and it needs to be put to an end. However I feel like I can safely say that this game is enjoyable and a great game for casual players and those looking for a high-paced fighter with depth too. I wouldn't say it's worth 59.99 unless you have money to burn like I did. I would suggest waiting for a price drop sale. Overall I think this game deserves a chance. I almost didn't give it one. I suggest trying this game out, and if it's not your cup of tea, you can refund it.

When someone calls a game a "walking simulator", it's usually meant as a knock against it.  The Stanley Parable is the only game that could reasonably be called that that manages to rise above the reasons that "walking simulator" has become a derogatory term.
A lot of game designers desperately want to tell a story but are not gamers themselves.  Thus we end up with a first person (because that's what the kids all like, these days) "walking simulator",  with very little to do except walk, that slowly dolls out its story over the course of 2-6 hours.  If they throw puzzles in there for some interactivity, it will take longer.
The Stanley Parable is not one of those games.  10 minutes in this game, and you'll understand why this is the exception in the genre.  I love this game.

I figured I'd play this game a few times over, before I decided to post a review.
After many rounds, I have to say I can fully recommend this game. The gameplay is really well done, hardly any bugs, and I love games that make me dream about what I should have, could have done.
A few things about the game, the screenshots don't do the beauty of this game justice. The character animations are quite well done, I was often wondering why there wasn't an option to zoom in to see how much depth was put into the character's animations. When the game first came into my radar I figured that this game would be a neat concept, but a quickly put together point and click; this is far from the case.
The replay ability is quite high, each run will have you wanting to try something new/different.
The mood and music are perfect for this type of game.  Also I cannot say that the game has ever cheated me. I have had moments of the game where I got upset that events played out the way they did but I was at fault for the results.
I'd also like to point out that there are constant interactions with characters during the game, which is really cool. It'll take a while to find out what I mean there but I won't spoil anything, but when I saw it I was like oh cool.
A few things that I'll bicker about. The game is too easily exploited. I found out during a crash, yes it does crash from time to time ( though I think it's due to a skype issue), that each day can be cheated. I'd say this is a total con point, but some people will like it. . . others won't but hey you're only cheating yourself, in a game like this.
I'd totally say that if you are on the fence to get This War of Mine.

Despite what some players say , about Crysis Warhead/Wars & Crysis2 , the original Crysis is a work of art in the gaming industry.  Crysis broke through a very important barrier with it's totally open concept , where you will never take the exact same steps in any replay of the single player campaign.  That "is" huge in terms of replay value.  I will admit there is alot more gameplay in Crysis , from the beginning that doesn't yet include any alien creatures that you have to overcome - unlike the sequels.  That is , a real foundation building asset to Crysis.
I can't say that I agree with players who claim that Crysis PC requirements are too high to consider.  When you can actually play with as little as a Pentium 4 @ 3ghz processor and as little as a 256mb memory capacity video card.  That is just not high at all in this day and age.  When you compare games such as :  Battlefield 2 / 3 & 4 , you know that they are quite a group of demanding titles to run on a PC.  One other good example which is not very common in terms of computer requirements , is :  Section 8 - which shows that you will need a Pentium 4 @ 4.3+ghz or Dual Core processor to run that game - yet only need a 256mb memory capacity video card as well.  256mb video cards have been around for quite a while now.
I have liked Crysis ever since I played the game , and the most likeable part is the single player campaign in the original Crysis because of the massive attacking and defending zones which you can't see the edges of or easily determine where they are.  The AI doesn't wait for you to attack or flank , the AI attacks and flanks you as well alot of the time.  So noted are the enemies who don't actually die sometimes and can surprise you - a nice touch.  I suppose I should also say I like the intensity of the AI , as if you don't react properly - you will end up losing the battle.  Great commentary and wisecracks etc. make Crysis a stand alone FPS - not the fact that it does take a good processor to run it on a PC.
On the latter side of praising the Crysis series , I have to say that Battlefield has captured the multiplayer crown over Crysis because it adapts the campaign right into the multiplayer maps at scales beyond many others.  Sure Crysis is a game that may be too big to capture without effort , but I'm sure it's multiplayer sessions would be so much better if they were put together better.  The way the multiplayer games in Crysis are set up - only those who have excellent computers have much fun , or get a good online experience on the servers.  Crysis is just too good a game to be put into a sandbox style of play and expect that it won't fail.  Battlefield took advantage of that fact in a big way.
If I had to choose between Crysis and the Battlefield series overall , after alot of consideration , I would have to side with Crysis.  The single player campaigns in the Crysis series are just too good to call what the Battlefield series has made since it's first games "better".  Although you could barely cut that margin with a knife between the 2 , as far as the latest Battlefield series games go.
Let's face it , Crysis has set a standard in the video game market , with the exception of authentic type war games (IE :  Call of Duty & Battlefield , just to mention 2) that doesn't belong to any other title - other than Crysis.  That is a very tough notch to attain and keep.  I would recommend this game and the rest of the Crysis series to anyone who likes FPS's.  Rendering the massive maps and foliage etc. - is a personal preference of the user , and should not be expectantly level across the entire playing field of computers and their components.  That's like asking for the same picture quality on an LCD screen , and the same size and dimensions - without the same component.  It's unrealistic.

Where to start... well lets just place the BLUF (Bottom line up Front)
The game is more like the red headed step chield of Civ predecessors.
Not saying this game is bad, but I have basicly the same grips with this game as there was in Pandora.  Another recent Space 4x.
Lets break this down into the basic 3 catigories that all 4x games have
1) Empire management
2) Militeristic Dominance
3) Diplomatic Actions
I still have not yet found that game that can make me keep coming back for more and this game is just like every 4x game since Civ3 too easy AI with a bad/simple code that alows you to win the game in any way you see fit.  Difficulty is so basic in this game (like civ5) where they have the same AI programing and just give them more buffs (aka cheating AI).  To me that's just lazy programming, but what do I know I'm just a gamer.
1) Empire management - This is split into groups such as health, food, production, culture, science and energy  You can specialize your civilization to excel at one thing, but only if you dont negate the others.  ultimately you can even wonder hord in a city.  Never understood the fact that I could place 50 wonders in a city, wish it would limit those.  Then even if you where doing great in science and production you would have to have a vast empire to build them all.  It plays out like anyone would know, and since civ 4 the auto city placement is more then enough to meet your basic needs, and just prioitizing can give you what you would manually get anyways unless you are going to split up your gains.  All in all the Empire management is what I was especting in a 4x game, nothing special and the same basic systems I know with new names and math.
2) Military Domination -  Would have to say this was a vast improvement on the former titles.  Instead of science giving more advanced units you have to ballance your afinity level to have better troops.  one of the best parts of this system was that it forces you to keep up with the other players if you wish to keep yourself defended, down side is like in most 4x games since civ3 the computer is too passive and lack unit tactics beyond trying to go after weeker units  plus I have yet to see the AI buy units in wartime, would love to see that if they had the coin (energy this game).  Also rarely see other AI try to stop wars or prevent non war wins with war.  Miss the days I built a science victory (space craft usually) and the whole world gos to war to prevent it.  All in all the military afinity is great but everything else is too passive for my tastes for such a short game
3)Diplomatic Actions - Yes I do place Covert Ops here, and would have to say I love how they work in this game, only wish the lower 2 max level building wasn't spamable for every city.  Not only that, but it is granted rather early after spycraft.  giving you little time to maxamize your subterfuge though spycraft.  Once those buildings are in play you basicly only take science and money or switch to your civ bonuses like +health.  You can trade now for favors or even science per turn, which I love, but too many times I see the AI bride me to stop a war and next turn they will try to get there energy back for a few favors.  I also have them tell me to stop having toops near my nation or that I have an afinity they dont like but dont have that option myself, WTF!  Would love to just rub an AI's face into the dirt telling him to switch his afinity or that he needs to keep his troops away from my stations.  All in all they did readd a few things from old games they took out, and that favor system was great in theory but bad in practice.
I still love the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of this game, great to play with other people hot seat that you like to hang out with, but as with almost all 4x players I play the game vs AI more, and would have to say it is lacking in more ways then one.  Well... at least it looks better then Civ3 and I don't have to worry about a stack of 40 units defending a city. which was even worse then just one.  would love to have like 3 or so, or even that civ 5 mechanic where you can populate a city and give it more str.
well if you like 4x and civ, beware.  since it will probably dissapoint, but for those that want a good stand alone 4x game that wont take alot of time to play, and has interesting mechanics you never seen much.  pick it up and enjoy
